1: In Genesis 1, what did God create in the beginning?
The Bible’s opening verse says, “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (1:1).
Genesis 1:1
Eden and Adam
Eden’s garden and the man come in Genesis 2 (2:7–8), not in the opening verse.
The heavens and the earth
The sun and the moon
The two great lights—never called sun and moon—are made on the fourth day (1:14–19), not “in the beginning.”
The sea and dry land
Seas and dry land are separated and named on the third day (1:9–10).
Angels and mankind
Mankind is created on the sixth day (1:26–27); Genesis 1 says nothing about the creation of angels.
In the opening creation account of Genesis, what was over the surface of the deep?
Before God spoke light into being, “darkness was over the surface of the deep” (1:2–3).
Genesis 1:2
Fire
Genesis 1:2 mentions no fire; darkness lay over the deep while the Spirit of God hovered over the waters.
Mist
No mist appears in 1:2; the deep lay in darkness until God said, “Let there be light” (1:3).
Darkness
Lightning
Lightning plays no part in Genesis 1; the deep was simply dark until light was created (1:3).
Clouds
Clouds are not mentioned in Genesis 1; the Bible’s first clouds hold the rainbow after the flood (Genesis 9:13).
According to Genesis chapter 1, who was hovering over the surface of the waters?
Verse 2 says “the Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters.”
Genesis 1:2
An angel of the LORD
The angel of the LORD first appears to Hagar in the desert (Genesis 16:7); in 1:2 it is the Spirit of God over the waters.
The Spirit of God
Adam
The man is not created until the sixth day (1:26–27), long after the Spirit hovered over the waters in 1:2.
Noah
Noah belongs to the flood story (Genesis 6–9); the one hovering over the primeval waters in 1:2 is the Spirit of God.
Cherubim
Cherubim first appear guarding the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24), not hovering over the waters.
In Genesis 1, what did God say before light appeared?
God’s first recorded words in the chapter are “Let there be light,” and there was light (1:3).
Genesis 1:3
Let the earth bring forth vegetation
“Let the earth bring forth vegetation” is the third-day command (1:11), after light already existed.
Let there be light
Let the waters teem
“Let the waters teem” opens the fifth day (1:20).
Let Us make man
“Let Us make man” comes on the sixth day (1:26), the last of the creative commands.
Let the dry land appear
God called for the dry land to appear on the third day (1:9), well after light.
In the first chapter of Genesis, what did God call the light?
“God called the light ‘day,’ and the darkness He called ‘night’” (1:5).
Genesis 1:5
Sun
The word “sun” never appears in Genesis 1; the sun is “the greater light” made on the fourth day (1:16).
Brightness
Brightness is not a name in Genesis 1; God called the light “day” (1:5).
Day
Glory
Genesis 1 never calls the light glory; God named it “day” (1:5).
Dawn
Dawn is not named in Genesis 1; each day closes with “there was evening, and there was morning” (1:5).
In Genesis 1, what did God call the darkness?
God named the darkness “night,” just as He named the light “day” (1:5).
Genesis 1:5
Shadow
Shadow does not appear in Genesis 1; God called the darkness “night” (1:5).
Deep
“The deep” is the dark water over which darkness lay in 1:2, not the name God gave the darkness.
Night
Evening
Evening belongs to the refrain “there was evening, and there was morning,” not to God’s naming of the darkness (1:5).
Abyss
No “abyss” appears in Genesis 1; darkness covered “the deep” (1:2) and was named “night” (1:5).
In Genesis 1, what did God separate after creating light?
After seeing that the light was good, God “separated the light from the darkness” (1:4).
Genesis 1:4
Land from sea
Dry land appeared when the waters were gathered on the third day (1:9–10).
Birds from fish
Sea creatures and birds are both made on the fifth day (1:20–21); God never separates them.
Light from darkness
Waters from birds
On the second day the expanse separated waters from waters (1:6–7); birds came on day five.
Man from animals
Man and the land animals are both made on the sixth day (1:24–27); no separation between them is described.
In Genesis 1, what did God call the expanse He made between the waters?
After making the expanse between the waters, “God called the expanse ‘sky’” (1:8).
Genesis 1:8
Heaven of heavens
“Heaven of heavens” is not used in Genesis 1; the BSB says simply that God called the expanse “sky” (1:8).
Firm foundation
“Firm foundation” is not in Genesis 1; the expanse divides the waters (1:6–7) and is named “sky” (1:8).
Sky
Eden
Eden is the garden the LORD God planted in the east (Genesis 2:8), not the expanse.
Canopy
Canopy is a modern picture of the expanse, but the name God gave it was “sky” (1:8).
In Genesis 1, what appeared when the waters under the sky were gathered into one place?
God gathered the waters under the sky into one place “so that the dry land may appear” (1:9).
Genesis 1:9
Stars
Stars are made on the fourth day (1:16), not when the waters were gathered on the third.
Dry land
Birds
Birds come on the fifth day (1:20–21).
Mountains of Ararat
The mountains of Ararat are where the ark came to rest after the flood (Genesis 8:4).
Rivers
No rivers are mentioned in Genesis 1; the first is the river flowing out of Eden (Genesis 2:10).
In the creation narrative of Genesis 1, what did God call the gathered waters?
“The gathering of waters He called ‘seas’” (1:10).
Genesis 1:10
Oceans
“Oceans” is not the BSB word; God called the gathered waters “seas” (1:10).
Deeps
“The deep” is the dark, formless water of 1:2; the gathered waters were named “seas” (1:10).
Rivers
Rivers first appear in Eden (Genesis 2:10); the gathered waters of 1:10 are called “seas.”
Seas
Fountains
The “fountains of the great deep” burst forth at the flood (Genesis 7:11); in 1:10 the gathered waters are “seas.”
According to Genesis 1, what did the earth bring forth on the third day?
God said, “Let the earth bring forth vegetation,” and the earth produced plants and fruit trees on the third day (1:11–13).
Genesis 1:11-12
Gold and precious stones
Gold and onyx are found in the land of Havilah near Eden (Genesis 2:11–12), not in the third-day account.
Vegetation
Animals
The earth brings forth living creatures on the sixth day (1:24), not the third.
Rain
Rain is absent from Genesis 1; Genesis 2:5 notes the LORD God “had not yet sent rain upon the earth.”
Mankind
Man is created in God’s image on the sixth day (1:26–27), not brought forth by the earth on day three.
In Genesis chapter 1, which two kinds of plant life are specifically mentioned?
The command names “seed-bearing plants and fruit trees, each bearing fruit with seed according to its kind” (1:11).
Genesis 1:11-12
Cedars and vines
Genesis 1 names no species; it speaks broadly of seed-bearing plants and fruit trees (1:11–12).
Herbs and reeds
Herbs and reeds are not mentioned; the two groups are seed-bearing plants and fruit trees (1:11–12).
Seed-bearing plants and fruit trees
Olives and figs
Genesis 1 names no particular trees; figs first appear when Adam and Eve sew fig leaves (Genesis 3:7).
Grass and flowers only
Neither grass nor flowers is named in the BSB of Genesis 1, and “only” leaves out the fruit trees (1:11–12).
In Genesis 1, what was made to rule the day?
“God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night” (1:16).
Genesis 1:16
The stars
The stars are added at the end of 1:16 with no ruling role; Psalm 136:9 pairs “the moon and stars to govern the night.”
The lesser light
The lesser light was made “to rule the night” (1:16).
The greater light
The expanse
The expanse separates the waters and is called “sky” (1:6–8); it is where the lights are set, not a ruler.
The rainbow
The rainbow is the sign of God’s covenant after the flood (Genesis 9:13), not part of creation week.
In Genesis 1, what was made to rule the night?
God made “the lesser light to rule the night” (1:16).
Genesis 1:16
The greater light
The greater light was made “to rule the day” (1:16).
The lesser light
The expanse
The expanse is the sky in which the lights are set (1:17), not itself a ruler of the night.
The deep
The deep is the dark water of 1:2, before light was even created.
The dawn
Dawn is not mentioned in Genesis 1; the night is ruled by the lesser light (1:16).
In Genesis 1, what else did God make along with the two great lights?
After the greater and lesser lights, 1:16 adds, “And He made the stars as well.”
Genesis 1:16
Clouds
Clouds are not in Genesis 1; the Bible first mentions them with the rainbow after the flood (Genesis 9:13).
Lightning
Lightning is not part of the Genesis 1 account; the fourth day lists only the two great lights and the stars (1:16).
Stars
Comets
Comets are not mentioned in Genesis 1; the fourth day adds only the stars (1:16).
Rain
Rain is absent from Genesis 1; Genesis 2:5 says the LORD God “had not yet sent rain upon the earth.”
In Genesis 1, the lights in the sky were to be signs for what?
God said of the lights, “Let them be signs to mark the seasons and days and years” (1:14).
Genesis 1:14
Covenants and sacrifices
The first sign of a covenant is the rainbow after the flood (Genesis 9:13), not the lights of 1:14.
Kingdoms and wars
Genesis 1 gives the lights no political role; they mark “the seasons and days and years” (1:14).
Seasons and days and years
Dreams and visions
Dreams and visions are promised when God pours out His Spirit (Joel 2:28); the lights of 1:14 mark time.
Harvest only
Harvest is not mentioned, and “only” is too narrow; the lights mark “seasons and days and years” (1:14).
In Genesis 1, what were the waters commanded to teem with?
God said, “Let the waters teem with living creatures” (1:20).
Genesis 1:20
Chariots of fire
Chariots of fire belong to the stories of Elijah and Elisha (2 Kings 2:11; 6:17), not the fifth day.
Living creatures
Fish only
Not fish only: the waters teemed with “the great sea creatures and every living thing that moves” (1:21); fish are named only in 1:26, 28.
Seaweed
Plant life came from the earth on the third day (1:11–12); the waters were to teem with living creatures (1:20).
Treasure
The waters were to teem with living creatures (1:20), not riches.
In Genesis 1, where were birds to fly?
God said, “Let birds fly above the earth in the open expanse of the sky” (1:20).
Genesis 1:20
Through the garden God planted in Eden
Eden is not mentioned until the LORD God plants a garden there (Genesis 2:8).
Over the high mountains and the valleys
Mountains are not in Genesis 1; the Bible first mentions them when the flood covered “all the high mountains” (Genesis 7:19).
Above the earth in the open expanse of the sky
Around the tabernacle in the wilderness
The tabernacle was built much later, in the wilderness at Sinai (Exodus 25:9).
Among the branches of the fruit trees
Birds “sing among the branches” in Psalm 104:12, but 1:20 places them “above the earth in the open expanse of the sky.”
In Genesis 1, which creatures first receive the blessing, “Be fruitful and multiply”?
On the fifth day “God blessed them and said, ‘Be fruitful and multiply’” to the sea creatures and birds (1:22), before He blesses mankind in 1:28.
Genesis 1:22
Land animals only
No blessing is recorded for the land animals made on the sixth day (1:24–25).
Man and woman
Man and woman hear “Be fruitful and multiply” on the sixth day (1:28), after the sea creatures and birds.
Sea creatures and birds
Trees and plants
Plants reproduce “with seed according to their kinds” (1:12), but they are never blessed or told to multiply.
Angels
Angels are not mentioned in Genesis 1 at all.
In Genesis 1, which three categories of land creatures are listed?
God said, “Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds: livestock, land crawlers, and beasts of the earth” (1:24).
Genesis 1:24
Lions, oxen, and serpents of the dust
Genesis 1 names no individual species; the serpent first appears in Genesis 3:1 and is told “dust you will eat” in 3:14.
Sheep, goats, and camels of the field
Genesis 1 names no individual species; 1:24 uses three broad groups—livestock, land crawlers, and beasts of the earth.
Livestock, land crawlers, and beasts of the earth
Birds of the air, fish, and cattle
Birds and sea creatures belong to the fifth day (1:20–21), not to the land creatures of 1:24.
Insects, reptiles, and creatures of the deep
Insects and reptiles are modern groupings, and the great sea creatures came on day five (1:21); 1:24 lists livestock, land crawlers, and beasts.
According to Genesis 1, in whose image was man created?
“So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him” (1:27).
Genesis 1:26-27
The angels’ image
Angels are not mentioned in Genesis 1; Psalm 8:5 says man was made “a little lower than the angels,” not in their image.
The image of the heavens
The heavens are created in 1:1, but man is made in the image of God (1:27).
God’s own image
The image of the earth
Genesis 2:7 says man was formed “from the dust of the ground,” but the image he bears is God’s (1:27).
No image at all
Verses 26–27 stress the image three times: “Our image,” “His own image,” and “the image of God.”
In Genesis 1:27, how does the text describe humanity’s creation?
Verse 27 ends, “male and female He created them.”
Genesis 1:27
Young and old He created them
Age plays no part in 1:27; the pairing is “male and female.”
Slave and free He created them
“Slave nor free” comes from Galatians 3:28, alongside “male nor female”; Genesis 1:27 has only male and female.
Male and female He created them
Priest and king He created them
Revelation 1:6 speaks of believers made “a kingdom, priests”; Genesis 1:27 says “male and female.”
Jew and Gentile He created them
Galatians 3:28 says “neither Jew nor Greek”; at creation, 1:27 names only “male and female.”
In Genesis 1, besides filling the earth, what were humans told to do with it?
God said, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it” (1:28).
Genesis 1:28
Divide it
The nations spread out over the earth after the flood (Genesis 10:32); 1:28 tells humanity to fill the earth and subdue it.
Abandon it
Humanity was told to fill the earth (1:28), the opposite of abandoning it.
Worship it
Deuteronomy 4:19 warns against worshiping even the sun, moon, and stars; in 1:28 humanity is to subdue the earth.
Subdue it
Hide from it
Hiding comes after the fall, when the man and his wife hid among the trees of the garden (Genesis 3:8).
In Genesis 1, what food did God give to humans?
God said, “I have given you every seed-bearing plant… and every tree whose fruit contains seed. They will be yours for food” (1:29).
Genesis 1:29
Every fish of the sea and every bird of the air
Animals were first given as food after the flood: “Everything that lives and moves will be food for you” (Genesis 9:3).
Quail each evening and manna each morning from heaven
Quail and manna fed Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16:13, 31), long after creation.
Every seed-bearing plant and every tree whose fruit contains seed
Milk from the flocks and honey from the rock
“Honey from the rock” is a later picture of God’s provision for Israel (Deuteronomy 32:13; Psalm 81:16).
Only the plants of the field, but no fruit of the trees
“You will eat the plants of the field” is said after the fall (Genesis 3:18); 1:29 also gives every tree whose fruit contains seed.
At the end of Genesis 1, how did God describe all that He had made?
“God looked upon all that He had made, and indeed, it was very good” (1:31).
Genesis 1:31
Unfinished
Far from unfinished, “the heavens and the earth were completed in all their vast array” (Genesis 2:1).
Blessed
God blessed the living creatures (1:22, 28) and later the seventh day (Genesis 2:3), but His verdict on all creation was “very good.”
Holy
It is the seventh day that God sanctified (Genesis 2:3); His verdict on all He had made was “very good” (1:31).
Very good
Abundant
The chapter’s final verdict is “very good” (1:31), not abundant.
In Genesis 1:2, how is the earth described before God says, “Let there be light”?
Before the first command, “the earth was formless and void, and darkness was over the surface of the deep” (1:2).
Genesis 1:2
Fruitful and full
Fruitfulness came later, as plants and creatures filled the earth (1:11–28); at first it was formless and void.
Dry and divided
Dry land did not appear until the third day (1:9); in 1:2 the earth lay under the deep.
Formless and void
Cursed and broken
The ground was cursed after Adam’s sin (Genesis 3:17), not before creation’s first day.
Hidden and sealed
Verse 2 calls the earth “formless and void,” not hidden or sealed.
In the Genesis 1 account, what did God place between the waters to separate them?
God said, “Let there be an expanse between the waters, to separate the waters from the waters” (1:6).
Genesis 1:6
Mountains
Mountains are not in Genesis 1; the Bible first mentions them when the flood covered them (Genesis 7:19).
An expanse
Dry land
Dry land appears on the third day, when the waters below are gathered (1:9).
Stars
Stars are made on the fourth day (1:16) and set in the expanse, not used to divide the waters.
Mist
No mist appears in Genesis 1; God made an expanse to divide the waters (1:6–7).
In Genesis 1, what was gathered into one place so that dry land could appear?
“Let the waters under the sky be gathered into one place, so that the dry land may appear” (1:9).
Genesis 1:9
Stars of the sky
Stars are made on the fourth day (1:16) and are never gathered.
All the animals
Gathering the animals recalls Noah’s ark (Genesis 6:19); in 1:9 it is the waters that are gathered.
The waters under the sky
The clouds above
Clouds are not in Genesis 1; the waters above were separated by the expanse (1:7), not gathered.
The trees of the earth
Trees are produced only after the dry land appears (1:11–12).
In Genesis 1, what did God call the dry land?
“God called the dry land ‘earth,’ and the gathering of waters He called ‘seas’” (1:10).
Genesis 1:10
World
Psalm 24:1 speaks of “the world and all who dwell therein,” but in 1:10 God names the dry land “earth.”
Earth
Ground of Eden
Eden’s garden is planted in Genesis 2:8; in 1:10 the dry land is called “earth.”
Field
The “field” appears in Genesis 2:5 (“no shrub of the field”); the dry land’s name in 1:10 is “earth.”
Wilderness
Verse 10 names the dry land “earth,” not wilderness.
In Genesis 1, on which day did dry land and vegetation both first appear?
On the third day the waters were gathered so dry land appeared (1:9–10), and then the earth produced vegetation (1:11–13).
Genesis 1:9-13
The first day
The first day brought light and its separation from darkness (1:3–5); there was no dry land yet.
The second day
The second day made the expanse between the waters (1:6–8); dry land had not yet appeared.
The third day
The fourth day
Day four added the lights (1:14–19); dry land and plants were already there, having first appeared on day three.
The fifth day
Day five added sea creatures and birds (1:20–23); dry land and vegetation had first appeared on day three.
In Genesis 1, what were the lights in the expanse meant to distinguish?
God set the lights in the expanse “to distinguish between the day and the night” (1:14).
Genesis 1:14
Sea from land
Sea and land were separated by gathering the waters on the third day (1:9–10), before the lights existed.
Day from night
Israel from the nations
Israel does not appear in Genesis 1; the lights of 1:14 distinguish day from night.
Summer from harvest
Jeremiah 8:20 laments, “The harvest has passed, the summer has ended”; the lights of 1:14 distinguish day from night.
Heaven from paradise
Paradise is never mentioned in Genesis 1; the lights distinguish “between the day and the night” (1:14).
In Genesis 1, what were the lights in the expanse set there to do for the earth?
The lights were to serve “in the expanse of the sky to shine upon the earth” (1:15, 17).
Genesis 1:15, 17
Cover it with rain
Rain is absent from Genesis 1; Genesis 2:5 says the LORD God “had not yet sent rain upon the earth.”
Warm Eden only
Eden is not mentioned until Genesis 2:8, and the lights shine upon the whole earth (1:17).
Shine upon it
Divide its nations
Nations do not appear until after the flood (Genesis 10:32); the lights shine upon the earth (1:15).
Hide it from darkness
The lights shine and “separate the light from the darkness” (1:18); they do not hide the earth.
According to Genesis 1, what were the heavenly lights to do over day and night?
God set the lights “to preside over the day and the night, and to separate the light from the darkness” (1:18).
Genesis 1:18
Judge the nations and peoples of the earth
The lights are given no judicial role in Genesis 1; they preside over day and night (1:18).
Preside over them and separate light from darkness
Gather the waters below into one place
The waters were gathered into one place by God’s command on the third day (1:9), before the lights existed.
Give every green plant to the beasts for food
God Himself gives every green plant to the beasts for food (1:30).
Hover over the surface of the deep waters
It is the Spirit of God who hovers over the surface of the waters in 1:2.
In Genesis 1, the stars are mentioned in the same verse with what other creations?
Verse 16 names the greater light and the lesser light, then adds, “And He made the stars as well.”
Genesis 1:16
The seas and the dry land called earth
The seas and the dry land called “earth” are named on the third day (1:10), a day before the stars.
The greater light and the lesser light
The great sea creatures and winged birds
The great sea creatures and winged birds come on the fifth day (1:21).
The seed-bearing plants and fruit trees
Seed-bearing plants and fruit trees are produced on the third day (1:11–12).
The man and woman made in God’s image
Man and woman are created in God’s image on the sixth day (1:27).
In Genesis 1, how are birds described in relation to kind?
Verse 21 says God created “every winged bird after its kind.”
Genesis 1:21
Every swift bird by its nest
Nests are not mentioned in Genesis 1; Psalm 84:3 speaks of the swallow’s nest near God’s altars.
Every clean bird by its wing
Clean and unclean birds are distinguished later, in Noah’s offering (Genesis 8:20) and the Law (Leviticus 11:13, 47).
Every winged bird after its kind
Every bird of prey by its strength
Birds of prey are not singled out in Genesis 1; 1:21 speaks of “every winged bird.”
Every flocking bird by its season
Seasons are tied to the lights in 1:14, not to birds.
In Genesis 1, what special term is used for the large creatures of the sea?
“So God created the great sea creatures and every living thing that moves” (1:21).
Genesis 1:21
Dragons of the deep
Psalm 74:13 speaks of “the dragons of the sea,” but Genesis 1:21 says “great sea creatures.”
Great sea creatures
Leviathans only
Leviathan appears in Job 41:1, Psalm 104:26, and Isaiah 27:1, not in Genesis 1.
Monsters of chaos
“Monsters of chaos” is a scholarly label; the BSB simply says “great sea creatures” (1:21).
Mighty fish
Fish are named only in the dominion lists (1:26, 28); the term in 1:21 is “great sea creatures.”
In Genesis 1, what repeated phrase shows ordered reproduction among living things?
“According to their kinds” (or “its kind”) runs through the plants (1:11–12), the sea creatures (1:21), and the land animals (1:24–25).
From dust to breath
Dust and breath come from the forming of man in Genesis 2:7, not from a reproduction formula.
By day and by night
Day and night are the realm of the lights (1:14–18), not a phrase about reproduction.
According to their kinds
From generation to generation
This phrase is not in Genesis 1; plants and animals reproduce “according to their kinds” (1:11–25).
After the flood
“After the flood” is how Genesis 10:32 dates the spread of the nations; it has nothing to do with creation.
In Genesis 1, who was given rule over fish, birds, livestock, and the earth itself?
God said, “Let Us make man… to rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air, over the livestock, and over all the earth itself” (1:26).
Genesis 1:26
The angels
Angels are not mentioned in Genesis 1; dominion was given to man (1:26).
Noah
After the flood the animals were “delivered into” the hand of Noah’s family (Genesis 9:2), but the original grant in 1:26 was to man.
Man
The priests
Priests do not appear in Genesis 1; rule over creation is given to mankind as a whole (1:26).
The elders
Elders belong to Israel’s later leadership; 1:26 gives dominion to man.
In Genesis 1, what blessing-command came to humanity before the command to rule creatures?
God blessed them, saying, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it,” before “rule over the fish of the sea” (1:28).
Genesis 1:28
Build an altar and call on the LORD
The Bible’s first altar is the one Noah built after the flood (Genesis 8:20); Abram later “called on the name of the LORD” (Genesis 12:8).
Name every bird and beast of the field
The man names the livestock, birds, and beasts in Genesis 2:19–20, not in the blessing of 1:28.
Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth
Leave father and mother for a wife
“A man will leave his father and mother” is said of marriage in Genesis 2:24.
Cultivate and keep the garden of Eden
Placing the man in Eden “to cultivate and keep it” comes in Genesis 2:15.
In Genesis 1, which exact pair of opposites did God separate on the first day?
On the first day God “separated the light from the darkness” (1:4).
Genesis 1:4
Sea and land
Sea and dry land were divided on the third day (1:9–10).
Above and below
The waters below and above were separated by the expanse on the second day (1:7).
Light and darkness
Male and female
Male and female were created together on the sixth day (1:27), not separated.
Sky and earth
The sky is named on day two (1:8) and the earth on day three (1:10); neither is the first day’s separation.
According to Genesis 1, which exact pair did the expanse separate on the second day?
God made the expanse “and separated the waters beneath it from the waters above” (1:7).
Genesis 1:7
Beasts and birds
Birds came on day five and beasts on day six (1:20–25); the expanse divided waters.
Waters below and waters above
Light and stars
Light was separated from darkness on day one (1:4); the stars came on day four (1:16).
Plants and trees
Plants and trees were produced together on the third day (1:11–12).
Man and woman
Male and female were created on the sixth day (1:27).
In Genesis 1, what had to happen to the waters under the sky before dry land appeared?
God said, “Let the waters under the sky be gathered into one place, so that the dry land may appear” (1:9).
Genesis 1:9
They had to freeze
Ice is not mentioned in Genesis 1; the waters were gathered into one place (1:9).
They had to evaporate
The waters did not vanish; they were gathered and named “seas” (1:10).
They had to be gathered into one place
They had to turn to blood
Water turned to blood in the first plague on Egypt (Exodus 7:20).
They had to be divided into rivers
A river branching into four headwaters flows out of Eden in Genesis 2:10; in 1:9 the waters are gathered into one place.
In the chapter where God creates the heavens and the earth, what is the first thing He explicitly calls “good”?
The first verdict of “good” in the chapter is “God saw that the light was good” (1:4).
Genesis 1:4
The sky
No “good” is pronounced on the second day, when the sky is made (1:6–8).
The seas
The seas are called good on the third day (1:10), after the light.
The light

Nothing was written in the sky; the man gave the names (2:19–20).
The number of its offspring
The number of a creature’s offspring is not mentioned; the man’s calling set the name (2:19).
Which groups did the man name in Genesis 2:20?
Genesis 2:20 says, “The man gave names to all the livestock, to the birds of the air, and to every beast of the field.”
Genesis 2:20
Fish of the sea, kings, and priests of the land
Fish are not listed in 2:20, and kings and priests do not yet exist; the man named livestock, birds and beasts.
Livestock, birds of the air, and beasts of the field
Rivers, mountains, and the stars of heaven
The rivers were described in 2:10–14, but the man named only living creatures in 2:20; mountains and stars are not named by him.
Nations, tribes, and tongues of the earth
Nations, tribes and tongues arise later, after the flood and Babel (Genesis 10; 11:9).
Angels, seraphim, and cherubim of heaven
Angels, seraphim and cherubim are not named by the man; seraphim appear in Isaiah 6:2 and cherubim in Genesis 3:24.
After the animals were named in Genesis 2, what was still not found for Adam?
Genesis 2:20 says, “But for Adam no suitable helper was found.”
Genesis 2:20
A garden river
The garden river is not what was missing; a river already flowed out of Eden (2:10).
A royal crown
A royal crown is not mentioned; what was missing was a suitable helper (2:20).
A suitable helper
A place to sleep
A place to sleep is not mentioned; the man was later put into a deep sleep (2:21).
A source of food
Food was not lacking; God had told the man he could eat freely from every tree (2:16).
What kind of sleep fell upon the man before the woman was made in Genesis 2?
Genesis 2:21 says, “the LORD God caused the man to fall into a deep sleep.”
Genesis 2:21
A troubled dream
No dream is mentioned; the LORD God caused a deep sleep (2:21).
A light nap
It was not a light nap but a deep sleep God caused (2:21).
A deep sleep
A deathlike trance for seven days
No trance lasting seven days is mentioned; the verse says only that God caused a deep sleep (2:21).
No sleep at all
The man did sleep: God caused a deep sleep before taking the rib (2:21).
What did God take from the man in Genesis 2 to make the woman?
Genesis 2:21 says God “took one of the man’s ribs,” and 2:22 says He made a woman from the rib.
Genesis 2:21-22
A tooth
A tooth is not mentioned; God took one of the man’s ribs (2:21).
One rib
A hand
A hand is not mentioned; God took one of the man’s ribs (2:21).
A lock of hair
A lock of hair is not mentioned; God took one of the man’s ribs (2:21).
His breath
God breathed breath into the man when he was formed (2:7), but the woman was made from a rib (2:22).
After taking the rib, what did God do to that place in the man’s body?
Genesis 2:21 says God “closed up the area with flesh.”
Genesis 2:21
Covered it with leaves
Leaves come later, when the couple sew fig leaves for themselves (Genesis 3:7); God closed the place with flesh (2:21).
Sealed it with stone
Stone is not mentioned; God closed up the area with flesh (2:21).
Closed it up with flesh
Washed it in the river
The river is not part of this scene; God closed the area with flesh (2:21).
Marked it with fire
Fire is not mentioned here; flame appears later in the sword guarding Eden (Genesis 3:24).
What did the LORD God make from the rib in Genesis 2?
Genesis 2:22 says, “from the rib that the LORD God had taken from the man, He made a woman and brought her to him.”
Genesis 2:22
A child
The first child, Cain, is born later (Genesis 4:1); from the rib God made a woman.
An altar
Altars come later, such as the one Noah built (Genesis 8:20); from the rib God made a woman.
A woman
A serpent
The serpent is one of the beasts of the field and first appears in Genesis 3:1; from the rib God made a woman.
A garment
God made garments of skin later (Genesis 3:21); from the rib He made a woman (2:22).
After making the woman in Genesis 2, what did God do next?
Genesis 2:22 says God “made a woman and brought her to him.”
Genesis 2:22
Sent her to name the rivers
Naming rivers is not mentioned; the man named the animals (2:19–20), and God brought the woman to him (2:22).
Hid her in the garden
She was not hidden; God brought her to the man (2:22). Hiding comes later, in Genesis 3:8.
Brought her to the man
Placed her outside Eden
She was not placed outside Eden; the couple is driven out later (Genesis 3:23–24).
Gave her a sword
A sword is not given to her; a flaming sword guards Eden later (Genesis 3:24).
In the man’s first words about the woman in Genesis 2, what completes the phrase “bone of my bones and ___ of my flesh”?
Genesis 2:23 records the man saying, “This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”
Genesis 2:23
Spirit
Spirit is not in the man’s words; he said, “bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”
Life
Life is not in the man’s words; God breathed the breath of life earlier (2:7), but the man said, “bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”
Flesh
Strength
Strength is not in the man’s words; he said, “bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”
Image
God’s image is mentioned in Genesis 1:27, but it is not in the man’s words here; he said, “bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”
Why did the man say the woman would be called “woman” in Genesis 2?
Genesis 2:23 says, “she shall be called ‘woman,’ for out of man she was taken.”
Genesis 2:23
Because she was named after the river
A river has nothing to do with her name; the man said she was called woman because out of man she was taken (2:23).
Because she was formed from dust only
The man was formed from dust (2:7); the woman was made from the rib God took from the man (2:22), which is the reason for her name (2:23).
Because she was taken out of man
Because she ruled the garden
Ruling the garden is not the reason given; she was called woman because out of man she was taken (2:23).
Because she spoke first
Speaking first is not mentioned; she was called woman because out of man she was taken (2:23).
According to Genesis 2, what does a man leave in order to be united to his wife?
Genesis 2:24 says, “a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife.”
Genesis 2:24
His flocks and tents
Flocks and tents are not mentioned; a man leaves his father and mother (2:24).
His father and mother
His city and king
City and king are not mentioned; a man leaves his father and mother (2:24).
His brothers and servants
Brothers and servants are not mentioned; a man leaves his father and mother (2:24).
His harvest and field
Harvest and field are not mentioned; a man leaves his father and mother (2:24).
In the marriage statement of Genesis 2, to whom is a man united?
Genesis 2:24 says a man will “be united to his wife.”
Genesis 2:24
His tribe
The verse speaks of a wife, not a tribe (2:24).
His servant
The verse speaks of a wife, not a servant (2:24).
His wife
His firstborn son
The verse speaks of a wife, not a firstborn son (2:24).
His sister
The verse speaks of a wife, not a sister (2:24).
What do the man and his wife become according to Genesis 2?
Genesis 2:24 says, “they will become one flesh.”
Genesis 2:24
One nation
A great nation is God’s promise to Abram later (Genesis 12:2), not what a husband and wife become in 2:24.
One spirit
The verse says one flesh, not one spirit (2:24).
One house
The verse says one flesh, not one house (2:24).
One flesh
One river
The rivers of Eden are four (2:10–14); the husband and wife become one flesh (2:24), not one river.
How does Genesis 2 describe the condition of the man and his wife at the end of the chapter?
Genesis 2:25 says, “the man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.”
Genesis 2:25
Clothed in linen and afraid
Clothing comes later, when they sew fig leaves (Genesis 3:7) and God makes garments of skin (Genesis 3:21). Fear also comes after the fall.
Naked and not ashamed
Hidden among the trees
Hiding among the trees happens only after the fall (Genesis 3:8); in 2:25 they were not ashamed.
Sleeping by the river
The woman had just been brought to the man (2:22), and nothing is said about them sleeping by the river.
Dressed in leaves and trembling
Leaves come later, when they sew fig leaves (Genesis 3:7); in 2:25 they were naked and not ashamed.
While naked in Genesis 2, what feeling did the man and his wife not have?
Genesis 2:25 says they “were not ashamed.”
Genesis 2:25
Hunger
Hunger is not mentioned; God had given the man every tree of the garden to eat from freely (2:16).
Fear
Fear appears only after the fall: “I was afraid because I was naked” (Genesis 3:10).
Shame
Sorrow
Sorrow is not mentioned in 2:25; the text says they were not ashamed.
Anger
Anger first appears later, in Cain (Genesis 4:5); in 2:25 the text says they were not ashamed.
Which phrase introduces the Genesis 2 section about creation and Eden?
Genesis 2:4 says, “This is the account of the heavens and the earth when they were created, in the day that the LORD God made them.”
Genesis 2:4
Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one
“Hear, O Israel” opens Moses’ call to love the LORD (Deuteronomy 6:4), not the Eden section.
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God
“In the beginning was the Word” is the opening of John 1:1, not Genesis 2.
This is the account of the heavens and the earth when they were created
These are the generations of Jacob and his twelve sons
A similar account formula, “This is the account of Jacob,” opens Joseph’s story in Genesis 37:2, but not Genesis 2.
Thus says the LORD to Pharaoh: Let My people go
The LORD’s demand to Pharaoh comes in Exodus 5:1, long after Eden.
In the summary statement of Genesis 2:4, what did the LORD God make?
Genesis 2:4 says, “This is the account of the heavens and the earth when they were created, in the day that the LORD God made them.”
Genesis 2:4
The sea and the dry land
The sea and dry land were gathered on the third day (Genesis 1:9–10), but 2:4 names the heavens and the earth as a whole.
The heavens and the earth
The moon and the stars
The sun, moon and stars were made on the fourth day (Genesis 1:14–19), but 2:4 names the heavens and the earth as a whole.
The tribes and the nations
Tribes and nations arise later (Genesis 10); 2:4 names the heavens and the earth.
The cherubim and seraphim
Cherubim appear later in Genesis 3:24, and seraphim in Isaiah 6:2; 2:4 names the heavens and the earth.
In the Garden of Eden narrative of Genesis 2, which divine title is repeatedly used?
From 2:4 on, the chapter repeatedly says “the LORD God,” for example in “the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground” (2:7).
Genesis 2:4-25
God Almighty
“God Almighty” is the name God uses with Abram in Genesis 17:1, not the repeated title in Genesis 2.
The Ancient of Days
“The Ancient of Days” is a title from Daniel 7:9, not from Genesis 2.
The LORD God
The God of Abraham
“The God of Abraham” is a title that appears later (Exodus 3:6), not in Eden.
The Holy One of Israel
“The Holy One of Israel” is found in Isaiah 1:4, not in Genesis 2.
What phrase describes the completed creation in Genesis 2:1?
Genesis 2:1 says, “Thus the heavens and the earth were completed in all their vast array.”
Genesis 2:1
Its full beauty
“Its full beauty” is not the wording of 2:1; the verse says all their vast array.
All their vast array
The host of heaven only
The heavens and the earth were completed in all their vast array (2:1), more than “the host of heaven only.”
Endless generations
“Endless generations” is not the wording of 2:1; the verse says all their vast array.
A holy remnant
A holy remnant is a later prophetic idea; 2:1 says all their vast array.
On the seventh day in Genesis 2, God rested from what?
Genesis 2:2 says God “rested from all His work.”
Genesis 2:2
Only from making animals
He rested from all His work, not only from making animals (2:2).
Only from planting the garden
He rested from all His work, not only from planting the garden (2:2); the garden is mentioned later in 2:8.
All His work
Speaking to the angels
Speaking to angels is not mentioned; He rested from all His work (2:2).
Judging the serpent
The serpent is not judged until Genesis 3:14; in 2:2 God rested from all His work.
Why did God bless and sanctify the seventh day in Genesis 2?
Genesis 2:3 says God blessed and sanctified the seventh day “because on that day He rested from all the work of creation that He had accomplished.”
Genesis 2:3
Because Adam finished naming all the livestock and birds that day
Naming the animals is described in 2:19–20, but the reason for the blessing in 2:3 is God’s rest.
Because the rivers began to flow out of Eden on that day
The river flowing from Eden is described in 2:10, but the reason for the blessing in 2:3 is God’s rest.
Because on that day He rested from all the work of creation He had accomplished
Because the woman was created and brought to the man that day
The woman’s creation is told in 2:22, but the reason for the blessing in 2:3 is God’s rest.
Because gold was found in the land of Havilah on that day
Gold in Havilah is mentioned in 2:11–12, but the reason for the blessing in 2:3 is God’s rest.
Before giving the man work in Genesis 2, where did God place him?
Genesis 2:8 says the LORD God planted a garden “in Eden, in the east,” and 2:15 says He placed the man there “to cultivate and keep it.”
Genesis 2:8, 15
In Ur of the Chaldeans
Ur of the Chaldeans is where Abram’s family started out (Genesis 11:31), not where the first man was placed.
In a garden in Eden, in the east
On Mount Sinai
Mount Sinai is where Moses later received the law (Exodus 19:20), not where the man was placed.
In the land of Nod
Nod is where Cain later settled, east of Eden (Genesis 4:16), not where the man was placed.
Beside the Dead Sea
The Dead Sea is the Salt Sea near the Valley of Siddim (Genesis 14:3), far from Eden.
Which river in Genesis 2 is linked with Havilah, where pure gold, bdellium, and onyx are found?
Genesis 2:11–12 says the first river “winds through the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold. And the gold of that land is pure, and bdellium and onyx are found there.”
Genesis 2:11-12
Gihon
The Gihon winds through Cush (2:13), not Havilah.
Euphrates
The Euphrates is the fourth river, and Genesis 2 gives it no description (2:14).
Jordan
The Jordan is not one of the four rivers of Eden (2:11–14).
Pishon
Tigris
The Tigris runs along the east side of Assyria (2:14), not through Havilah.
Which river is described in Genesis 2 as winding through the whole land of Cush?
Genesis 2:13 says the second river “winds through the whole land of Cush.”
Genesis 2:13
Pishon
The Pishon winds through Havilah (2:11).
Gihon
Euphrates
The Euphrates is the fourth river (2:14).
Jabbok
The Jabbok is where Jacob crossed before meeting Esau (Genesis 32:22), not one of the four rivers.
Kishon
The Kishon is a river of Israel (Judges 5:21), not one of the four rivers.
Which river is specifically said in Genesis 2 to run along the east side of Assyria?
Genesis 2:14 says, “The name of the third river is the Tigris; it runs along the east side of Assyria.”
Genesis 2:14
Tigris
Pishon
The Pishon winds through Havilah (2:11).
Gihon
The Gihon winds through Cush (2:13).
Nile
The Nile is not among the four rivers named in Genesis 2.
Euphrates
The Euphrates is the fourth river (2:14); no place is given for it in the verse.
In the four-river list of Genesis 2, which river is simply named as the fourth?
Genesis 2:14 says, “And the fourth river is the Euphrates.”
Genesis 2:14
Pishon
The Pishon is the first river (2:11).
Jordan
The Jordan is not among the four rivers of Eden (2:11–14).
Gihon
The Gihon is the second river (2:13).
Euphrates
Abana
The Abana is a river of Damascus (2 Kings 5:12), not one of Eden’s rivers.
Which pair of conditions explains why no shrub or plant of the field had yet appeared in Genesis 2?
Genesis 2:5 says, “the LORD God had not yet sent rain upon the earth, and there was no man to cultivate the ground.”
Genesis 2:5
No sunlight and no moonlight
The sun and moon were made on the fourth day (Genesis 1:14–19); 2:5 gives no rain and no man as the reasons.
No priest and no altar
Priests and altars come much later (Exodus 28:1); 2:5 gives no rain and no man as the reasons.
No rain and no man to cultivate the ground
No river and no animals
The river is described in 2:10, not as a missing condition; 2:5 gives no rain and no man as the reasons.
No seed and no seasons
Seed-bearing plants were made on the third day (Genesis 1:11); 2:5 gives no rain and no man as the reasons.
Which statement correctly describes the water source mentioned before regular agriculture in Genesis 2?
Genesis 2:6 says, “springs welled up from the earth and watered the whole surface of the ground.”
Genesis 2:6
Rain fell from heaven every evening and watered the whole earth
Rain had not yet been sent upon the earth (2:5).
Springs welled up from the earth and watered the whole surface of the ground
The Jordan overflowed its banks and soaked the whole surface of the ground
The Jordan is not mentioned in Genesis 2; it appears later in Lot’s choice of land (Genesis 13:10).
Dew alone kept Eden alive and watered the garden every single morning
Dew is not mentioned in Genesis 2; springs watered the ground (2:6).
A flood covered the mountains and watered the whole surface of the ground
The flood came much later, when the waters covered the mountains (Genesis 7:19).
Which statement best matches God’s command to the man in Genesis 2?
Genesis 2:16–17 says the man could “eat freely from every tree of the garden” but “must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.”
Genesis 2:16-17
He could eat only from the tree of life in the middle of the garden
The permission covered every tree of the garden, not only the tree of life (2:16).
He could eat freely from every tree except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil
He could not eat from any tree in the garden until the woman came
The command did not wait for the woman, and the permission covered every tree except one (2:16–17).
He could eat from the trees only after he had named all the animals
Naming the animals is not a condition for eating; the command was to eat freely from every tree except one (2:16–17).
He could eat from every tree of the garden with no exception at all
There was one exception, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (2:17).
Which statement about naming the creatures is correct in Genesis 2?
Genesis 2:19 says, “whatever the man called each living creature, that was its name.”
Genesis 2:19
The angels named them before Adam saw them
No angels named the creatures; God brought them to the man to name (2:19).
Their names came from the river they drank from
The names did not come from rivers; the man named the creatures (2:19).
Whatever the man called each living creature, that was its name
God refused to let the man name them
God did not refuse; He brought the creatures to the man to see what he would name them (2:19).
Only the birds were named
More than the birds were named; 2:20 says the man named the livestock, the birds and every beast of the field.
Which sequence correctly describes the making of the woman in Genesis 2?
Genesis 2:21–22 says God “caused the man to fall into a deep sleep,” took one of his ribs, “closed up the area with flesh,” and “made a woman and brought her to him.”
Genesis 2:21-22
The man awoke and named the rivers of Eden, then God made the woman from clay and brought her to him
The woman was made from a rib, not clay (2:22), and the man named animals (2:19–20), not rivers.
God sent rain, planted trees, then made the woman from the dust of the ground and gave her to the man
Rain had not yet been sent (2:5), and the woman was made from the man’s rib, not from dust (2:22).
God caused a deep sleep, took one rib, closed the place with flesh, made a woman, and brought her to the man
The woman was made first from the dust, then the man fell into a deep sleep and God formed him from her rib
The man was formed first (2:7), and the woman was then made from his rib (2:22), not the reverse.
The woman rose up out of the river, named herself, and was brought to the man by the animals
The woman did not come from the river; God made her from the man’s rib and brought her to him (2:22).
Which marriage statement is given in Genesis 2 after the woman is made?
Genesis 2:24 says, “a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh.”
Genesis 2:24
A man will leave his father and mother, be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh
A man will remain with his brothers and inherit the land alone
The statement is the opposite: a man leaves his father and mother (2:24).
A woman will leave the garden and rule the beasts
The statement speaks of a man and wife, not of a woman ruling the beasts; the woman has not left the garden (2:24).
Husband and wife will become one spirit but never one flesh
The statement says they will become one flesh, not one spirit alone (2:24).
A man will leave his wife and cleave to his tribe
The statement says he will be united to his wife, not to a tribe (2:24).
Which closing statement about the first couple is correct in Genesis 2?
Genesis 2:25 says, “the man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.”
Genesis 2:25
They were clothed in skins and afraid
Skins come later, when God makes garments of skin (Genesis 3:21), and fear appears after the fall (Genesis 3:10).
They were both naked and not ashamed
They hid among the trees because they were ashamed
Hiding among the trees comes after the fall (Genesis 3:8); in 2:25 they were not ashamed.
They departed Eden in sorrow
They left Eden later, when they were driven out (Genesis 3:23–24).
They built an altar by the river
Altars come later, such as the one Noah built (Genesis 8:20).
Which description of the trees in Eden is complete according to Genesis 2?
Genesis 2:9 says the trees were “pleasing to the eye and good for food,” and “in the middle of the garden were the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.”
Genesis 2:9
They were pleasing to the eye and good for food, with the tree of life in the middle of the garden and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil also there
They were thorny and barren, bearing no fruit at all except for one fig tree that stood beside the river in Eden
The trees were pleasing to the eye and good for food, not thorny and barren (2:9). Thorns come after the fall (Genesis 3:18).
They were useful only for shade and for building, and none of them were good for food, and none stood in the middle of the garden
The trees were good for food, not useful only for shade and building (2:9).
They grew only along the banks of the Euphrates and not within the garden itself, and no tree of life was found there
The trees were planted in the garden in Eden (2:8–9), not only along the Euphrates.
They were all forbidden to the man entirely, and he was told never to eat from any of them, not even the tree of life
Only one tree was forbidden (2:17); the others could be eaten from freely (2:16).
Which sequence best matches the early events of Genesis 2 before the garden command?

Genesis 2:5–7 says no rain had been sent and there was no man to cultivate the ground, “springs welled up from the earth,” and “the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils.”
Genesis 2:5-7
No rain and no man to cultivate, springs watered the ground, then God formed man from the dust and breathed life into him
The woman was formed first from a rib, then the animals were named, and last the man was made from the dust
The man was formed first, then the woman was made from his rib (2:7, 22).
Floodwaters came, the ark rested on the mountains of Ararat, and Noah planted a vineyard before God formed man
The flood and Noah come much later (Genesis 7–9), not before the trees grew.
Abraham left Ur of the Chaldeans for Canaan, and after that God formed the man from the dust of the ground
Abram left Ur long after the man was formed (Genesis 11:31–12:1).
Jacob dreamed of a ladder reaching up to heaven before any of the trees of the garden had grown from the ground
Jacob’s dream of a ladder comes much later (Genesis 28:12), not before the trees grew.
Which sequence best follows the overall order of Genesis 2?

Genesis 2 moves from the man’s formation (2:7) to the planting of the garden and placing the man there (2:8), the command about the trees (2:16–17), the naming of the animals and the lack of a suitable helper (2:19–20), and finally the woman made from the rib (2:21–22).
Genesis 2:7-22
Woman made, serpent speaks to her, man formed, garden planted, and then a flood begins to cover the earth and the animals are named
The man was formed before the woman, the serpent appears only in Genesis 3:1, and the flood is in Genesis 7.
Man formed, garden planted and man placed there, command about the trees, animals named and no suitable helper found, woman made from the man’s rib
Rivers named, the Exodus begins, manna falls in the wilderness, and then the woman is formed from the man’s rib in Eden
The Exodus, the manna and the woman’s formation are in the wrong order; the woman’s formation (2:22) comes long before Exodus 16.
A tower is built, languages are confused, the people scatter over the earth, and only then is the garden of Eden planted
The tower of Babel comes in Genesis 11:9, long after Eden was planted in 2:8.
Abraham is circumcised, Isaac is born to Sarah, and only then is the man formed from the dust of the ground
Abraham’s circumcision comes in Genesis 17:23, long after the man’s formation in 2:7.
In the Garden of Eden account of Genesis 3, which creature spoke to the woman?
The serpent spoke to the woman and opened the temptation (3:1).
Genesis 3:1
A dove
A dove appears later in Noah’s story (Genesis 8:8–12); no dove speaks in Eden.
A serpent
A lamb
Lambs are not mentioned in Genesis 3, and no lamb speaks anywhere in this account.
A lion
No lion appears in this chapter; the only animal that speaks is the serpent (3:1).
A raven
A raven appears in Noah’s story (Genesis 8:7), not in Eden.
In Genesis 3, how is the serpent compared to the other creatures the LORD God had made?
Genesis 3:1 says the serpent was “more crafty than any beast of the field that the LORD God had made.”
Genesis 3:1
More powerful than any beast
The serpent is called crafty, not powerful; Genesis 3:1 makes no comparison of strength.
More beautiful than any bird
Beauty is never mentioned, and birds are not part of the comparison; 3:1 speaks of craftiness among beasts of the field.
More crafty than any beast of the field
More feared than any animal
Fear is not the comparison; 3:1 says the serpent was more crafty than any beast of the field.
More swift than any creature
Speed is not mentioned; the serpent is singled out for being crafty (3:1).
In Eden, what did the serpent first ask the woman about God’s command?
In 3:1 the serpent opened with a question that cast doubt on God’s word: “Did God really say, ‘You must not eat from any tree in the garden?’”
Genesis 3:1
Whether the woman knew who had told her she was naked
The question about who told the woman something is not the serpent’s; God later asks the man who told him he was naked (3:11).
Why the woman was afraid to stand in God’s presence
Fear is not the serpent’s topic here; the man speaks of being afraid only after hiding (3:10).
Why the woman had not yet eaten from the tree of life
The woman’s tree of life is not at issue yet; the serpent’s question is about whether God forbade eating from any tree (3:1).
Whether God really said they must not eat from any tree in the garden
Where her husband had gone while she spoke with him
The serpent first asked a question, then said “You will not surely die” (3:4); it did not ask where the man had gone.
In the woman’s reply in Genesis 3, which tree’s fruit did she say was forbidden?
The woman said God had spoken about “the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden” (3:3).
Genesis 3:3
The fig tree near the river
No fig tree near a river is named in her reply; she points to the tree in the middle of the garden (3:3).
The tree in the middle of the garden

During Abram’s journey in Genesis 13, between which two places did he stop where his tent had formerly been?

Genesis 13:3
Shechem and Dothan
Abram built his first altar at Shechem (Genesis 12:6–7), but his earlier tent site was between Bethel and Ai.
Bethel and Ai
Hebron and Beersheba

Gerar and Gaza
Gerar is where Abraham later sojourned (Genesis 20:1); this journey does not take him to Gaza.
Sodom and Gomorrah
Lot, not Abram, moved toward Sodom (13:12); Abram’s tent had been between Bethel and Ai (13:3).

At the altar he had built earlier, “Abram called on the name of the LORD” (13:4).

Offered Isaac
Abraham bound Isaac on an altar in the land of Moriah, many years later (Genesis 22:2, 9).
Made a treaty with Abimelech

Called on the name of the LORD

Noah built the ark generations before Abram (Genesis 6:14–22).
In the chapter where Abram and Lot begin to separate, what did Lot also possess?

Only sheep and goats

Flocks, herds, and tents

Horses and chariots

In Genesis 13, why could the land not support both Abram and Lot while they stayed together?

A famine had begun

Their servants had rebelled

They had too many possessions to remain together

War comes in the next chapter (Genesis 14); here the problem was their many possessions (13:6).
In the account of Abram and Lot in Genesis 13, between whom did discord break out?

Abram and Lot themselves, over who should lead the household
Abram and Lot stayed on peaceful terms (13:8); the discord was between their herdsmen (13:7).
Sarai and the women of the camp, over who managed the tents
Sarai is not mentioned in the dispute; the quarrel was between the herdsmen (13:7).
The herdsmen of Abram’s livestock and the herdsmen of Lot’s livestock
Abram and the king of Sodom, over who owned the pastureland
Abram first meets the king of Sodom in the following chapter (Genesis 14:17).
Lot and the Canaanites, over wells and grazing in the land
The Canaanites and Perizzites were living in the land, but the discord was between the herdsmen (13:7).
Genesis 13 notes that which peoples were also living in the land at that time?

Hivites and Jebusites

Midianites and Amalekites

Canaanites and Perizzites
Philistines and Edomites

Moabites and Ammonites
Moab and Ammon came from Lot’s daughters later (Genesis 19:37–38).

“We serve the same king”

“We are kinsmen”
“The land belongs to Pharaoh”

It was not dry; the plain was well watered like the garden of the LORD (13:10).

Beersheba

Dan

Zoar
Bethel

Gerar
Gerar lies to the southwest, where Abraham later sojourned (Genesis 20:1).
In Genesis 13, to what two places is the Jordan plain compared before Lot chose it?

The cedars of Lebanon and the pastures of Bashan
Lebanon and Bashan are not part of this comparison; the plain is likened to the garden of the LORD and Egypt (13:10).
The hills of Gilead and the vineyards of Carmel

The garden of the LORD and the land of Egypt
The wilderness of Sinai and the oasis of Paran
Sinai and Paran are not mentioned in the comparison (13:10).

In the story of Abram and Lot’s separation in Genesis 13, what did Lot choose for himself?

The hill country of Ephraim
Lot chose the plain of the Jordan, not the hill country (13:11).

The whole plain of the Jordan
The oaks of Mamre

After choosing the plain in Genesis 13, in which direction did Lot set out?

North

South

East
West
Lot went east, not west (13:11).
Northwest

In Egypt

The stars of the sky

The sand on the seashore

The dew of the morning
Dew is not used in this promise; the comparison is dust (13:16).
The dust of the earth
The cedars of Lebanon
Cedars of Lebanon are not used in this promise; the comparison is dust (13:16).

If someone could count the dust of the earth

Rain is not used here; the comparison is dust (13:16).

Leaves of the trees are not used; the illustration is the dust of the earth (13:16).

Divide it among his servants by casting lots

Mark its boundaries by setting up stone pillars

Walk around it through its length and breadth

Near the oaks of Mamre at Hebron
Near the terebinths of Moreh at Shechem

Near the wells of Beersheba

An altar to the LORD

It was where his tent had formerly been and where he had built the altar

Joseph was sold at Dothan, generations later (Genesis 37:28).
Which sequence best matches Genesis 13 after Lot separated from Abram?

Bethel

Sodom
Gerar

Isaac

Abram
