While staying in Gerar, Abraham said of his wife Sarah, “She is my sister” (20:2).
Genesis 20:2
She is my wife
That was the truth he concealed; God later calls her a married woman (20:3), and Abraham admits she became his wife (20:12).
She is my cousin
Abraham called her his sister, in fact his half-sister (20:12), not his cousin.
She is my servant
Sarah was his wife, not his servant; the servant in Abraham’s household was Hagar, Sarah’s maidservant (Genesis 16:1).
She is my sister
She is my daughter
He said she was the daughter of his father, which made her his sister, not his daughter (20:12).
In the Gerar incident involving Sarah, who sent for her and took her?
Abimelech king of Gerar had Sarah brought to him (20:2).
Genesis 20:2
Pharaoh king of Egypt
Pharaoh took Sarai in an earlier, similar episode in Egypt (Genesis 12:15), not in Gerar.
Lot of Sodom
Lot, Abraham’s nephew, lived near Sodom and never took Sarah.
Abimelech king of Gerar
Isaac of Beersheba
Isaac was Abraham’s son; he later faced a similar problem with Rebekah in Gerar (Genesis 26:6–7), but he did not take Sarah.
Laban of Haran
Laban, Rebekah’s brother (Genesis 24:29), lived in Haran and had no part in Sarah’s story.
How did God warn Abimelech after he had taken Sarah into his household?
God came to Abimelech in a dream one night and warned him that he was as good as dead (20:3).
Genesis 20:3
Through a burning bush
God spoke to Moses from a burning bush (Exodus 3:2); that was a different time and person.
By thunder from heaven
Thunder accompanied God’s presence at Sinai (Exodus 20:18), not His warning to Abimelech.
Through a dream by night
By an angel at the city gate
Angels came to Lot at the gateway of Sodom (Genesis 19:1); here God spoke to Abimelech directly in a dream.
Through a prophet from Hebron
Abimelech is told that Abraham himself is the prophet (20:7); no prophet from Hebron brings the warning.
In God’s warning to Abimelech about Sarah, how did God describe her status?
God told Abimelech, “You are as good as dead because of the woman you have taken, for she is a married woman” (20:3).
Genesis 20:3
She was a widow
Abraham was alive, and God told Abimelech to return “the man’s wife” (20:7), so Sarah was not a widow.
She was pledged to another man
She was already married, not merely promised to someone; God said she is “a married woman” (20:3).
She was a married woman
She was a priestess
Nothing in the chapter makes Sarah a priestess; she is Abraham’s wife (20:2–3).
She was a servant in Abraham’s house
She was Abraham’s wife, not a servant; Abraham’s servants are listed separately among the gifts (20:14).
When God warned Abimelech in the dream, what was true of Abimelech and Sarah?
Verse 4 says Abimelech had not gone near Sarah, and God confirms that He kept him from touching her (20:6).
Genesis 20:4, 20:6
He had already given her gifts
Gifts came later, as restitution after God’s warning (20:14), so he had not yet given her any.
He had not gone near her
He had already sent her home
Abimelech returned Sarah only after the warning (20:14), so at that point she was still in his house.
He had already married her publicly
The chapter never says Abimelech married Sarah; he only had her brought to him (20:2), and God kept him from touching her (20:6).
He had already taken her to Egypt
Abimelech ruled Gerar; Sarah had been taken into Pharaoh’s palace in Egypt in an earlier episode (Genesis 12:15).
When Abimelech defended himself before God regarding Sarah, how did he describe his conduct?
Abimelech pleaded “the integrity of my heart and the innocence of my hands” (20:5), and God agreed he acted “with a clear conscience” (20:6).
Genesis 20:5
With zeal and courage
Abimelech did not claim zeal or courage; he claimed he had acted in ignorance and innocence (20:5).
With fear and trembling
His servants were terrified afterwards (20:8), but his own defense was a clear conscience, not fear.
With wisdom and patience
Abimelech did not boast of wisdom or patience; he pointed to his integrity and innocent hands (20:5).
With clear conscience and clean hands
With fasting and prayer
Abimelech fasted and prayed in no part of this scene; it was Abraham who was told to pray for him (20:7, 20:17).
When King Abimelech of Gerar asked Abraham why he had said Sarah was his sister, what reason did Abraham give?
Abraham said, “Surely there is no fear of God in this place. They will kill me on account of my wife” (20:11).
Genesis 20:11
He wanted to test whether Abimelech would be generous with gifts and livestock
Abraham gave fear for his life as his reason (20:11); the gifts came only afterwards from Abimelech (20:14).
He feared there was no fear of God there and that men would kill him because of Sarah
He had forgotten that Sarah was already his wife and spoke carelessly
Abraham knew Sarah was his wife and said so: “she became my wife” (20:12).
Sarah told him to say it so that they could gain political favor in Gerar
Abraham says he asked Sarah to say it as a sign of loyalty to him (20:13); there was no political motive.
He was obeying a command from Lot, who had warned him about the king of Gerar
Lot does not appear in this chapter; Abraham traces the plan to when God had him leave his father’s house (20:13).
In Abraham’s fuller explanation about Sarah in the Gerar episode, what family relationship did he say Sarah had to him?
Abraham explained, “she really is my sister, the daughter of my father—though not the daughter of my mother—and she became my wife” (20:12).
Genesis 20:12
She was his niece, the daughter of his younger brother
Abraham calls Sarah the daughter of his father, so a half-sister, not the child of a brother (20:12).
She was his cousin, the daughter of his father’s brother
Abraham calls Sarah the daughter of his father, so a half-sister, not the child of his father’s brother (20:12).
She was his half-sister, the daughter of his father but not of his mother
She was his stepdaughter, the child of his wife’s earlier marriage
Abraham says she is his father’s daughter who became his wife; he does not say she was a child of his wife by an earlier marriage (20:12).
She was no blood relation at all, only a close family friend
Abraham says she “really is my sister” (20:12), so she was a blood relative.
In God’s instruction to Abimelech about returning Sarah, what did God call Abraham?
God told Abimelech to return the man’s wife “for he is a prophet; he will pray for you and you will live” (20:7).
Genesis 20:7
A judge
Judges arose centuries later, when the LORD raised them up to save Israel (Judges 2:16); God did not call Abraham one.
A king
Abimelech was the king in this scene (20:2); God named Abraham a prophet.
A prophet
A priest
Melchizedek was the priest of God Most High in Abraham’s day (Genesis 14:18); God called Abraham a prophet.
A shepherd
Abraham owned flocks (20:14), but God described him as a prophet who would pray for Abimelech (20:7).
After Abimelech returned Sarah to Abraham, which gifts did he give Abraham?
Abimelech “brought sheep and cattle, menservants and maidservants” and gave them to Abraham when he restored Sarah (20:14).
Genesis 20:14
Chariots and horses, along with soldiers to guard the road
The list in 20:14 contains livestock and servants, with no chariots, horses or guards.
Gold, jewels, and garments of fine linen
Abimelech gave sheep, cattle and servants (20:14) and a thousand pieces of silver (20:16), but not gold or linen.
Sheep, cattle, and male and female servants
A fortified city and an army to defend it
He offered Abraham open land to settle in (20:15), but did not give him a city or an army.
Camels, donkeys, and a caravan loaded with spices
Camels and donkeys were part of what Pharaoh gave Abram in Egypt (Genesis 12:16), not what Abimelech gave here.
When Abimelech spoke directly to Sarah after restoring her, what did he say the thousand pieces of silver were meant to be?
Abimelech told Sarah the thousand pieces of silver were “your vindication before all who are with you; you are completely cleared” (20:16).
Genesis 20:16
Her dowry
Abimelech does not call the silver a dowry; Sarah was already married to Abraham (20:3).
Payment for Abraham’s livestock
The sheep, cattle and servants were given separately (20:14); the silver was for Sarah’s vindication.
A ransom for Gerar
Nothing is paid as a ransom; Abimelech says the silver clears Sarah’s name (20:16).
Her vindication before all who were with her
An offering for the altar at Bethel
No altar or offering is mentioned in the chapter; the silver was given to clear Sarah (20:16).
After Abraham prayed in the aftermath of the Gerar incident, whom did God heal?
After Abraham prayed, “God healed Abimelech and his wife and his maidservants, so that they could again bear children” (20:17).
Genesis 20:17
Abraham, Sarah, and the servants who had traveled with them from Haran
The healing was for Abimelech’s household (20:17), not Abraham’s family; Ishmael is not mentioned in this chapter.
Sarah, who could not bear children, and her servant Hagar the Egyptian
Sarah’s own son came later as the LORD’s promise (Genesis 21:1–2); here the healing was for Abimelech’s wife and maidservants (20:17).
Abimelech, his wife, and his female servants
Only Abimelech, who had been struck with a deadly illness
Verse 17 names Abimelech, his wife and his maidservants, and the trouble was closed wombs, not a deadly illness (20:18).
Only the men of Gerar, who had been struck down by a plague
The healing was for Abimelech’s own household (20:17), not for the men of Gerar, and no plague is mentioned.
Why did Abimelech’s household need healing after Sarah had been taken into the king’s house in Gerar?
On account of Abraham’s wife Sarah, “the LORD had completely closed all the wombs in Abimelech’s household” (20:18).
Genesis 20:18
The LORD had sent a famine on the land of Gerar, and the harvest had failed
Famine in Abraham’s and Isaac’s day sent them to Egypt and Gerar (Genesis 12:10, Genesis 26:1); no famine is mentioned here.
The LORD had struck the livestock of Gerar with a disease that spread through the herds
A plague on livestock struck Egypt in Moses’ day (Exodus 9:3); here the trouble was closed wombs (20:18).
The LORD had caused blindness in the palace, so that no one could find the door
Blindness struck the men at Lot’s door in Sodom (Genesis 19:11), not Abimelech’s palace.
The LORD had completely closed all the wombs in Abimelech’s household because of Sarah
The LORD had stopped the rain for three years, and the wells of Gerar had gone dry
No drought is mentioned in this chapter; the affliction was closed wombs, lifted after Abraham prayed (20:17–18).
In Genesis 21, when the LORD fulfilled His promise to Abraham’s household, whom did He attend to?
Genesis 21:1 says the LORD attended to Sarah as He had said and did for her what He had promised, so she conceived (21:2).
Genesis 21:1-2
Hagar
Hagar bore Ishmael to Abraham earlier (Genesis 16:16), but she was not the one through whom God’s promise was fulfilled here.
Rebekah
Rebekah became Isaac’s wife later (Genesis 24:67); she was not part of Abraham’s household when Isaac was born.
Sarah
Keturah
Keturah was the wife Abraham took after Sarah’s death (Genesis 25:1), not the woman God visited in this chapter.
Rachel
Rachel was Jacob’s wife (Genesis 29:28), a generation after Abraham and Sarah.
In the account of Sarah bearing Abraham a son in old age, what name did Abraham give the child?
Genesis 21:3 says Abraham gave the name Isaac to the son Sarah bore to him.
Genesis 21:3
Ishmael
Ishmael was the son born to Abraham by Hagar (Genesis 16:16), not the son Sarah bore.
Isaac
Jacob
Jacob was Isaac’s son, born to Rebekah when Isaac was sixty (Genesis 25:26).
Joseph
Joseph was Jacob’s son by Rachel (Genesis 30:24), two generations after Isaac.
Benjamin
Benjamin was Jacob’s youngest son (Genesis 35:18), not Abraham’s child.
When Abraham obeyed God regarding the sign of the covenant for baby Isaac, how old was Isaac?
Genesis 21:4 says that when Isaac was eight days old, Abraham circumcised him, as God had commanded him.
Genesis 21:4
Three days old
God’s command was not for the third day; Genesis 17:12 sets circumcision for a male when he is eight days old.
Seven days old
Seven days old is one day short; Genesis 17:12 and 21:4 both give the eighth day.
Eight days old
One month old
A month is far too late; God’s command in Genesis 17:12 required circumcision on the eighth day.
One year old
A year old is not the age the Bible gives; Isaac was circumcised at eight days (21:4).
In Genesis 21, how old was Abraham when Isaac was born to him?
Genesis 21:5 states that Abraham was a hundred years old when his son Isaac was born to him.
Genesis 21:5
Seventy-five was Abram’s age when he left Haran (Genesis 12:4), decades before Isaac’s birth.
Eighty-six was Abram’s age when Hagar bore Ishmael (Genesis 16:16), not when Isaac was born.
Ninety was not Abraham’s age at Isaac’s birth; Sarah, not Abraham, was ninety when Isaac was promised (Genesis 17:17).
One hundred twenty is too high; Genesis 21:5 gives a hundred.
After Isaac was born, what did Sarah say God had made her do?
In Genesis 21:6 Sarah says, “God has made me laugh, and everyone who hears of this will laugh with me.”
Genesis 21:6
Sing
Sarah does not say God made her sing; her joy is expressed as laughter, the root of Isaac’s name.
Laugh
Dance
Dancing is not mentioned in Sarah’s words; she says God has made her laugh (21:6).
Prophesy
Prophesying is not what Sarah says here; her words in 21:6–7 are about laughter and nursing a son in old age.
Rejoice silently
Sarah’s joy is not silent; she says everyone who hears will laugh with her (21:6).
In the Genesis narrative about Isaac’s early life, on what occasion did Abraham hold a great feast?
Genesis 21:8 says Abraham held a great feast on the day Isaac was weaned.
Genesis 21:8
When Isaac was named
The naming of Isaac (21:3) is not linked to a feast in this chapter.
When Isaac was circumcised
Genesis 21:4 mentions Isaac’s circumcision at eight days but no feast; the feast came when he was weaned.
When Isaac was weaned
When Isaac was married
Isaac’s marriage came when he was forty (Genesis 25:20), long after this event.
When Isaac blessed Jacob
Isaac blessed Jacob when he was old (Genesis 27:27), decades later.
After Isaac was weaned, whom did Sarah see mocking her son in Genesis 21?
Genesis 21:9 says Sarah saw that the son whom Hagar the Egyptian had borne to Abraham was mocking her son.
Genesis 21:9
Lot
Lot was Abraham’s nephew, who had parted from him earlier (Genesis 13:11); he is not in this scene.
Eliezer of Damascus
Eliezer of Damascus was the household steward Abraham once named as his heir (Genesis 15:2), not the one mocking Isaac.
Esau
Esau was Isaac’s son, born decades later (Genesis 25:25).
The son of Hagar the Egyptian
Abimelech
Abimelech appears later in this chapter making a covenant (21:22–32), not mocking Isaac.
After seeing Hagar’s son mocking, what did Sarah tell Abraham to do in Genesis 21?
In Genesis 21:10 Sarah tells Abraham, “Expel the slave woman and her son,” since the slave woman’s son will never share the inheritance with Isaac.
Genesis 21:10
Keep Hagar in the household as Abraham’s permanent wife
Sarah wanted Hagar gone, not kept as a permanent wife; Hagar had already been given to Abraham as a wife long before (Genesis 16:3).
Send Isaac away to live with other relatives
Sarah wanted Ishmael sent away, not her own son; she insists Isaac alone should inherit (21:10).
Drive out the slave woman and her son
Divide the household in two and give Hagar a half
Sarah asks for Hagar and Ishmael to be expelled from the household, not for the household to be divided between them.
Move the whole household to live in the land of Egypt
Sarah does not ask to move to Egypt; Hagar was the Egyptian, and she and her son were the ones sent away (21:14).
Why was Sarah’s demand about Hagar and her son very distressing to Abraham?
Genesis 21:11 says the matter distressed Abraham greatly because it concerned his son Ishmael.
Genesis 21:11
Because it threatened his livestock
Livestock is not mentioned; Genesis 21:11 says the distress was about his son.
Because it concerned his son Ishmael
Because Abimelech was offended
Abimelech’s dealings with Abraham come later (21:22–32) and are not what distressed him here.
Because Sarah was leaving him
Sarah is not leaving; she asks that Hagar and her son be expelled (21:10).
Because a famine had begun
No famine is mentioned in Genesis 21; Abraham’s grief concerned Ishmael (21:11).
When God spoke to Abraham about Sarah’s demand, through which son did God say Abraham’s offspring would be reckoned?
God told Abraham, “through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned” (Genesis 21:12).
Genesis 21:12
Ishmael
Ishmael was also Abraham’s son and God promised to make a nation of him (21:13), but the line of promise ran through Isaac.
Isaac
Lot
Lot was Abraham’s nephew, not his son (Genesis 14:12).
Midian
Midian was a son of Abraham by Keturah (Genesis 25:2), not the son of promise.
Zimran
Zimran was also a son of Abraham by Keturah (Genesis 25:2), not the line of promise.
Early the next morning, when Abraham sent Hagar away, what provisions did he give her?
Genesis 21:14 says Abraham took bread and a skin of water and put them on Hagar’s shoulders before sending her away with the boy.
Genesis 21:14
Silver and grain
Silver and grain are not mentioned; the only provisions named are bread and water (21:14).
Bread and a skin of water
A donkey and wine
No donkey or wine is given; Hagar carries bread and a skin of water on her shoulders (21:14).
Sheep and oil
No sheep or oil are listed; Genesis 21:14 names bread and a skin of water.
A tent and sandals
No tent or sandals are mentioned; she left with only bread, water and the boy (21:14).
After leaving Abraham’s household, in what place did Hagar wander?
Genesis 21:14 says Hagar left and wandered in the Wilderness of Beersheba.
Genesis 21:14
The Valley of Siddim
The Valley of Siddim was where the kings fought in Genesis 14:3, not Hagar’s wandering place.
The Wilderness of Shur
Hagar fled along the road to Shur earlier, when she ran from Sarah (Genesis 16:7); here she wandered in the Wilderness of Beersheba.
The Wilderness of Beersheba
The hill country of Ephraim
The hill country of Ephraim is far north of Hagar’s route and is not mentioned in this chapter.
The plains of Moab
The plains of Moab are east of the Dead Sea and are not part of Hagar’s story in this chapter.
When the water in the skin was gone, where did Hagar place the boy?
Genesis 21:15 says that when the water in the skin was gone, Hagar left the boy under one of the bushes.
Genesis 21:15
Beside a well
Hagar found a well only after God opened her eyes (21:19); she did not leave the boy beside one.
Under one of the bushes
In a cave
No cave is mentioned in this scene; she left him under one of the bushes (21:15).
On a rock
No rock is mentioned; the boy was placed under a bush (21:15).
Under a tamarisk tree
Abraham planted a tamarisk tree at Beersheba later (21:33), but Hagar left Ishmael under a bush.
In the wilderness scene of Genesis 21, about how far away did Hagar sit from the boy as she wept?
Genesis 21:16 says Hagar sat down nearby, about a bowshot away, because she could not bear to watch the boy die.
Genesis 21:16
A day’s journey
A day’s journey is far too great; she sat only about a bowshot away (21:16).
About a bowshot away
Seven cubits
Seven cubits is much too close; the text says about a bowshot (21:16).
Across the river
No river is mentioned in the scene; the nearby well appears only after God opens her eyes (21:19).
At the tent entrance
Hagar was in the wilderness, not at a tent entrance (21:14–16).
As Hagar wept in the wilderness, who called to her from heaven?
Genesis 21:17 says the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven, saying, “Do not be afraid, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he lies.”
Genesis 21:17
The angel of God
Abraham
Abraham had sent Hagar away and was not with her in the wilderness (21:14).
Melchizedek
Melchizedek is the king and priest who met Abraham in Genesis 14:18, not the voice that spoke to Hagar.
Isaac
Isaac was a young child at home with Abraham and Sarah, not present in the wilderness.
Phicol
Phicol is Abimelech’s army commander, who appears later in the chapter (21:22).
What did God enable Hagar to see so that she and the boy could live?
Genesis 21:19 says God opened Hagar’s eyes and she saw a well of water, so she filled the skin and gave the boy a drink.
Genesis 21:19
A flock of goats
No goats are mentioned; the life-saving provision was a well (21:19).
A spring of oil
No spring of oil appears here; she saw a well of water (21:19).
A well of water
A caravan to Egypt
No caravan is mentioned; God opened her eyes to a well (21:19).
Abraham returning
Abraham does not return; the rescue came from God through the well (21:17–19).
As Hagar’s son grew up in the wilderness, what skill is specifically mentioned in Genesis 21?
Genesis 21:20 says God was with the boy, who settled in the wilderness and became a great archer.
Genesis 21:20
He became a great shepherd
Ishmael became an archer, not a shepherd; the chapter names no shepherding skill for him (21:20).
He became a great archer
He became a skilled builder
Nothing is said about building; the skill named in 21:20 is archery.
He became a priest
Priests came later from the line of Aaron (Leviticus 21:1), not from Ishmael.
He became a scribe
No scribal skill is mentioned; Genesis 21:20 names only archery.
After settling in the Wilderness of Paran, from what land did Hagar obtain a wife for her son?
Genesis 21:21 says that while Ishmael lived in the Wilderness of Paran, his mother got a wife for him from the land of Egypt.
Genesis 21:21
Canaan
Canaan is not named; Hagar, who was Egyptian, chose a wife from her own homeland, Egypt (21:21).
Assyria
Assyria is not mentioned in Genesis 21; the wife came from Egypt.
Egypt
Babylon
Babylon is not mentioned here; Hagar was Egyptian and found Ishmael a wife in Egypt (21:9, 21).
Edom
Edom is not mentioned in the passage; it is the land named after Esau, who was not yet born.
Later in Genesis 21, which two men came to Abraham and said, “God is with you in all that you do”?
Genesis 21:22 says Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army said to Abraham, “God is with you in all that you do.”
Genesis 21:22
Lot and Mamre
Lot and Mamre do not speak these words; Lot had parted from Abraham long before (Genesis 13:11).
Isaac and Jacob
Isaac and Jacob are not part of this scene; Jacob was not yet born.
Abimelech and Phicol
Pharaoh and Potiphar
Pharaoh and Potiphar belong to the Egyptian stories of later chapters, not to this covenant at Beersheba.
Laban and Bethuel
Laban and Bethuel are Rebekah’s relatives (Genesis 25:20) and do not appear in this chapter.
In Abraham’s agreement with Abimelech, what did Abimelech ask Abraham to swear before God?
Abimelech said, “swear to me here before God that you will not deal falsely with me or my children or descendants” (Genesis 21:23).
Genesis 21:23

That he would not deal falsely with Abimelech or his descendants
That he would offer his son Isaac as a sacrifice at once

That he would move his household away from Abimelech’s land
Abimelech asks for kindness, not that Abraham relocate; he even lets Abraham stay in his land (21:34).
That he would serve as a captain in Abimelech’s army
Abimelech asks for an oath of fairness, not military service from Abraham (21:23).
During the covenant discussion, what specific complaint did Abraham raise against Abimelech?
Genesis 21:25 says Abraham complained to Abimelech about a well that Abimelech’s servants had seized.
Genesis 21:25
Abimelech had taken Sarah again
Abimelech had taken Sarah in Genesis 20:2, before Isaac’s birth, not in this dispute.
Abimelech’s servants had seized a well
Abimelech had stolen sheep
No stolen sheep are mentioned; the complaint was about a well (21:25).
Abimelech had broken an altar
No altar is mentioned in the dispute; the issue was a seized well (21:25).
Abimelech had refused circumcision
Circumcision is not mentioned in the covenant discussion; the complaint was about the well (21:25).
Before Abraham and Abimelech made their covenant, what did Abraham bring and give to Abimelech?
Genesis 21:27 says Abraham brought sheep and cattle and gave them to Abimelech, and the two men made a covenant.
Genesis 21:27
Silver and gold
No silver or gold changes hands in this covenant; Abraham gave animals (21:27).
Sheep and cattle
Bread and wine
Bread and wine appear with Melchizedek in Genesis 14:18, not in this agreement.
Doves and pigeons
Doves and pigeons are not mentioned in this covenant; Abraham gave sheep and cattle (21:27).
Garments and sandals
No garments or sandals are given here; the gift was livestock (21:27).
In the matter of the disputed well, how many ewe lambs did Abraham set apart from the flock?
Genesis 21:28 says Abraham separated seven ewe lambs from the flock.
Genesis 21:28
Three
Three is not the number given; the text says seven ewe lambs (21:28).
Five
Five is not the number given; Abraham set apart seven ewe lambs (21:28–30).
Seven
Ten
Ten is not the number given in this passage; it is seven (21:29).
Twelve
Twelve is not the number given; Abraham set apart seven ewe lambs (21:30).
What was the purpose of the seven ewe lambs Abraham gave Abimelech?
Abraham said, “You are to accept the seven ewe lambs from my hand as my witness that I dug this well” (Genesis 21:30).

To pay a bride-price for a daughter of Abimelech
The lambs were not a bride-price; no marriage is involved in this agreement (21:28–30).
To feed Abimelech’s army on its march home

To witness that Abraham had dug the well
To make atonement for a sin Abraham had done
The lambs were not an atonement offering; they were a witness that Abraham dug the well (21:30).
To celebrate the birth of Abraham’s son Isaac

In the account of Abraham’s oath with Abimelech, why was the place called Beersheba?

Because Sarah laughed there

Because Hagar found water there

Because the two men swore an oath there
Because Isaac was born there
Isaac’s birth is not tied to Beersheba’s name in this chapter (21:2–3).
Because a tamarisk forest grew there

After making the covenant at Beersheba, what kind of tree did Abraham plant there?
Genesis 21:33 says Abraham planted a tamarisk tree in Beersheba.
Genesis 21:33
Cedar
Cedar is not mentioned in this account; Abraham planted a tamarisk (21:33).
Olive
An olive tree is not named here; the tree was a tamarisk (21:33).
Tamarisk
Fig
A fig tree is not mentioned in this account (21:33).
Cypress

Gerar

Canaan

While Isaac was living in Gerar, how did he describe Rebekah when the men of that place asked about his wife?

“She is my sister”

Hundredfold

Jacob built no city walls; he was a herdsman putting up shelters for his animals (33:17).
Boats for crossing the Jordan
Nothing in the account involves boats; Jacob built a house and shelters for his livestock (33:17).
According to Genesis 33, after coming from Paddan-aram, at what city in the land of Canaan did Jacob arrive safely and camp before it?
After coming from Paddan-aram, Jacob arrived safely at the city of Shechem in Canaan and camped just outside it (33:18).
Genesis 33:18
Beersheba

Dothan
Dothan is where Joseph’s brothers later grazed their flocks (Genesis 37:17), not Jacob’s camp here.
Shechem
Jericho
Jericho is not on Jacob’s route; Israel conquered it generations later (Joshua 6).
Bethlehem
Bethlehem (Ephrath) is where Rachel was buried later (Genesis 35:19), after Jacob’s stay at Shechem.
Near Shechem in Genesis 33, from whom did Jacob buy the plot where he pitched his tent?
Jacob purchased the plot where he pitched his tent from the sons of Hamor, Shechem’s father, for a hundred pieces of silver (33:19).

The sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem

Laban was Jacob’s uncle in Paddan-aram, whom Jacob had left behind (Genesis 31:55), not the seller here.

Midianite traders appear later in Joseph’s story (Genesis 37:28); they did not sell Jacob this plot.
After Jacob set up an altar near Shechem in Genesis 33, what name did he give it?
At Shechem Jacob set up an altar and called it El-Elohe-Israel (33:20).

El-Bethel

Yahweh-Jireh

El-Elohe-Israel

El-Roi

In the incident at Shechem in Genesis 34, who saw Dinah, took her, and violated her?

According to Genesis 34, Shechem was the son of which man?

Illness is never mentioned; Jacob stayed silent until his sons came back from the field (34:5).

Jacob’s trip to Bethel comes later, in Genesis 35:1–7, after the events at Shechem.

In Genesis 34, what reason did Jacob’s sons give for refusing to give Dinah immediately to Shechem?

Egypt is not mentioned in this chapter; the promise concerned intermarriage and one people (34:16).
When Hamor and Shechem addressed the men at the city gate in Genesis 34, what self-interested argument did they use to persuade them?

No famine is mentioned in Genesis 34; the argument was that the men would gain Jacob’s livestock and goods (34:23).

Every male was circumcised

Near Bethel in Genesis 35, which woman, identified as Rebekah’s nurse, died and was buried under the oak?

Jacob wanted his body burned outside Egypt
Jacob was embalmed and buried in a tomb (50:2, 5, 13); nothing in the chapter speaks of burning his body.
Jacob had ordered burial in the Nile Delta
Jacob insisted on burial in Canaan, not Egypt (50:5), so a grave in the Nile Delta is the opposite of his charge.
Jacob had chosen a new grave in Goshen
Jacob lived in Goshen, but he asked to be buried with his fathers in Canaan (50:5; Genesis 49:29).
In Genesis 50, who told Joseph, “Go up and bury your father, as he made you swear”?
Pharaoh replied, “Go up and bury your father, as he made you swear to do” (50:6).
Genesis 50:6
Pharaoh
Potiphar
Potiphar was the officer of Pharaoh who bought Joseph as a slave (Genesis 39:1); he has no part in this scene.
The chief cupbearer
Joseph interpreted the chief cupbearer’s dream in prison (Genesis 40:12), but the cupbearer is not mentioned in the burial request.
Judah
Judah, Joseph’s brother, once pleaded with him for Benjamin (Genesis 44:18); he did not give permission here.
The high priest of On
Potiphera, priest of On, was Joseph’s father-in-law (Genesis 41:45), but Genesis 50:6 attributes the reply to Pharaoh.
When Joseph and the burial company traveled from Egypt, what was left behind in Goshen?
Only the children, flocks and herds stayed behind in Goshen while the rest went to bury Jacob (50:8).
Genesis 50:8
Jacob’s coffin and the elders of Egypt
The elders of Pharaoh’s household and of Egypt went along with Joseph (50:7); Jacob’s embalmed body was carried to Canaan.
Joseph’s silver and grain stores
No stores of silver or grain are mentioned in this scene; the verse names only the children, flocks and herds as left in Goshen (50:8).
The chariots and horsemen
The chariots and horsemen went up with Joseph, making an exceedingly large procession (50:9).
Their children, flocks, and herds
The physicians and embalmers
The physicians completed the embalming before the journey (50:2–3); the verse names only the children, flocks and herds as left in Goshen (50:8).
Along with Joseph’s family and Egyptian officials, what also accompanied Jacob’s funeral procession?
Chariots and horsemen went up with Joseph, making it an exceedingly large procession (50:9).
Genesis 50:9
Only shepherds from Goshen
Pharaoh’s servants and the elders of Egypt went along (50:7); shepherds of Goshen are not mentioned as part of the procession.
Camels and merchants from Midian
Midianite traders appear when Joseph was sold (Genesis 37:28), not in Jacob’s funeral procession.
Chariots and horsemen
Priests carrying the ark
The ark of the covenant was not made until the time of Moses (Exodus 25:10); no priests with an ark were in Jacob’s funeral.
Sailors from the Nile
No sailors are mentioned; 50:7–9 lists the servants, the elders, Joseph’s family, chariots and horsemen.
During the journey to bury Jacob, at what place beyond the Jordan did Joseph hold a great lamentation?
At the threshing floor of Atad, across the Jordan, they lamented and wailed loudly, and Joseph mourned seven days (50:10).
Genesis 50:10
The cave of Adullam
David later took refuge in the cave of Adullam (1 Samuel 22:1); it is not where Joseph mourned.
The Valley of Elah
The Valley of Elah is where Israel camped against the Philistines in Saul’s day (1 Samuel 17:2).
The field of Dothan
Dothan is where Joseph’s brothers had gone to pasture their flocks when he was sold (Genesis 37:17).
The oaks of Mamre
The oaks of Mamre are near the Machpelah cave where Jacob was buried (50:13), not the place of the great lamentation across the Jordan.
The threshing floor of Atad
What name did the Canaanites give to the mourning place beyond the Jordan after seeing Jacob’s funeral observance?
Because the Canaanites saw the mourning at the threshing floor of Atad, the place across the Jordan is called Abel-mizraim (50:11).
Genesis 50:11
Beth-el
Bethel is the name Jacob gave the place of his dream, formerly called Luz (Genesis 28:19).
Abel-mizraim
Kiriath-arba
Kiriath-arba is an older name of Hebron (Genesis 23:2), not the name given to this place across the Jordan.
En-mishpat
En-mishpat is another name for Kadesh (Genesis 14:7), not the mourning place across the Jordan.
Zoan
Zoan was an Egyptian city (Numbers 13:22), not the name given to the place across the Jordan.
When the inhabitants of Canaan saw the mourning at Atad, what did they say?
The Canaanites said, “This is a solemn ceremony of mourning by the Egyptians” (50:11), which is why the place was called Abel-mizraim.
Genesis 50:11
“This is a solemn ceremony of mourning by the Egyptians.”
“This is the wedding feast of a prince.”
The Canaanites saw a funeral, not a wedding; they said the mourning was by the Egyptians (50:11).
“This is a victory march of Pharaoh.”
No victory march is mentioned; the Canaanites interpreted what they saw as an Egyptian ceremony of mourning (50:11).
“This is a famine caravan from Canaan.”
The Canaanites saw mourners, not a caravan; they remarked on an Egyptian ceremony of mourning (50:11).
“This is a census gathering of the tribes.”
No census is involved; the crowd at Atad was a funeral procession for Jacob (50:10–11).
In the burial account of Genesis 50, where was Jacob laid to rest in Canaan?
Jacob’s sons carried him to Canaan and buried him in the cave at Machpelah in the field near Mamre (50:12–13).
Genesis 50:13
In a rock-cut tomb at Zoan in the Nile delta
Jacob was carried to Canaan to be buried (50:13); a rock-cut tomb in the Nile delta is the opposite of his charge.
In the plot near Shechem that Jacob had purchased
Jacob had bought a plot near Shechem (Genesis 33:19) and Joseph’s bones were later buried there (Joshua 24:32), but Jacob himself was laid in Machpelah (50:13).
In a cave near Beersheba in the far south
Isaac lies in the Machpelah cave with Rebekah (Genesis 49:31), and Jacob joined them there (50:13), not at Beersheba.
In the cave of the field of Machpelah near Mamre
In a royal tomb beside the Pharaohs at Memphis
Jacob was carried to Canaan and buried at Machpelah (50:13), not in an Egyptian royal tomb.
According to the description of Jacob’s burial place, which patriarch had originally bought the field of Machpelah?
Genesis 50:13 says Abraham had purchased the field of Machpelah from Ephron the Hittite as a burial site; the purchase is told in Genesis 23:16–20.
Genesis 50:13
Isaac
Isaac was buried in the Machpelah cave (Genesis 49:31), but Abraham, not Isaac, had bought the field (50:13).
Jacob
Jacob was buried in the cave (50:13), but Abraham had bought it long before.
Abraham
Joseph
Joseph did not buy the field; he buried his father in the cave Abraham had purchased (50:13).
Judah
Judah, Jacob’s son, had no part in the purchase; Genesis 50:13 names Abraham as the buyer.
From whom had the burial field and cave of Machpelah been purchased?
Abraham purchased the field and cave as a burial site from Ephron the Hittite (50:13), as told in Genesis 23:16–20.
Genesis 50:13
Abimelech the Philistine
Abraham dealt with Abimelech over a well that Abimelech’s servants had seized (Genesis 21:25), not over the burial field.
Laban the Aramean
Laban the Aramean was Rebekah’s brother and Jacob’s uncle (Genesis 28:5); he had nothing to do with the Machpelah field.
Mamre the Amorite
Mamre the Amorite was an ally of Abram (Genesis 14:13); the field near Mamre was bought from Ephron (50:13).
Melchizedek king of Salem
Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine for Abram (Genesis 14:18); he did not sell the burial field.
Ephron the Hittite
After Jacob had been buried and the family returned to Egypt, what did Joseph’s brothers fear?
With Jacob dead, the brothers said, “What if Joseph bears a grudge? Then he will surely repay us for all the evil that we did to him” (50:15).
Genesis 50:15
Pharaoh would take back the land of Goshen and drive them out of Egypt
Joseph had settled his family in the best part of Egypt (Genesis 47:11); their fear in 50:15 was Joseph’s revenge, not Pharaoh’s.
Joseph might hold a grudge and repay them for all the wrong they had done to him
The Canaanites who saw the mourning would pursue them back into Egypt
The Canaanites who watched the mourning only named the place Abel-mizraim (50:11); the brothers feared Joseph, not them.
Benjamin would accuse them before Pharaoh’s court of selling Joseph into slavery
Benjamin is not mentioned in chapter 50; the brothers feared that Joseph would repay them (50:15).
Another famine would strike the land and leave their families without grain
Famine is not mentioned in 50:15–21; Joseph promises to provide for them (50:21).
In the message sent to Joseph after Jacob’s death, what did the brothers ask him to forgive?
The message asked Joseph to forgive “the transgression and sin of your brothers, for they did you wrong” (50:17).
Genesis 50:16-17
Their transgression and sin—the wrong they had done to Joseph
The famine years they endured while living in Canaan
Famine drove them to Egypt (Genesis 42:1), but the message asks forgiveness for the wrong done to Joseph (50:17).
The silver they had found in their sacks after their first trip
Joseph himself had the silver returned in their sacks (Genesis 42:35); it was not a wrong they were asking him to forgive.
Their neglect of Rachel’s grave on the road to Bethlehem
Rachel was buried on the way to Ephrath (Genesis 35:19); no failure over her burial is mentioned in 50:16–17.
Their stealing of silver from Pharaoh’s treasury
No theft from Pharaoh is mentioned; the plea concerns their wrong against Joseph (50:17).
How did Joseph respond emotionally when his brothers’ message about forgiveness was delivered to him?
When their message came to him, Joseph wept (50:17).
Genesis 50:17
He laughed and dismissed the message
Joseph did not laugh; he wept and then reassured them (50:17, 21).
He sent them away in silence
Joseph did not send them away; he spoke kindly to them and reassured them (50:21).
He called Pharaoh to judge them
Joseph did not call Pharaoh to judge them; he said, “Am I in the place of God?” (50:19).
He rebuked them publicly
Joseph did not rebuke them; he said, “Do not be afraid” and spoke kindly (50:19–21).
He wept
When Joseph’s brothers came and bowed before him in Egypt, what did they say?
His brothers came to him, bowed down before him, and said, “We are your slaves!” (50:18).
Genesis 50:18
“We are your brothers.”
They called themselves his slaves, not his brothers, as they bowed in fear (50:18).
“We have come for grain.”
Their grain-buying trip to Egypt was long past (Genesis 42:3); here they were afraid of his revenge (50:15, 18).
“The LORD has judged us.”
They did not say that; they said, “We are your slaves!” (50:18).
“We are your slaves!”
“Please send us to Canaan.”
They remained in Egypt, and Joseph promised to provide for them (50:21); they did not ask to be sent away.
What question did Joseph ask his brothers to show that final judgment belonged to God, not to him?
Joseph asked, “Am I in the place of God?” (50:19), declining to take God’s role as judge.
Genesis 50:19
“Shall I not repay you for what you did?”
Joseph said the opposite: “Do not be afraid” and he would provide for them (50:19–21).
“Who can stand before Pharaoh?”
Nothing in the chapter has Joseph ask this; his question concerns God’s place (50:19).
“Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?”
Abraham asked this of God in Genesis 18:25; Joseph’s question in 50:19 was different.
“Why did you fear me?”
Joseph told them not to be afraid (50:19); he does not ask why they feared.
“Am I in the place of God?”
In Joseph’s famous reply to his brothers, what did he say God had intended through the evil done against him?
Joseph said, “what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this—to preserve the lives of many people” (50:20).
Genesis 50:20
To make Joseph king over Egypt forever
Joseph served under Pharaoh and was greater only with regard to the throne (Genesis 41:40); making him king is not the purpose stated in 50:20.
To accomplish the saving of many lives
To punish Jacob for leaving Canaan
Joseph invited Jacob to Egypt (Genesis 45:9); God’s purpose in 50:20 was good, not punishment.
To end the covenant with Abraham
Joseph speaks of God bringing Israel to the land promised to Abraham (50:24), not ending the covenant.
To scatter Israel among the nations
Joseph trusts God to bring Israel up to Canaan (50:24); scattering Israel is not what 50:20 says God intended.
After reassuring his brothers in Egypt, whom did Joseph promise to provide for?
Joseph said, “I will provide for you and your little ones” (50:21).
Genesis 50:21
Them and their little ones
Only Benjamin and his sons
Joseph addressed all of his brothers, not Benjamin alone (50:21).
Pharaoh’s household
Joseph already ran Pharaoh’s household (Genesis 41:40); his pledge in 50:21 was to his brothers and their little ones.
The priests of Egypt
Joseph protected the priests’ own land allotment in the famine (Genesis 47:22), but his pledge in 50:21 was to his brothers’ families.
Only the oldest brothers
Joseph promised for “you and your little ones,” not for the oldest brothers only (50:21).
At the end of Genesis 50, how old was Joseph when he died in Egypt?
Joseph died at the age of 110 (50:26), the age already given for his life in 50:22.
Genesis 50:26
90 years
Sarah was ninety when God promised her a son (Genesis 17:17); that is not Joseph’s age at death.
99 years
Abraham was ninety-nine when he was circumcised (Genesis 17:24); Joseph died at 110 (50:26).
103 years
103 is not tied to Joseph; the chapter says he died at 110 (50:26).
120 years
120 is the age at which Moses died (Deuteronomy 34:7); Joseph died at 110 (50:26).
110 years
In the final family notes about Joseph, which descendants did he live to see to the third generation?
Joseph saw Ephraim’s sons to the third generation (50:23).
Genesis 50:23
Reuben’s children
Reuben was one of Joseph’s older brothers; the verse names Ephraim’s sons as those Joseph lived to see (50:23).
Benjamin’s children
Benjamin was Joseph’s brother; the verse names Ephraim’s sons (50:23).
Levi’s children
Levi was Joseph’s brother and the ancestor of the priestly tribe; 50:23 names Ephraim’s sons.
Ephraim’s children
Judah’s children
Judah was Joseph’s brother; the descendants named in 50:23 are Ephraim’s sons.
In the closing verses of Genesis, whose sons were brought up on Joseph’s knees?
The sons of Machir son of Manasseh were brought up on Joseph’s knees (50:23).
Genesis 50:23
The sons of Perez son of Judah
Perez was Judah’s son by Tamar (Genesis 38:29); 50:23 names Machir’s sons.
The sons of Machir son of Manasseh
The daughters of Dinah
Dinah was Jacob’s daughter by Leah (Genesis 34:1); 50:23 names the sons of Machir.
The sons of Zebulun
Zebulun was one of Joseph’s brothers (Genesis 30:20); the verse names the sons of Machir.
The household of Asher
Asher was one of Joseph’s brothers (Genesis 30:13); the verse names the sons of Machir.
As Joseph approached death in Egypt, what did he say God would surely do for Israel?
Joseph said that God would surely visit them and bring them up from Egypt to the promised land (50:24), and that God would surely attend to them (50:25).
Genesis 50:24
Abandon Egypt to famine
Joseph speaks of God bringing Israel up from Egypt (50:24), not of leaving Egypt to famine.
Surely attend to them and bring them up out of that land
Make them rulers over all Canaan immediately
Joseph speaks only of God bringing them up to the land promised on oath (50:24); he says nothing about ruling Canaan immediately.
Build Joseph a tomb in Goshen
Joseph asked for his bones to be carried up (50:25); he does not ask for a tomb in Goshen.
Send them back one tribe at a time
Joseph says God will bring them up from the land (50:24); he does not describe a tribe-by-tribe return.
According to Joseph’s final words, to what land would God bring Israel?
Joseph said God would bring them up to the land He promised on oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (50:24).
Genesis 50:24
The land He swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
The land of Moab east of the Jordan
Israel later camped in the plains of Moab before crossing the Jordan (Numbers 22:1), but Joseph named the land promised to the patriarchs (50:24).
The plains of Shinar
Shinar is where Babel was built (Genesis 11:2); the promise in 50:24 concerns the land sworn to the patriarchs.
The coastlands of the Philistines
God did not lead Israel out along the road through the land of the Philistines (Exodus 13:17); Joseph names the promised land (50:24).
The mountains of Seir
Mount Seir is where Esau settled (Genesis 36:8); the promise in 50:24 was the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
Before Joseph died, whom did he make swear concerning his remains?
Joseph made the sons of Israel take an oath about carrying up his bones (50:25).
Genesis 50:25
The physicians of Egypt
The physicians embalmed Joseph (50:26), but the oath about his bones was taken by the sons of Israel (50:25).
The elders of Pharaoh’s house
The elders of Pharaoh’s house went with Joseph to bury Jacob (50:7), but they are not the ones who swore about his bones.
The inhabitants of Canaan
The Canaanites only named the mourning place Abel-mizraim (50:11); they took no oath about Joseph’s bones.
The horsemen who buried Jacob
The horsemen accompanied Jacob’s funeral (50:9), but Joseph’s oath was taken by the sons of Israel (50:25).
The sons of Israel
What did Joseph make the sons of Israel promise to carry up from Egypt when God attended to them?
Joseph said, “you must carry my bones up from this place” (50:25); Moses did so when Israel left Egypt (Exodus 13:19).
Genesis 50:25
Jacob’s staff
Jacob leaned on his staff as he worshiped near death (Hebrews 11:21), but Joseph’s oath concerned his own bones (50:25).
The silver cup
Joseph’s silver cup was found in Benjamin’s sack (Genesis 44:12); it has no part in the oath of 50:25.
His bones
The embalming spices
Spices were used to embalm Jacob (50:2); the oath concerned Joseph’s own bones (50:25).
His signet ring
Pharaoh gave Joseph his signet ring when he made him ruler (Genesis 41:42); the oath was about Joseph’s bones (50:25).
After Joseph died in Egypt, what two things were done to his body?
They embalmed Joseph’s body and placed it in a coffin in Egypt (50:26).
Genesis 50:26
He was burned and his ashes were scattered in the Nile
Joseph’s body was embalmed (50:26), not burned; Egyptian burial practice is what the chapter records.
He was buried at once in Canaan without preparation
Joseph’s bones were carried to Canaan much later (Exodus 13:19; Joshua 24:32), not buried at once without preparation.
He was laid in Jacob’s tomb near Mamre
Jacob was buried in the cave near Mamre (50:13); Joseph’s body stayed in Egypt in a coffin (50:26).
He was wrapped in linen and left in Goshen
The text says he was embalmed and placed in a coffin in Egypt (50:26); it does not mention linen or Goshen.
He was embalmed and placed in a coffin in Egypt
2: In the opening of Exodus 1, to what land did the sons of Israel come with Jacob, each with his family?
Exodus opens, “These are the names of the sons of Israel who went to Egypt with Jacob, each with his family” (1:1).
Exodus 1:1
Canaan
Canaan is the land they left behind; Jacob and all his offspring went from Canaan down to Egypt (Genesis 46:6).
Egypt
Midian
Midian is where Moses later fled from Pharaoh (Exodus 2:15), not where Jacob’s family settled.
Moab
Israel reached the plains of Moab only at the end of the wilderness years (Numbers 22:1).
Edom
Edom was the land of Esau’s descendants around Mount Seir (Genesis 36:8), not Jacob’s destination.
In Exodus 1, the sons listed as coming to Egypt are the sons of which patriarch, also called Israel?
The “sons of Israel” in 1:1 are the sons of Jacob, the man God renamed Israel (Genesis 32:28).
Exodus 1:1
Isaac
Isaac was Jacob’s father; the twelve listed in 1:2–4 are Isaac’s grandsons.
Abraham
Abraham was Jacob’s grandfather; the sons named in 1:2–4 are Jacob’s.
Jacob
Joseph
Joseph was one of the sons himself, already in Egypt when the family came (1:5).
Esau
Esau was Jacob’s twin brother (Genesis 25:26); his descendants became Edom, not Israel.
At the start of Israel’s story in Egypt in Exodus 1, what is specifically said about Joseph?
Jacob’s descendants numbered seventy, “including Joseph, who was already in Egypt” (1:5).
Exodus 1:5
He had returned to Canaan
Joseph went back to Canaan only to bury his father, then returned to Egypt (Genesis 50:14).
He was already in Egypt
He ruled in Midian
Joseph ruled in Egypt, where Pharaoh set him over all the land (Genesis 41:41), never in Midian.
He was imprisoned in Babylon
Joseph was imprisoned in Egypt (Genesis 39:20); Babylonian exile came centuries later (2 Kings 25:11).
He had died in the wilderness
Joseph died in Egypt at 110 (Genesis 50:26), and Moses carried his bones out at the exodus (Exodus 13:19).
In Exodus 1, how many descendants of Jacob were in Egypt in all?
“The descendants of Jacob numbered seventy in all, including Joseph” (1:5; compare Genesis 46:27).
Exodus 1:5
Twelve is the number of Jacob’s sons listed in 1:2–5, not the total of his descendants.
Forty is the number of years Israel later wandered in the wilderness (Numbers 14:33).
A hundred and twenty was Moses’ age when he died (Deuteronomy 34:7).
About 600,000 men on foot left Egypt at the exodus (Exodus 12:37), centuries after the seventy arrived.
According to Exodus 1, what happened to Joseph, his brothers, and that whole generation?
“Now Joseph and all his brothers and all that generation died” (1:6).
Exodus 1:6
They returned to Canaan
That generation died in Egypt; only Joseph’s bones were later carried back and buried at Shechem (Joshua 24:32).
They became rulers in Egypt
Joseph had ruled under Pharaoh (Genesis 41:41), but 1:6 records the death of that whole generation.
They were taken captive
No captivity is mentioned; the oppression began later under a new king who did not know Joseph (1:8–11).
They all died
They crossed the Red Sea
The Red Sea crossing came generations later under Moses (Exodus 14:21–22).
After that generation died, how are the Israelites described in Exodus 1?
“The Israelites were fruitful and increased rapidly; they multiplied and became exceedingly numerous” (1:7).
Exodus 1:7
They became weak and few
The opposite: they became so numerous that “the land was filled with them” (1:7).
They were fruitful and multiplied greatly
They scattered into the desert
They stayed in Egypt and filled the land (1:7); the desert journey began only after the exodus (Exodus 13:18).
They forgot their families
The chapter opens by listing each son “with his family” (1:1) and stresses growth, not lost family ties.
They built the temple
Solomon built the temple 480 years after Israel came out of Egypt (1 Kings 6:1).
In Exodus 1, what was the result of Israel’s growth in Egypt?
Israel multiplied and became exceedingly numerous, “so that the land was filled with them” (1:7).
Exodus 1:7
The land was filled with them
They all moved to Goshen alone
Goshen was where Jacob’s family first settled (Genesis 47:6, 27), but 1:7 says the land was filled with them.
Egypt drove them out at once
Egypt urged Israel out only after the tenth plague (Exodus 12:33); here the new king kept them as forced labor.
They settled in Jerusalem
Jerusalem became Israel’s city only when David captured Zion (2 Samuel 5:7).
The Nile dried up
The Nile did not dry up; in the first plague its water was turned to blood (Exodus 7:20).
In Exodus 1, why did the Egyptian king view the Israelites as a danger?
The king feared that “if a war breaks out, they may join our enemies, fight against us, and leave the country” (1:10).
Exodus 1:9-10
He feared they would steal the temple treasures
There was no temple yet; Solomon built the first one 480 years after the exodus (1 Kings 6:1).
He feared they would join Egypt’s enemies in war
He feared they would stop the Nile flooding
The king never mentions the Nile’s flooding; his fear was their numbers and possible alliance with enemies (1:9–10).
He feared they would destroy the pyramids
The Bible never mentions pyramids; the Israelites were forced to build the store cities Pithom and Rameses (1:11).
He feared they would crown Joseph again
Joseph and his generation had died (1:6), and the new king “did not know Joseph” (1:8).
To control the Israelites in Exodus 1, what officials did the Egyptians appoint over them?
“The Egyptians appointed taskmasters over the Israelites to oppress them with forced labor” (1:11).
Exodus 1:11
Prophets
No prophets were appointed; Israel’s great prophet Moses was not yet born (Exodus 2:2).
Priests
Egypt had priests, such as Potiphera priest of On (Genesis 41:45), but 1:11 says taskmasters were set over Israel.
Taskmasters
Judges
Judges over Israel came later, when Moses appointed leaders of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens (Exodus 18:25).
Shepherds
Shepherds were “detestable to the Egyptians” (Genesis 46:34); Egypt set taskmasters over Israel instead.
In Exodus 1, which store cities did the Israelites build for Pharaoh under forced labor?
Under forced labor the Israelites “built Pithom and Rameses as store cities for Pharaoh” (1:11).
Exodus 1:11
Jericho and Ai
Jericho and Ai were Canaanite cities Joshua later conquered (Joshua 6–8).
Pithom and Rameses
Sodom and Gomorrah
Sodom and Gomorrah had been destroyed by fire in Abraham’s day (Genesis 19:24).
Hebron and Beersheba
Hebron and Beersheba were places where the patriarchs lived in Canaan (Genesis 21:31; 23:2).
Tyre and Sidon
Tyre and Sidon were Phoenician cities, later named by Jesus (Matthew 11:21), not Egyptian store cities.
According to Exodus 1, what happened as the Israelites were increasingly oppressed?
“The more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and flourished” (1:12).
Exodus 1:12
They stopped having children
The opposite: oppression only increased their numbers (1:12), and later even more so (1:20).
They fled to Midian
Only Moses fled to Midian, years later, after killing an Egyptian (Exodus 2:15).
They multiplied and spread out even more
They chose a king
Israel first asked for a king in Samuel’s day (1 Samuel 8:5).
They blended into Egypt completely
They remained a distinct people whom the Egyptians “came to dread” (1:12).
How did the Egyptians feel about the Israelites as their numbers kept increasing in Exodus 1?
As Israel multiplied under oppression, “the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites” (1:12).
Exodus 1:12
They admired them
The Egyptians dreaded rather than admired them, and worked them ruthlessly (1:12–13).
They ignored them
Far from ignoring them, Egypt set taskmasters over them and imposed harsh labor (1:11–14).
They came to dread them
They worshiped them
No worship is involved; Egypt’s response was dread and oppression (1:12–14).
They married into every family
Rather than intermarrying, Egypt tried to kill every Hebrew son (1:16, 22).
In Exodus 1, how did the Egyptians make the Israelites work?
“They worked the Israelites ruthlessly” and made their lives bitter with hard labor (1:13–14).
Exodus 1:13
Cheerfully
The labor made their lives bitter, and every service imposed was harsh (1:14).
Ruthlessly
Voluntarily
The work was forced labor under taskmasters (1:11), not voluntary.
Secretly
The oppression was open state policy carried out by appointed taskmasters (1:11).
Briefly
The bondage was no brief episode; Israel’s stay in Egypt lasted 430 years (Exodus 12:40).
In the account of Israel’s slavery in Exodus 1, which kinds of labor embittered their lives?
The Egyptians made their lives bitter “with hard labor in brick and mortar, and with all kinds of work in the fields” (1:14).
Exodus 1:14
Fishing, weaving, and metalwork
Skilled metalwork appears later in building the tabernacle (Exodus 31:4); 1:14 names brick, mortar, and fieldwork.
Mortar, brickwork, and every kind of field labor
Herding camels and trading spices
Camels carrying spices belong to the Ishmaelite caravan that took Joseph to Egypt (Genesis 37:25).

The unit was an omer per person, not a homer per family; an omer is only a tenth of an ephah (16:16, 16:36).
An omer apiece for each person in the tent
Two ephahs for each household
An ephah is ten times an omer (16:36), and the command was per person, not per household.
One shekel’s worth per man
No shekel measure is used; manna was measured by the omer (16:16).
A basket for each tribe
The portion was by person, not by tribe (16:16).
When the Israelites measured their manna by omers in Exodus 16, what was true?
Exodus 16:18 says “he who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall.”
Exodus 16:18
The one who gathered much had no excess, and the one who gathered little had no shortfall
The elders received a double portion while the rest of the people went hungry
No one received a special double portion at this stage; everyone gathered as much as he needed (16:18).
The firstborn of every family gathered more than enough while others had too little
The firstborn are not singled out; each person gathered what he needed (16:18).
The Levites alone had no shortfall, while the other tribes went without
The Levites were not the only ones with enough; “Each one gathered as much as he needed to eat” (16:18).
Everyone had leftovers to last for a week, so no one gathered again
Leftovers spoiled when kept overnight (16:19–20), so no one had a week’s supply.
In Exodus 16, what command did Moses give about the manna at the end of the day?
Moses said, “No one may keep any of it until morning” (16:19).
Exodus 16:19
Burn it before sunset
Burning the manna is not commanded; the order was simply not to keep any until morning (16:19).
Store all of it for a month
Storing a month’s supply was forbidden; kept manna spoiled (16:19–20).
Sell the extra to neighboring tribes
Selling manna to other tribes is not mentioned; each person gathered what he needed (16:18).
Let no one keep any of it until morning
Mix it with oil before eating
Mixing it with oil is not commanded here; later the people prepared it by grinding and baking or boiling (Numbers 11:8).
What happened in Exodus 16 when some Israelites kept manna until morning against Moses’s command?
Those who kept it “did not listen to Moses; some people left part of it until morning, and it became infested with maggots and began to smell” (16:20).
Exodus 16:20
It turned into quail
Manna did not turn into quail; the quail came separately on the first evening (16:13).
It became sweet like honey
The leftover manna spoiled; the sweetness belongs to its taste when fresh, like wafers made with honey (16:31).
It bred worms and smelled foul
It doubled in size
The kept manna did not grow; it rotted (16:20).
It hardened into stones
Hardening into stones is not mentioned; the kept manna became infested and smelly (16:20).
According to the daily pattern in Exodus 16, what happened to the manna when the sun grew hot?
Exodus 16:21 says “when the sun grew hot, it melted away.”
Exodus 16:21
It multiplied
Heat did not multiply the manna; it melted what was left on the ground (16:21).
It blew into the sea
The text does not say the manna blew into the sea; it melted away (16:21).
It melted away
It turned bitter
The manna did not turn bitter; it tasted like wafers made with honey (16:31).
It sank into the sand
The manna melted away rather than sinking into the sand (16:21).
On the sixth day in Exodus 16, how much manna did the people gather compared with other days?
On the sixth day “they gathered twice as much food—two omers per person” (16:22).
Exodus 16:22
Half as much
The amount was doubled, not halved (16:22).
The same amount
The LORD had said the sixth-day amount would be twice as much as on other days (16:5).
Twice as much
None at all
They did gather on the sixth day, and twice as much (16:22).
Seven times as much
The increase was double, not sevenfold (16:5, 16:22).
In the sixth-day gathering account of Exodus 16, who came and reported the double amount to Moses?
“All the leaders of the congregation came and reported this to Moses” (16:22).
Exodus 16:22
The sons of Aaron who served as priests
Priests do not report the amount here; the leaders of the congregation did (16:22).
The firstborn sons of every family
The firstborn sons are not mentioned in this report (16:22).
The leaders of the congregation
Traders passing through from Egypt
Egyptian traders are not part of the camp; the Israelite leaders reported (16:22).
The women of Midian who lived nearby
The women of Midian are not in this scene; Israel’s leaders came to Moses (16:22).
In Exodus 16, what did Moses say the next day would be after the sixth-day gathering?
Moses said, “Tomorrow is to be a day of complete rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD” (16:23).
Exodus 16:23
A day of battle against the Amalekites
No battle is announced; the next day was a Sabbath of rest (16:23).
A feast of booths in honor of the harvest
The Feast of Booths is a later festival (Deuteronomy 16:13), not the next day’s purpose here.
A day of complete rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD
A day of mourning for those who had died
The next day was a holy day of rest, not mourning (16:23).
A day of circumcision for the sons born in the desert
Circumcision is not mentioned in this chapter; the day was a Sabbath (16:23).
What preparation did Moses command for the Sabbath in Exodus 16?
Moses said, “bake what you want to bake, and boil what you want to boil. Then set aside whatever remains and keep it until morning” (16:23).
Exodus 16:23
Fast from all food until the evening of the seventh day
No fast is commanded here; the people were to cook what they wanted and set aside the rest (16:23).
Bake what you want to bake and boil what you want to boil, then set aside the rest
Gather wood and light large fires throughout the whole day
Lighting fires all day is not the instruction; on the Sabbath itself they were to rest (16:23, 16:29).
Slaughter a lamb at sunrise and eat it before the others
No lamb is to be slaughtered here; the instructions concern baking and boiling the manna (16:23).
Go out early and hunt birds to store for the next day
On the seventh day there was nothing in the field to gather (16:25–26), and hunting was not commanded.
What happened to the manna that was set aside overnight for the Sabbath in Exodus 16?
Exodus 16:24 says the manna set aside “did not smell or contain any maggots.”
Exodus 16:24
It bred worms and began to smell
Bred worms describes the manna kept on other days against Moses’ command (16:20).
It disappeared before the morning came
It did not vanish; the manna set aside for the Sabbath stayed good (16:24).
It did not smell foul or contain maggots
It turned red and hard as stone
The text does not say it changed color; it stayed fresh (16:24).
It became bitter water by morning
Water is not mentioned; the manna kept without spoiling (16:24).
When some people still went out to gather manna on the seventh day in Exodus 16, what did they find?
“Yet on the seventh day some of the people went out to gather, but they did not find anything” (16:27).
Exodus 16:27
A double portion
The double portion came on the sixth day, not the seventh (16:22, 16:26).
Quail eggs
Quail came on the first evening (16:13), not on the seventh day.
Nothing
Bitter herbs
Bitter herbs are not mentioned; they found nothing (16:27).
Water from a rock
Water from a rock is a separate event at Rephidim (Exodus 17:6), not this story.
In the LORD’s Sabbath instruction in Exodus 16, what was each person told to do on the seventh day?
The LORD said, “On the seventh day, everyone must stay where he is; no one may leave his place” (16:29).
Exodus 16:29
Travel to Sinai
The command was to stay put, not to travel to Sinai (16:29).
Remain in his place
Offer incense at dawn
No incense is mentioned in these Sabbath instructions (16:29).
Cross the sea again
The crossing of the sea was already behind them (Exodus 14); the Sabbath instruction was to stay in place (16:29).
Count the tribes
Counting the tribes comes later in Numbers 1 and is not part of the Sabbath command.
How does Exodus 16 summarize the people’s response on the seventh day after the Sabbath instructions?
Exodus 16:30 says simply, “the people rested on the seventh day.”
Exodus 16:30
They marched toward Canaan
They did not march that day; they rested (16:30), and the march to Canaan was far off (16:35).
They built an altar
Building an altar is not mentioned; they rested (16:30).
They rested
They held a census
A census is not taken here; it is a later event (Numbers 1).
They returned to Elim
They were in the Desert of Sin, having left Elim before this (16:1), and they stayed put on the Sabbath (16:29–30).
In Exodus 16, what was the appearance of manna as described by the house of Israel?
The house of Israel called the bread manna, and “It was white like coriander seed” (16:31).
Exodus 16:31
Red like pomegranate seeds
The manna was not red; it was white like coriander seed (16:31).
White like coriander seed
Green like hyssop
It was not green; it was white (16:31).
Black like soot
It was not black like soot; it was white like coriander seed (16:31).
Blue like sapphire
Sapphire blue is not the color given; it was white (16:31).
According to Exodus 16, what did manna taste like?
Manna “tasted like wafers made with honey” (16:31).
Exodus 16:31
Bitter herbs
Bitter herbs are a Passover food (Exodus 12:8); manna tasted like wafers made with honey (16:31).
Roasted lamb
Roasted lamb is not how manna is described; its taste was like wafers made with honey (16:31).
Wafers made with honey
Salted fish
Salted fish is not mentioned in this chapter; manna tasted like wafers with honey (16:31).
Fresh figs
Fresh figs are not mentioned; manna tasted like wafers with honey (16:31).
In the concluding note of Exodus 16, for how long did the Israelites eat manna?
“The Israelites ate manna forty years” (16:35).
Exodus 16:35
Seven days
Seven days is the Sabbath week pattern (16:26), not how long manna lasted.
Forty days
Forty days is too short; the manna continued for forty years (16:35).
One year
One year is too short; they ate manna until they reached Canaan’s border (16:35).
Forty years
Until Moses died
They ate it until they reached Canaan’s border (16:35), and it stopped after they ate the produce of the land (Joshua 5:12).
According to Exodus 16, manna continued until the Israelites reached the border of which land?
Exodus 16:35 says “they ate manna until they reached the border of Canaan.”
Exodus 16:35
Edom
Edom lay on Israel’s route but is not named as the place where manna ended (16:35).
Moab
Israel camped in the plains of Moab late in the wilderness journey (Numbers 22:1), but the chapter names Canaan.
Philistia
Philistia is not named in this verse, which names Canaan (16:35).
Midian
Midian is not named in this verse, which names Canaan (16:35).
Canaan

Exodus 16:32-33
A handful
A handful is not the measure given; Moses specified an omer (16:32–33).
One basket
A basket is not the measure given; it was an omer in a jar (16:33).
An omer
Two ephahs
Two ephahs would be twenty times too much; the measure was an omer (16:32–33, 16:36).
A shekel’s weight
A shekel measures weight in silver or gold; the manna was to be preserved by the omer (16:32).
When Moses told Aaron to preserve manna in Exodus 16, what kind of container was he to use?
Moses told Aaron, “Take a jar and fill it with an omer of manna” (16:33).
Exodus 16:33
A wineskin
A wineskin is not mentioned; Aaron was to use a jar (16:33).
A bronze bowl
A bronze bowl is not mentioned; it was a jar (16:33).
A wooden chest
A wooden chest is not mentioned; it was a jar (16:33).
A jar
A clay lamp
A clay lamp is not a storage jar; the command was to use a jar (16:33).
According to the preservation command in Exodus 16, where did Aaron place the jar of manna?
“Aaron placed it in front of the Testimony, to be preserved just as the LORD had commanded Moses” (16:34).
Exodus 16:34
Before the Testimony
In Pharaoh’s storehouse
Pharaoh’s storehouse was in Egypt, which Israel had left (16:32).
Beside the bronze serpent
The bronze snake was made later, in Numbers 21:9.
At the spring of Marah
Marah was an earlier stop with bitter water (Exodus 15:23).
On Mount Carmel
The jar was placed before the Testimony (16:34), not on Mount Carmel.
In Exodus 16, why did the LORD say He would rain bread from heaven for Israel each day?
The LORD said, “In this way I will test whether or not they will follow My instructions” (16:4).
Exodus 16:4
To teach them how to farm the desert soil
Teaching farming is not the purpose; the bread was a daily provision and test (16:4).
To test whether they would follow His instructions
To make the priests wealthy among the tribes
The manna was for all the people, not for enriching the priests (16:4, 16:16).
To replace the Passover meal for all time
The Passover was not replaced; it was a remembrance of the exodus (Exodus 12:14).
To prepare the men for the coming battles
Preparing for battle is not stated as the reason; the purpose was a test of obedience (16:4).
As Aaron spoke to the whole congregation in Exodus 16, what appeared in the cloud when they looked toward the wilderness?
“As Aaron was speaking to the whole congregation of Israel, they looked toward the desert, and there in a cloud the glory of the LORD appeared” (16:10).
Exodus 16:10
A rainbow
The rainbow was the sign of God’s covenant with Noah (Genesis 9:13).
A pillar of fire only
The pillar of fire is a different guiding sign (Exodus 13:21); here the glory of the LORD appeared in the cloud (16:10).
The glory of the LORD
The ark of the covenant
The ark of the covenant had not yet been built (Exodus 25:10–22).
Twelve stars
Twelve stars are not mentioned; Joseph’s dream had eleven stars (Genesis 37:9).
In Moses’s rebuke in Exodus 16, against whom did he say the Israelites were really grumbling?
Moses said, “Your grumblings are not against us but against the LORD” (16:8).
Exodus 16:8
Against Joshua
Joshua is not the target of the grumbling; Moses said it was against the LORD (16:8).
Against the LORD
Against the elders
The elders are not named; Moses said the complaints were against the LORD (16:8).
Against Aaron alone
The grumbling was against Moses and Aaron (16:2), but Moses said it was ultimately against the LORD (16:8).
Against the tribes of Judah and Levi
Judah and Levi are not named; the complaint was against the LORD (16:8).
What future purpose did Moses give in Exodus 16 for preserving a measure of manna?
Moses said to keep an omer “so that they may see the bread I fed you in the wilderness when I brought you out of the land of Egypt” (16:32).
Exodus 16:32
So priests could burn it as a fragrant incense offering each day
Burning the manna as incense is not its purpose; it was preserved as a memorial (16:32–33).
So future kings could tax it for the support of the army
Taxation is not mentioned; the jar was a reminder of God’s provision (16:32).
So future generations could see the bread the LORD fed Israel in the wilderness
So it could be planted in Canaan to grow a new crop
Planting is not mentioned; the manna was preserved as a witness for future generations (16:32–33).
So it could be exchanged for silver among the nations
Exchanging the manna for silver is not mentioned; it was kept before the LORD (16:33).
On what point in time did Israel arrive at the Desert of Sin in the account of Exodus 16?
Exodus 16:1 says it was “the fifteenth day of the second month after they had left the land of Egypt.”
Exodus 16:1
The first day of the first month after leaving Egypt
The first day of the first month is not the date given; it was the fifteenth day of the second month (16:1).
The tenth day of the seventh month

The fifteenth day of the second month after departing from Egypt
The third day after crossing the Jordan
Crossing the Jordan comes after the wilderness years (Joshua 3), long after this event.
The fortieth day after Passover
No count of days from the Passover is given; the date is the fifteenth day of the second month (16:1).
In the travel notice at the start of Exodus 16, the Desert of Sin is said to be between which two places?

Exodus 16:1
Kadesh and Paran
Kadesh and Paran appear later in Israel’s journey (Numbers 13:26).
Elim and Sinai
Goshen and Succoth
Goshen and Succoth are in Egypt, on the way out (Exodus 12:37).
Jericho and Ai
Jericho and Ai are in Canaan, which Israel had not yet entered.
Horeb and Rephidim
Horeb and Rephidim come after the Desert of Sin (Exodus 17:1).
In their complaint recorded in Exodus 16, what did the Israelites say they had back in Egypt?
The people said, “There we sat by pots of meat and ate our fill of bread” (16:3).
Exodus 16:3
Vineyards and olive groves
Vineyards and olive groves are not named in this complaint; they spoke of pots of meat and bread (16:3).
Pots of meat and bread to the full
Wells of water and honey cakes
Honey cakes and wells are not named; the complaint was about meat and bread (16:3).
Priestly garments and incense
Priestly garments and incense are not mentioned in the complaint (16:3).
Fish and cucumbers beside the Nile
Fish and cucumbers are named in a later complaint (Numbers 11:5), not in this one.
After the dew evaporated in Exodus 16, how is the manna-like substance on the ground described?

Large stones like hail

Thick cakes like clay

Thin flakes like frost on the ground
Red dust like blood

Green leaves like coriander plants

In the detailed sixth-day report of Exodus 16, how much manna did they gather for each person?

Exodus 16:22
Half an omer

One omer

Two omers
Five omers
