Bezalel was the craftsman called to build the tabernacle (Exodus 31:2–3), not its priest.
Eleazar alone
Eleazar was among Aaron’s sons, who were anointed along with the others (40:14–15), not alone.
In the sanctuary layout described in Exodus 40, what was placed between the Tent of Meeting and the altar and filled with water?
40:7 says to place the basin between the Tent of Meeting and the altar and put water in it.
Exodus 40:7
The lampstand
The lampstand was set on the south side of the tabernacle, opposite the table (40:24).
The basin
The mercy seat
The mercy seat was set atop the ark (40:20).
The bronze serpent
The bronze serpent was not part of the tabernacle’s layout (Numbers 21:9).
The table
The table stood on the north side of the tabernacle, outside the veil (40:22).
In the tabernacle setup account of Exodus 40, what did Moses, Aaron, and Aaron’s sons wash at the basin?
From the basin Moses, Aaron, and his sons washed their hands and feet (40:31).
Exodus 40:31-32
Their faces and hair
Faces and hair are not mentioned; the washing was of hands and feet (40:31).
Their hands only
Hands alone is incomplete; they washed their feet as well (40:31).
Their feet only
Feet alone is incomplete; they washed their hands as well (40:31).
Their hands and feet
Their garments
Aaron’s sons were clothed in tunics (40:14), but the basin was for washing hands and feet (40:31).
At the entrance to the tabernacle in Exodus 40, which offerings did Moses present on the altar of burnt offering?
Moses placed the altar of burnt offering near the entrance and offered on it the burnt offering and the grain offering (40:29).
Exodus 40:29
Sin offering and drink offering
Sin offering and drink offering are not named in 40:29, which names the burnt and grain offerings.
Peace offering and vow offering
Peace offering and vow offering are not named in 40:29.
Burnt offering and grain offering
Incense offering and wave offering
Incense was burned on the gold altar inside the Tent (40:26–27), not on the altar of burnt offering.
Firstfruits and tithe
Firstfruits and tithe are not mentioned in 40:29, which names the burnt and grain offerings.
According to Exodus 40, when was the tabernacle actually set up?
40:17 says the tabernacle was set up on the first day of the first month of the second year.
Exodus 40:17
On the first day of the seventh month of the first year
The tabernacle was set up in the first month of the second year, not the seventh month of the first year (40:17).
On the tenth day of the first month of the second year
The tenth day of the first month was when Israel was to select Passover lambs (Exodus 12:3); the tabernacle went up on the first day (40:17).
On the first day of the first month of the second year
On the fifteenth day of the second month of the third year
Israel left Sinai on the twentieth day of the second month of the second year (Numbers 10:11), after the tabernacle was already up.
On the day after Passover in Canaan
The tabernacle was set up at Sinai, long before Israel reached Canaan (40:17).
In Exodus 40, before the ark was placed inside the tabernacle, what did Moses put into the ark?
Moses took the Testimony and placed it in the ark (40:20).
Exodus 40:20
Manna
Exodus 40:20 puts only the Testimony in the ark; Aaron placed the manna in front of the Testimony (Exodus 16:34).
Aaron’s rod
Aaron’s staff was put back in front of the Testimony (Numbers 17:10); 40:20 puts only the Testimony in the ark.
The Testimony
The book of the Law
The Book of the Law was placed beside the ark (Deuteronomy 31:26), not in it.
Incense
Incense was burned on the gold altar (40:27), not placed in the ark.
When the ark of the Testimony was brought into the tabernacle in Exodus 40, what screened it off?
Moses put up the veil for the screen and shielded off the ark of the Testimony (40:21).
Exodus 40:21
The outer covering of goats’ hair
The covering was put over the tent (40:19); the veil, not the covering, screened off the ark.
The curtain at the courtyard gate
That curtain hung at the entrance to the courtyard (40:33), not in front of the ark.
The veil
The bronze altar
The altar of burnt offering stood near the entrance to the tabernacle (40:29), far from the ark.
The pillar of cloud
The cloud covered the Tent only after all the work was finished (40:34).
In the arrangement of the Tent of Meeting in Exodus 40, where did Moses place the table?
Moses placed the table in the Tent of Meeting on the north side of the tabernacle, outside the veil (40:22).
Exodus 40:22-23
On the north side of the tabernacle, outside the veil
On the south side of the tabernacle, behind the veil
The lampstand, not the table, was set on the south side (40:24), and the table was outside the veil.
In the courtyard beside the altar of burnt offering
The altar of burnt offering stood near the entrance (40:29); the table was inside the Tent of Meeting (40:22).
On the west side of the tent, right next to the ark
The ark was behind the veil (40:21); the table stood outside it, on the north side (40:22).
At the entrance to the courtyard, near the curtain
The curtain at the courtyard entrance was hung later (40:33); the table was set inside the Tent (40:22).
As Moses arranged the furnishings in Exodus 40, where was the gold altar placed, and what was burned on it?
Moses placed the gold altar in the Tent of Meeting in front of the veil and burned fragrant incense on it (40:26–27).
Exodus 40:26-27
In the courtyard, and burnt offerings
Burnt offerings were made on the altar of burnt offering near the entrance (40:29), not on the gold altar in the Tent.
Behind the veil, and grain offerings
The gold altar stood in front of the veil, not behind it (40:26), and incense, not grain offerings, was burned on it (40:27).
In front of the veil, and fragrant incense
By the basin, and drink offerings
The basin stood between the Tent and the altar of burnt offering and held water for washing (40:30), not drink offerings.
Outside the camp, and sin offerings
The gold altar stood inside the Tent of Meeting (40:26), not outside the camp.
In the LORD’s instructions about Aaron’s sons in Exodus 40, what did their anointing qualify them for?
The LORD said their anointing would qualify Aaron’s sons for a permanent priesthood throughout their generations (40:15).
Exodus 40:15
Command of Israel’s armies in every war they fought
Joshua, not Aaron’s sons, was chosen to lead Israel’s men against Amalek (Exodus 17:9).
Kingship over the tribes of Israel for all time
Kingship was promised to Judah (Genesis 49:10), not to the priestly line of Aaron.
A permanent priesthood throughout their generations
Service as judges in the gates of every Israelite town
Judges and officials were appointed in each town (Deuteronomy 16:18); the anointing in 40:15 was for priesthood.
Sole guardianship of the ark on every journey of Israel
Carrying the holy objects fell to the Kohathites (Numbers 4:15), and the anointing in 40:15 was for priesthood.
In Exodus 40, which item was anointed with all its utensils and consecrated so that it would be “most holy”?
The LORD told Moses to anoint the altar of burnt offering and all its utensils and consecrate it so that it would be most holy (40:10).
Exodus 40:10
The lampstand
The lampstand was set up with its lamps (40:4, 40:25), but it is not called most holy in this chapter.
The basin
The basin and its stand were anointed and consecrated (40:11), but only the altar is called most holy.
The ark of the Testimony
The ark was screened off by the veil (40:21); the words “most holy” in 40:10 are about the altar of burnt offering.
The altar of burnt offering
The table of the bread
The table was brought in and set out (40:4, 40:22–23), but only the altar of burnt offering is called most holy.
At the close of Moses’ work in Exodus 40, what two things immediately marked the LORD’s presence at the sanctuary?
40:34 says the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle.
Exodus 40:34
Thunder and lightning shook the courtyard while all the people trembled
Thunder and lightning marked God’s arrival at Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:16), not the completion of the tabernacle.
The waters of the Jordan parted and the priests carried the ark across
The Jordan parted in the days of Joshua (Joshua 3:17), long after the tabernacle was set up.
The cloud covered the Tent of Meeting and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle
Manna fell inside the holy place and covered the floor of the Tent
Manna fell on the camp’s ground each morning (Exodus 16:14), not inside the holy place.
Fire from heaven consumed the basin and the lampstand before the people
Fire from the LORD consumed the offerings at a later event, Aaron’s first sacrifices (Leviticus 9:24), not the basin or lampstand.
In the final scene of Exodus 40, why could Moses not enter the Tent of Meeting?
Moses was unable to enter the Tent of Meeting because the cloud had settled on it and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle (40:35).
Exodus 40:35
Aaron had not yet arrived to open the entrance of the tent for him
Aaron was already present, washing with Moses at the basin (40:31).
The people were offering sacrifices there and had crowded the entrance
Moses himself had offered the burnt and grain offerings (40:29); no crowd of worshipers is mentioned.
The cloud had settled on it, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle
The veil had been torn and the sanctuary was no longer holy
The veil had been hung to screen the ark (40:21); nothing says it was torn.
The ark had been carried away and the tent stood empty
The ark had been brought in and placed in the tabernacle (40:21), not taken away.
During Israel’s wilderness journey as described at the end of Exodus 40, when would the Israelites set out?
Whenever the cloud was lifted from above the tabernacle, the Israelites set out on their journey (40:36).
Exodus 40:36
Whenever Moses blew the silver trumpets
Silver trumpets were sounded by Aaron’s sons, the priests (Numbers 10:8), but 40:36 makes the lifting of the cloud the signal to set out.
Whenever Aaron offered incense
Offering incense is never given as a signal to move; the cloud lifting was (40:36).
Whenever the cloud was lifted from above the tabernacle
Whenever the manna stopped
The manna stopped only after Israel ate the produce of Canaan (Joshua 5:12).
Whenever the moon was new
The new moon is not a signal for departure; the cloud decided when Israel moved (40:36–37).
In Exodus 40, what did the Israelites do if the cloud was not lifted from above the tabernacle?
If the cloud was not lifted, they would not set out until the day it was taken up (40:37).
Exodus 40:37
They set out anyway, trusting the sound of the trumpets
Israel did not march ahead on its own; it waited for the cloud to lift (40:37).
They fasted for seven days and then broke camp
No seven-day fast is mentioned; they simply stayed put until the cloud was taken up (40:37).
They turned back toward Egypt until the cloud lifted
Israel did not turn back to Egypt; they remained in camp until the cloud lifted (40:37).
They did not set out until the day it was taken up
They took down only the altar and stayed in camp
Nothing is said of dismantling the altar; they stayed in camp until the cloud was taken up (40:37).
At night in Exodus 40, what was seen in the cloud over the tabernacle in the sight of all the house of Israel?
40:38 says the cloud of the LORD was over the tabernacle by day, and fire was in the cloud by night, in the sight of all Israel.
Exodus 40:38
Lightning only
No lightning is described; the sign was fire in the cloud (40:38).
Smoke from the altar
Smoke from the altar is not mentioned; the fire was in the cloud itself (40:38).
Fire in the cloud
The sun’s reflection
The sun’s reflection is not mentioned; at night there was fire in the cloud (40:38).
A rainbow
The rainbow was the sign of God’s covenant with Noah (Genesis 9:13), not what Israel saw over the tabernacle.
As Moses physically assembled the tabernacle in Exodus 40, which sequence of construction is specifically given?
40:18 says Moses laid its bases, positioned its frames, inserted its crossbars, and set up its posts.
Exodus 40:18
Set up its posts, inserted its crossbars, positioned its frames, laid its bases
These are the right items in reverse order; 40:18 begins with the bases and ends with the posts.
Laid its bases, positioned its frames, inserted its crossbars, and set up its posts
Hung the veil, lit the lamps, burned incense, and washed at the basin
Those actions (the veil, lamps, incense, washing) come later in the chapter (40:21–32), after the framework was up.
Spread the covering, anointed Aaron, placed the ark, and raised the altar
Spreading the covering came after the frame was up (40:19), and anointing Aaron is a separate step (40:12–15).
Positioned its frames, laid its bases, hung the curtain, and set the table
The curtain and the table came later (40:22, 40:28); the bases were laid before the frames (40:18).
In the final assembly of the sanctuary in Exodus 40, what did Moses do with the ark before bringing it into the tabernacle?
Moses placed the Testimony in the ark, attached the poles to it, and set the mercy seat atop it (40:20).
Exodus 40:20
Filled it with manna, set Aaron’s rod inside it, and covered it with scarlet cloth
Exodus 40:20 mentions only the Testimony in the ark; manna and Aaron’s staff were kept in front of the Testimony (Exodus 16:34; Numbers 17:10).
Placed the Testimony in it, attached the poles to it, and set the mercy seat above it
Anointed it with blood, removed the poles, and set it beside the veil
Moses attached the poles to the ark (40:20), not removed them, and the ark was set behind the veil (40:21).
Carried it into the courtyard, lit lamps before it, and burned incense over it
The ark was brought into the tabernacle (40:21), not the courtyard, and incense was burned on the gold altar (40:27).
Placed the lampstand inside it, covered it with gold, and set it by the altar
The lampstand was set opposite the table (40:24), not placed inside the ark.
3: In the opening of Leviticus 1, from where did the LORD call to Moses to give Israel instructions about offerings?
“The LORD called to Moses and spoke to him from the Tent of Meeting” (1:1).
Leviticus 1:1
Mount Horeb
At Horeb God called Moses from the burning bush (Exodus 3:1–4), before the Tent existed.
The Tent of Meeting
The Ark of the Covenant
God promised to meet Moses above the mercy seat over the ark (Exodus 25:22), but 1:1 names the Tent of Meeting.
The wilderness of Paran
Israel reached the Wilderness of Paran only after leaving Sinai (Numbers 10:12).
The east gate of the camp
No gate is mentioned; the LORD spoke from the Tent of Meeting (1:1).
According to Leviticus 1, if a burnt offering was brought from the herd, what condition and sex was required?
A burnt offering from the herd had to be “an unblemished male” (1:3).
Leviticus 1:3
A female without blemish
A female from the herd was allowed for a peace offering (Leviticus 3:1), but the burnt offering had to be male.
A male without blemish
Any firstborn calf
Firstborn males belonged to the LORD (Exodus 13:2), but 1:3 requires simply an unblemished male.
A male with a broken horn
A defective animal would not be accepted (Leviticus 22:20); the offering had to be unblemished.
A pair of clean oxen
The worshiper brought a single unblemished male from the herd (1:3), not a pair.
According to Leviticus 1:3, where was a worshiper to bring a burnt offering from the herd for its acceptance before the LORD?
He was to “bring it to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting for its acceptance before the LORD” (1:3).
Leviticus 1:3
At the entrance to the Tent of Meeting
On the banks of the Jordan River
The Jordan is not in view; Israel was at Sinai, and offerings were brought to the Tent of Meeting (1:3).
On the summit of Mount Gerizim
Mount Gerizim was where the blessing would later be proclaimed in Canaan (Deuteronomy 11:29).
Inside the house of the high priest
No priest’s house is mentioned; the animal was presented at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting (1:3).
Outside the camp, beyond the gate
Outside the camp is where the remains of a sin offering bull were burned (Leviticus 4:12).
In Leviticus chapter 1, what was the purpose of laying a hand on the head of the burnt offering?
He laid his hand on its head “so it can be accepted on his behalf to make atonement for him” (1:4).
Leviticus 1:4
To mark the animal as a gift for the Levites’ support
The Levites were supported by Israel’s tithes (Numbers 18:21), not by burnt offerings.
To set the animal apart as payment for a special vow
Vows were fulfilled with peace offerings (Leviticus 22:21); 1:4 links the hand to atonement.
So it would be accepted to make atonement on the worshiper’s behalf
So it could be counted among the firstfruits of the harvest
Firstfruits were a sheaf from the harvest brought to the priest (Leviticus 23:10).
To hand the animal over to the high priest as his own portion
The officiating priest received only the hide (Leviticus 7:8); the rest was burned on the altar (1:9).
After the bull was slaughtered in the burnt-offering instructions of Leviticus 1, what were Aaron’s sons the priests to do with the blood?
Aaron’s sons were to “present the blood and splatter it on all sides of the altar at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting” (1:5).
Leviticus 1:5
Pour it into the bowls of the golden lampstand inside the Holy Place
The lampstand burned pure olive oil (Exodus 27:20), never blood.
Splash it on all sides of the altar at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting
Carry it behind the veil and sprinkle it on the mercy seat
Blood was sprinkled on the mercy seat only on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14), not for burnt offerings.
Mix it with fine flour and oil as a grain offering on the altar
Fine flour and oil make up the grain offering (Leviticus 2:1); blood was never mixed in.
Pour it out on the ground outside the camp and cover it with dirt
Draining blood and covering it with dirt was the rule for game killed in hunting (Leviticus 17:13).
When Leviticus 1 describes a sheep or goat as a burnt offering from the flock, on which side of the altar was the animal to be slaughtered before the LORD?
He was to slaughter it “on the north side of the altar before the LORD” (1:11).
Leviticus 1:11
South side
The south side is never named in Leviticus 1; 1:11 specifies the north side.
East side
The east side was the place for ashes, where the bird’s crop was thrown (1:16).
West side
The west side is not mentioned; 1:11 specifies the north side of the altar.
North side
Inside the sanctuary
The animal was killed beside the altar (1:11), not inside the sanctuary.
In the burnt-offering procedures of Leviticus 1, which parts of the animal were specifically to be washed with water before being burned on the altar?
“The entrails and legs must be washed with water” before the priest burned it all (1:9, 13).
Leviticus 1:9, 13
The horns and hooves
The horns that receive blood in Leviticus are the altar’s (Leviticus 4:7); 1:9 washes the entrails and legs.
The hide and ears
The hide went to the priest (Leviticus 7:8); ears figure in the priests’ ordination (Leviticus 8:23).
The entrails and legs
The liver and kidneys only
The kidneys and liver lobe are removed in the peace offering (Leviticus 3:4); 1:9 washes entrails and legs.
The neck and tail
The fat tail is part of the peace offering of sheep (Leviticus 3:9); 1:9 washes entrails and legs.
Later in Leviticus 1, if an Israelite’s burnt offering to the LORD was from the birds, which birds were permitted?
A bird burnt offering was to be “a turtledove or a young pigeon” (1:14).
Leviticus 1:14
Ravens or eagles
Eagles and ravens are listed among the detestable birds (Leviticus 11:13, 15).
Quail or sparrows
Quail fed Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16:13); sparrows appear in Jesus’ teaching (Matthew 10:29).
Doves or partridges
Doves are close, but only turtledoves or young pigeons are allowed (1:14); a partridge appears in 1 Samuel 26:20.
Turtledoves or young pigeons
Swans or cranes
Cranes appear in Hezekiah’s lament (Isaiah 38:14); only turtledoves or young pigeons qualified (1:14).
In the bird burnt offering described in Leviticus 1, what was the priest to remove and where was it to be thrown?
He was to “remove the crop with its contents and throw it to the east side of the altar, in the place for ashes” (1:16).
Leviticus 1:16
The wings, thrown to the west side of the altar toward the sanctuary
The bird was torn open by the wings, not separated from them (1:17); the crop went to the east side.
The feet, washed and then dropped into the bronze basin by the altar
The bronze basin was for washing (Exodus 30:18); nothing is said about the bird’s feet.
The crop with its contents, to the east side of the altar where the ashes were placed
The breast, given to Aaron and his sons as their share of the offering
The breast belonged to Aaron and his sons in the peace offering (Leviticus 7:31), not the bird burnt offering.
The feathers, carried outside the camp to a ceremonially clean place
Ashes were carried outside the camp to a clean place (Leviticus 6:11); the crop went beside the altar (1:16).
In the final preparation step for the bird burnt offering in Leviticus 1, how was the bird to be opened before being burned on the altar?
“He shall tear it open by its wings, without dividing the bird completely” (1:17).
Leviticus 1:17
Cut completely in two with a knife
The bird was not to be divided completely (1:17); likewise Abram did not cut his birds in half (Genesis 15:10).
Torn open by the wings, but not severed
Left whole without opening it
The bird was opened, torn by its wings (1:17), not left whole.
Broken at the neck and buried
The priest twisted off the bird’s head (1:15); breaking a neck belongs to the heifer rite of Deuteronomy 21:4.
Split at the breast and boiled
The bird was burned on the altar as a pleasing aroma (1:17), not boiled.
In Leviticus 2, when an Israelite brought a grain offering to the LORD, what was the offering to consist of?
Leviticus 2:1 says, “his offering must consist of fine flour.”
Leviticus 2:1
Cedar wood
Cedar wood appears in the purification for skin disease (Leviticus 14:4), not in the grain offering.
Fine flour
Turtledoves
Turtledoves are an animal offering (Leviticus 1:14), not a grain offering.
Grape juice
Grape juice is not part of the grain offering; wine belongs to the drink offering (Numbers 15:5).
Lamb fat
Fat from a lamb belongs to the animal offerings (Leviticus 3:3–4), not the grain offering.
According to the grain-offering law in Leviticus chapter 2, what was to be put on the fine flour before it was brought to Aaron’s sons the priests?
Leviticus 2:1 says, “He is to pour olive oil on it, put frankincense on it, and bring it to Aaron’s sons the priests.”
Leviticus 2:1
Salt and vinegar
Salt is added to the offering (2:13), but vinegar is not mentioned in the grain offering.
Oil and frankincense
Blood and hyssop
Blood and hyssop belong to other rites, not the grain offering (Leviticus 14:4–6).
Honey and leaven
Honey and leaven were not to be burned on the altar (2:11).
Wine and myrrh
Wine belonged to the drink offering (Numbers 15:5), and myrrh to the anointing oil (Exodus 30:23), not the grain offering.
In the instructions about the grain offering given through Moses, who received the remainder after the memorial portion was burned on the altar?
Leviticus 2:3 says, “The remainder of the grain offering shall belong to Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the food offerings to the LORD.”
Leviticus 2:3
Moses and Joshua
Moses and Joshua are not named as receiving the remainder; it belonged to Aaron and his sons (2:3).
The one who brought it
The one who brought the offering did not receive the remainder; it belonged to Aaron and his sons (2:3).
Aaron and his sons
The Levites only
The remainder belonged to Aaron and his sons, not to the Levites only (2:3).
The elders of Israel
The elders of Israel are not named as receiving the remainder; it belonged to Aaron and his sons (2:3).
In the oven-baked grain offering described in Leviticus 2, what form could the offering take?
Leviticus 2:4 says it “must consist of fine flour, either unleavened cakes mixed with oil or unleavened wafers coated with oil.”
Leviticus 2:4
Leavened loaves baked with honey and a little yeast
Leaven and honey were not to be burned on the altar (2:11).
Unleavened cakes mixed with oil or unleavened wafers coated with oil
Boiled grain cooked with wine and a little water
Boiling grain with wine is not part of the grain offering described in this chapter.
Roasted barley sprinkled with the sacrificial blood
Blood is not part of the grain offering; this offering was made of fine flour and oil (2:4).
Sweet cakes sweetened with dates, figs, and honey
Honey was not to be burned on the altar (2:11), and sweet cakes of dates and figs are not mentioned in this chapter.
When a grain offering was prepared on a griddle under the law of Leviticus 2, what was the worshiper told to do with it after preparing it?
Leviticus 2:6 says, “Crumble it and pour oil on it; it is a grain offering.”
Leviticus 2:5-6
Mix it with honey
Honey was not to be burned on the altar (2:11).
Crumble it and pour oil on it
Burn all of it outside the camp
Only the memorial portion was burned on the altar (2:9), not all of it outside the camp.
Add leaven before presenting it
Leaven was forbidden in the grain offering (2:11).
Boil it in water
Boiling in water is not mentioned; the griddle offering was to be crumbled and have oil poured on it (2:6).
In the grain-offering rules at the altar in Leviticus 2, which two substances were not to be burned as a food offering to the LORD?
Leviticus 2:11 says, “you are not to burn any leaven or honey as a food offering to the LORD.”
Leviticus 2:11
Oil and salt
Oil was poured on the flour (2:1), and salt was required (2:13); neither was forbidden.
Leaven and honey
Frankincense and oil
Frankincense and oil were part of the offering (2:1–2); they were not forbidden.
Flour and incense
Fine flour and incense were part of the offering (2:1–2).
Wine and myrrh
Wine and myrrh are not mentioned in this chapter.
In Leviticus 2, what had to season every grain offering as “the salt of the covenant of your God”?
Leviticus 2:13 says, “You must not leave the salt of the covenant of your God out of your grain offering.”
Leviticus 2:13
Ashes
Ashes are not mentioned as seasoning; the offering was seasoned with salt (2:13).
Frankincense
Frankincense was put on the offering (2:1), but the seasoning was salt (2:13).
Salt
Oil
Oil was poured on the offering (2:1), but the seasoning was salt (2:13).
Water
Water is not mentioned as seasoning; the offering was seasoned with salt (2:13).
In the law of firstfruits grain offerings in Leviticus chapter 2, what was an Israelite to present to the LORD?
Leviticus 2:14 says, “you shall offer crushed heads of new grain roasted on the fire.”
Leviticus 2:14
Fresh grapes from the vineyard
Fresh grapes are not mentioned in 2:14; the firstfruits offering was crushed heads of new grain roasted on the fire.
Crushed heads of new grain roasted on the fire
Pressed cakes of dried figs and raisins
Pressed cakes of dried figs and raisins are not mentioned in this chapter; 2:14 describes crushed heads of new grain roasted on the fire.
Boiled wheat with milk
Boiled wheat with milk is not mentioned; 2:14 describes crushed heads of new grain roasted on the fire.
Raw flour without oil
Raw flour without oil is not what 2:14 describes; oil and frankincense were put on the offering (2:15).
In the firstfruits exception stated in Leviticus 2, what was true about leaven and honey?
Leviticus 2:12 says, “You may bring them to the LORD as an offering of firstfruits, but they must not go up on the altar as a pleasing aroma.”
Leviticus 2:12
Both had to be burned completely on the altar as a pleasing aroma to the LORD
Leaven and honey were not to be burned on the altar (2:11); they could be brought only as firstfruits (2:12).
They could be presented to the LORD as an offering of firstfruits, but not offered on the altar as a pleasing aroma
Only honey could be burned on the altar, while leaven was not to be used at all
Both leaven and honey were excluded from the altar (2:11); neither was burned.
Only leaven could be burned on the altar, while honey was not to be used at all
Neither leaven nor honey was to be burned on the altar (2:11); honey was no exception.
They were required in every grain offering as the sign of the covenant of God
Salt, not leaven or honey, was required in every grain offering (2:13).
According to Leviticus 2:2, what did the priest take from a grain offering of fine flour to burn as the memorial portion?
Leviticus 2:2 says, “The priest shall take a handful of the flour and oil, together with all the frankincense, and burn this as a memorial portion on the altar.”
Leviticus 2:2
Half of the flour and oil, with half the frankincense
Only a handful of flour and oil was burned, and all of the frankincense went with it (2:2).
A handful of the flour and oil, with all the frankincense
A tenth of the flour, with none of the frankincense
The priest burned all the frankincense, not none of it, along with a handful of flour and oil (2:2).
All of the flour and oil, with none of the frankincense
The remainder of the flour belonged to Aaron and his sons (2:3), so not all of it was burned.
A handful of the flour only, keeping the frankincense
The frankincense was not kept back; all of it was burned with the memorial portion (2:2).
In Leviticus 3, what kind of sacrifice is Moses describing when an Israelite brings an animal before the LORD?
Leviticus 3:1 begins, “If one’s offering is a peace offering,” and the chapter gives the rules for it.
Leviticus 3:1
Burnt offering
The burnt offering is the subject of Leviticus 1, where the whole animal is burned.
Peace offering
Sin offering
The sin offering is covered in Leviticus 4, for unintentional sins.
Grain offering
The grain offering is covered in Leviticus 2 and is not an animal sacrifice.
Guilt offering
The guilt offering is covered in Leviticus 5, for wrongs that need restitution.
According to the peace offering law in Leviticus 3, if the offering comes from the herd, what kind of animal may be presented before the LORD?
Leviticus 3:1 says the herd offering may be “whether male or female,” but it “must present it without blemish before the LORD.”
Leviticus 3:1
Only a male without blemish
Leviticus 3:1 allows male or female, so a male only is too narrow (compare Leviticus 1:3, where the burnt offering must be male).
Only a female without blemish
Leviticus 3:1 allows male or female, so a female only is too narrow.
A male or female without blemish
Any firstborn animal, even blemished
Blemished animals are not accepted; the offering must be without blemish.
Any animal the worshiper chooses
The worshiper may not choose any animal; it must be from the herd, without blemish.
In the peace offering instructions of Leviticus 3, what must the worshiper do to the animal before slaughtering it at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting?
Leviticus 3:2 says, “He is to lay his hand on the head of the offering and slaughter it.”
Leviticus 3:2
Wash it with water
Washing is required for parts of the burnt offering (Leviticus 1:9), not here.
Lay his hand on its head
Anoint it with oil
Anointing with oil is not the act commanded here.
Shave part of it
Shaving is not mentioned for the offering.
Lead it around the altar seven times
Walking around the altar seven times is not mentioned here; compare Jericho in Joshua 6:15.
In Leviticus 3, where is the peace offering animal to be slaughtered?
Leviticus 3:2 says he is to slaughter it “at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.”
Leviticus 3:2
Outside the camp beyond the last tents
Outside the camp is where the remains of some sin offerings were burned (Leviticus 4:12), not where this was slaughtered.
At the entrance to the Tent of Meeting
Inside the Holy Place beside the lampstand
The Holy Place is for the priests, and the animal was slaughtered at the entrance.
At the city gate of the nearest town
City gates are not part of the tabernacle rules.
On a high hill overlooking the camp
High places are not used in the law of the peace offering.
After the peace offering animal is slaughtered in Leviticus 3, what are Aaron’s sons the priests commanded to do with the blood?
Leviticus 3:2 says Aaron’s sons the priests “shall splatter the blood on all sides of the altar.”
Leviticus 3:2
Pour it on the mercy seat
The mercy seat receives blood only on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14).
Drink it
Eating or drinking blood is forbidden (Leviticus 3:17).
Splatter it on all sides of the altar
Bury it outside the camp
Burying the blood outside the camp is not part of the law of the peace offering.
Place it on the people
Putting blood on the people occurs at the ordination of priests (Exodus 29:20), not here.
In Leviticus 3, if the peace offering comes from the flock, which animal is specifically mentioned first?
Leviticus 3:7 says, “If he is presenting a lamb for his offering.”
Leviticus 3:7
Lamb
Dove
Doves are mentioned in offerings for the poor (Leviticus 5:7), not in this section.
Camel
Camels are unclean (Leviticus 11:4), and are not offered.
Donkey
Donkeys are unclean as sacrifices, and are not mentioned here.
Stag
Stags are not sacrificial animals in the law.
If an Israelite brings a lamb as a peace offering in Leviticus 3, what extra fatty portion is specially mentioned?
Leviticus 3:9 mentions “the entire fat tail cut off close to the backbone.”
Leviticus 3:9
The wool sheared from the lamb’s back
Wool is not part of the offering described.
The hide stripped from the whole carcass
The hide is not listed among the portions burned.
The entire fat tail cut off close to the backbone
The left horn cut off near the head
A horn is not listed among the portions burned.
The foreleg cut off at the shoulder
The foreleg is not listed among the portions burned.
When Leviticus 3 lists the inner parts removed from a peace offering, which organ pair is specifically named?
Leviticus 3:4 says, “both kidneys with the fat on them near the loins.”
Leviticus 3:4
Lungs
Lungs are not mentioned in the list.
Kidneys
Eyes
Eyes are not offered; the portions are internal fat and organs.
Ears
Ears are not mentioned in the list.
Shoulders
Shoulders are not mentioned in the list.
In the peace offering law of Leviticus 3, what part connected to the liver is to be removed with the kidneys?
Leviticus 3:4 says, “the lobe of the liver, which he is to remove with the kidneys.”
Leviticus 3:4
The skin of the liver
The skin of the liver is not mentioned.
The lobe of the liver
The blood of the liver
Blood is not offered; Leviticus 3:17 forbids eating it.
The gall bladder only
The gall bladder is not mentioned.
The stomach lining
The stomach lining is not mentioned.
According to Leviticus 3:5, when the priest burns the peace offering portions, where are they placed?
Leviticus 3:5 says the sons are to burn it “on the altar atop the burnt offering that is on the burning wood.”
Leviticus 3:5
Beneath the altar on the ground by the ash heap
Under the altar is not the place described.
Atop the burnt offering on the burning wood on the altar
Inside the ark beneath the mercy seat
The ark is inside the Most Holy Place, and offerings are not placed in it.
Beside the bronze basin near the laver
The laver is a washing basin, not a place for burning offerings.
Outside the camp at the place of ashes
Burning outside the camp is for certain sin offerings (Leviticus 4:12), not this one.
In Leviticus 3, how are the burned peace offering portions described in relation to the LORD?
Leviticus 3:5 calls it “a food offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.”
Leviticus 3:5
A wave gift for Aaron and his sons
A wave gift is a different ritual, and it is not how the burned portions are described.
A memorial with frankincense on top
A memorial with frankincense belongs to the grain offering (Leviticus 2:2).
A food offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD
A drink offering of wine poured out
Drink offerings of wine are separate offerings (Numbers 15:5).
A trespass payment for the guilty
A trespass payment belongs to the guilt offering, not the peace offering.
At the close of Leviticus 3, what permanent statute is given to the Israelites throughout their generations wherever they live?
Leviticus 3:17 says, “You must not eat any fat or any blood.”
Leviticus 3:17
Eat no leaven and no honey
Leaven and honey are barred from offerings made by fire (Leviticus 2:11), but not in this verse.
Eat neither fat nor blood
Eat no fruit for seven days
Fasting from fruit is not commanded.
Eat only unleavened bread in the camp
Unleavened bread is for other occasions such as Passover.
Eat no fish without scales
Fish without scales are forbidden in Leviticus 11:10–12, but not here.
In the detailed peace offering instructions of Leviticus 3, where is the fat on the kidneys said to be located?
Leviticus 3:4 says, “both kidneys with the fat on them near the loins.”
Leviticus 3:4
Under the ribs
Under the ribs is not the location named.
Near the loins
On the neck
The neck is not the location named.
Beside the heart
Beside the heart is not the location named.
Above the eyes
Above the eyes is not the location named.
In the herd peace offering regulations of Leviticus 3, which complete set of portions is to be offered up on the altar?
Leviticus 3:3–4 lists the fat covering the entrails and all the fat on them, both kidneys with the fat, and the lobe of the liver removed with the kidneys.
Leviticus 3:3-4
The fat that covers the entrails, all the fat attached to them, both kidneys with the fat near the loins, and the lobe of the liver removed with the kidneys
The hide, the right thigh, the breast, and the heart, all burned on the altar
The hide, thigh, breast, and heart are not in the list in Leviticus 3:3–4.
The blood, the lungs, the stomach, and the left horn, all burned as a pleasing aroma
The blood, lungs, stomach, and horn are not in the list; blood is forbidden (3:17).
The entire animal including its hide and dung, burned whole on the altar
The whole animal is burned in the burnt offering (Leviticus 1), not in the peace offering’s list.
Only the fat tail and a grain offering mixed with oil and frankincense
The tail is listed for a lamb only (3:9), and a grain offering is not part of this list.
In the instructions of Leviticus 4, what kind of sin is being addressed when someone does what the LORD has commanded not to be done?
The chapter is about one who sins unintentionally against any of the LORD’s commandments (4:2).
Leviticus 4:1-2
Intentional rebellion
Defiant sin is treated differently (Numbers 15:30); Leviticus 4 deals with unintentional sin (4:2).
Unintentional sin
Theft from a neighbor
Theft is dealt with in Leviticus 6, not in these instructions about unintentional sin (4:2).
Failure to keep a vow
Vows are covered elsewhere; this chapter concerns unintentional sin against the LORD’s commandments (4:2).
Ceremonial uncleanness only
Uncleanness is handled in Leviticus 11–15; here the sin is breaking a commandment unintentionally (4:2).
In Leviticus 4, if the anointed priest sinned and brought guilt on the people, what offering was he to present to the LORD?
The anointed priest who sinned was to bring a young bull without blemish as a sin offering (4:3).
Leviticus 4:3
An unblemished ram
A ram is used for a guilt offering elsewhere (Leviticus 5:15); the priest’s sin offering was a young bull (4:3).
An unblemished male goat
A male goat is the leader’s offering (4:23), not the priest’s.
An unblemished young bull
Two turtledoves
Turtledoves are for those who cannot afford a lamb (Leviticus 5:7), not the anointed priest’s offering.
A grain offering of fine flour
A grain offering of fine flour is allowed only for the very poor (Leviticus 5:11); the priest brought a bull (4:3).
In Leviticus 4, if one of the common people sinned unintentionally and brought a goat as a sin offering, what kind of goat did it have to be?
A common person who brought a goat had to bring an unblemished female goat (4:28).
Leviticus 4:27-28
An unblemished female goat
An unblemished male goat
An unblemished male goat was the leader’s offering (4:23).
A firstborn goat only
Being firstborn is not required; the goat had to be an unblemished female (4:28).
A spotted female goat
Spots are not mentioned; the goat had to be unblemished and female (4:28).
Any goat from the flock
Not just any goat would do; it had to be an unblemished female (4:28).
In the sin offering of the anointed priest in Leviticus 4, how many times was some of the bull’s blood sprinkled before the LORD in front of the curtain of the sanctuary?
The priest dipped his finger in the blood and sprinkled some of it seven times before the LORD, in front of the veil of the sanctuary (4:6).
Leviticus 4:5-6
Three times
Three is not the number given; the sprinkling was seven times (4:6).
Five times
Five is not the number given; the sprinkling was seven times (4:6).
Seven times
Ten times
Ten is not the number given; the sprinkling was seven times (4:6).
Twelve times
Twelve is the number of stones in Joshua 4:3; the sprinkling here was seven times (4:6).
In Leviticus 4, for the sin offering of the anointed priest or of the whole congregation, where did the priest put some of the blood inside the Tent of Meeting?
In both cases the priest put some of the blood on the horns of the altar of fragrant incense in the Tent of Meeting (4:7, 18).
Leviticus 4:7, 17-18
On the bronze basin
The bronze basin stood in the courtyard for washing (Exodus 30:18); the blood went on the horns of the altar of incense (4:7).
On the horns of the altar of fragrant incense
On the Ark of the Covenant
Blood on the ark’s mercy seat belongs to the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14), not these sin offerings.
On the table of the Bread of the Presence
No blood is applied to the table of the Bread of the Presence; it went on the altar of incense (4:7).
On the lampstand
No blood is put on the lampstand; it went on the horns of the altar of incense (4:7).
In the case of a leader’s sin offering in Leviticus 4, on which altar did the priest put some of the blood?
For a leader the priest put some of the blood on the horns of the altar of burnt offering (4:25).
Leviticus 4:25
The golden altar of incense inside the tent
The golden altar of incense received blood for the priest and the congregation (4:7, 18), not the leader.
The altar of burnt offering
The altar on Mount Ebal
The altar on Mount Ebal was built by Joshua (Joshua 8:30); it is not part of this ritual.
The altar beside the Jordan stones
The stones by the Jordan were a memorial at Gilgal (Joshua 4:20), not an altar for blood.
The table of showbread
The table of showbread receives no blood in Leviticus 4; the leader’s blood went on the altar of burnt offering (4:25).
When the whole congregation of Israel discovered an unintentional sin in Leviticus 4, who laid their hands on the head of the bull before it was slaughtered before the LORD?
The elders of the congregation laid their hands on the bull’s head before the LORD (4:15).
Leviticus 4:13-15
Aaron and his sons
Aaron and his sons are not named here; the elders laid their hands on the bull (4:15).
The tribal musicians
Musicians are not mentioned in this chapter (4:15).
The elders of the congregation
Only the man who discovered the sin
A single man laying a hand on the head fits the individual sin offerings (4:24, 29), not the congregation’s (4:15).
The gatekeepers of the camp
Gatekeepers are not mentioned in this chapter (4:15).
After the fat was removed from the sin-offering bull for the anointed priest in Leviticus 4, what was done with the rest of the bull?
The rest of the bull was taken outside the camp to a ceremonially clean place where the ashes were poured out and burned on a wood fire (4:11–12).
Leviticus 4:11-12
It was eaten by the priests in a holy place in the court
Priests ate sin offerings whose blood was not brought into the tent (Leviticus 6:26, 30); this bull was burned outside the camp (4:12).
It was buried in a pit beside the altar of burnt offering
Burial is not mentioned; the bull was burned on a wood fire outside the camp (4:12).
It was taken outside the camp to a clean place where ashes were poured out and burned on wood
It was sent away alive into the wilderness for the people
Sending a goat into the wilderness belongs to the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:21–22); this bull was burned (4:12).
It was kept for the Levites to eat at the tent entrance
Nothing was kept for the Levites to eat; all the rest of the bull was burned outside the camp (4:11–12).

Looking across the cases in Leviticus 4, which two situations required the anointed priest to bring some of the blood into the Tent of Meeting, sprinkle it before the LORD, and put it on the horns of the altar of fragrant incense?

Both the anointed priest’s offering and the whole congregation’s offering involved bringing blood into the Tent of Meeting, sprinkling it, and putting it on the horns of the incense altar (4:5–7, 16–18).
Leviticus 4:3-7, 13-18
The sin of a leader and the sin of a common person
For a leader and a common person, the blood went on the altar of burnt offering (4:25, 30).
The sin of the anointed priest and the sin of the whole congregation
The cleansing of a leper and the vow of a Nazirite
Lepers and Nazirites are not treated in Leviticus 4; they are covered in Leviticus 14 and Numbers 6.
The guilt offering and the grain offering
Guilt and grain offerings are not the sin offerings of this chapter (see Leviticus 2 and 5).
The sin of a widow and the sin of a foreigner
Widows and foreigners are not mentioned in Leviticus 4.
In Leviticus 4, besides the fat, which parts of the anointed priest’s sin-offering bull were removed and burned on the altar of burnt offering?
Verse 9 names “both kidneys with the fat on them near the loins, and the lobe of the liver,” which were burned on the altar of burnt offering (4:9–10).
Leviticus 4:8-10
The heart and the lungs with their fat
The heart and lungs are not named; the fat, both kidneys and the lobe of the liver were burned on the altar (4:8–9).
The head and the legs with the entrails
The head, legs and entrails were taken outside the camp and burned on the ash heap (4:11–12), not on the altar.
Both kidneys and the lobe of the liver
The hide and all the flesh of the bull
The hide and all the flesh went outside the camp to be burned on a wood fire (4:11–12), not on the altar.
The breast and the right thigh
The breast and the right thigh were the priests’ share of the peace offering (Leviticus 7:31–32), not burned on the altar.
In Leviticus 5, when someone hears a public charge to testify about something he has seen or learned but stays silent, what happens?
Leviticus 5:1 says that if someone fails to testify when he hears a public charge about something he has witnessed, he shall bear the iniquity.
Leviticus 5:1
He remains innocent unless a judge questions him twice
Leviticus 5:1 puts the sin in failing to testify; there is no waiting for a judge to ask twice.
He becomes guilty and bears his iniquity
He is only unclean until evening
Being unclean until evening is the penalty for other contacts in Leviticus, not for silence about a charge (5:1).
He must fast for seven days
A seven-day fast is not part of Leviticus 5; the silent witness bears his iniquity (5:1).
He pays a small fine and goes free
Leviticus 5:1 gives no fine-and-release option; the person is held guilty and must bear iniquity.
In the laws of Leviticus 5, which contact could make a person guilty even if he realized it only later?
Leviticus 5:2 says touching the carcass of an unclean wild animal, livestock or crawling creature makes a person unclean and guilty, even if he is unaware of it.
Leviticus 5:2
Touching the carcass of an unclean wild animal, livestock animal, or swarming thing
Touching clean water in the basin set between the tent and the altar
Touching clean water is not a sin in Leviticus; priests washed in the bronze basin (Exodus 30:18).
Eating bread baked with clean flour at the autumn harvest feast
Eating bread from the harvest is not the contact named in Leviticus 5:2.
Standing near the bronze altar while the priests offered sacrifices
Standing near the altar is part of normal priestly service; Leviticus 5:2 names unclean carcasses.
Wearing a linen tunic and sash while serving in the tabernacle court
A linen tunic was priestly clothing (Exodus 28:39–40), not a source of guilt in Leviticus 5:2.
According to Leviticus 5, what kind of spoken commitment could make a person guilty when he later recognizes what he said?
Leviticus 5:4 says that if someone swears thoughtlessly to do anything good or evil, even unaware of it, he is guilty in the matter when he realizes it.
Leviticus 5:4
A blessing over a meal
A blessing over a meal is not mentioned in Leviticus 5:4; the guilt comes from a rash oath.
A rash oath to do evil or good
A marriage vow
A marriage vow is not named in Leviticus 5:4; the passage speaks of a thoughtless oath.
A king’s decree
A king’s decree is not part of this law; Leviticus 5:4 speaks of an individual’s rash oath.
A song of praise
A song of praise is not a spoken commitment; Leviticus 5:4 names a rash oath.
In Leviticus 5, after a person realizes guilt in one of these matters, what must he do first?
Leviticus 5:5 says that if someone incurs guilt in one of these ways, he must confess the sin he has committed.
Leviticus 5:5
Shave his head
Shaving the head belongs to the Nazirite vow (Numbers 6:18), not to this law.
Leave the camp
Leaving the camp is not required in Leviticus 5; confession comes first (5:5).
Confess how he has sinned
Bring incense only
Leviticus 5:5–6 gives confession and then a guilt offering; incense alone is not named.
Wait until the next feast
Leviticus 5:5 calls for confession now, not waiting for a feast.
In Moses’ instructions in Leviticus 5, what animal from the flock could a person bring for the sin he had committed?
Leviticus 5:6 says the person must bring a female lamb or goat from the flock as a sin offering.
Leviticus 5:6
A male bull
A male bull was the offering for the anointed priest’s sin (Leviticus 4:3), not the case in 5:6.
A female lamb or female goat
Two rams
Two rams are not named in Leviticus 5:6; the case calls for a female lamb or goat.
A young calf
A young calf is not the animal named in Leviticus 5:6, which calls for a female lamb or goat.
A male goat only
A male goat was for a leader’s sin (Leviticus 4:23); 5:6 names a female lamb or goat.
If an Israelite in Leviticus 5 could not afford a lamb, what substitute was permitted?
Leviticus 5:7 says that if he cannot afford a lamb, he may bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering.
Leviticus 5:7
Two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for a sin offering and one for a burnt offering
One ram and one dove, both of them presented together as sin offerings
Leviticus 5:7 does not name a ram and a dove; it names two birds, one for each offering.
Two lambs of the flock, both of them offered whole as burnt offerings
Lambs are what the poor could not afford (5:7); birds were the permitted substitute.
Five young pigeons, all of them offered together as one sin offering
Five pigeons is not the provision; Leviticus 5:7 names two birds.
One dove only, offered whole on the altar as a burnt offering alone
Leviticus 5:7 calls for two birds, one for a sin offering and one for a burnt offering, not one dove.
In the bird offering described in Leviticus 5, which offering did the priest present first?
Leviticus 5:8 says the priest shall first present the bird for the sin offering; 5:10 says the second bird is prepared as a burnt offering.
Leviticus 5:8, 10
The burnt offering first
The burnt offering bird came second (5:10), not first.
The grain offering first
No grain offering is part of the bird offering; the flour was a separate option for the very poor (5:11).
The sin offering first
The peace offering first
A peace offering is not part of this law in Leviticus 5.
Both birds together with no order
Leviticus 5:8 sets an order: the sin offering is presented first.
In Leviticus 5, where was the blood of the bird sin offering applied?
Leviticus 5:9 says the priest sprinkles some of the blood on the side of the altar, while the rest is drained out at the base of the altar.
Leviticus 5:9
All of it on the horns of the incense altar
Blood on the horns of the incense altar was for the anointed priest’s bull (Leviticus 4:7), not the bird in 5:9.
Some on the side of the altar, and the rest drained at the base
All of it poured outside the camp
Leviticus 5:9 has the blood at the altar, not outside the camp.
On the priest’s right ear and thumb
Blood on the right ear and thumb belongs to the priests’ ordination (Leviticus 8:23).
Mixed into the flour offering
The blood is not mixed into flour; Leviticus 5:9 says some is sprinkled and the rest drained.
If the person in Leviticus 5 could not afford two birds either, what could he bring, and what was forbidden with it?
Leviticus 5:11 says that if he cannot afford two birds, he may bring a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a sin offering, with no olive oil or frankincense on it.
Leviticus 5:11
A tenth of an ephah of fine flour, with no oil or frankincense
An ephah of barley, with oil only
Leviticus 5:11 names a tenth of an ephah of fine flour, with no oil, not an ephah of barley with oil.
Fine flour mixed with honey and incense
Honey is not named in Leviticus 5:11, and incense is forbidden on this offering.
Two-tenths of an ephah with wine
Two-tenths with wine is not what 5:11 says; it names a tenth of an ephah, with no oil or frankincense.
Unleavened cakes spread with oil
Cakes spread with oil go against 5:11, which forbids olive oil on this sin offering.
In the fine-flour sin offering of Leviticus 5, what happened to the remainder after the priest took a handful?
Leviticus 5:13 says the remainder of the flour offering belongs to the priest, like the grain offering.
Leviticus 5:12-13
It was eaten by the offerer
The offerer did not eat it; the remainder belonged to the priest (5:13).
It was burned completely
Only a handful was burned as a memorial portion (5:12), not all of it.
It belonged to the priest, like the grain offering
It was buried outside the camp
Burying outside the camp is not part of this law; Leviticus 5:13 gives the remainder to the priest.
It was stored for the next Sabbath
Leviticus 5:13 assigns the remainder to the priest, not to be stored for a Sabbath.
When Leviticus 5 addresses someone sinning unintentionally regarding the LORD’s holy things, what animal had to be brought?
Leviticus 5:15 says that for unintentional sin against the LORD’s holy things, he must bring an unblemished ram from the flock as a guilt offering.
Leviticus 5:15
A female lamb without blemish
A female lamb is for the sin offering in Leviticus 5:6, not the guilt offering for holy things.
A ram without blemish from the flock
A pair of turtledoves
Turtledoves are the poor person’s substitute in Leviticus 5:7, not the case in 5:15.
A young bull
A young bull was for a priest’s sin offering (Leviticus 4:3), not for this guilt offering.
A male goat for the people
A male goat was for a leader’s sin (Leviticus 4:23); 5:15 calls for a ram.
In the holy-things restitution law of Leviticus 5, how much extra had to be added to the repayment?
Leviticus 5:16 says he must make restitution by adding a fifth of its value to it and giving it to the priest.
Leviticus 5:16
Nothing extra
Leviticus 5:16 requires adding a fifth, so something extra was required.
One-tenth
A tenth is the tithe (Leviticus 27:30), not the amount added in 5:16.
One-fifth
One-third
One-third is not the fraction named in Leviticus 5:16.
Double
Double repayment applies to theft (Exodus 22:4), not the holy-things law in 5:16.
In Leviticus 5, by what standard was the ram for the guilt offering to be valued?
Leviticus 5:15 says the ram was to be of proper value in silver shekels according to the sanctuary shekel.
Leviticus 5:15, 18
By the market price in Egypt
Egyptian market prices are not named; the standard is the sanctuary shekel (5:15).
By silver shekels according to the sanctuary shekel
By the weight of barley
Barley weight is not the measure in Leviticus 5:15; silver shekels are.
By whatever amount the worshiper chose
The worshiper did not choose the value; the ram had to be of proper value in silver shekels (5:15).
By the number of feast days remaining
Feast days are not a measure of value in Leviticus 5; the sanctuary shekel is (5:15).
Near the end of Leviticus 5, if a person did what the LORD forbids but did not realize it at the time, which statement is correct?
Leviticus 5:17–18 says that if someone violates any of the LORD’s commandments even though he was unaware, he is guilty and must bring an unblemished ram as a guilt offering.
Leviticus 5:17-19
He was guiltless because it was unintentional
Leviticus 5:17 says he is guilty even though he was unaware.
He was only unclean until evening
Being unclean until evening is a different consequence; Leviticus 5:17 says he is guilty.
He was still guilty and had to bring a ram of proper value as a guilt offering
He needed only to confess, with no offering
Leviticus 5:18 requires a ram brought to the priest, not confession alone.

Gold, silver, and bronze are never used in this cleansing ritual.
A ram’s horn, salt, and myrrh
A ram’s horn, salt, and myrrh are not listed here; the items are cedar, scarlet yarn, and hyssop.
Fine flour, incense, and purple cloth
Fine flour comes later in the grain offering (14:10); incense and purple cloth are not part of this rite.
After the first washing, shaving, and bathing in Leviticus 14, what was the cleansed person allowed to do, and what restriction remained?
After washing his clothes, shaving, and bathing, the person could enter the camp but had to stay outside his tent for seven days (14:8).
Leviticus 14:8
Enter the camp but stay outside his tent for seven days
Enter his tent immediately but not the camp

Stay outside the camp for forty days
Forty days is not the period here; the restriction was seven days (14:8).
Go home with no restriction
He was not released without restriction; he had to stay outside his tent for seven days, then wash and shave again (14:8–9).
Live in the priest’s house for three days
No stay at the priest’s house is mentioned; he remained outside his own tent for seven days (14:8).
On the seventh day of cleansing in Leviticus 14, what hair was the person required to shave off?
On the seventh day he had to shave off all his hair, specifically his head, beard, eyebrows, and the rest of his hair (14:9).
Leviticus 14:9
Only the beard and the hair of the head

Only his eyebrows, leaving head and beard
The eyebrows were included, but so were the head, the beard, and all the rest of his hair (14:9).
Head, beard, eyebrows, and all remaining hair
Only the head and beard, not the eyebrows
The head and beard were included, but the eyebrows and all remaining hair were to be shaved too (14:9).
None, since he had already shaved on day one
He had already shaved once at the start (14:8), and the shaving was repeated on the seventh day (14:9), not postponed to the eighth.
On the eighth day in Leviticus 14, what animals did a person who could afford the full offering bring for cleansing?

Two unblemished male lambs and one unblemished year-old ewe lamb
One young bull, one ram, and one male goat without defect

Two turtledoves and one young pigeon, all without blemish

One male lamb and two goats, each one unblemished

Three male lambs, each of them a year old
Three male lambs is wrong; two were male lambs and the third was a year-old ewe lamb (14:10).
At the entrance to the Tent of Meeting in Leviticus 14, what did the priest wave before the LORD?
The priest took one of the male lambs and presented it as a guilt offering, along with the log of olive oil, and waved them before the LORD (14:12).

The burnt offering and incense
The burnt offering was slaughtered and offered on the altar later (14:19–20); it is not what was waved, and incense is not mentioned.
One male lamb as a guilt offering with the log of oil
The sin offering and flour

The two birds and hyssop
The two birds and hyssop belong to the earlier rite outside the camp (14:4–7), not to the wave offering at the tent.
The ewe lamb and the grain offering
The ewe lamb was the sin offering (14:10, 19), and the grain offering was not waved with the guilt offering.
In the cleansing of a healed skin disease in Leviticus 14, on which body parts was the blood of the guilt offering placed?

Left earlobe, thumb of the left hand, and big toe of the left foot
It was the right side that received the blood, not the left (14:14).
Forehead, palm of the right hand, and heel of the right foot
Forehead, palm, and heel are not the places named; they were the right earlobe, right thumb, and right big toe (14:14).
Right earlobe, thumb of the right hand, and big toe of the right foot
Tip of the nose, right wrist, and the right ankle bone
Nose, wrist, and ankle are not named; the blood went on the right ear, thumb, and big toe (14:14).
Both ears, both hands, and both feet of the one cleansed
Only the right ear, the right thumb, and the right big toe were touched, not both sides (14:14).
After putting oil on the right earlobe, right thumb, and right big toe in Leviticus 14, what did the priest do with the rest of the oil left in his palm?
The rest of the oil in his palm the priest put on the head of the one to be cleansed, to make atonement for him before the LORD (14:18).

Poured it out at the base of the altar of burnt offering

Incense is not part of this step; the leftover oil went on the person’s head (14:18).
Gave it to the family of the one being cleansed

Put it on the head of the one being cleansed
Poured it into the clay pot of fresh water
The oil was not poured into the pot of fresh water; the water and the bird’s blood belonged to the earlier rite (14:5–6), and the remaining oil went on the person’s head (14:18).
If a person was poor and could not afford the usual cleansing offerings in Leviticus 14, what birds could he bring?
A poor person was to bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons, whichever he could afford, one as a sin offering and one as a burnt offering (14:22).
Leviticus 14:21-22
Two ravens or two young hawks
Ravens were unclean birds (Deuteronomy 14:14) and could never serve as an offering.
Two quail or two young partridges
Quail were food for Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16:13), not an offering allowed for this cleansing.
Two turtledoves or two young pigeons
One eagle and one sparrow
Eagles were unclean birds (Deuteronomy 14:12), so an eagle could not be offered.
Three pigeons or three turtledoves
Three pigeons or turtledoves is wrong; the law names two birds, turtledoves or young pigeons (14:22).
In the section of Leviticus 14 about mildew in houses, when were these instructions to begin applying to Israel?

Leviticus 14:33-34
When Israel left Egypt

When they entered the land of Canaan
When the temple was built in Jerusalem
The temple is not mentioned here; the law is given for the time they enter the land of Canaan (14:34).
During the wilderness census
The wilderness years were spent in tents; the law is tied to houses in the land they would enter (14:34).

The exile came centuries later and has nothing to do with this law, which begins when Israel enters Canaan (14:34).

“Something like mildew has appeared in my house”

A house becoming holy is not the issue; the concern is possible mildew contamination (14:34–35).
“The plague has struck my field”
The law concerns a house, not a field; the report is that something like mildew has appeared in the house (14:35).
Before the priest entered a house to inspect suspected mildew in Leviticus 14, what had to happen first?
The priest ordered the house cleared before entering to examine the mildew, so that nothing in it would become unclean (14:36).

The priest alone inspected the house (14:36–37); neighbors were not part of the process.
According to the house-inspection law in Leviticus 14, what visible signs on the wall indicated possible mildew contamination?
The priest looked for green or red depressions that appeared to be beneath the surface of the wall (14:37).
Leviticus 14:37
White powder collecting on the floor along the walls
White powder is not mentioned; the sign was green or red depressions in the walls (14:37).
Black smoke stains across the ceiling beams
Black smoke on the ceiling is not mentioned; the warning signs were in the walls (14:37).
Cracks running from the doorway up to the roof
Cracks near the doorway are not the sign; it was green or red depressions in the wall (14:37).

Dripping water is not mentioned; the sign was green or red depressions beneath the wall’s surface (14:37).
After the priest first examined a house with suspicious mildew in Leviticus 14, how long was the house to be closed up?

Leviticus 14:38
Three days
Three days is too short; the house was shut for seven days (14:38).
Five days
Five days is not the period given; the law says seven days (14:38).
Seven days

Fourteen days is not mentioned in this law; the first closure was seven days (14:38).
Thirty days
Thirty days is far longer than the seven days the law sets (14:38).

Buried beneath the doorway of the same house
They were not buried beneath the doorway; they were dumped outside the city (14:40).
Pulled out and thrown into an unclean place outside the city
Set aside in the priest’s court for later reuse
They were not kept by the priest; they were thrown into an unclean place outside the city (14:40).

The house was holy and set apart
The house was declared unclean, not holy (14:44).

The priest judged the mildew; no king is involved (14:44).

A house declared unclean was torn down with its stones, timbers, and plaster, and taken outside the city to an unclean place (14:45).

It had to be torn down and its stones, timbers, and plaster taken to an unclean place outside the city

When a house was purified after the mildew was gone in Leviticus 14, which set of items did the priest use, and what happened to the live bird?

Two birds, cedar wood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop; the live bird was released into the open field outside the city
Two goats, olive branches, and incense; the live goat was sent into the wilderness
Goats and olive branches are not used in this rite, and no live goat is sent into the wilderness here; a live bird is released (14:49–53).
A ram, unleavened bread, and myrrh; the animal was burned completely
A ram, unleavened bread, and myrrh are not the materials; the live animal was released, not burned (14:49–53).

A bull and wool are not used; the priest used two birds, cedar wood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop (14:49).
Two doves, gold thread, and cassia; both birds were kept alive in the house
Gold thread and cassia are not used, and the live bird was released outside the city, not kept in the house (14:49–53).

Moses and Aaron
Eleazar and Ithamar

Moses and Miriam
Miriam is not addressed in this chapter; the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron (15:1).

One day
One day is too short; the impurity lasts seven days (15:19).
Seven days
Eight days
The eighth day is when a cleansed woman brings her offering (15:29), not the length of impurity.
Fourteen days
A daughter’s birth brings two weeks of impurity (Leviticus 12:5), not ordinary menstruation.
Forty days

Only his clothing
Clothing becomes unclean for those who touch his bed (15:5), but his bed and seat are unclean too (15:4).
Only the food he touches
Food is not mentioned; his bed, furniture and saddle become unclean (15:4, 9).
Any bed he lies on and anything he sits on

The entrance of his house is not mentioned; his bed and seat are unclean (15:4).
Only his sandals
Sandals are not mentioned; the chapter names bed, furniture and saddle (15:4, 9).

Burial is not prescribed; the clay pot is broken and the wooden utensil rinsed (15:12).

As the days of her menstrual impurity

Count off seven days, wash his clothes, and bathe in fresh water

Aaron
