She must be from the tribe of Judah
No tribe is specified; the conditions are unmarried and near to him (21:3).
According to the holiness rules for Aaron’s sons in Leviticus 21, which practice was forbidden to priests?
Leviticus 21:5 says priests must not make bald spots on their heads, shave off the edges of their beards, or make cuts in their bodies.
Leviticus 21:5
Washing their priestly garments in the Jordan River before serving
Washing garments is not what 21:5 forbids; Jordan washing is not mentioned in this passage.
Making bald patches on their heads, shaving off the edges of their beards, and making cuts in their bodies
Sitting in ashes for seven days after any death in the family
Sitting in ashes is not listed in 21:5; the rule names bald spots, beard edges and cuts.
Covering their heads with sackcloth during any season of mourning
Sackcloth is not mentioned in 21:5; the forbidden practices are bald spots, shaved beard edges and cuts.
Blowing ram’s horns at funerals for members of the congregation
Blowing ram’s horns is not part of this rule; the Day of Atonement horn is a different matter (Leviticus 25:9).
In Leviticus 21, why were priests to be regarded as holy by the Israelites?
Leviticus 21:6 says they present to the LORD the food offerings, the food of their God, so they must be holy; 21:8 says to regard them as holy since the priest presents the food of your God.
Leviticus 21:6, 8
Because they guarded the gates of Jericho
Jericho’s gates are not part of the priests’ role in Leviticus 21; no such duty is mentioned.
Because they wrote the Law on stone tablets
Writing the Law on stone tablets is not the priests’ role in this passage; their holiness is tied to presenting the offerings (21:6, 8).
Because they offered the food of God, the food offerings to the LORD
Because they ruled as kings over Israel
Priests were not kings; the reason for holiness in 21:6 and 21:8 is presenting the offerings.
Because they owned the land around Shiloh
Shiloh and land ownership are not mentioned in Leviticus 21; Levites had no tribal inheritance (Numbers 18:20).
When Leviticus 21 gives marriage restrictions for an ordinary priest, which woman is he specifically forbidden to marry?
Leviticus 21:7 says a priest must not marry a woman defiled by prostitution or divorced by her husband, for the priest is holy to his God.
Leviticus 21:7
A woman from the tribe of Benjamin who had never been married
The tribe of Benjamin is not mentioned as a restriction; the forbidden women are named in 21:7.
A woman defiled by prostitution or divorced by her husband
A widow whose husband had died without leaving children
A widow is not forbidden to an ordinary priest in 21:7; the high priest is restricted from marrying one (21:14).
A foreign queen from a neighboring nation’s royal house
A foreign queen is not mentioned in Leviticus 21; the named restrictions are prostitution and divorce (21:7).
A woman who owned no land or flocks of her own
Owning no land or flocks is not a restriction; the named restrictions are prostitution and divorce (21:7).
In the laws for priestly families in Leviticus 21, what was the penalty if a priest’s daughter defiled herself by prostitution?
Leviticus 21:9 says if a priest’s daughter defiles herself by prostituting herself, she profanes her father; she must be burned in the fire.
Leviticus 21:9
She had to shave her head
Shaving the head is not the penalty in 21:9; the verse requires burning.
She was sent outside the camp for seven days
Seven days outside the camp is not the penalty here; the verse prescribes burning (21:9).
She had to bring a grain offering
A grain offering is not the penalty; she profanes her father and must be burned (21:9).
She had to be burned in the fire
She lost her inheritance but remained in the camp
Loss of inheritance while remaining in the camp is not the penalty; Leviticus 21:9 says she must be burned in the fire.
Concerning the high priest in Leviticus 21, which outward signs of mourning was he forbidden to display?
Leviticus 21:10 says the high priest must not let his hair hang loose or tear his garments.
Leviticus 21:10
He must not put dust on his head or remove his sandals
Dust on the head and removing sandals are not listed in 21:10; the ban covers loose hair and torn garments.
He must not let his hair hang loose or tear his garments
He must not sit on the ground or fast until evening
Sitting on the ground and fasting are not mentioned in 21:10.
He must not cover his upper lip or wear sackcloth
Covering the mouth was a sign for a person with a skin disease (Leviticus 13:45), not the mourning ban here.
He must not close the sanctuary gates
The sanctuary gates are not mentioned; the ban is on loose hair and torn garments (21:10).
In Leviticus 21, how far did the high priest’s rule against corpse defilement extend?
Leviticus 21:11 says the high priest must not go near any dead body; he must not defile himself, even for his father or mother.
Leviticus 21:11
He could mourn only for his mother
Mourning only for his mother is not the rule; he must not defile himself even for his father or mother (21:11).
He could go near a dead body for any priest
The rule forbids him from going near any dead body, not only for a priest’s death (21:11).
He must not go near any dead body, even for his father or mother
He could touch only the body of a king
The rule does not name a king’s body as an exception; it bars contact with any dead body (21:11).
He could defile himself only during national festivals
No festival exception is given; the prohibition is stated without exception (21:11).
What reason does Leviticus 21 give for the high priest not leaving the sanctuary in a death-related defilement situation?
Leviticus 21:12 says he must not leave or desecrate the sanctuary of his God, for the consecration of the anointing oil of his God is on him.
Leviticus 21:12
The sanctuary was too far from his home
Distance from home is not the reason given; 21:12 cites the anointing oil.
The consecration of the anointing oil of his God was on him
He had to guard the Ark of the Covenant alone
Guarding the ark alone is not mentioned; the reason is the consecration of the anointing oil (21:12).
Only Moses was allowed outside the camp
Moses is not mentioned as the only one allowed outside; the reason in 21:12 is the anointing oil.
His tribe owned no burial ground
Burial grounds are not mentioned; the reason is the anointing oil on him (21:12).
In the marriage law for the priest who was highest among his brothers, what kind of wife was he to take?
Leviticus 21:13–14 says the woman he marries must be a virgin, and he is to marry a virgin from his own people.
Leviticus 21:13-15
A widow from any tribe
A widow is explicitly excluded for the high priest (21:14).
A divorced woman from the priestly clan
A divorced woman is explicitly excluded for the high priest (21:14).
A virgin from his own people
A foreign convert from Egypt
A foreign convert is not what the law says; he must marry a virgin from his own people (21:14).
A woman previously promised to another man
A woman previously promised to another man is not mentioned; the requirement is a virgin from his own people (21:13–14).
In the instructions given to Aaron in Leviticus 21, what general restriction is placed on his descendants who have a physical defect?
Leviticus 21:17 says none of Aaron’s descendants who has a physical defect may approach to offer the food of his God.
Leviticus 21:16-17, 21
They may not live inside Israel
They were not barred from living in Israel; the restriction concerns approaching to offer (21:17).
They may not eat any sacred food
They could still eat the most holy food and the holy food (21:22), so they were not barred from all sacred food.
They may not approach to offer the food of their God
They may not marry within the tribe of Levi
Marriage within Levi is not mentioned in this restriction (21:17–21).
They must serve as judges instead
Serving as judges is not mentioned; the restriction concerns approaching to offer (21:17).
Among the defects listed in Leviticus 21 that would prevent a descendant of Aaron from approaching the altar, which one below is not named in the chapter?
Leviticus 21:18–20 lists defects such as blind, lame, disfigured, deformed, hunchback, dwarf and crushed testicle, but deafness is not among them.
Leviticus 21:18-20
Blindness
Blindness is named in 21:18: “no man who is blind, lame, disfigured, or deformed.”
Lameness
Lameness is named in 21:18 as one of the defects that bar a descendant of Aaron from approaching the altar.
Hunchbacked
Hunchback is named in 21:20 among the defects.
Damaged testicles
A crushed testicle is named in 21:20; the question’s “damaged testicles” refers to that defect.
Deafness
According to Leviticus 21, what privilege still remained for a descendant of Aaron who had a physical defect?
Leviticus 21:22 says he may eat the most holy food of his God as well as the holy food.
Leviticus 21:22
He could become king over Israel
Kingship over Israel is not mentioned in Leviticus 21; the privilege named is eating the holy food (21:22).
He could eat the most holy food of his God as well as the holy food
He could enter the Most Holy Place once a year
The Most Holy Place was entered once a year by the high priest (Leviticus 16:2, 34), not a privilege of a priest with a defect.
He could offer incense at the altar
Offering incense at the altar is barred by 21:23; he may not approach the altar.
He could replace the high priest in an emergency
No replacement role for the high priest is mentioned; the privilege is eating the holy food (21:22).
In the closing part of Leviticus 21, which sacred places was a priest with a physical defect forbidden to approach?
Leviticus 21:23 says because he has a defect, he must not go near the veil or approach the altar, so as not to desecrate My sanctuaries.
Leviticus 21:23
The camp gate and the bronze basin
The bronze basin was for washing (Exodus 30:18), not named in 21:23; the places named are the veil and the altar.
The curtain and the altar
The Mount of Olives and the tabernacle roof
The Mount of Olives and a tabernacle roof are not mentioned in Leviticus 21; the forbidden places are the veil and the altar.
The city gate and the king’s court
The city gate and king’s court are not named in Leviticus 21; the forbidden places are the veil and the altar.
The Jordan River and Gilgal
The Jordan River and Gilgal are not part of this law; the forbidden places are the veil and the altar (21:23).
Which statement correctly combines two priestly rules given in Leviticus 21 about ordinary priests and the high priest?
Leviticus 21:1–3 allows ordinary priests to defile themselves for immediate family, while 21:11 says the high priest must not defile himself even for his father or mother.
Leviticus 21:1-3, 10-11
Ordinary priests could defile themselves for any Israelite, and the high priest could marry a widow
Ordinary priests could defile themselves only for close family (21:2–3), and the high priest could not marry a widow (21:14).
Ordinary priests could defile themselves for immediate family, but the high priest could not defile himself even for his father or mother
Ordinary priests had to marry only virgins, but the high priest could marry a divorced woman
Ordinary priests had no such rule limiting them to virgins; the high priest could not marry a divorced woman (21:14).
Both ordinary priests and the high priest were free to tear their garments in mourning
The high priest was forbidden to tear his garments in mourning (21:10), so they were not both free to do so.
Both ordinary priests and priests with physical defects could approach the altar if they were from Aaron’s line
Priests with physical defects could not approach the altar even if from Aaron’s line (21:21, 23).
When the LORD spoke to Moses about Aaron’s sons handling the holy offerings in Leviticus 22, what had an unclean priest do before he could eat the holy food after touching something unclean?
A man who touched something unclean “will remain unclean until evening. He must not eat from the sacred offerings unless he has bathed himself with water,” and after sunset he could eat (22:6–7).
Leviticus 22:6-7
Bring a ram immediately
No ram was required to end this kind of uncleanness; he had to bathe and wait until sunset (22:6–7).
Wash his body with water and wait until evening
Fast for seven days
A seven-day fast is not mentioned; he was unclean only until evening, after bathing (22:6–7).
Shave his head and his clothes
Shaving his head is not part of this law; he bathed with water and waited until evening (22:6–7).
Leave the camp permanently
He was not banished permanently; the uncleanness lasted until evening (22:6–7).
In the rules about priestly food in Leviticus 22, which person in a priest’s household was allowed to eat from the sacred offerings?
“If a priest buys a slave with his own money, or if a slave is born in his household, that slave may eat his food” (22:11).
Leviticus 22:10-11
A hired worker
A hired worker may not eat the offering (22:10).
A traveler staying overnight
A guest of a priest may not eat the offering (22:10).
A slave bought with the priest’s money
Any Israelite neighbor
No one outside a priest’s family may eat the sacred offering (22:10).
A priest’s daughter married to a layman
A priest’s daughter married to a man other than a priest is not to eat of the sacred contributions (22:12).
In Leviticus 22, what happened to the eating privileges of a priest’s daughter if she married a man outside the priestly family?
“If the priest’s daughter is married to a man other than a priest, she is not to eat of the sacred contributions” (22:12).
Leviticus 22:12
She could eat only on Sabbaths
A Sabbath exception is not mentioned; she could not eat the sacred contributions (22:12).
She could still eat after washing
Washing did not restore the privilege; she is not to eat of the sacred contributions (22:12).
She had to pay silver first
Paying silver is not mentioned; she is not to eat of the sacred contributions (22:12).
She could not eat the sacred contributions
She could eat only firstfruits
Firstfruits are not mentioned; she is not to eat of the sacred contributions (22:12).
In the holiness laws of Leviticus 22, if someone ate a holy offering unintentionally, what was that person required to do?
“If anyone eats a sacred offering in error, he must add a fifth to its value and give the sacred offering to the priest” (22:14).
Leviticus 22:14
Offer two pigeons only
Two pigeons are not mentioned in this law; he adds a fifth to its value (22:14).
Return nothing because it was accidental
Being accidental did not remove the duty; he must add a fifth and give it to the priest (22:14).
Add a fifth to its value and give it to the priest
Wait until the next festival
Waiting for a festival is not mentioned; he must add a fifth to its value and give it to the priest (22:14).
Bring a grain offering only
A grain offering alone is not what the law requires; he must add a fifth and give the offering to the priest (22:14).
In the laws for sacrifices in Leviticus 22, what kind of animal from the herd, sheep, or goats was required if an Israelite wanted his burnt offering or vow offering to be accepted?
Anyone presenting a burnt offering “must offer an unblemished male from the cattle, sheep, or goats in order for it to be accepted” (22:19).
Leviticus 22:19-20
Female without blemish
The animal had to be a male, not a female (22:19).
Male without blemish
Firstborn only
Being firstborn is not the requirement; it had to be an unblemished male (22:19).
Spotted but healthy
Spots or defects made it unacceptable; it had to be unblemished (22:19–20).
Any animal over one year old
The law set no minimum age of over a year here; it required an unblemished male (22:19).
In the sacrifice regulations of Leviticus 22:23, an ox or a sheep with a deformed or stunted limb could be presented in which way?
An ox or sheep with “a deformed or stunted limb” could be presented “as a freewill offering,” but it was “not acceptable in fulfillment of a vow” (22:23).
Leviticus 22:23
As a sin offering only
A sin offering is not mentioned for this case; it could be a freewill offering but not for a vow (22:23).
As a Passover offering
The Passover is not mentioned in this law; it could be a freewill offering but not for a vow (22:23).
As a freewill offering, but not for a vow
As the daily burnt offering
The daily burnt offering is not mentioned; it could be a freewill offering but not for a vow (22:23).
It could never be offered under any circumstance
It was not banned in every case; it could be a freewill offering, though not for a vow (22:23).
In Leviticus 22, what was the rule for a newborn ox, sheep, or goat before it could be accepted as an offering to the LORD?
“When an ox, a sheep, or a goat is born, it must remain with its mother for seven days. From the eighth day on, it will be acceptable” (22:27).
Leviticus 22:27
It had to be thirty days old, and from then on it was acceptable
Thirty days is not the rule; the animal stayed with its mother seven days (22:27).
It had to stay with its mother seven days, and from the eighth day it was acceptable
It had to be weaned first, and from then on it was acceptable
Weaning is not mentioned; the animal stayed with its mother seven days (22:27).
It had to be firstborn and male, and from birth it was acceptable
Being firstborn and male is not required here; the animal had to stay with its mother seven days (22:27).
It could be offered on the day of birth, since it was a newborn
Offering on the day of birth is not allowed; the animal had to stay seven days with its mother (22:27).
In Leviticus 22, which condition made a male animal expressly forbidden as an offering anywhere in the land of Israel?
“You are not to present to the LORD an animal whose testicles are bruised, crushed, torn, or cut; you are not to sacrifice them in your land” (22:24).
Leviticus 22:24
It had been used for plowing fields all year
Plowing is not given as a disqualification in this verse; the ban is on animals whose testicles are bruised, crushed, torn, or cut (22:24).
Its testicles were bruised, crushed, torn, or cut
It was more than three years old, past its prime
Age over three years is not mentioned; the ban is on animals whose testicles are bruised, crushed, torn, or cut (22:24).
It had crossed a river on the way to the altar
Crossing a river is not mentioned; the ban is on animals whose testicles are bruised, crushed, torn, or cut (22:24).
It had belonged to a foreigner living in Israel
A foreigner’s animal was not banned for that reason; foreign residents could present offerings too (22:18), but not damaged animals (22:24–25).
In Leviticus 22, under what circumstance could a priest’s daughter eat her father’s food again after having been married outside the priestly household?
If a priest’s daughter “with no children becomes widowed or divorced and returns to her father’s house, she may share her father’s food as in her youth” (22:13).
Leviticus 22:13
If she returned to her father’s house for a week-long feast
The Feast of Booths is not mentioned; the condition was being widowed or divorced with no children and returning home (22:13).
If she brought a thank offering to the priest with a fifth added
A thank offering is not the condition; she had to be widowed or divorced, childless, and back in her father’s house (22:13).
If she became widowed or divorced, had no children, and returned to her father’s house
If her husband gave permission while she remained married to him
Her husband’s permission is not the condition, and a priest’s daughter married to a layman may not eat (22:12–13).
If she paid a redemption price to the priest while still married
A redemption price is not mentioned; the condition was being widowed or divorced, childless, and back in her father’s house (22:13).
According to Leviticus 22:29–30, when was a thank offering to the LORD to be eaten?
Leviticus 22:30 says of the thank offering, “It must be eaten that same day. Do not leave any of it until morning.”
Leviticus 22:29-30
On that day and the next, but not the third
Eating on the next day was allowed for a vow or freewill offering (Leviticus 7:16), not a thank offering (22:30).
On that same day, leaving none until morning
Within seven days, before the next Sabbath
Seven days are not mentioned; the thank offering “must be eaten that same day” (22:30).
At any time, as long as it stayed clean
There was a time limit: “Do not leave any of it until morning” (22:30).
Only after the evening of the third day
Meat left to the third day had to be burned up (Leviticus 7:17); the thank offering was eaten the same day (22:30).
In Leviticus 23, when the LORD described Israel’s weekly sacred assembly, what was the seventh day to be?
Leviticus 23:3 says the seventh day is a Sabbath of complete rest, a day of sacred assembly on which no work is to be done.
Leviticus 23:3
A market day
A market day would involve work; 23:3 forbids any work on the Sabbath.
A Sabbath of complete rest
A day for gathering manna
Manna was gathered for six days and not on the Sabbath (Exodus 16:23–26), which is the opposite of 23:3.
A new moon feast
A new moon feast is a different observance (Numbers 28:11), not the weekly sacred assembly.
A day for military service
Military service is not a Sabbath activity; 23:3 forbids all work.
In the appointed feasts given through Moses in Leviticus 23, when does the Passover to the LORD begin?
Leviticus 23:5 says the Passover to the LORD begins at twilight on the fourteenth day of the first month.
Leviticus 23:5
At dawn on the first day of the first month
Dawn on the first day of the first month is not the Passover; the Passover is on the fourteenth (23:5).
At twilight on the fourteenth day of the first month
At noon on the tenth day of the seventh month
The tenth day of the seventh month is the Day of Atonement (23:27), not Passover.
At sunset on the fifteenth day of the third month
The fifteenth day is the start of Unleavened Bread in the first month (23:6), not the third month.
At midnight on the seventh day of the seventh month
The Passover is at twilight on the fourteenth day, not at midnight; midnight is when the firstborn of Egypt were struck (Exodus 12:29).
In Leviticus 23, what were the Israelites commanded to eat during the Feast of Unleavened Bread?
Leviticus 23:6 says that for seven days the people must eat unleavened bread.
Leviticus 23:6
Bread without yeast
Roasted lamb only
Roasted lamb was part of the Passover meal (Exodus 12:8), but the feast of Unleavened Bread in 23:6 is about bread without yeast.
Manna cakes
Manna cakes were the people’s food in the wilderness (Numbers 11:8), not the feast’s requirement.
Bitter herbs only
Bitter herbs were eaten with the Passover meal (Exodus 12:8), not the only food of the seven days.
Honey cakes
Honey was not to be burned on the altar (Leviticus 2:11) and is not a required food of this feast.
In the festival calendar of Leviticus 23, how long does the Feast of Unleavened Bread last?
Leviticus 23:6 says that the Feast of Unleavened Bread begins on the fifteenth day and lasts seven days.
Leviticus 23:6
One day
One day is not the length; the Day of Atonement lasts one day (23:27), but Unleavened Bread lasts seven.
Three days
Three days is not given for this feast; Unleavened Bread lasts seven days (23:6).
Seven days
Ten days
Ten days is not the length; the tenth day of the first month was when Passover lambs were chosen (Exodus 12:3).
Forty days
Forty days is the length of Moses’ stay on Sinai (Exodus 34:28), not of this feast.
In Leviticus 23, what marked the sacred assembly on the first day of the seventh month?
Leviticus 23:24–25 says the first day of the seventh month is a day of rest, a sacred assembly announced by trumpet blasts, with no regular work.
Leviticus 23:24-25
The waving of two loaves
Waving two loaves belongs to the Feast of Weeks (23:17), not the first day of the seventh month.
The release of a scapegoat
Releasing a scapegoat is part of the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:10), on the tenth day.
Trumpet blasts and complete rest
Crossing the Jordan River
Crossing the Jordan is a separate event in Israel’s history (Joshua 3), not a feast marker.
Lighting the menorah all night
Lighting the lamp all night is a tabernacle duty (Exodus 27:20–21), not described for this assembly.
When Leviticus 23 names the Day of Atonement, on which day of the seventh month does it fall?
Leviticus 23:27 says the tenth day of the seventh month is the Day of Atonement.
Leviticus 23:27
First day
The first day of the seventh month is the day of trumpet blasts (23:24).
Seventh day
The seventh day of the seventh month is not named as a feast; the Day of Atonement is on the tenth (23:27).
Tenth day
Fourteenth day
The fourteenth day of the first month is the Passover (23:5), not the Day of Atonement.
Twenty-fifth day
The twenty-fifth day is the day the wall of Jerusalem was finished in Elul (Nehemiah 6:15), not the Day of Atonement.
During the Feast of Tabernacles in Leviticus 23, where were native-born Israelites told to live for seven days?
Leviticus 23:42 says all the native-born of Israel must dwell in booths for seven days.
Leviticus 23:42
In stone houses
Stone houses were what they normally lived in; the feast called for temporary booths (23:42).
In booths
In caves
Caves were refuges in troubled times (Judges 6:2), not the feast’s requirement.
In upper rooms
Upper rooms appear in the New Testament (Acts 1:13), not in this command.
In Egypt
Egypt is what the booths remembered: God made the Israelites dwell in booths when He brought them out of Egypt (23:43).
In the harvest instruction attached to the appointed times in Leviticus 23, for whom were the edges of the field and the gleanings to be left?
Leviticus 23:22 tells Israel not to reap to the edges of the field or gather the gleanings, but to leave them for the poor and the foreign resident.
Leviticus 23:22
The king and his army
The king and his army are never mentioned as recipients of gleanings in 23:22.
The priests only
The priests received portions of offerings (Leviticus 7:34), not the field’s edges and gleanings.
The poor and the foreign resident
The oldest son of each family
The oldest son’s inheritance is a different matter (Deuteronomy 21:17); 23:22 sends the gleanings to the poor.
Traveling merchants
Traveling merchants are not named; 23:22 names the poor and the foreign resident.
In Leviticus 23, when Israel entered the land and reaped its harvest, what first item were they to bring to the priest?
Leviticus 23:10 says that when Israel entered the land and reaped its harvest, they were to bring to the priest a sheaf of the firstfruits of their harvest.
Leviticus 23:10
A basket of figs
A basket of figs is not named; Deuteronomy 26:2 speaks of a basket of firstfruits of all produce, but Leviticus 23:10 names a sheaf.
A pair of doves
A pair of doves is a poor person’s sacrifice (Leviticus 12:8), not the firstfruits offering.
The first sheaf of the harvest
Twelve stones from the Jordan
Twelve stones from the Jordan were set up as a memorial (Joshua 4:3), not given to the priest at harvest.
A jar of oil
A jar of oil is not what 23:10 requires; the offering was a sheaf of grain.
In the firstfruits instruction of Leviticus 23, when was the priest to wave the sheaf before the LORD?
Leviticus 23:11 says the priest is to wave the sheaf before the LORD on the day after the Sabbath.
Leviticus 23:11
On the day before the Sabbath
The day before the Sabbath is not the time; 23:11 says the day after the Sabbath.
On the day after the Sabbath
On the first day of the first month
The first day of the first month is not the time given; the sheaf was waved on the day after the Sabbath (23:11).
On the tenth day of the seventh month
The tenth day of the seventh month is the Day of Atonement (23:27), not the day of waving the sheaf.
On the eighth day after Passover
The day after the Sabbath is the one specified; no eighth day after Passover is named in 23:11.
According to Leviticus 23, which foods were forbidden until the day the firstfruits offering was brought to God?
Leviticus 23:14 says you must not eat any bread, roasted grain, or new grain until the very day you have brought the offering to your God.
Leviticus 23:14
Fish, figs, and milk
Fish, figs, and milk are not forbidden by 23:14, which names only bread, roasted grain, and new grain.
Bread, roasted grain, and new grain
Lamb, oil, and wine
Lamb, oil, and wine are not forbidden here; 23:13 uses oil and wine in the offering itself.
Dates, raisins, and honey
Dates, raisins, and honey are not mentioned in 23:14.
Garlic, leeks, and onions
Garlic, leeks, and onions are foods the Israelites craved in the wilderness (Numbers 11:5), not forbidden in 23:14.
In the Feast of Weeks instructions in Leviticus 23, how long were the Israelites to count from the day after the Sabbath until the new grain offering?
Leviticus 23:15–16 says to count off seven full weeks, which is fifty days, until the day after the seventh Sabbath.
Leviticus 23:15-16
Twelve days
Twelve days is not the count; 23:15–16 gives seven weeks and then fifty days.
Thirty days
Thirty days is not the count in 23:16, which gives fifty days.
Forty days
Forty days is the length of the flood rain (Genesis 7:12) and Moses’ stay on Sinai (Exodus 34:28), not this count.
Fifty days
Seventy days
Seventy days is not given; 23:16 gives fifty days, one day more than seven full weeks.
In Leviticus 23, how many loaves of bread were to be brought from the Israelites’ dwellings as a wave offering at the Feast of Weeks?
Leviticus 23:17 says to bring two loaves of bread from your dwellings as a wave offering.
Leviticus 23:17
One loaf
One loaf is not enough; 23:17 calls for two loaves.

Seven male lambs, one young bull, and two rams

Three young bulls and seven goats are not the animals named in 23:18.

One lamb for sin and seven goats for peace do not match 23:19.
On the Day of Atonement in Leviticus 23, what was to happen to anyone in Israel who did not humble himself on that day?

From sunrise to sunset on the tenth day only

From the new moon until the next Sabbath is not the pattern; the Day of Atonement is a single day from evening to evening (23:32).
In the instructions for the Feast of Tabernacles in Leviticus 23, what were the Israelites told to take on the first day as they rejoiced before the LORD?

Unleavened bread, bitter herbs, salt, and oil for the offering
Unleavened bread, bitter herbs, salt, and oil belong to Passover and offerings, not the first-day items of Tabernacles.
On the day the firstfruits sheaf was waved in Leviticus 23, what grain and drink offerings accompanied the year-old male lamb without blemish?

One-tenth of an ephah of flour with oil and half a hin of water

Two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil and a quarter hin of wine
Three-tenths of an ephah of barley meal and one full hin of wine

Aaron

Aaron was “to tend the lamps continually before the LORD from evening until morning” (24:3).

From evening until morning

In the bread instructions of Leviticus 24, how many loaves were to be baked from fine flour and set before the LORD?

In one stack of twelve
They were not stacked in one pile; they were set in two rows of six (24:6).
In two rows of six

Every new moon

Building houses and digging wells are not mentioned in the sabbatical law (25:4).
Threshing and baking
Threshing and baking are not forbidden; 25:4 names only sowing and pruning.

One full year

A murderer is put to death (35:16–21); stoning an unintentional killer is not prescribed.
Sell him as a servant to pay the family of the dead man
The text does not allow selling a manslayer; he was to stay in the city of refuge (35:25).
Protect him from the avenger of blood and return him to the city of refuge
Send him away to live among the foreigners in Egypt for good
Egypt is not mentioned; the assembly returned him to the city of refuge (35:25).
Require him to leave Israel permanently and never return
He was not banished; after the high priest’s death he could return to the land he owned (35:28).
In Numbers 35, how long was the manslayer to remain in the city of refuge?
“He must live there until the death of the high priest, who was anointed with the holy oil” (35:25).
Numbers 35:25, 28
For seven days of cleansing and sacrifice at the sanctuary
Seven days is not the term; he stayed until the high priest died (35:25).
For one full year, after which the avenger’s anger would have cooled
One year is not the term; the stay lasted until the high priest’s death (35:25, 35:28).
Until the next Jubilee year proclaimed throughout the land
The Jubilee returned land to families (Leviticus 25:10), but the manslayer’s release came at the death of the high priest (35:28).
Until the death of the high priest who was anointed with the holy oil
For the rest of his life, with no possibility of ever returning home
The stay was not for life: “only after the death of the high priest may he return to the land he owns” (35:28).
According to Numbers 35, what if the manslayer went outside the boundary of his city of refuge before the high priest died, and the avenger of blood killed him?
If the avenger found him outside the city of refuge and killed him, “the avenger will not be guilty of bloodshed” (35:27).
Numbers 35:26-28
The avenger was guilty of murder
The avenger was not guilty; the manslayer had to stay inside the city until the high priest died (35:26–28).
The avenger had to flee to a city of refuge
The avenger was not guilty, so he did not need to flee anywhere (35:27).
The congregation had to execute the avenger
The congregation was not to execute him; the verse says he is not guilty of bloodshed (35:27).
The avenger was not guilty of bloodshed
The high priest had to offer a sin offering for the avenger
No sin offering is mentioned; the manslayer’s confinement ended at the high priest’s death (35:28).
In the legal standard given in Numbers 35, which statement is true about convicting a murderer?
“The murderer is to be put to death on the testimony of the witnesses. But no one is to be put to death based on the testimony of a lone witness” (35:30).
Numbers 35:30
The testimony of one lone witness is enough to put a murderer to death
The text forbids execution on a lone witness’s testimony (35:30; compare Deuteronomy 17:6).
Only the avenger’s word is required, since he is the nearest relative
The law required witnesses, not just the avenger’s word (35:30).
The murderer may be put to death on the testimony of witnesses, but not on one lone witness
No witnesses are needed if a body is found and the killer is known
A death sentence required the testimony of witnesses; a body alone was not enough (35:30).
Only priests may testify, and the high priest must confirm every verdict
The law speaks of witnesses in general; it does not limit testimony to priests (35:30).
In Numbers 35, what payment was forbidden both for a murderer who deserved death and for a manslayer who wanted to return home before the death of the high priest?
“You are not to accept a ransom for the life of a murderer who deserves to die” (35:31), and “Nor should you accept a ransom for the person who flees to a city of refuge” (35:32).
Numbers 35:31-32
A tithe
Tithes supported Israel’s worship (Leviticus 27:30), but they could not buy off these penalties (35:31–32).
A grain offering
A grain offering (Leviticus 2:1) was an act of worship; it could not replace the death penalty or shorten a stay in refuge (35:31–32).
A peace offering
A peace offering (Leviticus 3:1) was a fellowship sacrifice; verses 31–32 forbid a ransom instead.
A ransom
A firstborn animal
The firstborn animal belonged to the LORD (Exodus 13:2); it is not what these verses forbid.
In Numbers 35, what alone could make atonement for land polluted by bloodshed?
“No atonement can be made for the land on which the blood is shed, except by the blood of the one who shed it” (35:33).
Numbers 35:33-34
The Day of Atonement sacrifices
The Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16) covered Israel’s sins, but verse 35:33 says land polluted by murder is cleansed only by the murderer’s blood.
The high priest’s intercession
The high priest’s death ended the manslayer’s stay in the city of refuge (35:28); it did not atone for polluted land.
Exile of the killer to another nation
Exile is not offered as atonement; the text says only the blood of the one who shed it (35:33).
Silver paid to the sanctuary
Silver paid as a ransom is forbidden (35:31–32); it could not atone for the land (35:33).
The blood of the one who shed the blood
In the closing chapter of the Book of Numbers, which women were at the center of the inheritance case brought before Moses and the Israelite leaders on the plains of Moab?
Numbers 36:1–2 says the family heads of Gilead’s clan came to Moses about the inheritance of Zelophehad’s daughters.
Numbers 36:1-2
The daughters of Zelophehad
The daughters of Caleb
Caleb is not connected to this case; the inheritance question concerns Zelophehad’s daughters (36:2).
The daughters of Aaron
Aaron’s family is not involved in this land case; the clan was from Manasseh (36:1).
The daughters of Korah
Korah’s daughters are not mentioned in the chapter; Zelophehad’s daughters are (36:2).
The daughters of Jethro
Jethro’s daughters are not part of this case; Zelophehad’s daughters held the inheritance (36:2).
In Numbers 36, Zelophehad is identified with which tribe of Israel?
Numbers 36:1 identifies the clan of Gilead son of Machir son of Manasseh, one of the clans of Joseph, as bringing the case about Zelophehad’s daughters.
Numbers 36:1
Judah
Judah is not the tribe in this case; the leaders were from Manasseh (36:1).
Levi
Levi received no tribal land allotment here; the case concerns Manasseh’s clan (36:1).
Manasseh son of Joseph
Benjamin
Benjamin is not named; the clan was of Manasseh son of Joseph (36:1).
Dan
Dan is not named in the chapter; the clan was of Manasseh (36:1).
When clan leaders from the descendants of Joseph spoke to Moses in Numbers 36, what did they fear would happen if Zelophehad’s daughters married men from another Israelite tribe?
Numbers 36:3 says that if the daughters married men from other tribes, their inheritance would be withdrawn from their fathers’ portion and added to the husbands’ tribe.
Numbers 36:3
Their names would be removed from the census
Census names are not mentioned; the worry was about land being transferred (36:3).
Their inheritance would be added to another tribe
Their marriages would be forbidden entirely
The leaders did not ask for marriage to be forbidden; Moses allowed them to marry anyone they pleased within their father’s tribe (36:6).
Their land would become temple property
Temple property is not mentioned; the fear was land added to another tribe (36:3).
Their husbands would move into Manasseh by force
Forced moves are not mentioned; the issue was the land passing to the husbands’ tribe (36:3).
In the appeal recorded in Numbers 36, which event did the leaders say would make that land transfer stand with the husbands’ tribe?
Numbers 36:4 says that when the Jubilee comes, their inheritance would be added to the tribe into which they marry.
Numbers 36:4
Passover
Passover is not mentioned in their argument; they cited the Jubilee (36:4).
The Feast of Weeks
The Feast of Weeks is not mentioned in this chapter; the appeal named the Jubilee (36:4).
The Day of Atonement
The Day of Atonement (Leviticus 23:27) is not what the leaders cited in 36:4.
The Year of Jubilee
The Sabbatical year
The sabbatical year is not mentioned in the appeal; the leaders spoke of the Jubilee (36:4).
What ruling did Moses give, at the LORD’s command in Numbers 36, concerning whom the daughters of Zelophehad could marry?
Numbers 36:6 says the LORD commanded that they may marry anyone they please, provided they marry within a clan of the tribe of their father.
Numbers 36:6
Only men who served as priests at the tabernacle
Priests are not specified; the only limit was marrying within their father’s tribe (36:6).
Only men from the tribe of Judah, the royal line
Judah is not named; the limit was their father’s tribe, which was Manasseh (36:6, 36:12).
Anyone they pleased, provided they married within a clan of their father’s tribe
Only the eldest sons of the leading tribes of Israel
No limit to eldest sons is given; they could marry anyone they pleased within the clan (36:6).
No one at all until after the next Jubilee had passed
The ruling did not delay marriage until the Jubilee; they could marry freely within the tribe (36:6).
At the end of Numbers 36, how does the chapter say the daughters’ marriages affected their inherited land?
Numbers 36:12 says they married within the clans of the descendants of Manasseh, and their inheritance remained within the tribe of their father’s clan.
Numbers 36:12
It was transferred to Judah
Judah is not mentioned; the land stayed in their father’s tribe (36:12).
It remained within the tribe of their father’s clan
It was divided among several tribes
The land was not divided among tribes; it stayed in one tribe (36:12).
It became property of the Levites
The Levites are not mentioned; the inheritance stayed with Manasseh’s clan (36:12).
It returned to Moses for reassignment
No reassignment by Moses took place; the inheritance remained within their father’s clan (36:12).
Which list correctly names the five daughters of Zelophehad mentioned in Numbers 36 as obeying Moses?
Numbers 36:11 names the daughters of Zelophehad as Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah.
Numbers 36:11
Tamar, Dinah, Abigail, Miriam, Deborah
Tamar, Dinah, Abigail, Miriam, and Deborah are other biblical women, none of them Zelophehad’s daughters (36:11).
Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, Noah
Ruth, Naomi, Orpah, Leah, Rachel
Ruth, Naomi, Orpah, Leah, and Rachel are from other stories, not Zelophehad’s family (36:11).
Jael, Judith, Esther, Vashti, Hadassah
Jael, Judith, Esther, Vashti, and Hadassah come from other settings, not Zelophehad’s daughters (36:11).
Sarah, Rebekah, Leah, Rachel, Dinah
Sarah, Rebekah, Leah, Rachel, and Dinah are Genesis matriarchs and daughters, not Zelophehad’s daughters (36:11).
According to Numbers 36, whom did Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah marry?
Numbers 36:11 says they were married to cousins on their father’s side.
Numbers 36:11
Men from the tribe of Judah
Marrying Judah’s men would have moved their inheritance to another tribe, the very thing forbidden (36:6–7).
Sons of Aaron
Aaron’s sons are not mentioned; the daughters married cousins (36:11).
Their cousins on their father’s side
Foreigners from Midian
Marrying foreigners is not mentioned; they married within their father’s tribe (36:11–12).
Princes from Ephraim
Ephraim’s princes are not mentioned; they married cousins within Manasseh (36:11–12).
In the opening of Numbers 36, which ancestry correctly identifies the family heads who brought this case before Moses?
Numbers 36:1 names the family heads of the clan of Gilead son of Machir son of Manasseh, one of the clans of Joseph.
Numbers 36:1
Gilead son of Machir, son of Manasseh, from the descendants of Joseph
Korah son of Izhar, son of Kohath, from Levi
Korah son of Izhar, of Levi, led a rebellion (Numbers 16:1), not this inheritance case.
Nahshon son of Amminadab, from Judah
Nahshon was a leader of Judah, not part of the Gilead clan of Manasseh (36:1).
Elishama son of Ammihud, from Ephraim
Elishama of Ephraim is not the ancestry given here; the family heads were from Manasseh (36:1).
Balaam son of Beor, from Pethor
Balaam son of Beor was from Pethor and is not connected with this case (36:1).
Which statement best matches the inheritance principle Moses repeated in Numbers 36 for all Israelite tribes?
Numbers 36:9 says no inheritance may be transferred from one tribe to another, for each tribe of Israel must retain its inheritance.
Numbers 36:7-9
Every inheritance must be reassigned at Jubilee
Numbers 36:7–9 says the opposite: inheritance was not reassigned between tribes.
Inheritance may pass freely from tribe to tribe through marriage
Moses ruled that inheritance may not pass from tribe to tribe (36:7, 36:9).
Each tribe of Israel must retain the inheritance of its fathers
Only sons may ever receive land in Israel
Zelophehad’s daughters inherited land, so daughters could receive it (36:2).
Priests must control all tribal property
Priests are not given control of tribal property; each tribe keeps its own inheritance (36:7).
5: In the opening of Deuteronomy 1, who is the speaker addressing all Israel in the wilderness east of the Jordan?
“These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel in the wilderness east of the Jordan” (1:1).
Deuteronomy 1:1
Aaron
Aaron had already died on Mount Hor (Numbers 20:28).
Joshua
Joshua is mentioned as the one who will lead Israel into the land (1:38), not the speaker.
Moses
Caleb
Caleb appears in the speech as the faithful exception (1:36), not as its speaker.
Eleazar
Eleazar succeeded Aaron as priest (Numbers 20:28); Moses is the speaker (1:1).
In Moses’ opening setting for this speech, where were these words spoken to Israel?
Moses spoke “in the wilderness east of the Jordan—in the Arabah” (1:1), “on the east side of the Jordan in the land of Moab” (1:5).
Deuteronomy 1:1, 5
West of the Jordan at Gilgal, after Israel had crossed into Canaan
Israel camped at Gilgal only after crossing the Jordan under Joshua (Joshua 4:19).
East of the Jordan in the wilderness, in the Arabah, in the land of Moab
In Jerusalem near the temple, before the assembly of all Israel
Solomon later stood before the assembly at the temple (1 Kings 8:22); Moses spoke east of the Jordan (1:1).
In Egypt beside the Nile, just before the night of the Passover
Israel had left Egypt forty years earlier (1:3); this speech was given in Moab (1:5).
At Hebron in the hill country of Canaan, near the cave of Machpelah
Hebron and the cave of Machpelah lay in Canaan (Genesis 23:19), which Moses never entered (1:37).
When Moses recalled the LORD’s command to Israel, at what mountain did God say, “You have stayed at this mountain long enough”?
“The LORD our God said to us at Horeb: ‘You have stayed at this mountain long enough’” (1:6).
Deuteronomy 1:6-7
Mount Carmel
Mount Carmel is where Elijah confronted the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18:20).
Mount Zion
Zion became the City of David (2 Samuel 5:7), long after Moses.
Mount Hor
Mount Hor is where Aaron died (Numbers 20:28).
Horeb
Mount Moriah
Moriah is where Abraham was told to offer Isaac (Genesis 22:2) and Solomon built the temple (2 Chronicles 3:1).
According to Moses’ review of Israel’s travels, how long was the journey from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea by way of Mount Seir?
“It is an eleven-day journey from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea by way of Mount Seir” (1:2).
Deuteronomy 1:2
3 days
Three days is the journey Moses asked Pharaoh for, to sacrifice in the wilderness (Exodus 3:18).
7 days
Seven days is not given; 1:2 says the journey took eleven days.
11 days
40 days
Forty days is how long the spies explored Canaan (Numbers 13:25).
70 days
Seventy days is how long the Egyptians mourned Jacob (Genesis 50:3).
Before Moses explained the law east of the Jordan, which two defeated kings did he mention?
Moses had defeated “Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon” and “Og king of Bashan” (1:4).
Deuteronomy 1:4
Balak king of Moab and Balaam son of Beor
Balak of Moab hired Balaam to curse Israel (Numbers 22:2, 5); neither is named as defeated in 1:4.
Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan
Saul king of Israel and Goliath of Gath
Saul and Goliath belong to David’s era (1 Samuel 17:2), centuries after Moses.
Jabin king of Canaan and his commander Sisera
Jabin and his commander Sisera oppressed Israel in the days of the judges (Judges 4:2).
Pharaoh king of Egypt and Abimelech of Gerar
Abimelech of Gerar dealt with Abraham (Genesis 20:2); neither he nor Pharaoh is named in 1:4.
In Deuteronomy 1, why did Moses say he needed help leading Israel?
Moses said, “How can I bear your troubles, burdens, and disputes all by myself?” (1:12).
Deuteronomy 1:9-12
He was too old and weak to go out and come in before them
Moses spoke of age only at the end, at 120 (Deuteronomy 31:2); in 1:9–12 the burden is the people’s size.
He could not bear their burdens, troubles, and disputes alone
He planned to return to his father-in-law’s home in Midian
Moses had long since left Jethro in Midian to return to Egypt (Exodus 4:18).
He had broken the stone tablets and lost the Book of the Law
Moses broke the first tablets at the golden calf (Exodus 32:19), but that is not his reason in 1:9–12.
He feared another attack by the Amalekites at Rephidim
The Amalekites attacked at Rephidim (Exodus 17:8), but Moses gave no such reason here.
When Moses told Israel to choose leaders from the tribes, what qualities were those men to have?
“Choose for yourselves wise, understanding, and respected men from each of your tribes” (1:13).
Deuteronomy 1:13
Tall, wealthy, and strong
Height marked Saul, a head taller than anyone (1 Samuel 9:2); Moses asked for wisdom and understanding.
Skilled in music and writing
Moses asked for character, not skills: wise, understanding, and respected men (1:13).
Wise, understanding, and respected
Young, unmarried, and swift
Nothing about age or marriage is said; the leaders were to be wise and respected (1:13).
Priests from Levi only
The leaders came “from each of your tribes” (1:13), not from Levi only.
In Moses’ appointment of leaders over Israel, which grouping matches the levels of command named in Deuteronomy 1?
Moses appointed them “as commanders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens” (1:15).
Deuteronomy 1:15
Thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens
Thousands, fifties, twenties, and fives
Twenties and fives are not mentioned; the levels were thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens (1:15).
Hundreds, seventies, thirties, and threes
Seventies, thirties, and threes are not among the levels named in 1:15.
Tens, nines, eights, and sevens
These numbers are invented; 1:15 names thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens.
Tribes, clans, households, and tents
Tribe, clan, family recalls the lot that exposed Achan (Joshua 7:14), not the command levels of 1:15.
While charging judges during Israel’s wilderness period, what standard did Moses command them to follow in disputes?
Moses charged, “Show no partiality in judging; hear both small and great alike” (1:17).
Deuteronomy 1:16-17
Favor the elder brother
Judges were to judge fairly “between a man and his brother” (1:16), with no favoritism.
Judge Israelites only, not foreigners
Foreigners were included: judges were to judge fairly between a man and “a foreign resident” (1:16).
Show no partiality and hear both small and great alike
Decide every case by lot
The land, not court cases, would be divided by lot (Numbers 26:55).
Delay every case until a priest arrived
Hard cases were to be brought to Moses himself (1:17), not delayed for a priest.
After traveling from Horeb through the “vast and terrifying wilderness,” what place did Israel reach before Moses urged them to take the land?
Leaving Horeb and crossing the terrifying wilderness, “we reached Kadesh-barnea” (1:19).
Deuteronomy 1:19-20
Beersheba
Beersheba was named in Abraham’s day (Genesis 21:31) and lay in southern Canaan.
Kadesh-barnea
Jericho
Jericho lay west of the Jordan, where Joshua later sent spies (Joshua 2:1); Israel had reached Kadesh-barnea (1:19).
Shiloh
Shiloh is where the Tent of Meeting was set up after the conquest (Joshua 18:1).
Ramah
Ramah was Samuel’s home town (1 Samuel 7:17).
In Moses’ retelling of events at Kadesh-barnea, why did the people ask to send men ahead?
They asked to send men “to search out the land and bring us word of what route to follow and which cities to enter” (1:22).
Deuteronomy 1:22
To count the fighting men of the tribes once more
The tribes were numbered in the two censuses (Numbers 26:2); the scouts in 1:22 were to search out the land.
To find water for the people from the rock at Horeb
Water came from the rock at Horeb in an earlier episode (Exodus 17:6).
To spy out the land and report the route and the cities
To ask the king of Edom for passage through his land
Moses later sent messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom (Numbers 20:14), but that was not this request.
To choose a site for an altar in the hill country
No altar is mentioned; the scouts were to report the route and the cities (1:22).
When Moses agreed to the plan to scout the land, how many men did he choose, and how were they selected?
Moses “selected twelve men from among you, one from each tribe” (1:23).
Deuteronomy 1:23
10 men, all from Judah
The scouts came “one from each tribe” (1:23); Judah’s scout was Caleb (Numbers 13:6).
12 men, one from each tribe
70 elders, chosen by lot
Seventy elders were gathered on another occasion (Numbers 11:16).
2 men, both Levites
Two spies were sent to Jericho by Joshua (Joshua 2:1), not by Moses here.
40 soldiers, five from each tribe
Forty is the number of days the spies spent exploring (Numbers 13:25), not the number of men.
After the spies returned with fruit in Moses’ account, how did they describe the land the LORD was giving Israel?
The scouts reported, “It is a good land that the LORD our God is giving us” (1:25).
Deuteronomy 1:25
Too barren for settlement
They brought back some of its fruit (1:24–25), proof that the land was productive.
Good
Full of idols and unusable
The scouts’ report in 1:25 was simply that the land is good.
Better left for Egypt
The people later wanted to return to Egypt (Numbers 14:4), but the scouts called the land good (1:25).
Suitable only for shepherds
Grazing land was what Reuben and Gad wanted east of the Jordan (Numbers 32:1).
In the account of the spies that Moses retold, which valley did they reach while exploring the hill country?
The scouts “came to the Valley of Eshcol and spied out the land” (1:24).
Deuteronomy 1:24
Valley of Siddim
The Valley of Siddim was the site of the kings’ battle in Abraham’s day (Genesis 14:3).
Valley of Elah
The Valley of Elah is where Israel faced the Philistines and Goliath (1 Samuel 17:2).
Valley of Eshcol
Valley of Jezreel
The Valley of Jezreel is where Midian camped against Gideon (Judges 6:33).
Valley of Aijalon
The Valley of Aijalon is where Joshua commanded the moon to stand still (Joshua 10:12).
In their grumbling at Kadesh-barnea, what fear did the Israelites report about the land’s inhabitants and cities?
They said, “The people are larger and taller than we are; the cities are large, with walls up to the heavens. We even saw the descendants of the Anakim there” (1:28).
Deuteronomy 1:27-28
The land had no water and no roads
Lack of water was the complaint at Meribah (Numbers 20:2); here they feared giants and walled cities (1:28).
The people were larger and taller, the cities were fortified to the heavens, and Anakites were there
The sea blocked the entrance and Philistines held iron chariots
Iron chariots appear later, in the plains Judah could not take (Judges 1:19).
Snow covered the land all year
No weather is mentioned; they feared the people’s size and the walled cities (1:28).
Wild beasts had taken every city
Wild animals come up in Deuteronomy 7:22, as a reason for driving out the nations little by little.
To reassure the frightened nation, what picture did Moses use for God’s care in the wilderness?
The LORD carried them in the wilderness “as a man carries his son” (1:31).
Deuteronomy 1:29-31
A shepherd finding one lost sheep
The lost sheep is Jesus’ parable (Luke 15:4).
An eagle stirring up its nest
The eagle stirring its nest comes in Moses’ later song (Deuteronomy 32:11), not in chapter 1.
A king building a fortress
No fortress image appears; Moses pictured a man carrying his son (1:31).
A man carrying his son
A priest lighting the lampstand
Aaron tended the lamps of the Tent (Leviticus 24:3), but this image is not used in 1:31.
In Moses’ reminder of the LORD’s guidance on the journey, how did God go ahead of Israel to show them the route they should travel?
God went before them “in the fire by night and in the cloud by day” to show them the road (1:33).
Deuteronomy 1:32-33
By thunder in the day and stars at night
Thunder came at Sinai when God descended on the mountain (Exodus 19:16), not as a daily guide.
By an angel with a drawn sword
The angel with a drawn sword stood in Balaam’s path (Numbers 22:31).
By fire at night and cloud by day
By dreams to the elders only
No dreams are mentioned; God led openly by fire and cloud (1:33).
By the Urim and Thummim alone
The Urim was later consulted through Eleazar for Joshua (Numbers 27:21), not the guide on the journey.
When the LORD swore that the evil generation would not see the good land, which man was singled out as the exception because he followed the LORD wholeheartedly?
No one of that generation would see the land “except Caleb son of Jephunneh … because he followed the LORD wholeheartedly” (1:36).
Deuteronomy 1:34-36
Aaron son of Amram
Aaron son of Amram (Exodus 6:20) died on Mount Hor without entering the land (Numbers 20:28).
Korah son of Izhar
Korah rebelled and was swallowed by the earth (Numbers 16:32).
Caleb son of Jephunneh
Eleazar son of Aaron
Eleazar later helped allot the land (Joshua 14:1), but 1:36 singles out only Caleb for wholehearted devotion.
Othniel son of Kenaz
Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb’s nephew, became Israel’s first judge (Judges 3:9).
In Moses’ retelling of God’s judgment after Israel’s rebellion, who was told he would enter the land and enable Israel to inherit it?
“Joshua son of Nun, who stands before you, will enter it … for he will enable Israel to inherit the land” (1:38).
Deuteronomy 1:37-38
Phinehas son of Eleazar
Phinehas son of Eleazar is remembered for his zeal at Peor (Numbers 25:7).
Joshua son of Nun
Gershon son of Levi
Gershon was one of Levi’s three sons (Exodus 6:16), long dead by this time.
Hur son of Caleb
Hur helped hold up Moses’ hands at the battle with Amalek (Exodus 17:12).
Samuel son of Elkanah
Samuel son of Hannah and Elkanah was born centuries later (1 Samuel 1:20).
After Israel went up into the Amorite hill country against God’s warning, how did Moses describe their defeat?
“The Amorites who lived in the hills came out against you and chased you like a swarm of bees. They routed you from Seir all the way to Hormah” (1:44).
Deuteronomy 1:42-44
The Amalekites captured the ark of the covenant and burned the camp at Kadesh
Amalekites joined this attack (Numbers 14:45), but the ark was captured only centuries later, by the Philistines (1 Samuel 4:11).
The Amorites chased them like a swarm of bees and routed them from Seir as far as Hormah
The Moabites drove them back across the Jordan and drowned many in its waters
No river battle is described; the Amorites chased them from Seir to Hormah (1:44).
The Canaanites took them captive and sold them as slaves back into Egypt
No one was taken captive; Israel returned and wept before the LORD (1:45).
The Midianites swept down on them in the Valley of Jezreel and scattered them
The Midianites camped in the Valley of Jezreel against Gideon (Judges 6:33).
In Deuteronomy 2, after Israel had traveled around the hill country of Seir for many days, what direction did the LORD tell them to turn?
Deuteronomy 2:3 records the LORD saying the people had wandered around the hill country long enough and telling them to turn to the north.
Deuteronomy 2:1-3
East
East is not the direction given; the LORD said to turn north (2:3).
West
West is not the direction given; the LORD said to turn north (2:3).
North
South
South is not the direction given; the LORD said to turn north (2:3).
Back toward Egypt
Going back toward Egypt was never the command; they were turned north toward the land God had promised (2:3).
While Moses retold Israel’s route near Seir in Deuteronomy 2, he said they would pass through the territory of the descendants of which man?

Lot

Esau
Ishmael

Jacob
Jacob’s descendants are Israel itself; Esau’s descendants were called Israel’s brothers (2:4).
Caleb
Caleb son of Jephunneh was a faithful man of Israel’s generation (Joshua 14:14), not the ancestor of the people of Seir.
As Israel passed near the descendants of Esau in Seir in Deuteronomy 2, how were they told to obtain food and water?

Deuteronomy 2:6
Take it by force

Pray and wait for manna only

Buy it with silver
Receive it as tribute
Israel was not told to demand tribute; it was told to pay for what it ate and drank (2:6).
In Deuteronomy 2, which mountain region had the LORD given to Esau as his possession, so Israel was not to provoke his descendants?
Deuteronomy 2:5 says the LORD had given Mount Seir to Esau as his possession, so Israel was not to provoke his descendants.
Deuteronomy 2:5
Mount Nebo
Mount Nebo is east of the Jordan, where Moses would later view the land (Deuteronomy 34:1), not Esau’s possession.
Mount Carmel
Mount Carmel is in Israel’s later land near the Mediterranean, not Esau’s possession (2:5).
Mount Hermon
Mount Hermon was part of the territory of Og, which Israel took (Deuteronomy 3:8–9), not Esau’s.
Mount Sinai
Mount Sinai (Horeb) is where Israel received the law, not the land God gave Esau (2:5).
Mount Seir
When Israel came near Moab in Deuteronomy 2, what place had the LORD given to the descendants of Lot as their possession?

Heshbon

Ar
Gilead
Gilead was a region Israel later received (Deuteronomy 3:12), not Lot’s land.
Bashan
Bashan was Og’s kingdom, which Israel took (Deuteronomy 3:3–4), not Lot’s land.
Hebron
Hebron was in Canaan, west of the Jordan, and was not part of Lot’s possession (2:9).
Looking back on the journey from Kadesh-barnea in Deuteronomy 2, how many years passed before Israel crossed the Brook Zered?

12 years
Twelve is the number of men sent as spies from Kadesh (Deuteronomy 1:23), not the years of travel.
20 years
Twenty falls short; Moses says thirty-eight years passed (2:14).
38 years
40 years

70 years
Seventy years is not tied to this journey; Moses gives thirty-eight (2:14).
In the wilderness review of Deuteronomy 2, what brook did Israel cross after that long period from Kadesh-barnea?
Deuteronomy 2:13 records the LORD saying, “Now arise and cross over the Brook of Zered.”
Deuteronomy 2:13
Jabbok
The Jabbok marked the border of the Ammonites (Deuteronomy 3:16), not this crossing.
Arnon
The Arnon Valley came after the Zered, when Israel moved against Sihon (2:24).
Kidron
The Kidron is a valley by Jerusalem (2 Samuel 15:23), far from this route.
Zered
Cherith
The brook Cherith is where Elijah was fed in a later era (1 Kings 17:3), not part of this journey.
In Moses’ description of ancient Moab in Deuteronomy 2, what were the former inhabitants called, a people great and many and as tall as the Anakites?
Deuteronomy 2:10–11 says the Emites used to live there, a people great and many, as tall as the Anakites; the Moabites called them Emites.
Deuteronomy 2:10-11
Horites
The Horites lived in Seir, not in the land of Ar (2:12).
Emites
Zamzummites
Zamzummites is the Ammonites’ name for the Rephaim in their land (2:20), not the Moabites’ name.
Avvim
The Avvim lived in villages as far as Gaza until the Caphtorites destroyed them (2:23).
Hivites
The Hivites were a Canaanite people (Genesis 10:17), not the former inhabitants of Moab’s land.
According to the historical note in Deuteronomy 2, which people formerly lived in Seir before the descendants of Esau dispossessed them?
Deuteronomy 2:12 says the Horites used to live in Seir, but the descendants of Esau drove them out and settled in their place.
Deuteronomy 2:12
Amalekites
The Amalekites are not named in Deuteronomy 2; the people displaced in Seir were the Horites (2:12).
Horites
Jebusites
The Jebusites held Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:6), not Seir.
Kenites
The Kenites are not named in Deuteronomy 2; the former Seir dwellers were the Horites (2:12).
Rephaim
The Rephaim lived in Moab and Ammon’s lands (2:11, 20), not Seir; Seir’s former people were the Horites.
As Israel came near the Ammonites in Deuteronomy 2, what did the LORD specifically forbid Israel to do?
Deuteronomy 2:19 tells Israel, when they got close to the Ammonites, not to harass them or provoke them, since the land was given to the descendants of Lot.
Deuteronomy 2:19
Intermarry with them
Intermarriage is not mentioned here; the command was not to harass or provoke them (2:19).
Harass them or provoke them
Build an altar in their land
No altar-building ban is given; the command was not to harass or provoke them (2:19).
Demand tribute from them
Israel was not told to demand tribute; it was told not to harass or provoke them (2:19).
Camp in Rabbah
Rabbah is the Ammonite capital (Deuteronomy 3:11), but camping there is not forbidden by name; the command was not to harass or provoke them (2:19).
In Deuteronomy 2’s note about Ammon, what name did the Ammonites use for the great people who once lived in that land?
Deuteronomy 2:20–21 says the Ammonites called the Rephaim who lived there Zamzummites, a people great and many, as tall as the Anakites.
Deuteronomy 2:20-21
Emites
Emites is the Moabites’ name for the Rephaim in their land (2:10–11), not the Ammonites’ name.
Anakites
The Anakites are the people these giants were compared with for height (2:21), not the Ammonites’ name for them.
Zamzummites
Avvim
The Avvim lived in villages as far as Gaza (2:23).
Caphtorites
The Caphtorites came out of Caphtor and destroyed the Avvim (2:23).
In the historical aside about the region near Gaza in Deuteronomy 2, who destroyed the Avvim and settled in their place?
Deuteronomy 2:23 says the Avvim, who lived in villages as far as Gaza, were destroyed by the Caphtorites, who came out of Caphtor and settled in their place.
Deuteronomy 2:23
Edomites
The Edomites (Esau’s descendants) drove out the Horites in Seir (2:12), not the Avvim.
Midianites
The Midianites are not named in this chapter; the Avvim were destroyed by the Caphtorites (2:23).
Hittites
The Hittites are not named in this chapter; the Avvim were destroyed by the Caphtorites (2:23).
Caphtorites
Amalekites
The Amalekites are not named in this chapter; the Avvim were destroyed by the Caphtorites (2:23).
After Israel was told to cross the Valley of Arnon in Deuteronomy 2, which ruler did the LORD say He had delivered into their hand?
Deuteronomy 2:24 says, “See, I have delivered into your hand Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land.”

Og king of Bashan, ruler of sixty cities

Balak king of Moab, son of Zippor

Sihon the Amorite king of Heshbon
Jabin king of Hazor, in northern Canaan
Jabin king of Hazor was a later enemy, in the days of Joshua and the judges (Joshua 11:1), not in this passage.
Eglon king of Moab, who oppressed Israel
Eglon king of Moab oppressed Israel in the time of the judges (Judges 3:12), long after this event.
From where did Moses send messengers with words of peace to Sihon king of Heshbon, according to Deuteronomy 2?

Deuteronomy 2:26
Wilderness of Paran
The Wilderness of Paran was where the spies returned to Kadesh (Numbers 13:26), not where Moses sent this message.
Wilderness of Kedemoth
Wilderness of Sin
The Wilderness of Sin was early in the exodus journey (Exodus 16:1), long before this message (2:26).
Plains of Jericho
The plains of Jericho were reached much later (Joshua 5:10), not where Moses sent this message (2:26).
Valley of Elah
The Valley of Elah is where Israel later faced the Philistines (1 Samuel 17:2), not here.
In Moses’ peace proposal to Sihon in Deuteronomy 2, what route did Israel promise to follow through the land?
Deuteronomy 2:27 has Moses promise Sihon, “we will stay on the main road. We will not turn to the right or to the left.”
Deuteronomy 2:27-28
The seacoast road through the lowlands
Israel did not propose a seacoast route; it promised to stay on the main road (2:27).
The shepherds’ trail through the hills
Israel did not propose a shepherds’ trail; it promised to stay on the main road (2:27).
The river path along the valley floor
Israel did not propose a river path; it promised to stay on the main road (2:27).
The main road, without turning right or left
A mountain pass traveled at night
Israel did not propose a mountain pass by night; it promised to stay on the main road (2:27).
According to Moses in Deuteronomy 2, why did Sihon king of Heshbon refuse to let Israel pass through his land?
Deuteronomy 2:30 says Sihon would not let Israel pass because the LORD “had made his spirit stubborn and his heart obstinate,” so that He might deliver him into their hand.
Deuteronomy 2:30
The Jordan was in flood at harvest time
The Jordan is not mentioned as a reason; the text points to the LORD making Sihon’s heart obstinate (2:30).
Israel refused to pay for food and water
Israel offered to pay silver for food and water (2:28), so refusing to pay was not the reason.
Balaam had warned him against Israel
Balaam is not mentioned in Deuteronomy 2; Sihon refused because the LORD made his heart obstinate (2:30).
Egypt had threatened war against him
Egypt is not mentioned as a reason; Sihon refused because the LORD made his heart obstinate (2:30).
The LORD made his spirit stubborn and his heart obstinate
When Sihon came out against Israel in Deuteronomy 2, at what place did the battle occur?
Deuteronomy 2:32 says Sihon and his whole army came out for battle against Israel at Jahaz.
Deuteronomy 2:32
Edrei
Edrei was where Og of Bashan fought Israel (Deuteronomy 3:1), not Sihon.
Jahaz
Ai
Ai was attacked in the days of Joshua (Joshua 8:1–2), not here.
Gilgal
Gilgal was Israel’s camp after crossing the Jordan (Joshua 4:19), not the site of Sihon’s battle.
Hormah
Hormah is where Israel was defeated after the spies’ report (Deuteronomy 1:44), not the site of Sihon’s battle.
Even after conquering Sihon’s territory in Deuteronomy 2, which land did Israel not go near because the LORD had forbidden it?
Deuteronomy 2:37 says Israel did not go near the land of the Ammonites, the banks of the Jabbok River, or any place the LORD had forbidden.
Deuteronomy 2:37
The land of Bashan, ruled by King Og
Bashan was conquered under Og (Deuteronomy 3:3–4).
The territory of Sihon around Heshbon
Sihon’s land around Heshbon was what Israel was told to take, and it did (2:24, 33–34).
The land of the Ammonites along the Jabbok
The cities of Gilead, as far as Aroer
Israel took the cities of Gilead; not one city had walls too high for it (2:36).
The town of Aroer on the rim of the Arnon
Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley was inside the territory Israel captured (2:36).
After the victory over Sihon in Deuteronomy 2, what did Israel keep for themselves even though the cities were devoted to destruction?
Deuteronomy 2:34–35 says the cities’ people were devoted to destruction, but Israel carried off “only the livestock and the plunder from the cities we captured.”
Deuteronomy 2:34-35
Only the idols and gold of the cities

Only the silver from Sihon’s palace
Silver from Sihon’s palace is not singled out; what Israel kept was the livestock and plunder from the cities (2:35).
Nothing, since everything was devoted to destruction
Israel did keep something: the livestock and the plunder (2:35).
Livestock and plunder from the cities
Firstfruits and tithes from the surrounding fields
Firstfruits and tithes were given to the LORD, not taken from the captured cities; Israel kept the livestock and plunder (2:35).
In Moses’ summary of the conquest in Deuteronomy 2, what stretch of territory had no city too strong for Israel?
Deuteronomy 2:36 says that from Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley, along with the city in the valley, even as far as Gilead, not one city had walls too high for Israel.

From Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley, and from the city in the valley, as far as Gilead
From Beersheba in the south to Dan in the far north

From Jericho in the Jordan valley to Bethel in the hills

From Kadesh-barnea in the south to Elath on the Red Sea

Deuteronomy 3:1
Sihon king of Heshbon
Sihon king of Heshbon had already been defeated; the LORD held up his fall as the pattern for what would happen to Og (3:2).
Og king of Bashan
Balak king of Moab
Balak king of Moab saw what Israel did to the Amorites (Numbers 22:2) but never met them in battle at Edrei.
Jabin king of Hazor
Jabin king of Hazor led a northern coalition against Israel under Joshua (Joshua 11:1), long after this campaign east of the Jordan.
Arad king of the Negev
The Canaanite king of Arad attacked Israel earlier in the Negev (Numbers 21:1), far from Bashan and Edrei.
At the start of Deuteronomy 3, after defeating Sihon, where did Israel turn and go?
Moses says that Israel turned and went up the road to Bashan (3:1), where Og came out to fight them.

To Kadesh
Kadesh lay far to the south; the road here led north into Bashan (3:1).
To Jericho

Up the road to Bashan
Back to Egypt

Make peace with him

Do not fear him

When Moses described Israel’s victory over Og’s kingdom in Bashan, how many cities did Israel capture in the whole region of Argob?

Mount Hermon

Rephaim
Hivites

Cedar

Bronze

Gold
Gold is not mentioned here; Og’s bed was of iron (3:11).
Iron
Stone

Machir
