When Moses encouraged Joshua after the defeats of Sihon and Og in Deuteronomy 3, why did he say Joshua should not fear the kingdoms ahead?
Moses told Joshua not to be afraid of the coming kingdoms, “for the LORD your God Himself will fight for you” (3:22).
Deuteronomy 3:21-22
Because Egypt would support Israel
Egypt is never offered as support; the confidence came from the LORD Himself (3:22).
Because Moab had surrendered
Moab is not said to have surrendered; Joshua’s courage rested on the LORD’s fighting for him (3:22).
Because the LORD your God Himself would fight for you
Because Israel had more horses
Horses are never given as the reason; Moses points to the LORD’s own action (3:21–22).
Because the Canaanites were unarmed
Nothing says the Canaanites were unarmed; Moses points to the LORD who would fight for Israel (3:22).
At the close of Deuteronomy 3, after the LORD told Moses he would not cross the Jordan, which combination of viewing place and camp location is correct?
The LORD told Moses to go to the top of Pisgah and view the land (3:27), and Israel stayed in the valley opposite Beth-peor (3:29).
Deuteronomy 3:27, 29
Top of Tabor / plains of Mamre
Tabor and Mamre are west of the Jordan; Moses was sent to Pisgah and Israel stayed opposite Beth-peor (3:27, 29).
Top of Pisgah / valley opposite Beth-peor
Mount Carmel / valley of Elah
Carmel and the valley of Elah lie in Canaan west of the Jordan, which Moses could only view from Pisgah (3:27).
Mount Ebal / opposite Ai
Ebal and Ai are in central Canaan, west of the Jordan, and belong to Joshua’s later campaigns.
Mount Seir / brook Zered
Seir is Edom’s mountain region and the Zered a brook crossed earlier (Deuteronomy 2:13), not Moses’ viewpoint here.
In Deuteronomy 4, as Moses urged Israel to obey before entering the land, what did he say they must not do to the LORD’s commandment?
Moses told Israel, “You must not add to or subtract from what I command you” (4:2).
Deuteronomy 4:2
Hide it from foreigners
Moses did not tell them to hide the commandments; he told them not to add or subtract (4:2).
Add to it or subtract from it
Read it only at feasts
Reading the law at feasts is not the warning here; the warning was against adding or subtracting (4:2).
Give it only to the Levites
Moses did not restrict the commandments to the Levites (4:1–2).
Replace it with local customs
Replacing the commandments with local customs would be adding and subtracting, which Moses forbade (4:2).
In Moses’ reminder about Baal-peor in Deuteronomy 4, what happened to the Israelites who followed Baal of Peor?
The LORD destroyed from among them all who followed Baal of Peor (4:3).
Deuteronomy 4:3
They were made servants
They were destroyed, not made servants (4:3).
They fled to Egypt
Fleeing to Egypt is not mentioned; the LORD destroyed them (4:3).
They were destroyed by the LORD
They became judges in Israel
They did not become judges; the LORD destroyed them (4:3).
They inherited extra land
They inherited nothing; the LORD destroyed them (4:3).
In Deuteronomy 4, what did Moses say the nations would conclude if Israel kept the LORD’s statutes and ordinances?
The nations would say, “Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people” (4:6).
Deuteronomy 4:6
Israel is a rich trading nation
Trade and wealth are not what Moses mentions; he spoke of wisdom and understanding (4:6).
Israel is a mighty naval power
A naval power is not mentioned; the nations would say Israel was wise (4:6).
Israel is a wise and understanding people
Israel is invincible in battle
Invincibility is not claimed; the nations would call Israel wise and understanding (4:6).
Israel is ruled by angels
Angels ruling Israel are not mentioned; the nations would call Israel wise and understanding (4:6).
As Moses spoke in Deuteronomy 4, what made Israel uniquely blessed among the nations?
Moses asked what nation has a god as near to them as the LORD is to Israel whenever they call on Him (4:7).
Deuteronomy 4:7
Their kings never died
Kings never dying is not claimed anywhere in the chapter (4:7).
Their God was near whenever they called on Him
Their land had no enemies
Israel was told it would face enemies in the land; its blessing was the LORD’s nearness (4:7, 38).
Their priests ruled the army
The priests ruling the army is not mentioned; the blessing was the LORD’s nearness (4:7).
Their temple was already built
The temple was not built until long after Moses; the blessing was the LORD’s nearness (4:7).
In Deuteronomy 4, what did Moses tell Israel to teach to their children and grandchildren?
Moses told Israel not to forget the things their eyes had seen and to teach them to their children and grandchildren (4:9).
Deuteronomy 4:9
Only tribal borders
Tribal borders are not mentioned in 4:9; they were to teach what they had seen.
The things their eyes had seen
Egyptian literature
Egyptian literature is not mentioned; they were to teach what their eyes had seen (4:9).
Military formations
Military formations are not mentioned; they were to teach what their eyes had seen (4:9).
The names of foreign gods
Foreign gods are to be avoided (4:19, 23), not taught (4:9).
Recalling Mount Horeb in Deuteronomy 4, what did the Israelites hear and not see when the LORD spoke from the fire?
The LORD spoke from the fire; they heard the sound of the words but saw no form, only a voice (4:12).
Deuteronomy 4:11-12, 15
They heard thunder and saw an angel
No angel is mentioned; they heard the sound of the words and saw no form (4:12).
They heard music and saw a throne
No throne is mentioned; they saw no form at all (4:12).
They heard a voice but saw no form
They heard silence and saw lightning
They heard the voice of the LORD, not silence (4:12).
They heard Moses and saw the ark
Moses is not the one they heard; the LORD spoke out of the fire (4:12).
In Deuteronomy 4, what covenant did Moses say the LORD declared and write on two tablets of stone?
The LORD declared His covenant, the Ten Commandments, which He wrote on two tablets of stone (4:13).
Deuteronomy 4:13
The covenant of circumcision
The covenant of circumcision was given to Abraham (Genesis 17:10), not written on tablets.
The priestly covenant
The priestly covenant is the lasting priesthood given to Phinehas (Numbers 25:13).
The covenant with David
The covenant with David comes much later, in 2 Samuel 7.
The Ten Commandments
The laws of the Jubilee
The laws of the Jubilee are in Leviticus 25, not the covenant written on the tablets (4:13).
In his warning against idolatry in Deuteronomy 4, which human-shaped images did Moses specifically mention?
Moses warned against making an idol in the likeness of a male or female (4:16).
Deuteronomy 4:16
King or judge
King or judge is not among the images listed (4:16).
Prophet or priest
Prophet or priest is not among the images listed (4:16).
Man or woman
Bride or groom
Bride or groom is not among the images listed (4:16).
Parent or child
Parent or child is not among the images listed (4:16).
In Deuteronomy 4, when Moses warned Israel not to look up to heaven and worship created things, which heavenly lights did he name?
Moses warned against being enticed to worship the sun, moon and stars, all the host of heaven (4:19).
Deuteronomy 4:19
Clouds, wind, and rain
Clouds, wind and rain are not the named objects of worship; the sun, moon and stars are (4:19).
Sun, moon, and stars
Dawn, noon, and dusk
Dawn, noon and dusk are not named; the sun, moon and stars are (4:19).
Comets, planets, and meteors
Comets, planets and meteors are not named; the sun, moon and stars are (4:19).
Lightning, thunder, and hail
Lightning, thunder and hail are not named; the sun, moon and stars are (4:19).
In Deuteronomy 4, from what place, described as “the iron furnace,” did the LORD bring Israel out?
The LORD brought Israel out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt (4:20).
Deuteronomy 4:20
Babylon
Babylon is where Judah is exiled much later; the iron furnace is Egypt (4:20).
Assyria
Assyria is not the iron furnace; Moses meant Egypt (4:20).
Midian
Midian is where Moses lived in exile (Exodus 2:15), not the iron furnace.
Egypt
Edom
Edom is not the iron furnace; Moses meant Egypt (4:20).
Speaking east of the Jordan in Deuteronomy 4, what did Moses say he himself would not be allowed to do?
Moses said the LORD swore that he would not cross the Jordan to enter the good land (4:21–22).
Deuteronomy 4:21-22
Enter the city of Jerusalem and worship there
Jerusalem is not named in the chapter; Moses said he would not cross the Jordan (4:22).
Build the tabernacle that the LORD had described
Moses did take part in building the tabernacle (Exodus 39:32); what he was denied was entering the good land (4:21).
Cross the Jordan into the good land
Appoint Joshua as the next leader of Israel
Moses did appoint Joshua as his successor (Numbers 27:22–23); what he was denied was entering the land (4:21).
See the good land from the top of Mount Nebo
Moses was shown the land from Mount Nebo (Deuteronomy 34:1–4); what he was denied was crossing the Jordan (4:21).
In Deuteronomy 4, how did Moses describe the LORD while warning Israel not to forget the covenant and make idols?
Moses said, “the LORD your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God” (4:24).
Deuteronomy 4:23-24
A gentle shepherd only
Moses does not call the LORD a gentle shepherd in this passage; he calls Him a consuming fire (4:24).
A consuming fire, a jealous God
A distant ruler
Moses stressed how near the LORD is (4:7), not that He is distant.
A silent judge
The LORD spoke from the fire (4:12); He is not called a silent judge.
A wandering spirit
The LORD is not called a wandering spirit; He is a consuming fire, a jealous God (4:24).
In Deuteronomy 4, whom did Moses call as witnesses against Israel if they became corrupt in the land and made idols?
Moses said, “I call heaven and earth as witnesses against you this day” (4:26).
Deuteronomy 4:25-26
The priests and Levites
The priests and Levites are not called as witnesses (4:26).
Joshua and Caleb
Joshua and Caleb are not called as witnesses (4:26).
Heaven and earth
The elders and judges
The elders and judges are not called as witnesses (4:26).
The tribes of Reuben and Gad
Reuben and Gad are not called as witnesses (4:26).
Moses warned in Deuteronomy 4 that if Israel were scattered among the nations, they would serve what kind of gods there?
Moses said Israel would serve man-made gods of wood and stone, which cannot see or hear or eat or smell (4:28).
Deuteronomy 4:27-28
Living gods who hear and answer every prayer
Idols cannot answer prayer; they cannot see or hear (4:28).
Gods of gold that speak plainly to their servants
The gods Moses names are wood and stone, not gold, and they cannot speak (4:28).
Gods of wood and stone that cannot see, hear, eat, or smell
River gods that control the floods in the land
River gods are not mentioned; the idols are of wood and stone (4:28).
Star gods that write laws for all the nations
Star gods are warned against in 4:19, but the scattered Israelites would serve gods of wood and stone (4:28).
In Deuteronomy 4, how did Moses say Israel would find the LORD after being scattered, if they sought Him from there?
Moses said, “you will find Him if you seek Him with all your heart and with all your soul” (4:29).
Deuteronomy 4:29
By building a larger army
Building a larger army is not the way; Moses pointed to seeking the LORD with heart and soul (4:29).
By returning to Egypt
Returning to Egypt is not the way; they were to seek the LORD (4:29).
By seeking Him with all their heart and soul
By making a vow to a prophet
A vow to a prophet is not mentioned; they were to seek the LORD (4:29).
By offering silver and gold
Silver and gold are not what Moses mentions; they were to seek the LORD with all their heart and soul (4:29).
In Deuteronomy 4, what extraordinary event did Moses say no other people had experienced and survived as Israel had?
Moses asked whether a people had ever heard the voice of God speaking out of the fire, as Israel had, and lived (4:33).
Deuteronomy 4:32-33
Seeing the ark float on the sea
Seeing the ark float on the sea is not in the chapter; the wonder was hearing God’s voice from the fire (4:33).
Hearing the voice of God speaking from the fire and living
Eating manna for one day
Eating manna for one day is not mentioned; the unique event was hearing God’s voice from the fire (4:33).
Crossing the Nile on foot
Israel crossed the Red Sea and the Jordan, not the Nile; the unique event here was hearing God from the fire (4:33).
Watching the sun stand still at Horeb
The sun standing still happens in Joshua 10:13, not at Horeb.
In Deuteronomy 4, what reason did Moses give for the LORD bringing Israel out of Egypt by His presence and great power?
Moses said that because He loved their fathers, the LORD chose their descendants and brought them out of Egypt (4:37).
Deuteronomy 4:37
Because Egypt had become weak and was falling apart
Egypt’s weakness is not given as the reason; the reason was His love for their fathers (4:37).
Because Moses requested it on behalf of the people
Moses’ request is not given as the reason; the reason was His love for their fathers (4:37).
Because He loved their fathers and chose their descendants
Because Israel had never sinned against the LORD
Israel had sinned, and the reason was God’s love, not Israel’s merit (4:37).
Because Pharaoh offered them a land of their own
Pharaoh offered them no land; God acted because He loved their fathers (4:37).
Near the end of Moses’ teaching in Deuteronomy 4, what truth was Israel to know and take to heart about the LORD?
Moses told Israel to know and take to heart that the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth below; there is no other (4:39).
Deuteronomy 4:39
He rules only over the land and people of Israel
Moses said the LORD is God in heaven and on earth, not only in Israel (4:39).
He is the first and greatest among many gods
Moses said there is no other god; the LORD is not first among many (4:39).
He is God in heaven above and on earth below; there is no other
He changes His nature from one age to the next
Moses does not say the LORD changes; he says He is God, and there is no other (4:39).
He speaks only through the kings of the nations
The LORD spoke to Israel directly from the fire (4:12), not only through kings.
In the section about the three cities east of the Jordan in Deuteronomy 4, who was allowed to flee there for safety?
The cities were for a manslayer who killed his neighbor unintentionally, without prior malice (4:41–42).
Deuteronomy 4:41-42
A thief caught stealing livestock from his neighbor
Theft is not the reason; the cities were for unintentional killing (4:42).
A king defeated in battle by the neighboring tribes
Defeated kings are not mentioned; the cities were for unintentional killers (4:42).
A manslayer who killed his neighbor accidentally without prior hostility
A false prophet who had led the people astray
False prophets are not mentioned; the cities were for unintentional killers (4:42).
A runaway slave who had left his master in Israel
Runaway slaves are not mentioned; the cities were for unintentional killers (4:42).
At the close of Deuteronomy 4, which answer correctly matches the three cities Moses set apart east of the Jordan with their tribes?
Moses set aside Bezer for the Reubenites, Ramoth in Gilead for the Gadites, and Golan in Bashan for the Manassites (4:43).
Deuteronomy 4:41-43
Kedesh for Judah, Shechem for Ephraim, and Hebron for Benjamin in the hill country
Kedesh, Shechem and Hebron are the cities of refuge west of the Jordan (Joshua 20:7).
Zoar for Reuben, Dibon for Gad, and Ashtaroth for Manasseh beside the Jordan
Zoar, Dibon and Ashtaroth are not the cities named here (4:43).
Bezer in the wilderness plateau for the Reubenites, Ramoth in Gilead for the Gadites, and Golan in Bashan for the Manassites
Jericho for Reuben, Jabesh for Gad, and Dan for Manasseh in the plains
Jericho, Jabesh and Dan are not the cities named here (4:43).
Heshbon for Reuben, Rabbah for Gad, and Edrei for Manasseh beyond the river
Heshbon, Rabbah and Edrei are not the cities named here (4:43).
In Deuteronomy 5, who summoned all Israel and told them to hear the statutes and ordinances?
Deuteronomy 5:1 says Moses summoned all Israel and said to them, “Hear, O Israel, the statutes and ordinances that I declare in your hearing this day.”
Deuteronomy 5:1
Aaron
Aaron was Moses’ brother and the first high priest, but he is not the speaker here (5:1).
Joshua
Joshua succeeded Moses later (Deuteronomy 34:9); Moses is speaking here.
Moses
Caleb
Caleb is not mentioned in Deuteronomy 5; Moses summoned Israel (5:1).
Eleazar
Eleazar served as priest (Numbers 20:26–28), but he did not summon Israel in Deuteronomy 5:1.
When Moses reviewed the covenant in Deuteronomy 5, at what place did the LORD make this covenant with Israel?
Deuteronomy 5:2 says the LORD our God made a covenant with us at Horeb.
Deuteronomy 5:2
Kadesh-barnea
Kadesh-barnea is where the spies were sent (Numbers 13:26), not where this covenant was made.
Mount Nebo
Mount Nebo is where Moses saw the land before he died (Deuteronomy 34:1).
Gilgal
Gilgal is where Israel camped after crossing the Jordan (Joshua 4:19).
Horeb
Beersheba
Beersheba is a site in the patriarchal stories (Genesis 21:31), not the covenant site in Deuteronomy 5:2.
In the Ten Commandments as repeated in Deuteronomy 5, from what land did the LORD say He had brought Israel out?
Deuteronomy 5:6 says, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.”
Deuteronomy 5:6
Canaan
Canaan is the land Israel was heading toward (Deuteronomy 5:31), not the land they were brought out of.
Assyria
Assyria had no part in Israel’s deliverance here; the LORD brought them out of Egypt (5:6).
Egypt
Midian
Midian is where Moses lived for a time (Exodus 2:15), not the land of slavery.
Babylon
Babylon is where Judah was later exiled, long after Moses’ time; Deuteronomy 5:6 names Egypt.
In Moses’ retelling of the first commandment in Deuteronomy 5, what was Israel forbidden to have before the LORD?
Deuteronomy 5:7 says, “You shall have no other gods before Me.”
Deuteronomy 5:7
Graven altars
Altars are not forbidden in Deuteronomy 5:7; the commandment forbids other gods.
Other gods
Kings
Kings are not forbidden by the first commandment; Deuteronomy 5:7 forbids other gods.
Priests
Priests are not forbidden in Deuteronomy 5:7; the commandment forbids other gods.
Judges
Judges are not forbidden in Deuteronomy 5:7; the commandment forbids other gods.
In Deuteronomy 5, which day was Israel commanded to observe and keep holy?
Deuteronomy 5:12 says, “Observe the Sabbath day by keeping it holy.”
Deuteronomy 5:12
New Moon day
The New Moon is not the day named in Deuteronomy 5:12.
Day of Atonement
The Day of Atonement is in Leviticus 16, not the Sabbath command of Deuteronomy 5:12.
Sabbath day
Passover day
Passover is a yearly feast (Exodus 12), not the day of this commandment.
Feast of Booths
The Feast of Booths is a yearly feast (Leviticus 23:34), not the day of this commandment.
In the Sabbath command of Deuteronomy 5, how many days were given for labor?
Deuteronomy 5:13 says, “Six days you shall labor and do all your work.”
Deuteronomy 5:13
Five
Five is not the number of work days in Deuteronomy 5:13.
Six
Seven
Seven is the total week; the seventh day is the Sabbath, so six are for labor (5:13–14).
Eight
Eight is not part of the Sabbath command in Deuteronomy 5:13.
Ten
Ten is not the number of work days in Deuteronomy 5:13.
According to the Sabbath instructions in Deuteronomy 5, which person was specifically included among those who must rest?
Deuteronomy 5:14 includes the foreigner within your gates among those who must not work on the Sabbath.
Deuteronomy 5:14
Only the priests and Levites serving in the tabernacle
The Sabbath rest was not limited to priests; it covered sons, daughters, servants, animals and the foreigner (5:14).
Only the firstborn sons of each household
The rest was not limited to firstborn sons (5:14).
The resident alien within your gates
Only the landowners who held a share of the inheritance
The rest was not limited to landowners; servants and animals rested too (5:14).
Only the Levites who lived among the other tribes
The rest was not limited to Levites (5:14).
In Deuteronomy 5, whom was Israel commanded to honor so that their days might be long?
Deuteronomy 5:16 says, “Honor your father and your mother, … so that your days may be long.”
Deuteronomy 5:16
Prophets and judges
Prophets and judges are not named in the fifth commandment (5:16).
Father and mother
Priests and Levites
Priests and Levites are not named in the fifth commandment (5:16).
Elders and chiefs
Elders and chiefs are not named in the fifth commandment (5:16).
Kings and captains
Kings and captains are not named in the fifth commandment (5:16).
Which sin against human life is directly forbidden in the commandments repeated in Deuteronomy 5?
Deuteronomy 5:17 says, “You shall not murder.”
Deuteronomy 5:17
Kidnapping
Kidnapping is forbidden in Exodus 21:16, but it is not one of the commandments repeated in Deuteronomy 5.
Hatred
Hatred is condemned in Leviticus 19:17, not in this list of commandments.
Murder
Revenge
Revenge is addressed in Leviticus 19:18, not in Deuteronomy 5:17.
Strife
Strife is not named in the Ten Commandments of Deuteronomy 5.
Which sin against marriage is forbidden in Deuteronomy 5?
Deuteronomy 5:18 says, “You shall not commit adultery.”
Deuteronomy 5:18
Divorce
Divorce is regulated in Deuteronomy 24:1, not forbidden in the commandments of chapter 5.
Polygamy
Polygamy is not forbidden in Deuteronomy 5.
Adultery
Betrothal
Betrothal is not forbidden in Deuteronomy 5.
Celibacy
Celibacy is not addressed in Deuteronomy 5; the commandment forbids adultery (5:18).
Which sin against property is forbidden in Moses’ recitation of the commandments in Deuteronomy 5?
Deuteronomy 5:19 says, “You shall not steal.”
Deuteronomy 5:19
Trespassing
Trespassing is not named among the commandments of Deuteronomy 5.
Borrowing
Borrowing is not forbidden in Deuteronomy 5:19.
Stealing
Taxing
Taxing is not forbidden in Deuteronomy 5:19.
Inheriting
Inheriting is not forbidden in Deuteronomy 5:19.
In Deuteronomy 5, what false act against a neighbor is prohibited?
Deuteronomy 5:20 says, “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.”
Deuteronomy 5:20
Bearing false witness
Lending without interest
Lending without interest is commanded for the poor (Leviticus 25:37), not forbidden.
Moving a boundary stone
Moving a boundary stone is forbidden in Deuteronomy 19:14, not in the commandments of chapter 5.
Withholding wages
Withholding wages is forbidden in Leviticus 19:13, not in the commandments of Deuteronomy 5.
Breaking an oath to a king
Breaking an oath to a king is not named in Deuteronomy 5:20.
In the final commandment as given in Deuteronomy 5, what person is mentioned first as something not to covet?
Deuteronomy 5:21 begins, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.”
Deuteronomy 5:21
Your neighbor’s daughter
A neighbor’s daughter is not named in Deuteronomy 5:21.
Your neighbor’s wife
Your neighbor’s servant
A servant is named later in the verse, after the wife and house or field.
Your neighbor’s brother
A neighbor’s brother is not named in Deuteronomy 5:21.
Your neighbor’s judge
A neighbor’s judge is not named in Deuteronomy 5:21.
According to Deuteronomy 5:21, which of these belonging to a neighbor is named alongside his house as something not to covet?
Deuteronomy 5:21 says, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house or field,” so his field is named with his house.
Deuteronomy 5:21
Vineyard
A vineyard is not named in Deuteronomy 5:21, which lists house, field, servants, ox and donkey.
Gold
Gold is not named in Deuteronomy 5:21.
Chariot
A chariot is not named in Deuteronomy 5:21.
His field
Well
A well is not named in Deuteronomy 5:21.
When Moses described the second commandment in Deuteronomy 5, from which realms were carved images forbidden?
Deuteronomy 5:8 forbids an idol in the form of anything in the heavens above, on the earth below, or in the waters beneath.
Deuteronomy 5:8
Desert, sea, and sky
Desert, sea, and sky are not the three realms named in Deuteronomy 5:8.
Heaven above, earth beneath, and waters below
Mountains, valleys, and plains
Mountains, valleys, and plains are not the realms named in Deuteronomy 5:8.
Sun, moon, and stars only
Deuteronomy 4:19 warns against worshiping the sun, moon and stars, but 5:8 names heavens, earth and waters.
Temple, field, and city
Temple, field and city are not the realms named in Deuteronomy 5:8.
In Deuteronomy 5, how far does the LORD say He visits the iniquity of those who hate Him?
Deuteronomy 5:9 says the LORD visits “the iniquity of the fathers on their children to the third and fourth generations of those who hate Me.”
Deuteronomy 5:9
To the second and third generations
Second and third generations is not what Deuteronomy 5:9 says; it says third and fourth.
To the third and fourth generations
To the fifth generation only
The fifth generation is not named in Deuteronomy 5:9.
To seven generations
Seven generations is not named in Deuteronomy 5:9.
Forever without limit
The LORD’s loving devotion extends to a thousand generations of those who love Him (5:10), but iniquity is visited on the third and fourth (5:9).
In Deuteronomy 5, what warning is attached to taking the name of the LORD in vain?
Deuteronomy 5:11 says, “for the LORD will not leave anyone unpunished who takes His name in vain.”
Deuteronomy 5:11
The land will mourn
Deuteronomy 5:11 does not say the land will mourn.
The priests will judge him
Deuteronomy 5:11 puts the punishment in the LORD’s hands, not the priests’.
The LORD will not leave him unpunished
He will be cut off from Israel immediately
Being cut off immediately is not what Deuteronomy 5:11 says; the LORD will not leave him unpunished.
His offerings will be rejected for seven days
Rejected offerings are not named in Deuteronomy 5:11.
In Moses’ explanation of the Sabbath in Deuteronomy 5, what reason is given for keeping it?
Deuteronomy 5:15 says, “Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD your God brought you out of there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm.”
Deuteronomy 5:15
Because manna fell on that day to feed the people in the wilderness
Manna fell on six days and not on the Sabbath (Exodus 16:26); it is not the reason in Deuteronomy 5:15.
Because the ark of the covenant had come to rest in the tabernacle
The ark’s resting place is not the reason given in Deuteronomy 5:15.
Because Israel had been slaves in Egypt and the LORD brought them out
Because Abraham had kept that day as holy before the covenant at Horeb
Abraham is not named in the Sabbath command of Deuteronomy 5.
Because the elders of the tribes had asked Moses to set apart a rest day
Joshua is not named as the source of the Sabbath command in Deuteronomy 5.
Recounting the scene at Horeb in Deuteronomy 5, how did Moses say the LORD spoke to Israel on the mountain?
Deuteronomy 5:4 says, “The LORD spoke with you face to face out of the fire on the mountain.”
Deuteronomy 5:4
In a whisper from the cave
A still, small voice came to Elijah (1 Kings 19:12), not to Israel at Horeb.
Through a dream at night
Deuteronomy 5:4 describes a voice from the fire, not a dream at night.
Face to face out of the fire
By an angel in a cloud only
Deuteronomy 5:4 says the LORD Himself spoke, not an angel only.
By writing in the sand
Writing in the sand appears in John 8:6; at Horeb the LORD spoke from the fire (5:4) and wrote on stone (5:22).
In Deuteronomy 5, why did Moses stand between the LORD and Israel at that time?
Deuteronomy 5:5 says Moses stood between the LORD and the people because they were afraid of the fire and would not go up the mountain.
Deuteronomy 5:5
Because Moses alone understood the language in which God spoke
Language is not the issue; the people were afraid of the fire (5:5).
Because the people were afraid of the fire and did not go up the mountain
Because Aaron was absent and Moses had to speak in his place
Aaron’s absence is not mentioned in Deuteronomy 5:5; the people’s fear is.
Because the elders refused to listen and Moses had to intervene
Deuteronomy 5:5 gives fear of the fire, not an elders’ refusal, as the reason.
Because the tablets were already broken and had to be restored
The tablets were not broken until Exodus 32:19; Deuteronomy 5:5 gives the people’s fear.
After Israel heard the voice out of the darkness in Deuteronomy 5, who came near to Moses?
Deuteronomy 5:23 says all the heads of your tribes and your elders approached Moses.
Deuteronomy 5:23
The singers and gatekeepers
Singers and gatekeepers are not named in Deuteronomy 5:23.
The chiefs of the tribes and the elders
Only Aaron and Hur
Deuteronomy 5:23 names the tribal heads and elders, not only Aaron and Hur.
The women and children only
Deuteronomy 5:23 names tribal leaders, not women and children only.
The foreign sojourners
Foreign sojourners are not named in Deuteronomy 5:23.
What did the Israelites say they had seen happen in Deuteronomy 5 after hearing God speak from the fire?
Deuteronomy 5:24 says, “Today we have seen that a man can live even if God speaks with him.”
Deuteronomy 5:24
That no one can see God’s glory and live
“No one can see Me and live” is what the LORD told Moses in Exodus 33:20; in Deuteronomy 5:24 the people say a man can live if God speaks with him.
That angels must interpret every word
Deuteronomy 5:24 says nothing about angels interpreting God’s words.
That God speaks with man, yet he still lives
That the mountain would never burn again
The mountain’s fire is not said to stop in Deuteronomy 5:24.
That the priesthood should replace Moses
Deuteronomy 5:24 does not mention replacing Moses with priests.
In Deuteronomy 5, what did the people fear would happen if they heard the voice of the LORD any longer?
Deuteronomy 5:25 says, “this great fire will consume us, and we will die, if we hear the voice of the LORD our God any longer.”
Deuteronomy 5:25
They would forget the law
Forgetting the law is not the fear in Deuteronomy 5:25; they feared dying.
They would become blind
Blindness is not mentioned in Deuteronomy 5:25.
They would die
They would be exiled at once
Exile is not mentioned in Deuteronomy 5:25.
Their flocks would perish
Flocks perishing is not mentioned in Deuteronomy 5:25; they feared they themselves would die.
In the question Israel asked in Deuteronomy 5, whose voice had they heard speaking from the fire and lived?
Deuteronomy 5:26 says, “For who of all flesh has heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the fire, as we have, and survived?”
Deuteronomy 5:26
The Angel of the LORD
The Angel of the LORD is not named in Deuteronomy 5:26; they heard the voice of the living God.
Moses
They heard the voice of the living God, not only Moses (5:26).
The living God
A prophet like Elijah
Elijah is not named in Deuteronomy 5:26.
The cherubim
Cherubim are not named in Deuteronomy 5:26.
What request did the Israelites make of Moses in Deuteronomy 5 after the terrifying display at Horeb?
Deuteronomy 5:27 says, “Go near and listen to all that the LORD our God says. Then you can tell us everything the LORD our God tells you; we will listen and obey.”
Deuteronomy 5:27
Build an altar immediately so that sacrifices can be offered for us
Building an altar is not their request in Deuteronomy 5:27.
Ask Joshua to lead us on to the land while you remain here
They asked Moses to go near and listen, not for Joshua to lead (5:27).
Go near and hear all the LORD says, then tell us, and we will listen and do it
Hide the stone tablets from the people so that they do not fear
Hiding the tablets is not their request in Deuteronomy 5:27.
Bring water from the rock so that the people and herds may drink
Water from the rock is a different episode (Numbers 20), not their request in Deuteronomy 5:27.
How did the LORD respond to the people’s words spoken to Moses in Deuteronomy 5?
In Deuteronomy 5:28 the LORD said, “They have done well in all that they have spoken.”
Deuteronomy 5:28
“They have spoken rebelliously”
The LORD did not call their words rebellious; He said they had done well (5:28).
“They have done well in all that they have spoken”
“They must fast for seven days”
A seven-day fast is not mentioned in Deuteronomy 5:28.
“Aaron shall answer them instead”
Aaron answering them is not mentioned in Deuteronomy 5:28.
“They have seen too little”
The LORD’s response in 5:28 is approval, not a complaint that they had seen too little.
In Deuteronomy 5, what did the LORD say He wished the people had always?
In Deuteronomy 5:29 the LORD said, “If only they had such a heart to fear Me and keep all My commandments always.”
Deuteronomy 5:29
Such strength to conquer the nations living in the land
Strength to conquer nations is not what the LORD wished in Deuteronomy 5:29.
Such wisdom to judge one another fairly in every town
Wisdom to judge is not what the LORD wished in Deuteronomy 5:29.
Such a heart to fear Me and keep all My commandments always
Such wealth to build great cities throughout the land
Wealth to build cities is not what the LORD wished in Deuteronomy 5:29.
Such courage to go up the mountain and meet with Him
Courage to go up the mountain is not what the LORD wished; He wished for a heart to fear Him (5:29).
After approving the people’s request in Deuteronomy 5, what instruction did the LORD give the people, and what did He require of Moses?
In Deuteronomy 5:30–31 the LORD said, “Go and tell them: ‘Return to your tents,’” and told Moses to stand with Him so He could speak all the commandments, statutes and ordinances to teach them.
Deuteronomy 5:30-31
Return to your tents, and Moses was to stand there to receive commandments, statutes, and ordinances to teach Israel
Cross the Jordan at once, and Moses was to appoint judges over every tribe to govern the land after him
Crossing the Jordan and appointing judges are not in Deuteronomy 5:30–31.
Gather manna for the journey, and Moses was to take a census of every tribe before they left the mountain
Gathering manna and numbering the tribes are not in Deuteronomy 5:30–31.
Build the tabernacle without delay, and Moses was to anoint Aaron and his sons as priests before the people
Building the tabernacle and anointing Aaron are not in Deuteronomy 5:30–31 (see Exodus 28 and 40).
Circle Mount Seir, and Moses was to strike the rock so that water would flow for the whole assembly
Circling Mount Seir (Deuteronomy 2:1) and striking the rock (Numbers 20:11) are different episodes.

Summarizing the giving of the commandments in Deuteronomy 5, what did the LORD do after speaking with a loud voice from the midst of the fire, cloud, and thick darkness to the whole assembly at the mountain?
Deuteronomy 5:22 says He added nothing more, and He wrote them on two tablets of stone and gave them to Moses.
Deuteronomy 5:22
He sent the people into battle
Nothing in Deuteronomy 5:22 sends the people into battle.
He added many more sayings that day
Deuteronomy 5:22 says He added nothing more.
He wrote the words on two stone tablets and gave them to Moses
He commanded Aaron to read them aloud from a scroll
Aaron reading from a scroll is not mentioned in Deuteronomy 5:22.
He hid the words in the ark immediately
The tablets were placed in the ark later, by Moses (Deuteronomy 10:5), not hidden there immediately.
In Moses’ famous command in Deuteronomy 6, whom was Israel to love with all heart, soul, and strength?
Moses commands Israel to love “the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength” (6:5).
Deuteronomy 6:5
Moses the servant of the LORD
Moses is the one speaking to Israel; the command in 6:5 directs wholehearted love to the LORD, not to His servant.
Aaron the priest
Aaron was Israel’s high priest, but the love with all heart, soul, and strength is owed to the LORD alone (6:5).
The LORD your God
Your neighbor as yourself
Loving your neighbor as yourself is a separate command, found in Leviticus 19:18, not the object of the love in 6:5.
Abraham your father
Abraham appears in 6:10 as a patriarch to whom God swore the land, not as the one Israel must love with all their being.
In the declaration that begins “Hear, O Israel” in Deuteronomy 6, what is said about the LORD?
The Shema declares, “The LORD our God, the LORD is One” (6:4).
Deuteronomy 6:4
The LORD is hidden
The LORD is not hidden; Moses says He is “among you” (6:15) and has acted openly before Israel’s eyes (6:22).
The LORD is One
The LORD sleeps not
God’s watchfulness is taught elsewhere (Psalm 121:4), but the declaration in 6:4 is that the LORD is One.
The LORD changes not
God’s unchanging nature is stated in Malachi 3:6; the declaration “Hear, O Israel” in 6:4 is about His oneness.
The LORD is far off
Far from being distant, the LORD is described as dwelling “among you” (6:15), and the Shema stresses that He is One.
In Deuteronomy 6, where were the words God commanded that day to be kept?
Moses says the words he was commanding that day “are to be upon your hearts” (6:6).
Deuteronomy 6:6
In the ark only
The ark held the tablets (Deuteronomy 10:5), but 6:6 says God’s words are to be on the people’s own hearts.
Upon your hearts
On the altar stones
Altar stones are not mentioned here; Moses puts God’s words on the hearts of the people (6:6).
In the king’s house
The king’s house is never mentioned in the chapter; the words belong on every Israelite’s heart (6:6).
Among the tribes’ weapons
Weapons are not where God’s words were to be kept; Moses places them inwardly on the heart (6:6).
In Moses’ instructions for family life in Deuteronomy 6, to whom were these words to be taught diligently?
Moses says, “you shall teach them diligently to your children” (6:7).
Deuteronomy 6:7
Foreign kings
Foreign kings are never named as recipients of this teaching; the instruction is for Israelite parents and their children (6:7).
Priests only
The command is not limited to priests; every Israelite household was to teach the words to its children (6:7).
Your children
The Levites only
Levites had teaching duties elsewhere, but 6:7 addresses all parents, not only the Levites.
Traveling merchants
Traveling merchants are not mentioned; the teaching was for the family circle (6:7).
According to Deuteronomy 6, when were Israelites to speak of God’s commands in daily life?
Moses says to speak of God’s words “when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up” (6:7).
Deuteronomy 6:7
Only during the annual feasts when the whole nation gathered together
The feasts were important, but 6:7 calls for talk of God’s words every day, not just at annual gatherings.
Only at times of war when the army marched out to battle
Battle is not mentioned in 6:7; the words were to fill ordinary life at home and on the road.
When sitting at home, walking along the road, lying down, and getting up
Only on the Sabbath day when the people rested from all work
The Sabbath is not named here; 6:7 lists four everyday settings, from sitting at home to getting up.
Only on the occasions when they entered the tabernacle to worship
Entering the tabernacle is not in the list; 6:7 stresses speaking of God’s words in everyday places, not just in worship.
In Deuteronomy 6, where were God’s words to be tied and bound as reminders?
Moses says, “Tie them as reminders on your hands and bind them on your foreheads” (6:8).
Deuteronomy 6:8
On your staff and sandals
Staff and sandals are not named; 6:8 mentions the hands and the foreheads.
On your hands and foreheads
On your cloak and belt
A cloak and belt are not in the text; the reminders go on the hands and foreheads (6:8).
On your tent ropes and pegs
Tent ropes and pegs are not mentioned; the words were to be worn on the body, on hands and foreheads (6:8).
On your ears and neck
Ears and neck are not named in 6:8; the reminders go on the hands and foreheads.
In Deuteronomy 6, what kind of land did Moses say Israel would enter if they obeyed?
Moses promises “a land flowing with milk and honey” (6:3).
Deuteronomy 6:3
A land of cedar and snow
Cedar and snow are not part of the promise; 6:3 describes a land flowing with milk and honey.
A land flowing with milk and honey
A land of iron and bronze
Iron and copper are mentioned in Deuteronomy 8:9, but the description in 6:3 is milk and honey.
A land beside the great sea only
The promised land is not described as lying beside the sea only; 6:3 stresses its milk and honey.
A land of figs and pomegranates only
Figs and pomegranates appear in a longer list in Deuteronomy 8:8, but 6:3 names milk and honey, not these alone.
In the opening of Deuteronomy 6, whom were Israel, their children, and their grandchildren to fear all the days of their lives?
Moses wants Israel, their children, and their grandchildren to “fear the LORD your God all the days of your lives” (6:2).
Deuteronomy 6:2
The nations around them
The nations around them were not to be feared or followed; 6:14 warns against their gods, and 6:2 calls for fear of the LORD.
The king of Egypt
Egypt’s king is the oppressor from whom the LORD rescued Israel (6:21–22), not the one Israel was to fear.
The LORD your God
The Amorite armies
The Amorite armies are not mentioned in the chapter; the fear Moses commands is reverence for the LORD (6:2).
The judges of Israel
No judges are mentioned in this chapter; the fear Moses commands is reverence for the LORD, across generations (6:2).
In Deuteronomy 6:3, what two results did Moses connect with careful obedience in the promised land?
Moses says to be careful to observe God’s commands “so that you may prosper and multiply greatly” (6:3).
Deuteronomy 6:3
Rest and silence
Rest and silence are not the stated results; 6:3 promises prospering and multiplying.
Victory and riches only
Victory is promised elsewhere (6:19), but 6:3 pairs obedience with prospering and multiplying, not riches.
Prospering and multiplying greatly
Longer harvests and shorter wars
Harvests and wars are not mentioned in 6:3; the two results are prospering and multiplying.
Wisdom and songs
Wisdom and songs are not the results named in 6:3, which are prospering and multiplying greatly.
In Moses’ charge before Israel crossed the Jordan, which three generations are specifically named as those who should fear the LORD?
Moses names “you and your children and grandchildren” as those who should fear the LORD (6:2).
Deuteronomy 6:2
Fathers, mothers, and sons
Fathers and mothers are not the generations named; 6:2 lists you, your children, and your grandchildren.
Prophets, priests, and kings
Prophets, priests, and kings are offices, not the generations named in 6:2.
You, your children, and your grandchildren
Elders, captains, and judges
Elders, captains, and judges are offices, not generations; 6:2 names you, your children, and grandchildren.
Brothers, sisters, and cousins
Brothers, sisters, and cousins are not the generations named; 6:2 lists you, your children, and grandchildren.
According to Deuteronomy 6, what did Moses say would be prolonged if Israel kept God’s statutes and commandments?
Moses says that by keeping God’s statutes and commandments “your days may be prolonged” (6:2).
Deuteronomy 6:2
Your crops
Crops are not mentioned in 6:2; the promise is of long days.
Your kingdom
A kingdom is not promised in 6:2; the promise is that their days may be prolonged.
Your days
Your journeys
Journeys are not what 6:2 says will be prolonged; it says your days.
Your tents
Tents are not mentioned in 6:2; the text promises prolonged days.
According to Deuteronomy 6:1, what were the Israelites about to do?
Moses taught the commandments for Israel to follow “in the land that you are about to enter and possess” (6:1).
Deuteronomy 6:1
Return to slavery in Egypt
Israel had been brought out of Egypt; 6:1 looks ahead to entering the land, not going back.
Build a permanent temple in the wilderness
No temple is mentioned; 6:1 speaks of the land they were about to enter and possess.
Enter and possess the land
Appoint Moses as their king
Moses was not made king; he taught the commandments for life in the new land (6:1).
Abandon the LORD’s commandments
The opposite: Moses taught the commandments so they would follow them in the land (6:1).
At the start of Deuteronomy 6, what three kinds of instruction did Moses say the LORD had told him to teach Israel?
Moses calls what the LORD told him to teach “the commandments and statutes and ordinances” (6:1).
Deuteronomy 6:1
Songs, feasts, and sacrifices
Songs, feasts, and sacrifices are not the three terms Moses uses; he names commandments, statutes, and ordinances (6:1).
Commandments, statutes, and ordinances
Dreams, visions, and riddles
Dreams, visions, and riddles are not the instruction Moses describes in 6:1.
Prayers, hymns, and psalms
Prayers, hymns, and psalms are not the three terms Moses uses in 6:1.
Tithes, vows, and fasts
Tithes, vows, and fasts are not the three terms; 6:1 names commandments, statutes, and ordinances.
In Deuteronomy 6, to which three patriarchs had the LORD sworn to give the land?
Moses says the LORD swore the land “to your fathers, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (6:10).
Deuteronomy 6:10
Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
Noah, Shem, and Eber
Noah, Shem, and Eber are earlier ancestors in Genesis; the land oath was made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (6:10).
Moses, Aaron, and Miriam
Moses, Aaron, and Miriam led Israel out of Egypt, but the land oath was sworn to the patriarchs (6:10).
Joshua, Caleb, and Eleazar
Joshua, Caleb, and Eleazar were part of the generation that would enter the land; the oath was sworn to the patriarchs (6:10).
Levi, Kohath, and Amram
Levi, Kohath, and Amram are Moses’ ancestors in the line of Levi, not the patriarchs named in 6:10.
When Deuteronomy 6 describes Israel entering the promised land, what kind of cities does it say they would receive without building them?
Moses describes “great and splendid cities that you did not build” (6:10).
Deuteronomy 6:10
Walled and cursed cities
Walled cities are mentioned elsewhere, but 6:10 calls the cities great and splendid, not cursed.
Deserted and broken cities
The cities are described as great and splendid, not deserted and broken (6:10).
Great and splendid cities
Coastal and trading cities
Coastal and trading cities are not mentioned; 6:10 calls them great and splendid.
Small and hidden cities
Small and hidden cities do not fit 6:10, which says great and splendid cities.
In the list of blessings in Deuteronomy 6, what were the houses said to be full of?
Moses describes “houses full of every good thing with which you did not fill them” (6:11).
Deuteronomy 6:11
Gold and silver only
Gold and silver are not singled out; 6:11 says the houses are full of every good thing.
Every good thing
Grain and new wine only
Grain and new wine are not named in 6:11; the houses are full of every good thing.
Armor and weapons
Armor and weapons are not mentioned; 6:11 says the houses are full of every good thing.
Cedar and purple cloth
Cedar and purple cloth are not mentioned in 6:11, which says every good thing.
In Deuteronomy 6:11, what water source is mentioned as something Israel did not make for themselves?
Moses lists “wells that you did not dig” among the gifts Israel would receive (6:11).
Deuteronomy 6:11
Canals
Canals are not mentioned in 6:11; the water source named is wells.
Springs
Springs are mentioned in Deuteronomy 8:7 as part of the land, but 6:11 names wells that Israel did not dig.
Wells
Riverbanks
Riverbanks are not in the list; 6:11 names wells that you did not dig.
Fountains
Fountains appear in Deuteronomy 8:7 as a feature of the land, but 6:11 names wells that Israel did not dig.
In Deuteronomy 6, after Israel had eaten and was satisfied in the land, what were they warned not to do?
After eating and being satisfied, Israel was told, “be careful not to forget the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (6:11–12).
Deuteronomy 6:11-12
Forget the LORD
Neglect the feasts
The feasts are not the warning here; 6:12 warns against forgetting the LORD who brought them out of Egypt.
Tear down the cities
Tearing down cities is not mentioned; the cities were gifts they did not build (6:10).
Return to Egypt
Returning to Egypt is not the warning; Moses warns against forgetting the LORD who brought them out (6:12).
Give up the Sabbath
The Sabbath is not mentioned in this chapter; the warning in 6:12 is about forgetting the LORD.
In Deuteronomy 6:12, which two expressions describe the place from which the LORD rescued Israel?
The LORD brought Israel out of “the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (6:12).
Deuteronomy 6:12
The wilderness and the desert
The wilderness and desert were the route Israel traveled after rescue, not the place from which the LORD rescued them (6:12).
Canaan and the famine
Canaan was the destination, not the place of rescue; 6:12 names Egypt and the house of slavery.
Egypt and the house of slavery
Moab and the exile
Moab is not the place from which Israel was rescued, and the exile came centuries later; 6:12 names Egypt and the house of slavery.
Sinai and the fire
Sinai and the fire belong to the giving of the law (Deuteronomy 4:11–12), not to the place of rescue named in 6:12.
In Deuteronomy 6:13, besides fearing the LORD, what else was Israel commanded to do?
Moses commands, “Fear the LORD your God, serve Him only, and take your oaths in His name” (6:13).
Deuteronomy 6:13
Serve Him only and take oaths in His name
Build Him images and offerings
Building images for Him is the opposite of what the LORD wants; 6:13 commands serving Him only.
Consult prophets from every nation
Consulting prophets from other nations is not in 6:13, which calls for serving the LORD only.
Store manna for future years
Storing manna is not a command in 6:13; it commands serving the LORD only and taking oaths in His name.
Swear by the names of the patriarchs
Oaths are to be taken in the LORD’s name, not by the names of the patriarchs (6:13).
In Moses’ warning about idolatry in Deuteronomy 6, whose gods were the Israelites not to follow?
Moses says, “Do not follow other gods, the gods of the peoples around you” (6:14).
Deuteronomy 6:14
The gods of the peoples around them
The gods of their ancestors
The gods of their ancestors are not named in 6:14, which mentions the gods of the peoples around them.
The gods of the wilderness only
The text does not restrict the warning to the wilderness; 6:14 names the gods of the peoples around them.
The gods of Egypt alone
Egypt’s gods are not singled out here; 6:14 warns against the gods of the surrounding peoples.
The gods of distant islands
Distant islands are not mentioned; 6:14 names the gods of the peoples around them.
What reason does Deuteronomy 6 give for Israel not following other gods?
Moses warns, “For the LORD your God, who is among you, is a jealous God” (6:15).
Deuteronomy 6:15
Because the priests of Israel would strongly object to such worship
The priests’ objections are never given as a reason; 6:15 says the LORD is a jealous God.
Because the promised land was too small for so many different gods
The size of the land is not a reason in the text; 6:15 gives the LORD’s jealousy.
Because the LORD your God who is among you is a jealous God
Because the kings of the nations would punish them for it
The kings’ punishment is not the reason; 6:15 points to the LORD’s jealousy and anger.
Because the ark of the covenant would leave them if they did
The ark leaving them is not the stated reason; 6:15 points to the LORD’s jealousy.
In Deuteronomy 6:16, Moses tells Israel not to test the LORD as they did at what place?
Moses says, “Do not test the LORD your God as you tested Him at Massah” (6:16).
Deuteronomy 6:16
Horeb
Horeb is where the law was given; the testing Moses recalls took place at Massah (6:16).
Kadesh
Kadesh is another place of Israel’s unbelief, but 6:16 names Massah as the place of testing.
Massah
Gilgal
Gilgal is where Israel would later camp after entering the land (Joshua 4:19), not the place of testing named in 6:16.
Shiloh
Shiloh is not mentioned in the chapter; the place of testing named in 6:16 is Massah.
In Deuteronomy 6:17, what were the Israelites to keep diligently?
Moses commands Israel to “diligently keep the commandments of the LORD your God and the testimonies and statutes He has given you” (6:17).
Deuteronomy 6:17
Only the annual feasts and the laws of the harvest season
The feasts are not singled out in 6:17, which calls for keeping all the commandments, testimonies, and statutes.
The commandments, testimonies, and statutes of the LORD
The songs of praise that Moses and Miriam had sung at the sea
Moses and Miriam’s songs (Exodus 15) celebrated the sea crossing; 6:17 commands keeping the LORD’s commandments, testimonies, and statutes.
The genealogies of the tribes and the family records of Israel
The tribal genealogies are not mentioned in 6:17, which is about keeping the LORD’s commandments.
The customs and traditions that the elders had handed down
The elders’ customs are not the standard; 6:17 points to what the LORD has given.
According to Deuteronomy 6:18, what was Israel to do in the sight of the LORD?
Moses commands, “Do what is right and good in the sight of the LORD” (6:18).
Deuteronomy 6:18
What is ancient and memorable
Being ancient and memorable is not the standard; 6:18 asks for what is right and good.
What is right and good
What is difficult and hidden
Difficult and hidden is not the standard; 6:18 asks for what is right and good.
What is prosperous and admired
Prosperity follows obedience (6:24), but the command in 6:18 is to do what is right and good.
What is severe and feared
Severe and feared is not the standard; 6:18 asks for what is right and good.
In Deuteronomy 6:18-19, what two results are connected with doing what is right and good?
Doing what is right and good is linked to two results, “that it may be well with you and that you may enter and possess the good land” (6:18).
Deuteronomy 6:18
Israel would appoint a king and build a temple
A king and temple are not mentioned in the chapter; 6:18 promises well-being and possession of the land.
It would go well with them, and they would enter and possess the good land
Manna would fall again, and the sea would divide
Manna and the dividing of the sea were in the past; 6:18 promises well-being and possession of the land.
The priesthood would expand, and Moab would submit
Neither the priesthood nor Moab’s submission is mentioned; the promised results are well-being and entering the land (6:18).
The wilderness would blossom, and Amalek would repent
The wilderness blossoming and Amalek repenting are not in the passage; 6:18 promises well-being and the good land.
In Deuteronomy 6, whose future question is specifically anticipated about the meaning of God’s laws?
Moses anticipates, “when your son asks, ‘What is the meaning of the decrees and statutes and ordinances…’” (6:20).
Deuteronomy 6:20
Your daughter
Moses names a son, not a daughter, in 6:20.
Your servant
A servant is not the questioner; 6:20 anticipates a son asking.
Your son
Your neighbor
A neighbor is not the questioner; 6:20 anticipates a son asking.
Your king
A king is not the questioner; 6:20 anticipates a son asking.
When the son asks in Deuteronomy 6:20, what three terms does he use for God’s commands?
The son asks about “the decrees and statutes and ordinances that the LORD our God has commanded you” (6:20).
Deuteronomy 6:20
Laws, songs, and feasts
Laws, songs, and feasts are not the son’s three terms; 6:20 has decrees, statutes, and ordinances.
Decrees, statutes, and ordinances
Visions, dreams, and signs
Visions, dreams, and signs are not the son’s three terms in 6:20.
Covenants, sacrifices, and vows
Covenants, sacrifices, and vows are not the son’s three terms in 6:20.
Tithes, sabbaths, and jubilees
Tithes, sabbaths, and jubilees are not the son’s three terms in 6:20.
In the answer parents were to give in Deuteronomy 6, how is Israel’s past in Egypt summarized?
Parents were to say, “We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt” (6:21).
Deuteronomy 6:21
We were guests in Pharaoh’s palace
Israel was not a guest in Pharaoh’s palace; the answer begins with slavery (6:21).
We traded with Pharaoh in Egypt
Israel did not trade with Pharaoh; the answer says they were slaves (6:21).
We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt
We fled from Pharaoh into Egypt
Israel did not flee into Egypt; the LORD brought them out of Egypt (6:21).
We ruled under Pharaoh in Egypt
Israel did not rule in Egypt; the answer says they were slaves of Pharaoh (6:21).
According to that same answer, how did the LORD bring Israel out of Egypt?
The answer says the “LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand” (6:21).
Deuteronomy 6:21
With a still small voice
A still small voice belongs to Elijah’s story (1 Kings 19:12), not the Exodus; 6:21 says a mighty hand.
With a mighty hand
With fire from heaven only
Fire from heaven is not named in 6:21, which says the LORD brought them out with a mighty hand.
With the rod of Aaron alone
Aaron’s rod is not named in 6:21, which credits the LORD’s mighty hand.

The capital city
