According to Deuteronomy 21, what animal must the elders of the nearest city take in the case of an unsolved killing?
Deuteronomy 21:3 says the elders of the city nearest the victim shall take a heifer that has never been yoked or used for work.
Deuteronomy 21:3
A ram without any blemish or defect
A ram without blemish is a guilt offering in Leviticus 5:15, but this ritual calls for a heifer (21:3).
A young male goat without any blemish
A goat is not called for in this ritual; the elders take a heifer (21:3).
A heifer that has never been worked or yoked
A red heifer to be burned outside the camp
A red heifer was burned for purification (Numbers 19:2), whereas this heifer’s neck was broken in a valley (21:4).
A pair of turtledoves or young pigeons
Turtledoves are not part of this ritual; the elders take a heifer (21:3).
In Moses’ instruction about an unknown murderer in Deuteronomy 21, where is the heifer to be taken?
Deuteronomy 21:4 says to bring the heifer to a valley with running water that has not been plowed or sown, and break its neck there by the stream.
Deuteronomy 21:4
To the city gate where the elders sit in judgment
The city gate is where elders judge a rebellious son (21:19), not where the heifer’s neck is broken.
To the altar of the tabernacle in the camp
The tabernacle altar is not part of this rite; the heifer’s neck is broken in a valley (21:4).
To a wadi with flowing water that has not been plowed or sown
To the summit of a mountain far from any city
A mountain summit is not mentioned; the rite took place in a valley with running water (21:4).
To a plowed field beside the nearest city’s wall
A plowed field would defeat the rule; the valley must not be plowed or sown (21:4).
In the Deuteronomy 21 case of a slain man with no known killer, why do the Levitical priests come forward?
Deuteronomy 21:5 says the priests, the sons of Levi, come forward for the LORD has chosen them to serve Him, pronounce blessings in His name, and give a ruling in every dispute and case of assault.
Deuteronomy 21:5
To count the fighting men of every nearby city so they could be called up for war
Counting for war is not the priests’ role in this passage (21:5).
Because they were chosen to minister before the LORD, pronounce blessings in His name, and settle disputes and assaults
To divide the surrounding land by lot among the cities nearest to the body
Dividing the land by lot is not mentioned in this law (21:5).
To appoint new tribal leaders and judges to replace the elders of the city
Appointing tribal leaders is not mentioned; the priests give rulings in disputes and assaults (21:5).
To inspect the body and declare whether the dead man had become unclean
Inspecting for uncleanness is not mentioned; the priests give rulings in disputes and assaults (21:5).
As the elders wash their hands over the heifer in Deuteronomy 21, what do they declare?
Deuteronomy 21:7 says they shall declare, “Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it.”
Deuteronomy 21:6-8
“We have fasted and prayed for this land”
Fasting and prayer are not part of the declaration; the elders speak of their innocence (21:7).
“This blood is avenged before the LORD”
The declaration is not about vengeance; the elders ask the LORD to accept atonement (21:8).
“The murderer will surely be found”
The declaration does not promise that the murderer will be found; the elders claim innocence (21:7).
“We have offered a pleasing sacrifice”
The declaration is not about a sacrifice; the elders claim innocence and ask for atonement (21:7–8).
“Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it”
In Deuteronomy 21, if an Israelite desired to marry a beautiful woman taken captive in war, which set of actions had to happen first in his house?
Deuteronomy 21:12–13 says she must shave her head, trim her nails, put aside the clothing of her captivity, and mourn her father and mother for a full month before he may marry her.
Deuteronomy 21:11-13
She was to shave her head, trim her nails, remove her captive clothing, and mourn her father and mother
She was to bring a lamb as a sin offering and be washed at the altar for a week
Offering a lamb and washing at the altar are not mentioned in this law (21:12–13).
She was to remain outside the camp for forty days of purification and fasting
A forty-day stay outside the camp is not mentioned; she is brought into his house (21:12).
She was to be given jewelry and festive clothing and a wedding feast at once
Jewelry and festive clothing are the opposite of what the law requires; she puts aside her captive clothing (21:13).
She was to return to her homeland for a year to bury her dead and then come back
She does not return to her homeland; she stays in his house a month (21:13).
In the law about a captive woman in Deuteronomy 21, how long was she to mourn her father and mother before the man could become her husband?
Deuteronomy 21:13 says she shall live in his house a full month and mourn her father and mother before he may be her husband.
Deuteronomy 21:13
Seven days
Seven days is not the period; the text says a full month (21:13).
Fourteen days
Fourteen days is not the period; the text says a full month (21:13).
One full month
Three months
Three months is not the period; the text says a full month (21:13).
One year
One year is not the period; the text says a full month (21:13).
According to Deuteronomy 21, if a man later was not pleased with the captive woman he had married, what was he forbidden to do?
Deuteronomy 21:14 says if you are not pleased with her, you are to let her go wherever she wishes, but you must not sell her for money or treat her as a slave, since you have dishonored her.
Deuteronomy 21:14
Send her to the priests for service
The law does not send her to the priests; he must let her go wherever she wishes (21:14).
Force her to remain unmarried for life
He may not hold her to a life unmarried; she goes wherever she wishes (21:14).
Return her to battle as a prisoner
He may not make her a prisoner again; she must be allowed to go free (21:14).
Sell her for money or treat her as a slave
Put her outside the camp for uncleanness
Uncleanness and the camp are not mentioned; the law forbids selling her or treating her as a slave (21:14).
In Deuteronomy 21, if a man had two wives and the true firstborn was the son of the unloved wife, what could the father not do when assigning his inheritance?
Deuteronomy 21:16–17 says the man must not appoint the son of the beloved wife as the firstborn over the son of the unloved wife, but must give the unloved wife’s firstborn a double portion.
Deuteronomy 21:15-16
Bless the firstborn son before his younger brother
The law does not forbid blessing the firstborn; it forbids giving his birthright to another (21:16).
Set aside land for both of his sons at his death
Setting aside land for both sons is not forbidden; the issue is the firstborn’s double portion (21:17).
Make the son of the loved wife the firstborn instead
Call the priests to witness how he divided his goods
Calling priests as witnesses is not mentioned in this law (21:15–17).
Divide his movable goods before dividing the land
Dividing goods in a particular order is not mentioned; the issue is the birthright (21:16–17).
When parents bring a stubborn and rebellious son to the elders in Deuteronomy 21, which accusation do they make?
Deuteronomy 21:20 says they tell the elders, “This son of ours is stubborn and rebellious; he does not obey us.” Then they add, “He is a glutton and a drunkard.”
Deuteronomy 21:18-20
That he had stolen sheep from the flock and hidden them away in the hills
Stealing sheep is not the charge in Deuteronomy 21:20; the charge is rebellion, disobedience, gluttony and drunkenness.
That their son is stubborn and rebellious, does not obey them, and is a glutton and a drunkard
That he had spoken falsely before the priests in the sanctuary
Speaking falsely in the sanctuary is not the charge in 21:20.
That he had refused to serve in the army when Israel went to war
Refusing military service is not the charge in 21:20; Deuteronomy 20 deals with who is exempt from war.
That he had moved his neighbor’s boundary stone and seized the field
Moving a boundary stone is a different crime (Deuteronomy 19:14), not the charge against a rebellious son in 21:20.
In the Deuteronomy 21 law about a rebellious son, what are the men of his city commanded to do after the case is presented at the gate?
Deuteronomy 21:21 says all the men of his city will stone him to death, so you must purge the evil from among you.
Deuteronomy 21:21
Exile him for seven years
Exile for seven years is not the penalty; the law says stoning (21:21).
Shave his head publicly
Shaving the head is not the penalty here; the law says stoning (21:21).
Beat him and release him
Beating and releasing him is not the penalty; the law says stoning (21:21).
Make him serve at the sanctuary
Sanctuary service is not the penalty; the law says stoning (21:21).
Stone him to death
In Deuteronomy 21, if a man guilty of a capital offense is executed and hung on a tree, what must be done with his body before nightfall, and why?
Deuteronomy 21:23 says you must not leave the body on the tree overnight but bury him that day, because anyone who is hung on a tree is under God’s curse, and the land must not be defiled.
Deuteronomy 21:22-23
Leave it hanging until morning so that all the people can see the warning
The body may not be left overnight; the law says it must be buried that day (21:23).
Burn it outside the camp so that the defilement of the land is removed
Burning outside the camp is not the instruction; the body is buried that day (21:23).
Bury it the same day, because anyone hung on a tree is under God’s curse and the land must not be defiled
Place it in the city gate until the elders have given their judgment
The city gate is not where the body is placed; it is to be buried that day (21:23).
Cover it with a heap of stones but leave it unburied in the open
Covering with stones without burying contradicts the command to bury him that day (21:23).
In Deuteronomy 22, when Moses gave laws about caring for a fellow Israelite’s property, what was a person to do if he saw an ox or sheep going astray?
Deuteronomy 22:1 says you “must not ignore” a brother’s straying ox or sheep but must return it to him.
Deuteronomy 22:1
Leave it until evening
The command is the opposite of delay: the stray animal was not to be ignored but returned (22:1), with a way to hold it safely if the owner lived far away (22:2).
Keep it if no one was watching
Keeping a found animal is exactly what the law forbids; it is held only until the brother comes seeking it, then returned (22:2).
Return it to its owner
Sell it at the gate
Nothing in the law lets the finder sell the animal; it belongs to the brother and must be returned to him (22:1–2).
Offer it at the sanctuary
Stray livestock was not an offering; Deuteronomy 22:1–2 treats it as a neighbor’s property to be given back.
In the lost-property commands of Deuteronomy 22, what was to be done with a fellow Israelite’s garment or any other lost item that someone found?
Deuteronomy 22:3 extends the command to a donkey, a cloak, or anything a brother has lost: “You must not ignore it.”
Deuteronomy 22:3
Burn it to prevent theft
Burning lost property would destroy a neighbor’s goods; the law commands returning them (22:1–3).
Return it and not ignore it
Keep it for personal use
Personal use is ruled out; the finder keeps the item only until the brother comes for it (22:2–3).
Give it to the priest
Lost property was returned to its owner, not handed to the priest (22:3).
Only return animals, not clothing
The command names the cloak and “anything your brother has lost,” so it covers more than animals (22:3).
In Moses’ instruction about a fallen animal in Deuteronomy 22, what should an Israelite do if he saw a fellow Israelite’s donkey or ox fallen on the road?
Deuteronomy 22:4 commands that if you see a brother’s donkey or ox fallen on the road, “you must help him lift it up.”
Deuteronomy 22:4
Walk past it
Walking past is the very thing forbidden: “you must not ignore it” (22:4).
Report it later
The law demands immediate help, not a later report (22:4).
Help lift it up
Slaughter it
Nothing in the command calls for killing the animal; the fallen animal is to be lifted up (22:4).
Take it home as a pledge
Taking the animal as a pledge would profit from the owner’s trouble; the law calls for help to lift it up (22:4).
In the bird’s nest law of Deuteronomy 22, if someone came across a nest with young birds or eggs and the mother was sitting on them, what could be taken?
Deuteronomy 22:7 says “You may take the young, but be sure to let the mother go,” so that it may be well with you.
Deuteronomy 22:6-7
The mother only
Taking the mother alone is backward; the mother is the one to be let go (22:7).
The young or eggs, but not the mother
The mother and the young
Taking the mother along with the young is explicitly forbidden (22:6).
The nest itself only
The law speaks of taking the young or eggs; it says nothing about taking only the nest (22:6–7).
Nothing at all
Something could be taken: the young were permitted, only the mother was to be released (22:7).
In the rooftop safety law of Deuteronomy 22:8, what was an Israelite to construct around the roof of a new house?
Deuteronomy 22:8 commands a new house to have a railing around its roof so you do not bring bloodguilt on your house if someone falls.
Deuteronomy 22:8
A watchtower
A watchtower is a military structure; Deuteronomy 22:8 requires a railing to keep people from falling off the roof.
A railing
A tent of meeting
The tent of meeting was the place where the LORD met with Israel (Exodus 33:7), not a safety feature for a house roof.
A storehouse
A storehouse holds grain; the roof law is about a railing to prevent bloodguilt from falls (22:8).
A stone altar
Altars were built for sacrifice; the roof law concerns a safety railing, not worship (22:8).
In Deuteronomy 22, what were Israelites told to make on the four corners of the cloak they wore?
Deuteronomy 22:12 says: “You are to make tassels on the four corners of the cloak you wear.”
Deuteronomy 22:12
Bells
Bells were sewn on the hem of the high priest’s robe, not commanded for every Israelite’s cloak (Exodus 28:33).
Embroidered cherubim
Embroidered cherubim belonged to the tabernacle curtains (Exodus 26:1), not to ordinary cloaks.
Tassels
Leather patches
No leather patches are commanded; the cloak was to have tassels on its four corners (22:12).
Silver clasps
Silver clasps are not mentioned; the command is for tassels on the four corners (22:12).
In the holiness instructions of Deuteronomy 22, what practice is called detestable to the LORD?
Deuteronomy 22:5 says a woman must not wear men’s clothing and a man must not wear women’s clothing, for whoever does so “is detestable to the LORD your God.”
Deuteronomy 22:5
A woman wearing a man’s apparel and a man wearing a woman’s garment
A traveler taking the young birds but letting the mother go
Taking the young birds while letting the mother go is permitted in the verses that follow (22:6–7), not called detestable.
A homeowner building a railing around his new roof
Building a railing around a new roof is commanded to avoid bloodguilt (22:8), not condemned.
A farmer returning a lost ox to his brother
Returning a lost ox to a brother is required by the law (22:1), not called detestable.
A man helping lift his neighbor’s fallen donkey
Helping lift a neighbor’s fallen donkey is commanded (22:4), not called detestable.
Deuteronomy 22 forbids wearing clothes woven from which two materials together?
Deuteronomy 22:11 says: “Do not wear clothes of wool and linen woven together.”
Deuteronomy 22:11
Silk and goat hair
Silk and goat hair are not named in this command; the forbidden mixture is wool and linen (22:11).
Wool and linen
Leather and flax
Leather and flax are not mentioned; the verse names wool and linen woven together (22:11).
Wool and purple cloth
Purple cloth is not part of this law; wool is forbidden with linen (22:11).
Cotton and hemp
Cotton and hemp are not mentioned in the chapter; the ban is on wool and linen together (22:11).
In the farming laws of Deuteronomy 22, which two animals were not to be yoked together for plowing?
Deuteronomy 22:10 says: “Do not plow with an ox and a donkey yoked together.”
Deuteronomy 22:10
Two oxen
Two oxen yoked together was ordinary; the ban is on yoking an ox with a donkey (22:10).
A horse and a mule
Horses and mules are not named in the law; the pair forbidden is an ox and a donkey (22:10).
An ox and a donkey
Two donkeys
Two donkeys are not mentioned; the prohibition is about mixing an ox with a donkey (22:10).
A camel and an ox
Camels are not mentioned here; the command names an ox and a donkey (22:10).
In the vineyard law of Deuteronomy 22, what was the result if a person planted a vineyard with two types of seed?
Deuteronomy 22:9 warns that if you plant your vineyard with two types of seed, the entire harvest will be defiled, both the crop you plant and the fruit of your vineyard.
Deuteronomy 22:9
Only the second planting failed
The verse does not say only the second planting fails; the entire harvest, both crop and vineyard fruit, is defiled (22:9).
Both the seed crop and the vineyard’s produce became defiled
The land had to rest for seven years
A seven-year rest for the land is the Sabbath year law (Leviticus 25:4), not the penalty for mixed seed.
The vineyard automatically belonged to the Levites
The text gives no transfer of the vineyard to the Levites; the result is a defiled harvest (22:9).
The owner paid fifty shekels
Fifty shekels is the payment for seizing an unbetrothed virgin (22:29), not for mixed seed.
According to the bird’s nest instruction in Deuteronomy 22, what blessing was attached to letting the mother bird go free?
Deuteronomy 22:7 says to let the mother go “so that it may be well with you and that you may prolong your days.”
Deuteronomy 22:7
Exemption from military service for a whole year
Exemption from war for a year was given to a newly married man (Deuteronomy 24:5), not as a reward for sparing a mother bird.
A double harvest in the very next season
No double harvest is promised here; the stated reward is well-being and long life (22:7).
That it may go well with you and you may prolong your days
Automatic cleansing from every kind of uncleanness
Cleansing from uncleanness is not the promise of this law; it is that things go well and days are prolonged (22:7).
Freedom from paying the tithes for a year
Release from tithes is not offered; the blessing attached is well-being and long life (22:7).
In the case law of Deuteronomy 22, if a husband accused his new wife of not being a virgin, what were her parents to bring to the city elders at the gate?
The girl’s father and mother were to bring “the proof of her virginity” to the elders at the gate and spread out the cloth before them (22:15–17).
Deuteronomy 22:15-17
The marriage contract
The law calls for proof of her virginity spread before the elders, not a marriage contract (22:15–17).
A list of wedding guests
The elders did not need a guest list; her parents brought the proof of her virginity (22:15).
The evidence of her virginity
A lamb for a guilt offering
No guilt offering is required; the parents bring proof of her virginity (22:15–17).
A written appeal from the priest
No letter from a priest is involved; her parents present the proof to the city elders (22:15).
When a husband falsely defamed a virgin in Israel in Deuteronomy 22, what fine was he required to pay, and to whom?
Because he gave a virgin of Israel a bad name, the husband was fined a hundred shekels of silver, paid to the young woman’s father (22:19).
Deuteronomy 22:18-19
Fifty shekels to the elders
Fifty shekels is the sum the seducer of an unbetrothed virgin pays her father (22:29), not this fine.
One hundred shekels to the woman’s father
Twenty shekels to the priests
No fine of twenty shekels to priests is set; the fine was a hundred shekels to the father (22:19).
One hundred shekels to the woman herself
The amount is right but the recipient is wrong: the silver goes to the young woman’s father (22:19).
No fine, only a warning
He was not merely warned: the elders punished him and fined him a hundred shekels (22:18–19).
If the accusation against a bride was proven true under Deuteronomy 22, where was the young woman taken, and what penalty followed?
If the accusation was true, she was brought to the door of her father’s house, where the men of her city stoned her to death (22:21).
Deuteronomy 22:20-21
To the sanctuary, where the priests made atonement for her
Purification at the sanctuary is not the law’s answer; it calls for stoning at her father’s door (22:21).
To the city gate, where the elders publicly rebuked her
A public rebuke was the fate of the false accuser (22:18), not the guilty bride, who faced death by stoning (22:21).
To the door of her father’s house, where the men of her city stoned her to death
To the king’s court, where a heavy fine was imposed on her
No king’s court or fine is involved; the men of her city carried out the penalty (22:21).
Out beyond the camp, where she was driven into exile
Exile outside the camp is not the penalty here; the law prescribes stoning at her father’s house (22:21).
In Deuteronomy 22, if a man was found lying with another man’s wife, who was to die?
Deuteronomy 22:22 says that if a man is found lying with another man’s wife, “both the man who slept with her and the woman must die.”
Deuteronomy 22:22
Only the man
Both are guilty; the woman is not spared (22:22).
Only the woman
Both are guilty; the man is not spared (22:22).
Both the man and the woman
The woman’s husband
The husband was the wronged party, not the one to die (22:22).
No one, if witnesses were lacking
The verse does not excuse them for lack of witnesses; it says both must die when they are found (22:22).
In Moses’ law about a betrothed virgin inside a city in Deuteronomy 22, what was the judgment if a man lay with her and she did not cry out?
If a betrothed virgin was taken in the city and did not cry out, both were taken to the city gate and stoned: she for not crying out, he for violating his neighbor’s wife (22:23–24).
Deuteronomy 22:23-24
The man paid a bride-price and married her
A bride-price marriage is the outcome for an unbetrothed virgin (22:28–29), not a betrothed one (22:24).
Only the man died
Only the man dies in the open country case, where she cried out (22:25), not in the city case.
Both were brought to the gate of that city and stoned to death
The woman was sent back to her father and the man was whipped
No whipping or return to her father is prescribed here; both were stoned (22:24).
Both brought sacrifices and were forgiven
The law prescribes stoning, not forgiveness through sacrifices (22:24).
In the field-assault case of Deuteronomy 22, what was the verdict if a man found a betrothed virgin in the field and forced her to lie with him?
In the open country the woman is not punished because “she has committed no sin worthy of death,” so only the man who attacked her must die (22:25–26).
Deuteronomy 22:25-27
Both were to die
Both die in the city case because she did not cry out (22:24), not in the field.
Only the man was to die
Only the woman was to die
The woman is not to be punished; she committed no sin worthy of death (22:26).
The man paid fifty shekels and married her
Fifty shekels and marriage is for an unbetrothed virgin (22:28–29), not a betrothed one assaulted in the field.
Both were declared innocent
The man is guilty and must die; only the woman is declared free of blame (22:25–26).
Deuteronomy 22 says the assault of a betrothed virgin in the field is like what other crime?
Deuteronomy 22:26 says this case is just like one in which a man attacks his neighbor and murders him.
Deuteronomy 22:26-27
Kidnapping a Hebrew servant
Kidnapping is a different capital crime (Exodus 21:16), not the comparison given here (22:26).
Bearing false witness
False witness is not the comparison; the text compares it to a man attacking and murdering his neighbor (22:26).
Attacking and murdering another person
Stealing a neighbor’s ox
Stealing an ox is covered by other laws, not by this comparison (22:26).
Burning a field
Burning a field is not mentioned; the comparison is murder (22:26).
In the law about an unbetrothed virgin in Deuteronomy 22, what was required if a man seized her, lay with her, and they were discovered?
Deuteronomy 22:29 requires the man to pay the young woman’s father fifty shekels of silver, marry her, and never divorce her as long as he lives.
Deuteronomy 22:28-29
He paid thirty shekels to her father and was free to leave her
Thirty shekels is the price for a gored servant (Exodus 21:32), not this penalty; the sum here is fifty shekels paid to her father (22:29).
He paid fifty shekels to her father, married her, and could never divorce her
Both were taken to the city gate and stoned for the offense
Stoning at the city gate is for a betrothed virgin in the city (22:23–24), not for an unbetrothed one.
He served her father seven years without any wages
Seven years of service is Jacob’s arrangement for Rachel (Genesis 29:18), not this law.
He brought a ram for a guilt offering and was forgiven
No ram or forgiveness is mentioned; the man pays fifty shekels and must marry her (22:29).
The closing command of Deuteronomy 22 forbids a man to do what?
The chapter closes with “A man is not to marry his father’s wife, so that he will not dishonor his father’s marriage bed” (22:30).
Deuteronomy 22:30
Marry his brother’s widow
Marrying a brother’s widow was actually commanded when he died without a son (Deuteronomy 25:5), and it is not forbidden in 22:30.
Marry a woman from a foreign city
Nothing in the chapter bans marrying a woman from a foreign city; the closing command concerns the father’s wife (22:30).
Marry his father’s wife and dishonor his father’s bed
Take two wives from one family
The chapter does not forbid taking two wives from one family; its last verse concerns the father’s wife (22:30).
Remarry a divorced wife after her second marriage
That ban appears in Deuteronomy 24:4, not in the closing verse of Deuteronomy 22.
In Deuteronomy 23, when someone entered a neighbor’s vineyard, what was he allowed to do?
Deuteronomy 23:24 says that when you enter your neighbor’s vineyard you may eat your fill of grapes, but you must not put any in your basket.
Deuteronomy 23:24
Harvest enough grapes to feed his whole family
Harvesting for a household is exactly what 23:24 forbids; you may eat on the spot but not carry grapes away.
Eat his fill of grapes but put none in a basket
Take only the fallen grapes lying on the ground
The law is not limited to fallen grapes; it allows eating one’s fill from the vine (23:24). Leaving fallen gleanings for the poor is a separate rule (Leviticus 19:10).
Cut one cluster of grapes to carry home with him
Cutting a cluster to carry home is forbidden; nothing may go in the basket (23:24).
Eat nothing there unless the owner had invited him
No invitation was required; a person entering a neighbor’s vineyard may eat his fill (23:24).
In the law of Deuteronomy 23, what could a person do when entering a neighbor’s standing grain?
Deuteronomy 23:25 says you may pluck the heads of grain with your hand, but must not put a sickle to your neighbor’s grain.
Deuteronomy 23:25
Reap with a sickle if he was poor
A sickle is exactly what 23:25 forbids, whether the person is poor or not.
Fill a sack with grain
Filling a sack is not allowed; 23:25 permits only plucking heads of grain by hand.
Pluck heads of grain with his hand, but not use a sickle
Take only what was left after harvest
The permission applies to the standing grain, not only what is left after harvest; leftovers for the poor are a separate law (Leviticus 23:22).
Burn a handful as an offering
Nothing in 23:25 mentions burning grain as an offering.
In Moses’ instruction about a slave who escaped and took refuge in Israel, what was the Israelites’ command?
Deuteronomy 23:15–16 says not to return a slave to his master if he has taken refuge with you; he may live among you wherever he chooses.
Deuteronomy 23:15
Do not return him to his master
Keep him chained for seven days
No chaining is permitted; 23:16 says not to oppress him.
Send him to the Levites
Sending him to the Levites is not mentioned; he may live wherever he chooses (23:16).
Make him pay a ransom
No ransom is demanded; the slave is not to be returned (23:15).
Return him at the next new moon
Returning him at the new moon is the opposite of 23:15, which forbids returning him.
When Deuteronomy 23 spoke about neighboring peoples, which people were not to be despised because he was Israel’s brother?
Deuteronomy 23:7 says, “Do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother.”
Deuteronomy 23:7
Moabite
Moabites were barred from the assembly of the LORD to the tenth generation (23:3).
Ammonite
Ammonites were barred from the assembly of the LORD to the tenth generation (23:3).
Amalekite
Amalekites were to be remembered as Israel’s enemy and blotted out (Deuteronomy 25:17–19), not treated as brothers.
Edomite
Philistine
Philistines are not mentioned in this passage; the Edomites are the kin of Israel, descended from Esau (Genesis 36:1).
Regarding vows to the LORD in Deuteronomy 23, what if a person chose not to make a vow?
