Ephraim appears with Manasseh as the myriads and thousands of Joseph’s blessing (33:17).
Zebulun
Zebulun is told to rejoice in his journeys (33:18).
At the end of Joseph’s blessing in Deuteronomy 33, which two tribal groups are named together?
Joseph’s blessing ends, “Such are the myriads of Ephraim, and such are the thousands of Manasseh” (33:17).
Deuteronomy 33:17
Reuben and Simeon
Reuben is blessed alone in 33:6, and Simeon is not named in the chapter.
Judah and Benjamin
Judah and Benjamin each have their own blessings (33:7, 12).
Zebulun and Issachar
Zebulun and Issachar share the blessing in 33:18, not Joseph’s.
Ephraim and Manasseh
Dan and Naphtali
Dan and Naphtali are blessed in 33:22–23, not in Joseph’s blessing.
In Deuteronomy 33, which tribe is said to teach God’s ordinances to Jacob and place incense and burnt offerings on His altar?
Of Levi, Moses said, “He will teach Your ordinances to Jacob and Your law to Israel; he will set incense before You and whole burnt offerings on Your altar” (33:10).
Deuteronomy 33:10
Levi
Judah
Judah’s blessing is a prayer for help against foes (33:7).
Benjamin
Benjamin is the beloved of the LORD who rests secure (33:12).
Gad
Gad enlarges his domain and lies down like a lion (33:20–21).
Naphtali
Naphtali is full of the blessing of the LORD (33:23).
In Moses’ blessing over Levi in Deuteronomy 33, at which two places did he say God tested and contended with His godly one?
Moses spoke of God’s godly one “whom You tested at Massah and contested at the waters of Meribah” (33:8).
Deuteronomy 33:8
Bethel and Ai
Ai was a city Joshua later conquered (Joshua 8), and Bethel is unrelated to Levi’s testing.
Kadesh and Hormah
Hormah is where Israel was defeated by Canaanites after its unbelief at Kadesh (Numbers 14:45), not where Levi was tested.
Massah and Meribah
Gilgal and Shiloh
Gilgal and Shiloh were Israel’s camp and the tabernacle’s site in Joshua’s day (Joshua 4:19; 18:1), not Levi’s testing places.
Sinai and Horeb
Sinai appears in 33:2 and Horeb is the mountain of God (Exodus 3:1), but neither is named as Levi’s testing place.
In Deuteronomy 33, what did Moses call the law that he gave to Israel?
Moses called the law “the possession of the assembly of Jacob” (33:4).
Deuteronomy 33:4
The rod of Joseph
Joseph’s blessing speaks of dew and a firstborn bull (33:13–17), not a rod; the law is not called a rod of Joseph.
The inheritance of Judah
Judah’s blessing is a prayer for help (33:7); the law is not called an inheritance of Judah.
The possession of the assembly of Jacob
The sword of Jeshurun
The sword in which Israel boasts is the LORD (33:29); the law is not called the sword of Jeshurun.
The song of the wilderness
Moses’ song is recorded in Deuteronomy 31:30–32:43; the law in 33:4 is the possession of the assembly of Jacob.
In the line about Jeshurun in Deuteronomy 33, who became King when the leaders of the people assembled with the tribes of Israel?
The LORD became King in Jeshurun when the leaders of the people gathered and the tribes of Israel came together (33:5).
Deuteronomy 33:5
Moses
Moses is the man of God who pronounced the blessing (33:1); he is not called the King.
Joshua
Joshua takes over leadership after Moses’ death (Deuteronomy 34:9), but 33:5 names the LORD as King.
Aaron
Aaron served as priest and had died before this blessing (Numbers 33:38); he is not called king.
The LORD
The high priest
The high priest serves under the LORD, who is the King (33:5).
Near the close of Deuteronomy 33, Moses says, “The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are…” what?
Moses said, “The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms” (33:27).
Deuteronomy 33:27
Chariots of fire
Chariots of fire appear when Elijah is taken up (2 Kings 2:11), not in this verse.
Everlasting arms
Pillars of cloud
A pillar of cloud guided Israel by day (Exodus 13:21), but this verse speaks of everlasting arms.
Foundations of stone
Foundations of stone are not named in this verse; underneath are the everlasting arms (33:27).
Rivers of peace
Isaiah 66:12 speaks of peace like a river, but this verse names everlasting arms.
Looking at the tribes explicitly named in Moses’ blessings in Deuteronomy 33, which son of Jacob is not mentioned by name?
Reuben, Judah, Levi, Benjamin, Joseph, Zebulun, Issachar, Gad, Dan, Naphtali, and Asher are named in 33:6–25; Simeon is not.
Deuteronomy 33:6-25
Simeon
Reuben
Reuben is named in the first blessing (33:6).
Dan
Dan is named in 33:22.
Asher
Asher is named in 33:24.
Naphtali
Naphtali is named in 33:23.
At the close of Moses’ life in Deuteronomy 34, from which mountain did he view the land the LORD showed him?
Deuteronomy 34:1 says Moses “went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, which faces Jericho.”
Deuteronomy 34:1
Mount Sinai
Mount Sinai is where Moses received the tablets (Exodus 34:2), far from the plains of Moab.
Mount Nebo
Mount Hor
Mount Hor is where Aaron died (Numbers 20:25–28), not where Moses viewed the land.
Mount Carmel
Mount Carmel is where Elijah met the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18:19).
Mount Gerizim
Mount Gerizim is where the blessing was to be proclaimed (Deuteronomy 11:29), not where Moses viewed the land.
In the land-viewing scene of Deuteronomy 34, which city is called “the City of Palms”?
34:3 describes “the region from the Valley of Jericho (the City of Palms) all the way to Zoar.”
Deuteronomy 34:3
Hebron
34:3 gives the title “City of Palms” to Jericho, not Hebron.
Jerusalem
34:3 gives the title “City of Palms” to Jericho, not Jerusalem.
Jericho
Bethel
34:3 gives the title “City of Palms” to Jericho, not Bethel.
Beersheba
34:3 gives the title “City of Palms” to Jericho, not Beersheba.
When the LORD spoke to Moses about the promised land in Deuteronomy 34, which patriarchs did He name?
34:4 says, “This is the land that I swore to give Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.”
Deuteronomy 34:4
Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
Noah, Shem, and Eber
Noah, Shem, and Eber lived before Abraham; the land oath was sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (34:4).
David, Solomon, and Samuel
David, Solomon, and Samuel lived centuries after the oath; 34:4 names Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Caleb, Joshua, and Eleazar
Caleb, Joshua, and Eleazar were Moses’ contemporaries, not the patriarchs of the oath (34:4).
Terah, Nahor, and Haran
Terah, Nahor, and Haran were Abraham’s father and brothers (Genesis 11:26), not the patriarchs of the oath.
Before Moses died in Moab, what did the LORD tell him he would do with the land, but not do?
The LORD said, “I have let you see it with your own eyes, but you will not cross into it” (34:4).
Deuteronomy 34:4
Divide it by lot but not live in it himself
Moses did not divide the land; Eleazar and Joshua were to assign it (Numbers 34:17).
See it with his own eyes but not cross into it
Measure it with a line but not settle in it
Measuring the land is not mentioned; the LORD let Moses see it but not cross (34:4).
Bless it from the mountain but not name it
Blessing it from the mountain is not mentioned; 34:4 says he would see it but not cross into it.
Enter it with Joshua but not lead the people
Moses was not allowed to enter at all (34:4); Joshua led the people instead (34:9).
In Deuteronomy 34’s account of Moses’ death, in what land did Moses die?
34:5 says, “Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, as the LORD had said.”
Deuteronomy 34:5
Canaan
Moses did not cross into Canaan (34:4); he died in Moab (34:5).
Midian
Moses once lived in Midian after fleeing Egypt (Exodus 2:15), but he died in Moab (34:5).
Edom
Edom is not where Moses died; 34:5 says the land of Moab.
Moab
Egypt
Moses left Egypt in the exodus; he died in the land of Moab (34:5).
After Moses died, how long did the Israelites weep for him in the plains of Moab?
“The Israelites grieved for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days” (34:8), the same length as the mourning for Aaron (Numbers 20:29).
Deuteronomy 34:8
7 days
Seven days was the mourning for Jacob (Genesis 50:10), not for Moses.
14 days
Fourteen days is not given; 34:8 says thirty.
30 days
40 days
Forty days were the days of embalming Jacob (Genesis 50:3), not the weeping for Moses.
70 days
Seventy days was the Egyptians’ mourning for Jacob (Genesis 50:3), not Israel’s for Moses.
In the leadership transition at the end of Deuteronomy, who was filled with the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him?
“Joshua son of Nun was filled with the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him” (34:9).
Deuteronomy 34:9
Caleb son of Jephunneh
Caleb son of Jephunneh was Judah’s leader in dividing the land (Numbers 34:19); 34:9 names Joshua.
Joshua son of Nun
Eleazar son of Aaron
Eleazar the priest helped assign the land (Numbers 34:17); 34:9 names Joshua as the one Moses laid hands on.
Phinehas son of Eleazar
Phinehas is not named in 34:9; Joshua is.
Othniel son of Kenaz
Othniel was a later judge on whom the Spirit of the LORD came (Judges 3:9–10), not Moses’ successor.
When Deuteronomy 34 reports Moses’ condition at death, which description is correct?
34:7 says Moses “was a hundred and twenty years old when he died, yet his eyes were not weak, and his vitality had not diminished.”
Deuteronomy 34:7
He was 90 years old, and his sight had failed
Moses was eighty when he stood before Pharaoh (Exodus 7:7) and a hundred and twenty at death, with his eyes not weak (34:7).
He was 100 years old, but his strength was gone
He was a hundred and twenty, not a hundred, and his vitality had not diminished (34:7).
He was 120 years old, yet his eyes were not weak and his vitality had not diminished
He was 130 years old, and he could no longer hear clearly
He was a hundred and twenty, not a hundred and thirty, and no loss of hearing is mentioned (34:7).
He was 140 years old, but he still fought in battle
He was a hundred and twenty, not a hundred and forty, and he was not fighting in battle at his death (34:7).
In the account of Moses’ burial in Deuteronomy 34, which statement is correct?
“He buried him in a valley in the land of Moab facing Beth-peor, and no one to this day knows the location of his grave” (34:6).
Deuteronomy 34:6
He was buried in the cave at Hebron beside Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, in the family tomb
The patriarchs were buried in the cave of Machpelah near Mamre (Genesis 25:9), not Moses; his grave is unknown (34:6).
He was buried on top of Mount Nebo, and Israel marked the tomb with a stone pillar there
Moses was buried in a valley in Moab, and no one knows where his grave is (34:6); no marked tomb is mentioned.
He was buried in the valley in the land of Moab, opposite Beth-peor, and no one knows his grave to this day
He was buried at Gilgal beside the Jordan, where the people built a memorial to him
Gilgal is not named in the burial account; Moses’ grave is in a valley in Moab and is unknown (34:6).
He was buried near Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin, beside his sister Miriam’s grave
Miriam died and was buried at Kadesh (Numbers 20:1); Moses was buried in Moab (34:6).
In the closing tribute of Deuteronomy 34, why is Moses said to be unmatched among Israel’s prophets?
34:10–11 says no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses, “whom the LORD knew face to face,” who did the signs and wonders in the land of Egypt.
Deuteronomy 34:10-12
He built the temple in Jerusalem and ruled Israel as its king
Moses never ruled as king, and the temple was built by Solomon (1 Kings 6:1); neither is the tribute in 34:10–12.
The LORD knew him face to face, and he did signs and wonders in Egypt
He conquered all of Canaan by himself, without any army
Moses was not allowed to enter Canaan (34:4); Joshua succeeded him (34:9).
He appointed every judge in Israel and ruled over each tribe
Later judges, such as Othniel, were raised up long after Moses (Judges 3:9); this is not the tribute in 34:10–12.
He never left the Promised Land once he had entered it
Moses could not enter the land at all (34:4); he did not live in it and then leave.
6: At the start of Joshua 1, after whose death did the LORD speak to Joshua son of Nun?
Joshua 1:1 opens, “Now after the death of His servant Moses, the LORD spoke to Joshua son of Nun.”
Joshua 1:1
Aaron
Aaron had died long before on the mountain, with Eleazar taking his garments (Numbers 20:28); the chapter opens after Moses’ death.
Moses
Caleb
Caleb was still alive and later came to Joshua at Gilgal to ask for Hebron (Joshua 14:6).
Samuel
Samuel was born to Hannah generations later (1 Samuel 1:20), long after Joshua’s day.
Eli
Eli was the priest at Shiloh in Hannah’s day (1 Samuel 1:9), long after Joshua.
In the opening of Joshua 1, to whom did the LORD speak?
The LORD spoke “to Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ assistant” (1:1).
Joshua 1:1
Caleb son of Jephunneh
Caleb son of Jephunneh was Joshua’s fellow faithful spy (Numbers 14:6), but the commission in 1:1–9 is spoken to Joshua.
Eleazar the priest
Eleazar the priest later helped Joshua distribute the land (Joshua 14:1); the LORD’s words in 1:1 go to Joshua.
Joshua son of Nun
Phinehas
Phinehas son of Eleazar appears later, sent to the eastern tribes in Gilead (Joshua 22:13).
Gideon
Gideon lived in the time of the judges and was called at Ophrah by the angel of the LORD (Judges 6:11).
In Joshua 1:1, how is Joshua described in relation to Moses?
Joshua 1:1 calls Joshua “Moses’ assistant,” the role he had filled since the wilderness years (Exodus 33:11).
Joshua 1:1
Moses’ brother
Moses’ brother was Aaron (Exodus 4:14); Joshua was the son of Nun (1:1).
Moses’ assistant
Moses’ father-in-law
Moses’ father-in-law was Jethro, the priest of Midian (Exodus 18:1).
Moses’ scribe
Joshua is never called Moses’ scribe; 1:1 calls him Moses’ assistant.
Moses’ judge
Joshua is not called a judge in 1:1; the judges arose only after his death (Judges 2:16).
In God’s first command to Joshua in this chapter, which river was Israel told to cross?
The LORD said, “arise, you and all these people, and cross over the Jordan” (1:2).
Joshua 1:2
Nile
The Nile was Egypt’s river, which Aaron struck with the staff (Exodus 7:20).
Euphrates
The Euphrates appears in 1:4 as the far boundary of the promised territory, not the river to be crossed.
Jabbok
Jacob crossed the ford of the Jabbok on his way back to Canaan (Genesis 32:22).
Jordan
Kishon
The River Kishon swept away Sisera’s army in Deborah’s song (Judges 5:21).
In Joshua 1, what were Joshua and all the people going to receive?
God told them to cross “into the land that I am giving to the children of Israel” (1:2).
Joshua 1:2
A king
Israel did not ask for a king until Samuel was old (1 Samuel 8:5).
A temple
The temple was begun by Solomon 480 years after the exodus (1 Kings 6:1).
The land
New laws
Joshua received no new laws; he was to observe “all the law that My servant Moses commanded” (1:7).
Silver from Egypt
Israel took silver and gold from the Egyptians at the exodus (Exodus 12:35), forty years earlier.
In the opening verses of Joshua 1, how is Moses identified?
Moses is “His servant” and “Moses My servant” in 1:1–2, and “the servant of the LORD” in 1:13 and 1:15.
Joshua 1:1-2
Prophet of Baal
The prophets of Baal opposed Elijah on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:19); Moses is the LORD’s servant.
Servant of the LORD
Priest of Israel
The priesthood belonged to Moses’ brother Aaron and his sons (Exodus 28:1).
King of Jeshurun
Moses’ blessing says the LORD became King in Jeshurun (Deuteronomy 33:5); Moses himself is never called king.
Captain of Judah
Moses came from the house of Levi (Exodus 2:1), not Judah, and is never called a captain.
In Joshua 1, who said, “Moses My servant is dead”?
The LORD speaks these words to Joshua: “Moses My servant is dead” (1:1–2).
Joshua 1:2
Joshua
Joshua is the one addressed; he hears the news from the LORD (1:1–2).
Eleazar
Eleazar the priest does not speak in Joshua 1.
Caleb
Caleb does not speak in this chapter; his first words in Joshua come when he asks for Hebron (Joshua 14:6).
The LORD
The people
The people speak only at the end of the chapter, pledging obedience to Joshua (1:16–18).
In the LORD’s commission to Joshua, what was Joshua told to do next?
The LORD said, “Now therefore arise, you and all these people, and cross over the Jordan” (1:2).
Joshua 1:2
Build an altar
Joshua later built an altar on Mount Ebal (Joshua 8:30); the first command was to cross the Jordan.
Arise and cross the Jordan
Count the tribes
The census of the tribes was taken under Moses (Numbers 26:2); Joshua was told to cross the Jordan.
Appoint a king
Israel had no king until Saul was presented by Samuel (1 Samuel 10:24).
Return to Egypt
The LORD had said, “You are never to go back that way again” (Deuteronomy 17:16); Joshua was to lead them into Canaan.
In Joshua 1:2, who was to go across the Jordan with Joshua?
God said, “arise, you and all these people, and cross over the Jordan” (1:2).
Joshua 1:2
Only the priests
The priests carried the ark ahead (Joshua 3:6), but the entire nation crossed the Jordan (Joshua 3:17).
Only the army
The command was not limited to soldiers; Joshua was to cross with “all these people” (1:2).
Joshua and all these people
The tribe of Judah only
Judah is singled out to go up first in Judges 1:2; here all the people were to cross (1:2).
Moses’ family
Moses’ family is not mentioned; the command covered Joshua and the whole nation (1:2).
In God’s promise to Joshua, every place where the sole of what would tread was given to Israel?
God promised, “I have given you every place where the sole of your foot will tread” (1:3).
Joshua 1:3
Your foot
Your staff
A staff was Moses’ tool at the Red Sea (Exodus 14:16); the promise in 1:3 is about the sole of the foot.
Your hand
The verse speaks of the sole of the foot, not the hand (1:3).
Your sandal strap
Sandals come up when Joshua is told to take them off before the Commander of the LORD’s army (Joshua 5:15).
Your chariot wheel
Chariot wheels wobbled for Pharaoh’s army in the sea (Exodus 14:25); Israel’s promise is tied to the foot.
In Joshua 1:3, God said He had given the land just as He had promised to whom?
God said, “I have given you every place where the sole of your foot will tread, just as I promised to Moses” (1:3).
Joshua 1:3
Abraham
God first promised the land to Abram (Genesis 12:7), but 1:3 points to His promise to Moses.
Isaac
God confirmed the oath to Isaac (Genesis 26:3), but 1:3 says “just as I promised to Moses.”
Jacob
God promised the land to Jacob at Bethel (Genesis 28:13); in 1:3 the reference is to Moses.
Moses
David
David lived centuries after Joshua; 1:3 refers to what God promised Moses.
In the early part of Joshua 1, what quality did God tell Joshua to have?
God says “Be strong and courageous” in 1:6, “be strong and very courageous” in 1:7, and repeats the charge in 1:9.
Joshua 1:6-9
Silence
Far from silence, Joshua was to keep the Book of the Law in his mouth (1:8).
Wealth
Prosperity was promised as a result of obedience (1:8), but the quality commanded was strength and courage.
Strength and courage
Speed
Speed is never commanded; the repeated charge is to be strong and courageous (1:6–9).
Cunning
Cunning is not commended; Joshua’s success hinged on careful obedience to the law (1:7–8).
In Joshua 1, what book was not to depart from Joshua’s mouth?
“This Book of the Law must not depart from your mouth; meditate on it day and night” (1:8).
Joshua 1:8
The Book of Judges
The book of Judges records events after Joshua’s death (Judges 2:8).
The Book of the Covenant
Moses read the Book of the Covenant to the people at Sinai (Exodus 24:7); 1:8 names the Book of the Law.
The Book of the Law
The Book of Psalms
The Psalms come largely from David’s era and later; Joshua was to keep the Book of the Law (1:8).
The Book of the Kings
The books of Kings record Israel’s monarchy, centuries after Joshua.
According to Joshua 1:8, when was Joshua to meditate on the Book of the Law?
Joshua was told to “meditate on it day and night” (1:8).
Joshua 1:8
At harvest only
Joshua’s meditation was not seasonal; 1:8 says “day and night.”
Once a year
The law was read to all Israel every seven years at the Feast of Tabernacles (Deuteronomy 31:10–11), but Joshua was to meditate on it continually.
Morning only
Not mornings only: 1:8 calls for meditation both day and night.
Day and night
On Sabbaths only
The Sabbath was the weekly holy day (Exodus 20:8), but Joshua’s meditation was to be daily, day and night (1:8).
In Joshua’s instruction to the officers, what were the people to prepare?
The officers told the people, “Prepare your provisions, for within three days you will cross the Jordan” (1:11).
Joshua 1:11
Altars
Altars come later, such as the one Joshua built on Mount Ebal (Joshua 8:30).
Provisions
Tents
Tents are not mentioned; the people were to prepare provisions for the crossing (1:11).
Trumpets
Rams’ horns sounded later at Jericho (Joshua 6:4); here the people prepared provisions.
Shields
Weapons are mentioned only for the eastern tribes’ warriors, who were to cross “armed for battle” (1:14).
In Joshua 1, within how many days were the Israelites told they would cross the Jordan?
The officers announced, “within three days you will cross the Jordan” (1:11).
Joshua 1:11
One day
The people had three days to prepare, not one (1:11).
Two days
The time given in 1:11 was three days, not two.
Three days
Seven days
Seven days belongs to the Jericho march, six days once around and the seventh day seven times (Joshua 6:3–4).
Forty days
Forty days was the length of the spies’ mission under Moses (Numbers 13:25).
In Joshua 1:10-11, whom did Joshua command to carry his message through the camp?
“Then Joshua commanded the officers of the people” to go through the camp with his message (1:10–11).
Joshua 1:10-11
The priests
The priests’ role came at the crossing itself, carrying the ark ahead of the people (Joshua 3:6).
The Levites
The Levites are not mentioned in Joshua 1; the messengers were the officers (1:10).
The elders
Elders appear among Joshua’s leaders at Shechem (Joshua 24:1), but in 1:10 he commanded the officers.
The officers of the people
The judges
Judges are listed with the officers at Shechem (Joshua 24:1), but in 1:10 only the officers are sent through the camp.
In Joshua 1, which tribal groups did Joshua address about land already given beyond the Jordan?
Joshua spoke “to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh” (1:12), to whom Moses had given land east of the Jordan (Numbers 32:33).
Joshua 1:12
Judah, Benjamin, and Levi
Judah and Benjamin received land west of the Jordan (Joshua 18:11), and Levi received no land inheritance (Joshua 13:14).
Ephraim, Issachar, and Zebulun
Ephraim, Issachar, and Zebulun all received allotments west of the Jordan (Joshua 16; 19).
Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh
Dan, Naphtali, and Asher
Dan, Naphtali, and Asher received their land by lot west of the Jordan (Joshua 19).
Simeon, Levi, and Judah
Simeon’s inheritance lay within Judah’s territory (Joshua 19:1), and Levi received no land (Joshua 13:14).
In Joshua’s reminder to the eastern tribes, who could remain in the land beyond the Jordan?
“Your wives, your young children, and your livestock may remain in the land that Moses gave you on this side of the Jordan” (1:14).
Joshua 1:14
Only the priests
Priests are not mentioned; the families and livestock stayed behind (1:14).
Wives, children, and livestock
Only the firstborn sons
Firstborn sons get no special mention; wives, young children, and livestock remained (1:14).
No one at all
Some did stay: the wives, young children, and livestock (1:14).
The fighting men only
The fighting men were the very ones who had to cross over ahead of their brothers (1:14).
In Joshua 1:14, who had to cross over to help the other tribes?
“All your mighty men of valor must be armed for battle to cross over ahead of your brothers and help them” (1:14).
Joshua 1:14
The singers
Singers belong to David’s Levitical worship (1 Chronicles 15:16), not to Joshua 1:14.
The shepherds
The livestock stayed behind (1:14); those who crossed were the mighty men of valor.
The mighty men of valor
The old men only
Not old men but the mighty men of valor were to cross (1:14).
The foreign servants
No foreign servants are mentioned; the eastern tribes’ own warriors crossed (1:14).
In what manner were the eastern tribes’ warriors to cross over in Joshua 1?
The mighty men were to “be armed for battle to cross over ahead of your brothers” (1:14), and they did so (Joshua 4:12).
Joshua 1:14
Secretly at night
Joshua later marched all night from Gilgal to surprise the Amorites (Joshua 10:9), but this crossing was openly armed for battle.
Armed for battle
One tribe at a time
They crossed over before the other Israelites as one armed force (Joshua 4:12), not tribe by tribe.
Without weapons
The opposite is true: they were to cross “armed for battle” (1:14).
By ship
Israel crossed the Jordan on dry ground when the waters stopped (Joshua 3:17).
In Joshua’s command to the eastern tribes, whom were they supposed to help?
The warriors were to cross over “ahead of your brothers and help them” (1:14).
Joshua 1:14
The Egyptians
Israel had left Egypt forty years earlier; the help was for their fellow Israelites (1:14).
The Philistines
The Philistines were enemies of Israel, later fought by Samson and David.
Their brothers
The Moabites
Moab was a neighbor Israel was told not to harass (Deuteronomy 2:9); the help was for their brothers.
The Canaanite kings
The Canaanite kings were the ones Israel was about to conquer (Joshua 12:7).
According to Joshua 1:15, how long were the eastern tribes to help the others?
They were to help “until the LORD gives them rest as He has done for you, and your brothers also possess the land” (1:15); Joshua released them in Joshua 22:4.
Joshua 1:15
Until the ark of the covenant was carried up to Shiloh
The Tent of Meeting was set up at Shiloh (Joshua 18:1), but their service lasted until the LORD gave their brothers rest (1:15).
Until Jericho fell and Ai had been captured as well
Jericho and Ai fell early in the conquest (Joshua 6; 8); the eastern warriors stayed until the LORD gave their brothers rest (Joshua 22:4).
Until their brothers received rest and took possession of the land
Until the spring barley harvest was gathered in the land
The crossing came during the harvest season (Joshua 3:15), but their duty was measured by rest for their brothers, not a season.
Until the elders of Israel had chosen a king for them
Israel had no king until Saul (1 Samuel 10:24); the warriors were released when their brothers had rest (Joshua 22:4).
In Joshua 1:15, after helping the other tribes, where could the eastern tribes return?
They could “return to the land of your inheritance” which Moses had given them “on the east side of the Jordan” (1:15).
Joshua 1:15
Back to Egypt, the land of their former slavery
Egypt was the land of slavery Israel had left; the LORD had said they were never to go back that way (Deuteronomy 17:16).
To Mount Sinai, where the law had been given
Sinai was where the LORD gave the law (Exodus 19:20); the eastern tribes’ inheritance lay east of the Jordan (1:15).
The land Moses gave them on the east side of the Jordan
To Jerusalem, the stronghold of the Jebusites
Jerusalem was still held by the Jebusites (Joshua 15:63) and lay west of the Jordan.
To the Wilderness of Paran where they had camped
Israel camped in the Wilderness of Paran during the wanderings (Numbers 10:12); their own land was east of the Jordan (1:15).
In God’s description of Israel’s territory in Joshua 1, which region is named near the beginning?
The territory runs “from the wilderness and Lebanon to the great River Euphrates” (1:4).
Joshua 1:4
Bashan
Bashan was Og’s kingdom, already given east of the Jordan (Numbers 32:33); it is not named in 1:4.
Lebanon
Edom
Edom bordered Israel on the south (Numbers 34:3) but is not named in 1:4.
Goshen
Goshen was where Jacob’s family lived in Egypt (Genesis 47:6).
Samaria
Samaria was founded much later by King Omri (1 Kings 16:23–24).
In Joshua 1:4, which great river is named as part of the territory?
The territory extends “to the great River Euphrates” (1:4).
Joshua 1:4
Nile
The Nile was Egypt’s river (Exodus 7:20), not named in Israel’s borders in 1:4.
Jordan
The Jordan is the river Israel had to cross (1:2), not the great river of 1:4.
Tigris
The Tigris is one of Eden’s rivers alongside the Euphrates (Genesis 2:14); it is not named in 1:4.
Euphrates
Arnon
The Arnon was the border between Moab and the Amorites (Numbers 21:13).
In Joshua 1, what body of water marks the western extent of the land?
The land reaches “west as far as the Great Sea” (1:4), the Mediterranean.
Joshua 1:4
The Red Sea
Israel crossed the Red Sea leaving Egypt (Exodus 15:4); it is not the western border in 1:4.
The Dead Sea
The Salt Sea (Dead Sea) marked the southeastern corner of Canaan (Numbers 34:3); the western limit is the Great Sea.
The Great Sea
The Sea of Galilee
The Sea of Chinnereth (Galilee) lies on the eastern border (Numbers 34:11), not the west.
The Nile Delta
The Nile belongs to Egypt; the western border in 1:4 is the Great Sea.
What did God promise Joshua about his enemies in Joshua 1:5?
God promised, “No one shall stand against you all the days of your life” (1:5).
Joshua 1:5
They would all become allies
Only the Gibeonites made peace, and by deception (Joshua 9:15); God promised that no one would stand against Joshua.
No man would stand against him
They would flee only at harvest
No seasonal limit was given; the promise covered “all the days of your life” (1:5).
They would surrender without battle
Joshua fought many battles; thirty-one kings were defeated in all (Joshua 12:24).
They would be judged by Samuel
Samuel judged Israel generations later (1 Samuel 7:15).
In Joshua 1:5, what comparison did God make between Moses and Joshua?
God said, “As I was with Moses, so will I be with you” (1:5).
Joshua 1:5
Joshua would live longer than Moses
Joshua died at 110 (Joshua 24:29), younger than Moses, who died at 120 (Deuteronomy 34:7).
Joshua would speak more laws than Moses
Joshua was to keep the law Moses commanded (1:7), not add new laws.
As God was with Moses, so He would be with Joshua
Joshua would perform more signs than Moses
Scripture says no prophet arose in Israel like Moses (Deuteronomy 34:10).
Joshua would return to Sinai like Moses
Joshua was sent across the Jordan into Canaan (1:2), not back to Sinai.
In the LORD’s promise to Joshua, what two things did He say He would never do?
God said, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (1:5), the same promise Moses gave in Deuteronomy 31:6.
Joshua 1:5
Sleep or slumber
“Neither slumber nor sleep” describes the Protector of Israel in Psalm 121:4, not the promise to Joshua.
Leave or forsake him
Rebuke or correct him
Rebuke and correction are not mentioned in 1:5; God promised never to leave or forsake him.
Test or discipline him
Testing and discipline are not in view; 1:5 is a pure promise of God’s presence.
Hide or wait
God promised constant presence, not hiding: “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (1:5).
In Joshua 1:6, to whom had God sworn He would give the land?
Joshua would give the people the land “that I swore to their fathers I would give them” (1:6).
Joshua 1:6
The judges
The judges arose only after Joshua’s death (Judges 2:16).
The prophets
The oath was made to the patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Deuteronomy 34:4), not to prophets.
Their fathers
The kings
Israel had no kings yet; the oath was to the fathers (1:6).
The priests
The Levitical priests received no land inheritance at all (Joshua 13:14).
In Joshua 1:7, how does God intensify His command to Joshua?
In 1:7 the charge grows: “Above all, be strong and very courageous.”
Joshua 1:7
Be calm and quiet
The charge in 1:7 is to strength and courage, not calm and quiet.
Be strong and very courageous
Be swift and hidden
Hiding fits the spies concealed by Rahab (Joshua 2:4), not God’s charge to Joshua.
Be patient and silent
God called for courage, not silence; the law was to stay in Joshua’s mouth (1:8).
Be wise and rich
Prosperity is promised as the result of obedience (1:7), not commanded as a quality.
In the LORD’s instruction about the law, what was Joshua not to turn from to the right or to the left?
“Be careful to observe all the law that My servant Moses commanded you. Do not turn from it to the right or to the left” (1:7).
Joshua 1:7
The ark
The ark led the crossing (Joshua 3:6), but in 1:7 “it” refers to the law.
The priesthood
The priesthood is not mentioned in 1:7; Joshua was not to turn from the law.
The whole law
The tabernacle curtains
The tabernacle’s curtains are described in Exodus 26; 1:7 concerns all the law.
The feast calendar
The feasts are set out in Leviticus 23; 1:7 speaks of all the law Moses commanded.
According to Joshua 1:7, what would happen if Joshua did not turn from the law?
Joshua was not to turn aside “so that you may prosper wherever you go” (1:7).
Joshua 1:7
He would become king over all nations
Joshua never became a king; Israel’s first king was Saul (1 Samuel 10:24).
He would prosper wherever he went
He would never fight another battle
Joshua fought many more battles (Joshua 12:24); the promise was success, not an end to war.
He would build the temple
The temple was built by Solomon (1 Kings 6:1).
He would live forever
Joshua died at the age of 110 (Joshua 24:29).
In Joshua 1:8, what was Joshua commanded to do with the Book of the Law day and night?
Joshua was to “meditate on it day and night” (1:8).
Joshua 1:8
Hide it
Rather than hide it, Joshua was to keep it in his mouth; the Book of the Law was later lost and found in Josiah’s day (2 Kings 22:8).
Copy it once
Joshua did inscribe a copy of the law on stones at Mount Ebal (Joshua 8:32), but 1:8 calls for daily meditation.
Meditate on it
Burn it as an offering
King Jehoiakim burned Jeremiah’s scroll (Jeremiah 36:23); Joshua was to meditate on the law.
Give it to the priests only
Moses had entrusted the law to the priests and elders (Deuteronomy 31:9), but Joshua himself was to meditate on it.
In the commission of Joshua, why was he to meditate on the law constantly?
He was to meditate “so that you may be careful to do everything written in it” (1:8).
Joshua 1:8
So he could impress the surrounding nations with his wisdom
Wisdom that drew men from all nations is linked to Solomon (1 Kings 4:34); Joshua meditated in order to obey (1:8).
So he could carefully observe everything written in it
So he could replace the words of Moses with his own
Joshua was to observe “all the law that My servant Moses commanded you” (1:7), not replace it.
So he could write new laws for the coming generation
Joshua was no new lawgiver; he was to do everything already written in the Book of the Law (1:8).
So he could avoid the priests and rule Israel alone
Joshua worked alongside Eleazar the priest (Joshua 14:1); nothing in 1:8 sets him against the priests.
According to Joshua 1:8, what result would follow Joshua’s meditation and obedience?
“For then you will prosper and succeed in all you do” (1:8).
Joshua 1:8
He would avoid all enemies forever
Joshua still faced many enemies (Joshua 12:24); the promise was success, not escape from battle.
He would prosper and succeed in all he did
He would never need counsel
Joshua still needed the LORD’s counsel; Israel went wrong with the Gibeonites when they did not seek it (Joshua 9:14).
He would become a priest
Joshua was from the tribe of Ephraim (Numbers 13:8); the priesthood belonged to Aaron’s family (Exodus 28:1).
He would reign from Jerusalem
Jerusalem was still a Jebusite city (Joshua 15:63); David later captured Zion (2 Samuel 5:7).
In Joshua 1:9, which two negative feelings was Joshua told to reject?
God said, “Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged” (1:9).
Joshua 1:9
Anger and envy
Anger and envy are not mentioned; 1:9 addresses fear and discouragement.
Hunger and weariness
The people were told to prepare provisions (1:11), but 1:9 addresses fear and discouragement.
Fear and discouragement
Doubt and laughter
Laughter at God’s promise belongs to Sarah (Genesis 18:12), not Joshua 1:9.
Pride and sorrow
Pride and sorrow are not mentioned; Joshua was told not to be afraid or discouraged (1:9).
What reason does Joshua 1:9 give for Joshua not to be afraid or discouraged?
“For the LORD your God is with you wherever you go” (1:9).
Joshua 1:9
Israel’s army was larger than any army in Canaan
Verse 9 gives no military reason; even the spies said, “The LORD has surely delivered the entire land into our hands” (Joshua 2:24).
Moses had left him detailed maps of the land
The land was mapped later by men Joshua sent out from Shiloh (Joshua 18:8–9), not by maps from Moses.
The LORD his God would be with him wherever he went
The gates of Jericho had been left wide open
Jericho was “tightly shut up because of the Israelites” (Joshua 6:1).
Egypt had been too weakened to pursue them again
Egypt is not mentioned in 1:9; Joshua’s courage rested on the LORD’s presence.
When Joshua passed instructions through the camp, to whom did the officers speak?
Joshua told the officers, “Go through the camp and tell the people” (1:11).
Joshua 1:10-11
The kings of Canaan
The kings of Canaan heard about Israel only after the crossing (Joshua 5:1); no message was sent to them.
The people
The priests only
The message was for all the people, not the priests alone (1:11).
The women only
The message was for all the people, not the women alone (1:11).
The Levites only
The Levites are not singled out; the officers spoke to all the people (1:11).
In Joshua 1:11, what two major actions were the people told would happen within three days?
“Within three days you will cross the Jordan to go in and take possession of the land” (1:11).
Joshua 1:11
Build an altar and appoint judges
Joshua built an altar later on Mount Ebal (Joshua 8:30), and judges arose only after his death (Judges 2:16).
Cross the Jordan and take possession of the land
March around Jericho and shout
Marching around Jericho and shouting came later (Joshua 6:3–5).
Gather manna and rest
Manna stopped once Israel ate the produce of Canaan (Joshua 5:12); 1:11 is about crossing and possessing.
Leave Canaan and return east
The people were entering Canaan westward across the Jordan, not leaving it (1:11).
In Joshua’s reminder to the eastern tribes, whose earlier command were they to remember?
Joshua said, “Remember what Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you” (1:13).
Joshua 1:13
Aaron’s
Aaron had died on the mountain (Numbers 20:28); the command recalled was Moses’ (Numbers 32:20).
Caleb’s
It was Moses, not Caleb, who required the eastern tribes’ men to cross over armed (Deuteronomy 3:18).
Moses’
Samuel’s
Samuel was born generations later (1 Samuel 1:20).
David’s
David reigned centuries later; Joshua reminded them of Moses’ command (1:13).
According to Joshua 1:13, besides land, what had the LORD given the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-Manasseh?
Moses had told them, “The LORD your God will give you rest, and He will give you this land” (1:13).
Joshua 1:13
A monarchy
Israel had no monarchy until Saul (1 Samuel 10:24).
Rest
A temple
The temple was built by Solomon (1 Kings 6:1).
A prophet
A prophet like Moses is promised in Deuteronomy 18:15, but 1:13 speaks of rest and land.
New manna
Manna fed all Israel in the wilderness and stopped after they entered Canaan (Joshua 5:12).
In Joshua 1:15, what were the eastern tribes permitted to do only after helping the others?
“Then you may return to the land of your inheritance and take possession of that which Moses the servant of the LORD gave you” (1:15).
Joshua 1:15
Offer incense in Jerusalem
Burning incense was the priests’ duty (Exodus 30:7), and Jerusalem was not yet Israel’s (Joshua 15:63).
Return to their own land
Appoint a new leader
Joshua remained leader; the tribes pledged to obey him as they had obeyed Moses (1:17).
Sail across the sea
Their land lay across the Jordan (1:15), not across the sea.
Divide the priesthood
The priesthood belonged to Aaron’s family (Exodus 28:1) and was not theirs to divide.
In the tribes’ answer to Joshua, what did they say about his commands?
They answered, “Everything you have commanded us we will do, and everywhere you send us we will go” (1:16).
Joshua 1:16
We will weigh each command before we act
The tribes made no conditions; they promised, “everywhere you send us we will go” (1:16).
We will obey whichever commands seem right
Doing what seemed right in one’s own eyes marks the close of Judges (Judges 21:25), not this pledge of full obedience.
Everything you have commanded us we will do
We will first ask Moses whether to obey you
Moses was already dead (1:2); they promised to obey Joshua as they had obeyed Moses (1:17).
We will obey you once the harvest is finished
No delay was offered; the crossing came within three days (1:11), during harvest season (Joshua 3:15).
In Joshua 1:17, whom did the tribes mention as the leader they had previously obeyed?
“Just as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we will obey you” (1:17).
Joshua 1:17
Aaron
Aaron was the high priest and had already died (Numbers 20:28); the tribes named Moses.
Moses
Samuel
Samuel was born generations later (1 Samuel 1:20).
Saul
Saul, Israel’s first king, was anointed by Samuel long after Joshua (1 Samuel 10:1).
Eli
Eli was the priest at Shiloh in Hannah’s day (1 Samuel 1:9).
What blessing did the tribes speak over Joshua in Joshua 1:17?
“And may the LORD your God be with you, as He was with Moses” (1:17), echoing God’s promise in 1:5.
Joshua 1:17
May your enemies become your servants
“May peoples serve you” is Isaac’s blessing on Jacob (Genesis 27:29), not the tribes’ words to Joshua.
May the LORD your God be with you, as He was with Moses
May your sons inherit Jerusalem
Jerusalem was still held by the Jebusites (Joshua 15:63).
May your throne endure forever
An enduring throne was promised to David (2 Samuel 7:16).
May your flocks increase greatly
Flocks are not mentioned; their blessing was that the LORD be with Joshua (1:17).
In the final verse of Joshua 1, what punishment did the tribes declare for anyone who rebelled against Joshua’s command?
“Anyone who rebels against your order and does not obey your words … will be put to death” (1:18).
Joshua 1:18
Exile
Exile came centuries later under Babylon (2 Kings 25:11); the tribes named death.
Fasting
Fasting is not a penalty in 1:18; the rebel was to be put to death.
Loss of land
Their land is not mentioned in 1:18; the penalty named is death.
Death
Fines of silver
No fine is mentioned; the tribes said a rebel would be put to death (1:18).
What final encouragement did the tribes give Joshua at the end of Joshua 1?
The tribes close with “Above all, be strong and courageous!” (1:18), echoing God’s words in 1:6–9.
Joshua 1:18
Wait for a prophet
No prophet is mentioned; the tribes urged Joshua to be strong and courageous (1:18).
Be strong and courageous
Count the warriors
No count of warriors is asked for in 1:18.
Build a memorial
Joshua later set up twelve stones from the Jordan at Gilgal (Joshua 4:20), but that is not the tribes’ word here.
Rest for seven days
No rest is mentioned; the crossing was coming within three days (1:11).
Which statement belongs to the LORD’s charge in Joshua 1 rather than to another Bible event?
The LORD told Joshua to “meditate on it day and night” (1:8).
Joshua 1:8
March around the city for seven days
Marching around Jericho is from Joshua 6:3–4: once a day for six days, then seven times on the seventh.
Stretch out your staff over the sea
Stretching out the staff over the sea was God’s command to Moses at the Red Sea (Exodus 14:16).
Meditate on the Book of the Law day and night
Choose five smooth stones
David chose five smooth stones to face Goliath (1 Samuel 17:40).
Build an ark of gopher wood
Building an ark of gopher wood was God’s command to Noah (Genesis 6:14).
In the border description of Joshua 1, which place is specifically named along with the wilderness?
The territory runs “from the wilderness and Lebanon to the great River Euphrates” (1:4).
Joshua 1:4
Zion
Zion was the fortress David captured (2 Samuel 5:7), not part of 1:4.
Lebanon
Bethel
Bethel, formerly Luz (Genesis 28:19), is not named in 1:4.
Hebron
Hebron, formerly Kiriath-arba, was given to Caleb (Joshua 15:13).
Gilgal
Gilgal was Israel’s first camp after the crossing (Joshua 4:19).
In Joshua 1:4, which named people group appears inside the territorial description?
The territory includes “all the land of the Hittites” (1:4).
Joshua 1:4
Hittites
Amalekites
The Amalekites attacked Israel at Rephidim (Exodus 17:8); they are not in 1:4.
Jebusites
The Jebusites held Jerusalem (Joshua 15:63); they are not named in 1:4.
Amorites
The Amorites under Sihon were defeated east of the Jordan (Numbers 21:21); they are not named in 1:4.
Moabites
Moab’s land was not given to Israel (Deuteronomy 2:9).
When Joshua said the eastern tribes could go home later, where did he say their land lay?
Moses had given them land “on the east side of the Jordan” (1:15).
Joshua 1:15
Beside the Great Sea
The Great Sea marks the western limit of the promised territory (1:4).
In the hill country of Ephraim
The hill country of Ephraim, west of the Jordan, held Joshua’s own inheritance (Joshua 24:30).
On the east side of the Jordan
In the Negev near Arad
The Negev near Arad is where the Kenites settled with Judah (Judges 1:16).
Beyond the great River Euphrates
Beyond the Euphrates is where Israel’s fathers once lived and served other gods (Joshua 24:2).
Counting both God’s words and the people’s response in Joshua 1, how many times does the chapter use the exhortation “be strong and courageous” or “be strong and very courageous”?
The LORD says it in 1:6, 1:7 (“be strong and very courageous”), and 1:9, and the people say it once in 1:18: four times.
Two
Two would count only 1:6 and 1:7; the charge also appears in 1:9 and 1:18.
Three
God alone says it three times (1:6, 1:7, 1:9), but the people add a fourth in 1:18.
Four
Five
Five overcounts; the occurrences are 1:6, 1:7, 1:9, and 1:18 only.
Six
Six overcounts; the same words in Deuteronomy 31:6–7 and 31:23 lie outside Joshua 1.
In Joshua 1, which body part is linked to Israel’s possession of the land?
“I have given you every place where the sole of your foot will tread” (1:3).
Joshua 1:3
Hand
Hands come up when Moses laid his hands on Joshua (Numbers 27:18), not in the land promise of 1:3.
Heart
The heart is not mentioned in 1:3; the promise is tied to the sole of the foot.
Eye
The eye is not mentioned in 1:3; the promise is tied to the sole of the foot.
Sole of the foot
Ear
The ear is not mentioned in 1:3; the promise is tied to the sole of the foot.
In God’s boundary description to Joshua, which comes first?
The territory runs “from the wilderness and Lebanon to the great River Euphrates” (1:4).
Joshua 1:4
The Euphrates
The Euphrates comes after the wilderness and Lebanon in 1:4.
The Great Sea
The Great Sea comes last, as the western limit (1:4).
The wilderness
The land of the Hittites
The land of the Hittites follows the Euphrates in 1:4.
Mount Hermon
Mount Hermon is not named in 1:4; it appears among Joshua’s conquests (Joshua 11:17).
In the tribes’ reply to Joshua, which idea appears before the death penalty for rebels?
In 1:17 the tribes say, “may the LORD your God be with you, as He was with Moses,” and only then declare the death penalty in 1:18.
Joshua 1:17-18
A blessing that the LORD be with Joshua as with Moses
A command for Joshua to build an altar at Gilgal
Joshua’s altar was built on Mount Ebal (Joshua 8:30), and at Gilgal he set up stones (Joshua 4:20); the tribes gave no such command.
A warning that Jericho’s walls were too strong
Jericho’s walls fell at the people’s shout (Joshua 6:20); the tribes say nothing about Jericho.
A census of every warrior from the eastern tribes
About 40,000 armed troops crossed over (Joshua 4:13), but no census appears in 1:17–18.
A plan for dividing the cities among the tribes
The cities were assigned by lot later (Joshua 14:2), not in the tribes’ reply.
In the opening verse of Joshua 1, which title belongs to Joshua rather than to Moses?
In 1:1 Moses is “His servant,” while Joshua is “Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ assistant.”
Joshua 1:1
Servant of the LORD
In Joshua 1 “servant of the LORD” belongs to Moses (1:13); Joshua gets the title only at his death (Joshua 24:29).
Son of Amram
Moses and Aaron were sons of Amram (Exodus 6:20); Joshua was the son of Nun.
Moses’ assistant
Priest of Israel
The priesthood belonged to Aaron and his sons (Exodus 28:1).
Man of God
“Man of God” is used of Moses (Deuteronomy 33:1), not Joshua.
In Joshua 1:11, which phrase shows that Israel’s task involved both movement and inheritance?
The officers said, “within three days you will cross the Jordan to go in and take possession of the land” (1:11).
Joshua 1:11
Count your tents and number your households by clans
Israel was counted by clans under Moses (Numbers 26:2); 1:11 gives no census command.
Cross the Jordan to go in and take possession of the land
Return to the land your fathers lived in beyond the river
Israel’s fathers lived beyond the Euphrates (Joshua 24:2); 1:11 points forward into Canaan.
Call the elders up to Sinai to renew the covenant
Moses went up Sinai with seventy elders (Exodus 24:9); Joshua later made a covenant at Shechem (Joshua 24:25).
Build cities with strong walls on the east side
The eastern tribes built cities for their little ones (Numbers 32:16), but 1:11 is about crossing and possessing.
In Joshua’s reminder to the eastern tribes, what were they specifically to remember that Moses had said?
Moses had said, “The LORD your God will give you rest, and He will give you this land” (1:13).
Joshua 1:13
The LORD your God will give you rest, and He will give you this land
You must go back to Egypt whenever famine strikes the land
Going down to Egypt in famine is Abram’s story (Genesis 12:10); Moses never commanded it.
You must camp beside the tabernacle for the rest of your lives
The eastern tribes settled east of the Jordan (1:15); no one was told to camp beside the tabernacle.
You will never cross the Jordan to fight with your brothers
The opposite: Moses required their men to cross over armed ahead of their brothers (Deuteronomy 3:18).
You must appoint a king over you as soon as you settle
Israel did not ask for a king until Samuel was old (1 Samuel 8:5).
In Joshua 1:14, which group was not allowed to remain behind east of the Jordan?
“All your mighty men of valor must be armed for battle to cross over ahead of your brothers” (1:14).
Joshua 1:14
Wives
Wives were allowed to remain east of the Jordan (1:14).
Children
Young children were allowed to remain east of the Jordan (1:14).
Livestock
Livestock were allowed to remain east of the Jordan (1:14).
Mighty men of valor
Families
The families, wives and young children, stayed behind (1:14); only the warriors crossed.
In the first command to “be strong and courageous” in Joshua 1, what reason does God give?
“Be strong and courageous, for you shall give these people the inheritance of the land that I swore to their fathers” (1:6).
Joshua 1:6
Because the walls of Jericho are weak and will soon crumble
Jericho was “tightly shut up because of the Israelites” (Joshua 6:1); its wall fell only at the shout (Joshua 6:20).
Because Joshua will give the people possession of the land sworn to their fathers
Because the priests will go before him carrying the ark into battle
The priests carried the ark into the Jordan (Joshua 3:6), but the reason in 1:6 is the inheritance.
Because no battles will be needed to take the land from Canaan
Many battles followed; thirty-one kings were defeated (Joshua 12:24).
Because Moses will return from the mountain to lead them again
Moses had died in the land of Moab (Deuteronomy 34:5).
In the second courage command of Joshua 1, why must Joshua be “very courageous”?
“Above all, be strong and very courageous. Be careful to observe all the law that My servant Moses commanded you” (1:7).
Joshua 1:7
To write a new covenant to replace Moses’ law
Joshua later made a covenant at Shechem (Joshua 24:25), but 1:7 calls for keeping Moses’ law, not replacing it.
To carefully observe the whole law Moses commanded
To defeat Og king of Bashan in open battle
Og king of Bashan had already been struck down under Moses (Numbers 21:35).
To rebuild the tabernacle that Moses had made
The tabernacle was set up at Shiloh (Joshua 18:1), not rebuilt.
To choose twelve judges to rule over the tribes
The judges arose after Joshua (Judges 2:16); Joshua chose twelve men to carry stones from the Jordan (Joshua 4:2).
In the third courage command of Joshua 1, what reason is given for not being afraid or discouraged?
“Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go” (1:9).
Joshua 1:9
Israel has many horses
Israel did not trust in horses; Joshua later hamstrung the Canaanites’ horses (Joshua 11:9).
The Canaanites are already fleeing
The Canaanites’ hearts melted (Joshua 2:11), but 1:9 grounds courage in God’s presence.
The LORD your God is with you wherever you go
The river will dry up at once
The Jordan stopped when the priests’ feet touched the water (Joshua 3:15–16), but that is not the reason given in 1:9.
The ark alone will fight
The ark led the march at Jericho (Joshua 6:4), but 1:9 rests on the LORD being with Joshua.
Which name appears both in God’s promise to Joshua and in the people’s pledge to Joshua as the comparison point for leadership?
God says, “As I was with Moses, so will I be with you” (1:5), and the people say, “Just as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we will obey you” (1:17).
Joshua 1:5, 17
Aaron
Aaron is not named in Joshua 1; Moses is the comparison in 1:5 and 1:17.
Moses
Caleb
Caleb does not appear in Joshua 1; he comes to Joshua at Gilgal in Joshua 14:6.
Eleazar
Eleazar the priest is not mentioned in Joshua 1; he helped divide the land later (Joshua 14:1).
Abraham
Abraham is not named in Joshua 1, though the land had been sworn to the fathers (1:6).
Which set of geographical markers matches the territory statement in Joshua 1 most fully?
God set the bounds “from the wilderness and Lebanon to the great River Euphrates—all the land of the Hittites—and west as far as the Great Sea” (1:4).
Joshua 1:4

Trumpets belong to the later march around Jericho (Joshua 6:4), not this command (3:8).
Just before describing the miracle at the Jordan, Joshua told Israel to choose men from the tribes. How many men were to be chosen, one from each tribe?
Joshua told Israel to choose twelve men from the tribes, one from each tribe (3:12).
Joshua 3:12
Seven
Seven is not the number; one man from each of the twelve tribes was to be chosen (3:12).
Ten
Ten would leave two tribes out; Joshua said one from each tribe, which is twelve (3:12).
Twelve
Twenty-four
Twenty-four would be two from each tribe; the instruction was one from each (3:12).
Seventy
Seventy is the number of elders in Numbers 11:16, but here twelve men were chosen (3:12).
As the ark went ahead into the Jordan in Joshua 3, by what title did Joshua describe the LORD connected with that ark?
Joshua called Him “the Lord of all the earth,” saying the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth would go ahead into the Jordan (3:11, 13).
Joshua 3:11, 13
The LORD of Hosts
“LORD of Hosts” is a familiar title but is not the one Joshua uses in this chapter (3:11, 13).
The God of Abraham
“God of Abraham” is not Joshua’s title for the LORD in this passage (3:11, 13).
The Lord of all the earth
The Holy One of Israel
“Holy One of Israel” is not the title used here; Joshua says Lord of all the earth (3:11, 13).
The Mighty One of Jacob
“Mighty One of Jacob” is not Joshua’s phrase in this chapter; he says Lord of all the earth (3:11, 13).
In Joshua’s words before the crossing, which complete list names the peoples that the living God would surely drive out before Israel?
Joshua listed seven peoples God would drive out: the Canaanites, Hittites, Hivites, Perizzites, Girgashites, Amorites and Jebusites (3:10).
Joshua 3:10
Canaanites, Hittites, Hivites, Perizzites, Girgashites, Amorites, and Jebusites
Moabites, Edomites, Ammonites, Midianites, Amalekites, Philistines, and Sidonians
This list names peoples such as the Philistines and Amalekites who are not in Joshua’s list of seven (3:10).
Canaanites, Kenites, Rephaim, Horites, Edomites, Hivites, and Amalekites
Kenites, Rephaim and Horites do not appear in Joshua’s list; he names Canaanites, Hittites and others (3:10).
Amorites, Moabites, Perizzites, Arameans, Hittites, Jebusites, and Gibeonites
Moabites, Arameans and Gibeonites are not among the seven peoples Joshua names (3:10).
Girgashites, Israelites, Philistines, Canaanites, Sidonians, Hivites, and Zebulunites
Israelites and Zebulunites are God’s people, not peoples to be driven out (3:10).
When the priests carrying the ark came to the Jordan River, what was true of the Jordan at that time of year?
The Jordan overflows its banks throughout the harvest season, which makes the crossing even more miraculous (3:15).
Joshua 3:15
It was frozen solid across its whole width
The Jordan was in flood, not frozen, at harvest time (3:15).
It had dried up from a long drought
Far from drying up, the Jordan overflowed its banks (3:15).
It overflowed all its banks throughout harvest season
It flowed only at night and ran dry by day
Nothing says the river flowed only at night; it was in flood throughout harvest season (3:15).
It had turned bitter and undrinkable
The Jordan’s trouble was flooding, not bitter water (3:15); bitter water is Marah’s story (Exodus 15:23).
According to Joshua’s prediction beside the Jordan, what exact action by the priests carrying the ark would cause the river’s downstream waters to be cut off and stand in a heap?
Joshua said that when the priests’ feet touch down in the waters of the Jordan, its flowing waters will be cut off and stand up in a heap (3:13).
Joshua 3:13
Their shouting a battle cry
Shouting is not what Joshua said would stop the river; the priests’ feet touching the water would (3:13).
Their lifting the ark above their heads
Lifting the ark overhead is not mentioned; the sign was their feet touching the water (3:13).
The soles of their feet touching down in the Jordan waters
Their circling the river seven times
Circling a river seven times is not part of this account; it echoes Jericho’s walls (Joshua 6:3–4).
Their offering sacrifice on the bank
No sacrifice is called for; their feet touching the water was the trigger (3:13).
During Israel’s crossing of the Jordan, where did the priests carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD stand while the entire nation crossed?
The priests carrying the ark stood firm on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan while all Israel crossed (3:17).
Joshua 3:17
On the west bank near Jericho
The priests were in the riverbed, not on the bank near Jericho; Israel crossed opposite Jericho (3:16–17).
On dry ground in the middle of the Jordan

Mount Nebo is where Moses viewed the land (Deuteronomy 34:1), not where the priests stood.
In the camp at Shittim
Shittim is where Israel set out from (3:1); the priests stood in the Jordan (3:17).

Gilgal is where Israel camped after crossing (Joshua 4:19), not where the priests stood.
In the description of the Jordan miracle, what happened to the waters flowing down toward the Sea of the Arabah, that is, the Salt Sea?
The water flowing toward the Sea of the Arabah (the Salt Sea) was completely cut off (3:16).
Joshua 3:16

The water did not split into channels; it stood still and was cut off (3:16).
They were completely cut off

The water flowing downstream was cut off, so it could not flood the plain (3:16).
They flowed back into the Red Sea
The Red Sea is not in view; the water toward the Salt Sea was cut off (3:16).
In Joshua 3, when the priests’ feet touched the water, the flowing water stood still and backed up as far upstream as which place?
The flowing water stood still and backed up as far upstream as Adam, a city in the area of Zarethan (3:16).
Joshua 3:16
At Gilgal near Bethel
Gilgal is where Israel camped after the crossing (Joshua 4:19), not where the water backed up.
At Adam, a city in the area of Zarethan
At Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin
Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin is far south of the Jordan (3:16 places the water at Adam).
At Jazer beyond the Arnon
Jazer lies east of the Jordan, not upstream on the river where the water stopped (3:16).
At Gibeon near Ai
Gibeon and Ai are in the hill country, not on the Jordan; the water stopped at Adam (3:16).
In Joshua 4, after all Israel had finished crossing the Jordan River, how many men was Joshua told to choose, one from each tribe?
The LORD told Joshua, “Choose twelve men from among the people, one from each tribe” (4:2).
Joshua 4:1-4
Seven is not the number; the LORD said twelve, one from each tribe (4:2).
Ten is not the number; the LORD said twelve (4:2).
Twenty-four is double the number; the LORD said twelve (4:2).
Seventy is not the number; the LORD said twelve (4:2).
In the Jordan-crossing account of Joshua 4, how many stones were the chosen men commanded to take from the river?
The men were to take twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan (4:3, 8).
Joshua 4:3, 8
Two is not the number; the men took twelve stones (4:8).
Five is not the number; the men took twelve stones (4:8).
Ten is not the number; the men took twelve stones, one for each tribe (4:8).
Forty is not the number; the men took twelve stones (4:8). Forty thousand is the number of troops in 4:13.
In Joshua 4, from what exact place were the twelve stones to be taken?
The LORD said to take twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan where the priests were standing (4:3).

Gilgal is where the stones were set up (4:20), not where they were taken from (4:3).
During Israel’s crossing in Joshua chapter 4, how was each selected man to carry his stone?
Each man was to take a stone upon his shoulder, according to the number of the tribes (4:5).

In both hands
They were to carry the stones on their shoulders, not in both hands (4:5).
In a cart
No cart is mentioned; each man took a stone upon his shoulder (4:5).
On his shoulder
Tied to the ark
The stones were not tied to the ark; the men carried them (4:5).
In a basket
No basket is mentioned; each man took a stone upon his shoulder (4:5).
In Joshua 4, what were the twelve stones from the Jordan meant to be for Israel in future generations?
The stones were to serve as a sign and a memorial to the Israelites forever (4:6–7).
Joshua 4:6-7
A store of building material
They were a memorial, not building material (4:6–7).
A sign and memorial
A weapon cache
They were a memorial of the Jordan crossing, not weapons (4:6–7).
A royal throne base
They were not a throne base; they were a sign and a memorial (4:6–7).
A grain marker
They were not grain markers; they were a sign and a memorial (4:6–7).

Israel crossed the Jordan on dry ground

No boats are mentioned; Israel crossed on dry ground (4:22).
Moses stretched out his staff over the Jordan
Moses stretched out his staff at the Red Sea (Exodus 14:16), not in this account of the Jordan.
The Canaanites made a bridge for Israel
No bridge is mentioned; the LORD dried up the waters (4:23).

The river returned to its course once the priests came up (4:18); it did not stay dry for a year.
After coming up from the Jordan in Joshua 4, where did the Israelites camp?
The people camped at Gilgal on the eastern border of Jericho (4:19).
Joshua 4:19-20
Shiloh in Ephraim
Shiloh in Ephraim is not where they camped (4:19).
Bethel in the hill country
Bethel is not where they camped (4:19).
Gilgal on the eastern border of Jericho
Hebron in Judah
Hebron in Judah is not where they camped (4:19).
Shechem between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim
Shechem is between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim; Israel camped at Gilgal (4:19).

Judah, Benjamin, and Levi
Judah, Benjamin and Levi are not the tribes named in 4:12.
Ephraim, Issachar, and Zebulun
Ephraim, Issachar and Zebulun are not the tribes named in 4:12.
Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh
Simeon, Asher, and Naphtali
Simeon, Asher and Naphtali are not the tribes named in 4:12.
Dan, Judah, and Ephraim
Dan, Judah and Ephraim are not the tribes named in 4:12.

He made Joshua king over Canaan
Joshua was not made king over Canaan (4:14).
He hid Joshua from the people

Joshua was not sent back to the wilderness (4:14).

Eleazar did not replace Joshua; Israel revered Joshua all his life (4:14).

Joshua 4:15-17
The ark of the Testimony
The bronze serpent
The bronze serpent is a different object, made later in Numbers 21:9.
The altar of incense
The altar of incense is not the object the priests carried (4:16).
The lampstand of gold
The golden lampstand is not the object the priests carried (4:16).
The chest of manna
The chest of manna is not a title used here; the priests carried the ark of the Testimony (4:16).
In Joshua 4, what happened when the priests carrying the ark stepped up from the Jordan onto dry land?
When the priests’ feet touched dry land, the waters of the Jordan returned to their course and overflowed all the banks as before (4:18).
Joshua 4:18
The river stayed dry for seven more days afterward
The river did not stay dry; it returned as soon as the priests came up (4:18).
The Jordan returned to its place and overflowed its banks as before
Fire came down from heaven and dried the riverbed
Fire coming down on the river is not mentioned (4:18).

Water turning to blood belongs to the plagues (Exodus 7:20), not to this crossing.

The river did not split into twelve streams; the twelve stones were the memorial (4:3, 18).
In Joshua chapter 4, on what date did the people come up from the Jordan and camp at Gilgal?
The people went up from the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month and camped at Gilgal (4:19).
Joshua 4:19
The first day of the first month
The first day of the first month is not the date given (4:19).
The tenth day of the first month
The fourteenth day of the first month
The fourteenth day of the first month is the Passover date (Exodus 12:6), not the date in 4:19.
The seventh day of the third month
The seventh day of the third month is not the date given (4:19).
The tenth day of the seventh month
The tenth day of the seventh month is the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29), not the date in 4:19.
Besides setting up stones at Gilgal, what else did Joshua himself do with twelve stones in Joshua 4?
Joshua also set up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan, where the priests who carried the ark of the covenant stood (4:9).
Joshua 4:9
He built an altar of them on Mount Ebal for the LORD
Joshua built an altar on Mount Ebal later (Joshua 8:30), not with these stones.
He placed them at the gate of Jericho as a marker
Nothing is said about stones at the gate of Jericho (4:9).
He set them up in the middle of the Jordan where the priests’ feet had stood
He buried them under the oak tree at Shechem
Burying stones under an oak at Shechem is not mentioned in this chapter (4:9).
He used them to mark the new border near Ai
Marking the border of Ai is not mentioned in this chapter (4:9).
In Joshua 4, why did Joshua say the LORD dried up the Jordan, just as He had done at the Red Sea?
Joshua said the LORD dried up the Jordan so that all the peoples of the earth would know His hand is mighty and so that Israel would always fear the LORD (4:23–24).
Joshua 4:23-24
So Israel could avoid every future war in Canaan
Avoiding future wars is not the stated purpose (4:24).
So Joshua could build a royal palace at Gilgal
A palace at Gilgal is not the stated purpose (4:24).
So all the peoples of the earth might know the LORD’s hand is mighty, and so Israel would always fear the LORD
So the priests could stay in the riverbed for good
The priests left the riverbed once the waters returned (4:18); staying there was not the purpose (4:24).
So Jericho would give up without any fighting
Jericho is not mentioned in Joshua’s explanation (4:23–24).
In Joshua 5, after the LORD dried up the Jordan before Israel, how did the Amorite kings west of the Jordan and the Canaanite kings along the coast respond?

Joshua 5:1
They crossed the river to attack
The kings were paralyzed with fear, not attacking (5:1).
They sent tribute to Gilgal
No tribute is mentioned in Joshua 5:1; their hearts melted for fear.
Their hearts melted and their spirit failed
They asked Moses for peace
Moses had died (Deuteronomy 34:5), so no one asked him for peace; Joshua 5:1 describes fear, not a peace request.
They rebuilt Ai
Ai was destroyed later (Joshua 8:28), not rebuilt here.
In Joshua 5, what did the LORD command Joshua to do “once again” for the sons of Israel?
Joshua 5:2 says the LORD told Joshua, “Make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Israel once again.”

Count them by tribes
Counting the tribes happened earlier in Numbers 1 and 26, not here.
Circumcise them
Teach them the Law
Teaching the Law is not the command in Joshua 5:2.
Divide the land
Dividing the land comes later (Joshua 13–19).
Send spies to Jericho
Spies were sent to Jericho in Joshua 2, before this command.
In Joshua 5, what kind of knives did Joshua make when he circumcised the sons of Israel?
Joshua 5:2–3 says the LORD told Joshua to make flint knives, and Joshua made flint knives and circumcised the sons of Israel.
Joshua 5:2
Flint knives
Bronze knives
Joshua 5:2–3 names flint, not bronze.
Iron knives
Joshua 5:2–3 names flint, not iron.
Wooden knives
Joshua 5:2–3 names flint, not wood.
Gold knives
Joshua 5:2–3 names flint, not gold.
During Israel’s encampment near Jericho in Joshua 5, at what named place did Joshua circumcise the sons of Israel?

Joshua 5:3
Gilgal
Gilgal is where they camped and where the reproach of Egypt was rolled away (5:9–10), not the circumcision site named in 5:3.
Shiloh
Shiloh is where the Tent of Meeting was later set up (Joshua 18:1).
Shechem
Shechem is where Joshua later assembled the tribes (Joshua 24:1).
Gibeath-haaraloth
Kadesh-barnea
Kadesh-barnea is where the spies reported earlier (Numbers 13:26).

They had broken the covenant at Sinai
Joshua 5:5–7 gives the reason as the wilderness birth, not a covenant breach at Sinai.
They had been circumcised in Egypt but needed it repeated
Those who came out of Egypt had been circumcised (5:5), but their sons born in the wilderness had not.
They had not been circumcised along the way

The reason is not priestly service; the sons had simply not been circumcised along the way (5:7).
They were about to cross the Red Sea
The Red Sea crossing was long past (Exodus 14); the issue was uncircumcised sons born in the wilderness (5:5, 5:7).
In Joshua 5, what had happened to the fighting men who came out of Egypt, and why did they not enter Canaan?
Joshua 5:6 says the nation’s men of war who had come out of Egypt died in the wilderness, since they did not obey the LORD.
Joshua 5:6
They settled in Moab because they feared battle
The men of war died in the wilderness; they did not settle in Moab (5:6).
They perished in the wilderness because they did not obey the LORD
They returned to Egypt because of hunger
Joshua 5:6 does not say they returned to Egypt; it says they died because they did not obey.
They became judges over Israel
Joshua 5:6 does not say they became judges; they died without seeing the land.
They were taken captive by Midian
Joshua 5:6 does not say Midian took them captive; they died because they did not obey the LORD.
When Joshua 5 explains the wilderness years, how long had the Israelites walked in the wilderness before that Exodus generation was gone?

Joshua 5:6
12 years
Twelve years is not the length given in Joshua 5:6; it says forty.
20 years
Twenty years is not the length given in Joshua 5:6; it says forty.
25 years
Twenty-five years is not the length given in Joshua 5:6; it says forty.
38 years
Thirty-eight years is the time from Kadesh-barnea to the Brook of Zered (Deuteronomy 2:14), but Joshua 5:6 says forty.
40 years
After the entire nation had been circumcised in Joshua 5, what did the Israelites do next?
Joshua 5:8 says that after all the nation had been circumcised, they stayed in the camp until they were healed.

They stayed in camp until they were healed
They marched around Jericho
Marching around Jericho comes in Joshua 6, after this chapter.
They crossed back over the Jordan

They built the temple

Milk and honey from the hill villages
