They pointed to Achan son of Zerah, who was unfaithful regarding what was set apart for destruction and brought wrath on the whole congregation (22:20).
Joshua 22:20
Nadab son of Aaron
Nadab son of Aaron died for offering unauthorized fire (Leviticus 10:1–2), not as the example cited here.
Abimelech son of Gideon
Abimelech son of Gideon belongs to the time of the judges, later than Joshua (Judges 9:1).
Achan son of Zerah
Hophni son of Eli
Hophni son of Eli lived much later (1 Samuel 2:34); the delegation named Achan (22:20).
Joab son of Zeruiah
Joab son of Zeruiah served David, centuries later; the example given was Achan (22:20).
When Phinehas and the chiefs spoke to the eastern tribes in Joshua 22, what solution did they offer if the land east of the Jordan was unclean?
They urged: “cross over to the land of the LORD’s possession, where the LORD’s tabernacle stands, and take possession of it among us” (22:19).
Joshua 22:19
Retreat into the wilderness of Sinai until Israel calmed down
Retreating into the wilderness of Sinai was never proposed; they offered land among them where the tabernacle stood (22:19).
Build a second tabernacle in Gilead beside their new altar
They warned against building any altar other than the LORD’s (22:19), so a second tabernacle was no solution.
Cross into the LORD’s land where His tabernacle stood and settle there
Ask the king of Moab to give them land east of the Arnon
No request to the king of Moab for territory is suggested; they offered land west of the Jordan (22:19).
Suspend all sacrifices until Joshua gave a ruling
Suspending sacrifices is not proposed; they urged crossing over and not rebelling (22:19).
In their defense in Joshua 22, what future claim did the eastern tribes fear the western tribes’ descendants might make because the Jordan stood between them?
They feared that descendants of the western tribes might say, “You have no share in the LORD!” because the Jordan was a border (22:24–25).
Joshua 22:24
“You cannot own flocks here”
Ownership of flocks is not the concern; the fear was of being told “You have no share in the LORD” (22:24–25).
“You have no share in the LORD”
“You must return to Egypt”
Return to Egypt is not mentioned; their fear was of losing their share in the LORD (22:25).
“You are not sons of Abraham”
Their descent from Abraham is not questioned; the fear was of being told they had no share in the LORD (22:25).
“You must worship on Mount Gerizim”
Mount Gerizim is not mentioned in the chapter; the fear concerned having no share in the LORD (22:25).
According to the reply of the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-Manasseh in Joshua 22, what was the real purpose of the altar by the Jordan?
They said the altar was to be “a witness between us and you and the generations to come” (22:27).
Joshua 22:27
To serve as a rallying point for war against the western tribes
They denied any rebellious purpose (22:29); the altar was no preparation for war.
To replace the altar at Shiloh as their place of sacrifice
They explicitly said it was not to replace the altar of the LORD at the tabernacle (22:29).
To serve as a witness between the tribes and future generations
To mark the place where a king of the eastern tribes would be crowned
No king is mentioned; the altar was a witness between the tribes (22:27).
To store the tribes’ tithes and offerings for the Levites
They said the altar was not for burnt offerings or sacrifices (22:26), so it was not a storehouse.
In Joshua 22, if future generations questioned the eastern tribes, what did they say their descendants could point to as evidence?
They said they would answer: “Look at the replica of the altar of the LORD that our fathers made” (22:28).
Joshua 22:28
The bronze serpent Moses made
The bronze serpent is not mentioned in this account (Numbers 21:9 records it); they pointed to the replica of the altar (22:28).
The replica of the altar of the LORD their fathers had made
Aaron’s budding staff
Aaron’s staff (Numbers 17:8) is not mentioned here; the evidence was the replica altar (22:28).
The twelve stones from the Jordan at Gilgal
The twelve stones at Gilgal (Joshua 4:19–20) are not mentioned here; the evidence was the replica altar (22:28).
Joshua’s written covenant scroll
No covenant scroll is mentioned; they pointed to the replica of the LORD’s altar (22:28).
In Joshua 22, which use did the eastern tribes specifically deny for the altar they built near the Jordan?
They insisted the altar was not for “burnt offerings, grain offerings, or sacrifices, other than the altar of the LORD our God” (22:29).
Joshua 22:29
Gathering the tribes there to read the Law of Moses aloud
Reading the Law at the altar is never mentioned; what they denied was offering sacrifices on it (22:29).
Defending the Jordan crossing against foreign invaders
Defending a crossing is never mentioned; what they denied was offering sacrifices on it (22:29).
Offering burnt offerings, grain offerings, or sacrifices on it
Holding court there to judge disputes among the eastern tribes
Holding court is never mentioned; what they denied was offering sacrifices on it (22:29).
Training the eastern tribes’ soldiers for the next campaign
Military training is never mentioned; what they denied was offering sacrifices on it (22:29).
After hearing the eastern tribes’ explanation in Joshua 22, what did Phinehas say Israel knew “today”?
Phinehas said, “Today we know that the LORD is among us, because you have not committed this breach of faith against Him” (22:31).
Joshua 22:31
That Gilead was unclean
Phinehas did not call Gilead unclean; he said they had not committed a breach of faith (22:31).
That the LORD is among us
That Joshua should divide the land again
The land was not to be divided again; the delegation was satisfied (22:30–31).
That a second tabernacle was needed
A second tabernacle was not needed; the altar was only a witness (22:27, 22:31).
That Moab would soon attack
No attack by Moab is mentioned; Phinehas said the LORD was among them (22:31).
At the end of Joshua 22, what name did the Reubenites and Gadites give the altar by the Jordan?
The Reubenites and Gadites named the altar Witness, saying, “It is a witness between us that the LORD is God” (22:34).
Joshua 22:34
Ebenezer
Ebenezer is the stone Samuel set up much later (1 Samuel 7:12); this altar was named Witness (22:34).
Witness
The LORD Provides
“The LORD Provides” is not the name given here; the altar was named Witness (22:34).
Peace
Peace is not the name given; the altar was named Witness (22:34).
Remembrance
Remembrance is not the name given; the altar was named Witness (22:34).

At the end of the conquest, after the LORD had given Israel rest from all the enemies around them, which aged successor of Moses summoned the elders, leaders, judges, and officers of Israel for a farewell address?
Joshua 23:1–2 says that when Joshua was old and well along in years, he summoned all Israel, including its elders, leaders, judges, and officers.
Joshua 23:1-2
Moses
Moses had already died (Deuteronomy 34:5) and could not give this address.
Joshua
Caleb
Caleb was Joshua’s companion who received Hebron (Joshua 14:13), but he did not summon Israel in 23:2.
Eleazar
Eleazar was the high priest (Joshua 14:1), but 23:2 says Joshua summoned Israel.
Gideon
Gideon was a later judge (Judges 6:11), centuries after this scene.
In Joshua’s farewell address recorded in Joshua 23, what did he say Israel had seen the LORD do to the nations for their sake?
Joshua told Israel that they had seen everything the LORD their God had done to all these nations for their sake, because the LORD their God fought for them (23:3).
Joshua 23:3
The LORD fought for Israel
The LORD made peace treaties with every king
No peace treaties were made with every king; no city made peace with Israel except the Hivites living in Gibeon (Joshua 11:19).
The LORD moved the tabernacle to Jerusalem
The tabernacle was set up at Shiloh (Joshua 18:1), not moved to Jerusalem in Joshua’s time.
The LORD crowned Joshua as king
Joshua was never crowned king; he led as Moses’ successor (Deuteronomy 34:9).
The LORD sent Israel back into Egypt
The LORD brought Israel out of Egypt and never sent them back there (Deuteronomy 17:16).
When Joshua described the inheritance in Joshua 23, he said it stretched from the Jordan to what western boundary?
Joshua said he had allotted the remaining nations as an inheritance to the tribes from the Jordan westward to the Great Sea (23:4).
Joshua 23:4
The Salt Sea
The Salt Sea is part of Canaan’s eastern boundary (Numbers 34:3), not its western limit.
The Sea of Chinnereth
The Sea of Chinnereth is on the eastern side of the land (Numbers 34:11), not the western boundary.
The Red Sea
The Red Sea is a southern boundary in other promises (Exodus 23:31), not the western boundary in 23:4.
The Great Sea
The Euphrates River
The Euphrates is the northeastern limit in the promise to Abraham (Genesis 15:18), not the western boundary of 23:4.
Speaking to Israel’s leaders in Joshua 23, Joshua told them to be very strong to keep and do everything written in what book?
Joshua told Israel to be very strong so that they could keep and obey all that is written in the Book of the Law of Moses (23:6).
Joshua 23:6
The Book of Jashar
The Book of Jashar is cited about the sun standing still (Joshua 10:13), not as the law they were to obey.
The Book of the Law of Moses
The Book of Judges
The Book of Judges records a later period, after Joshua’s death.
The Book of the Covenant at Shechem
The covenant at Shechem is described in Joshua 24:25–26, after this speech.
The Scroll of Samuel
The Scroll of Samuel refers to a later era; Samuel wrote in a scroll centuries later (1 Samuel 10:25).
In Joshua’s warning about the nations still remaining in the land, what did he say Israel must not do with the names of their gods?
Joshua said, “You must not call on the names of their gods or swear by them” (23:7).
Joshua 23:7
Carve them on memorial stones
Carving the names on memorial stones is not mentioned; Joshua forbade invoking or swearing by them (23:7). Memorial stones in Joshua commemorate the Jordan crossing (Joshua 4:20).
Invoke them or swear by them
Carry them into battle
Carrying gods into battle is not mentioned; Joshua forbade calling on their names or swearing by them (23:7).
Offer grain offerings to them only at harvest
Grain offerings to foreign gods are forbidden entirely, not only at harvest (23:7).
Write them in the Book of the Law
Writing their names in the Book of the Law is not mentioned; the Book is to be obeyed (23:6).
Near the middle of Joshua’s final charge, what did he tell Israel to be very careful to do?
Joshua said, “Therefore watch yourselves carefully, that you love the LORD your God” (23:11).
Joshua 23:11
Love the LORD your God
Rebuild Jericho
Rebuilding Jericho is a matter on which Joshua pronounced a curse (Joshua 6:26), not part of this charge.
Choose a king from Judah
Choosing a king from Judah is not part of Joshua’s charge; Israel had no king until Saul (1 Samuel 10:24).
Move the ark to Bethel
Moving the ark to Bethel is not part of Joshua’s charge; the ark was there in later years (Judges 20:27).
Fast for forty days
A forty-day fast is something Moses did (Exodus 34:28), not part of Joshua’s charge in 23:11.
Joshua warned Israel about the remnant nations in Canaan. What specific bond did he forbid with them?
Joshua warned Israel not to intermarry and associate with the remaining nations (23:12).
Joshua 23:12
Trading horses with Egypt
Trading horses with Egypt is not mentioned in Joshua 23; Deuteronomy 17:16 forbids a king to acquire many horses from Egypt.
Intermarrying with them
Letting them farm the land for seven years
Letting them farm the land is not mentioned; the warning is about intermarrying and associating with them (23:12).
Appointing them as Levites
Appointing them as Levites is not mentioned in Joshua 23.
Sending them across the Jordan
Sending them across the Jordan is not mentioned; the LORD would drive them out (23:5).
As the aged Joshua concluded his words in Joshua 23, what expression did he use for his approaching death?
Joshua said, “Now behold, today I am going the way of all the earth” (23:14).
Joshua 23:14
I am going into the wilderness
Going into the wilderness is not the phrase; Joshua said he was going the way of all the earth (23:14).
I am ascending the mountain of God
Ascending the mountain of God is what Moses did on Sinai (Exodus 24:18), not Joshua’s phrase.
I am going the way of all the earth
I am crossing the Jordan at last
Crossing the Jordan at last is not Joshua’s phrase; Israel crossed it in Joshua 3.
I am being carried to Shiloh
Being carried to Shiloh is not his phrase; Shiloh is where the Tent of Meeting stood (Joshua 18:1).
At the end of Joshua 23, what did Joshua say would happen if Israel transgressed the covenant of the LORD, served other gods, and bowed down to them?
Joshua said that if Israel transgressed the covenant, served other gods and bowed down to them, the anger of the LORD would burn against them and they would quickly perish from the good land (23:16).
Joshua 23:15-16
They would gain the remaining land more quickly
The opposite is promised; if they turned away, the LORD would no longer drive out the nations (23:13).
They would wander in the wilderness for forty more years
Forty more years of wandering was the penalty for the unbelief at Kadesh (Numbers 14:33), not what Joshua said here.
The LORD’s anger would burn against them, and they would quickly perish from the good land
They would be moved to live permanently east of the Jordan
Living east of the Jordan is the choice of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh (Numbers 32:33), not a penalty in 23:16.
The priesthood would immediately pass to the Canaanites
The priesthood passing to the Canaanites is not mentioned anywhere in Joshua 23.
In Joshua 23:10, because the LORD fought for Israel, how many enemies did Joshua say one Israelite could put to flight?
Joshua said, “One of you can put a thousand to flight, because the LORD your God fights for you, just as He promised” (23:10).
Joshua 23:10
A hundred
A hundred is the number five would pursue in Leviticus 26:8; Joshua said one could put a thousand to flight (23:10).
Ten thousand
Ten thousand is the number put to flight by two in Deuteronomy 32:30; Joshua said one would rout a thousand (23:10).
A thousand
Five hundred
Five hundred is not the number given; Joshua 23:10 says a thousand.
Fifty
Fifty is not mentioned; one Israelite could put a thousand to flight (23:10).
In Joshua’s closing assembly, where did he gather all the tribes of Israel before God?
“Joshua assembled all the tribes of Israel at Shechem” (24:1).
Joshua 24:1
Gilgal
Gilgal was Israel’s first camp west of the Jordan (Joshua 4:19), not the site of this assembly.
Shiloh
Shiloh was where the tabernacle stood and the land was apportioned (Joshua 18:1), not the site of this assembly.
Shechem
Hebron
Hebron was given to Caleb (Joshua 14:13), not the site of this assembly.
Bethel
Bethel was a Canaanite city Joshua defeated (Joshua 12:16), not the site of this assembly.
In Joshua 24, what decision did Joshua tell the people to make “this day”?
Joshua said, “choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve” (24:15).
Joshua 24:15
Where to camp
Where to camp is not the choice Joshua posed; it was whom to serve (24:15).
Whom they would serve
How to divide the land
Dividing the land was handled earlier (Joshua 13–19); the choice here was whom to serve (24:15).
Which judge to appoint
Appointing a judge is not the decision here; it was whom to serve (24:15).
When to attack Jericho
Attacking Jericho was long past (24:11); the choice here was whom to serve (24:15).
In Joshua’s famous declaration to Israel, whom did he say he and his house would serve?
Joshua declared, “As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD!” (24:15).
Joshua 24:15
The gods of the Amorites
Joshua listed the gods of the Amorites as an alternative he was rejecting, not as the one he would serve (24:15).
The LORD
The angels of heaven
He did not say he would serve the angels of heaven; he said, “we will serve the LORD” (24:15).
The ark of the covenant
The ark was the symbol of the LORD’s presence, not whom Joshua served; he said “we will serve the LORD” (24:15).
The gods beyond the Euphrates
Joshua listed the gods beyond the Euphrates as an alternative he was rejecting, not as the one he would serve (24:15).
Near the end of Joshua 24, how old was Joshua son of Nun when he died?
“Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at the age of 110” (24:29).
Joshua 24:29
Ninety is not his age; Joshua died at 110 (24:29).
Abraham was 100 when Isaac was born (Genesis 21:5); Joshua died at 110 (24:29).
Moses died at 120 (Deuteronomy 34:7); Joshua died at 110 (24:29).
Jacob told Pharaoh he was 130 (Genesis 47:9); Joshua died at 110 (24:29).
At Shechem in Joshua 24, which group of Israelite leaders did Joshua summon?
Joshua “summoned the elders, leaders, judges, and officers of Israel” (24:1).
Joshua 24:1
Priests, Levites, singers, and gatekeepers
Priests, Levites, singers and gatekeepers resemble the temple staff in 1 Chronicles 9:17–19, not Joshua’s list (24:1).
Elders, leaders, judges, and officers
Captains, horsemen, charioteers, and archers
Captains, horsemen, charioteers and archers are not the list given in 24:1.
Prophets, scribes, princes, and merchants
Prophets, scribes, princes and merchants are not the list given in 24:1.
Kings, elders, builders, and guards
Israel had no kings yet; the list in 24:1 is elders, leaders, judges and officers.
In the covenant renewal scene of Joshua 24, before whom did the leaders and tribes present themselves?
The leaders and tribes “presented themselves before God” (24:1).
Joshua 24:1
Before the ark only
The ark is not named here; the text says they presented themselves before God (24:1).
Before Eleazar
Eleazar is not named in the scene; his death is noted at the end of the chapter (24:33).
Before Joshua alone
They did not appear before Joshua alone; the text says before God (24:1).
Before God
Before the people
The leaders and tribes were the people; the text says they presented themselves before God (24:1).
When Joshua reviewed Israel’s earliest history at Shechem, what did he say Terah’s family had served beyond the Euphrates?
Joshua said Terah and Nahor “lived beyond the Euphrates and worshiped other gods” (24:2).
Joshua 24:2
Idols of Egypt
Terah’s family lived beyond the Euphrates, far from Egypt; Egyptian idols are not named (24:2).
Carved images of Canaan
Terah’s family was not yet in Canaan; Canaanite images are not named (24:2).
Other gods
The stars of heaven
Star worship is warned against in Deuteronomy 4:19, but 24:2 says only that they worshiped other gods.
No gods at all
The verse says they worshiped other gods, not that they worshiped no gods at all (24:2).
In Joshua’s retelling of Israel’s beginnings, which patriarch did God take from beyond the River and lead through Canaan?
“I took your father Abraham from beyond the Euphrates and led him through all the land of Canaan” (24:3).
Joshua 24:3
Isaac
Isaac is mentioned next as the son God gave Abraham (24:3), not the one taken from beyond the Euphrates.
Jacob
Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt (24:4); they were not taken from beyond the Euphrates.
Joseph
Joseph’s bones were buried at Shechem (24:32), but he was not the one led through Canaan here.
Abraham
Lot
Lot is not mentioned in Joshua 24; God took Abraham (24:3).
In the historical summary of Joshua 24, which son did God give to Abraham?
God said, “I gave him Isaac” (24:3).
Joshua 24:3
Ishmael
Ishmael was Abraham’s son by Hagar (Genesis 16:15), but Joshua names Isaac as the son God gave him (24:3).
Isaac
Esau
Esau was Isaac’s son (24:4), not a son of Abraham.
Jacob
Jacob was Isaac’s son (24:4), not a son of Abraham.
Joseph
Joseph was Jacob’s son, buried at Shechem (24:32), not a son of Abraham.
As Joshua recounted the patriarchs, which two sons were given to Isaac?
“To Isaac I gave Jacob and Esau” (24:4).
Joshua 24:4
Ephraim and Manasseh
Ephraim and Manasseh were Joseph’s sons (Genesis 41:50–52).
Cain and Abel
Cain and Abel were Adam’s sons (Genesis 4:1–2).
Jacob and Esau
Perez and Zerah
Perez and Zerah were Judah’s twin sons by Tamar (Genesis 38:29–30).
Nadab and Abihu
Nadab and Abihu were Aaron’s sons (Exodus 6:23).
In Joshua 24, what mountain region did God assign to Esau as his possession?
“I gave Esau Mount Seir to possess” (24:4).
Joshua 24:4
Carmel
Carmel is where Elijah met the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18:19), not Esau’s possession.
Hermon
Hermon marked the northern limit of Israel’s conquests (Joshua 12:1), not Esau’s possession.
Seir
Sinai
Sinai is where Israel received the law (Exodus 19:20), not Esau’s possession.
Tabor
Tabor is where Barak gathered his troops (Judges 4:6), not Esau’s possession.
In Joshua’s review of Israel’s family history, where did Jacob and his sons go down?
“Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt” (24:4).
Joshua 24:4
Moab
Moab lay east of the Dead Sea; Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt (24:4).
Egypt
Assyria
Assyria is not where Jacob’s family went; they went down to Egypt (24:4).
Edom
Edom was Esau’s land, given Mount Seir (24:4); Jacob’s sons went to Egypt.
Babylon
Babylon is not where Jacob’s family went; they went down to Egypt (24:4).
In Joshua’s account of the exodus, which two brothers did God send before bringing Israel out of Egypt?
“Then I sent Moses and Aaron, and I afflicted the Egyptians by what I did there, and afterward I brought you out” (24:5).
Joshua 24:5
Moses and Aaron
Joshua and Caleb
Joshua and Caleb were the spies who gave a good report (Numbers 14:6–9), not those sent before the exodus.
Nadab and Abihu
Nadab and Abihu were Aaron’s sons (Exodus 24:1), not those sent before the exodus.
Saul and Jonathan
Saul and Jonathan were Israel’s first king and his son, centuries later (1 Samuel 13:22).
Peter and Andrew
Peter and Andrew were disciples of Jesus (Matthew 4:18), not Old Testament figures.
In Joshua 24, to what body of water did the Egyptians pursue Israel with chariots and horsemen?
“The Egyptians pursued them with chariots and horsemen as far as the Red Sea” (24:6).
Joshua 24:6
The Dead Sea
The Dead Sea is not where the Egyptians pursued Israel (24:6).
The Jordan River
Israel crossed the Jordan River later (24:11); the pursuit ended at the Red Sea (24:6).
The Sea of Galilee
The Sea of Galilee is not mentioned; the pursuit ended at the Red Sea (24:6).
The Red Sea
The Nile
The Nile was in Egypt, which Israel had left; the pursuit reached the Red Sea (24:6).
In Joshua’s summary of the exodus, what did the LORD place between Israel and the Egyptians?
“He put darkness between you and the Egyptians” (24:7).
Joshua 24:7
Hail
Hail was among the plagues (Exodus 9:23–24), not what God placed between Israel and the Egyptians at the sea.
Darkness
Fire from heaven
Fire from heaven is not what Joshua names; he says darkness was put between them (24:7).
An earthquake
An earthquake is not mentioned; Joshua says darkness was put between them (24:7).
An army of angels
An army of angels is not mentioned; Joshua says darkness was put between them (24:7).
After the deliverance at the sea, where does Joshua 24 say Israel lived for a long time?
“Then you lived in the wilderness for a long time” (24:7).
Joshua 24:7
In the hill country
The hill country was part of the promised land, which Israel entered later (24:11).
In the wilderness
In the land of Goshen
Goshen was in Egypt, which Israel left at the exodus (Genesis 47:27).
On Mount Sinai
Israel camped at Mount Sinai for about a year (Numbers 10:11–12), not a long time.
In Philistia
Israel avoided the way of the Philistines (Exodus 13:17); the long stay was in the wilderness (24:7).
In Joshua’s review of victories east of the Jordan, which people fought Israel and lost their land?
“I brought you to the land of the Amorites who lived beyond the Jordan. They fought against you, but I delivered them into your hand” (24:8).
Joshua 24:8
Philistines
The Philistines are not named in this part of Joshua’s review; the people beyond the Jordan were the Amorites (24:8).
Midianites
Israel fought Midian later (Numbers 31:7); the people beyond the Jordan in 24:8 were the Amorites.
Amorites
Sidonians
The Sidonians are not named in this part; the people beyond the Jordan were the Amorites (24:8).
Amalekites
Israel fought Amalek at Rephidim (Exodus 17:8), but beyond the Jordan it was the Amorites (24:8).
In the Shechem address of Joshua 24, which king of Moab summoned Balaam to curse Israel?
“Balak son of Zippor, the king of Moab, set out to fight against Israel. He sent for Balaam son of Beor to curse you” (24:9).
Joshua 24:9
Eglon son of Chemosh
Eglon king of Moab oppressed Israel (Judges 3:12–14), but he did not summon Balaam.
Balak son of Zippor
Sihon son of Og
Sihon was king of the Amorites (Numbers 21:21–26); he was not the Moabite king who summoned Balaam.
Mesha son of Omri
Mesha king of Moab rebelled against Israel in 2 Kings 3:4–5, centuries after Balaam’s time.
Abimelech son of Gideon
Abimelech son of Gideon ruled at Shechem (Judges 9:6), not Moab.
In Joshua’s historical review, Balaam is identified as the son of whom?
Joshua says Balak “sent for Balaam son of Beor to curse you” (24:9).
Joshua 24:9
Peor
Peor was a mountain and a god tied to Moab (Numbers 23:28; 25:3), not Balaam’s father.
Beor
Bosor
Bosor is not the name Joshua gives; he says Balaam son of Beor (24:9).
Nahor
Nahor was Abraham’s brother (24:2), not Balaam’s father.
Kish
Kish was Saul’s father (1 Samuel 9:1), not Balaam’s father.
According to Joshua 24, what did Balaam do repeatedly instead of cursing Israel?
“I would not listen to Balaam. So he blessed you again and again” (24:10).
Joshua 24:10
Fled from Israel
Balaam did not flee from Israel; he returned to his homeland (Numbers 24:25).
Cursed Israel in secret
Balaam never cursed Israel; the LORD would not listen to him and he blessed them (24:10).
Blessed Israel
Fought Israel
Balak set out to fight Israel (24:9); Balaam blessed them.
Joined Israel
Balaam did not join Israel; he was later killed fighting against them (Numbers 31:8).
In Joshua’s summary of the conquest, which city did Israel come to after crossing the Jordan?
“You crossed the Jordan and came to Jericho” (24:11).
Joshua 24:11
Ai
Ai was taken after Jericho (Joshua 7:2; 8:1), not the first city they came to.
Hazor
Hazor was conquered in the northern campaign (Joshua 11:10), not the first city after the Jordan.
Jerusalem
The Jebusites held Jerusalem; Judah could not dislodge them (Joshua 15:63).
Jericho
Gibeon
Gibeon made a treaty with Israel (Joshua 9:3–15), after Jericho.
In Joshua 24, what did God say He sent before Israel to drive out the two kings of the Amorites?
“I sent the hornet ahead of you, and it drove out the two Amorite kings before you” (24:12).
Joshua 24:12
Thunder
Thunder is not named in this verse; God sent the hornet ahead of Israel (24:12).
Hailstones
Hailstones fell at Beth-horon (Joshua 10:11), but 24:12 says God sent the hornet.
The hornet
A plague
A plague is not named in this verse; God sent the hornet (24:12).
A whirlwind
A whirlwind is not named in this verse; God sent the hornet (24:12).
In Joshua 24, what kind of settlements did God say He gave Israel that they had not built?
“I gave you a land on which you did not toil and cities that you did not build” (24:13).
Joshua 24:13
Towers
Towers are not named; the verse says cities Israel did not build (24:13).
Cities
Wells
Wells you did not dig are mentioned in Deuteronomy 6:11, but Joshua 24:13 says cities you did not build.
Altars
Altars are not named; the verse says cities Israel did not build (24:13).
Palaces
Palaces are not named; the verse says cities Israel did not build (24:13).
In Joshua’s reminder of God’s gifts, what did Israel eat from even though they had not planted them?
“Now you live in them and eat from vineyards and olive groves that you did not plant” (24:13).
Joshua 24:13
Wheat fields and fig trees
Wheat fields and fig trees are not named; the verse says vineyards and olive groves (24:13).
Date palms and almond groves
Date palms and almond groves are not named; the verse says vineyards and olive groves (24:13).
Vineyards and olive groves
Barley fields and pomegranates
Barley fields and pomegranates are not named; the verse says vineyards and olive groves (24:13).
Flax fields and cedars
Flax fields and cedars are not named; the verse says vineyards and olive groves (24:13).
In Joshua’s call to covenant faithfulness, how were the people told to serve the LORD?
“Fear the LORD and serve Him in sincerity and truth” (24:14).
Joshua 24:14
With fasting and ashes
Fasting and ashes are not mentioned; Joshua called for service in sincerity and truth (24:14).
In sincerity and truth
With power and wealth
Power and wealth are not how Joshua said to serve; he said in sincerity and truth (24:14).
In silence and fear
Silence and fear are not what Joshua asked; he said to serve in sincerity and truth (24:14).
By sacrifices alone
Joshua did not say by sacrifices alone; he said to serve in sincerity and truth (24:14).
In the farewell challenge at Shechem, which gods did Joshua tell Israel to cast aside?
“Cast aside the gods your fathers served beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt, and serve the LORD” (24:14).
Joshua 24:14
Only the gods of Jericho and the other Canaanite cities
Joshua named the gods beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt, not only those of Jericho (24:14).
The gods their fathers served beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt
Only the gods of Moab, Ammon, and Edom
Joshua named the gods beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt, not only those of Moab and its neighbors (24:14).
Only Baal and Asherah, the gods of Canaan
Joshua named the gods beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt, not only Baal and Asherah (24:14).
Only the household gods Jacob’s family kept in Haran
Joshua named the gods beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt, not only household gods from Haran (24:14).
In Joshua 24:15, Joshua contrasts serving the LORD with serving the gods of the people in whose land Israel was then dwelling. Whose land was it?
Joshua spoke of “the gods of the Amorites in whose land you are living” (24:15).
Joshua 24:15
Hivites
Hivites were one of the peoples of Canaan (24:11), but 24:15 names the Amorites.
Jebusites
Jebusites were one of the peoples of Canaan (24:11), but 24:15 names the Amorites.
Amorites
Midianites
Midian lay to the east, and Israel was not living in its land (24:15).
Philistines
The Philistines lived on the coast; 24:15 names the Amorites as the people of the land.
When the people promised to serve the LORD, why did Joshua warn that they were not able to serve Him?
Joshua said, “You are not able to serve the LORD, for He is a holy God; He is a jealous God” (24:19).
Joshua 24:19
Because they had no priest
No lack of a priest was given as the reason; Joshua pointed to God’s holiness and jealousy (24:19).
Because they lacked weapons
No lack of weapons was given as the reason; Joshua pointed to God’s holiness and jealousy (24:19).
Because He is a holy and jealous God
Because the ark was far away
The ark’s location was not the reason; Joshua pointed to God’s holiness and jealousy (24:19).
Because the land was not fully conquered
Unfinished conquest was not the reason; Joshua pointed to God’s holiness and jealousy (24:19).
In Joshua’s warning at Shechem, what did he say God would not forgive if the people turned away?
Joshua said God “will not forgive your rebellion or your sins” (24:19).
Joshua 24:19
Their hunger and thirst
Hunger and thirst are not what God would not forgive; it was their rebellion and sins (24:19).
Their transgressions and sins
Their tithes and offerings
Tithes and offerings are not named; God would not forgive their rebellion and sins (24:19).
Their fear and weakness
Fear and weakness are not named; God would not forgive their rebellion and sins (24:19).
Their debts and pledges
Debts and pledges are not named; God would not forgive their rebellion and sins (24:19).
According to Joshua 24, what would God do if Israel forsook Him and served foreign gods after He had been good to them?
Joshua said God “will turn and bring disaster on you and consume you, even after He has been good to you” (24:20).
Joshua 24:20
Ignore their rebellion and keep on blessing them
God would not ignore them; Joshua said He would bring disaster on them (24:19–20).
Send them manna again to bring them back
Manna was a gift in the wilderness (Exodus 16:35), not what Joshua said God would send (24:20).
Turn and bring disaster upon them and consume them
Send them back to Egypt to serve Pharaoh again
Joshua did not say God would send them back to Egypt; he said disaster would consume them (24:20).
Raise up another Moses to plead for them
Joshua did not say God would raise up another Moses; he said He would bring disaster on them (24:20).
In the people’s answer to Joshua, from what place did they say the LORD had brought them and their fathers up?
“The LORD our God brought us and our fathers out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (24:17).
Joshua 24:17
The land of Midian
Midian is where Moses lived in exile (Exodus 2:15), not where Israel was enslaved (24:17).
The house of slavery
The plains of Moab
The plains of Moab were where Israel camped (Numbers 22:1), not the house of slavery (24:17).
The land of Uz
Uz was Job’s land (Job 1:1), not where Israel was enslaved (24:17).
The valley of Achor
The valley of Achor is where Achan was stoned (Joshua 7:24–26), not the house of slavery (24:17).
In Joshua 24, whom did Joshua say were witnesses against themselves that they had chosen to serve the LORD?
Joshua told them, “You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen to serve the LORD” (24:22).
Joshua 24:22
The priests
The priests were not the witnesses; Joshua told the people they were witnesses against themselves (24:22).
The elders
The elders were not the only witnesses; Joshua told all the people they were witnesses against themselves (24:22).
The people themselves
The Levites
The Levites were not the witnesses; Joshua told the people they were witnesses against themselves (24:22).
The judges
The judges were not the witnesses; Joshua told the people they were witnesses against themselves (24:22).
After the people renewed their promise at Shechem, what did Joshua tell them to get rid of?
“Get rid of the foreign gods among you and incline your hearts to the LORD, the God of Israel” (24:23).
Joshua 24:23
Their tents
Their tents were not to be discarded; the foreign gods were (24:23).
Their foreign wives
Foreign wives were an issue later (Ezra 10:3), but Joshua told them to get rid of the foreign gods (24:23).
The foreign gods among them
Their weapons
Weapons were not to be discarded; the foreign gods were (24:23).
The bronze serpent
The bronze serpent was destroyed by Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:4), long after Joshua.
In Joshua’s final instructions at Shechem, to whom were the people told to incline their hearts?
“Incline your hearts to the LORD, the God of Israel” (24:23).
Joshua 24:23
Moses the servant of God
Moses was dead by then (Deuteronomy 34:5); the people were told to incline their hearts to the LORD (24:23).
Eleazar the priest
Eleazar the priest is not who they were to incline their hearts to; it was the LORD (24:23).
The LORD, the God of Israel
The ark of the covenant
The ark was a symbol of God’s presence; the people were told to incline their hearts to the LORD (24:23).
The elders of Ephraim
The elders of Ephraim are not mentioned; the people were told to incline their hearts to the LORD (24:23).
On that day at Shechem, what did Joshua make with the people?
“On that day Joshua made a covenant for the people” (24:25).
Joshua 24:25
A census
A census was taken under Moses (Numbers 26:1–4), not made at Shechem.
A covenant
A military alliance
A military alliance is not mentioned; Joshua made a covenant (24:25).
A temple tax
A temple tax is not mentioned; there was no temple yet, and Joshua made a covenant (24:25).
A pilgrimage vow
A pilgrimage vow is not mentioned; Joshua made a covenant (24:25).
In addition to making a covenant at Shechem, what did Joshua establish for the people there?
“There at Shechem he established for them a statute and ordinance” (24:25).
Joshua 24:25
A festival and fast
A festival and fast are not named; Joshua established a statute and ordinance (24:25).
A throne and scepter
A throne and scepter are not named; Israel had no king yet (24:25).
A statute and ordinance
A sacrifice and altar
A sacrifice and altar are not named here; Joshua established a statute and ordinance (24:25).
A census and tribute
A census and tribute are not named; Joshua established a statute and ordinance (24:25).
In Joshua 24, where did Joshua record the words and actions of this covenant renewal?
“Joshua recorded these things in the Book of the Law of God” (24:26).
Joshua 24:26
The Book of Jasher
The Book of Jasher is cited in Joshua 10:13, but Joshua recorded these things in the Book of the Law of God (24:26).
The Book of the Law of God
The chronicles of the priests
The chronicles of the priests are not mentioned; Joshua used the Book of the Law of God (24:26).
The scroll of Samuel
Samuel lived centuries later (1 Samuel 10:25), so he is not the source of this record.
The book of the kings of Canaan
A book of the kings of Canaan is not mentioned; Joshua used the Book of the Law of God (24:26).
As a witness to the covenant at Shechem, what object did Joshua set up?
Joshua “took a large stone and set it up there under the oak” (24:26).
Joshua 24:26
A bronze altar
Joshua built an altar on Mount Ebal earlier (Joshua 8:30), but at Shechem he set up a large stone (24:26).
A large stone
A wooden pillar
A wooden pillar is not mentioned; Joshua set up a large stone (24:26).
A golden lampstand
The golden lampstand belonged to the tabernacle (Exodus 25:31), not to this scene.
A heap of twelve jars
Twelve stones were set up at the Jordan crossing (Joshua 4:20), but at Shechem it was one large stone (24:26).
In the closing covenant scene of Joshua 24, where was the witness stone placed?
Joshua “took a large stone and set it up there under the oak that was near the sanctuary of the LORD” (24:26).
Joshua 24:26
Beside the Jordan under a tamarisk
A tamarisk by the Jordan is not mentioned; the stone was under the oak near the sanctuary (24:26).
Beneath the oak near the sanctuary of the LORD
On Mount Ebal beside the altar
The altar on Mount Ebal was built earlier (Joshua 8:30); the stone was under the oak at Shechem (24:26).
At Gilgal near the camp
Gilgal is where stones from the Jordan were set up (Joshua 4:20), not this stone (24:26).
Before the gate of Jericho
Jericho’s gate is not mentioned; the stone was under the oak near the sanctuary (24:26).
What did Joshua say the witness stone had heard?
Joshua said, “it has heard all the words the LORD has spoken to us” (24:27).
Joshua 24:27
All the songs Israel sang at the sea
The songs Israel sang at the sea (Exodus 15:1) are not what the stone heard; it heard all the words the LORD had spoken (24:27).
All the words the LORD had spoken to them
The trumpet blasts at the walls of Jericho
Trumpets sounded at Jericho (Joshua 6:20), but the stone heard all the words the LORD had spoken (24:27).
The words of Moses’ final blessing on the tribes
Moses blessed the tribes in Deuteronomy 33, but the stone heard all the words the LORD had spoken (24:27).
The vow Jacob made at Bethel long before
Jacob’s vow at Bethel is in Genesis 28:20–22, but the stone heard all the words the LORD had spoken (24:27).
After the covenant ceremony in Joshua 24, where did Joshua send the people?
“Joshua sent the people away, each to his own inheritance” (24:28).
Joshua 24:28
To Shiloh
Shiloh is where the tabernacle stood (Joshua 18:1); Joshua sent the people each to his own inheritance (24:28).
To the tabernacle
The tabernacle is not where he sent them; each went to his own inheritance (24:28).
Each to his own inheritance
To the plains of Moab
The plains of Moab were left behind long before; each went to his own inheritance (24:28).
To the wilderness
The wilderness was behind them; each went to his own inheritance in the land (24:28).
In the death notice near the end of Joshua 24, what title is Joshua son of Nun given?
“Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at the age of 110” (24:29).
Joshua 24:29
Prophet of the LORD
Joshua is not called a prophet of the LORD here; the text calls him the servant of the LORD (24:29).
Captain of Israel
A commander appeared to Joshua in Joshua 5:14, but the title in 24:29 is servant of the LORD.
Servant of the LORD
Judge in Israel
Joshua is not called a judge here; the title in 24:29 is servant of the LORD.
Prince of Ephraim
Joshua was buried in Ephraim (24:30), but he is not called prince of Ephraim; he is the servant of the LORD (24:29).
According to Joshua 24, where was Joshua buried?
“They buried him in the land of his inheritance, at Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim” (24:30).
Joshua 24:30
Hebron in the hill country of Judah
Hebron was Caleb’s inheritance (Joshua 14:13–14), not Joshua’s burial place.
Ramah in Benjamin
Ramah in Benjamin is where Samuel lived (1 Samuel 7:17), not where Joshua was buried.
Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim
Shiloh near the tabernacle
Shiloh is where the tabernacle stood (Joshua 18:1), not where Joshua was buried.
Gibeah of Saul
Gibeah is where Eleazar was buried (24:33), not Joshua.
Joshua’s burial place in Joshua 24 is described as north of what landmark?
Joshua was buried at Timnath-serah “north of Mount Gaash” (24:30).
Joshua 24:30
Mount Nebo
Mount Nebo is where Moses saw the land before he died (Deuteronomy 34:1), not the landmark in 24:30.
Mount Carmel
Mount Carmel is not mentioned in 24:30; the landmark is Mount Gaash.
Mount Gaash
Mount Ebal
Mount Ebal is where the altar was built (Joshua 8:30), not the landmark in 24:30.
Mount Gerizim
Mount Gerizim is where the blessings were spoken (Joshua 8:33), not the landmark in 24:30.
After Joshua’s death, which group does Joshua 24 say continued to serve the LORD because they had known His works for Israel?
“Israel had served the LORD throughout the days of Joshua and of the elders who outlived him” (24:31).
Joshua 24:31
The priests who served at Shiloh
Priests at Shiloh are not named in 24:31; the text names the elders who outlived Joshua.
The elders who outlived Joshua
The kings of the tribes
Israel had no kings of the tribes; 24:31 names the elders who outlived Joshua.
The judges after Othniel
The judges came after this period, and Israel then turned away (Judges 2:10–11); 24:31 names the elders.
The sons of Korah
The sons of Korah are not mentioned here; 24:31 names the elders who outlived Joshua.
In the final burial notices of Joshua 24, whose bones were buried at Shechem?
“The bones of Joseph, which the Israelites had brought up out of Egypt, were buried at Shechem” (24:32).
Joshua 24:32
Moses’
Moses’ burial place was unknown (Deuteronomy 34:6), and his bones were not buried at Shechem.
Aaron’s
Aaron died on Mount Hor (Numbers 20:28), not at Shechem.
Joseph’s
Caleb’s
Caleb received Hebron (Joshua 14:13), not Shechem.
Samuel’s
Samuel was buried at Ramah (1 Samuel 25:1), not Shechem.
The plot at Shechem where Joseph’s bones were buried had originally been bought by Jacob from whom?
The plot was one “that Jacob had purchased from the sons of Hamor, Shechem’s father, for a hundred pieces of silver” (24:32).
Joshua 24:32
Ephron the Hittite, owner of the cave at Machpelah
Abraham bought the cave at Machpelah from Ephron the Hittite (Genesis 23:16–18); Jacob bought the Shechem plot from Hamor’s sons (24:32).
The sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem
Laban the Aramean, in the hill country of Gilead
Laban made a covenant with Jacob in Gilead (Genesis 31:44–47), but Jacob bought the Shechem plot from Hamor’s sons (24:32).
Abimelech of Gerar, near the well at Beersheba
Abimelech made a covenant with Abraham at Beersheba (Genesis 21:27–32), but the Shechem plot came from Hamor’s sons (24:32).
The sons of Anak, the giants of Hebron
The sons of Anak lived around Hebron (Joshua 15:13–14), not at Shechem; the plot came from Hamor’s sons (24:32).
According to Joshua 24, what price did Jacob pay for the plot at Shechem that became the inheritance of Joseph’s descendants?
Jacob bought the plot “for a hundred pieces of silver” (24:32).
Joshua 24:32
Thirty shekels of silver
Thirty shekels of silver was the price for a gored slave (Exodus 21:32), not the Shechem plot (24:32).
Ten talents of gold
Ten talents of gold are not mentioned; the price was a hundred pieces of silver (24:32).
Fifty shekels of silver
David paid fifty shekels of silver for Araunah’s threshing floor (2 Samuel 24:24), not Jacob for the Shechem plot.
A hundred pieces of silver
Twenty minas of bronze
Twenty minas of bronze are not mentioned; the price was a hundred pieces of silver (24:32).
At the very end of Joshua 24, where was Eleazar son of Aaron buried?
“Eleazar son of Aaron also died, and they buried him at Gibeah, which had been given to his son Phinehas in the hill country of Ephraim” (24:33).
Joshua 24:33
At Gibeah allotted to his son Phinehas in the hill country of Ephraim
At Hebron in the allotment given to Caleb in the hill country of Judah
Hebron was Caleb’s inheritance (Joshua 14:13–14), but Eleazar was buried at Gibeah (24:33).
At Shiloh beside the sanctuary where the tabernacle stood in Ephraim
Shiloh is where the tabernacle stood (Joshua 18:1), but Eleazar was buried at Gibeah (24:33).
At Timnath-serah beside Joshua north of Mount Gaash in Ephraim
Joshua was buried at Timnath-serah (24:30), while Eleazar was buried at Gibeah (24:33).
On Mount Hor beside his father Aaron at the edge of Edom
Aaron died on Mount Hor (Numbers 20:28), but Eleazar was buried at Gibeah in Ephraim (24:33).
7: In Judges 1, after Joshua died, which tribe did the Israelites ask the LORD should go up first to fight the Canaanites?
The LORD answered, “Judah shall go up… I have delivered the land into their hands” (1:2).
Judges 1:1-2
Ephraim
Ephraim belonged to the house of Joseph, which later attacked Bethel (1:22).
Judah
Benjamin
Benjamin is mentioned for failing to drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem (1:21).
Dan
Dan was pushed into the hill country by the Amorites (1:34).
Reuben
Reuben had already received land east of the Jordan from Moses (Joshua 13:8).
In the opening events of Judges 1, which tribe did Judah invite to go up with them to fight the Canaanites in their allotted territory?
Judah said to “their brothers the Simeonites, ‘Come up with us to our allotted territory’” (1:3).
Judges 1:3
Levi
Levi received no land inheritance (Joshua 13:14) and is not invited in 1:3.
Issachar
Issachar is not mentioned anywhere in Judges 1.
Simeon
Naphtali
Naphtali appears later, failing to drive out Beth-shemesh and Beth-anath (1:33).
Gad
Gad’s inheritance lay east of the Jordan (Joshua 13:8); it is not mentioned in Judges 1.
At Bezek in Judges 1, Judah and Simeon struck which two groups in battle?
“The LORD delivered the Canaanites and Perizzites into their hands, and they struck down ten thousand men at Bezek” (1:4).
Judges 1:4
Philistines and Moabites
Judah took the Philistine cities later (1:18), and Moab oppressed Israel under Eglon (Judges 3:12).
Canaanites and Perizzites
Jebusites and Hivites
The Jebusites held Jerusalem (1:21), and the Hivites were the Gibeonites who tricked Joshua (Joshua 9:7).
Amalekites and Midianites
The Midianites and Amalekites raided Israel in Gideon’s day (Judges 6:3).
Amorites and Edomites
The Amorites hemmed in the Danites (1:34); Edom is not in Judges 1.
In the battle at Bezek described in Judges 1, what was the name of the ruler who fled and was captured?
At Bezek “they found Adoni-bezek”; he fled, but they pursued and seized him (1:5–6).
Judges 1:5-6
Adoni-zedek
Adoni-zedek was king of Jerusalem in Joshua’s day (Joshua 10:1).
Adoni-bezek
Sihon
Sihon was king of the Amorites, defeated under Moses (Numbers 21:21).
Og
Og was king of Bashan, defeated under Moses (Numbers 21:33).
Jabin
Jabin was a king of Hazor who oppressed Israel in Deborah’s day (Judges 4:2).
When Adoni-bezek was captured in Judges 1, what did the men of Judah do to him?
They “cut off his thumbs and big toes” (1:6), as he had done to seventy kings (1:7).
Judges 1:6-7
They blinded him
Blinding was done to Samson by the Philistines (Judges 16:21).
They shaved his head
Samson’s hair, not Adoni-bezek’s, was shaved off (Judges 16:19).
They cut off his thumbs and big toes
They bound him in chains
Chains are not mentioned; Samson and later Zedekiah were bound with bronze shackles (2 Kings 25:7).
They exiled him
He was not exiled; they brought him to Jerusalem, where he died (1:7).
In Judges 1, Judah fought against a city later called Hebron. What had that city formerly been called?
Hebron was “formerly known as Kiriath-arba” (1:10).
Judges 1:10
Kiriath-jearim
Kiriath-jearim was a Gibeonite town (Joshua 9:17) where the ark was later kept (1 Samuel 7:1).
Kiriath-sepher
Kiriath-sepher was the former name of Debir (1:11).
Kiriath-arba
Beth-shean
Beth-shean was a town Manasseh failed to capture (1:27).
Luz
Luz was the former name of Bethel (1:23).
When Judah attacked Hebron in Judges 1, which three descendants were defeated there?
At Hebron Judah “struck down Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai” (1:10), descendants of Anak (Numbers 13:22).
Judges 1:10
Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai
Hophni, Phinehas, and Eliab
Hophni and Phinehas were Eli’s sons (1 Samuel 1:3), and Eliab was David’s eldest brother (1 Samuel 17:13).
Nadab, Abihu, and Eleazar
Nadab, Abihu, and Eleazar were sons of Aaron (Exodus 6:23).
Gershon, Kohath, and Merari
Gershon, Kohath, and Merari were the sons of Levi (Exodus 6:16).
Oreb, Zeeb, and Zalmunna
Oreb and Zeeb were princes of Midian (Judges 7:25), and Zalmunna was a Midianite king (Judges 8:5).
In the campaign of Judges 1, what was the former name of Debir, the city Caleb challenged others to capture?
Judah marched against “Debir (formerly known as Kiriath-sepher)” (1:11).
Judges 1:11
Hormah
Hormah was the new name of Zephath (1:17).
Kiriath-sepher
Beth-anath
Beth-anath was a town Naphtali failed to drive out (1:33).
Gezer
Gezer was where Ephraim failed to drive out the Canaanites (1:29).
Aijalon
Aijalon was one of the places the Amorites held onto (1:35).
In Judges 1, what reward did Caleb promise to the man who would strike Kiriath-sepher and capture it?
Caleb said, “To the man who strikes down Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give my daughter Acsah in marriage” (1:12).
Judges 1:12
A field in Hebron
Acsah later asked for a field (1:14), and Hebron was given to Caleb himself (1:20).
A spring in the Negev
Springs were given later, when Acsah asked her father for them (1:15).
His daughter Acsah in marriage
A place among the elders
No place among the elders is offered; Caleb offered his daughter (1:12).
His armor and sword
Armor appears when Saul dressed David in his own (1 Samuel 17:38).
Who captured Kiriath-sepher in Judges 1 and received Acsah, Caleb’s daughter, as his wife?
“Othniel son of Caleb’s younger brother Kenaz captured the city, and Caleb gave his daughter Acsah to him in marriage” (1:13).
Judges 1:13
Ehud son of Gera
Ehud son of Gera was the left-handed judge who delivered Israel from Moab (Judges 3:15).
Othniel son of Kenaz
Shamgar son of Anath
Shamgar son of Anath struck down six hundred Philistines (Judges 3:31).
Jair the Gileadite
Jair the Gileadite judged Israel twenty-two years (Judges 10:3).
Abdon son of Hillel
Abdon son of Hillel judged Israel after Elon (Judges 12:13).
In Judges 1, after Acsah came to Caleb, what additional gift did she ask from her father besides the land in the Negev?
She said, “Since you have given me land in the Negev, give me springs of water as well,” and Caleb gave her the upper and lower springs (1:15).
Judges 1:14-15
Wells of oil
A jar of oil was the widow’s only possession when Elisha helped her (2 Kings 4:2).
Vineyards
Vineyards recall Naboth’s vineyard in Jezreel (1 Kings 21:1), not Acsah’s request.
Springs of water
Herds of cattle
Herds are not mentioned; Acsah asked for springs of water (1:15).
A fortified city
A city is not mentioned; Acsah asked for springs of water (1:15).
According to Judges 1, the descendants of Moses’ father-in-law, the Kenite, went up from which place before settling near Arad in the Wilderness of Judah?
The Kenites “went up with the men of Judah from the City of Palms to the Wilderness of Judah in the Negev near Arad” (1:16); the City of Palms is Jericho (Deuteronomy 34:3).
Judges 1:16
Shiloh
Shiloh was where Israel set up the Tent of Meeting (Joshua 18:1).
Gilgal
Gilgal was Israel’s first camp after crossing the Jordan (Joshua 4:19).
The City of Palms
Bethel
Bethel was the city the house of Joseph attacked (1:22).
Mizpah
Mizpah was where Israel later assembled before the LORD (Judges 20:1).
After Judah and Simeon struck the Canaanites living in Zephath and devoted the city to destruction in Judges 1, what was the city called?
They “devoted the city to destruction. So it was called Hormah” (1:17).
Judges 1:17
Hormah
Hebron
Hebron was the city formerly called Kiriath-arba (1:10).
Bethel
Bethel was the city formerly called Luz (1:23).
Ekron
Ekron was a Philistine city Judah captured (1:18).
Debir
Debir was the city formerly called Kiriath-sepher (1:11).
In Judges 1, although the LORD was with Judah, why could Judah not drive out the inhabitants of the plain?
They could not drive out the inhabitants of the plains “because they had chariots of iron” (1:19).
Judges 1:19
They had fortified towers
No towers are mentioned; the obstacle was chariots of iron (1:19).
They had iron chariots
A famine stopped the campaign
No famine is mentioned in Judges 1; a famine in the judges’ era drove Elimelech to Moab (Ruth 1:1).
Judah made a peace treaty

Judges 5:31 says, “But may those who love You shine like the sun at its brightest.”
Judges 5:31
Like cedars of Lebanon standing tall
Cedars of Lebanon are not named in Judges 5:31.
Like stars shining forever and ever
Stars fought against Sisera (5:20), but those who love the LORD are compared to the sun (5:31).
Like the sun when it rises in strength
Like rivers in flood sweeping the land
Rivers in flood are not compared to those who love the LORD (5:31); the River Kishon swept enemies away (5:21).
Like lions among the sheep of the fold
Lions among sheep are not named in Judges 5:31.
In the opening of Judges 6, which people oppressed Israel after the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD?
The LORD gave Israel into the hand of Midian because of their evil, and the Midianites then ravaged the land (6:1–6).
Judges 6:1
Moabites
Moab under King Eglon oppressed Israel earlier, in Judges 3:12, not in this chapter.
Midianites
Philistines
The Philistines oppressed Israel later, in Judges 13:1, for forty years.
Ammonites
The Ammonites joined the Philistines in oppressing Israel in Judges 10:7, in a different cycle.
Canaanites
Jabin king of Canaan oppressed Israel earlier, in Judges 4:2–3, in the days of Deborah.
In Judges 6, for how many years did the LORD give Israel into the hand of Midian?
Judges 6:1 says the LORD delivered Israel into the hand of Midian for seven years.
Judges 6:1
Three years
Abimelech reigned over Israel three years (Judges 9:22), but Midian’s oppression lasted seven years (6:1).
Seven years
Ten years
Ten years is not the length given; Judges 6:1 says seven years.
Twenty years
Twenty years was how long Jabin harshly oppressed Israel (Judges 4:3), not Midian.
Forty years
Forty years was the rest the land enjoyed in Gideon’s days after Midian was subdued (Judges 8:28), not the length of the oppression.
Because of Midian in Judges 6, where did the Israelites make hiding places for themselves?
Because of Midian, the Israelites prepared shelters for themselves in the mountains, caves, and strongholds (6:2).
Judges 6:2
In fortified cities only
Fortified cities did not protect them; 6:2 says they hid in the mountains, caves, and strongholds.
In tents by the Jordan
It was the Midianites who came with tents (6:5); Israel hid in mountain shelters (6:2).
In mountains, caves, and strongholds
In the tabernacle courts
No tabernacle is mentioned here; Israel’s hiding places were mountains, caves, and strongholds (6:2).
In Philistine towns
Israel hid in its own hill country, not in Philistine towns, which are not mentioned in this chapter (6:2).
Whenever Israel planted crops in Judges 6, which additional groups came up with Midian against them?
Whenever Israel planted crops, the Midianites, Amalekites, and other people of the east came up and invaded (6:3).
Judges 6:3
Amalekites and the people of the east
Philistines and Sidonians
The Philistines would oppress Israel later (Judges 13:1); this chapter names Amalekites and people of the east alongside Midian (6:3).
Moabites and Edomites
Moab and Edom are not named here; 6:3 lists the Amalekites and other people of the east.
Egyptians and Cushites
Egypt is the land the LORD had brought Israel out of (6:8), not one of the raiding groups.
Hittites and Jebusites
Hittites and Jebusites were peoples of Canaan (Exodus 3:8), not the eastern raiders of 6:3.
According to Judges 6, what did these raiders do to Israel’s food supply?
The raiders encamped against Israel and destroyed the produce of the land, leaving no sustenance (6:4).
Judges 6:4
They taxed the harvest
The invaders did not tax the harvest; they destroyed the produce (6:4).
They destroyed the produce and left no sustenance
They traded for grain fairly
There was no fair trade; the Midianites came to ravage the land (6:5).
They stored Israel’s crops in Samaria
Samaria did not yet exist; Omri founded it much later (1 Kings 16:24), and the raiders destroyed the crops rather than storing them (6:4).
They took only the sheep
They took far more than sheep: 6:4 says they left Israel neither sheep nor oxen nor donkeys, and destroyed the produce.
After Israel became greatly impoverished in Judges 6, what did the Israelites do?
Israel was greatly impoverished by Midian, and the Israelites cried out to the LORD (6:6).
Judges 6:6
They crowned a king
Israel did not ask for a king until much later, in 1 Samuel 8:5.
They fled to Egypt
Nothing here says they fled to Egypt; they hid in the mountains and caves (6:2).
They cried out to the LORD
They made peace with Midian
They did not make peace with Midian; they cried out to the LORD (6:6).
They rebuilt Jericho
Jericho was rebuilt much later, in the days of Ahab (1 Kings 16:34).
Before calling Gideon in Judges 6, what did the LORD send to Israel after they cried out?
When the Israelites cried out because of Midian, the LORD sent them a prophet (6:7–8).
Judges 6:7-8
A judge
The deliverer, Gideon, came after the prophet’s message; what the LORD sent first was a prophet (6:8).
A prophet
A king
Israel had no king in this period (Judges 21:25).
A priest from Shiloh
Priests at Shiloh appear in 1 Samuel 1:3; here the LORD sent a prophet (6:8).
An army from Judah
No army from Judah is sent; the LORD first sent a prophet and then called Gideon of Manasseh (6:8, 6:15).
In the prophet’s message in Judges 6, from what land did the LORD say He had brought Israel up?
The prophet said the LORD brought Israel up out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery (6:8).
Judges 6:8
Babylon
Israel’s exile to Babylon came centuries later (2 Kings 25:21); the prophet spoke of Egypt (6:8).
Aram
Aram was where Jacob once sojourned (Genesis 28:5), not the land of Israel’s slavery.
Edom
Edom was where Esau settled (Genesis 36:8); Israel was not enslaved there.
Egypt
Moab
Israel camped in the plains of Moab before entering Canaan (Numbers 22:1), but Moab was not the house of slavery.
In the rebuke recorded in Judges 6, whose gods had the LORD told Israel not to fear in the land where they lived?
The prophet quotes the LORD: “You must not fear the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell.” (6:10)
Judges 6:10
The gods of the Amorites
The gods of the Philistines
Israel did later serve the gods of the Philistines (Judges 10:6), but the rebuke in 6:10 names the Amorites.
The gods of the Egyptians
Egypt’s gods belong to the land Israel left behind (6:8); the warning concerns the land where they now lived.
The gods of the Hivites
The Hivites were another people of Canaan (Joshua 9:7), but the LORD’s words in 6:10 name the Amorites.
The gods of the Arameans
Israel later served the gods of Aram (Judges 10:6), but the rebuke here names the Amorites (6:10).
When the Angel of the LORD found Gideon in Judges 6, where was Gideon threshing wheat to hide it from the Midianites?
Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites (6:11).
Judges 6:11
In a barn
Threshing in a barn would have exposed the grain; Gideon worked in a winepress to hide it (6:11).
On a rooftop
A rooftop is not mentioned; 6:11 places Gideon in a winepress.
In a winepress
At the city gate
The city gate was where elders sat (Ruth 4:1), not where Gideon hid his wheat.
By the altar at Shiloh
Shiloh does not appear here; Gideon was at Ophrah (6:11).
In Gideon’s call at Ophrah in Judges 6, under what tree did the Angel of the LORD sit at the property of Joash the Abiezrite?
The angel of the LORD sat down under the oak in Ophrah that belonged to Joash the Abiezrite (6:11).
Judges 6:11
Palm
Deborah sat under a palm tree (Judges 4:5), not the tree in Gideon’s story.
Cedar
Cedar was the wood of Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 6:9); the tree at Ophrah was an oak (6:11).
Oak
Olive
Olive wood was used for the temple cherubim (1 Kings 6:23); the tree at Ophrah was an oak (6:11).
Sycamore
Zacchaeus climbed a sycamore (Luke 19:4); the angel sat under an oak (6:11).
According to Judges 6:12, how did the angel of the LORD greet Gideon at Ophrah?
The angel of the LORD appeared to Gideon and said, “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor.” (6:12)
Judges 6:12
“Fear not, prophet of Israel”
Gideon was no prophet; the prophet had already been sent (6:8), and the angel’s greeting was that the LORD was with him (6:12).
“The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor”
“Rise up, son of Jesse”
‘Son of Jesse’ is David (1 Samuel 17:58); Gideon was the son of Joash (6:11).
“Blessed are you among men”
The angel did not pronounce a blessing on Gideon; he declared that the LORD was with him (6:12).
“Go, priest of Manasseh”
Gideon was not a priest; he was a young man threshing wheat in a winepress (6:11).
In Gideon’s reply in Judges 6, what famous act of deliverance did he say their fathers had told them about?
Gideon asked where were all the LORD’s wonders “of which our fathers told us,” namely that the LORD had brought them up out of Egypt (6:13).
Judges 6:13
The walls of Jericho falling down
Jericho fell in Joshua’s day (Joshua 6:20), but Gideon pointed to the exodus from Egypt (6:13).
The waters of the Jordan parting
The Jordan parted for Joshua (Joshua 3:16), but Gideon’s example was the exodus from Egypt (6:13).
The conquest of Ai under Joshua
Ai was burned by Joshua (Joshua 8:28), but Gideon’s example was the exodus from Egypt (6:13).
The LORD bringing Israel up out of Egypt
David defeating Goliath in battle
David lived generations after Gideon (1 Samuel 17:50), so Gideon’s fathers could not have told him of it.
What reason did Gideon give in Judges 6 for feeling unqualified to save Israel?
Gideon said, “my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the youngest in my father’s house” (6:15).
Judges 6:15
He was far too old and nearly blind to lead any army into battle against Midian
Gideon never claimed to be old or blind; he said he was the youngest in his father’s house (6:15).
He had no sword or shield, and Israel had no army left to follow him into battle
He did not mention weapons; his reasons were his weak clan and his youth (6:15).
His clan was the weakest in Manasseh, and he was the youngest in his father’s house
His clan came from Judah rather than Manasseh, so the tribes of Israel would not follow him
Gideon’s clan was in Manasseh (6:15), not Judah.
He had been exiled from Israel by Midian and had no home or tribe to speak for him
Gideon lived at home in Ophrah (6:11); he was not an exile.
What promise did the LORD make Gideon about Midian in Judges 6?
The LORD told Gideon, “you will strike down all the Midianites as one man” (6:16).
Judges 6:16
“You will strike down all the Midianites as one man”
“You will avoid battle entirely”
God sent Gideon to save Israel from Midian’s hand (6:14); the promise was victory in battle, not avoiding it.
“You will make peace with Midian”
God promised Gideon victory over Midian, not peace with it (6:16).
“You will need Egypt’s help”
The LORD said, “Am I not sending you?” (6:14); Gideon’s strength came from Him, not from Egypt.
“You will reign over Midian”
Gideon later refused even to rule over Israel (Judges 8:23), and no promise of ruling Midian is given.
When Gideon prepared an offering in Judges 6, what food did he bring to the visitor under the oak?
Gideon prepared a young goat and unleavened bread and an ephah of flour, and brought them out to present under the oak (6:19).
Judges 6:19
A lamb and leavened bread baked from a bushel of barley flour
Gideon prepared a young goat and unleavened bread, not a lamb and leavened bread (6:19).
Fish and cakes of raisins served with a basket of fresh figs
Cakes of raisins appear in David’s gifts to the people (2 Samuel 6:19), not in Gideon’s offering (6:19).
A young goat and unleavened bread from an ephah of flour
Doves and oil cakes served with a jar of olive oil and honey
Doves were an offering for those who could not afford a lamb (Leviticus 5:7); Gideon brought a young goat (6:19).
Manna and quail gathered from the wilderness camp of Israel
Manna and quail were God’s provision in the wilderness (Exodus 16:13), long before Gideon.
In the offering scene of Judges 6, where was Gideon told to place the meat and unleavened bread?
The angel told Gideon to take the meat and the unleavened bread, lay them on “this rock,” and pour out the broth (6:20).
Judges 6:20
On a bronze altar
Gideon built his altar only afterward (6:24); the angel directed him to a rock (6:20).
On a stone table
No table is mentioned; the angel told him to lay the food on a rock (6:20).
On the ground before the oak
Gideon brought the food to the oak (6:19), but the angel told him to put it on the rock (6:20).
On a rock
In a basket by the doorway
The meat was already in a basket (6:19); the angel told him to lay it on the rock (6:20).
What happened when the Angel of the LORD touched Gideon’s offering with the tip of his staff in Judges 6?
The angel touched the meat and bread with his staff; fire flared from the rock and consumed it, and the angel vanished from his sight (6:21).
Judges 6:21
Rain fell from heaven and put out the fire of the offering
Fire, not rain, consumed the offering in 6:21.
The food turned into bread that Gideon shared with the Angel
There was no shared meal; the food was consumed by fire and the angel vanished (6:21).
Fire sprang from the rock and consumed it, and the Angel vanished
The basket filled with grain, and the Angel blessed the harvest
The offering was consumed, not multiplied or replaced by grain (6:21).
The altar collapsed, and the Angel struck Gideon to the ground
Gideon built an altar only afterward, and it still stands (6:24); the angel simply vanished (6:21).
After Gideon feared he had seen the Angel of the LORD face to face in Judges 6, what did God tell him?
The LORD said to him, “Peace be with you. Do not be afraid, for you will not die.” (6:23)
Judges 6:23
“Leave this place at once before the fire returns”
God did not send him away; He reassured him (6:23).
“Peace be with you. Do not be afraid, for you will not die”
“Fast for seven days and then return to this rock”
No fast is commanded; Gideon responded by building an altar called The LORD Is Peace (6:24).
“Call the elders of Ephraim and tell them what you saw”
Gideon’s call to Ephraim came later (Judges 7:24); at this moment God reassured him (6:23).
“Hide in the mountains until the Midianites have gone”
Israel was hiding in the mountains (6:2), but God told Gideon not to be afraid (6:23).
What name did Gideon give the altar he built in Ophrah after this encounter in Judges 6?
Gideon built an altar to the LORD there and called it The LORD Is Peace (6:24).
Judges 6:24
The LORD Our Banner
Moses named an altar The LORD Is My Banner (Exodus 17:15), not Gideon.
Ebenezer
Ebenezer is the stone Samuel set up (1 Samuel 7:12).
The LORD Is Peace
House of Mercy
That is not a name given in this passage; Gideon’s altar was called The LORD Is Peace (6:24).
Rock of Refuge
The rock appears in 6:20–21, but the altar’s name was The LORD Is Peace (6:24).
On the night of Gideon’s commission in Judges 6, what was he told to tear down at his father’s house?
The LORD told Gideon to tear down his father’s altar to Baal and cut down the Asherah pole beside it (6:25).
Judges 6:25
A shrine of Molech and a sacred grove
Molech worship is condemned in Leviticus 18:21; Gideon’s assignment concerned Baal’s altar and the Asherah pole (6:25).
An altar to Baal and the Asherah pole beside it
A golden calf and a high place
The golden calf was Aaron’s (Exodus 32:4) and Jeroboam’s (1 Kings 12:28); Gideon’s task was Baal’s altar (6:25).
A pillar of Dagon and a Philistine image
Dagon was the Philistines’ god (1 Samuel 5:2); Gideon’s assignment was Baal’s altar (6:25).
The city gate and watchtower
Gideon’s task was at his father’s house, an altar and an Asherah pole, not a city gate (6:25).
Which animal did the LORD specifically tell Gideon to use for the burnt offering in Judges 6?
The LORD told Gideon to take his father’s second bull, seven years old, and offer it as a burnt offering (6:25–26).
Judges 6:25-26
A firstborn lamb
A lamb is not mentioned here; the LORD specified the second bull (6:25–26).
Two doves
Two doves were an offering for the poor (Leviticus 5:7); Gideon was told to use a bull (6:26).
A heifer without blemish
A red heifer was for purification (Numbers 19:2); Gideon was told to use the second bull (6:26).
The second bull, seven years old
A ram caught in a thicket
A ram caught in a thicket was Abraham’s offering (Genesis 22:13); Gideon’s was a bull (6:26).
In Judges 6, what wood was Gideon told to use for that burnt offering after destroying the pagan shrine?
The LORD said to offer the second bull as a burnt offering using the wood of the Asherah pole Gideon cut down (6:26).
Judges 6:26
Cedar beams from the house
The wood was not from a house; it came from the Asherah pole (6:26).
Olive wood from the grove
Olive wood is used elsewhere for the temple cherubim (1 Kings 6:23); here the fuel was the Asherah pole (6:26).
Wood from the city gate
No city gate wood is mentioned; the fuel was the Asherah pole (6:26).
Wood of the Asherah pole he cut down
Acacia wood from the tabernacle
Acacia wood was used for the tabernacle’s ark (Exodus 25:10); Gideon used the Asherah pole’s wood (6:26).
How did Gideon carry out this act against Baal’s altar in Judges 6?
Gideon took ten of his servants and obeyed, but because he was too afraid of his father’s household and the men of the city, he did it by night (6:27).
Judges 6:27
Alone in broad daylight, since he feared no one in his father’s household or city
Gideon did not act in daylight; fear made him do it by night (6:27).
With ten servants at night because he feared his father’s household and the men of the city
With the elders of the city at noon, during a public feast in the town square
No elders helped him; he took ten of his servants and went by night (6:27).
With three hundred men at dawn, ready to fight off anyone who objected
Gideon’s three hundred men came later, against Midian (Judges 7:7), not here.
Publicly at the town square on the Sabbath, as the men of the city looked on
He acted by night, not publicly; the city found the work in the morning (6:27–28).
When the men of the city investigated the destroyed altar in Judges 6, whom did they say had done it?
After investigating thoroughly, the men of the city were told, “Gideon son of Joash did it.” (6:29)
Judges 6:29
Samson son of Manoah
Samson, son of Manoah, appears in Judges 13–16, after Gideon.
Gideon son of Joash
Jephthah the Gileadite
Jephthah the Gileadite comes later, in Judges 11:1.
Abimelech son of Jerubbaal
Abimelech was Gideon’s own son, born later (Judges 8:31), not the one who tore down the altar.
Jonathan son of Gershom
Jonathan son of Gershom was a priest for the tribe of Dan (Judges 18:30), not in this story.
How did Joash defend Gideon before the angry townsmen in Judges 6?
Joash told the crowd, “If Baal is a god, let him contend for himself with the one who has torn down his altar.” (6:31)
Judges 6:31
He denied that Gideon had been anywhere near the altar
Joash did not deny it; he challenged the crowd to let Baal contend for himself (6:31).
He blamed the Midianites for tearing down the altar
The Midianites are not blamed; Joash defended Gideon by pointing to Baal (6:31).
He said Baal was too weak to notice what happened
Joash did not say Baal was weak; he said that if Baal is a god, he can contend for himself (6:31).
He said, “If Baal is a god, let him contend for himself”
He offered silver to the crowd to rebuild Baal’s altar
No silver was offered; Joash warned that whoever pleads Baal’s case would be put to death by morning (6:31).
After Gideon tore down Baal’s altar in Judges 6, what new name was he given?
Gideon was called Jerubbaal that day, meaning “Let Baal contend with him,” because he had torn down Baal’s altar (6:32).
Judges 6:32
Israel
Jacob received the name Israel (Genesis 32:28), not Gideon.
Boanerges
Boanerges was the name Jesus gave James and John (Mark 3:17).
Jerubbaal
Ichabod
Ichabod was the name given to Phinehas’s son (1 Samuel 4:21).
Maher-shalal-hash-baz
Maher-shalal-hash-baz was the name of Isaiah’s son (Isaiah 8:3).
Later in Judges 6, where did the gathered Midianites, Amalekites, and people of the east camp?
The Midianites, Amalekites, and other people of the east crossed the Jordan and camped in the Valley of Jezreel (6:33).
Judges 6:33
Valley of Elah
The Valley of Elah is where Saul faced the Philistines (1 Samuel 17:2).
Plain of Sharon
The Plain of Sharon lay along the coast; the enemy crossed the Jordan and camped in the Valley of Jezreel (6:33).
Valley of Jezreel
Wilderness of Zin
The Wilderness of Zin lay far to the south (Numbers 20:1).
Mount Carmel
Mount Carmel is where Elijah met the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18:19).
After the Spirit of the LORD came upon Gideon in Judges 6, which tribes besides Manasseh did he summon by messengers?
Gideon sent messengers throughout Manasseh, as well as Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali (6:35).
Judges 6:34-35
Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin
Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin are not named; 6:35 lists Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali.
Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali
Ephraim, Dan, and Issachar
Ephraim was summoned later (Judges 7:24); Dan and Issachar are not named in 6:35.
Reuben, Gad, and Levi
Reuben and Gad are not named in 6:35, and Levi had no tribal inheritance (Joshua 13:33).
Judah, Ephraim, and Benjamin
Ephraim was summoned later (Judges 7:24); Judah and Benjamin are not named in 6:35.
In Gideon’s second fleece test in Judges 6, what exact overnight sign did he ask God to give?
Gideon asked that the fleece be dry and the ground covered with dew, and that night God did so (6:39–40).
Judges 6:39-40
Dew only on the fleece and dry ground
That was the first test, when only the fleece was wet (6:37–38).
Frost on the fleece and rain on the ground
Frost and rain are not mentioned; Gideon asked for a dry fleece and dew on the ground (6:39).
Fire on the fleece and darkness on the ground
Fire appears in this chapter only in the offering on the rock (6:21).
A dry fleece and dew on all the ground
A wet fleece and hail on the ground
Hail is not mentioned; the second sign was a dry fleece and a dew-covered ground (6:39–40).
In Judges 7, what other name is Gideon called when he rose early and camped beside the spring of Harod?
Judges 7:1 calls him “Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon).”
Judges 7:1
Barak
Barak was Deborah’s general (Judges 4:6), not another name for Gideon.
Jerubbaal
Abimelech
Abimelech was Gideon’s son (Judges 8:31), not his other name.
Othniel
Othniel was the first judge (Judges 3:9), a different man.
Elon
Elon was a judge from Zebulun (Judges 12:11), not Gideon.
In the Gideon narrative of Judges 7, beside what spring did Gideon and his men camp?
Judges 7:1 says Gideon and his men camped beside the spring of Harod.
Judges 7:1
Spring of Jezreel
Jezreel is the valley region, but the spring named is Harod.
Spring of En-gedi
En-gedi is on the Dead Sea, far to the south (1 Samuel 24:1).
Spring of Harod
Spring of Beersheba
Beersheba is far south in the Negev; Gideon camped by Harod.
Spring of Gihon
Gihon is a spring at Jerusalem (1 Kings 1:33), not where Gideon camped.
In Judges 7, which enemy people had a camp set against Gideon?
Judges 7:1 says “the camp of Midian was north of them in the valley.”
Judges 7:1
Midian
Philistia
The Philistines were later oppressors (Judges 13:1), not Gideon’s enemy here.
Moab
Moab oppressed Israel in Ehud’s day (Judges 3:12), not in Gideon’s.
Edom
Edom is not part of Gideon’s story; the enemy was Midian.
Ammon
Ammon oppressed Israel in Jephthah’s day (Judges 10:7–9), not Gideon’s.
In the account of Gideon in Judges 7, where was the camp of Midian located relative to Gideon’s camp?
The camp of Midian “was north of them in the valley near the hill of Moreh” (7:1).
Judges 7:1
South of him in the hill country near Hebron
The camp was to the north, not the south, and not near Hebron.
West of him along the coast near the sea
Midian was north of Gideon, in the valley, not west by the sea.
East of him in the plain near Jericho
Jericho lies in the Jordan plain; the camp was north of Gideon near the hill of Moreh.
North of him in the valley near the hill of Moreh
On the slopes of Mount Carmel above him
The Midianites were in the valley near Moreh, not on Mount Carmel.
In Judges 7, why did the LORD say Gideon had too many troops?
The LORD said, “You have too many men for Me... lest Israel glorify themselves over Me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me’” (7:2).

They had no weapons

They were too tired to fight

They were from the wrong tribe
Tribe was not the issue; the army was simply too large.
They had not crossed the Jordan
The Jordan is not mentioned here; the concern was pride.
Israel might boast that its own hand saved it
In Gideon’s preparation for battle in Judges 7, how many men turned back after the fearful were told they could leave?
“So twenty-two thousand of them turned back, but ten thousand remained” (7:3).
Judges 7:3
The number who left was 22,000, not 12,000.
Seven thousand is not the number; 22,000 turned back.
Thirty thousand is not given; 22,000 left and 10,000 stayed.
Three thousand is far too small; 22,000 went home.
In Judges 7, how many men remained with Gideon after the fearful returned home?
After 22,000 turned back, “ten thousand remained” (7:3).
Judges 7:3
Three hundred is the number after the second test (7:6), not the first.
Thirty-two thousand is the starting figure (22,000 left plus 10,000 stayed), not the number left.
Five thousand is not given; the text says ten thousand remained.
One thousand is not the number; 10,000 remained until the water test.
In the water test of Judges 7, what drinking behavior marked the men God selected?

They lay flat on the ground and drank straight from the stream

They lapped water from their hands to their mouths like a dog
