There was no fast; the test was how they drank.
They washed their hands and faces before drinking
Washing before drinking is not part of the test.
In Judges 7, how many men were chosen after the water test?
“With the three hundred men who lapped the water I will save you” (7:7).
Judges 7:6-7

Doubled silver is not mentioned; the reason was a Levite as priest (17:13).
Because a Levite had become his priest
Because he had gone up to Shiloh
Going up to Shiloh is not mentioned; the reason was a Levite as priest (17:13).
Because the tribe of Judah approved his shrine
Judah’s approval is not mentioned; the reason was a Levite as priest (17:13).
In Judges 18, which tribe of Israel was looking for a place to settle because it had not yet come into an inheritance among the tribes of Israel?
Judges 18:1 says the tribe of the Danites was looking for territory to occupy because they had not yet come into an inheritance among the tribes of Israel.
Judges 18:1
Judah
Judah had already received a large allotment in the south (Joshua 15:1), so it was not looking for land.
Benjamin
Benjamin’s lot lay just north of Judah, between Judah and Joseph (Joshua 18:11), so it already had its territory.
Dan
Simeon
Simeon’s inheritance was drawn from within Judah’s portion (Joshua 19:1), and it is not the tribe seeking land here.
Levi
Levi was given towns within the other tribes’ territory rather than a tribal allotment (Joshua 21:41), and is not the tribe on the move in this chapter.
In the account of the Danite spies in Judges 18, from which two towns were the five brave men sent out to explore the land?
Judges 18:2 says the Danites sent five men of valor from Zorah and Eshtaol to spy out the land.
Judges 18:2
Hebron and Beersheba
Hebron and Beersheba lay far to the south in Judah’s country, not among the Danite towns that sent the spies.
Zorah and Eshtaol
Ramah and Gibeah
Ramah and Gibeah were Benjamite towns north of Jerusalem (Judges 19:13), not the Danite home towns.
Bethel and Shiloh
Bethel and Shiloh were in the hill country to the north, and Shiloh is where the house of God stood (18:31), not where the spies set out.
Gaza and Ekron
Gaza and Ekron were Philistine cities, not Danite towns.
When the five Danite scouts entered the hill country of Ephraim in Judges 18, at whose house did they spend the night?
Judges 18:2 says the five men entered the hill country of Ephraim and came to the house of Micah, where they spent the night.
Judges 18:2
Eli’s house
Eli served as priest at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:9) and is not mentioned in this story.
Manoah’s house
Manoah of Zorah was Samson’s father (Judges 13:2), but the spies stayed with Micah.
Micah’s house
Jesse’s house
Jesse was David’s father in Bethlehem (1 Samuel 16:1), in a much later period than this account.
Abinadab’s house
Abinadab of Kiriath-jearim later housed the ark (1 Samuel 7:1); he does not appear in this chapter.
Near Micah’s house in Judges 18, whose voice did the Danite spies recognize?
Judges 18:3 says that near Micah’s house the spies recognized the voice of the young Levite and asked him why he was there.
Judges 18:3
Micah’s mother
Micah’s mother appears earlier, giving silver for the idol (Judges 17:2–4), but the voice the spies knew was the Levite’s.
A young Levite
Gideon
Gideon’s story is told earlier, in Judges 6–8, and he does not appear in this scene.
Samson
Samson was a Danite from Zorah (Judges 13:2), but his exploits are in Judges 13–16, not this scene.
Samuel
Samuel belongs to the later period of 1 Samuel and is not part of this account.
In the story of Micah and the Danites in Judges 18, what did the five spies ask the Levite priest to do for them?
In Judges 18:5 the spies said to the priest, “Please inquire of God to determine whether we will have a successful journey.”
Judges 18:5
Bless their swords before the fighting begins
The spies never asked for weapons to be blessed; they asked for God’s guidance about their journey (18:5).
Inquire of God whether their mission would succeed
Interpret a strange dream they had on the road
No dream appears in this scene; the request was to inquire of God about the success of their trip (18:5).
Call an assembly of the tribes at Shiloh
No assembly at Shiloh was requested; Shiloh is mentioned only at the end of the chapter (18:31).
Anoint a king to lead their expedition
Anointing a king is never mentioned here; the chapter opens by noting there was no king in Israel (18:1).
What answer did the priest give the Danite spies about their journey in Judges 18:6?
In Judges 18:6 the priest told them, “Go in peace. The LORD is watching over your journey.”
Judges 18:6
“Turn back at once, for the road is not safe”
The priest told them to go in peace, not to turn back (18:6).
“Wait seven days for a clear word from God”
No waiting period was set; the priest sent them on their way at once (18:6).
“Go in peace. The LORD is watching over your journey.”
“Carry the ark of God before you in battle”
The ark is not mentioned in this story; the priest simply assured them of the LORD’s watchful care (18:6).
“Offer a sacrifice at the altar before you go”
No sacrifice was required; the priest’s answer was an immediate blessing on their journey (18:6).
When the five men reached Laish in Judges 18, how were the people living there described?
Judges 18:7 says the five men saw that the people of Laish were living securely, like the Sidonians, quiet and unsuspecting.
Judges 18:7
Warlike and heavily fortified, guarded day and night by a large army
Laish was the opposite of fortified and warlike: its people were quiet and unsuspecting (18:7).
Quiet and unsuspecting, living securely after the manner of the Sidonians
Starving under a long Philistine siege that had cut off all supplies
No Philistine siege is mentioned; Laish was at peace and lacking nothing (18:7).
Hiding in caves and mountain strongholds from raiding Midianites
Hiding from Midian describes Israel’s plight earlier in Judges (Judges 6:2), not the people of Laish.
Serving under an Egyptian governor who collected heavy tribute
Laish had no oppressive ruler at all (18:7), and no Egyptian governor is mentioned.
After returning from Laish in Judges 18, how did the spies describe the land to their fellow Danites?
Judges 18:9–10 records the spies saying they had seen the land, “it is very good,” and that God had delivered it into their hand.
Judges 18:9-10
Barren and dangerous
The spies called the land very good, with nothing on earth lacking (18:9–10), not barren.
Very good and spacious, with God giving it into their hands
Already occupied by Judah
The land belonged to an unsuspecting people far from help, not to Judah (18:7, 18:10).
Full of giants and impossible to take
Giants figure in the earlier spy report at Kadesh (Numbers 13:33), but these spies said God had delivered the land into their hand.
Cursed because of idolatry
The spies said nothing about a curse; they urged the Danites to take possession without hesitating (18:9).
In Judges 18, how many Danite men armed with weapons of war set out from Zorah and Eshtaol?
Judges 18:11 says six hundred Danites departed from Zorah and Eshtaol, armed with weapons of war.
Judges 18:11
Three hundred is Gideon’s famous band (Judges 7:7), not the Danite force here.
Four hundred recalls the men who gathered to David (1 Samuel 22:2); the Danites numbered six hundred (18:11).
Five was the number of spies (18:2); the armed force that followed numbered six hundred (18:11).
A thousand recalls Samson’s victory with the jawbone (Judges 15:15); this force numbered six hundred (18:11).
As the Danites traveled in Judges 18, what name was given to the camp west of Kiriath-jearim?
Judges 18:12 says the Danites camped at Kiriath-jearim in Judah, which is why the place west of it is called Mahaneh-dan to this day.
Judges 18:12
Gilgal
Gilgal was Israel’s first camp west of the Jordan (Joshua 4:19), not the Danite camp.
Mahaneh-dan
Mizpah
Mizpah was a gathering place for Israel (Judges 20:1), not the name of this camp.
Ebenezer
Ebenezer was where Israel camped before a defeat by the Philistines (1 Samuel 4:1).
Ramath-lehi
Ramath-lehi is where Samson threw away the jawbone (Judges 15:17), not this camp.
In Judges 18, which set of objects did the five spies report was in one of the houses near Micah?
In Judges 18:14 the five spies said that one of the houses had an ephod, household gods, a graven image, and a molten idol.
Judges 18:14
The ark of the covenant, the stone tablets, and a jar of manna
The ark and the tablets were not in Micah’s neighborhood; the objects named were Micah’s idolatrous items (18:14).
An ephod, household idols, a carved image, and a molten image
A bronze altar, a washing basin, and a golden lampstand
A bronze altar and basin belonged to the tabernacle, not to the list the spies gave (18:14).
A royal crown, a gold scepter, and a scroll of the law
No crown, scepter, or scroll is mentioned; the list was of ephod, household gods, and images (18:14).
Silver trumpets, oil lamps, and the bread of the Presence
Trumpets, lamps, and showbread are not named; the spies listed Micah’s ephod and idols (18:14).
During the seizure at Micah’s house in Judges 18, where did the 600 armed Danites stand while the five spies went in?
Judges 18:16–17 says the six hundred armed Danites stood at the entrance of the gate while the five spies went inside to take the idols.
Judges 18:16-17
At the altar
No altar is mentioned in the scene; the six hundred stood at the gate (18:16).
On the roof
No one is said to stand on a roof; the armed men and the priest were at the gate’s entrance (18:17).
At the entrance of the gate
In the inner room
The five spies went inside the house; the six hundred stayed outside at the gate (18:17).
Outside the city wall
The scene is at Micah’s house, not at a city wall; the Danites stood at the gate entrance (18:16).
What did the Danites say to persuade the young Levite to leave Micah and join them in Judges 18:19?

Judges 18:19
“Stay here, and we will send silver later”
No promise of later payment is made; they offered him a larger priesthood over a tribe (18:19).
“Be our captain in battle”
They asked him to be a father and priest, not a battle captain (18:19).
“be a father and a priest to us”
“Take us to Shiloh and inquire there”
The inquiry of God happened earlier (18:5); the persuasion here was the offer of a tribal priesthood (18:19).
“Teach us the Law of Moses first”
The Law of Moses is not mentioned in their appeal; they argued that a tribe was a better charge than one house (18:19).
When the priest was glad and went with the Danites in Judges 18:20, which items did he take?
Judges 18:20 says the priest was glad and took the ephod, the household idols, and the graven image, and went with the people.
Judges 18:20
The ephod, household idols, and carved image
The molten image, silver, and robe
Verse 20 lists the ephod, household idols, and graven image; no silver or robe is named.
The ark, lampstand, and table
The ark, lampstand, and table belong to the tabernacle, not to Micah’s collection (18:20).
Only a priestly garment
He took the ephod, the household idols, and the graven image (18:20), not just a garment.
A sword, trumpet, and staff
No sword, trumpet, or staff is mentioned in what he carried (18:20).
As the Danites departed from Micah’s area in Judges 18, what did they place in front of them?
Judges 18:21 says that putting their small children, their livestock, and their possessions in front of them, the Danites turned and departed.
Judges 18:21
The ark of God, carried by priests and singers
The ark is not mentioned in this story; the Danites put their families and goods in front (18:21).
Chariots, horsemen, and the strongest warriors
No chariots or horsemen are mentioned; it was children, livestock, and possessions that went in front (18:21).
The little ones, livestock, and possessions
Only the priest, the idols, and the ephod
The priest and idols had already gone with them (18:20); verse 21 describes the children and goods placed ahead.
Prisoners captured from Micah’s household
No prisoners are mentioned in the departure (18:21).
When Micah caught up with the Danites in Judges 18:24, what was his main complaint?
In Judges 18:24 Micah cried, “You took the gods I had made, and my priest, and went away. What else do I have?”
Judges 18:24
“You stole my harvest and burned my fields”
Micah never mentions a harvest or burned fields; his complaint was about his gods and priest (18:24).
“You took the gods I had made, and my priest, and went away”
“You broke my covenant and killed my servants”
No covenant or servants are mentioned; the complaint was the taking of his gods and priest (18:24).
“You seized my land in Ephraim”
Micah did not complain about land; he lost his idols and priest (18:24).
“You refused me justice at Shiloh”
Shiloh is mentioned only at the chapter’s end (18:31); Micah’s complaint was about his stolen gods and priest.
What warning did the Danites give Micah in Judges 18:25 that caused him to turn back?
Judges 18:25 has the Danites say, “Do not raise your voice against us, or angry men will attack you,” and Micah turned back because they were too strong for him (18:26).

“The Philistines are coming up behind us, so go home now”
The Philistines are not mentioned in this scene; the Danites simply threatened Micah with angry men (18:25).
“The priest will curse your household and your descendants”
The priest uttered no curse; the Danites warned of an attack by angry men (18:25).
“Do not raise your voice against us, or angry men will attack you”
“We will bring you before the elders at Shiloh for judgment”
They made no threat of the elders; they warned him he and his family would lose their lives (18:25).
“The king will hear of this and punish your whole house”
There was no king in Israel at that time (18:1), so no king could hear of it.
After taking Micah’s idols and priest in Judges 18, what did the Danites do to the people of Laish and their city?
Judges 18:27 says the Danites struck the quiet, unsuspecting people of Laish with their swords and burned down the city.
Judges 18:27-28
They made peace with the people and demanded yearly tribute
The Danites made no treaty; they struck the people with the sword (18:27).
They struck the people with the sword and burned down the city
They left the city alone after camping outside its walls
They did not leave Laish; they attacked it and burned it (18:27).
They carried the people off to live in the hill country of Ephraim
The people of Laish were not deported to Ephraim; they were struck down and the city burned (18:27).
They built an altar and sealed a treaty with the city
Laish had no alliance with anyone (18:28), and no treaty altar was built.
Once the Danites rebuilt the captured city in Judges 18, what new name did they give it, and why?
Judges 18:29 says they named the city Dan after their forefather Dan, who was born to Israel, though it was formerly named Laish.
Judges 18:29
Bethel, after Jacob’s vision
Bethel was named by Jacob after his vision (Genesis 28:19), not by the Danites.
Dan, after their forefather Dan
Hebron, after Caleb
Hebron was Caleb’s city in Judah (Joshua 14:13), not the Danite conquest.
Naphtali, after Barak
Barak came from Naphtali (Judges 4:6), but the Danites named the city for their own forefather Dan (18:29).
Jerusalem, after Melchizedek
Melchizedek was king of Salem (Genesis 14:18); the Danites did not rename Laish Jerusalem.
According to the closing line of Judges 18, how long did the Danites keep Micah’s carved image set up?
Judges 18:31 says Micah’s graven image was set up and remained there the whole time the house of God was in Shiloh.
Judges 18:31
Only during Micah’s lifetime
The verse ties the image to the time of the house of God at Shiloh, not to Micah’s lifetime (18:31).
Until Samuel became judge
Samuel is not mentioned in the verse; the image stood as long as the house of God was in Shiloh (18:31).
For the whole time the house of God was in Shiloh
Until David brought the ark to Jerusalem
David brought the ark to Jerusalem long after (2 Samuel 6:12); the verse gives the Shiloh period.
Until Solomon built the temple
Solomon built the temple generations later (1 Kings 6:1); the verse speaks of Shiloh.
In Judges 19, what condition in Israel is stated at the beginning of the account of the Levite and his concubine?
Judges 19:1 opens, “in those days, when there was no king in Israel.”
Judges 19:1
Israel had no temple
The verse names the lack of a king, not a temple; Israel’s worship was centered on the Tent of Meeting at Shiloh (Joshua 18:1).
Israel had no king
Israel had no prophet
The verse says nothing about prophets; the problem it names is the absence of a king.
Israel had no judge
Judges 19:1 names no missing judge; the stated lack is a king.
Israel had no priest
The verse names no lack of priests; the Levite himself is traveling toward the house of the LORD (19:18).
In the Judges 19 account, where was the Levite living when he took a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah?
The Levite lived “in the remote hill country of Ephraim” (19:1).
Judges 19:1
The plains of Moab
The plains of Moab lay east of the Jordan (Numbers 22:1), not where the Levite lived.
The hill country of Judah
Bethlehem in Judah was his concubine’s home, not his own (19:1–2).
The remote hill country of Ephraim
The Valley of Jezreel
The Valley of Jezreel is not mentioned; his home was in Ephraim (19:1).
The wilderness of Paran
The wilderness of Paran lies far to the south (Genesis 21:21) and is not part of this story.
In the story of Judges 19, from what town did the Levite take his concubine?
The Levite took a concubine “from Bethlehem in Judah” (19:1).
Judges 19:1
Shiloh
Shiloh is not mentioned in Judges 19; she was from Bethlehem.
Hebron
Hebron, another town in Judah, is not named; her home was Bethlehem (19:2).
Bethlehem in Judah
Jericho
Jericho does not appear in this story; she came from Bethlehem (19:1).
Beersheba
Beersheba lies far south in Simeon’s land (Joshua 19:2); she came from Bethlehem.
After leaving the Levite in Judges 19, where did the concubine go?
She left him “to return to her father’s house in Bethlehem in Judah” (19:2).
Judges 19:2
To her father’s house in Bethlehem in Judah
To Shiloh to serve at the tabernacle
Nothing says she served at the tabernacle; she went home to her father (19:2).
To Jerusalem in Jebus
Jebus (Jerusalem) is where the Levite later refused to stay (19:10–12), not where she went.
To Ramah in Benjamin
Ramah was a town the Levite later considered for a night’s stay (19:13).
To Hebron with relatives
She went to her father in Bethlehem, not to relatives in Hebron (19:2).
Before the Levite went after his concubine in Judges 19, how long had she remained at her father’s house in Bethlehem in Judah?
She had been at her father’s house in Bethlehem for “four months” before her husband went after her (19:2).
Judges 19:2
Four days
The text says four months, not four days (19:2).
Four weeks
The text says four months, not four weeks (19:2).
Four months
One year
Judges 19:2 gives four months, not a full year.
Three years
Judges 19:2 gives four months, not three years.
When the Levite traveled to Bethlehem in Judah in Judges 19, what was his purpose?
He went “to speak kindly to her and bring her back” (19:3).

To demand payment from her father
He went to win her back, not to demand payment from her father (19:3).
To speak kindly to her and bring her back
To move permanently to Bethlehem
He intended to bring her home to Ephraim (19:3, 9), not to move to Bethlehem.
To summon the elders for judgment
The tribes are summoned only after her death (19:29), not at the start of his trip.
To enlist men for war
He took only a servant and a pair of donkeys (19:3), not a force of soldiers.
In Judges 19, who accompanied the Levite when he went to his concubine’s father’s house?
He took “his servant and a pair of donkeys” (19:3).
Judges 19:3
His two sons and an ox cart
He took a servant and a pair of donkeys, not sons or an ox cart (19:3).
His servant and a pair of donkeys
A priest and a lamb
No priest or lamb accompanied him (19:3); that would suit a sacrifice, not this errand.
His brother and three camels
Only a servant and donkeys are mentioned (19:3), not a brother or camels.
A troop of Benjamites
Benjamites were the men of Gibeah, whom he met later (19:16), not his companions.
When the concubine’s father saw the Levite in Bethlehem in Judah in Judges 19, how did he respond?
When her father saw him, “he gladly welcomed him” (19:3).
Judges 19:3
He feared him
The father welcomed him gladly (19:3), not with fear.
He accused him
The father welcomed him; he did not accuse him (19:3).
He rejoiced to meet him
He ignored him
The father did not ignore him; he persuaded him to stay (19:3–4).
He sent him away
He did not send him away; he urged him to stay several days (19:4–9).
After arriving at his concubine’s father’s house in Judges 19, how many days did the Levite stay eating, drinking, and lodging there before rising early on the fourth day?

Judges 19:4-5
One day
He stayed three days before the fourth-day attempt to leave (19:4–5), not one.
Two days
He stayed three days before the fourth-day attempt to leave (19:4–5), not two.
Three days
Five days
The fifth day comes later, when he tried to leave again (19:8).
Seven days
He stayed three days at first (19:4); the visit never reached seven days.
On the return journey in Judges 19, which city did the servant suggest for lodging, but the Levite refused because it was a city of foreigners?
The servant said, “let us stop at this Jebusite city,” but the master replied, “We will not turn aside to the city of foreigners” (19:11–12).
Judges 19:11-12
Bethel
Bethel was never proposed; the Levite named Gibeah and Ramah instead (19:12–13).
Jebus, that is Jerusalem
Jericho
Jericho lay far to the east in the Jordan valley and is not named on this journey (19:11–14).
Shechem
Shechem lay to the north in Ephraim and is not named on this trip (19:11–14).
Hebron
Hebron lay south of Jebus and is not named here (19:11–14).
As evening fell in Judges 19, to which town did the travelers actually turn aside to spend the night?

Judges 19:14-15
Mizpah
Mizpah is not mentioned in the chapter; they stayed at Gibeah (19:14–15).
Ramah
Ramah was the second option the Levite named, but they stopped at Gibeah (19:13–15).
Gibeah
Shiloh
Shiloh is not part of this journey (19:10–15).
Bethlehem
Bethlehem was the place they left (19:10).

Judges 19:14, 16
Judah
Bethlehem in Judah was where they started (19:1), but Gibeah lay in Benjamin (19:14).
Ephraim
The Levite and the old man came from Ephraim’s hill country (19:1, 16), but Gibeah lay in Benjamin.
Levi
Levi had no tribal territory (Joshua 13:14); the Levite was a visitor in Gibeah.
Benjamin
Issachar
Issachar’s land lay in the north (Joshua 19:17–23), not at Gibeah.
Before anyone offered hospitality in Gibeah in Judges 19, where did the Levite and his party remain?
The Levite “sat down in the city square, but no one would take them into his home” (19:15).
Judges 19:15
At the city gate
The text places him in the city square, not at a gate (19:15).
In the open square of the city
In the tabernacle court
The tabernacle was at Shiloh, not Gibeah (Joshua 18:1).
By the threshing floor
No threshing floor is mentioned; he sat in the city square (19:15).
In a cave outside the wall
He sat in the city square (19:15), not in a cave outside the town.
Who finally invited the travelers into his house in the Gibeah account of Judges 19?

Judges 19:16-21
A young Benjamite soldier who lived beside the city wall

An old man from the hill country of Ephraim who was staying in Gibeah
The chief elder of Gibeah, a Benjamite who ruled the city
The chapter names no chief elder of Gibeah; the host was an old man from Ephraim (19:16).
A priest from Shiloh who was staying in Gibeah that week
No priest from Shiloh appears; the host was an old man from Ephraim (19:16).
A merchant from Tyre who was lodging in Gibeah that night
No merchant appears; the host was an old man coming in from his field (19:16).
After hearing the travelers’ situation in Judges 19, what did the old man in Gibeah promise to do?

Send them to Ramah
Ramah was the Levite’s own alternative (19:13); the old man offered his house instead (19:21).
Report them to the elders

Supply everything they needed
Keep only the servant

Make them sleep in the stable
He fed the donkeys and gave them a meal (19:21) rather than putting them in a stable.
When speaking to the old man in Judges 19, which provisions did the Levite say he already had?

Judges 19:19
Oil and flour for a grain offering, and incense for the altar
He mentioned straw, feed, bread, and wine (19:19), not oil, flour, or incense.
Straw and fodder for the donkeys, and bread and wine for the travelers
Fish and dates for supper, and fresh water for the donkeys
He listed straw, feed, bread, and wine (19:19); no tents or water skins are mentioned.
Tents and water skins for camping, and wool for bedding
He said they lacked nothing, naming straw, feed, bread, and wine (19:19), not silver or garments.
Silver and garments to pay for lodging, and a lamb for supper
Fish and dates are not mentioned; the Levite named straw, feed, bread, and wine (19:19).
In the night scene at Gibeah in Judges 19, what did the wicked men of the city demand from the old man?

That he hand over his livestock and his donkeys to feed the crowd
The mob wanted the guest himself (19:22), not the old man’s livestock.
That he bring out the man who had entered his house so they could know him

That he send the Levite’s servant out to fight the men in the street

In response to the mob in Judges 19, whom did the old man offer instead?

Judges 19:23-24
His wife and his son
He offered his own virgin daughter and the Levite’s concubine, not his wife or a son (19:24).
Two servant girls
He offered his virgin daughter and the concubine, not two servant girls (19:24).
His virgin daughter and the Levite’s concubine

The elders planned to say that the fathers had not actually given their daughters, so they had no guilt, and that wives had not been secured for each man in the war (21:22).
Judges 21:22
The daughters had volunteered to go with the Benjamites, so no one could object
21:22 gives no such claim; the elders did not say the daughters had volunteered.
Benjamin had paid a full bride-price to every family before the feast
No bride-price is mentioned; the Benjamites seized the women (21:21).
The fathers had not directly given their daughters, and not enough wives had been secured in battle
The high priest had publicly annulled the oath sworn earlier at Mizpah
The oath was never annulled by the high priest; the elders worked around it (21:22).
The law of the feast required each family to provide a bride that year
No law of the feast required a bride; the elders’ argument was that the fathers had not actually given their daughters (21:22).
What closing statement sums up the spiritual and political condition of Israel at the end of Judges 21?
Judges ends: “In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (21:25).
Judges 21:25
“So the land had rest for forty years, until Othniel son of Kenaz died.”
“So the land had rest for forty years, until Othniel son of Kenaz died” is Judges 3:11, from early in the book, not its closing line.
“And Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as his father David had done.”
“And Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as his father David had done” is 1 Kings 15:11, from a king’s reign long after Judges.
“So Moab was subdued under the hand of Israel that day, and the land had rest for eighty years.”
“So Moab was subdued under the hand of Israel that day, and the land had rest for eighty years” is Judges 3:30, an early victory, not the closing line.
“So they set up for themselves Micah’s graven image, and it was there the whole time the house of God was in Shiloh.”
“So they set up for themselves Micah’s graven image, and it was there the whole time the house of God was in Shiloh” is Judges 18:31, not the final verse.
“In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes.”
8: In the opening of Ruth 1, during what period did the story take place?
Ruth opens, “In the days when the judges ruled, there was a famine in the land” (1:1).
Ruth 1:1
In the days when the kings ruled
The judges’ era was a time when “there was no king in Israel” (Judges 21:25).
In the days when the judges ruled
During the Babylonian exile
The Babylonian exile came centuries later (2 Kings 25:11).
In the days of Samuel alone
Samuel judged Israel later (1 Samuel 7:15); Ruth was the great-grandmother of David, whom Samuel anointed (Ruth 4:17).
After the temple was rebuilt
The temple was rebuilt after the exile (Ezra 6:15), long after Ruth.
In Ruth chapter 1, what crisis in the land caused a family from Bethlehem to leave?
“There was a famine in the land” (1:1), so Elimelech took his family to Moab.
Ruth 1:1
A plague
Plagues struck Egypt in Moses’ day (Exodus 9:3); Ruth 1:1 names a famine.
A war
No war is mentioned in Ruth 1; the family left because of famine (1:1).
A famine
A flood
The great flood is Noah’s story (Genesis 7); Ruth 1:1 names a famine.
An invasion of locusts
A locust invasion is described in Joel 1:4; Ruth 1:1 names a famine.
According to Ruth 1, from which town and region did Naomi’s family come?
“A certain man from Bethlehem in Judah” went to Moab with his family (1:1).
Ruth 1:1
Hebron in Judah
Hebron, formerly Kiriath-arba, was where Sarah died (Genesis 23:2); Naomi’s family was from Bethlehem.
Bethlehem in Judah
Jericho in Benjamin
Jericho was the City of Palms (Deuteronomy 34:3); the family came from Bethlehem in Judah.
Shiloh in Ephraim
Shiloh was where the Tent of Meeting stood (Joshua 18:1), not Naomi’s home.
Beersheba in the Negev
Beersheba is not mentioned in Ruth; the family was from Bethlehem in Judah (1:1).
In the first verse of Ruth, to which land did Elimelech move his family to reside for a time?
The family “went to reside in the land of Moab” (1:1).
Ruth 1:1
Edom
Edom was where Esau settled, at Mount Seir (Genesis 36:8).
Ammon
Ammon is not mentioned in Ruth; the family went to Moab (1:1).
Midian
Midian was where Moses fled from Pharaoh (Exodus 2:15).
Moab
Philistia
Isaac went to the Philistines at Gerar in a famine (Genesis 26:1); Elimelech went to Moab.
In Ruth 1, what was the name of Naomi’s husband who moved with the family from Bethlehem?
“The man’s name was Elimelech, his wife’s name was Naomi” (1:2).
Ruth 1:2
Boaz
Boaz was a relative from Elimelech’s clan who appears in chapter 2 (Ruth 2:1).
Elimelech
Mahlon
Mahlon was one of Naomi’s sons (1:2).
Obed
Obed was the son later born to Ruth and Boaz (Ruth 4:17).
Jesse
Jesse was Obed’s son and David’s father (Ruth 4:17).
In Ruth chapter 1, what were the names of Naomi’s two sons?
“The names of his two sons were Mahlon and Chilion” (1:2).
Ruth 1:2
Perez and Zerah
Perez and Zerah were the twin sons of Judah and Tamar (Genesis 38:29–30).
Nadab and Abihu
Nadab and Abihu were sons of Aaron (Exodus 6:23).
Mahlon and Chilion
Hophni and Phinehas
Hophni and Phinehas were Eli’s sons (1 Samuel 1:3).
Gershom and Eliezer
Gershom and Eliezer were the sons of Moses (Exodus 18:3–4).
In Ruth 1:2, how is Elimelech’s family further described besides being from Bethlehem in Judah?
“They were Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah” (1:2); Ephrath is an old name for Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19).
Ruth 1:2
Levites from Shiloh
No Levites from Shiloh are mentioned; the family were Ephrathites (1:2).
Ephrathites
Benjamites from Gibeah
Gibeah was a town in Benjamin (Judges 19:14); this family was from Bethlehem in Judah.
Kenites from Midian
Kenites settled with Judah near Arad (Judges 1:16); Elimelech’s family were Ephrathites.
Simeonites from the south
Simeon is not mentioned in Ruth; the family were Ephrathites from Bethlehem (1:2).
In the early events of Ruth 1, what happened to Elimelech after the family arrived in Moab?
“Then Naomi’s husband Elimelech died, and she was left with her two sons” (1:3).
Ruth 1:3
He returned to Judah
Elimelech never returned; only Naomi came back with Ruth (1:22).
He became a judge
Elimelech is never called a judge; he died in Moab (1:3).
He bought land
He bought no land in Moab; his field in Israel was later sold by Naomi (Ruth 4:3).
He died
He remarried
He did not remarry; he died and left Naomi a widow (1:3).
In Ruth 1, what kind of women did Mahlon and Chilion take as wives while living in Moab?
Naomi’s sons “took Moabite women as their wives” (1:4).
Ruth 1:4
Israelite women
They were living in Moab and married Moabite women (1:4).
Egyptian women
Joseph, not Naomi’s sons, married an Egyptian, Asenath (Genesis 41:45).
Philistine women
Samson sought a Philistine wife from Timnah (Judges 14:2).
Moabite women
Edomite women
No Edomites appear in Ruth; the wives were Moabite women (1:4).
In Ruth chapter 1, what were the names of Naomi’s two daughters-in-law?
The Moabite wives were named “Orpah and the other named Ruth” (1:4).
Ruth 1:4
Ruth and Esther
Esther lived in Persia centuries later (Esther 2:7).
Orpah and Ruth
Tamar and Rahab
Tamar (Genesis 38:6) and Rahab (Joshua 2:1) are other women in David’s line, not Naomi’s daughters-in-law.
Leah and Rachel
Leah and Rachel were Laban’s daughters, Jacob’s wives (Genesis 29:16).
Deborah and Jael
Deborah was a prophetess (Judges 4:4), and Jael killed Sisera (Judges 4:21).
After Naomi’s sons married in Moab, about how long did they live there, according to Ruth 1?
“After they had lived in Moab about ten years,” both sons died (1:4–5).
Ruth 1:4
About one year
The text says about ten years, not one (1:4).
About three years
The text says about ten years, not three (1:4).
About seven years
The text says about ten years, not seven (1:4).
About ten years
About forty years
Forty years was Israel’s wilderness wandering; Ruth 1:4 says about ten years.
In Ruth 1, what happened to Naomi’s sons, Mahlon and Chilion?
“Both Mahlon and Chilion also died” (1:5).
Ruth 1:5
They returned to Bethlehem
They never returned; only Naomi and Ruth came back to Bethlehem (1:19).
They became shepherds
Nothing is said of their work; the text records that both died (1:5).
They both died
They separated from Naomi
They did not separate from Naomi; they died in Moab (1:5).
They had many children
They left no children; Ruth’s son Obed was later born to Boaz (Ruth 4:13).
After the deaths in Ruth 1, what does the chapter say Naomi was left without?
“Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband” (1:5).
Ruth 1:5
Her land and her house
Elimelech’s land still existed, and Naomi later sold it (Ruth 4:3).
Her two children and her husband
Her health and her sight
Nothing is said about Naomi’s health or sight; she lost her sons and husband (1:5).
Her parents and her brothers
Her parents and brothers are never mentioned in Ruth.
Her servants and her flocks
No servants or flocks are mentioned; Naomi said she came back empty (1:21).
In Ruth 1, why did Naomi decide to return from Moab to Judah?
“When Naomi heard in Moab that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food,” she prepared to leave (1:6).
Ruth 1:6
She saw a vision of the LORD during the night in Moab
No vision is mentioned; Naomi acted on what she “heard in Moab” (1:6).
She learned she had inherited a large house in Bethlehem
Elimelech’s land remained, and Naomi later sold it (Ruth 4:3), but she returned because of news of food (1:6).
She heard the LORD had attended to His people with food
She was summoned home by one of the judges of Israel
No judge summoned her; she heard that the LORD had provided food (1:6).
She was forced out of Moab by a war against Israel
Eglon of Moab had once oppressed Israel (Judges 3:12), but Ruth 1 mentions no war.
When Naomi left the place where she had been living in Ruth 1, who went with her at first?
“Accompanied by her two daughters-in-law,” Naomi set out for Judah (1:7).
Ruth 1:7
Boaz and his servants
Boaz first appears in Bethlehem in chapter 2 (Ruth 2:1).
Her two daughters-in-law
The elders of Moab
No Moabite elders are mentioned; her daughters-in-law went with her (1:7).
Her brothers and sisters
Naomi’s brothers and sisters are never mentioned in Ruth.
No one at all
She did not leave alone; her two daughters-in-law went with her (1:7).
In Naomi’s roadside speech in Ruth 1, where did she tell each daughter-in-law to return?
Naomi said, “Go back, each of you to your mother’s home” (1:8).
Ruth 1:8
To her father’s field
Naomi said “your mother’s home,” not a father’s field (1:8).
To her husband’s grave
No grave is mentioned; Naomi sent them to their mothers’ homes (1:8).
To her mother’s home
To Bethlehem’s gate
Bethlehem’s gate is where Boaz later settled the redemption (Ruth 4:1).
To the tabernacle at Shiloh
Shiloh was where the Tent of Meeting stood (Joshua 18:1), not where Naomi sent them.
In Ruth 1, what did Naomi ask the LORD to show Orpah and Ruth as they parted?
Naomi prayed, “May the LORD show you loving devotion, as you have shown to your dead and to me” (1:8).
Ruth 1:8
Great wealth
Naomi asked for loving devotion, not wealth (1:8).
Long life
Long life is not mentioned; Naomi prayed for loving devotion and rest in a new home (1:8–9).
Victory in battle
Battle has no place in Naomi’s prayer; she asked for loving devotion (1:8).
Loving devotion
Prophetic dreams
Dreams are not mentioned; Naomi prayed for loving devotion (1:8).
After Naomi told Orpah and Ruth to return home in Ruth 1, how did both women first respond?
Both women said, “Surely we will return with you to your people” (1:10).
Ruth 1:10
“We will stay in Moab.”
At first both insisted on going with Naomi, not staying in Moab (1:10).
“We will seek other husbands.”
Seeking husbands was Naomi’s suggestion (1:9), not their first response.
“Surely we will return with you to your people.”
“We will send you ahead alone.”
They did not send Naomi ahead; both said they would go with her (1:10).
“We will go back after harvest.”
They did not mention the harvest; they insisted on going with her (1:10).
In Ruth 1, what reason did Naomi give for why Orpah and Ruth should not continue with her?
Naomi asked, “Are there still sons in my womb to become your husbands?” (1:11).
Ruth 1:11
She had no food for them on the journey
Food for the journey is not mentioned; her argument was about future husbands (1:11).
She had no sons in her womb to become their husbands
She feared robbers on the road
Robbers are not mentioned; Naomi’s concern was that she had no sons for them (1:11).
She had vowed to travel alone
Naomi made no vow to travel alone; she argued that she had no more sons (1:11).
She was returning to another nation
Naomi was returning to her own people in Judah (1:7), not to another nation.
In Naomi’s continued argument in Ruth 1, what did she say about herself and marriage?
Naomi said, “Go on, for I am too old to have another husband” (1:12).
Ruth 1:12
She was promised to a kinsman
The kinsman-redeemer theme comes later, with Boaz (Ruth 3:9).
She was too poor to marry
Naomi spoke of her age, not poverty, as the barrier to marriage (1:12).
She was too old to have another husband
She was under a vow to remain single
There is no vow; Naomi said she was too old to have another husband (1:12).
She was returning to her father’s house
Naomi told her daughters-in-law to go to their mothers’ homes (1:8); she spoke of her own age (1:12).
In Ruth 1, if Naomi were to have a husband that very night and bear sons, what did she ask Orpah and Ruth?
Naomi asked, “would you wait for them to grow up?” (1:13).
Would you name them after the dead?
Naming children after the dead is not in Naomi’s question; she asked if they would wait for them to grow up (1:13).
Would you wait for them to grow up?
Would you return to Moab at once?
She was already urging them to return; her question was about waiting for sons to grow up (1:13).
Would you give them your inheritance?
No inheritance is mentioned; she asked whether they would wait (1:13).
Would you leave Bethlehem forever?
They had not yet reached Bethlehem; she asked if they would wait for sons to grow up (1:13).
In Ruth 1, what strong statement did Naomi make about her suffering and the LORD?
Naomi said, “it is much more bitter for me than for you, because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me” (1:13).
Ruth 1:13
“The LORD has hidden His face from me.”
“How long will You hide Your face from me?” is David’s lament in Psalm 13:1, not Naomi’s words.
“The hand of the LORD has gone out against me.”
“The LORD has forgotten His covenant.”
Naomi never says the LORD forgot His covenant; she speaks of His hand against her (1:13).
“The angel of the LORD blocked my way.”
The angel of the LORD stood in the road to oppose Balaam (Numbers 22:22).
“The LORD has cast me from Judah.”
Naomi was returning to Judah; she said the LORD’s hand had gone out against her (1:13).
After more weeping in Ruth 1, which daughter-in-law kissed Naomi goodbye?
“Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her” (1:14).
Ruth 1:14
Ruth
Ruth did not say goodbye; she clung to Naomi (1:14).
Tamar
Tamar was Judah’s daughter-in-law (Genesis 38:6), not Naomi’s.
Orpah
Rachel
Rachel was Jacob’s wife (Genesis 29:16), invoked later in the elders’ blessing (Ruth 4:11).
Abigail
Abigail was Nabal’s wife and later David’s (1 Samuel 25:3).
In contrast to Orpah in Ruth 1, what did Ruth do after the farewell scene?
“Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her” (1:14).
Ruth 1:14
She returned to Moab’s king
No king of Moab appears in Ruth; Ruth stayed with Naomi (1:14).
She clung to Naomi
She went ahead to Bethlehem alone
Ruth traveled together with Naomi to Bethlehem (1:19), not ahead alone.
She asked for silver and bread
Ruth asked for nothing; she clung to Naomi (1:14).
She stayed by her husband’s grave
Ruth left Moab with Naomi (1:22) rather than stay by any grave.
When Naomi tried again to persuade Ruth in Ruth 1, what did Naomi say Orpah had gone back to?
Naomi said, “your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods” (1:15).
Ruth 1:15
Her house and her fields
Naomi spoke of Orpah’s people and gods, not her house and fields (1:15).
Her people and her gods
Her husband’s brothers and her city
Naomi said Orpah went back “to her people and her gods” (1:15).
Her flocks and her family tomb
No flocks or tombs are mentioned; Orpah returned to her people and gods (1:15).
Her vows and her altars in Judah
Orpah went back to Moab, not to altars in Judah (1:15).
In Ruth 1, how did Ruth begin her famous reply to Naomi’s urging?
Ruth began, “Do not urge me to leave you or to turn from following you” (1:16).
Ruth 1:16
“Do not fear for me in Bethlehem.”
Ruth did not speak about fear; she refused to leave Naomi (1:16).
“Do not urge me to leave you or to turn from following you.”
“Do not send me empty to my mother’s house.”
“Do not go back to your mother-in-law empty-handed” is Boaz’s word to Ruth later (Ruth 3:17).
“Do not test me, for I have chosen Judah.”
Ruth did not speak of testing; her reply begins with a refusal to leave Naomi (1:16).
“Do not speak again of Moab to me.”
Ruth did not forbid talk of Moab; she refused to leave Naomi (1:16).
In Ruth’s pledge in chapter 1 of the Book of Ruth, which promise about journey and dwelling did she make to Naomi?
Ruth said, “wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live” (1:16).
Ruth 1:16
“Wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live.”
“Wherever you sow, I will reap, and wherever you reap, I will thresh.”
Sowing and reaping are not in Ruth’s pledge; her later gleaning is told in Ruth 2:2.
“Wherever you pray, I will offer, and wherever you sing, I will praise.”
Ruth’s pledge speaks of going and living, not praying and singing (1:16).
“Wherever you lead, I will judge, and wherever you fight, I will stand.”
Ruth does not speak of judging or fighting; she pledged to go and live where Naomi did (1:16).
“Wherever you rest, I will watch, and wherever you sleep, I will guard.”
Ruth does not speak of guarding Naomi’s sleep; she pledged to go and live with her (1:16).
In Ruth 1, what did Ruth say about Naomi’s people and God?
Ruth said, “your people will be my people, and your God will be my God” (1:16).
Ruth 1:16
“Your tribe will be my tribe, and your judges my judges.”
Ruth spoke of Naomi’s people and God, not tribe and judges (1:16).
“Your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.”
“Your city will be my city, and your king will be my king.”
Ruth did not speak of a city or a king; Israel had no king then (Judges 21:25).
“Your altar will be my altar, and your priest my priest.”
Ruth did not speak of an altar or priest; she claimed Naomi’s God as her own (1:16).
“Your language will be my language, and your customs my customs.”
Ruth did not mention language or customs; she said Naomi’s people and God would be hers (1:16).
In Ruth’s vow to Naomi in Ruth 1, what did Ruth promise concerning death and burial?
“Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried” (1:17).
Ruth 1:17
“If you die in Moab, I will return to Judah.”
Ruth pledged to stay with Naomi even in death, not to leave if Naomi died (1:17).
“Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried.”
“When you die, I will build you a monument.”
Ruth spoke of being buried where Naomi died, not of a monument (1:17).
“If I die first, return my bones to Bethlehem.”
Ruth asked for no bones to be carried; she would die and be buried where Naomi was (1:17).
“We will die together before entering Judah.”
Ruth did not speak of dying before Judah; they arrived in Bethlehem together (1:19).
In the strongest part of Ruth’s oath in chapter 1, what did she call down upon herself if she left Naomi before death?
Ruth swore, “May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me” (1:17).
Ruth 1:17
“May I never see another harvest if I ever return to my mother’s house.”
Ruth swore by the LORD, not by the harvest; they did arrive at the barley harvest (1:22).
“May the people of Moab reject me forever if I turn back from you now.”
Ruth’s oath called on the LORD to punish her, not on Moab’s rejection (1:17).
“May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me.”
“May the elders of Bethlehem cast me out if I ever leave your side.”
The elders of Bethlehem appear later as witnesses at the gate (Ruth 4:11), not in Ruth’s oath.
“May my name be forgotten in Israel if I go back to my own people.”
Ruth called on the LORD to punish her (1:17); her name was in fact remembered in David’s line (Ruth 4:13–17).
In Ruth 1, what made Naomi stop trying to persuade Ruth to turn back?
“When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her” (1:18).
Ruth 1:18
Ruth became silent
Ruth was not silent; she had just made a strong vow (1:16–17).
Ruth’s brothers arrived from Moab
No brothers of Ruth appear in the story.
Naomi was too tired to speak
Naomi’s weariness is not mentioned; she saw Ruth’s determination (1:18).
Ruth was determined to go with her
A messenger called them to Bethlehem
No messenger is mentioned; Naomi gave in to Ruth’s determination (1:18).
In the final travel scene of Ruth 1, to what town did Naomi and Ruth come together?
“So Naomi and Ruth traveled until they came to Bethlehem” (1:19).
Ruth 1:19
Hebron
Hebron is not mentioned in Ruth; they went to Bethlehem (1:19).
Jerusalem
Jerusalem was still held by the Jebusites (Judges 1:21); they came to Bethlehem.
Bethlehem
Jericho
Jericho was the City of Palms (Deuteronomy 34:3); they came to Bethlehem.
Mizpah
Mizpah was where Israel gathered before the LORD (Judges 20:1); they came to Bethlehem.
When Naomi and Ruth arrived in Bethlehem in Ruth 1, how did the town react?
“When they entered Bethlehem, the whole town was stirred because of them” (1:19).
Ruth 1:19
The whole town was stirred because of them
The elders shut the gates
The gates were not shut; the town was stirred and the women asked about Naomi (1:19).
No one noticed them
Everyone noticed: “the whole town was stirred because of them” (1:19).
The priests met them with sacrifices
No priests or sacrifices are mentioned at their arrival (1:19).
The men of war gathered around them
No soldiers are mentioned; it was the women of the town who spoke (1:19).
In Bethlehem, what did the women exclaim when Naomi returned in Ruth 1?
“The women of the town exclaimed, ‘Can this be Naomi?’” (1:19).
Ruth 1:19
“Blessed is the woman who has come home!”
The women did not pronounce a blessing at this point; they asked if this could be Naomi (1:19).
“Is this Ruth of Moab?”
The women asked about Naomi, not Ruth (1:19).
“Can this be Naomi?”
“Has Elimelech returned?”
Elimelech had died in Moab (1:3); the women asked about Naomi.
“Who will redeem her field?”
Redeeming Elimelech’s land comes up later (Ruth 4:3), not at their arrival.
In response to the women of Bethlehem in Ruth 1, what name did Naomi ask to be called instead of Naomi?
“Do not call me Naomi,” she replied. “Call me Mara” (1:20).
Ruth 1:20
Hadassah
Hadassah was Esther’s Hebrew name (Esther 2:7).
Mara
Tirzah
Tirzah was one of Zelophehad’s daughters (Numbers 26:33).
Michal
Michal was Saul’s younger daughter (1 Samuel 14:49).
Shiphrah
Shiphrah was a Hebrew midwife in Egypt (Exodus 1:15).
In Ruth 1, what reason did Naomi give for wanting to be called Mara?
Naomi said, “Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me” (1:20).
Ruth 1:20
“Because Moab has broken me.”
Naomi blamed no nation; she said the Almighty had dealt bitterly with her (1:20).
“Because the judges have wronged me.”
The judges are not blamed; Naomi spoke of the Almighty (1:20).
“Because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me.”
“Because my enemies have mocked me.”
No enemies are mentioned; Naomi said the Almighty had dealt bitterly with her (1:20).
“Because famine has consumed my house.”
Famine had driven the family away (1:1), but Naomi’s reason for “Mara” names the Almighty (1:20).
In Naomi’s lament in Ruth 1, how did she contrast her departure from Bethlehem with her return?
Naomi said, “I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty” (1:21).
Ruth 1:21
“I went away poor, but the LORD brought me back rich.”
The reverse is true: she went away full and came back empty (1:21).
“I went away alone, but the LORD brought me back with many children.”
She had gone away with a husband and two sons and came back without them (1:5, 1:21).
“I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty.”
“I went away hopeful, but the LORD brought me back joyful.”
Naomi spoke of coming back empty, not joyful (1:21).
“I went away in mourning, but the LORD brought me back dancing.”
Mourning turned into dancing is the psalmist’s praise (Psalm 30:11); Naomi said the LORD brought her back empty (1:21).
At the close of Ruth chapter 1, which statement correctly summarizes Naomi’s return to Bethlehem?
“So Naomi returned from the land of Moab with her daughter-in-law Ruth the Moabitess. And they arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest” (1:22).
Ruth 1:22
Naomi returned from Egypt with Ruth the Judahite at wheat harvest
Naomi returned from Moab, not Egypt, and Ruth was a Moabitess (1:22); the wheat harvest comes later (Ruth 2:23).
Naomi returned from Moab with Orpah the Moabitess at the grape harvest
Orpah went back to her people (1:15); Naomi returned with Ruth at the barley harvest (1:22).
Naomi returned from Moab with Ruth the Moabitess at the beginning of barley harvest
Naomi returned from Edom with Ruth the Israelite at the olive harvest
Naomi returned from Moab, not Edom, with Ruth the Moabitess (1:22).
Naomi returned from Ammon with her sons at the beginning of barley harvest
Naomi’s sons had died in Moab (1:5); she returned from Moab with Ruth (1:22).
In the Bethlehem harvest story in Ruth 2, Ruth the Moabitess went to glean in a field. Whose field did she happen to enter?
Ruth 2:3 says Ruth happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz, who was from the clan of Elimelech.
Ruth 2:3
Elimelech
Elimelech was Naomi’s late husband (Ruth 1:2); Boaz was from his clan and owned the field (2:3).
Boaz
Mahlon
Mahlon was Naomi’s son, who had died in Moab (Ruth 1:2), not the owner of the field.
Jesse
Jesse was the grandson of Boaz and Ruth (Ruth 4:17), born long after this harvest.
Nahshon
Nahshon was an earlier ancestor in Boaz’s family line (Ruth 4:20), not the field’s owner.
When Boaz arrived to check on the harvesters in Ruth 2, from which town did he come?
Ruth 2:4 says, “Just then Boaz arrived from Bethlehem.”
Ruth 2:4
Hebron
Hebron is where David was later anointed king over Judah (2 Samuel 2:4), not where Boaz came from (2:4).
Jerusalem
Jerusalem is not named in Ruth 2; Boaz came from Bethlehem (2:4).
Bethlehem
Jericho
Jericho is the city Rahab lived in (Joshua 2:1), not Boaz’s town.
Tekoa
Tekoa is not named in Ruth 2; Boaz came from Bethlehem (2:4).
At the beginning of Ruth 2, what did Ruth ask Naomi for permission to do during harvest?
Ruth 2:2 has Ruth say, “Please let me go into the fields and glean heads of grain after someone in whose sight I may find favor.”
Ruth 2:2
Reap with a sickle beside the men
Ruth asked to glean behind the harvesters, not to reap with a sickle alongside the men (2:2).
Glean heads of grain after the harvesters
Sell grain in the town gate
Selling grain at the gate is not mentioned; she asked to glean (2:2).
Draw water from Bethlehem’s well
Drawing water is not what she asked for; she asked to glean (2:2).
Gather grapes from a vineyard
Gathering grapes is not what she asked for; she asked to glean heads of grain (2:2).
In the field near Bethlehem, what greeting did Boaz give the harvesters?
Ruth 2:4 says Boaz said to the harvesters, “The LORD be with you,” and they replied, “The LORD bless you.”
Ruth 2:4
Peace be to this house
“Peace to this house” is what Jesus told His disciples to say on entering a home (Luke 10:5), not Boaz’s greeting.
The LORD watch between you and me
A prayer that the LORD keep watch between two men comes from Laban and Jacob (Genesis 31:49), not Boaz’s greeting.
The LORD be with you
Grace and peace to you
“Grace and peace” is a New Testament greeting, as in Romans 1:7, not Boaz’s.
May your barns be filled
Boaz did not wish them full barns; his greeting was “The LORD be with you” (2:4).
When Boaz noticed Ruth in his field, how did the foreman identify her?
Ruth 2:6 has the foreman answer, “She is the Moabitess who returned with Naomi from the land of Moab.”
Ruth 2:6
She is Naomi’s sister from Bethlehem
The foreman does not call her Naomi’s sister; he says she returned with Naomi from Moab (2:6).
She is the young Moabite woman who returned with Naomi from the land of Moab
She is Boaz’s servant from Judah
She was not Boaz’s servant; she was a Moabitess who asked to glean (2:6–7), and she said she was not like one of his servant girls (2:13).
She is the widow from Jericho who came with Rahab
Rahab lived in Jericho in Joshua’s day (Joshua 2:1); she has no place in this scene.
She is a daughter of Jesse helping the poor
Jesse’s family appears at the end of the book (Ruth 4:17); the foreman called her the Moabitess who came back with Naomi (2:6).
In Ruth 2, what did Boaz first tell Ruth about where she should glean?
In Ruth 2:8 Boaz says, “Do not go and glean in another field, and do not go away from this place, but stay here close to my servant girls.”
Ruth 2:8
Go wherever the best barley grows
Boaz did not send her wherever the best barley grew; he told her to stay in his field (2:8).
Do not go and glean in another field, and do not go away from here
Work only in the vineyards south of Bethlehem
Boaz did not mention vineyards; he told her to stay with his servant girls (2:8).
Return to Naomi until the wheat harvest
Boaz did not send her back to Naomi; he told her to stay close to his servant girls (2:8).
Follow the men into every neighboring field
Boaz told her to follow his servant girls, not the men or neighboring fields (2:8–9).
According to Boaz’s instructions in the harvest account of Ruth 2, what could Ruth do when she became thirsty?
Ruth 2:9 has Boaz say, “when you are thirsty, go and drink from the jars the young men have filled.”
Ruth 2:9
Drink from what the young men had drawn
Return to Naomi’s house for water
She did not need to go home for water; the young men’s jars were available (2:9).
Draw water only from the city well
She was not limited to a city well; she could drink from jars the young men had filled (2:9).
Ask the foreman for wine
Boaz did not say to ask the foreman for wine; he offered the filled jars (2:9).
Wait until evening to drink
She did not have to wait for evening; Boaz told her to drink when thirsty (2:9).
When Boaz explained why he had shown kindness to Ruth, what had he heard about her?

In Ruth 2:11 Boaz says he had been told of all she had done for her mother-in-law since her husband’s death, how she left her father and mother and the land of her birth, and came to a people she did not know before.
Ruth 2:11
She had won a harvest contest among the women of Moab
A harvest contest in Moab is not mentioned; Boaz praised her devotion to Naomi (2:11).
She had brought gold and silver from Moab to Bethlehem
Gold from Moab is not mentioned; Boaz praised her devotion to Naomi (2:11).
She had cared for Naomi, left her parents and homeland, and come to a people she had not known
She had been promised the field by the elders at the gate
No promise of the field by the elders is mentioned; Boaz praised her devotion to Naomi (2:11).
She had been born in Bethlehem and had come back home
Ruth was born in Moab, not Bethlehem; she left the land of her birth (2:11).
In Boaz’s blessing over Ruth in Ruth 2, under whose wings did he say she had taken refuge?
Ruth 2:12 has Boaz say she had taken refuge under the wings of “the LORD, the God of Israel.”
Ruth 2:12
Under Naomi’s wings
Naomi is not the one whose wings gave refuge; Boaz said the LORD’s wings (2:12).
Under Boaz’s wings
Boaz did not claim to be her refuge; he named the LORD, the God of Israel (2:12).
Under the wings of the God of Israel
Under the wings of the elders of Bethlehem
The elders of Bethlehem are not mentioned in the blessing; Boaz named the LORD (2:12).
Under the wings of the harvesters
The harvesters are not mentioned in the blessing; Boaz named the LORD (2:12).
At mealtime in the field, what did Boaz invite Ruth to eat and drink in Ruth 2?
Ruth 2:14 has Boaz say, “have some bread and dip it into the vinegar sauce,” and he offered her roasted grain.
Ruth 2:14
Fish and honey from the river
Fish and honey are not mentioned; Boaz offered bread dipped in vinegar sauce and roasted grain (2:14).
Bread dipped in vinegar, and he offered her roasted grain
Milk and figs from the vineyard
Milk and figs are not mentioned; Boaz offered bread dipped in vinegar sauce and roasted grain (2:14).
Lentil stew and honey cakes
Lentil stew and cakes are not mentioned; Boaz offered bread dipped in vinegar sauce and roasted grain (2:14).
Manna and quail from the wilderness
Manna and quail were Israel’s food in the wilderness (Exodus 16:13); Ruth ate bread and roasted grain (2:14).
After Ruth rose from the meal to glean again, what instructions did Boaz give his young men about her?
Ruth 2:15–16 has Boaz order his young men: “Even if she gathers among the sheaves, do not insult her,” and “pull out for her some stalks from the bundles and leave them for her to gather.”
Send her home before sunset so she is safe
Boaz did not send her away; he let her keep gleaning until evening (2:15–17).
Let her gather among the sheaves, do not insult her, and even pull out some stalks for her
Count every stalk she collects and report it
Boaz did not tell them to count her stalks; he told them to leave extra for her (2:16).
Keep her away from the bundles and sheaves
Boaz did not keep her from the bundles; he told them to pull stalks out of the bundles for her (2:16).
Make her work only with the reapers, not the gleaners
Boaz did not limit her to working with the reapers; she could glean among the sheaves (2:15).
By evening, after gleaning in Boaz’s field near Bethlehem, about how much barley did Ruth beat out?
Ruth 2:17 says Ruth gathered grain until evening, and when she beat out what she had gleaned, it was about an ephah of barley.
Ruth 2:17
About a homer of wheat
The harvest she gleaned was barley, not wheat, and the amount was an ephah, not a homer (2:17).
About a seah of flour
A seah of flour is not mentioned; the amount was an ephah of barley (2:17).
About an ephah of barley
About ten omers of manna
Manna fell in the wilderness (Exodus 16:35) and has nothing to do with this harvest; she beat out about an ephah of barley (2:17).
About a basket of grapes
Grapes are not mentioned; she gleaned barley, about an ephah (2:17).
When Ruth returned to Naomi in town after working in Boaz’s field, what did she give Naomi besides the grain she had gleaned?
Ruth 2:18 says she “brought out what she had saved from her meal and gave it to Naomi.”
Ruth 2:18
A new cloak from Boaz
A cloak from Boaz is not mentioned; she gave Naomi what she had saved from her meal (2:18).
Silver from the foreman
Silver from the foreman is not mentioned; she gave Naomi what she had saved from her meal (2:18).
Water from the workers
Water from the workers is not mentioned; she gave Naomi what she had saved from her meal (2:18).
What she had left over from her meal
Oil and wine
Oil and wine are not mentioned; she gave Naomi what she had saved from her meal (2:18).
After Ruth told Naomi that the man’s name was Boaz, how did Naomi describe Boaz in relation to their family?
Ruth 2:20 has Naomi say, “The man is a close relative. He is one of our kinsman-redeemers.”
Ruth 2:20
He is a prophet from Ephraim who serves at Shiloh
Naomi did not call Boaz a prophet; she called him a close relative and kinsman-redeemer (2:20).
He is a distant trader from Moab who knew Ruth’s father
Naomi did not call him a trader from Moab; he was a relative from Elimelech’s clan (2:1, 20).
He is a close relative, one of our kinsman-redeemers
He is the judge of Bethlehem who rules the town
Naomi did not call him a judge; she called him a close relative and kinsman-redeemer (2:20).
He is Ruth’s brother from Judah, come to look for her
Naomi did not call him Ruth’s brother; she called him a close relative of the family (2:20).
At the end of Ruth 2, how long did Ruth stay close to the servant girls of Boaz, and where did she live during that time?
Ruth 2:23 says Ruth stayed close to the servant girls of Boaz “until the barley and wheat harvests were finished. And she lived with her mother-in-law.”
Ruth 2:23
Until the grape harvest, and she lived in Boaz’s house
The harvest named is barley and wheat, not grapes, and she lived with Naomi, not in Boaz’s house (2:23).
Until the barley and wheat harvests were finished, and she lived with her mother-in-law
Until Passover, and she lived at the city gate
Passover is not mentioned, and she lived with Naomi, not at the city gate (2:23).
Until the olive harvest, and she lived alone in the field
The olive harvest is not mentioned, and she lived with Naomi, not in the field (2:23).
Until the census, and she lived in Moab
No census is mentioned, and she lived with Naomi in Bethlehem, not in Moab (2:23).
In Ruth 3, who said to Ruth, “My daughter, should I not seek a resting place for you, that it may be well with you?”
Naomi, Ruth’s mother-in-law, said, “My daughter, should I not seek a resting place for you, that it may be well with you?” (3:1).
Ruth 3:1
Orpah
Orpah kissed Naomi goodbye and went home (Ruth 1:14); she is not in Ruth 3.
Naomi
Hannah
Hannah is the mother of Samuel (1 Samuel 1:20), not a relative of Ruth.
Abigail
Abigail was one of David’s wives (2 Samuel 3:3), not a character in the book of Ruth.
Deborah
Deborah was a prophetess who judged Israel (Judges 4:4), not a relative of Ruth.
In Bethlehem during Ruth 3, where did Naomi say Boaz would be winnowing barley that night?
Naomi told Ruth that Boaz was winnowing barley that night on the threshing floor (3:2).
Ruth 3:2
At the city gate
The city gate is where Boaz later settled the matter with the nearer redeemer (Ruth 4:1), not where he was winnowing that night (3:2).
In the vineyard
Naomi said nothing of a vineyard; the winnowing was on the threshing floor (3:2).
On the threshing floor
By the well
A well is not the place Naomi names; she says the threshing floor (3:2).
In the synagogue
Synagogues belong to a much later age; Boaz was winnowing barley on the threshing floor (3:2).
Before Ruth went down to meet Boaz in Ruth 3, what preparations did Naomi tell her to make?
Naomi told Ruth to wash herself, put on perfume and wear her best clothes before going down to the threshing floor (3:3).
Ruth 3:3
Fast, mourn, and wear sackcloth
Mourning and sackcloth would be the opposite of preparing for a meeting like this (3:3).
Wash, put on perfume, and wear her best clothes
Shave her head and sit in ashes
Shaving her head and sitting in ashes are signs of grief; Naomi told her to wash and dress well (3:3).
Bring a lamb and oil
Naomi never mentions bringing a lamb and oil; her instructions were to wash, perfume and dress (3:3).
Take a staff and sandals only
Naomi told her to put on her best clothes, not to go with only a staff and sandals (3:3).
In Naomi’s instructions to Ruth in Ruth 3, when was Ruth to let Boaz notice her presence?
Naomi said Ruth should not let Boaz know she was there until he had finished eating and drinking (3:3).
Ruth 3:3
Before he started working
Boaz was already working in the day; Naomi’s plan was for the night (3:2–3).
While he was speaking to the reapers
Ruth was to stay unnoticed, not to approach while Boaz was speaking to the reapers (3:3).
After he had finished eating and drinking
As soon as he entered Bethlehem
Naomi’s plan took place at the threshing floor that night, not on Boaz’s entering town (3:2–3).
At sunrise
Sunrise comes only after the night scene; Ruth was to reveal herself after he had eaten and drunk (3:3).
At the threshing floor in Ruth 3, what did Naomi tell Ruth to observe once Boaz lay down?
Naomi told Ruth, “When he lies down, note the place where he lies,” and then to uncover his feet (3:4).
Ruth 3:4
The amount of barley in the pile
The amount of barley is not what Naomi asked her to note; it was the place where Boaz lay (3:4).
The place where he lay
The names of his servants
Naomi did not ask for the servants’ names; she asked Ruth to note where Boaz lay (3:4).
The time of the moonrise
Moonrise is not mentioned; Ruth was to note the place where he lay (3:4).
The location of the gate
The gate is not part of the instructions; Ruth was to note where Boaz lay (3:4).
Near the grain pile in Ruth 3, what did Ruth do after Boaz had eaten, drunk, and lain down?
After Boaz had finished eating and drinking and lain down, Ruth went in secretly, uncovered his feet and lay down (3:7).
Ruth 3:7
She called to him from the doorway
Ruth came in secretly, not calling from a doorway (3:7).
She sat beside Naomi
Naomi was at home; Ruth was on the threshing floor with Boaz (3:6–7).
She uncovered his feet and lay down
She took barley and returned home
Barley was given to her by Boaz only later, in the morning (3:15), not taken now.
She stood at the city gate
The scene is the threshing floor, not the city gate (3:6–7).
Around midnight in Ruth chapter 3, what startled Boaz awake on the threshing floor?
At midnight Boaz was startled, turned over, and there lying at his feet was a woman (3:8).
Ruth 3:8
A fire in the grain
Fire is not mentioned; it was the woman at his feet that startled him (3:8).
Thieves in Bethlehem
No thieves appear in the story; Boaz was startled by a woman at his feet (3:8).
A strong wind from Moab
No wind is mentioned; what woke Boaz was a woman at his feet (3:8).
A woman lying at his feet
The cry of a child
No child is mentioned in the scene; the cause was a woman lying at his feet (3:8).
When Boaz asked who was at his feet in Ruth 3, what appeal did Ruth make?
Ruth answered Boaz’s question with “I am your servant Ruth” and asked him to “spread the corner of your garment over me,” since he was a kinsman-redeemer (3:9).
Ruth 3:9
“I am your servant Ruth” and “Spread the corner of your garment over me”
“I am Naomi” and “Take me into your house”
Ruth was not Naomi, and Ruth asked for Boaz’s protection as a redeemer, not a place in his house (3:9).
“I am Orpah” and “Send me back to Moab”
Orpah went back to Moab earlier (Ruth 1:14); Ruth identified herself as Ruth (3:9).
“I am your servant” and “Give me water and bread”
Ruth asked Boaz to act as kinsman-redeemer, not for water and bread (3:9).
“I am a gleaner” and “Let me remain among the sheaves”
Ruth had gleaned in the fields (Ruth 2:3), but at the threshing floor she asked Boaz to spread his garment over her as redeemer (3:9).
In Boaz’s reply to Ruth in Ruth 3, why did he say her later kindness was greater than her earlier kindness?
Boaz said her kindness was greater now than before because she had not run after the younger men, whether rich or poor (3:10).
Ruth 3:10
She had gathered more grain than the servants
Gathering more grain than the servants is not what Boaz praised; it was her not running after younger men (3:10).
She had returned to Moab and come back
Ruth had not gone back to Moab; she stayed with Naomi (Ruth 1:14–15 and 3:10).
She had not run after the younger men, whether rich or poor
She had given all her barley to Naomi
Boaz does not mention giving barley to Naomi as the reason; it was her loyalty in marriage choice (3:10).
She had spoken before the elders at the gate
Ruth had not spoken before the elders; Boaz later meets them at the gate (Ruth 4:1).
During the nighttime conversation in Ruth 3, how did Boaz describe Ruth’s reputation among his fellow townspeople?
Boaz said all his fellow townspeople knew that she was a woman of noble character (3:11).
Ruth 3:11
A skilled singer
Singing is not what Boaz praised; he spoke of her noble character (3:11).
A woman of noble character
A wise judge in Israel
Ruth is not called a judge; Boaz says the townspeople knew her as a woman of noble character (3:11).
A wealthy landowner
Ruth owned no land; Boaz speaks of her character, not wealth (3:11).
A daughter of the king
Ruth was a Moabite widow, not a king’s daughter; Boaz praised her noble character (3:11).
What complication did Boaz explain to Ruth at the threshing floor in Ruth 3 regarding redemption?
Boaz said that he was a kinsman-redeemer but that there was a redeemer nearer than he (3:12).
Ruth 3:12
Naomi had already sold the land to another family
Naomi’s land is not mentioned as already sold in this scene; the complication was a nearer redeemer (3:12).
Ruth had to return to Moab first
Ruth did not need to return to Moab; the obstacle was a nearer redeemer (3:12).
There was a kinsman-redeemer closer than Boaz
The harvest had not yet ended
The harvest timing is not the complication; Boaz pointed to a nearer redeemer (3:12).
The elders of Bethlehem had forbidden the marriage
The elders had not forbidden anything; Boaz named a nearer redeemer (3:12).
In Ruth 3, what solemn promise did Boaz make if the closer redeemer did not want to redeem Ruth?
Boaz said that if the nearer redeemer did not want to redeem her, “as surely as the LORD lives, I will” (3:13).
Ruth 3:13
He would send her back to her people
Boaz said he would redeem her himself, not send her back to her people (3:13).
He would ask the priest to decide
Boaz did not defer to a priest; he swore by the LORD that he would redeem her (3:13).
He would wait until the next harvest
Boaz promised action, not waiting for a later harvest (3:13).
As surely as the LORD lives, he would redeem her
He would give Naomi silver instead
Boaz’s promise was to redeem her, not to give Naomi silver (3:13).
Before dawn in Ruth 3, why did Boaz have Ruth leave the threshing floor before she could be recognized?
Boaz told her, “Do not let it be known that a woman came to the threshing floor,” so she got up before anyone else could recognize her (3:14).
Ruth 3:14
The reapers were about to arrive and start the day’s threshing
No singing reapers are mentioned; Boaz’s concern was that no one know a woman had come (3:14).
Naomi had sent a servant to call her home at dawn
Naomi did not call her home; Boaz himself sent her off to keep it unknown (3:14).
He said it must not be known that a woman came to the threshing floor
The nearer redeemer had arrived suddenly at the threshing floor
The nearer redeemer did not arrive that night; Boaz later meets him at the gate (Ruth 4:1).
A band of Philistines was approaching Bethlehem that morning
No Philistines are mentioned in Ruth 3; Boaz wanted to keep the visit unknown (3:14).
As Ruth prepared to return to Naomi in Ruth 3, what did Boaz tell her to hold out, and what did he put into it?
Boaz told Ruth to bring the shawl she was wearing and hold it out, and he poured in six measures of barley (3:15).
Ruth 3:15
Her basket, and five loaves of bread
No basket or loaves are mentioned; it was her shawl, filled with six measures of barley (3:15).
Her shawl, and six measures of barley
Her jar, and olive oil
Oil is not mentioned; she held out her shawl for six measures of barley (3:15).
Her cloak, and silver coins
No silver is involved; the gift was six measures of barley (3:15).
Her pouch, and roasted grain
She held out a shawl, not a pouch, and received barley, not roasted grain (3:15).
After Ruth returned to Naomi in Bethlehem in Ruth 3, what did Naomi say Boaz would not do until the matter was settled?
Naomi said Boaz would not rest unless he had resolved the matter that day (3:18).
Ruth 3:18
Eat another meal
Eating is not what Naomi said he would give up; she said he would not rest until the matter was resolved (3:18).
Leave the threshing floor
Leaving the threshing floor is not the point; Naomi said he would not rest until it was resolved (3:18).
Speak to the elders
Boaz does go to the elders later, but Naomi’s point was that he would not rest until it was settled today (3:18; Ruth 4:1–2).
Rest until he had resolved it that day
Return to his field
Naomi’s concern was Boaz not resting before the matter was resolved, not his field (3:18).
In Ruth 4, where did Boaz go in Bethlehem to settle the redemption matter publicly?
Boaz went to the gate and sat down there, and the kinsman-redeemer he had mentioned soon came along (4:1).
Ruth 4:1
The threshing floor
The threshing floor is where Ruth lay at Boaz’s feet in the night (Ruth 3:7), not the site of the legal hearing.
The city gate
The barley field
The barley field is where Ruth gleaned (Ruth 2:2–3), earlier in the story.
Naomi’s house
Naomi’s house is not where Boaz settled the matter; he sat at the gate with the elders (4:1–2).
The court of the priests
No court of the priests is mentioned; the matter was settled at the city gate (4:1).
In the opening scene of Ruth 4, who came by while Boaz was sitting at the gate?
The kinsman-redeemer of whom Boaz had spoken came along while Boaz sat at the gate (4:1).
Ruth 4:1
Mahlon’s surviving brother, come back from Moab
Mahlon and Chilion were both dead (4:9–10); the man who came was a nearer kinsman, not a surviving brother.
The nearer kinsman-redeemer Boaz had mentioned
The prophet Samuel, sent to bless the transaction
Samuel appears generations later in 1 Samuel and plays no part in Ruth 4.
Jesse, the father of David, hoping to sell land
Jesse is named only at the end of the chapter as Obed’s son (4:17), long after this scene.
A Moabite official arriving to claim Ruth’s land
No Moabite official appears; the man who came was a fellow Israelite kinsman (4:1).
In the legal meeting in Ruth chapter 4, how many elders of the city did Boaz ask to sit down?
Boaz took ten of the elders of the city and told them to sit (4:2).
Ruth 4:2
Five
Boaz took ten elders (4:2), not five.
Seven
Boaz took ten elders (4:2), not seven.
Ten
Twelve
Twelve is the number of Solomon’s governors in 1 Kings 4:7, not the elders here.
Twenty
Twenty is the number of barley loaves in 2 Kings 4:42; Boaz took ten elders (4:2).
In Ruth 4, Boaz said that which woman had returned from the land of Moab?
Boaz said that Naomi, who had returned from the land of Moab, was selling the piece of land that belonged to Elimelech (4:3).
Ruth 4:3
Ruth
Ruth also came from Moab, but Boaz named Naomi as the one who had returned and was selling the land (4:3).
Orpah
Orpah stayed in Moab (Ruth 1:14), so she did not return.
Naomi
Leah
Leah was Jacob’s wife, mentioned in the elders’ blessing (4:11).
Tamar
Tamar is mentioned only as the mother of Perez (4:12).
In Boaz’s statement at the gate in Ruth 4, the piece of land Naomi was selling had belonged to whom?
Boaz said the land Naomi was selling had belonged to “our brother Elimelech” (4:3).
Ruth 4:3
Boaz
Boaz was the buyer, not the former owner (4:9).
Mahlon
Mahlon was Elimelech’s son and Ruth’s late husband (4:10).
Chilion
Chilion was Elimelech’s other son (4:9), not the original owner of the land.
Elimelech
Jesse
Jesse is Obed’s son (4:17), a later generation than these events.
In Ruth 4, when Boaz first offered the nearer relative the chance to redeem the property, what was the man’s initial reply?
When Boaz offered the redemption, the man replied, “I will redeem it” (4:4).
Ruth 4:4
“I will ask Naomi first”
The man did not say he would ask Naomi first; he said he would redeem it (4:4).
“I cannot redeem it”
“I cannot redeem it” was his later reply, after Boaz mentioned Ruth (4:6).
“I will redeem it”
“Boaz should redeem it”
Boaz said only that he was next after him (4:4); the man did not tell Boaz to redeem it at first.
“Let the elders decide”
The man did not defer to the elders; he agreed to redeem the land (4:4).
In the Bethlehem gate scene of Ruth 4, which woman did Boaz name when he explained that redeeming the field also involved raising up the name of the deceased?
Boaz said that on the day the man bought the land from Naomi he must also acquire “Ruth the Moabitess” to raise up the name of the deceased (4:5).
Ruth 4:5
Naomi the Judahite
Naomi was the one selling the land (4:3); Boaz added Ruth the Moabitess as the widow to be acquired (4:5).
Orpah the Moabitess
Orpah stayed in Moab (Ruth 1:14) and is not mentioned in Ruth 4.
Ruth the Moabitess
Tamar the Canaanite
Tamar the Canaanite appears only as the mother of Perez (4:12), not in this obligation.
Hannah of Ramah
Hannah belongs to 1 Samuel and plays no part in Ruth 4.
In Boaz’s public declaration in Ruth 4, Ruth the Moabitess is identified as whose widow?
Boaz said, “I have acquired Ruth the Moabitess, Mahlon’s widow, as my wife” (4:10).
Ruth 4:10
Elimelech’s widow
Naomi, not Ruth, was Elimelech’s widow (4:3, 4:9).
Boaz’s former widow
Ruth was never Boaz’s widow; she became his wife (4:10, 4:13).
Mahlon’s widow
Chilion’s widow
Chilion also died (4:9), but Ruth was identified as Mahlon’s widow (4:10).
Nahshon’s widow
Nahshon is a distant ancestor of Boaz (4:20), not Ruth’s husband.
In Ruth 4, why did the nearer kinsman-redeemer refuse to complete the redemption himself?
The nearer kinsman-redeemer said, “I cannot redeem it myself, or I would jeopardize my own inheritance” (4:6).
Ruth 4:6
He was leaving Bethlehem
His stated reason was his own inheritance, not leaving Bethlehem (4:6).
He feared the Philistines
The Philistines play no part in this story; he feared for his inheritance (4:6).
He had no money
He gave no reason about money; he said he would jeopardize his own inheritance (4:6).
He might jeopardize his own inheritance
Naomi refused his offer
Naomi did not refuse him; she was the one selling the land (4:3).
