In the explanation of ancient legal custom in Ruth 4, what object was removed to confirm the redemption and transfer of property?
To make a matter legally binding in Israel, a man would remove his sandal and give it to the other party; the kinsman-redeemer did this (4:7–8).
Ruth 4:7-8
A robe
A robe sealed Jonathan’s covenant with David (1 Samuel 18:4), not a property transfer.
A staff
Judah left his staff as a pledge with Tamar (Genesis 38:18), not as a mark of redemption.
A sandal
A ring
Pharaoh gave Joseph his signet ring (Genesis 41:42), but no ring confirmed the sale here.
A seal
Jeremiah’s deed of purchase was signed and sealed (Jeremiah 32:10), but a seal is not the object used here.
In Ruth chapter 4, whom did Boaz address as witnesses when he finalized the purchase?
Boaz said to the elders and all the people, “You are witnesses today” (4:9).
Ruth 4:9-10
Only Naomi and Ruth
Naomi and Ruth were the ones to benefit, but Boaz addressed the elders and all the people (4:9).
Only the priests
No priests are mentioned in the scene; Boaz spoke to the elders and all the people (4:9).
The elders and all the people
Only his servants
Servants are not mentioned; the witnesses were the elders and all the people at the gate (4:9, 4:11).
The women of Bethlehem only
The women of Bethlehem speak later, after the birth (4:14); the witnesses at the gate were the elders and all the people (4:11).
In Boaz’s legal statement in Ruth 4, he said he had bought from Naomi all that belonged to which three deceased men?
Boaz said, “You are witnesses today that I am buying from Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech, Chilion, and Mahlon” (4:9).
Ruth 4:9
Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are not named in Ruth 4; Boaz named Elimelech, Chilion, and Mahlon (4:9).
Elimelech, Chilion, and Mahlon
Perez, Hezron, and Ram
Perez, Hezron, and Ram are ancestors in the closing genealogy (4:18–19), not owners of the property.
Jesse, David, and Solomon
Jesse and David appear at the end of the genealogy (4:22), long after these men.
Boaz, Salmon, and Nahshon
Boaz, Salmon, and Nahshon are in the genealogy (4:20–21); Boaz was the buyer, not one of the three.
In the blessing spoken at the gate in Ruth 4, the people prayed that the woman entering Boaz’s home would be like which two women who built the house of Israel?
The elders and people prayed that the LORD would make the woman entering Boaz’s home “like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel” (4:11).
Ruth 4:11
Sarah and Rebekah
Sarah and Rebekah were earlier matriarchs (Genesis 21:2, 24:67), but the blessing named Rachel and Leah (4:11).
Rachel and Leah
Miriam and Deborah
Miriam and Deborah were women prophets (Exodus 15:20, Judges 4:4), not the women named in this blessing.
Hannah and Abigail
Hannah and Abigail belong to later books (1 Samuel 1:20, 25:3), not this blessing.
Naomi and Ruth
Naomi and Ruth are the women in this story, not the comparison used in the blessing (4:11).
In Ruth 4, the witnesses blessed Boaz by saying, “May you be prosperous” in which place?
The witnesses said, “May you be prosperous in Ephrathah and famous in Bethlehem” (4:11).
Ruth 4:11
Jerusalem
Jerusalem is not named in the blessing, which pairs Ephrathah with Bethlehem (4:11).
Hebron
Hebron is where Abraham settled (Genesis 13:18), not the place named in this blessing.
Ephrathah
Moab
Moab is where Naomi’s family had lived as outsiders (Ruth 1:1), not the place of Boaz’s hoped-for prosperity.
Shiloh
Shiloh housed the tabernacle (1 Samuel 1:3) and is not mentioned in Ruth 4.
In the blessing spoken at Bethlehem’s gate in Ruth 4, in which town did the people hope Boaz’s name would become famous?
The witnesses prayed that Boaz would be “famous in Bethlehem” (4:11).
Ruth 4:11
Gibeah
Gibeah is Saul’s hometown (1 Samuel 10:26), not the town named in this blessing.
Bethlehem
Jericho
Jericho is the city of Joshua’s conquest (Joshua 6), not part of this blessing.
Bethel
Bethel lay in Ephraim’s hill country (Judges 4:5) and is not named in this blessing.
Tekoa
Tekoa is the hometown of Amos (Amos 1:1), not the town named here.
In Ruth 4, whose house did the people say Boaz’s house should be like through the offspring the LORD would give by Ruth?
The people said, “May your house become like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah” (4:12).
Ruth 4:12
Joseph, whom Rachel bore to Jacob
Joseph was Rachel’s son by Jacob (Genesis 30:23), but the blessing named Perez (4:12).
Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah
Isaac, whom Sarah bore to Abraham
Isaac was Sarah’s son by Abraham (Genesis 21:2), but the blessing named Perez (4:12).
Samuel, whom Hannah bore to Elkanah
Samuel was Hannah’s son by Elkanah (1 Samuel 1:20), who lived after this scene.
Benjamin, whom Rachel bore to Jacob
Benjamin was Rachel’s son by Jacob (Genesis 35:18), but the blessing named Perez (4:12).
In the closing events of Ruth 4, after Boaz took Ruth as his wife, what did the LORD enable Ruth to do?
After Boaz took Ruth as his wife, “the LORD enabled her to conceive, and she gave birth to a son” (4:13).
Ruth 4:13
Return to Moab
Ruth had already chosen to stay with Naomi rather than return to Moab (Ruth 1:16).
Glean in another field
Gleaning in another field belongs to Ruth’s earlier days (Ruth 2:8–9).
Conceive
Speak before the elders
Speaking before the elders was Boaz’s role in the scene at the gate (4:9–10).
Buy the land
Boaz, not Ruth, bought the land (4:9).
In Ruth 4, after Ruth gave birth, who said to Naomi, “Blessed be the LORD”?
The women said to Naomi, “Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a kinsman-redeemer” (4:14).
Ruth 4:14
Boaz and the elders
Boaz and the elders spoke earlier at the gate (4:9–11); the blessing after the birth came from the women (4:14).
The women
The priests of Bethlehem
No priests of Bethlehem are mentioned in Ruth 4.
The shepherds nearby
Shepherds are not mentioned in Ruth 4; the women spoke to Naomi (4:14).
Ruth’s Moabite relatives
Ruth’s Moabite relatives never appear in the book; the women said this (4:14).
In the words spoken to Naomi in Ruth 4, what did the women say the LORD had not left her without “this day”?
The women praised the LORD “who has not left you this day without a kinsman-redeemer” (4:14).
Ruth 4:14
A harvest
A harvest is not what the women mentioned; they spoke of a kinsman-redeemer (4:14).
A field
The field was settled earlier at the gate (4:9); the women spoke of a kinsman-redeemer (4:14).
A husband
Naomi’s husband Elimelech was dead (Ruth 1:3), and the women did not speak of a husband.
A kinsman-redeemer
A servant
No servant is mentioned; the blessing was for a kinsman-redeemer (4:14).
In Ruth 4, how did the women of Bethlehem describe Ruth’s love for Naomi in comparison with sons?
The women said Ruth, who loves Naomi, “is better to you than seven sons” (4:15).
Ruth 4:15
Equal to three sons
The women said seven sons, not three (4:15).
Better to you than seven sons
Greater than many daughters
The comparison was to sons, not daughters (4:15).
Like the love of one firstborn son
The comparison was to seven sons, not one firstborn (4:15).
Worth ten servants
The women compared Ruth to seven sons, not to servants (4:15).
In the blessing spoken over Naomi in Ruth 4, what two things did the women say the child would do for her?
The women said of the child, “He will renew your life and sustain you in your old age” (4:15).
Ruth 4:15
Guard her field and judge her case
The women did not mention fields or judging cases; they spoke of renewed life and care in old age (4:15).
Renew her life and sustain her in old age
Restore her wealth and avenge her enemies
Restored wealth and vengeance are not promised; the blessing is renewed life and sustenance (4:15).
Lead Israel and defeat Moab
Leading Israel and defeating Moab are not what the women said; that came later with David’s line (4:17).
Comfort her grief and enlarge her house
The women did not mention grief or an enlarged house; they said he would renew her life (4:15).
In Ruth 4, what did Naomi do with the child after his birth?
Naomi took the child, placed him on her lap, and became a nurse to him (4:16).
Ruth 4:16
Dedicated him at Shiloh
Nothing is said about Shiloh; Naomi herself held and nursed the child (4:16).
Sent him to live with Boaz’s relatives
The child stayed with Naomi; she did not send him away (4:16).
Placed him on her lap and became a nurse to him
Hid him from the townspeople
Naomi did not hide the child; the neighbor women celebrated his birth (4:17).
Took him to Moab
Naomi did not take the child to Moab; she had returned from there (4:3).
In the final family scene of Ruth 4, what did the neighbor women say had been born to Naomi?
The neighbor women said, “A son has been born to Naomi” (4:17).
Ruth 4:17
A daughter
The women said a son, not a daughter, had been born (4:17).
A prophet
No prophet is mentioned; the child was a son named Obed (4:17).
A redeemer of Israel
The women called the baby a son; the redeemer language comes in their blessing (4:14), not their announcement (4:17).
A son
A judge
No judge is mentioned; the child became the father of Jesse, the father of David (4:17).
In Ruth 4, what name did the neighbor women give to the son born in Boaz’s household?
The neighbor women named the boy Obed, and “He became the father of Jesse, the father of David” (4:17).
Ruth 4:17
Jesse
Jesse was Obed’s son (4:17), not the baby’s name.
Obed
Perez
Perez was an ancestor several generations earlier (4:18).
Salmon
Salmon was Boaz’s father (4:21), not the child.
David
David was Obed’s grandson (4:17, 4:22).
In the family line named at the end of Ruth 4, what was Obed’s relation to David?
Obed was the father of Jesse, and Jesse was the father of David (4:22), so Obed was David’s grandfather.
Father
Jesse, not Obed, was David’s father (4:22).
Grandfather
Great-grandfather
Great-grandfather would require one more generation; Obed’s son Jesse fathered David (4:22).
Brother
Obed was in an earlier generation than David (4:17, 4:22), not a brother.
Uncle
Obed was not David’s uncle; Jesse, Obed’s son, was David’s father (4:22).
In the genealogy at the end of Ruth 4, which man comes between Amminadab and Salmon?
The genealogy reads, “Amminadab was the father of Nahshon, Nahshon was the father of Salmon” (4:20).
Ruth 4:20
Ram
Ram was the father of Amminadab, so he comes before him (4:19).
Nahshon
Boaz
Boaz was Salmon’s son and comes after Salmon (4:21).
Hezron
Hezron was the father of Ram (4:19), earlier in the line.
Obed
Obed was Boaz’s son and comes after Boaz (4:21).
In the genealogy that closes Ruth 4, which pair is given in the correct father-to-son order?
Ruth 4:21 says, “Salmon was the father of Boaz, Boaz was the father of Obed.”
Hezron—Perez
The order is reversed; Perez was the father of Hezron (4:18).
Ram—Hezron
The order is reversed; Hezron was the father of Ram (4:19).
Salmon—Boaz
Obed—Salmon
Obed was Boaz’s son and Salmon’s grandson (4:21), so the order is wrong.
David—Jesse
The order is reversed; Jesse was the father of David (4:22).
In the legal exchange at Bethlehem’s gate in Ruth 4, which option correctly combines the nearer redeemer’s reason for declining and the act that confirmed the transfer?
The nearer redeemer declined because he feared jeopardizing his inheritance (4:6), and he confirmed the transfer by removing his sandal (4:7–8).
Ruth 4:6-8
He lacked silver, and he tore his cloak
His reason was his inheritance, not lack of silver, and he removed his sandal rather than tearing a cloak (4:6–8).
He feared jeopardizing his inheritance, and he removed his sandal
Naomi refused him, and he broke a staff
Naomi did not refuse him, and the confirming act was the sandal, not a broken staff (4:3, 4:7–8).
Ruth returned to Moab, and he signed a scroll
Ruth did not return to Moab, and no scroll was signed; the man removed his sandal (4:8).
The elders objected, and he offered grain
The elders did not object, and the man gave a sandal, not grain (4:8, 4:11).
In the genealogy that concludes Ruth 4, which sequence is correct from Perez to David?
The genealogy in 4:18–22 runs Perez, Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed, Jesse, David.
Perez, Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed, Jesse, David
Perez, Ram, Hezron, Nahshon, Amminadab, Salmon, Boaz, Jesse, Obed, David
This swaps Ram with Hezron, Nahshon with Amminadab and Jesse with Obed; the text says Hezron fathered Ram, and Obed fathered Jesse (4:19, 4:22).
Perez, Hezron, Amminadab, Ram, Nahshon, Boaz, Salmon, Obed, Jesse, David
This places Amminadab before Ram and Boaz before Salmon; the text has Ram fathering Amminadab and Salmon fathering Boaz (4:19, 4:21).
Perez, Hezron, Ram, Salmon, Amminadab, Nahshon, Boaz, Obed, David, Jesse
This puts Salmon too early and David before Jesse; the text has Jesse fathering David (4:20, 4:22).
Perez, Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, Salmon, Nahshon, Obed, Boaz, Jesse, David
This puts Salmon before Nahshon and Obed before Boaz; the text has Nahshon fathering Salmon and Boaz fathering Obed (4:20–21).
In Boaz’s public declaration at Bethlehem’s gate in Ruth 4, what did he say was his purpose in acquiring Ruth the Moabitess as his wife?
Boaz said he had acquired Ruth “to raise up the name of the deceased through his inheritance, so that his name will not disappear from among his brothers or from the gate of his home” (4:10).
Ruth 4:10
To increase his harvest, enlarge his vineyards, and gain the best barley land in all of Bethlehem
Boaz said nothing of increasing his harvest or vineyards; his purpose was to preserve the deceased’s name (4:10).
To make peace with Moab, secure a trade route, and unite the two nations under a single marriage
Moab and trade are not mentioned; the purpose was to raise up the name of the deceased (4:10).
To raise up the name of the deceased on his inheritance so it would not vanish from among his brothers or from the gate of his home
To fulfill a vow made at the threshing floor and gain honor among the elders of the city and the people
No vow at the threshing floor is mentioned; the stated purpose was to keep the deceased’s name alive (4:10).
To provide Naomi with servants and rebuild Elimelech’s house in Jerusalem as a new family estate
Nothing is said of servants or Jerusalem; the purpose was to preserve the deceased’s name and inheritance (4:10).
9: In the opening of 1 Samuel 1, what was the name of the man from Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim who had two wives?
The chapter opens, “Now there was a man named Elkanah who was from Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim,” and he had two wives, Hannah and Peninnah (1:1–2).
1 Samuel 1:1-2
Elkanah
Eli
Eli was the priest at Shiloh, sitting by the doorpost of the temple of the LORD (1:9), not the Ephraimite husband of Hannah and Peninnah.
Samuel
Samuel is the son later born to Elkanah and Hannah in answer to her prayer (1:20).
Kish
Kish was a Benjamite, the father of Saul (1 Samuel 9:1), not the Ephraimite from Ramathaim-zophim.
Jesse
Jesse was from Bethlehem and was the father of David (1 Samuel 16:1); the man of 1:1 is Elkanah.
In 1 Samuel 1, which wife of Elkanah had no children at the beginning of the account?
1:2 says, “Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none.”
1 Samuel 1:2
Abigail
Abigail was the wife of Nabal and later of David (1 Samuel 25:3, 42); she does not appear in 1 Samuel 1.
Michal
Michal was Saul’s daughter, given to David in marriage (1 Samuel 18:27), not a wife of Elkanah.
Hannah
Peninnah
Peninnah is the wife who did have children; it was Hannah who had none (1:2).
Bathsheba
Bathsheba was the wife of Uriah the Hittite and later of David (2 Samuel 11:3), not of Elkanah.
In the family story at the start of 1 Samuel, what was the name of Elkanah’s other wife, the one who had children?
Elkanah “had two wives, one named Hannah and the other Peninnah. And Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none” (1:2).
1 Samuel 1:2
Peninnah
Naomi
Naomi was Elimelech’s wife from Bethlehem and Ruth’s mother-in-law (Ruth 1:2–4), not a wife of Elkanah.
Rizpah
Rizpah was Saul’s concubine (2 Samuel 3:7), not Elkanah’s wife.
Tamar
Tamar was the wife of Judah’s son Er (Genesis 38:6), and another Tamar was David’s daughter (2 Samuel 13:1); neither was married to Elkanah.
Deborah
Deborah was a prophetess who judged Israel (Judges 4:4), not Elkanah’s other wife.
Each year in 1 Samuel 1, to what place did Elkanah go with his household to worship and sacrifice to the LORD?
“Year after year Elkanah would go up from his city to worship and sacrifice to the LORD of Hosts at Shiloh,” where Hophni and Phinehas were priests (1:3).
1 Samuel 1:3
Bethel
Bethel is where Jacob dreamed of the stairway (Genesis 28:19); Elkanah’s yearly worship was at Shiloh (1:3).
Jerusalem
Jerusalem was still a Jebusite city until David captured it (2 Samuel 5:6–7); the house of the LORD was then at Shiloh.
Hebron
Hebron later became David’s first capital (2 Samuel 2:1, 11); Elkanah went up to Shiloh (1:3).
Shiloh
Beersheba
Beersheba is where Samuel’s sons later served as judges (1 Samuel 8:2), not where Elkanah worshiped yearly.
At Shiloh in 1 Samuel 1, who was the priest while Hannah prayed at the house of the LORD?
1:9 says, “Eli the priest was sitting on a chair by the doorpost of the temple of the LORD,” and Eli is the one who watched Hannah pray (1:12).
1 Samuel 1:9
Zadok
Zadok was a priest in the days of David and Solomon (2 Samuel 8:17), long after Hannah.
Abiathar
Abiathar was the son of Ahimelech who escaped to David (1 Samuel 22:20), a later generation of priests.
Eli
Ahimelech
Ahimelech was the priest at Nob who met David (1 Samuel 21:1), not the priest at Shiloh in Hannah’s day.
Hilkiah
Hilkiah was the high priest in King Josiah’s day (2 Kings 22:4), centuries after Hannah prayed at Shiloh.
In the worship setting of 1 Samuel 1, what were the names of Eli’s two sons who served as priests of the LORD at Shiloh?
1:3 says that at Shiloh “Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests to the LORD.”
1 Samuel 1:3
Nadab and Abihu
Nadab and Abihu were Aaron’s sons who offered unauthorized fire (Leviticus 10:1), not Eli’s sons.
Hophni and Phinehas
Jonathan and Ahimaaz
Jonathan and Ahimaaz were the sons of Abiathar and Zadok in David’s day (2 Samuel 15:36).
Eleazar and Ithamar
Eleazar and Ithamar were Aaron’s sons who served as priests in the wilderness (Numbers 3:4).
Joel and Abijah
Joel and Abijah were Samuel’s sons, who judged in Beersheba (1 Samuel 8:2).
During the sacrificial meal in 1 Samuel 1, what did Elkanah give to Hannah because he loved her?
“To Hannah he would give a double portion, for he loved her even though the LORD had closed her womb” (1:5).
1 Samuel 1:5
The firstborn lamb
The firstborn males of the livestock belonged to the LORD (Exodus 13:12); 1:5 says Elkanah gave Hannah a double portion.
A double portion
A priestly garment
Clothing comes later, when Hannah made Samuel a little robe each year (1 Samuel 2:19); Elkanah gave her a double portion.
A gold bracelet
Gold bracelets were given to Rebekah by Abraham’s servant (Genesis 24:22); Elkanah gave Hannah a double portion (1:5).
A separate tent
No tent is mentioned in the chapter; Elkanah’s gift was a double portion of the sacrifice (1:5).
In 1 Samuel 1, why did Peninnah provoke Hannah so bitterly year after year?
“Because the LORD had closed Hannah’s womb, her rival would provoke her viciously to taunt her” (1:6).
1 Samuel 1:6
Hannah had stolen her inheritance
No inheritance dispute appears in the chapter; the only special gift was Elkanah’s double portion to Hannah (1:5).
Hannah had mocked her sons
Hannah is never said to have mocked anyone; it was Peninnah who taunted Hannah over her barrenness (1:6–7).
Hannah refused to travel to Shiloh
Hannah went up to the house of the LORD year after year (1:7); she stayed home only once, after Samuel was born (1:22).
The LORD had closed Hannah’s womb
Eli had favored Hannah
Eli did not favor Hannah; at first he mistook her for a drunken woman (1:13–14).
When Peninnah provoked Hannah during their visits to the house of the LORD in 1 Samuel 1, how did Hannah commonly respond?
“Whenever Hannah went up to the house of the LORD, her rival taunted her until she wept and would not eat” (1:7).
1 Samuel 1:7
She laughed and sang
Hannah’s song of praise comes after she gives Samuel to the LORD (1 Samuel 2:1); under Peninnah’s taunts she wept.
She left the family
Hannah stayed with the family and went up with them year after year (1:7); she did not leave.
She wept and would not eat
She argued with Eli
Hannah spoke to Eli only once, respectfully, explaining she was not drunk (1:15–16); this was not her response to Peninnah.
She returned to Ramah alone
The family returned to Ramah together after worshiping (1:19); Hannah never went home alone.
In 1 Samuel 1, when Elkanah tried to comfort Hannah, he asked whether he was better to her than how many sons?
Elkanah asked, “Am I not better to you than ten sons?” (1:8).
1 Samuel 1:8
Three
Hannah would later bear three more sons (1 Samuel 2:21), but Elkanah’s question named ten sons (1:8).
Five
Five is not the number Elkanah used; he asked, “Am I not better to you than ten sons?” (1:8).
Seven
Seven appears in Hannah’s later song: “The barren woman gives birth to seven” (1 Samuel 2:5); Elkanah said ten.
Ten
Twelve
Twelve was the number of Jacob’s sons (Genesis 35:22); Elkanah spoke of ten sons (1:8).
At Shiloh in 1 Samuel 1, what specific gift did Hannah ask the LORD to give her?
In her vow Hannah asked the LORD to remember her, “not forgetting Your maidservant but giving her a son” (1:11).
1 Samuel 1:11
A long life
Long life is what Solomon did not ask for (2 Chronicles 1:11); Hannah asked for a son (1:11).
Wealth for her household
Hannah’s vow mentions no wealth; she asked for a son whom she would dedicate to the LORD (1:11).
Victory over enemies
Hannah speaks of her enemies only later, in her song (1 Samuel 2:1); her vow asked for a son.
A son
A daughter
Hannah asked specifically for a son (1:11); she later also bore two daughters (1 Samuel 2:21).
When Eli watched Hannah praying in 1 Samuel 1, what did he wrongly think about her?
Because her lips moved but her voice could not be heard, “Eli thought she was drunk” and said, “How long will you be drunk?” (1:13–14).
1 Samuel 1:13-14
She was ill
Eli did not think Hannah was ill; he told her, “Put away your wine!” (1:14).
She was possessed
Eli never suggested possession; he accused her of drunkenness, and she replied that she was “troubled in spirit” (1:14–15).
She was drunk
She was a foreigner
Hannah was the wife of the Ephraimite Elkanah (1:1–2), and Eli never questioned where she was from.
She was hiding something from Elkanah
Eli’s mistake had nothing to do with Elkanah; he thought she was drunk (1:13).
In Hannah’s prayer scene at Shiloh, how was she speaking before the LORD?
“Hannah was praying in her heart, and though her lips were moving, her voice could not be heard” (1:13), which is why Eli thought she was drunk.
1 Samuel 1:13
Aloud before the assembly, with her hands raised to heaven
Hannah did not pray aloud; “her voice could not be heard” (1:13).
In a loud song of praise, with tambourines and dancing
Hannah’s song of praise comes later, when she gives Samuel to the LORD (1 Samuel 2:1); at first she prayed silently in her heart (1:13).
In her heart, with her lips moving but no voice heard
Through Eli the priest, who spoke her request at the altar
Hannah prayed directly to the LORD (1:10); Eli only watched her mouth and misjudged her (1:12–13).
In a dream, while she slept in the house of the LORD
Hannah was awake and praying in the house of the LORD (1:9–10); it was Samuel who later lay down to sleep in the temple (1 Samuel 3:3).
After Eli accused her in 1 Samuel 1, what did Hannah say she had not consumed?
Hannah replied, “I have not had any wine or strong drink, but I have poured out my soul before the LORD” (1:15).
1 Samuel 1:15
Bread or meat
Hannah’s earlier refusal to eat (1:7) is a different matter; to Eli she denied drinking wine or strong drink (1:15).
Water or milk
Milk is paired with honey in the description of the promised land (Exodus 3:8); Hannah denied having wine or strong drink (1:15).
Oil or vinegar
Vinegar appears when Boaz invited Ruth to dip her bread (Ruth 2:14); Hannah spoke of wine and strong drink (1:15).
Wine or strong drink
Honey or dates
Honey belongs to Jonathan’s story, when he tasted the honeycomb (1 Samuel 14:27); Hannah denied wine and strong drink (1:15).
In response to Hannah’s explanation in 1 Samuel 1, what blessing did Eli pronounce over her?
Eli replied, “Go in peace,” and added, “may the God of Israel grant the petition you have asked of Him” (1:17).
1 Samuel 1:17
May the ark return safely
The ark was captured only later, when Hophni and Phinehas died (1 Samuel 4:11); Eli’s blessing concerned Hannah’s petition.
May your husband honor you
Eli did not mention Elkanah; he asked the God of Israel to grant Hannah’s petition (1:17).
May the God of Israel grant your petition
May your enemies fall before you
Eli’s words were not about enemies; he sent her off in peace with a prayer for her petition (1:17).
May your daughters be many
Eli did not speak of daughters, though Hannah later had two (1 Samuel 2:21); he blessed her petition (1:17).
After speaking with Eli in 1 Samuel 1, what immediate change is noted about Hannah?
After Eli’s blessing, Hannah “went on her way, and she began to eat, and her face was no longer downcast” (1:18).
1 Samuel 1:18
She went home at once
The family did not leave at once; they rose early the next morning to worship and then returned home to Ramah (1:19).
She stopped praying permanently
Hannah did not stop praying; she prayed again in her song when she gave Samuel to the LORD (1 Samuel 2:1).
She ate, and her face was no longer downcast
She confronted Peninnah
Hannah never confronts Peninnah in the chapter; the change noted is that she ate and was no longer downcast (1:18).
She gave away her portion
The portions were Elkanah’s gift to her (1:5); 1:18 says she began to eat, not that she gave her portion away.
After Elkanah and Hannah returned home to Ramah in 1 Samuel 1, what happened next?
At Ramah, “Elkanah had relations with his wife Hannah, and the LORD remembered her,” and in time she conceived and bore a son (1:19–20).
1 Samuel 1:19-20
Peninnah moved away
Peninnah’s whereabouts are never mentioned after the taunting (1:6–7); the next event is that the LORD remembered Hannah (1:19).
Eli visited them
Eli did not visit Ramah; Hannah later brought the boy to Eli at Shiloh (1:25).
The LORD remembered Hannah, and she conceived
Samuel was immediately taken to Shiloh
Samuel was not taken to Shiloh until he was weaned (1:22–24).
Elkanah became priest
Elkanah was an Ephraimite (1:1), not a priest; the priests at Shiloh were Hophni and Phinehas (1:3).
In the birth account of 1 Samuel 1, what name did Hannah give her son?
Hannah “gave birth to a son. She named him Samuel” (1:20).
1 Samuel 1:20
Ichabod
Ichabod was the son of Phinehas’s wife, named when the ark was captured (1 Samuel 4:21).
Nathan
Nathan was the prophet of David’s day (2 Samuel 7:2), not Hannah’s son.
Samuel
Joel
Joel was Samuel’s own firstborn son (1 Samuel 8:2), not the name Hannah gave her child.
Abner
Abner was the commander of Saul’s army (1 Samuel 14:50).
Why did Hannah say she named the child Samuel in 1 Samuel 1?
She named him Samuel, “saying, ‘Because I have asked for him from the LORD’” (1:20).
1 Samuel 1:20
Because he was born in Shiloh
Samuel was born after the family returned home to Ramah (1:19–20), not at Shiloh.
Because he looked like Eli
The chapter never compares the child to Eli; Hannah explained the name by her prayer (1:20).
Because he was the firstborn of Elkanah
Peninnah already had sons and daughters by Elkanah (1:2, 4), so Samuel was not Elkanah’s firstborn.
Because she had asked for him from the LORD
Because Peninnah chose the name
Hannah named the boy herself (1:20); Peninnah had no part in it.
When Elkanah went up again for the yearly sacrifice in 1 Samuel 1, why did Hannah stay home?
Hannah told her husband, “After the boy is weaned … I will take him to appear before the LORD and to stay there permanently” (1:22).
1 Samuel 1:22
She was angry with Eli
Hannah had parted from Eli in peace with his blessing (1:17–18); she stayed home to wean the boy (1:22).
She was waiting until the child was weaned
She was too old to travel
Age is never mentioned for Hannah (that was Sarah’s situation in Genesis 18:11); she stayed home until the boy was weaned (1:22).
She had taken a Nazirite vow herself
Hannah’s vow concerned her son—“no razor shall ever touch his head” (1:11)—not a Nazirite vow for herself.
She was caring for Peninnah’s children
Peninnah’s children are not mentioned here; Hannah stayed home to nurse her own son until he was weaned (1:23).
In Hannah’s plan for Samuel in 1 Samuel 1, what did she intend to do after he was weaned?
Hannah said, “After the boy is weaned … I will take him to appear before the LORD and to stay there permanently” (1:22).
1 Samuel 1:22
Send him to live with relatives in Bethlehem
Bethlehem is where Samuel would later go to anoint David (1 Samuel 16:4); Hannah planned to leave Samuel before the LORD at Shiloh.
Present him before the LORD so he would stay there forever
Dedicate him as a soldier under Saul
Saul was not yet king; Samuel himself would later anoint Saul (1 Samuel 10:1).
Enroll him among the musicians of David
David’s appointment of musicians came generations later (1 Chronicles 25:1); Hannah meant Samuel to stay before the LORD (1:22).
Return him to Ramah after one feast
Hannah intended him “to stay there permanently” (1:22), not to return home after a feast.
How did Elkanah respond to Hannah’s decision to wait before bringing Samuel to Shiloh in 1 Samuel 1?
Elkanah replied, “Do what you think is best,” and told her to “stay here until you have weaned him. Only may the LORD confirm His word” (1:23).
1 Samuel 1:23
He forbade any delay, since the vow had to be kept at once
Elkanah did not forbid the delay; he told her, “Do what you think is best” (1:23).
He told her to do what she thought best and stay until he was weaned
He insisted she bring the boy to Shiloh with him that year
Elkanah let Hannah stay home that year (1:23); she brought the boy only after he was weaned (1:24).
He told her to go and ask Eli the priest to decide the matter
Eli had no part in the decision; Elkanah left it to Hannah’s judgment (1:23).
He sent Peninnah to Shiloh in her place to fulfill the vow
Peninnah was not sent in her place; Hannah herself later brought the boy to Shiloh (1:24).
When Hannah finally took the young Samuel to the house of the LORD at Shiloh in 1 Samuel 1, which offering accompanied him?
Hannah brought the boy “along with a three-year-old bull, an ephah of flour, and a skin of wine” (1:24).
1 Samuel 1:24
A lamb, oil, and incense
Lambs were the daily burnt offering under the Law (Exodus 29:38); Hannah brought a bull, flour, and wine (1:24).
A three-year-old bull, an ephah of flour, and a skin of wine
Two doves, barley, and salt
Doves recall the offering of Mary and Joseph (Luke 2:24); Hannah brought a three-year-old bull, flour, and wine (1:24).
A ram, figs, and honey
Figs were among Abigail’s gifts to David (1 Samuel 25:18); Hannah’s offering was a bull, an ephah of flour, and a skin of wine.
Three lambs and a drink offering of water
Water was poured out to the LORD by David (2 Samuel 23:16); Hannah brought a bull, flour, and a skin of wine (1:24).
After the bull was slaughtered in 1 Samuel 1, to whom did Hannah and her household bring the boy Samuel?
“When they had slaughtered the bull, they brought the boy to Eli” (1:25).
1 Samuel 1:25
To Hophni
Hophni was one of Eli’s sons (1:3), but the boy was brought to Eli himself (1:25).
To Phinehas
Phinehas served as a priest at Shiloh (1:3), but the boy was brought to Eli (1:25).
To the elders of Ephraim
No elders of Ephraim are mentioned; the boy was brought to Eli (1:25).
To Eli
To a Levite from Ramah
No Levite from Ramah appears in the chapter; the boy was brought to Eli the priest (1:25).
Standing before Eli again in 1 Samuel 1, how did Hannah identify herself?
Hannah said, “I am the woman who stood here beside you praying to the LORD” (1:26).
1 Samuel 1:26
As Peninnah’s sister, who had come up with Elkanah’s household
Hannah and Peninnah were rival wives of Elkanah (1:2, 6), not sisters.
As the woman who stood there praying to the LORD
As a singer from Ephraim who served at the house of the LORD
Hannah did not call herself a singer; she reminded Eli that she had stood there praying (1:26).
As a servant who kept watch over the ark of God
Hannah identified herself by her earlier prayer (1:26); the ark is not mentioned in the chapter.
As a widow from Ramah who had come to seek a blessing
Hannah was not a widow; her husband Elkanah was alive and with her (1:23).
In Hannah’s words to Eli in 1 Samuel 1, what did she say about Samuel?
Hannah told Eli, “I prayed for this boy, and since the LORD has granted me what I asked of Him, I now dedicate the boy to the LORD” (1:27–28).
1 Samuel 1:27
“I prayed for this boy”
“This child was born during harvest”
The chapter never says when Samuel was born; Hannah tied him to her prayer (1:27).
“He will judge Israel”
Samuel did judge Israel all his life (1 Samuel 7:15), but Hannah did not say this to Eli.
“He belongs to my husband alone”
Hannah said the opposite: she dedicated the boy to the LORD for as long as he lived (1:28).
“He was promised by Peninnah”
Peninnah promised nothing; Hannah said the LORD had granted what she asked (1:27).
What did Hannah do with Samuel once the LORD had granted her request in 1 Samuel 1?
Hannah said, “I now dedicate the boy to the LORD. For as long as he lives, he is dedicated to the LORD” (1:28), fulfilling her vow of 1:11.
1 Samuel 1:28
She crowned him before the people
Samuel was never crowned; years later he himself anointed Saul (1 Samuel 10:1).
She dedicated him to the LORD for all his life
She sent him to study in Egypt
It was Moses who was raised in Pharaoh’s household (Exodus 2:10); Samuel stayed to minister before Eli (1 Samuel 2:11).
She kept him hidden from Eli
Hannah did the opposite and brought the boy directly to Eli (1:25).
She gave him to Peninnah to raise
Samuel stayed at Shiloh ministering before Eli the priest (1 Samuel 2:11), not with Peninnah.
In the prayer scene of 1 Samuel 1, where was Eli sitting when Hannah began praying in bitterness of soul?
1:9 says, “Eli the priest was sitting on a chair by the doorpost of the temple of the LORD.”
1 Samuel 1:9
Beside the altar of burnt offering in the courtyard
Eli was seated by the doorpost of the temple (1:9), not at the altar.
At the city gate among the elders of Shiloh
Eli later sat on his chair by the city gate when he heard the ark was taken (1 Samuel 4:18); in 1:9 he sat by the doorpost of the temple.
On his chair by the doorpost of the temple of the LORD
Inside the Most Holy Place before the ark of God
Eli sat at the doorpost of the temple of the LORD (1:9), not inside the Most Holy Place.
Under an oak tree at Ramah near Elkanah’s house
Ramah was Elkanah’s home (1:19); the prayer scene took place at Shiloh, with Eli by the temple doorpost (1:9).
In Hannah’s vow concerning the son she asked for in 1 Samuel 1, what outward sign did she promise would mark his life?
Hannah vowed, “I will dedicate him to the LORD all the days of his life, and no razor shall ever touch his head” (1:11).
1 Samuel 1:11
He would wear royal robes
Hannah’s vow said nothing of royal robes; the sign was that no razor would touch his head (1:11).
He would eat no grain
The Nazirite law restricted wine and grapes (Numbers 6:3), not grain; Hannah’s vow named the uncut hair (1:11).
No razor would ever touch his head
He would never leave Ramah
Samuel later traveled a circuit to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah (1 Samuel 7:16); the vow concerned his uncut hair (1:11).
He would carry the ark
Hannah’s vow did not mention the ark; the sign was that no razor would touch his head (1:11).
In the formal introduction to Elkanah in 1 Samuel 1, which ancestral sequence is given after his own name?
Elkanah is introduced as “the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuph, an Ephraimite” (1:1).
1 Samuel 1:1
Son of Jesse, son of Obed, son of Boaz, son of Salmon
Salmon, Boaz, Obed, and Jesse belong to David’s line (Ruth 4:21–22), not to Elkanah’s.
Son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph
Son of Kish, son of Ner, son of Abiel, son of Zeror
Kish, Ner, Abiel, and Zeror are Saul’s Benjamite ancestors (1 Samuel 9:1; 1 Chronicles 8:33).
Son of Amram, son of Kohath, son of Levi, son of Jacob
Levi, Kohath, and Amram are the ancestors of Moses and Aaron (Exodus 6:18, 20).
Son of Hilkiah, son of Shallum, son of Zadok, son of Ahitub
Hilkiah, Shallum, Zadok, and Ahitub appear in Ezra’s priestly genealogy (Ezra 7:1–2).
In the opening prayer of 1 Samuel 2, after young Samuel had been dedicated at Shiloh, whose heart rejoiced in the LORD?
1 Samuel 2:1 begins, “At that time Hannah prayed: ‘My heart rejoices in the LORD.’”
1 Samuel 2:1
Miriam
Miriam sang after the Red Sea crossing (Exodus 15:20–21), not at Samuel’s dedication.
Hannah
Abigail
Abigail was the widow of Nabal and later David’s wife (2 Samuel 2:2), not the one praying here.
Deborah
Deborah sang after Barak’s victory (Judges 5:1), not at Shiloh.
Elizabeth
Elizabeth is from the New Testament (Luke 1:5), not this prayer.
In the Shiloh account of 1 Samuel 2, where did Elkanah go while the boy Samuel remained to minister before the LORD?
1 Samuel 2:11 says Elkanah went home to Ramah while the boy began ministering to the LORD before Eli the priest.
1 Samuel 2:11
Bethlehem
Bethlehem is not named in 1 Samuel 2:11; Elkanah went home to Ramah.
Hebron
Hebron is not named in 1 Samuel 2:11; Elkanah went home to Ramah.
Ramah
Gibeah
Gibeah was Saul’s hometown later (1 Samuel 10:26), not Elkanah’s.
Beersheba
Beersheba is not named in 1 Samuel 2:11; Elkanah went home to Ramah.
According to 1 Samuel 2, under which priest did the boy Samuel minister before the LORD?
1 Samuel 2:11 says the boy began ministering to the LORD before Eli the priest.
1 Samuel 2:11
Zadok
Zadok became priest under Solomon (1 Kings 2:35), long after Samuel’s boyhood.
Abiathar
Abiathar served David later (1 Kings 2:35), not Samuel in his boyhood.
Ahimelech
Ahimelech was a priest at Nob in David’s time (1 Samuel 21:1), not at Shiloh in Samuel’s boyhood.
Eli
Jehoiada
Jehoiada was a priest in the days of the kings (2 Kings 11:4), centuries later.
In the description of young Samuel serving at Shiloh in 1 Samuel 2, what was he wearing?
1 Samuel 2:18 says Samuel was ministering before the LORD, “a boy wearing a linen ephod.”
1 Samuel 2:18
A crown of gold
A golden crown is not mentioned; Samuel wore a linen ephod (2:18).
A linen ephod
A camel-hair cloak
A camel-hair cloak was John the Baptist’s clothing (Matthew 3:4), not Samuel’s.
A soldier’s tunic
A soldier’s tunic is not mentioned; Samuel wore a linen ephod (2:18).
A scarlet sash
A scarlet sash is not mentioned; Samuel wore a linen ephod (2:18).
Each year in 1 Samuel 2, what did Hannah make and bring to Samuel when she came with Elkanah to offer the annual sacrifice?
1 Samuel 2:19 says his mother would make him a little robe and bring it to him each year when she went with her husband to offer the annual sacrifice.
1 Samuel 2:19
A little robe
A silver cup
A silver cup is not mentioned; Hannah brought a little robe each year (2:19).
A pair of sandals
Sandals are not mentioned; Hannah brought a little robe each year (2:19).
A basket of grain
A basket of grain is not mentioned; Hannah brought a little robe each year (2:19).
A scroll
A scroll is not mentioned; Hannah brought a little robe each year (2:19).
After Samuel was dedicated, how many additional children did God give Hannah according to 1 Samuel 2?
1 Samuel 2:21 says the LORD attended to Hannah, and she gave birth to three sons and two daughters.
1 Samuel 2:21
Two sons and one daughter
Two sons and one daughter is too few; she had three sons and two daughters (2:21).
One son and three daughters
One son and three daughters is not the count; she had three sons and two daughters (2:21).
Three sons and two daughters
Four sons only
Four sons only is not the count; she had three sons and two daughters (2:21).
No more children
The LORD attended to Hannah, and she had more children (2:21).
In 1 Samuel 2, how are Eli’s sons Hophni and Phinehas described before their sins at Shiloh are detailed?
1 Samuel 2:12 says, “Now the sons of Eli were wicked men; they had no regard for the LORD.”
1 Samuel 2:12
Faithful priests who served the LORD well
Eli’s sons were priests, but not faithful ones; they had no regard for the LORD (2:12).
Wise elders who judged the people
Eli’s sons are not called wise elders; they were wicked men (2:12).
Wicked men who had no regard for the LORD
Mighty warriors who defended Shiloh
They are not described as warriors; they are described as wicked men (2:12).
Skilled musicians who led the worship
They are not described as musicians; they are described as wicked men (2:12).
In the account of abused sacrifices at Shiloh in 1 Samuel 2, what utensil did the servant of Eli’s sons use to take meat from worshipers’ offerings?
1 Samuel 2:13 says the servant of the priest would come with a three-pronged meat fork while the meat was boiling.
1 Samuel 2:13-14
A golden censer
A golden censer is used for incense; the servant used a three-pronged meat fork (2:13).
A two-edged sword
A two-edged sword is not mentioned; the servant used a three-pronged meat fork (2:13).
A three-pronged fork
A measuring reed
A measuring reed is not mentioned; the servant used a three-pronged meat fork (2:13).
A pruning hook
A pruning hook is not mentioned; the servant used a three-pronged meat fork (2:13).
In 1 Samuel 2, what kind of meat did Eli’s sons demand from the man offering sacrifice at Shiloh?
1 Samuel 2:15 has the servant say, “he will not accept boiled meat from you, but only raw.”
1 Samuel 2:15
Dried meat
Dried meat is not mentioned; the demand was for raw meat to roast (2:15).
Raw meat
Salted fish
Salted fish is not mentioned; the demand was for raw meat to roast (2:15).
Boiled lentils
Lentils are not mentioned; the demand was for raw meat to roast (2:15).
Roasted grain
Roasted grain is not mentioned; the demand was for raw meat to roast (2:15).
In the sacrificial abuse described in 1 Samuel 2, when did Eli’s sons demand meat from the worshiper?
1 Samuel 2:15 says the servant would come “Even before the fat was burned.”
1 Samuel 2:15-16
After the feast ended
The demand came before the offering was finished, not after the feast ended (2:15).
Before the fat was burned
Only after the priestly blessing
There was no waiting for a priestly blessing; the demand came before the fat was burned (2:15).
On the next day
The demand came at once, not the next day (2:15–16).
After the Ark was carried out
The ark is not mentioned in this scene; the demand came before the fat was burned (2:15).
Besides taking the offerings improperly, what sin of Hophni and Phinehas did Eli hear about in 1 Samuel 2?
1 Samuel 2:22 says Eli heard “how they were sleeping with the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.”
1 Samuel 2:22
They burned incense to Baal on the high places
Burning incense to Baal is not mentioned; the sin was sleeping with the women at the Tent of Meeting (2:22).
They stole silver from the tabernacle treasury
The ark was captured in battle later (1 Samuel 4:11); Eli’s complaint here was about sexual sin (2:22).
They slept with the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting
They publicly cursed the boy Samuel
Cursing Samuel is not mentioned; the sin was sleeping with the women at the Tent of Meeting (2:22).
They refused to keep the Passover each year
Refusing Passover is not mentioned; the sin was sleeping with the women at the Tent of Meeting (2:22).
In Eli’s rebuke to his sons in 1 Samuel 2, why did Hophni and Phinehas not listen to their father’s voice?
1 Samuel 2:25 says they would not listen to their father, “since the LORD intended to put them to death.”
1 Samuel 2:25
Because the people supported them
The people’s support is not given as the reason; the LORD intended to put them to death (2:25).
Because Eli was too old to discipline them
Eli’s age is not given as the reason; the LORD intended to put them to death (2:25).
Because Samuel had already judged them
Samuel had not judged them; he was still a boy growing in favor with the LORD (2:26).
Because the LORD intended to put them to death
Because they had fled from Shiloh
They had not fled Shiloh; the reason was that the LORD intended to put them to death (2:25).
According to Hannah’s prayer in 1 Samuel 2:2, there is no one holy like the LORD, and there is no what like our God?
1 Samuel 2:2 has Hannah say, “And there is no Rock like our God.”
1 Samuel 2:2
Shepherd
The shepherd image is used of the LORD in Psalm 23:1, but Hannah’s line is about a Rock (2:2).
Rock
Vine
The vine image appears in John 15:1, not in Hannah’s line about a Rock (2:2).
Lamp
The lamp image appears in Psalm 119:105, not in Hannah’s line about a Rock (2:2).
Fortress gate
A fortress gate is not in Hannah’s line; she says there is no Rock like our God (2:2).
According to Hannah’s song in 1 Samuel 2, what does she say cannot make a person prevail?
1 Samuel 2:9 says, “for by his own strength shall no man prevail.”
1 Samuel 2:9
Wealth
Wealth is not what she names; she says no man prevails by his own strength (2:9).
Noble birth
Noble birth is not what she names; she says no man prevails by his own strength (2:9).
Military skill
Military skill is not what she names; she says no man prevails by his own strength (2:9).
His own strength
Long life
Long life is not what she names; she says no man prevails by his own strength (2:9).
At the close of Hannah’s prayer in 1 Samuel 2, to whom will the LORD give power, and whose horn will He exalt?
1 Samuel 2:10 says the LORD “will give power to His king. He will exalt the horn of His anointed.”
1 Samuel 2:10
His priest and His Levite
A priest and a Levite are not named; the LORD gives power to His king and exalts His anointed (2:10).
His prophet and His messenger
A prophet and messenger are not named; the LORD gives power to His king and exalts His anointed (2:10).
His king and His anointed
His people and Jerusalem
His people and Jerusalem are not named; the LORD gives power to His king and exalts His anointed (2:10).
His judge and Israel
A judge and Israel are not named; the LORD gives power to His king and exalts His anointed (2:10).
When the man of God confronted Eli in 1 Samuel 2, what did he say Eli was doing above the LORD?
1 Samuel 2:29 says, “You have honored your sons more than Me by fattening yourselves with the best of all the offerings of My people Israel.”
1 Samuel 2:29
Honoring his sons above Him
Moving the sanctuary to Ramah
Moving the sanctuary to Ramah is not charged; Eli honored his sons more than the LORD (2:29).
Hiding the ephod
Hiding the ephod is not charged; Eli honored his sons more than the LORD (2:29).
Refusing to teach the Law
Refusing to teach the Law is not charged; Eli honored his sons more than the LORD (2:29).
Trusting Pharaoh for help
Trusting Pharaoh is not charged; the LORD recalls that He revealed Himself to Eli’s father’s house in Egypt (2:27), and Eli honored his sons above Him (2:29).
In the prophecy against Eli’s house in 1 Samuel 2, what principle did the LORD declare about honor and contempt?
1 Samuel 2:30 says, “I will honor those who honor Me, but those who despise Me will be disdained.”
1 Samuel 2:30
Those who honor Me I will honor, but those who despise Me will be disdained
Those who fast will rule, but those who feast will fall
Fasting and feasting are not the principle; the LORD honors those who honor Him (2:30).
Those who sacrifice much will become kings
Sacrificing much is not the principle; the LORD honors those who honor Him (2:30).
Those who fear Eli will be blessed
Fearing Eli is not the principle; the LORD honors those who honor Him (2:30).
Those who judge Israel will never die
Judging Israel is not the principle, and Eli’s line was told it would not reach old age (2:31–32).
What sign did the man of God give Eli in 1 Samuel 2 to confirm that judgment would come on his house?
1 Samuel 2:34 says, “this sign shall come to you concerning your two sons Hophni and Phinehas: They will both die on the same day.”
1 Samuel 2:34
Fire would fall on Shiloh
Fire falling on Shiloh is not the sign given; the sign is that both sons die on the same day (2:34).
The Ark would disappear for a year
The ark’s disappearance is not the sign given; the sign is that both sons die on the same day (2:34). The ark was captured later (4:11).
Hophni and Phinehas would both die on the same day
The altar would split in two
The altar splitting is not the sign given; the sign is that both sons die on the same day (2:34).
A famine would strike Ephraim
A famine in Ephraim is not the sign given; the sign is that both sons die on the same day (2:34).
After announcing judgment on Eli’s line in 1 Samuel 2, what kind of servant did the LORD promise to raise up for Himself?
1 Samuel 2:35 has the LORD say, “I will raise up for Myself a faithful priest. He will do whatever is in My heart and mind.”
1 Samuel 2:35
A warrior king who would defeat the Philistines
A warrior king is not promised here; the LORD promises a faithful priest (2:35).
A faithful priest who would do according to God’s heart and mind
A prophet from Bethlehem who would anoint kings
A prophet from Bethlehem is not promised here; the LORD promises a faithful priest (2:35).
A Levite singer who would lead the worship
A Levite singer is not promised here; the LORD promises a faithful priest (2:35).
A judge from Dan who would deliver Israel
A judge from Dan is not promised here; the LORD promises a faithful priest (2:35).
According to the closing prophecy against Eli’s descendants in 1 Samuel 2, what humiliating request would those left in his house make?

1 Samuel 2:36 says everyone left in Eli’s house would bow down to the faithful priest for a piece of silver or a morsel of bread, pleading, “Please appoint me to some priestly office so that I can eat a piece of bread.”
1 Samuel 2:36
A vineyard and a field
A vineyard and a field are not requested; they beg for a priestly office to eat (2:36).
A place among the royal guards
A place among the royal guards is not requested; they beg for a priestly office to eat (2:36).
Some priestly office so they could eat a piece of bread
A seat among the singers for oil and wine
A seat among the singers for oil and wine is not requested; they beg for a priestly office to eat (2:36).
A judge’s robe and staff
A judge’s robe and staff are not requested; they beg for a priestly office to eat (2:36).
In the opening of 1 Samuel 3 at Shiloh, under whom did the boy Samuel minister before the LORD?
The boy Samuel ministered to the LORD before Eli (3:1).
1 Samuel 3:1
Ahimelech
Ahimelech served as a priest in Saul’s day, after Samuel’s boyhood.
Eli
Zadok
Zadok became a leading priest in David’s time, long after Eli.
Phinehas
Phinehas was Eli’s son, a priest who died with his brother when the ark was captured (1 Samuel 4:11), not Samuel’s master.
Abiathar
Abiathar was a priest in David’s reign, not the one Samuel served as a boy.
In Samuel’s call narrative, what was said to be rare in those days?
In those days the word of the LORD was rare, and visions were scarce (3:1).
1 Samuel 3:1
Sacrifices

Samuel did not summon the elders; he spoke privately with Saul.
He told the servant to go on ahead while Saul stayed
He sent Saul back to Kish immediately
Samuel did not send Saul home; he kept him for the word of God.
He ordered a trumpet to be blown
No trumpet is mentioned at the edge of the city.
He called for the ark
The ark is not mentioned in this chapter.
In 1 Samuel 10, when Samuel privately anointed Saul as ruler, what did he pour on Saul’s head?
Samuel “took a flask of oil, poured it on Saul’s head” as the sign of anointing (10:1).
1 Samuel 10:1
Water
Water was for washing and cleansing; Scripture’s anointings of kings use oil, as when Samuel later anoints David with the horn of oil (1 Samuel 16:13).
Honey
Honey is food in Scripture, as in the land “flowing with milk and honey” (Exodus 3:8), not anointing material.
Oil
Wine
Wine appears in this chapter only as a skin carried by one of the three men Saul would meet (10:3), not as the anointing substance.
Ashes
Ashes marked mourning, as when Mordecai put on sackcloth and ashes (Esther 4:1); they were no sign of a ruler’s anointing.
In Samuel’s first sign to Saul in 1 Samuel 10, what animals were reported as already found?
Samuel said the two men near Rachel’s tomb would tell Saul that the donkeys he sought had been found (10:2).
1 Samuel 10:2
Sheep
Sheep belong to David’s story (1 Samuel 16:11); Saul had been searching for his father’s donkeys, not sheep.
Donkeys
Goats
Goats appear in the next sign, where one of the three men carries three young goats (10:3), but they were not the lost animals.
Oxen
Oxen come up later when Saul cuts a pair of them into pieces to rally Israel (1 Samuel 11:7); the lost animals were donkeys.
Camels
No camels are mentioned here; the animals that wandered off were the donkeys of Saul’s father Kish (1 Samuel 9:3).
After Saul left Samuel, what message were the two men near Rachel’s tomb at Zelzah on the border of Benjamin supposed to give him?
Samuel told Saul the two men would say the donkeys had been found and that his father had stopped worrying about the donkeys and started worrying about him (10:2).
1 Samuel 10:2
The Philistines were attacking Gibeah and Saul must return to fight them
The Philistines have an outpost at Gibeah of God (10:5), but the two men report no attack there.
Samuel had gone up to Bethel and Saul must follow him there at once
Bethel is where the three men of the next sign were headed (10:3); the two men at Rachel’s tomb say nothing of Samuel going there.
His servant had gone back home, and his father was worried about the servant
Saul’s servant stays with him throughout (10:14); the message concerns the donkeys and Saul’s father.
The donkeys had been found, and his father was worried about him
Samuel had anointed David in Bethlehem, and Saul must now return to Gibeah
David’s anointing in Bethlehem comes later (1 Samuel 16:13) and is no part of this message to Saul.
In the sign Samuel gave Saul about the oak of Tabor, where were the three men going up to worship?
Samuel said three men “going up to God at Bethel” would meet Saul at the Oak of Tabor (10:3).
1 Samuel 10:3
Bethel
Shiloh
Shiloh was where the tabernacle stood in Joshua’s day (Joshua 18:1), but it is not the place named in Samuel’s sign.
Hebron
Hebron is where David was later anointed king over Judah (2 Samuel 2:4), not where these men were headed.
Beersheba
Beersheba was where Samuel’s sons served as judges (1 Samuel 8:2); the three men were going to Bethel.
Jerusalem
Jerusalem is not mentioned in this chapter’s signs; the three men were going up to God at Bethel.
At the oak of Tabor in 1 Samuel 10, how many loaves of bread would the travelers give to Saul?
One man carried three loaves, but Samuel said the three men would greet Saul and give him two loaves of bread (10:3–4).
1 Samuel 10:3-4
One
The men give two loaves, not one (10:4).
Two
Three
Three is the number of loaves one man carried (10:3), but only two were given to Saul (10:4).
Four
Four loaves are never mentioned; the sign says two loaves (10:4).
Five
Five loaves are not mentioned in this sign; Saul would receive two loaves (10:4).
Near Gibeah of God, where the Philistine garrison was stationed, what group was Saul told he would meet coming down from the high place?
Samuel said that as Saul approached the city he would meet a group of prophets coming down from the high place (10:5).
1 Samuel 10:5
Priests
Priests are not mentioned in this sign; it is a group of prophets who come down from the high place.
Soldiers
The only military force here is the Philistine outpost in Gibeah of God (10:5), not the group Saul would meet.
Prophets
Shepherds
Shepherds do not appear in this sign; Saul meets prophets with musical instruments.
Scribes
Scribes are not mentioned in this passage; the group coming down from the high place is a company of prophets.
In the scene near Gibeah of God in 1 Samuel 10, which set of instruments was associated with the prophets?
The prophets would come down “preceded by harps, tambourines, flutes, and lyres” as they prophesied (10:5).
1 Samuel 10:5
Harp, cymbals, flute, and trumpet
Cymbals and a trumpet are not in the list; 10:5 names harps, tambourines, flutes, and lyres.
Harp, tambourine, flute, and lyre
Lyre, trumpet, drum, and cymbals
Trumpets, drums, and cymbals are not named in 10:5; the instruments there are harps, tambourines, flutes, and lyres.
Tambourine, horn, lyre, and harp
A horn is not among the instruments in 10:5, which lists harps, tambourines, flutes, and lyres.
Flute, harp, trumpet, and shofar
Trumpets and shofars are not in the list; 10:5 names harps, tambourines, flutes, and lyres.
According to Samuel’s word to Saul in 1 Samuel 10, what would happen when the Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon him?
Samuel said the Spirit of the LORD would rush upon Saul, he would prophesy, and he would “be transformed into a different person” (10:6).
1 Samuel 10:6
He would defeat the Philistines immediately
The Philistines appear only as holding an outpost (10:5); Saul’s clashes with them come later and are not promised here.
He would become high priest
Saul never becomes high priest; Samuel’s word is that he would prophesy and be changed.
He would prophesy and be transformed into a different person
He would return at once to his father’s house
Samuel told Saul to do as the occasion demanded because God was with him (10:7), not to go home at once.
He would build an altar at Mizpah
Mizpah is where Samuel later gathers the people (10:17), not a place where Saul builds an altar.
In Samuel’s instructions after the anointing, to which place was Saul told to go ahead and wait seven days?
Samuel told Saul to go ahead of him to Gilgal and wait seven days until Samuel came to offer sacrifices and show him what to do (10:8).
1 Samuel 10:8
Mizpah
Mizpah is where Samuel later summoned the people to choose a king (10:17), not the place Saul was told to wait.
Bethel
Bethel was the destination of the three men in the second sign (10:3), not the place of Saul’s seven-day wait.
Nob
Nob is not mentioned in this chapter; Samuel sent Saul to Gilgal.
Gilgal
Carmel
Carmel is not mentioned in this chapter; Samuel’s instruction was to go to Gilgal.
When people at Gibeah saw Saul prophesying with the prophets, what saying became a proverb?
When people saw Saul prophesying with the prophets, “Is Saul also among the prophets?” became a proverb (10:11–12).
1 Samuel 10:11-12
“Can anything good come from Nazareth?”
“Can anything good come from Nazareth?” is Nathanael’s question about Jesus (John 1:46), unrelated to Saul.
“Is Saul also among the prophets?”
“The battle is the LORD’s”
“The battle is the LORD’s” echoes David’s declaration to Goliath (1 Samuel 17:47), not the saying about Saul.
“Whoever is for the LORD, come to me.”
“Whoever is for the LORD, come to me” is Moses’ call at the golden calf (Exodus 32:26), not the saying about Saul.
“Does the LORD speak only through Moses?”
“Does the LORD speak only through Moses?” is what Miriam and Aaron said (Numbers 12:2), not a saying about Saul.
When Saul prophesied at Gibeah in 1 Samuel 10 and people questioned what was happening, what question did a man there ask?
A man who lived there replied, “And who is their father?” (10:12), and the saying about Saul among the prophets became a proverb.
1 Samuel 10:12
“Where is Samuel?”
The people do not ask about Samuel; their wonder is about Saul among the prophets (10:11).
“Who anointed him?”
Nobody asks who anointed Saul; the onlookers ask what has happened to the son of Kish (10:11).
“Is this not Kish’s son?”
The onlookers ask “What has happened to the son of Kish?” (10:11), which is not the question the man at Gibeah asked.
“Why has he come here?”
No one asks why Saul has come; the man’s reply is the question about the prophets’ father (10:12).
“And who is their father?”
When Saul’s uncle asked what Samuel had told him, what did Saul report?
Saul told his uncle that Samuel had assured them the donkeys had been found, but he did not tell him what Samuel had said about the kingship (10:16).
1 Samuel 10:14-16
That he had been chosen king over Israel
Saul deliberately did not tell his uncle about the kingship (10:16).
That Samuel told him plainly the donkeys had been found
That he must move to Shiloh
Nothing is said of a move to Shiloh anywhere in the chapter.
That he was to fight the Ammonites that day
The Ammonites are not mentioned in this chapter; Saul says nothing about fighting.
That he must build an altar
Building an altar is not part of Saul’s report; he mentions only the donkeys.
In the public selection of Israel’s king in 1 Samuel 10, to what town did Samuel summon the people before the LORD?
Samuel summoned the people to the LORD at Mizpah to choose a king (10:17).
1 Samuel 10:17
Mizpah
Bethlehem
Bethlehem is where David is later anointed (1 Samuel 16:13), not where Israel assembled to choose Saul.
Gilgal
Gilgal is where Samuel told Saul to wait (10:8), not the site of the public selection.
Ramah
Ramah was Samuel’s hometown (1 Samuel 7:17), not the place where he summoned the people.
Jericho
Jericho is not mentioned in this chapter.
At Mizpah, when Samuel had Israel come forward by tribes, which tribe was taken?
Samuel had all the tribes of Israel come forward, “and the tribe of Benjamin was selected” (10:20).
1 Samuel 10:20
Judah
Judah is not selected here; the choice falls on Benjamin, Saul’s tribe.
Ephraim
Ephraim was not selected; the choice narrowed to Benjamin (10:20).
Levi
Levi was the priestly tribe and is not part of this selection; Benjamin was taken.
Benjamin
Issachar
Issachar is not named in this selection; the lot fell on Benjamin (10:20).
After the tribe of Benjamin was taken in 1 Samuel 10, which clan was selected next?
Samuel had Benjamin come forward by its clans, “and the clan of Matri was selected,” and then Saul son of Kish was taken (10:21).
1 Samuel 10:21
The clan of Merari
Merari was a Levite clan, not a clan of Benjamin.
The clan of Korah
Korah was a Levite family, not a clan of Benjamin.
The Matrite clan
The clan of Caleb
Caleb belonged to Judah; the selection was narrowing within Benjamin.
The clan of Gershon
Gershon was a Levite clan, not a clan of Benjamin.
When Saul son of Kish was chosen at Mizpah and the people looked for him, where was he found?
When they looked for Saul and could not find him, the LORD replied, “he has hidden himself among the baggage” (10:21–22).
1 Samuel 10:21-22
In the tabernacle
Saul was not in the tabernacle; the LORD said he was hiding among the baggage (10:22).
Hidden among the supplies
At Rachel’s tomb
Rachel’s tomb was where the first sign was to happen (10:2), not where Saul hid.
With the prophets
Saul had prophesied with the prophets earlier (10:10), but when sought he was hiding among the baggage.
In his father’s field
His father’s field is not mentioned; Saul was hiding among the baggage (10:22).
When Saul stood among the people after being brought out, how does 1 Samuel 10 describe his height?
When Saul stood among the people, “he was a head taller than any of the others” (10:23).
1 Samuel 10:23
He was shorter than Samuel
Saul was not shorter than Samuel; he was a head taller than any of the others (10:23).
He was the same height as everyone else
Saul was taller than all the others, not the same height as everyone.
He was taller only than his servants
The text says he was taller than any of the others, not only taller than his servants.
He was two cubits taller than Abner
Abner is not mentioned in this chapter; Saul stood a head taller than the others (10:23).
He was a head taller than any of the people
After Samuel presented Saul to all Israel, what did the people shout?
Samuel said, “Do you see the one the LORD has chosen?” and all the people shouted, “Long live the king!” (10:24).
1 Samuel 10:24
“The LORD is one!”
“The LORD is One” is Moses’ confession in Deuteronomy 6:4, not the cry at Saul’s presentation.
“Blessed is the son of Kish!”
Blessing the son of Kish is not recorded; the people shouted for the king (10:24).
“Long live the king!”
“Give us a sign!”
A request for a sign is not part of this scene; Samuel had already given Saul the signs (10:2–7).
“Let the ark come here!”
The ark is not mentioned in this chapter.
In 1 Samuel 10, what did Samuel write on a scroll and lay up before the LORD after Saul was presented as king?
Samuel “explained to the people the rights of kingship,” wrote them on a scroll, and laid it up before the LORD (10:25).
1 Samuel 10:25
The genealogy of Benjamin
No genealogy of Benjamin is mentioned; the scroll recorded the rights of kingship.
The boundaries of the kingdom
The boundaries of the kingdom are not mentioned on the scroll.
A list of military officers
A list of military officers is not mentioned on the scroll.
The rights and duties of kingship
The songs of the prophets
The songs of the prophets are not mentioned on the scroll; it was about the rights of kingship.
At the end of 1 Samuel 10, what did some worthless men say about Saul?
Some worthless men said, “How can this man save us?” and despised Saul, but he remained silent about it (10:27).
1 Samuel 10:27
“Can Saul offer sacrifices?”
Sacrifices come up in Samuel’s instructions about Gilgal (10:8), not in the scoffers’ words.
“Why has Samuel deceived us?”
Nobody accuses Samuel of deceit in this scene.
“How can this man save us?”
“Let Jonathan be king!”
Jonathan does not appear in 1 Samuel 10; the scoffers question Saul himself.
“Benjamin is too small to rule!”
Benjamin’s small size is not mentioned here; the scoffers question Saul’s ability to save (10:27).
In the opening of 1 Samuel 11, Nahash the Ammonite besieged which Israelite city in Gilead?
Nahash the Ammonite laid siege to Jabesh-gilead, whose men offered to serve him if he would make a treaty (11:1).
1 Samuel 11:1
Gibeah
Gibeah was Saul’s hometown, where the messengers brought the news (11:4); it was not the city under siege.
Jabesh-gilead
Gilgal
Gilgal is where the people later renewed the kingship (11:14–15), not the city Nahash besieged.
Ramah
Ramah was Samuel’s hometown (1 Samuel 7:17), not a city Nahash besieged.
Bethlehem
Bethlehem was David’s hometown in Judah (1 Samuel 16:1), far from Gilead and not part of this story.
In Saul’s early reign, who was the enemy leader threatening Jabesh-gilead in 1 Samuel 11?
The enemy was Nahash the Ammonite, who besieged Jabesh-gilead (11:1).
1 Samuel 11:1
Goliath the Philistine
Goliath was a Philistine champion killed by David (1 Samuel 17:50), not the Ammonite who threatened Jabesh.
Agag the Amalekite
Agag was king of the Amalekites, whom Saul captured later (1 Samuel 15:8), not the besieger of Jabesh.
Nahash the Ammonite
Achish of Gath
Achish was the Philistine king of Gath who hosted David (1 Samuel 21:10), not an Ammonite.
Sisera the Canaanite
Sisera was a Canaanite commander defeated in the days of the judges (Judges 4:15), long before Saul.
According to 1 Samuel 11, on what humiliating condition would Nahash make a treaty with the men of Jabesh-gilead?
Nahash agreed to a treaty only on the condition that he could put out everyone’s right eye and bring reproach on all Israel (11:2).
1 Samuel 11:2
They must shave their heads
Shaved heads are never mentioned; Nahash demanded the loss of every right eye (11:2).
They must surrender their children
No demand for children is recorded; his condition was putting out every right eye (11:2).
They must pay silver every year
No yearly tribute is mentioned; the humiliating price was the right eye of each man (11:2).
He would gouge out everyone’s right eye
They must leave the city forever
Exile is not mentioned; the men offered to serve Nahash (11:1), and he set the right-eye condition (11:2).
When the elders of Jabesh-gilead answered Nahash in 1 Samuel 11, how long did they ask for to send messengers throughout Israel?
The elders asked Nahash to hold off for seven days so they could send messengers throughout Israel (11:3).
1 Samuel 11:3
3 days
They asked for seven days, not three (11:3).
5 days
They asked for seven days, not five (11:3).
7 days
10 days
They asked for seven days, not ten (11:3).
14 days
They asked for seven days, not fourteen (11:3).
When the messengers arrived at Gibeah of Saul with news from Jabesh-gilead, how did the people respond?
When the messengers relayed the words in the hearing of the people at Gibeah of Saul, they all wept aloud (11:4).
1 Samuel 11:4
They laughed at the threat
No one laughed; the people wept aloud at the news (11:4).
They immediately marched in silence
They did not march at once; they wept, and only after Saul heard did the army gather (11:4–8).
They hid in their houses
No hiding is recorded; the people wept aloud (11:4).
They all wept aloud
They stoned the messengers
The messengers were not harmed; the people wept aloud at their report (11:4).
After Saul heard the words from Jabesh-gilead in 1 Samuel 11, what came upon him?
When Saul heard the words, the Spirit of God rushed upon him and he burned with great anger (11:6).
1 Samuel 11:6
Fear of the Ammonites
Saul was not afraid; the Spirit of God rushed upon him and he burned with anger (11:6).
The Spirit of God, and great anger
A dream in the night
Saul received no dream here; the Spirit of God came upon him as he heard the news (11:6).
A plague on his household
No plague is mentioned; Saul was seized by the Spirit of God and by anger (11:6).
A message from a Philistine scout
No Philistine scout appears; the news came from the messengers of Jabesh (11:4–5).
To summon Israel to battle in 1 Samuel 11, what did Saul do with a pair of oxen?
Saul took a pair of oxen, cut them into pieces, and sent the pieces by messengers throughout Israel as a summons to war (11:7).
1 Samuel 11:7
He offered them as a sacrifice to the LORD at Shiloh
Saul did not sacrifice the oxen; he cut them up and sent the pieces out (11:7).
He yoked them to a war cart and led the army out
Saul did not use the oxen for a war cart; he cut them in pieces as a summons (11:7).
He traded them to the Philistines for swords
Israel had few weapons (1 Samuel 13:19), but Saul did not trade the oxen; he used them as a warning (11:7).
He cut them in pieces and sent the pieces throughout Israel
He gave them to Samuel as a gift for the altar
Saul did not give the oxen to Samuel; he sent the pieces out and named Samuel only in the threat (11:7).
In Saul’s warning sent across Israel with the pieces of oxen, whom did he say the people must follow?
The message threatened that this would be done to the oxen of anyone who did not march behind Saul and Samuel (11:7).
1 Samuel 11:7
Saul and Jonathan
Jonathan is not named in the summons; the call named Saul and Samuel (11:7).
Saul and Samuel
Samuel and Eli
Eli had died long before (1 Samuel 4:18); the summons named Saul and Samuel (11:7).
Saul and Abner
Abner was Saul’s army commander (1 Samuel 14:50), but he is not named in the summons (11:7).
Saul and David
David had not yet entered Saul’s service (1 Samuel 16:21); the summons named Samuel with Saul (11:7).
When Saul mustered the troops to rescue Jabesh-gilead, which report is correct?
Saul numbered the army at Bezek: 300,000 Israelites and 30,000 men of Judah (11:8).
1 Samuel 11:8
At Bezek, 300,000 Israelites and 30,000 men of Judah
At Gilgal, 30,000 Israelites and 300,000 men of Judah
The numbers are swapped and the place is wrong; the muster was at Bezek with 300,000 Israelites and 30,000 men of Judah (11:8).
At Mizpah, 120,000 Israelites and 12,000 men of Judah
Mizpah is where Saul was publicly chosen (1 Samuel 10:17), not where this muster took place, and the totals are wrong (11:8).
At Gibeah, 600,000 Israelites and 60,000 men of Judah
Gibeah was Saul’s home (11:4); the muster was at Bezek and the counts were far smaller (11:8).
At Jabesh-gilead, 40,000 Israelites and 4,000 men of Judah
The army was numbered at Bezek, not in Jabesh-gilead, and the totals were much larger (11:8).
What message was sent back to the men of Jabesh-gilead after the army gathered in 1 Samuel 11?
Saul’s men told the messengers to say: “Deliverance will be yours tomorrow by the time the sun is hot” (11:9).
1 Samuel 11:9
“Barricade the city and hold out for seven more weeks”
No long wait was promised; the message promised deliverance by the next day (11:9).
“Deliverance will be yours tomorrow by the time the sun is hot”
“Wait for the ark to come before you go out to fight”
The ark is not part of this campaign; the promise was deliverance by tomorrow (11:9).
“Cross the Jordan tonight and flee into the hill country”
No flight was advised; the message promised rescue by the time the sun was hot (11:9).
“Surrender to Nahash now and rebuild your city later”
Surrender was Jabesh’s own fallback (11:3), not Saul’s message; he promised deliverance (11:9).
To mislead Nahash and the Ammonites, what did the men of Jabesh-gilead say in 1 Samuel 11?
The men of Jabesh told Nahash: “Tomorrow we will come out, and you can do with us whatever seems good to you” (11:10), and Saul’s attack came at dawn (11:11).
1 Samuel 11:10
“Tonight we will break out of the city and strike your camp at dawn”
They pretended to surrender; they did not threaten an attack (11:10). The attack came from Saul’s army at dawn (11:11).
“Tomorrow we will come out, and you can do with us whatever seems good to you”
“Samuel has already cursed your army, and the LORD will destroy it”
Samuel is not mentioned in their message to Nahash (11:10).
“The Philistines are coming against you, so hurry home to defend your land”
No warning about Philistines was given; the men of Jabesh pretended to surrender (11:10).
“We have escaped across the Jordan, so there is no one left to conquer”
They stayed in the city and offered to come out the next day (11:10); they had not escaped anywhere.
In Saul’s attack on the Ammonite camp, how were the troops arranged and when did they strike?
Saul organized the troops into three divisions, and during the morning watch they invaded the Ammonite camp (11:11).
1 Samuel 11:11
In two divisions at sunset
Saul used three divisions, not two, and struck in the morning watch, not at sunset (11:11).
In three companies during the morning watch
In seven ranks at noon
The attack came at the morning watch and lasted until the hottest part of the day; seven ranks are not mentioned (11:11).
In one column at midnight
The army was in three divisions, not one column, and struck at the morning watch, not midnight (11:11).
In four divisions after the evening sacrifice
Four divisions and the evening sacrifice are not mentioned; it was three divisions in the morning watch (11:11).
After the victory of 1 Samuel 11, some people wanted to kill the men who had doubted Saul’s rule. What did Saul say?
Saul spared his critics, saying: “No one shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel” (11:13).
1 Samuel 11:13
“Bring them here at once, and let them answer to the whole assembly”
Saul refused to have anyone brought for execution (11:13).
“Let Samuel judge them before the LORD and then decide their punishment”
Saul did not hand the men over to Samuel; he ruled that no one would be put to death (11:13).
“No one shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel”
“Exile them beyond the Jordan, and let them never return to Gibeah”
No exile was ordered; Saul spared them all and credited the LORD with the victory (11:13).
“Take their property but spare their lives, and let them serve the army”
Saul did not seize property either; he simply said no one would be put to death that day (11:13).
After the deliverance in 1 Samuel 11, where did Samuel lead the people to renew the kingship, and what did they sacrifice there?
Samuel led the people to Gilgal to renew the kingship, and there they sacrificed peace offerings before the LORD (11:14–15).
1 Samuel 11:14-15
Shiloh, burnt offerings
They went to Gilgal, not Shiloh, and offered peace offerings, not burnt offerings (11:14–15).
Bethel, grain offerings
Bethel and grain offerings are not mentioned; the place was Gilgal and the offerings were peace offerings (11:14–15).
Mizpah, sin offerings
Mizpah was where Saul was first publicly chosen (1 Samuel 10:17), but here they went to Gilgal and offered peace offerings (11:14–15).
Gilgal, peace offerings
Hebron, guilt offerings
Hebron is where David was later anointed (2 Samuel 2:4); here the place was Gilgal and the offerings were peace offerings (11:14–15).
In Samuel’s address to all Israel after a king had been set over them, who did Samuel say was now “walking before” the people?
In 12:2 Samuel says, “Now here is the king walking before you,” pointing to the king the people had asked for.
1 Samuel 12:1-2
Eli
Eli had died years earlier (1 Samuel 4:18); he is not the one Samuel points to in 12:2.
The king
The high priest
Samuel speaks of the king, not of a priest, as walking before the people (12:2).
The commander of the army
The army’s commander is not mentioned in 12:2; Samuel points to the king himself.
The ark of God
The ark of God is not named in this address; Samuel points to the king (12:2).
In 1 Samuel 12, how did Samuel describe himself when he spoke about his years of serving Israel?
In 12:2 Samuel says, “I am old and gray,” and adds that he had walked before them from his youth.
1 Samuel 12:2
Strong and ready for war
Samuel stresses his age, not strength for war, in 12:2.
Sick and near death
Samuel says he is old and gray (12:2), not sick or near death.
Old and gray
Blind and weak
Samuel does not call himself blind or weak here; he says he is old and gray (12:2). Eli was the blind one (1 Samuel 4:15).
Rich and honored
Samuel claims no wealth; he asks whether he took anything from anyone (12:3).
During Samuel’s challenge for Israel to examine his leadership, which pair did he say he had not taken from anyone?
In 12:3 Samuel asks, “Whose ox or donkey have I taken?”
1 Samuel 12:3
Sheep and goats
Sheep and goats are not named in Samuel’s challenge; he names an ox and a donkey (12:3).
Silver and gold
Silver and gold are not mentioned in 12:3; the property named is an ox or a donkey.
Houses and vineyards
Houses and vineyards are what Samuel warned a king would take (1 Samuel 8:14), but his own challenge names an ox and a donkey.
Ox and donkey
Bread and wine
Bread and wine are not in Samuel’s list; he mentions an ox or donkey, cheating, oppression, and a bribe (12:3).
In Samuel’s appeal for testimony about his conduct, before whom did he ask Israel to speak?
In 12:3 Samuel says, “Bear witness against me before the LORD and before His anointed.”
1 Samuel 12:3, 5
The elders and priests
Elders and priests are not named as witnesses; Samuel calls on the LORD and His anointed (12:3).
The army and the king
Samuel does not ask the army to testify; he names the LORD and His anointed (12:3).

While chasing the Amalekites after the attack on Ziklag, whom did David’s men find in the open country?
