1 Samuel 30:11-13
A Philistine captain of Achish’s army
A Philistine captain is not mentioned in this scene.
An Egyptian servant of an Amalekite
An Edomite priest from Mount Seir
An Edomite priest is not mentioned in this scene.
A Judean shepherd with his father’s flock
A Judean shepherd is not mentioned in this scene.
A Benjamite scout sent out by Saul
A Benjamite scout is not mentioned in this scene.
What did David’s men give the abandoned Egyptian to restore his strength in 1 Samuel 30?
They “gave the man water to drink and food to eat—a piece of a fig cake and two clusters of raisins” (30:11–12).
1 Samuel 30:11-12
Roasted grain, dried fish, and a skin of wine
Fish is not mentioned; the food was fig cake and raisins (30:12).
Curds, milk, and honey from the Amalekite camp
Milk and honey are not mentioned in this scene (30:11–12).
Water, food, a piece of fig cake, and two clusters of raisins
A bowl of lentil stew with olive oil and bread
Lentil stew and oil are not mentioned; the food was fig cake and raisins (30:12).
Dates, cheese, and a skin of goat’s milk
Dates and cheese are not mentioned; the food was fig cake and raisins (30:12).
Why had the Egyptian servant been abandoned by his Amalekite master before David found him?
The Egyptian said, “My master abandoned me three days ago when I fell ill” (30:13).
1 Samuel 30:13
He stole some spoil
Stealing is not mentioned; he was left because he fell ill.
He refused to fight
Refusing to fight is not mentioned; he fell ill.
He became ill three days earlier
He got lost in the desert
Getting lost is not mentioned; his master abandoned him when he fell ill (30:13).
He tried to escape to Judah
Trying to escape is not mentioned; he was abandoned when he fell ill (30:13).
According to the Egyptian servant in 1 Samuel 30, which regions had the raiders attacked before burning Ziklag?
He said, “We raided the Negev of the Cherethites, the territory of Judah, and the Negev of Caleb, and we burned down Ziklag” (30:14).
1 Samuel 30:14
The Negev of the Cherethites, the territory of Judah, and the Negev of Caleb
The hill country of Ephraim, the plains of Sharon, and the valley of Jezreel
Galilee, Samaria and Moab are not what the Egyptian names (30:14).
The territory of Benjamin, the hill country of Ephraim, and the land of Gilead
Benjamin, Ephraim and Gilead are not what the Egyptian names (30:14).
The Phoenician coast, the hill country of Lebanon, and the land of Tyre
Tyre, Sidon and Philistia are not what the Egyptian names (30:14).
The plains of Edom, the land of Ammon, and the hill country of Moab
Edom, Ammon and Moab are not what the Egyptian names (30:14).
Before the Egyptian servant agreed to lead David to the Amalekite band, what did David promise him?
The man asked, “Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or deliver me into the hand of my master,” and then he led David to them (30:15).
1 Samuel 30:15
To make him a captain in his own army
Making him a captain is not mentioned.
To send him safely back home to Egypt
Returning him to Egypt is not mentioned; his request was not to be killed or handed back to his master (30:15).
Not to kill him or hand him over to his master
To give him the town of Ziklag as his own
Giving him Ziklag is not mentioned; Ziklag was David’s own city.
To bring him before Saul as a prisoner
Sending him to Saul is not mentioned.
When the Egyptian led David to the Amalekites who had plundered Ziklag, what were they doing?
They were “spread out over all the land, eating, drinking, and celebrating the great amount of plunder” (30:16).
1 Samuel 30:16
Building defenses
Building defenses is not mentioned; they were feasting.
Offering sacrifices
Sacrifices are not mentioned; they were eating, drinking and celebrating.
Eating, drinking, and celebrating
Burying their dead
Burying the dead is not mentioned; they were celebrating (30:16).
Marching toward Hebron
Marching toward Hebron is not mentioned; they were spread out, feasting (30:16).
After David attacked the Amalekites, how many of them escaped, and how did they get away?
“Not a man escaped, except four hundred young men who fled, riding off on camels” (30:17).
1 Samuel 30:17
70 on chariots
Seventy is not the number, and camels, not chariots, were used (30:17).
200 on horses
Two hundred is the number who stayed at the brook (30:10), not the number who escaped.
400 on camels
600 on foot
Six hundred is the number with David at the start (30:9); the escapees were four hundred on camels.
None escaped
Four hundred young men did escape on camels (30:17).
After the battle to recover the captives from Ziklag, how much did David recover from the Amalekites?
“David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, including his two wives... Nothing was missing” (30:18–19).
1 Samuel 30:18-19
Only his two wives
He recovered his wives and everything else (30:18–19).
Only the livestock
He recovered everything, not only the livestock.
Everything; nothing was missing
About half of what was taken
He recovered all, not half (30:19).
Only the children
He recovered all, not only the children (30:19).
When David returned to the Brook Besor, what did some wicked men among the fighters want to deny the 200 exhausted men who had stayed behind?
“we will not share with them the plunder we recovered, except for each man’s wife and children” (30:22).
1 Samuel 30:21-22
Water and food for their journey back to Ziklag
Food and water are not what the wicked men wanted to deny them.
Their share of the spoil, except for their wives and children
Permission to rejoin the camp of David’s fighters
The men were not barred from the camp; David greeted them (30:21).
The right to travel home with David to Ziklag
Returning to Ziklag is not mentioned.
Protection from the Philistines on their way home
Protection from the Philistines is not mentioned; the issue was the plunder (30:22).
What rule did David establish after the Ziklag recovery regarding those who went into battle and those who stayed with the supplies?
David said, “The share of the one who went to battle will match the share of the one who stayed with the supplies. They will share alike” (30:24).
1 Samuel 30:23-25
Leaders receive double
Leaders did not receive double; the share was equal.
Only fighters receive spoil
Fighters did not receive spoil alone; those who stayed with the supplies shared equally (30:24).
Priests decide the division
Priests were not given the decision; David set the rule (30:25).
Both groups share alike
The king keeps half
The king did not keep half; the share was equal (30:24).
In the closing verses of 1 Samuel 30, David sent part of the plunder to elders in towns of Judah. Which of these places is specifically named as one of the recipients?
David sent gifts “to those in Hebron and in all the places where David and his men had roamed” (30:31).
1 Samuel 30:26-31
Jerusalem
Jerusalem is not on the list (30:27–31).
Hebron
Jericho
Jericho is not on the list (30:27–31).
Gibeah
Gibeah is not on the list (30:27–31).
Damascus
Damascus is not on the list (30:27–31).
In the account of Israel’s defeat by the Philistines at the end of Saul’s reign, on which mountain did the men of Israel fall slain?
1 Samuel 31:1 says the men of Israel fled before the Philistines “and many fell slain on Mount Gilboa.”
1 Samuel 31:1
Mount Carmel
Mount Carmel is where Elijah met the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18:19), not where Saul’s army fell.
Mount Gilboa
Mount Tabor
Mount Tabor is not mentioned in this chapter; the slain fell on Mount Gilboa (31:1).
Mount Gerizim
Mount Gerizim is where the blessing was to be proclaimed (Deuteronomy 11:29), not the site of this battle.
Mount Sinai
Mount Sinai is where Moses received the law (Exodus 31:18), far from this battlefield.
In Saul’s final battle against the Philistines, which son of Saul is specifically named among those killed?
1 Samuel 31:2 says the Philistines “killed Saul’s sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua.”
1 Samuel 31:2
Ish-bosheth
Ish-bosheth survived the battle; Abner made him king at Mahanaim (2 Samuel 2:8).
Jonathan
Mephibosheth
Mephibosheth was Jonathan’s young son (2 Samuel 4:4), not a son of Saul.
Absalom
Absalom was a son of David, killed by Joab (2 Samuel 18:14).
Eleazar
Eleazar was Aaron’s son (Exodus 6:23), not Saul’s.
During the fighting near Mount Gilboa, who overtook Saul and wounded him critically?
1 Samuel 31:3 says, “the archers overtook him and wounded him critically.”
1 Samuel 31:3
Charioteers
Charioteers are not named in 31:3; the archers overtook Saul (compare the report of chariots in 2 Samuel 1:6).
Slingers
Slingers are not mentioned; 31:3 names the archers.
Archers
Spearmen
Spearmen are not named; 31:3 says the archers overtook Saul.
Horsemen
Horsemen are not named in 31:3; the archers overtook Saul.
When Saul feared what the Philistines might do to him if they reached him alive, what did he ask his armor-bearer to do?
In 31:4 Saul said, “Draw your sword and run me through with it, or these uncircumcised men will come and run me through and torture me!”
1 Samuel 31:4
Hide his crown and royal robes from the enemy
Saul did not ask to hide his crown; he feared torture by the uncircumcised (31:4).
Carry him to Gibeah before the Philistines came
Saul did not ask to be carried to Gibeah; he asked to be run through with a sword (31:4).
Blow the trumpet to call the men of Israel
Saul did not ask for a trumpet; he asked his armor-bearer to run him through (31:4).
Draw his sword and run him through
Summon a priest to pray for him before he died
Saul did not ask for a priest; he asked his armor-bearer to run him through (31:4).
In the narrative of Saul’s death, how did Saul die after his armor-bearer refused his request?
1 Samuel 31:4 says that when the armor-bearer refused, “Saul took his own sword and fell on it.”
1 Samuel 31:4
He was captured and executed
Saul feared being captured, which is why he asked to be run through (31:4); he was not executed by captors.
He was struck by a Philistine spear
A Philistine spear is not mentioned; 31:4 says Saul fell on his own sword.
He fell on his own sword
He died in a burning tent
There was no burning tent; Saul fell on his sword (31:4).
He drowned while fleeing
Saul did not drown; he fell on his own sword on Mount Gilboa (31:4, 31:8).
After Israelites in the valley and beyond the Jordan learned that Saul and his sons were dead, what did they do?
1 Samuel 31:7 says they “abandoned their cities and ran away. So the Philistines came and occupied their cities.”
1 Samuel 31:7
They attacked Beth-shan

They crowned a new king immediately
A new king was not crowned immediately; Abner later made Ish-bosheth king (2 Samuel 2:8).
They hid in caves near En-gedi
Caves near En-gedi are not mentioned; the Israelites abandoned their cities (31:7).
They abandoned their cities and fled
They gathered at Shiloh to mourn
Gathering at Shiloh is not mentioned; they abandoned their cities and the Philistines occupied them (31:7).
After the battle, where did the Philistines fasten Saul’s body?
1 Samuel 31:10 says the Philistines “hung his body on the wall of Beth-shan.”
1 Samuel 31:10
The wall of Jericho
Jericho is not mentioned in this chapter; the body was hung on the wall of Beth-shan (31:10).
The gate of Jerusalem
Jerusalem is not mentioned; the body was hung on the wall of Beth-shan (31:10).
The wall of Beth-shan
The tower of Jezreel
Jezreel is not named for this; the body was hung on the wall of Beth-shan (31:10).
The stronghold of Hebron
Hebron is not mentioned; the body was hung on the wall of Beth-shan (31:10).
After the Philistines found Saul among the slain on Mount Gilboa, where did they place his armor?
1 Samuel 31:10 says, “They put his armor in the temple of the Ashtoreths,” after they had stripped Saul’s body (31:9).
1 Samuel 31:9-10
In the temple of the Ashtoreths
In the house of Dagon
The house of Dagon is where the ark was placed (1 Samuel 5:2), not where Saul’s armor was put.
In the tabernacle at Shiloh
The Tent at Shiloh was Israel’s sanctuary (Joshua 18:1); the Philistines would not put their trophy there.
In the treasury of Ekron
Ekron’s treasury is not mentioned; the armor went into the temple of the Ashtoreths (31:10).
In the temple of Baal at Samaria
A temple of Baal at Samaria is not mentioned; the armor went into the temple of the Ashtoreths (31:10).
When the people of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul, who went to retrieve the bodies from Beth-shan?
1 Samuel 31:11–12: “all their men of valor set out, journeyed all night, and retrieved the bodies of Saul and his sons.” Saul had once rescued Jabesh-gilead (1 Samuel 11:1, 11:11).
1 Samuel 31:11-12
The priests of Nob
The priests of Nob are not mentioned; the men of valor of Jabesh-gilead went (31:11–12).
The elders of Hebron
The elders of Hebron are not mentioned; the men of Jabesh-gilead went (31:11–12).
All the valiant men of Jabesh-gilead
The warriors of Ephraim
The warriors of Ephraim are not mentioned; the men of Jabesh-gilead went (31:11–12).
David’s mighty men
David’s men are not mentioned in this chapter; the men of Jabesh-gilead went (31:11–12).
After the valiant men of Jabesh-gilead recovered Saul and his sons, what did they do with them?
1 Samuel 31:12–13: “they burned the bodies there. Then they took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and they fasted seven days.”
1 Samuel 31:12-13
They embalmed the bodies, buried them in Hebron, and mourned three days
They did not embalm the bodies; they burned them, buried the bones at Jabesh, and fasted seven days (31:12–13).
They burned them there, buried their bones under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and fasted seven days
They laid them in a cave at Adullam and sounded trumpets for seven days
A cave at Adullam is not mentioned; the bones were buried at Jabesh (31:13).
They buried them under an oak at Shechem and offered sacrifices
Shechem is not mentioned; the bones were buried under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh (31:13).
They took them to Jerusalem and placed them in the king’s tomb
Jerusalem is not mentioned; the bones were buried under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh (31:13).
10: After Saul’s death, when David returned from striking down the Amalekites, in which town did he remain for two days?
“After the death of Saul, David returned from the slaughter of the Amalekites and stayed in Ziklag two days” (1:1).
2 Samuel 1:1
Hebron
David moved to Hebron only later, at the LORD’s direction (2 Samuel 2:1); in 1:1 he was at Ziklag.
Bethlehem
Bethlehem was David’s hometown (1 Samuel 17:12), but after the Amalekite raid he stayed in Ziklag (1:1).
Ziklag
Mahanaim
Mahanaim is where Abner took Ish-bosheth to make him king (2 Samuel 2:8), not where David waited.
Gibeah
Gibeah was Saul’s hometown (1 Samuel 10:26); David was at Ziklag (1:1).
In the account of the messenger arriving to David at Ziklag, on which day did the man come from Saul’s camp?

2 Samuel 1:2
The first day
On the first day David had only just returned to Ziklag (1:1); the man came on the third day (1:2).
The second day
David stayed in Ziklag two days (1:1), and the messenger arrived on the third (1:2).
The third day
The seventh day
Seven days was how long the men of Jabesh fasted after burying Saul (1 Samuel 31:13).
The fortieth day

When the messenger came to David with news from Saul’s camp, what showed outward signs of grief or distress?
The man arrived “with torn clothes and dust on his head” (1:2), the customary signs of mourning.
2 Samuel 1:2
A purple robe and clean sandals
A purple robe and clean sandals would not signal grief; he came with torn clothes and dust on his head (1:2).
Torn clothes and dust on his head
Sackcloth and a ram’s horn
Sackcloth was Jacob’s sign of mourning for Joseph (Genesis 37:34); this man had torn clothes and dust on his head (1:2).
Armor and a drawn sword
The messenger came in mourning, not in armor; he had torn clothes and dust on his head (1:2).
A priestly ephod and ashes on his hands
Ashes were Tamar’s sign of grief (2 Samuel 13:19); this messenger wore torn clothes and had dust on his head (1:2).
At Ziklag, what did the man from Saul’s camp do when he reached David?
“When he came to David, he fell to the ground to pay him homage” (1:2).
2 Samuel 1:2
He sat in silence at the gate
He did not sit silently; he fell to the ground before David and then answered his questions (1:2–3).
He fell to the ground to pay respect
He sounded a trumpet
No trumpet is mentioned; he fell to the ground to pay David homage (1:2).
He embraced Joab
Joab does not appear in 2 Samuel 1; the man bowed to the ground before David (1:2).
He asked for food first
He did not ask for food; he fell to the ground before David (1:2).
In the report given to David, from where did the messenger say he had escaped?
Asked where he came from, he replied, “I have escaped from the Israelite camp” (1:3).
2 Samuel 1:3
The cave of Adullam
The cave of Adullam was David’s refuge from Saul (1 Samuel 22:1), not the place this man fled.
The camp of Israel
Jabesh-gilead
Jabesh-gilead is where Saul’s body was taken after the battle (1 Samuel 31:11–12), not the camp the man escaped from.
The wilderness of En-gedi
En-gedi’s wilderness was where David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 24:1); the man escaped from the Israelite camp (1:3).
The tabernacle at Nob
Nob, the city of the priests, had been destroyed by Saul (1 Samuel 22:19); the man came from the Israelite camp (1:3).
In the news brought to David after the battle, which two people were specifically said to be dead?
He reported, “Saul and his son Jonathan are also dead” (1:4).
2 Samuel 1:4
Saul and Abner
Abner survived the battle and later made Ish-bosheth king (2 Samuel 2:8).
Jonathan and Abishai
Abishai was David’s nephew and still alive afterward (2 Samuel 2:18); the report named Saul and Jonathan (1:4).
Saul and Jonathan
Saul and Michal
Michal was alive, and David later demanded her return (2 Samuel 3:14).
Jonathan and Ish-bosheth
Ish-bosheth survived and was made king at Mahanaim (2 Samuel 2:8); the dead named were Saul and Jonathan (1:4).
When David asked how the messenger knew Saul was dead, on which mountain did the man say he found Saul?
The man said, “I happened to be on Mount Gilboa,” and that there he saw Saul “leaning on his spear” (1:6).
2 Samuel 1:6
Mount Carmel
Mount Carmel is where Elijah confronted the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18:19).
Mount Sinai
Mount Sinai is where the LORD gave Moses the law (Exodus 19:20).
Mount Gilboa
Mount Zion
Zion was the Jebusite fortress David captured later (2 Samuel 5:7).
Mount Hor
Mount Hor is where Aaron died (Numbers 20:28).
In the Amalekite’s story about the battle on Mount Gilboa, what was Saul leaning on?

2 Samuel 1:6
His shield
Saul’s shield appears only in David’s lament: “the shield of Saul, no longer anointed with oil” (1:21).
His bow
The bow in the lament belongs to Jonathan, which “did not retreat” (1:22); Saul was leaning on his spear (1:6).
His spear
His chariot
The chariots were the enemy’s, “closing in on him” (1:6); Saul was leaning on his spear.
An altar stone
No altar appears in the Amalekite’s story; Saul was leaning on his spear (1:6).
According to the man who came to David from Mount Gilboa, what two items did he take from Saul and bring to David?
The Amalekite said, “I took the crown that was on his head and the band that was on his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord” (1:10).
2 Samuel 1:10
A sword and sandals
No sword or sandals were taken; he brought Saul’s crown and the band from his arm (1:10).
A crown and an arm band
A robe and ring
A robe and ring were Pharaoh’s gifts to Joseph (Genesis 41:42); the Amalekite brought a crown and an arm band (1:10).
A spear and helmet
David once took Saul’s spear and water jug while Saul slept (1 Samuel 26:12); here the items were a crown and an arm band (1:10).
A scepter and scroll
No scepter or scroll is mentioned; he brought the crown and the band from Saul’s arm (1:10).
After hearing the report about Saul and Jonathan, how long did David and his men mourn, weep, and fast?
“They mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Saul and his son Jonathan” (1:12).
2 Samuel 1:11-12
Until noon
Their mourning lasted until evening, not just until noon (1:12).
Until evening
For three days
Three days was the length of Esther’s fast (Esther 4:16); David’s men fasted until evening (1:12).
For seven days
Seven days was the fast of the men of Jabesh after burying Saul (1 Samuel 31:13), not David’s.
For forty days
Forty days were the days of Jacob’s embalming (Genesis 50:3); David and his men fasted until evening (1:12).
In 2 Samuel 1, for whom did David and his men mourn after hearing the battle report?

2 Samuel 1:12
Only Jonathan, his closest friend, and none of the others
The mourning was not only for Jonathan; it included Saul, the people of the LORD, and the house of Israel (1:12).
Only Saul’s armor-bearer, who died beside the king
Saul’s armor-bearer died beside Saul (1 Samuel 31:5), but 1:12 names Saul, Jonathan, the people of the LORD, and Israel.
Saul, Jonathan, the people of the LORD, and the house of Israel
Only the men of Judah who had fallen on Mount Gilboa
The mourning was for the people of the LORD and the house of Israel as a whole (1:12), not Judah alone.
Samuel the prophet and Saul, who had both recently died
Samuel had died earlier and been mourned by all Israel (1 Samuel 25:1); here they mourned Saul, Jonathan, and the people (1:12).
When David asked the young messenger about his origin, how did he identify himself?
Asked where he was from, he answered, “I am the son of a foreigner,” and added, “I am an Amalekite” (1:13).
2 Samuel 1:13
“I am a Benjamite from Gibeah”

“I am Doeg the Edomite”
Doeg the Edomite was Saul’s servant who killed the priests (1 Samuel 22:18), not this messenger.
“I am the son of a foreigner,” he answered. “I am an Amalekite.”
“I am an Ephraimite from Shiloh”
The man was a foreigner, an Amalekite (1:13), not an Ephraimite.
“I am the son of Jesse’s servant”
He did not claim any link to Jesse’s household; he said he was the son of a foreigner, an Amalekite (1:13).
After hearing the Amalekite’s claim about Saul, what question did David ask that revealed the seriousness of the act?
David asked, “Why were you not afraid to lift your hand to destroy the LORD’s anointed?” (1:14).
2 Samuel 1:14
“Why did you leave the king’s body unburied on the mountain?”

“Why were you not afraid to lift your hand to destroy the LORD’s anointed?”
“Why did you flee from the Philistines instead of defending Saul?”
David did not ask about fleeing; his question was why the man was not afraid to destroy the LORD’s anointed (1:14).
“Why did you strip the king’s armor and keep it for yourself?”
David never asked about armor; the man had brought Saul’s crown and arm band (1:10).
“How did you escape the battle when all the king’s men died?”
David had already asked about the battle (1:4); his question in 1:14 was about striking the LORD’s anointed.
In David’s judgment of the Amalekite messenger, what did David command one of his young men to do?
David said, “Go, execute him!” and “the young man struck him down, and he died” (1:15), because the man’s own mouth had testified against him (1:16).
2 Samuel 1:15-16
Crown him
David did the opposite of honoring him; he ordered his execution (1:15).
Imprison him
There was no imprisonment; the young man struck him down at once (1:15).
Send him to Hebron
David himself later went up to Hebron (2 Samuel 2:1); the Amalekite was executed at Ziklag (1:15).
Strike him down
Make him a witness before the elders
No elders were involved; David said, “Your own mouth has testified against you” (1:16).
What was the name of the lament David ordered taught to the sons of Judah after the deaths of Saul and Jonathan?
David “ordered that the sons of Judah be taught the Song of the Bow” (1:18).
2 Samuel 1:17-18
The Song of Moses
The Song of Moses celebrated the crossing of the sea (Exodus 15:1), not Saul’s death.
The Song of the Sword
The lament mentions “the sword of Saul” (1:22), but its title is the Song of the Bow (1:18).
The Song of the Bow
The Song of Deborah
The Song of Deborah was sung by Deborah and Barak after Sisera’s defeat (Judges 5:1).
The Song of the Vineyard
The song of a vineyard is Isaiah’s parable of Israel (Isaiah 5:1), not David’s lament.
In the chapter about David’s lament over Saul and Jonathan, where does the text say this song was written?
1:18 says of the Song of the Bow, “It is written in the Book of Jashar.”
2 Samuel 1:18
The Book of the Wars of the LORD
The Book of the Wars of the LORD is quoted in Numbers 21:14, not in David’s lament.
The Book of Jashar
The Annals of the Kings of Judah
The Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah is cited for later kings like Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:29).
The Scroll of Samuel
No scroll of Samuel is mentioned in the chapter; the lament is written in the Book of Jashar (1:18).
The Book of the Covenant
The Book of the Covenant was the law Moses read at Sinai (Exodus 24:7).
In David’s lament over Saul and Jonathan, which two Philistine places did he say should not hear the news?
David sang, “Tell it not in Gath; proclaim it not in the streets of Ashkelon” (1:20).
2 Samuel 1:20
Ekron and Gaza
Ekron and Gaza were Philistine cities too (1 Samuel 6:17), but the lament names Gath and Ashkelon (1:20).
Tyre and Sidon
Tyre and Sidon were Phoenician cities, not the ones named in the lament (1:20).
Gath and Ashkelon
Ashdod and Joppa

In the family note included in 2 Samuel 4 about Jonathan son of Saul, which statement about Mephibosheth is true?

The chapter about Ish-bosheth identifies Rechab and Baanah as sons of Rimmon from which town?

No meeting with elders is mentioned; the king was taking his midday nap (4:5).

They did not claim to be messengers; they entered as if to get wheat (4:6).
They came to get wheat

Weapons were not the pretext; they entered as if to get some wheat (4:6).
The background note in 2 Samuel 4 says the Beerothites had fled and remained as foreigners in which place?

Ziklag

Gittaim
Jericho

Shiloh
Shiloh is not named in this chapter; the Beerothites fled to Gittaim (4:3).
After Rechab and Baanah killed Ish-bosheth and cut off his head, by which route did they travel all night to bring it to David at Hebron?

By way of the Arabah
Through the Valley of Elah

Mount Carmel is not named in 2 Samuel 4; the route was the Arabah (4:7).
Through the Wilderness of Paran
The Wilderness of Paran is not named here; the night route was the Arabah (4:7).
When the brothers brought Ish-bosheth’s head to David in Hebron, David recalled an earlier incident at Ziklag. What did he say he did to the man who announced Saul’s death?

At the end of 2 Samuel 4, which statement correctly describes David’s final response to Rechab and Baanah and what was done with Ish-bosheth’s head?

David rewarded the brothers with silver for their loyalty, and then buried the head of Ish-bosheth beside Saul in the tomb at Zela

Shiloh

Gilgal

Solomon
Ibhar
Ibhar was one of David’s sons born in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:15); Adonijah invited “all his royal brothers” except Solomon (1:9–10).
Elishama
Elishama was another son born in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:16); Solomon is the brother singled out as not invited (1:10).
In David’s command concerning Solomon in 1 Kings 1, what animal was Solomon told to ride to Gihon?
David said, “Set my son Solomon on my own mule and take him down to Gihon” (1:33).
1 Kings 1:33
A white horse
A white horse appears in John’s vision (Revelation 19:11), not in Solomon’s anointing.
A camel
No camel is mentioned; Solomon rode King David’s mule (1:38).
David’s own mule
A war chariot
Chariots were what Adonijah had acquired for himself (1:5); Solomon rode David’s mule.
A donkey from Bethlehem
A king riding on a donkey is Zechariah’s prophecy (Zechariah 9:9); Solomon rode David’s own mule (1:33).
In the enthronement account of 1 Kings 1, to what place was Solomon brought to be anointed king?
They “set Solomon on King David’s mule, and they escorted him to Gihon” (1:38), where Zadok anointed him (1:39).
1 Kings 1:38
Hebron
Hebron is where David himself was anointed king over Israel (2 Samuel 5:3).
Gihon
En-rogel
En-rogel was the site of Adonijah’s rival feast (1:9).
Mizpah
Mizpah is where Samuel assembled the people when Saul was chosen (1 Samuel 10:17).
Bethel
Bethel is not mentioned in 1 Kings 1; Solomon was anointed at Gihon (1:38–39).
In 1 Kings 1, which two men were told to anoint Solomon king over Israel at Gihon?
David ordered, “There Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet are to anoint him king over Israel” (1:34).
1 Kings 1:34
Abiathar the priest and Joab son of Zeruiah
Abiathar and Joab were supporting Adonijah (1:7).
Samuel the prophet and Saul son of Kish
Samuel anointed Saul long before (1 Samuel 10:1); neither had any part in Solomon’s anointing.
Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet
Bathsheba his mother and Abishag the Shunammite
Bathsheba appealed to David for Solomon (1:17), and Abishag served the king (1:15); neither anointed him.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada and Jonathan son of Abiathar
Benaiah escorted Solomon to Gihon (1:38), and Jonathan son of Abiathar brought the news to Adonijah (1:42–43).
During Solomon’s anointing in 1 Kings 1, what did Zadok the priest take from the tabernacle?
“Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the tabernacle and anointed Solomon” (1:39).
1 Kings 1:39
The Ark of the Covenant
The ark was in the tent David had pitched for it (2 Samuel 6:17); Zadok took a horn of oil (1:39).
A silver trumpet
The silver trumpets were made in Moses’ day (Numbers 10:2); at Gihon they blew the ram’s horn (1:39).
A horn of oil
A golden lampstand
The golden lampstand was part of the tabernacle furnishings (Exodus 25:31); Zadok took the horn of oil.
The book of the law
The Book of the Law was found much later by Hilkiah (2 Kings 22:8).
After Solomon was anointed in 1 Kings 1, what did the people shout?
“They blew the ram’s horn, and all the people proclaimed, ‘Long live King Solomon!’” (1:39).
1 Kings 1:39
“The sword of the LORD and of Gideon!”
Gideon’s men shouted, “A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!” (Judges 7:20).
“Long live King Solomon!”
“Blessed is the kingdom of David!”
“Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David!” was shouted at Jesus’ entry into Jerusalem (Mark 11:10).
“Let Israel go up to Hebron!”
No one called for going up to Hebron; the people shouted, “Long live King Solomon!” (1:39).
“Great is the LORD in Zion!”
“Great is the LORD in Zion” is a line from Psalm 99:2, not the crowd’s shout.
As Adonijah’s guests were finishing their feast in 1 Kings 1, who arrived with the news that David had made Solomon king?
“Jonathan the son of Abiathar the priest arrived” and told Adonijah, “Our lord King David has made Solomon king” (1:42–43).
1 Kings 1:42
Jonathan son of Abiathar the priest
Ahimaaz son of Zadok the priest
Ahimaaz son of Zadok ran with news of Absalom’s defeat (2 Samuel 18:19), not of Solomon’s anointing.
Hushai the Archite, David’s friend
Hushai, David’s friend, served during Absalom’s revolt (2 Samuel 15:37) and does not appear here.
Mephibosheth son of Jonathan son of Saul
Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s son, plays no part in 1 Kings 1; the news came from Jonathan son of Abiathar (1:42).
Eleazar son of Aaron the priest
Eleazar son of Aaron lived centuries earlier (Numbers 20:28).
In 1 Kings 1, after hearing that Solomon sat on the royal throne, what did King David do on his bed?
Jonathan reported that “the king has bowed in worship on his bed,” saying, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel!” (1:47–48).
1 Kings 1:47
Tore his robe
David tore his clothes when he heard of Saul’s death (2 Samuel 1:11), not at Solomon’s enthronement.
Sounded the trumpet
The ram’s horn was blown at Gihon by those anointing Solomon (1:39), not by David on his bed.
Bowed in worship
Called for Joab
Joab was among Adonijah’s guests (1:41); David bowed in worship (1:47).
Went down to Gihon
David stayed behind; Solomon was escorted to Gihon by Zadok, Nathan, and Benaiah (1:38).
When Adonijah feared Solomon in 1 Kings 1, where did he go and what did he seize?
“Adonijah, in fear of Solomon, got up and went to take hold of the horns of the altar” (1:50).
1 Kings 1:50
He went to Hebron and seized the city gate
Adonijah did not go to Hebron; he took hold of the horns of the altar (1:50).
He went to the tabernacle and seized the lampstand
Adonijah grasped the horns of the altar (1:50), not the lampstand.
He went to the altar and took hold of its horns
He went to Bethlehem and seized a storehouse
No storehouse appears; Adonijah sought refuge at the altar (1:50–51).
He went to the palace and seized the throne
Solomon was the one who took his seat on the royal throne (1:46).
In Solomon’s first judgment in 1 Kings 1, under what condition did he say Adonijah would not lose a hair of his head?
Solomon said, “If he is a man of character, not a single hair of his will fall to the ground. But if evil is found in him, he will die” (1:52).
1 Kings 1:52
If Adonijah returned the royal treasury he had seized
No treasury is mentioned; Solomon’s condition was that Adonijah prove a man of character (1:52).
If Adonijah fled to Egypt and never returned to Israel
Fleeing to Egypt was Jeroboam’s later escape from Solomon (1 Kings 11:40); Solomon sent Adonijah home (1:53).
If he proved himself a worthy man and no wickedness was found in him
If Joab son of Zeruiah stood surety for his good conduct
Joab was not asked to vouch for him; Solomon’s condition concerned Adonijah’s own character (1:52).
If Abiathar the priest swore an oath for him at the altar
Abiathar had no role in Solomon’s terms; Adonijah would live if no evil was found in him (1:52).
In the account of King David’s final charge before his death, which son did David tell to “be strong” and keep the LORD’s charge?
David charged Solomon, “be strong and prove yourself a man,” and keep the charge of the LORD his God (1 Kings 2:2–3).
1 Kings 2:1-4
Absalom
Absalom rebelled against David and was killed before David’s death (2 Samuel 18:14); he received no such charge.
Adonijah
Adonijah tried to take the throne for himself (1 Kings 1:5) and was later put to death by Solomon (2:25).
Solomon
Amnon
Amnon, David’s firstborn, was killed by Absalom’s men years earlier (2 Samuel 13:28–29).
Rehoboam
Rehoboam was Solomon’s son who reigned after him (1 Kings 11:43), not the son David charged here.
In David’s last recorded words in 1 Kings 2, what did he say he was about to do?
David said, “I am about to go the way of all the earth” (1 Kings 2:2), a way of saying he was about to die.
1 Kings 2:2
Cross the Jordan
David had crossed the Jordan years earlier while fleeing Absalom (2 Samuel 17:22); here he speaks of dying.
Go into exile
David was no exile at this point; he was handing his kingdom to Solomon on his deathbed.
Go the way of all the earth
Return to Hebron
David had reigned in Hebron seven years (2:11), but he speaks here of dying, not of travel.
Stand before the priests
David’s words concern his death and his charge to Solomon, not a visit to the priests.
In the chapter describing David’s death, where was King David buried?
David “rested with his fathers and was buried in the City of David” (1 Kings 2:10).
1 Kings 2:10
Bethlehem
Bethlehem was David’s hometown (1 Samuel 17:12), but it was not his burial place.
Hebron
David reigned in Hebron for seven years (2:11), but he was buried in Jerusalem.
Shiloh
Shiloh was the early home of the tabernacle and of Eli’s house (1 Samuel 1:3), not David’s tomb.
The City of David
Gibeon
Gibeon was where Solomon later offered sacrifices and received wisdom (1 Kings 3:4–5), not David’s burial site.
In the summary of David’s reign given before Solomon’s kingdom was firmly established, how many years had David reigned over Israel?
1 Kings 2:11 says David’s reign over Israel was forty years: seven in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem.
1 Kings 2:11
20 years
Twenty years is too short; David reigned forty years in all (2:11).
30 years
Thirty years is the age David began to reign (2 Samuel 5:4), not the length of his reign.
33 years
Thirty-three years is only the time David reigned in Jerusalem (2:11), not his whole reign.
40 years
50 years
Fifty years is too long; seven plus thirty-three years is forty (2:11).
In David’s instructions to Solomon, whose sons were to be shown kindness and allowed to eat at the king’s table because their father helped David when he fled from Absalom?
David told Solomon to “show loving devotion to the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite” and have them eat at his table, because they stood by him when he fled from Absalom (2:7).
1 Kings 2:7
The sons of Zadok the priest
Zadok the priest stood with Solomon against Adonijah (1:8), but David’s request here concerns Barzillai’s family.
The sons of Barzillai the Gileadite
The sons of Joab son of Zeruiah
Joab’s descendants were warned of coming judgment (2:33), not honored at the king’s table.
The sons of Abiathar the priest
Abiathar was banished to Anathoth for backing Adonijah (2:26–27), so his sons were not honored.
The sons of Shimei son of Gera
David told Solomon to keep an eye on Shimei, who had cursed him (2:8–9), not to reward his sons.
In the episode where Adonijah came to Bathsheba with a request, which woman did he ask to have as his wife?
Adonijah asked Bathsheba to have Solomon give him Abishag the Shunammite as his wife (2:17), a request Solomon saw as a grab for the kingdom (2:22).
Michal
Michal was Saul’s daughter and David’s first wife (1 Samuel 18:27), not part of Adonijah’s request.
Tamar
Tamar, David’s daughter, was assaulted by Amnon (2 Samuel 13:14); she is not the woman Adonijah requested.
Abishag the Shunammite
Rizpah
Rizpah was Saul’s concubine, whom Abner took (2 Samuel 3:7); Adonijah asked for Abishag.
Bathsheba
Bathsheba was the one Adonijah asked to speak for him; the wife he asked for was Abishag (2:17).
In 1 Kings 2, through whom did Adonijah try to present his request to King Solomon?
Adonijah asked Bathsheba, Solomon’s mother, to speak to the king for him, and she agreed (2:13–18).
Nathan the prophet
Nathan the prophet backed Solomon against Adonijah (1:8) and was not Adonijah’s go-between.
Zadok the priest
Zadok the priest also refused to join Adonijah (1:8), so Adonijah did not use him.
Joab son of Zeruiah
Joab had supported Adonijah (2:22, 28), but Adonijah’s request here went through Bathsheba.
Bathsheba, Solomon’s mother
Benaiah son of Jehoiada
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was Solomon’s man, who carried out Adonijah’s execution (2:25).
After Solomon judged Adonijah’s request to be worthy of death, whom did the king send to strike Adonijah down?
King Solomon “gave orders to Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and he struck down Adonijah and he died” (2:25).
Benaiah son of Jehoiada
Abishai son of Zeruiah
Abishai, Joab’s brother, led a third of David’s troops (2 Samuel 18:2), but he is not named in Adonijah’s death.
Zadok the priest
Zadok the priest was installed in Abiathar’s place (2:35), not sent to kill Adonijah.
Nathan the prophet
Nathan the prophet sided with Solomon (1:8), but the executioner was Benaiah.
Adoram
Adoram oversaw forced labor and was stoned in Rehoboam’s reign (1 Kings 12:18); he did not execute Adonijah.
In Solomon’s response to those connected with Adonijah’s cause, which priest was sent away to his fields in Anathoth instead of being executed?
Solomon told Abiathar the priest, “Go back to your fields in Anathoth,” sparing his life because he had carried the ark before David (2:26).
Zadok
Zadok took Abiathar’s place as priest (2:35); he was not the one sent to Anathoth.
Abiathar
Ahimelech
Ahimelech was Abiathar’s father, killed at Nob by Doeg (1 Samuel 22:18–20), long before this.
Azariah
Azariah son of Zadok was a priest in Solomon’s court (1 Kings 4:2), not the one banished to Anathoth.
Jehoiada
Jehoiada was the father of Benaiah (2:25); he was not the priest sent away.
When news of Adonijah’s death reached one of his former supporters, which commander fled to the tent of the LORD and took hold of the horns of the altar?
Joab, who had conspired with Adonijah, “fled to the tent of the LORD and took hold of the horns of the altar” (2:28).
1 Kings 2:28
Abner son of Ner
Abner was killed by Joab at Hebron (2 Samuel 3:27), long before this scene.
Amasa son of Jether
Amasa was also killed by Joab (2 Samuel 20:10); he was not the one who fled to the altar.
Joab son of Zeruiah
Shimei son of Gera
Shimei son of Gera had cursed David (2 Samuel 16:5) and was dealt with later (2:36–46), not at the altar.
Asahel
Asahel, Joab’s brother, was killed by Abner (2 Samuel 2:23) many years before this.
In Solomon’s explanation for Joab’s execution, which two men did he say Joab had struck down with the sword unjustly?
Solomon said Joab struck down “two men more righteous and better than he,” Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether (2:32).
1 Kings 2:32
Saul son of Kish and Jonathan son of Saul
Saul and Jonathan fell in battle against the Philistines (1 Samuel 31:2–3), not by Joab’s sword.
Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether
Ish-bosheth son of Saul and Mephibosheth son of Jonathan
Ish-bosheth was killed by Rechab and Baanah (2 Samuel 4:5–7), not by Joab; Solomon named only Abner and Amasa.
Adonijah son of Haggith and Amnon son of David
Adonijah was struck down by Benaiah at Solomon’s order (2:25); Amnon was killed by Absalom’s servants (2 Samuel 13:28–29).
Nadab son of Aaron and Abihu son of Aaron
Nadab and Abihu died for offering unauthorized fire (Leviticus 10:1–2), centuries before Joab.
After Joab was killed and buried at his home in the wilderness, whom did Solomon appoint over the army in Joab’s place?
“The king appointed Benaiah son of Jehoiada in Joab’s place over the army” (2:35).
1 Kings 2:35
Abishai son of Zeruiah
Abishai, Joab’s brother, led part of David’s army (2 Samuel 18:2), but Solomon put Benaiah in Joab’s place.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada
Adoniram
Adoniram son of Abda was in charge of the forced labor (1 Kings 4:6), not the army.
Azariah son of Nathan
Azariah son of Nathan was in charge of the governors (1 Kings 4:5), not the army.
Elihoreph
Elihoreph was one of Solomon’s secretaries (1 Kings 4:3), not a military commander.
Solomon’s removal of Abiathar from the priesthood fulfilled a word the LORD had spoken at Shiloh against which house?
Solomon banished Abiathar and so “fulfilled the word that the LORD had spoken at Shiloh against the house of Eli” (2:27).
1 Kings 2:27
The house of Aaron
Eli was of Aaron’s priestly line, but the word of judgment at Shiloh was aimed at Eli’s own house (1 Samuel 2:31).
The house of Korah
Korah led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness (Numbers 16:1–3); that is not the house in view here.
The house of Eli
The house of Phinehas
Phinehas received a covenant of peace and a lasting priesthood (Numbers 25:12–13), the opposite of this judgment.
The house of Samuel
Samuel was Eli’s young successor, not the target of the judgment on Eli’s house (1 Samuel 3:12).
When Solomon placed Shimei son of Gera under restriction, in which city was Shimei commanded to build a house and remain?
Solomon told Shimei, “Build a house for yourself in Jerusalem and live there, but do not go anywhere else” (2:36).
1 Kings 2:36
Bahurim
Bahurim was Shimei’s hometown (2:8), but Solomon told him to live in Jerusalem.
Hebron
Hebron was where David reigned seven years (2:11); Shimei was not told to live there.
Jerusalem
Jericho
Jericho is not mentioned in Solomon’s order to Shimei (2:36).
Bethlehem
Bethlehem is not mentioned in Solomon’s order to Shimei (2:36).
In Solomon’s warning to Shimei, which valley was named as the boundary Shimei must not cross if he wanted to live?
Solomon warned Shimei, “On the day you go out and cross the Kidron Valley, know for sure that you will die” (2:37).
1 Kings 2:37
Valley of Elah
The Valley of Elah is where Israel faced Goliath and the Philistines (1 Samuel 17:2), not Shimei’s boundary.
Valley of Kidron
Valley of Achor
The Valley of Achor is where Achan was punished (Joshua 7:24–26), not the boundary Solomon set for Shimei.
Valley of Jezreel
The Valley of Jezreel is where the Midianites camped in Gideon’s day (Judges 6:33), not Shimei’s boundary.
Valley of Siddim
The Valley of Siddim is where the kings fought in Abraham’s time (Genesis 14:3), not Shimei’s boundary.
In the account of Shimei’s eventual disobedience, how long did he remain in Jerusalem before leaving to pursue his servants?
“After three years” two of Shimei’s slaves ran away to Gath, and he set out after them (2:39–40).
1 Kings 2:39
Three days
Three days is too short; Shimei lived in Jerusalem for a long time before he left (2:38–39).
Seven months
Seven months is not what the text says; it records three years (2:39).
One year
One year is too short; the text gives three years (2:39).
Three years
Ten years
Ten years is too long; the text gives three years (2:39).
In the event that led to Shimei’s execution, why did Shimei travel from Jerusalem to Gath?
Two of Shimei’s slaves ran away to Gath, so he saddled his donkey and “brought them back from Gath” (2:39–40).
To offer sacrifices to the LORD
Shimei went to Gath after his runaway slaves, not to offer sacrifices (2:40).
To negotiate a peace treaty
Peace talks are not mentioned; Shimei went to recover his slaves (2:40).
To join Achish in a battle
Shimei went to Gath for his slaves, not for a battle (2:40).
To collect tribute for Solomon
The text mentions no tribute; Shimei went to search for his slaves (2:40).
To recover his runaway servants
The two servants who fled from Shimei went to which ruler and city?
Shimei was told, “Look, your slaves are in Gath,” after they ran away “to Achish son of Maacah, king of Gath” (2:39).
1 Kings 2:39
Hiram king of Tyre
Hiram king of Tyre was a friend of David and supplier of cedar (1 Kings 5:1), not the ruler Shimei’s slaves fled to.
Achish son of Maacah king of Gath
Talmai king of Geshur
Talmai king of Geshur was Absalom’s grandfather (2 Samuel 3:3); he is not the ruler in this story.
Nahash king of Ammon
Nahash king of Ammon besieged Jabesh-gilead in Saul’s day (1 Samuel 11:1), long before this event.
Ben-hadad king of Damascus
Ben-hadad of Damascus came later, when Asa sought his help (1 Kings 15:18); he is not the ruler here.
In David’s difficult final instruction about Joab son of Zeruiah, what two items did David say Joab had stained with blood shed in peacetime?
David said Joab “stained with the blood of war the belt around his waist and the sandals on his feet” (2:5).
1 Kings 2:5
His robe and turban
Joab’s robe and turban are not mentioned; David names his belt and sandals (2:5).
His chariot and spear
Chariot and spear are not named; David speaks of Joab’s belt and sandals (2:5).
His belt and sandals
His tent and altar
Joab later fled to the tent of the LORD and its altar (2:28), but David spoke of blood on his belt and sandals.
His sword and shield
Sword and shield are not named; the blood was on Joab’s belt and sandals (2:5).
In Solomon’s early reign in 1 Kings 3, Solomon made a marriage alliance with which ruler by marrying his daughter?
Solomon “formed an alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt by marrying his daughter” (3:1).
1 Kings 3:1
Hiram king of Tyre
Hiram king of Tyre was Solomon’s friendly partner in the temple project (2 Chronicles 2:11), but he is not the father-in-law named in 3:1.
Pharaoh king of Egypt
Ben-hadad king of Aram
Ben-hadad king of Aram was a later enemy of Israel who besieged Samaria (1 Kings 20:1), not Solomon’s father-in-law.
Achish king of Gath
Achish king of Gath was the Philistine ruler who sheltered David (1 Samuel 27:2), not a ruler Solomon married into.
Hadadezer king of Zobah
Hadadezer king of Zobah was an enemy defeated by David (2 Samuel 8:3); Solomon’s marriage alliance was with Egypt.
After marrying Pharaoh’s daughter in 1 Kings 3, to what place did Solomon bring her?
Solomon brought Pharaoh’s daughter to the City of David “until he had finished building his palace and the house of the LORD, as well as the wall around Jerusalem” (3:1).
1 Kings 3:1
Hebron
Hebron was David’s first capital, where he reigned seven years and six months (1 Chronicles 3:4); Solomon housed his bride in the City of David.
Shiloh
Shiloh was an earlier worship center where Eli’s sons served as priests (1 Samuel 1:3), not where Solomon took his bride.
The City of David
Bethel
Bethel became a rival worship site when Jeroboam set up a calf there (1 Kings 12:29), long after this marriage.
Ramah
Ramah was the hometown of Samuel (1 Samuel 7:17), not the place Solomon lodged Pharaoh’s daughter.
In the opening of 1 Kings 3, why were the people sacrificing on the high places?
The people kept sacrificing on the high places “because a house for the Name of the LORD had not yet been built” (3:2).
1 Kings 3:2
The ark of the covenant had been lost to the Philistines
The ark was not lost; Solomon later stood before the ark of the covenant in Jerusalem (3:15).
No house had yet been built for the Name of the LORD
Jerusalem had been destroyed by Pharaoh’s army
Jerusalem was not destroyed; Solomon had brought his bride to the City of David and was building the wall around it (3:1).
The priesthood had ended with the death of David
The chapter never says the priesthood ended; the stated reason is that no temple for the Name of the LORD existed yet.
No altar to the LORD remained anywhere in Israel
Altars did exist, such as the one at Gibeon where Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings (3:4).
In 1 Kings 3, what does the narrator say Solomon loved?
The narrator says “Solomon loved the LORD and walked in the statutes of his father David” (3:3).
1 Kings 3:3
Wealth
Wealth was something Solomon did not ask for; God gave it as an unrequested gift (3:13).
Horses
Horses are not what the narrator says Solomon loved here; Deuteronomy 17:16 warns that the king must not acquire many horses for himself.
The LORD
Foreign alliances
Solomon made an alliance with Pharaoh (3:1), but the narrator says his love was for the LORD; foreign wives only became a problem later (1 Kings 11:1).
Music
Solomon did compose songs (1 Kings 4:32), but 3:3 names the LORD as the object of his love.
Even though Solomon loved the LORD, where did 1 Kings 3 say he still sacrificed and burned incense?
Although Solomon loved the LORD, 3:3 says “he sacrificed and burned incense on the high places.”
1 Kings 3:3
In Philistine temples
Solomon’s sacrifices here were on Israel’s own high places (3:2–4), not in Philistine temples.
On the high places
At Dan and Bethel
Dan and Bethel became centers of calf worship under Jeroboam (1 Kings 12:29), after Solomon’s time.
In Egypt
Solomon’s marriage tied him to Egypt (3:1), but the chapter places his sacrifices on the high places, not in Egypt.
In Baal shrines
Chapter 3 describes Solomon’s sacrifices at the high places and Gibeon as offerings to the LORD, not as worship at Baal shrines.
In 1 Kings 3, to what place did King Solomon go to sacrifice because it was the great high place?
Solomon went to Gibeon to sacrifice, “for it was the great high place” (3:4).
1 Kings 3:4
Gibeon
Shechem
Shechem is where all Israel gathered to make Rehoboam king (1 Kings 12:1), not where Solomon sacrificed.
Beersheba
Beersheba is where Abraham planted a tamarisk tree and called on the LORD (Genesis 21:33), not the high place of 3:4.
Gilgal
Gilgal was Israel’s first camp west of the Jordan (Joshua 4:19), not Solomon’s sacrifice site.
Nob
Nob was a priestly town where David met Ahimelech (1 Samuel 21:1), not the great high place.
At Gibeon in 1 Kings 3, how many burnt offerings did Solomon offer on that altar?
“Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on the altar there” at Gibeon (3:4).
1 Kings 3:4
Twelve matches the tribes of Israel, but the chapter says Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings.
Seventy is not a number given in this chapter; Solomon’s offering was a thousand burnt offerings.
Three hundred understates the scale; 3:4 says Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings.
Ten thousand overstates it ten times over; 3:4 says Solomon offered a thousand.
During Solomon’s visit to Gibeon in 1 Kings 3, how did the LORD appear to him?
The LORD appeared to Solomon “in a dream” one night at Gibeon (3:5).
1 Kings 3:5
In a pillar of fire
A pillar of fire guided Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21), not Solomon at Gibeon.
By an angel at noon
No angel is mentioned, and the encounter came by night in a dream, not at noon.
In thunder on the mountain
Thunder on the mountain belongs to Sinai (Exodus 19:16); at Gibeon God spoke to Solomon in a dream.
Through the high priest
No high priest is involved; God spoke to Solomon directly in the dream (3:5).
In a dream by night
In Solomon’s dream at Gibeon in 1 Kings 3, what did God invite him to do?
In the dream God said, “Ask, and I will give it to you!” (3:5).
1 Kings 3:5

Sennacherib said Hezekiah had removed the LORD’s high places and altars and told Judah and Jerusalem to worship before one altar (2 Chronicles 32:12).
2 Chronicles 32:12
Hezekiah had forbidden anyone in Jerusalem to pray to the LORD
Hezekiah forbidding prayer in Jerusalem is not part of the taunt; he and Isaiah prayed in the crisis (2 Chronicles 32:20).
Hezekiah had removed high places and altars, directing worship to one altar
Hezekiah had closed the temple and sent its priests away for good
Hezekiah had reopened and repaired the temple (2 Chronicles 29:3), and the taunt does not say he closed it.
Hezekiah had moved the Passover celebration from Jerusalem to Bethel
Hezekiah’s great Passover was held in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 30), and Sennacherib does not say it was moved to Bethel.
Hezekiah had sold the temple vessels to the king of Babylon
Sennacherib’s taunt does not mention the temple vessels or Babylon; Babylon’s envoys come only later (2 Chronicles 32:31).
When the Assyrian servants shouted to the people standing on Jerusalem’s wall, what language did they use to frighten them?
The Assyrians called out loudly in Hebrew to the people of Jerusalem on the wall, to frighten and terrify them in order to capture the city (2 Chronicles 32:18).
2 Chronicles 32:18
Aramaic
Judah’s officials asked the Assyrians to speak Aramaic in 2 Kings 18:26, but in this chapter the Assyrians shouted in Hebrew.
Egyptian
Egyptian was the language of Egypt; the Assyrians used the language of the people on the wall.
Greek
Greek was not the language of the Assyrian envoys; 2 Chronicles 32:18 says they called out in Hebrew.
Hebrew
Latin
Latin was not in use in Hezekiah’s day, and the Assyrians shouted in Hebrew.
In response to Sennacherib’s blasphemous threats, which prophet prayed to heaven together with King Hezekiah?
King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz cried out to heaven in prayer (2 Chronicles 32:20).
2 Chronicles 32:20
Elijah the Tishbite
Elijah the Tishbite prophesied in the northern kingdom in the days of Ahab, long before Hezekiah.
Elisha son of Shaphat
Elisha son of Shaphat succeeded Elijah in the northern kingdom generations before Hezekiah’s time.
Isaiah son of Amoz
Jeremiah of Anathoth
Jeremiah of Anathoth prophesied about a century later, near the fall of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 32:1–2).
Amos of Tekoa
Amos of Tekoa prophesied in the days of Uzziah and Jeroboam II, before Hezekiah’s reign.
How did the LORD strike the Assyrian camp after Hezekiah and Isaiah prayed in the crisis described in 2 Chronicles 32?
The LORD sent an angel who annihilated every mighty man of valor and every leader and commander in the camp of the king of Assyria (2 Chronicles 32:21).
2 Chronicles 32:21
By sending an earthquake that swallowed up the Assyrian camp outside Jerusalem
The chapter describes no earthquake; the LORD sent an angel who destroyed the Assyrian warriors and commanders.
By sending confusion among the Assyrian horses so they trampled their own men
There is no mention of confusion among horses; the angel annihilated the mighty men, leaders and commanders.
By sending an angel who annihilated the mighty warriors, commanders, and officers
By sending hailstones that fell on the Assyrian camp and drove it away
No hail fell in this story; hail is a plague of Egypt (Exodus 9:23), but here an angel struck the Assyrian camp.
By sending fire from the temple altar that consumed the Assyrian commanders
Fire from the temple altar is not mentioned; the destruction came when the LORD sent an angel into the Assyrian camp.
After returning in disgrace to his own land, where was Sennacherib when some of his own sons struck him down with the sword?
Sennacherib withdrew to his own land in disgrace, and when he entered the temple of his god, some of his own sons struck him down with the sword (2 Chronicles 32:21).
2 Chronicles 32:21
In the gate of Nineveh
The gate of Nineveh is not mentioned; he was killed inside a temple (see also 2 Kings 19:37).
In the palace garden
A palace garden is where Manasseh was buried (2 Kings 21:18), not where Sennacherib was killed.
In the temple of his god
At the Euphrates River
The Euphrates is not mentioned in the account of his death; he fell in a temple in his own land.
In the house of Hezekiah
He never entered Hezekiah’s house; the Assyrian king withdrew in disgrace and was killed in the temple of his god.
After the LORD saved Jerusalem from Assyria, what did many people bring according to the record of Hezekiah’s reign?
Many brought offerings to Jerusalem for the LORD and valuable gifts for Hezekiah king of Judah, who was exalted in the eyes of all nations (2 Chronicles 32:23).
2 Chronicles 32:23
Only war horses and chariots to strengthen Judah’s army
War horses are not mentioned; people brought offerings and valuable gifts after the LORD’s deliverance.
Offerings to the LORD in Jerusalem and valuable gifts for Hezekiah
Idols and altars from the nations to set up in Jerusalem
Idols from the nations are not mentioned; the gifts were offerings for the LORD and gifts for Hezekiah.
Timber from Lebanon for building a new palace for Hezekiah
Timber from Lebanon is not mentioned; the verse speaks of offerings and valuable gifts.
Tribute and silver to pay off the king of Assyria
Nothing was paid to Assyria; the LORD saved Jerusalem and others honored Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 32:22–23).
In the later part of 2 Chronicles 32, when Hezekiah became mortally ill and prayed, what did the LORD give him?
When Hezekiah became mortally ill he prayed to the LORD, who spoke to him and gave him a sign (2 Chronicles 32:24).
2 Chronicles 32:24
A new army
No new army was given; the LORD answered Hezekiah’s prayer for healing with a sign.
A book of the Law
A book of the Law is not mentioned here; God spoke to Hezekiah and gave him a sign.
A sign
A foreign alliance
A foreign alliance is not part of this verse; the LORD gave a sign in response to Hezekiah’s prayer.
A crown of gold
A crown of gold is not mentioned; the verse says the LORD spoke to Hezekiah and gave him a sign.
What spiritual problem in Hezekiah brought wrath on him and on Judah and Jerusalem before he humbled himself?
Because Hezekiah’s heart was proud and he did not repay the favor shown to him, wrath came upon him and upon Judah and Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 32:25).
2 Chronicles 32:25-26
Cowardice
Hezekiah showed courage, not cowardice, when he encouraged the people against the Assyrians (2 Chronicles 32:7–8).
Greed alone
Greed is not named; the chapter says his heart was proud.
His heart was proud
Open idolatry in the temple
No idolatry in the temple is mentioned here; Hezekiah had cleansed the temple (2 Chronicles 29), and his sin was pride.
Refusal to keep Passover
Hezekiah kept a great Passover (2 Chronicles 30), so refusing to keep it is not the problem named.
Which water-engineering project is specifically credited to Hezekiah in the history of Judah?
Hezekiah blocked the upper outlet of the Spring of Gihon and channeled it down to the west side of the City of David (2 Chronicles 32:30).
2 Chronicles 32:30
He split the Jordan River near Jericho so that the people could cross
The Jordan was parted by the LORD for Joshua’s people (Joshua 3:17), not by Hezekiah.
He blocked the upper outlet of Gihon and channeled the water westward to the City of David
He dug wells in Beersheba so that his flocks and camels could drink
Isaac reopened wells in the Negev region (Genesis 26:18); Hezekiah’s work was at the Gihon spring.
He diverted the Kishon River toward Mount Carmel to water the fields
The Kishon is a river mentioned in the days of Deborah (Judges 4:7), and no diversion of it is credited to Hezekiah.
He built aqueducts from the Jordan to Samaria to supply the northern kingdom
Aqueducts to Samaria are not credited to Hezekiah; his water project brought the Gihon spring into the City of David.
When envoys from the rulers of Babylon came to visit Hezekiah, what were they asking about?
The ambassadors of the rulers of Babylon were sent to inquire about the wonder that had happened in the land, and God left Hezekiah alone to test him (2 Chronicles 32:31).
2 Chronicles 32:31
The rebuilding of the walls of Jericho
The rebuilding of Jericho is told in 1 Kings 16:34 and has nothing to do with the Babylonian envoys.
The famine that had struck Samaria
A famine in Samaria is told in the days of Elisha (2 Kings 6) and is not why the envoys came.
The wonder that had happened in the land
The death of Ahab in battle at Ramoth
Ahab died in battle generations earlier (1 Kings 22:37); the envoys asked about the wonder in the land.
The census that David had taken in Israel
David’s census (2 Samuel 24) happened centuries earlier and is not the subject of the envoys’ inquiry.
Why did God leave Hezekiah alone during the visit from the Babylonian envoys in the account of 2 Chronicles 32?
God left Hezekiah alone to test him, “that He might know all that was in Hezekiah’s heart” (2 Chronicles 32:31).
2 Chronicles 32:31
To punish Babylon at once for sending the envoys
The text gives no punishment of Babylon at that time; God left Hezekiah alone to test his heart.
To test Hezekiah and know everything in his heart
To force Judah into exile in Babylon that year
Exile is not the stated reason here; the purpose was to test Hezekiah and know what was in his heart.
To appoint a new high priest in his place
No new high priest is mentioned in this passage; the point is the testing of Hezekiah’s heart.
To end the temple worship Hezekiah had restored
Ending temple worship is not suggested; God left Hezekiah alone to test what was in his heart.
At the end of Hezekiah’s life, where was he buried according to the closing verses of 2 Chronicles 32?
Hezekiah was buried in the upper tombs of David’s descendants, and all Judah and the people of Jerusalem paid him honor at his death (2 Chronicles 32:33).
2 Chronicles 32:33
In the cave of Machpelah with the patriarchs
The cave of Machpelah is where Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and their wives were buried (Genesis 49:31), not Hezekiah.
In the field of Ephron the Hittite
The field of Ephron the Hittite is the site Abraham bought at Machpelah for Sarah’s burial (Genesis 23:19), far earlier.
In the upper tombs of David’s descendants
In the valley of Megiddo
Megiddo is where Josiah was killed, and it is not Hezekiah’s burial place.
In the Garden of Uzza
The garden of Uzza is where his son Manasseh was buried (2 Kings 21:18), not Hezekiah.
In 2 Chronicles 33, when Manasseh became king of Judah in Jerusalem, how old was he?
Manasseh was twelve years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem fifty-five years (33:1).
2 Chronicles 33:1
Eight is Josiah’s age when he became king (2 Chronicles 34:1), not Manasseh’s.
Sixteen is Uzziah’s age when he became king (2 Chronicles 26:1), not Manasseh’s.
Twenty is Ahaz’s age when he became king (2 Chronicles 28:1), not Manasseh’s.
Twenty-five is Hezekiah’s age when he became king (2 Chronicles 29:1); his son Manasseh was only twelve.
According to the record of King Manasseh in 2 Chronicles 33, how long did he reign in Jerusalem?
Manasseh reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem (33:1).
2 Chronicles 33:1
22 years
Twenty-two is Amon’s age when he became king (33:21), not the length of Manasseh’s reign.
29 years
Twenty-nine years was Hezekiah’s reign (2 Chronicles 29:1), Manasseh’s father.
40 years
Forty years was Joash’s reign (2 Chronicles 24:1), not Manasseh’s.
55 years
70 years
Seventy years is the length of the Babylonian servitude in Jeremiah 25:11, not Manasseh’s reign.
In the account of Manasseh’s idolatry in 2 Chronicles 33, where did he build altars to all the host of heaven?
Manasseh built altars to all the host of heaven in both courtyards of the house of the LORD (33:5).
2 Chronicles 33:5
On the heights of Mount Carmel and Mount Tabor
Elijah’s contest with Baal’s prophets took place on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:19), not Manasseh’s altars for the host of heaven.
At Bethel and Dan, beside the golden calves
The golden calves at Bethel and Dan were set up by Jeroboam (1 Kings 12:29), not by Manasseh.
In the king’s garden, behind the palace wall
The king’s garden is not mentioned; Manasseh built the altars in the courtyards of the LORD’s house (33:5).
Beside the Valley Gate on the city wall
The Valley Gate is not part of this account; Manasseh’s altars were in the temple courtyards (33:5).
In both courts of the house of the LORD
During King Manasseh’s evil practices described in 2 Chronicles 33, in which valley did he sacrifice his sons in the fire?
Manasseh sacrificed his sons in the fire in the Valley of Ben-hinnom (33:6).
2 Chronicles 33:6
Valley of Kidron
The Kidron Valley lay east of Jerusalem (2 Samuel 15:23); the chapter names the Valley of Ben-hinnom.
Valley of Elah
The Valley of Elah is where David faced Goliath (1 Samuel 17:2), not where Manasseh sacrificed his sons.
Valley of Ben Hinnom
Valley of Jezreel
The Valley of Jezreel is where the Midianites camped in Gideon’s day (Judges 6:33), not the place named here.
Valley of Aijalon
The Valley of Aijalon appears in Joshua’s victory (Joshua 10:12), not in Manasseh’s sins.
When the LORD spoke to Manasseh and the people of Judah in 2 Chronicles 33, how did they respond?
The LORD spoke to Manasseh and his people, but they did not listen (33:10).
2 Chronicles 33:10
They listened and repented at once
They did not repent at that time; Manasseh humbled himself later, in distress in Babylon (33:12–13).
They asked the priests for counsel
No request for the priests’ counsel is recorded; the people did not listen (33:10).
They fled from Jerusalem
No flight from Jerusalem is recorded here; they simply did not listen (33:10).
They did not listen
They removed the high places
Manasseh removed the foreign gods only later, after his return (33:15); at this point they did not listen.
After Manasseh ignored the LORD, what did the commanders of the king of Assyria do to him according to 2 Chronicles 33?
The commanders of the king of Assyria captured Manasseh, put a hook in his nose, bound him with bronze shackles, and took him to Babylon (33:11).
2 Chronicles 33:11
They made him a vassal of Assyria, left him on his throne, and returned home
Manasseh was taken away to Babylon, not left ruling in Jerusalem (33:11).
They captured him, put a hook in his nose, bound him with bronze shackles, and took him to Babylon
They blinded him, chained him, and carried him off to the city of Nineveh
Blinding is what Babylon did to Zedekiah (2 Kings 25:7); Manasseh was captured, shackled, and taken to Babylon (33:11).
They stoned him outside the temple and put his young son on the throne
No stoning is recorded; the commanders captured and bound him (33:11).
They imprisoned him in Samaria and forced him to labor in the fields
The Assyrian commanders took Manasseh to Babylon, not to Samaria (33:11).
In Manasseh’s distress, after he earnestly humbled himself before the God of his fathers and prayed, what happened?
The LORD received his plea, heard his petition, and brought him back to Jerusalem and to his kingdom (33:13).
2 Chronicles 33:12-13
He died in an Assyrian prison, and Judah chose another man as king
Manasseh did not die in prison; the LORD received his plea and restored him (33:13).
He remained in Babylon for the rest of his life as a captive king
He did not stay in Babylon for life; the LORD brought him back to Jerusalem (33:13).
He was replaced by his son Amon at once, while still in captivity
Amon reigned only after Manasseh’s death (33:20), not in his place while he was in captivity.
He was ignored by God, who refused to listen to his prayer
The LORD did not ignore him; He received his plea and heard his petition (33:13).
The LORD heard him and brought him back to Jerusalem and his kingdom
After Manasseh returned to Jerusalem and restored the altar of the LORD, what did he sacrifice on it?
Manasseh restored the altar of the LORD and sacrificed peace offerings and thank offerings on it (33:16).
2 Chronicles 33:16
Burnt offerings and grain offerings
Burnt and grain offerings were also part of Israel’s worship (Leviticus 1–2), but this chapter names peace and thank offerings.
Sin offerings and guilt offerings
Sin and guilt offerings are described in Leviticus 4–5, but the chapter names peace and thank offerings.
Peace offerings and thank offerings
Drink offerings and wave offerings
Drink and wave offerings are not the ones named here; Manasseh sacrificed peace offerings and thank offerings (33:16).
Firstfruits and tithes
Firstfruits and tithes are not mentioned in this passage; Manasseh sacrificed peace offerings and thank offerings (33:16).
At the end of 2 Chronicles 33, what did King Amon of Judah fail to do, unlike his father Manasseh?
Amon “did not humble himself before the LORD as his father Manasseh had done; instead, Amon increased his guilt” (33:23).
2 Chronicles 33:23
Humble himself before the LORD
Strengthen the fortified cities of Judah
Manasseh, not Amon, stationed military commanders in Judah’s fortified cities (33:14).
Return from exile in Babylon
Manasseh, not Amon, was taken to Babylon and brought back (33:11–13).
Repair the temple courts
The temple repairs came later under Josiah (2 Chronicles 34:8), not from Amon.
Bury his father in Jerusalem
Manasseh was buried at his palace (33:20); the text does not say Amon failed to bury him.
Following Manasseh’s restoration, which fortification work in Jerusalem is specifically described in 2 Chronicles 33?
Manasseh rebuilt the outer wall of the City of David from west of Gihon in the valley to the entrance of the Fish Gate, and brought it around the hill of Ophel (33:14).
2 Chronicles 33:14
He rebuilt the walls of Jericho from the spring to the king’s palace and set gates in them
Jericho’s walls fell in Joshua 6, long before; Manasseh’s wall work was in Jerusalem (33:14).
He enclosed Bethlehem with towers and cisterns and stored grain inside its walls
Bethlehem is not part of this account; Manasseh stationed commanders in Judah’s fortified cities (33:14).
He repaired the temple steps from the east court to the altar and covered them in bronze
Manasseh’s temple work was removing the idols and restoring the altar (33:15–16), not repairing steps.
He rebuilt the outer wall of the City of David west of Gihon in the valley, as far as the entrance of the Fish Gate, encircling Ophel
He fortified Samaria and the hill of Moreh with a double wall and new gates
Samaria belonged to the northern kingdom; Manasseh’s fortification work was in Jerusalem and Judah (33:14).
In the account of King Josiah in Judah, how old was he when he became king in Jerusalem?
“Josiah was eight years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem thirty-one years” (34:1).
2 Chronicles 34:1
6 years old
Six is not Josiah’s age at accession; 34:1 says eight.
8 years old
12 years old
Twelve was Manasseh’s age when he became king (2 Chronicles 33:1); Josiah’s twelfth year is when his cleansing began (34:3).
16 years old
Sixteen was Uzziah’s age at accession (2 Chronicles 26:1), not Josiah’s.
20 years old
Twenty was Ahaz’s age at accession (2 Chronicles 28:1), not Josiah’s.
In the opening of 2 Chronicles 34, how long did Josiah reign in Jerusalem?
34:1 says Josiah “reigned in Jerusalem thirty-one years.”
2 Chronicles 34:1
21 years
Twenty-one years is not the length of Josiah’s reign; 34:1 says thirty-one.
29 years
Twenty-nine years was Hezekiah’s reign (2 Chronicles 29:1), not Josiah’s.
31 years
40 years
Forty years was Joash’s reign (2 Chronicles 24:1), not Josiah’s.
52 years
Fifty-two years was Uzziah’s reign (2 Chronicles 26:3), not Josiah’s.
According to the record of Josiah’s character, in whose ways did he walk as he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD?
Josiah “did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and walked in the ways of his father David; he did not turn aside to the right or to the left” (34:2).
2 Chronicles 34:2
Solomon
Solomon was David’s son; 34:2 says Josiah walked in the ways of David.
Hezekiah
Hezekiah himself followed David (2 Chronicles 29:2); 34:2 says Josiah walked in David’s ways.
David
Samuel
Samuel is not named in 34:2; the model for Josiah was David.
Jehoshaphat
Jehoshaphat walked in David’s earlier ways (2 Chronicles 17:3), but 34:2 names David as Josiah’s model.
While still young, what did King Josiah begin to do in the eighth year of his reign?
“In the eighth year of his reign, while he was still young, Josiah began to seek the God of his father David” (34:3).
2 Chronicles 34:3
Seek the God of his father David
Build a new palace
Building a new palace is not mentioned in this chapter; Josiah began to seek God (34:3).
Number the fighting men
Counting the fighting men was David’s census (1 Chronicles 21:2), not Josiah’s act in 34:3.
Move the ark to Zion
Bringing the ark to Zion was David’s act (2 Samuel 6:12); in the eighth year Josiah began to seek God (34:3).
Marry a foreign princess
Marrying a foreign princess was Solomon’s alliance with Pharaoh (1 Kings 3:1), not Josiah’s act in 34:3.
In the twelfth year of Josiah’s reign over Judah, what did he begin to purge from Judah and Jerusalem?
“In the twelfth year he began to cleanse Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, the Asherah poles, the carved idols, and the cast images” (34:3).
2 Chronicles 34:3
High places, Asherah poles, carved idols, and cast images
Foreign merchants and tax collectors
Merchants and tax collectors are not mentioned; the purge targeted idolatry (34:3).
Chariots and horses from the army
Chariots and horses are not mentioned in this purge; it was aimed at idols and high places (34:3).
Priests and Levites from the temple
Priests and Levites were not purged from the temple; the bones of idolatrous priests were burned (34:5), and Levites served in the repairs (34:12).
Vineyards and olive groves from royal land
Vineyards and olive groves are not mentioned; the purge was of idolatry (34:3).
During Josiah’s destruction of idols in Judah and Jerusalem, what did he scatter over the graves of those who had sacrificed to idols?
Josiah “crushed them to dust, and scattered them over the graves of those who had sacrificed to them” (34:4).
2 Chronicles 34:4
Ashes from the altar
Ashes from the altar are not mentioned; he scattered the crushed idols over the graves (34:4).
The dust of the idols he had ground to powder
Water from the bronze sea
Water from the bronze sea is not mentioned; he scattered dust of the idols (34:4).
Cedar shavings from the temple
Cedar shavings are not mentioned; he scattered the dust of crushed idols (34:4).
Incense from the sanctuary
Josiah cut the incense altars to pieces (34:4); he did not scatter incense over the graves.
As part of cleansing Judah and Jerusalem, what did Josiah burn on the idolatrous altars?
“Then he burned the bones of the priests on their altars. So he cleansed Judah and Jerusalem” (34:5).
2 Chronicles 34:5
Scrolls of false prophets
Scrolls are not mentioned; he burned the bones of the priests on their altars (34:5).
Dead animals from the high places
Dead animals are not mentioned; the bones burned were those of the priests (34:5).
The bones of the priests
Weapons taken in battle
Weapons are not mentioned; the bones of the priests were burned (34:5).
The robes of pagan worshipers
Robes are not mentioned; the bones of the priests were burned (34:5).
In the record of Josiah’s wider reforms beyond Jerusalem, the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon were purged as far as what place?
Josiah “did the same in the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, as far as Naphtali” (34:6).
2 Chronicles 34:6
Beersheba
Beersheba is in the far south of Judah; 34:6 reaches north to Naphtali.
Gilead
Gilead is east of the Jordan and is not named in 34:6.
Naphtali
Hebron
Hebron is in the hill country of Judah and is not the limit named in 34:6.
Ashdod
Ashdod is a Philistine city, not one of the Israelite cities of 34:6.
In the eighteenth year of Josiah’s reign, what task did he assign to Shaphan son of Azaliah, Maaseiah the governor of the city, and Joah son of Joahaz the recorder?
“In the eighteenth year of his reign … Josiah sent Shaphan son of Azaliah, Maaseiah the governor of the city, and Joah son of Joahaz, the recorder, to repair the house of the LORD his God” (34:8).
2 Chronicles 34:8
Gather an army against Egypt

Repair the house of the LORD his God
Rebuild the walls of Jerusalem

Divide the land among the tribes
Dividing the land among the tribes was done in the days of Moses and Joshua (Numbers 34:17), not Josiah’s task here.
Lead a mission to Babylon
Babylonian ambassadors came to Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 32:31); Josiah sent no mission to Babylon in 34:8.
In the temple-repair account under King Josiah, who had collected the money brought into the house of God?

The captains of the army

The Levites who kept the doors
The elders of Benjamin
The people of Benjamin were among the givers (34:9), not the collectors.
The sons of Aaron at the altar
The sons of Aaron at the altar are not named as collectors; the Levites who guarded the doors were (34:9).
The singers of Asaph alone
The singers of Asaph are not named in this verse; the Levites who guarded the doors collected the money (34:9).

Shaphan the scribe

Hilkiah the priest
Maaseiah the governor

Joah the recorder

Asaiah the king’s servant

He fell asleep

Deborah the prophetess in Ephraim

Anna the prophetess in the temple

Huldah the prophetess in the Second District
Miriam the prophetess by the wilderness

Jezebel in Samaria
