2 Chronicles 34:24-25
Because the city walls had fallen into ruin and the gates stood unrepaired for many long years
Broken walls are the later complaint in Nehemiah 1:3; Huldah’s reason was idolatry (34:25).
Because the people had refused to pay the temple tax and had neglected the tithes of the harvest
No temple tax is mentioned; Huldah’s reason was that they had forsaken the LORD for other gods (34:25).
Because the priests had stopped the daily offerings and left the altar cold throughout the land
The daily offerings are not mentioned in Huldah’s message; the reason was idolatry (34:25).
Because the king had delayed a census and neglected to muster the army of the whole nation
A delayed census is not mentioned; Huldah’s reason was that they had forsaken the LORD and burned incense to other gods (34:25).
Because they had forsaken the LORD, burned incense to other gods, and provoked Him by the works of their hands
What personal assurance did Huldah give King Josiah because his heart was tender and he humbled himself before God?
Huldah told Josiah, “Now I will indeed gather you to your fathers, and you will be gathered to your grave in peace. Your eyes will not see all the calamity that I will bring on this place” (34:28).
2 Chronicles 34:27-28
He would never face an enemy in battle, and no army would threaten Judah in his lifetime
Huldah promised a peaceful grave, not freedom from every battle (34:28).
He would be gathered to his fathers and to his grave in peace, and his eyes would not see all the calamity
All of his sons would rule after him, and his dynasty would never end in Judah
No promise about his sons ruling is made; the assurance concerned his own death and burial in peace (34:28).
Jerusalem would never be judged, because the LORD had forgiven the whole nation
Jerusalem was still to be judged (34:24–25); Josiah would not live to see it (34:28).
The kingdom would expand to the Euphrates, and Egypt would pay tribute to him
No expansion to the Euphrates is promised; the assurance was a peaceful grave (34:28).
After hearing the Book of the Covenant, what public action did Josiah take at the house of the LORD, and what result followed during his reign?
34:31–33: the king made a covenant before the LORD, had everyone take a stand in agreement to it, and “throughout his reign they did not turn aside from following the LORD, the God of their fathers.”
2 Chronicles 34:31-33
He made a covenant before the LORD to follow Him wholeheartedly, had the people stand to it, and they did not turn aside from following the LORD during his reign
He closed the temple and sealed the scroll away, and the people kept worshiping at the high places for the rest of his reign, ignoring the Law
Josiah did not close the temple; he went up to it and read the Book of the Covenant there (34:30).
He crowned his young son as co-regent, and the people soon returned to the worship of Baal despite the covenant they had made together
No co-regent is mentioned; throughout his reign the people did not turn aside from the LORD (34:33).
He moved the center of worship from Jerusalem to Bethel, and all the people of Judah followed him there for the rest of his days
Worship was not moved to Bethel; Josiah made the covenant at the house of the LORD in Jerusalem (34:30–32).
He abolished the priesthood so that the Levites ruled the land, and the people lived in peace and idleness until the exile
The priests and Levites were present at the reading of the covenant (34:30); they were not abolished.
In the report about money for temple repairs during Josiah’s reign, from which groups had the Levites who kept the doors collected it?

34:9 says the Levites who guarded the doors collected the money “from the people of Manasseh and Ephraim, from all the remnant of Israel, from all Judah and Benjamin, and from the people of Jerusalem.”
2 Chronicles 34:9
Only from the families of Judah and the citizens of Jerusalem, and from no other tribe
The money came from more than Judah and Jerusalem; Manasseh, Ephraim, and the remnant of Israel gave too (34:9).
Only from the priests serving in Jerusalem and the Levites who guarded the doors
The Levites collected it from the people, not only from priests (34:9).
From Dan, Asher, and Zebulun only, the tribes of the far north of the land
The givers were far more than Dan, Asher, and Zebulun; they included Manasseh, Ephraim, Judah, Benjamin, and Jerusalem (34:9).
From Manasseh, Ephraim, all the remnant of Israel, all Judah and Benjamin, and the people of Jerusalem
From Moab, Ammon, Edom, and Philistia, as tribute paid by the neighboring nations
The givers were Israelites, not the nations around them; no tribute from Moab, Ammon, Edom, or Philistia is mentioned (34:9).
According to the temple restoration details in 2 Chronicles 34, what were the workers buying with the money given to carpenters and builders?
The money was given to the carpenters and builders “to buy dressed stone, as well as timbers for couplings and beams for the buildings that the kings of Judah had allowed to deteriorate” (34:11).
2 Chronicles 34:11
Dressed stone and timber for couplings and beams
Gold shields and silver trumpets
Gold shields and silver trumpets are not mentioned; the money bought stone and timber for repairs (34:11).
Chariots, horses, and spears
Chariots, horses, and spears are not mentioned; the money went to repairs (34:11).
Purple cloth and priestly garments
Purple cloth and priestly garments are not mentioned; the money bought stone and timber (34:11).
Grain, wine, and oil for a siege
Grain, wine, and oil for a siege are not mentioned; the money bought stone and timber (34:11).
Which Levites were named as the supervisors directing the temple repair work in the days of Josiah?
34:12 says, “The Levites overseeing them were Jahath and Obadiah, descendants of Merari, and Zechariah and Meshullam, descendants of Kohath.”
2 Chronicles 34:12
Jahath and Obadiah from Merari; Zechariah and Meshullam from the Kohathites
Asaph and Heman from Gershon; Ethan and Jeduthun from Merari
Heman, Asaph, and Ethan were Levite musicians (1 Chronicles 15:19), not the overseers named in 34:12.
Nathan and Gad from Judah; Eliab and Benaiah from Levi
Nathan and Gad were prophets of David’s day, not the Levite overseers of 34:12.
Hilkiah and Azariah from Aaron; Joab and Abishai from Benjamin
Hilkiah was the priest (34:9), but Azariah, Joab, and Abishai are not the overseers named in 34:12.
Uzziah and Jotham from Judah; Shemaiah and Hananiah from Ephraim
Uzziah and Jotham were kings of Judah (2 Chronicles 26:1; 27:1), not the Levite overseers of 34:12.
When King Josiah ordered men to inquire of the LORD about the discovered book, which exact group did he send?
34:20 says the king “commanded Hilkiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Abdon son of Micah, Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah the servant of the king.”
2 Chronicles 34:20-21
Hilkiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Abdon son of Micah, Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah the king’s servant
Hilkiah, Eliakim son of Hilkiah, Shebna the secretary, Joah, and Isaiah the prophet
Eliakim, Shebna, and the priests were sent to Isaiah in Hezekiah’s day (2 Kings 19:2), not by Josiah.
Azariah the priest, Zadok, Nathan, Gad, and Benaiah
Azariah, Zadok, Nathan, Gad, and Benaiah belong to the days of David and Solomon, not Josiah’s delegation.
Jeremiah, Baruch, Seraiah, Ebed-melech, and Gedaliah
Jeremiah, Baruch, Seraiah, Ebed-melech, and Gedaliah belong to a later period, not Josiah’s delegation in 34:20.
Hilkiah, Achbor son of Micaiah, Huldah, Shallum, and Maaseiah
Huldah was the prophetess they consulted (34:22), not one of those sent; the list in 34:20 names Abdon son of Micah, not Achbor (2 Kings 22:12).
In 2 Chronicles 35, which king of Judah kept a Passover unlike any observed in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet?
“Josiah kept the Passover to the LORD in Jerusalem” (35:1), and “No such Passover had been observed in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet” (35:18).
2 Chronicles 35:1
Hezekiah
Hezekiah also kept a notable Passover (2 Chronicles 30:1), but 35:18 says none matched Josiah’s.
Josiah
Jehoshaphat
Jehoshaphat is not credited with a Passover like this; 35:18 says no king’s Passover matched Josiah’s.
Amaziah
Amaziah is not credited with this Passover; the chapter names Josiah (35:1).
Manasseh
Manasseh, Josiah’s grandfather, was known for idolatry (2 Chronicles 33:2–3), not for this Passover.
According to 2 Chronicles 35, in what city did Josiah celebrate this Passover to the LORD?
“Josiah kept the Passover to the LORD in Jerusalem” (35:1).
2 Chronicles 35:1
Bethel
Josiah did tear down the altar at Bethel in his reforms (2 Kings 23:15), but the Passover was kept in Jerusalem (35:1).
Hebron
Hebron is not where this Passover was held; it was kept in Jerusalem (35:1).
Samaria
Samaria was the old northern capital; the Passover was kept in Jerusalem (35:1).
Jerusalem
Shiloh
Shiloh once held the tabernacle (Joshua 18:1), but this Passover was in Jerusalem (35:1).
In Josiah’s Passover account, on which day of the first month were the Passover lambs slaughtered?
“The Passover lamb was slaughtered on the fourteenth day of the first month” (35:1).
2 Chronicles 35:1
10th day
The tenth day was when the lamb was chosen (Exodus 12:3), not slaughtered.
12th day
The twelfth day is not a Passover date; the lambs were slaughtered on the fourteenth (35:1).
14th day
15th day
The Feast of Unleavened Bread began on the fifteenth day (Leviticus 23:6).
21st day
The twenty-first was the last day of Unleavened Bread (Exodus 12:18).
After the Passover in 2 Chronicles 35, which seven-day festival did the Israelites who were present keep?
The Israelites present “observed the Passover at that time, as well as the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days” (35:17).
2 Chronicles 35:17
Feast of Weeks
The Feast of Weeks came seven weeks later, at the end of the grain harvest (Leviticus 23:15–16).
Feast of Booths
The Feast of Booths also lasted seven days, but it was in the seventh month (Leviticus 23:34), not after this Passover.
Day of Atonement
The Day of Atonement was a single day on the tenth of the seventh month (Leviticus 16:29).
Feast of Trumpets
The Feast of Trumpets was a one-day observance on the first day of the seventh month (Leviticus 23:24).
Feast of Unleavened Bread
In the temple preparations described in 2 Chronicles 35, whom did King Josiah appoint to their duties and encourage in the service of the house of the LORD?
“He appointed the priests to their duties and encouraged them in the service of the house of the LORD” (35:2).
2 Chronicles 35:2
The prophets
Josiah consulted the prophetess Huldah earlier (2 Kings 22:14), but here he appointed the priests (35:2).
The priests
The army commanders
Army commanders are not mentioned; Josiah appointed the priests (35:2).
The city elders
Josiah gathered the elders in his earlier covenant ceremony (2 Kings 23:1), but here he appointed the priests (35:2).
The foreign servants
No foreign servants are mentioned; Josiah appointed the priests (35:2).
When Josiah addressed the Levites in 2 Chronicles 35, what sacred object did he tell them to place in the temple that Solomon son of David had built?
Josiah told the Levites, “Put the holy ark in the temple built by Solomon son of David king of Israel” (35:3).
2 Chronicles 35:3
The bronze altar
The bronze altar already stood in Solomon’s temple (2 Chronicles 4:1); the Levites were told to put the ark there (35:3).
The lampstand
Solomon’s temple already held ten golden lampstands (2 Chronicles 4:7); Josiah’s order concerned the ark (35:3).
The holy ark
The table of showbread
The tables for the Bread of the Presence were already in the temple (2 Chronicles 4:19); Josiah’s order concerned the ark (35:3).
The bronze sea
The Sea of cast metal stood in Solomon’s temple already (2 Chronicles 4:2); Josiah’s order concerned the ark (35:3).
As the Levites prepared by family divisions for Josiah’s Passover, whose written instructions were they told to follow?
The Levites were to prepare “according to the instructions written by David king of Israel and Solomon his son” (35:4).
2 Chronicles 35:4
Moses the lawgiver and Joshua son of Nun
Josiah also cites “the word of the LORD given by Moses” (35:6), but the family divisions follow David and Solomon (35:4).
Samuel the prophet and Saul son of Kish
Samuel’s days are only the benchmark for how long since such a Passover (35:18); Saul left no such instructions here.
David king of Israel and Solomon his son
Elijah the Tishbite and Elisha son of Shaphat
Elijah and Elisha were prophets of the northern kingdom, and are not cited here (35:4).
Ezra the scribe and Nehemiah the governor
Ezra and Nehemiah lived after the exile (Ezra 7:6), long after Josiah.
In the Passover service of 2 Chronicles 35, who skinned the animals after the Passover lambs were slaughtered?
“The priests splattered the blood handed to them and the Levites skinned the animals” (35:11).
2 Chronicles 35:11
The priests
The priests splattered the blood; the Levites did the skinning (35:11).
The Levites
The singers
The singers, the descendants of Asaph, stayed at their stations (35:15).
The gatekeepers
The gatekeepers stayed at their gates, since other Levites prepared for them (35:15).
The king’s guards
The king’s guards are not part of the service described in 35:11.
During Josiah’s Passover in Jerusalem, how were the Passover animals prepared for eating?
“They roasted the Passover animals on the fire according to the regulation” (35:13).
2 Chronicles 35:13
They were eaten raw on the day they were slaughtered
The Passover meat could not be eaten raw (Exodus 12:9); it was roasted (35:13).
They were baked in ovens with oil and flour
The Passover animals were roasted (Exodus 12:8; 35:13); only the other holy offerings were boiled (35:13).
They were roasted on the fire according to the regulation
They were dried in the sun and stored for later use
Drying in the sun is not mentioned; the animals were roasted on the fire (35:13).
They were salted overnight and eaten the next morning
Nothing was to be left until morning (Exodus 12:10), so the meat was roasted and eaten, not salted overnight.
In the worship arrangements of 2 Chronicles 35, which group of singers remained at their stations according to the command of David, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun?
“The singers, the descendants of Asaph, were at their stations according to the command of David, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun the king’s seer” (35:15).
2 Chronicles 35:15
The sons of Korah
The Korahites were also Levite singers (2 Chronicles 20:19), but 35:15 names the descendants of Asaph.
The sons of Aaron
The sons of Aaron were the priests, offering burnt offerings until nightfall (35:14).
The sons of Asaph
The men of Gibeon
The men of Gibeon are not mentioned in the worship arrangements of this chapter (35:15).
The sons of Zadok
The sons of Zadok were priests (Ezekiel 44:15), not the singers named here.
In 2 Chronicles 35, whose own flocks and herds supplied 30,000 lambs and goats plus 3,000 bulls for the Passover offerings for all the people?
“From his own flocks and herds Josiah contributed 30,000 lambs and goats plus 3,000 bulls for the Passover offerings” (35:7).
2 Chronicles 35:7
David’s
David gave his personal treasures for the temple (1 Chronicles 29:3), but these Passover animals came from Josiah’s own flocks and herds (35:7).
Solomon’s
Solomon offered many oxen and sheep at the temple’s dedication (1 Kings 8:63), not at this Passover.
Hezekiah’s
Hezekiah contributed bulls and sheep for his own great Passover assembly (2 Chronicles 30:24), not for this one (35:7).
Josiah’s
Jehoshaphat’s
Jehoshaphat is not named as a donor; the gift came from Josiah’s own flocks and herds (35:7).
In 2 Chronicles 35, which officials of God’s house gave the priests 2,600 Passover offerings from the flock and 300 cattle?
“Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, the chief officials of the house of God, gave the priests 2,600 Passover offerings and 300 bulls” (35:8).
2 Chronicles 35:8
Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel
Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah
Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah were royal officials in Hezekiah’s day (Isaiah 36:3), not donors at Josiah’s Passover.
Azariah, Maaseiah, and Joel
These names do not appear in the list of donors; the gift to the priests came from Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel (35:8).
Conaniah, Shemaiah, and Nethanel
Conaniah, Shemaiah, and Nethanel were among the Levite officers who gave to the Levites, not the priests (35:9).
Urijah, Meremoth, and Hananiah
These names are not the donors; the gift to the priests came from Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel (35:8).
When 2 Chronicles 35 compares Josiah’s Passover with earlier times, since the days of which prophet had no Passover like it been observed in Israel?
“No such Passover had been observed in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet” (35:18).
2 Chronicles 35:18
Isaiah
Isaiah prophesied under Hezekiah and later kings (Isaiah 1:1), long after Samuel.
Jeremiah
Jeremiah appears at the end of this chapter, lamenting over Josiah (35:25), not as the benchmark.
Samuel
Elijah
Elijah is not the benchmark; the chapter points back to the days of Samuel (35:18).
Ezekiel
Ezekiel prophesied in the exile, long after Josiah; the benchmark is Samuel (35:18).
According to the historical note in 2 Chronicles 35, in which year of King Josiah’s reign was this remarkable Passover held?
“In the eighteenth year of Josiah’s reign, this Passover was observed” (35:19).
2 Chronicles 35:19
8th year
In Josiah’s eighth year he began to seek the God of his father David (2 Chronicles 34:3).
12th year
In his twelfth year he began to cleanse Judah of its high places and idols (2 Chronicles 34:3).
16th year
The sixteenth year is not the date given; the Passover came in the eighteenth year (35:19).
18th year
31st year
Josiah reigned thirty-one years in all (2 Chronicles 34:1), so the thirty-first year is when his reign ended.
After the temple had been set in order in 2 Chronicles 35, which foreign king marched up to fight at Carchemish on the Euphrates?
“Neco king of Egypt marched up to fight at Carchemish by the Euphrates” (35:20).
2 Chronicles 35:20
Sennacherib king of Assyria
Sennacherib attacked Judah in Hezekiah’s time (2 Chronicles 32:1), not Josiah’s.
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon
Nebuchadnezzar later defeated Neco at Carchemish (Jeremiah 46:2); in this account Neco is the one marching up (35:20).
Neco king of Egypt
Hazael king of Aram
Hazael king of Aram lived in earlier days (2 Kings 12:17), not Josiah’s.
Cyrus king of Persia
Cyrus king of Persia lived after the exile (2 Chronicles 36:22).
In King Josiah’s final battle narrative, what message did Neco send to Josiah about God?
Neco said, “God has told me to hurry. So stop opposing God, who is with me, or He will destroy you!” (35:21).
2 Chronicles 35:21
God wanted Josiah to join Egypt in war
Neco did not ask Josiah to join him; he told Josiah to stop opposing God (35:21).
God had told Neco to hurry, and Josiah should stop opposing Him
God had promised Judah victory at Megiddo
Neco’s message was a warning, not a promise of victory for Judah (35:21).
God wanted the temple moved to Egypt
Moving the temple to Egypt is not mentioned; Neco’s message concerned the war he was hurrying to fight (35:21).
God had rejected Jerusalem forever
Neco said God was with him in the campaign and warned Josiah, but he did not say God had rejected Jerusalem forever (35:21).
In spite of Neco’s warning in 2 Chronicles 35, what did King Josiah do before going to fight on the plain of Megiddo?
“Josiah, however, did not turn away from him; instead, in order to engage him in battle, he disguised himself” (35:22).
2 Chronicles 35:22
He fled to Lachish
Josiah went out to fight on the Plain of Megiddo, not to flee to Lachish (35:22).
He asked Jeremiah to lead the army
Jeremiah appears only at the end, lamenting Josiah’s death (35:25); he did not lead the army.
He disguised himself
He made peace with Egypt
Josiah did not make peace; he went to fight Neco (35:22).
He waited at Jerusalem
Josiah did not wait; he went out to battle on the Plain of Megiddo (35:22).
In the mourning account at the end of 2 Chronicles 35, where does the text say the laments for Josiah were written?
The laments for Josiah “are written in the Book of Laments” (35:25).
2 Chronicles 35:25
In the Book of the Wars of the LORD
The Book of the Wars of the LORD is cited in Numbers 21:14, not for Josiah’s laments.
In the Scroll of Isaiah
No Scroll of Isaiah is named in this chapter; the laments are in the Book of Laments (35:25).
In the Book of Nathan the Prophet
Nathan’s records are cited for Solomon’s reign (2 Chronicles 9:29), not for Josiah’s laments.
In the Book of Laments
In the Proverbs of Solomon
Solomon’s Proverbs are a collection of wisdom sayings (Proverbs 1:1), not the place of these laments (35:25).
In 2 Chronicles 36, after King Josiah died, whom did the people of the land make king in Jerusalem?
2 Chronicles 36:1 says the people of the land took Jehoahaz son of Josiah and made him king in Jerusalem in place of his father.
2 Chronicles 36:1
Jehoiakim
Jehoiakim was Jehoahaz’s brother, made king by Neco (36:4).
Jehoahaz
Zedekiah
Zedekiah was made king much later by Nebuchadnezzar (36:10).
Hezekiah
Hezekiah was an earlier king of Judah, long before Josiah’s death.
Manasseh
Manasseh also ruled long before Josiah and is not named in this chapter.
When Jehoahaz was deposed, what tribute did the king of Egypt impose on the land of Judah?
2 Chronicles 36:3 says the king of Egypt imposed on Judah a levy of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold.
2 Chronicles 36:3
10 talents of silver and 100 talents of gold
The amounts are reversed; the levy was 100 talents of silver and one of gold (36:3).
100 talents of silver and 1 talent of gold
30 talents of silver and 30 talents of gold
Thirty talents is not given in the chapter; the levy was 100 talents of silver and 1 of gold (36:3).
50 talents of silver and 5 talents of gold
Fifty and five are not the amounts given in the chapter (36:3).
1,000 talents of silver and 100 talents of gold
A thousand and a hundred talents is far larger than the levy in 36:3.
In the record of King Neco’s actions in Judah, what new name did he give Eliakim son of Josiah?
2 Chronicles 36:4 says Neco king of Egypt made Eliakim king and changed his name to Jehoiakim.
2 Chronicles 36:4
Jehoahaz
Jehoahaz was Eliakim’s brother, whom Neco carried off to Egypt (36:4).
Jehoiakim
Jehoiachin
Jehoiachin was Jehoiakim’s son, who reigned in his place (36:8).
Azariah
Azariah is not a name Neco gave; Eliakim became Jehoiakim (36:4).
Mattaniah
Mattaniah was the original name of Zedekiah, changed by the king of Babylon (2 Kings 24:17).
According to 2 Chronicles 36, what did Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon do to Jehoiakim?
2 Chronicles 36:6 says Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against Jehoiakim and bound him with bronze shackles to take him to Babylon.
2 Chronicles 36:6
He crowned him again in a ceremony at Hebron
Nothing is said of a coronation at Hebron; Nebuchadnezzar bound him instead (36:6).
He bound him with bronze shackles to take him to Babylon
He seized him and took him to Egypt in iron chains
It was Neco who carried off Jehoiakim’s brother Jehoahaz to Egypt (36:4), not Nebuchadnezzar who took Jehoiakim there.
He put out his eyes at Riblah and bound him
Blinding at Riblah describes what happened to Zedekiah (2 Kings 25:7), not Jehoiakim.
He confirmed him as a vassal and restored his throne
Nebuchadnezzar did not restore Jehoiakim to the throne; he bound him (36:6).
In the spring, after Nebuchadnezzar took Jehoiachin to Babylon, whom did he make king over Judah and Jerusalem?
2 Chronicles 36:10 says that in the spring, Nebuchadnezzar brought Jehoiachin to Babylon and made his relative Zedekiah king over Judah and Jerusalem.
2 Chronicles 36:10
Jehoahaz
Jehoahaz was deposed by the king of Egypt years earlier (36:3).
Eliakim
Eliakim was renamed Jehoiakim and was already dead by then (36:4–8).
Zedekiah
Uzziah
Uzziah was a much earlier king of Judah and is not named in the chapter.
Josiah
Josiah was the father of Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim (36:1, 36:5), already dead by this time.
According to 2 Chronicles 36:12, what did King Zedekiah fail to do?
2 Chronicles 36:12 says Zedekiah did evil and “did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke for the LORD.”
2 Chronicles 36:12
He did not heed Ezekiel’s vision of the dry bones in the valley
The chapter does not mention Ezekiel; it faults Zedekiah for not humbling himself before Jeremiah (36:12).
He did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke for the LORD
He did not rebuild Jericho, as Joshua’s curse had warned
The chapter does not mention Jericho; Joshua’s curse concerns its rebuilding (Joshua 6:26), not Zedekiah’s failure here.
He did not return the ark of the covenant to its place
The chapter does not mention the ark; Zedekiah’s failure was pride before the prophet (36:12).
He did not keep the Passover in the first month
Josiah kept the Passover (2 Chronicles 35:1); this chapter does not charge Zedekiah with missing it.
What specific rebellion of Zedekiah is named in this chapter about Jerusalem’s fall?
2 Chronicles 36:13 says he rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God.
2 Chronicles 36:13
He attacked Samaria and seized its treasure for himself
Samaria is not mentioned here; Zedekiah’s rebellion was against Nebuchadnezzar (36:13).
He burned the temple treasury to hide its gold
The chapter says the Babylonians carried off the temple treasures (36:18), not that Zedekiah burned them.
He rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear an oath by God
He executed Ezra the priest in the temple court
Ezra lived much later, after the exile (Ezra 7), so Zedekiah could not have executed him.
He moved the capital to Bethel and abandoned Jerusalem
The capital stayed in Jerusalem until the Chaldeans burned it (36:19).
Before Jerusalem was destroyed, what did the leaders of the priests and the people do to the house of the LORD in Jerusalem?
2 Chronicles 36:14 says the leaders of the priests and the people multiplied their unfaithful deeds and defiled the house of the LORD, which He had consecrated in Jerusalem.
2 Chronicles 36:14
They purified it and restored its worship
The verse says the opposite: they followed the abominations of the nations and defiled the house (36:14).
They moved it to Gibeon
The house stayed in Jerusalem until the Chaldeans burned it (36:19).
They enlarged it with cedar from Lebanon
The leaders defiled the house; enlarging it is not mentioned (36:14).
They polluted it while following the abominations of the nations
They turned it into a royal palace
The house was defiled, but it was not turned into a palace; the Chaldeans burned both (36:19).
According to 2 Chronicles 36, why did the LORD God of their fathers keep sending messengers to His people again and again?
2 Chronicles 36:15 says the LORD sent word to His people again and again through His messengers because He had compassion on them and on His dwelling place.
2 Chronicles 36:15
Because Babylon demanded that Judah’s prophets be sent to its court
Babylon did not ask for prophets; the LORD sent messengers out of compassion (36:15).
Because He wanted monthly sacrifices offered in the temple courts
Monthly sacrifices are not given as the reason; His compassion is (36:15).
Because He had compassion on His people and on His dwelling place
Because Egypt had asked Judah’s kings for warnings of coming war
Egypt is not mentioned in this connection; the cause was God’s compassion (36:15).
Because the princes of Judah had already repented and asked for guidance
The leaders had not repented; they mocked the messengers (36:16).

“Ask the priests at Bethel for permission, and then we will let you help”
No permission from priests at Bethel is involved; they cited Cyrus’s command (4:3).
After their offer was refused in Ezra 4, what did the people of the land try to do to the people of Judah?
The people of the land set out to discourage the people of Judah and make them afraid to build (4:4).
Ezra 4:4
Teach them the Law of Moses
They did not teach Judah anything; they set out to discourage the builders (4:4).
Discourage them and make them afraid to build
Help them repair the gates
They sought to hinder the work, not to help repair gates (4:4–5).
Send them grain for the workers
No grain was sent; they hired counselors to frustrate the builders’ plans (4:5).
Invite them to Samaria for peace talks
No peace talks are mentioned; the people of the land worked against Judah (4:4–5).
In Ezra 4, the opponents hired counselors against the builders during whose reign, continuing until the reign of which later Persian king?
They hired counselors to frustrate the builders’ plans throughout the reign of Cyrus and down to the reign of Darius, kings of Persia (4:5).
Ezra 4:5
From Saul to David
Saul and David were Israel’s kings, centuries before the Persian period.
From Nebuchadnezzar to Belshazzar
Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar were Babylonian kings, before Cyrus of Persia.
From Cyrus to Darius
From Xerxes to Artaxerxes
Xerxes and Artaxerxes come after Darius in this chapter (4:6–7), not as the span of the hired counselors (4:5).
From Solomon to Rehoboam
Solomon and Rehoboam were kings of Israel and Judah long before the Persian kings of Ezra 4.
According to Ezra 4, at the beginning of whose reign was an accusation lodged against the people of Judah and Jerusalem?
At the beginning of the reign of Xerxes, an accusation was lodged against the people of Judah and Jerusalem (4:6).
Ezra 4:6
Xerxes
Artaxerxes
Artaxerxes is the king to whom a later letter was written (4:7), not the king at the accusation in 4:6.
Darius
Darius is the king in whose second year the work resumed (4:24), not the Xerxes of 4:6.
Cyrus
Cyrus’s reign is where the opposition began (4:5), earlier than the accusation under Xerxes.
Belshazzar
Belshazzar was a Babylonian ruler (Daniel 5:1), long before Xerxes’ Persian reign.
In the section of Ezra 4 that records a complaint to King Artaxerxes about Jerusalem, which two officials are named as writing the letter?
Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe wrote the letter against Jerusalem to King Artaxerxes (4:8).
Ezra 4:8
Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite
Sanballat and Tobiah opposed the wall in Nehemiah’s day (Nehemiah 4:1–3), not in this letter.
Zerubbabel the governor and Jeshua the priest
Zerubbabel and Jeshua were the Jewish leaders who rejected the opponents’ offer (4:3), not the accusers.
Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the prophet
Haggai and Zechariah encouraged the builders later (Ezra 5:1); they did not write against Jerusalem.
Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe
Ezra the priest and Shecaniah son of Jehiel
Ezra and Shecaniah do not appear in this chapter.
How does Ezra 4 describe the form of the letter sent to Artaxerxes?
Ezra 4:7 says the letter to Artaxerxes was written in Aramaic and then translated.
Ezra 4:7
Written in Hebrew only
The letter was written in Aramaic and then translated (4:7), not Hebrew only.
Written on stone tablets
Stone tablets are not mentioned; the letter was a written document (4:7–8).
Written in Aramaic and then translated
Spoken orally by a messenger
The letter was written, not spoken by a messenger (4:7); the king replied that it had been translated and read in his presence (4:18).
Written in Greek for the court
Greek is not mentioned; the letter was written in Aramaic (4:7).
In the accusation sent to Artaxerxes in Ezra 4, how was the city of Jerusalem described?
The accusers called Jerusalem a rebellious and wicked city that was restoring its walls and foundations (4:12).
Ezra 4:12
A peaceful and faithful city
They said the opposite, calling the city rebellious and wicked (4:12).
A rebellious and wicked city
A small and defenseless village
They described a city rebuilding its walls and foundations (4:12), not a small village.
A city full of prophets
Prophets are not mentioned in the accusation; it centers on rebellion and lost revenue (4:12–13).
A trading port by the sea
No seaport is mentioned; they warned of lost tribute, duty, and toll (4:13).
In the warning sent to King Artaxerxes about rebuilding Jerusalem, which three kinds of revenue did the accusers say would no longer be paid?
The accusers warned that if the city were rebuilt, the Jews would not pay tribute, duty, or toll, and the royal treasury would suffer (4:13).
Ezra 4:13
Tithes, offerings, and firstfruits
Tithes, offerings, and firstfruits were obligations to the LORD, not the Persian revenues named in 4:13.
Tribute, duty, and toll
Gold, frankincense, and myrrh
Gold, frankincense, and myrrh are the gifts of the Magi (Matthew 2:11), not the revenues named here.
Grain, wine, and oil
Grain, wine, and oil are produce, not the three payments named in 4:13.
Silver, iron, and bronze
Silver, iron, and bronze are metals; the payments named in 4:13 are tribute, duty, and toll.
In Ezra 4, what reason did the officials west of the Euphrates give for informing the king about Jerusalem?
They said that because they were in the service of the palace, it was not fitting to allow the king to be dishonored (4:14).
Ezra 4:14
They wanted the regional capital moved to Samaria
Moving a capital is never suggested; they claimed loyalty to the king (4:14).
They were in service to the palace and did not want to see the king dishonored
They needed priests from Persia to serve the temple
Priests for the temple are not mentioned in their reasoning (4:14).
They wanted Jerusalem to become a free city exempt from tribute
They wanted Jerusalem stopped, not freed; they feared lost revenue and a challenge to the king (4:13–16).
They feared a famine would strike Judah and the region
No famine is mentioned; their stated worry was the king’s honor and treasury (4:13–14).
In the list of peoples settled in the cities of Samaria in Ezra 4, who is called “the great and honorable” and said to have deported and settled them there?
The letter describes the peoples settled in Samaria as those whom the great and honorable Ashurbanipal deported and settled there (4:10).
Ezra 4:10
Esarhaddon
Esar-haddon is named in 4:2 as the king who brought settlers, not as the one called great and honorable in 4:10.
Ashurbanipal
Shalmaneser
Shalmaneser is not named in this chapter.
Nebuchadnezzar
Nebuchadnezzar was a Babylonian king and is not named in the letter.
Tatnai
Tatnai is a Persian-period official (see Ezra 5:3), not an Assyrian king.
In King Artaxerxes’ reply in Ezra 4, over what region did he say mighty kings from Jerusalem had once ruled?
Artaxerxes’ reply says mighty kings ruled over Jerusalem and exercised authority over the whole region west of the Euphrates (4:20).
Ezra 4:20
Only the hill country of Judah
The reply speaks of the whole region west of the Euphrates, not only Judah’s hill country (4:20).
Egypt and Cush
Egypt and Cush are not named in the king’s reply (4:20).
The whole region west of the Euphrates
The islands of the sea
The islands of the sea are not mentioned; the region was west of the Euphrates (4:20).
The land east of the Jordan only
The land east of the Jordan is not named; the king said west of the Euphrates (4:20).
After Artaxerxes’ letter was read in Ezra 4, what did Rehum, Shimshai, and their associates do in Jerusalem, and what happened to the work on God’s house?
On reading Artaxerxes’ letter, Rehum, Shimshai, and their associates went to the Jews and forcibly stopped them, and the work stood still until the second year of Darius (4:23–24).
They joined the builders, and the temple was finished that same year
The opposition forced a halt rather than joining the builders; the temple was not finished then (4:24).
They asked for a new decree from Cyrus, and the work moved to Samaria instead
No new decree from Cyrus was sought; they acted on Artaxerxes’ letter (4:23).
They forcibly stopped the Jews, and the work stood still until the second year of Darius king of Persia
They rebuilt the city wall and appointed gatekeepers to guard it
The chapter ends with the work on the house of God halted, not a wall rebuilt and gatekeepers appointed (4:24).
They returned to Babylon and left the builders in peace for many years
They went to the Jews in Jerusalem and stopped them by force (4:23); they did not return to Babylon.
In Ezra 5, which two prophets spoke in Judah and Jerusalem in the name of the God of Israel, prompting the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem to continue?
The prophets Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo prophesied to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem in the name of the God of Israel (5:1).
Ezra 5:1
Elijah and Elisha son of Shaphat
Elijah and Elisha prophesied centuries earlier in the northern kingdom, not in the days of Darius.
Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo
Isaiah and Jeremiah son of Hilkiah
Isaiah and Jeremiah prophesied before the exile, not during the rebuilding (5:1).
Joel son of Pethuel and Amos
Joel and Amos are not the prophets named in 5:1.
Nathan and Gad the seer
Nathan and Gad were prophets in David’s day, not in the days of Ezra 5.
According to Ezra 5, which two leaders rose up in Jerusalem to begin rebuilding the house of God after the prophets spoke?
Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak rose up and began to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem (5:2).
Ezra 5:2
Nehemiah son of Hacaliah and Ezra the scribe
Nehemiah and Ezra worked later and are not the leaders named in 5:2.
Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak
Sheshbazzar and Daniel
Sheshbazzar laid the foundation earlier (5:16), and Daniel is not named in 5:2.
Rehum and Shimshai
Rehum and Shimshai are opponents of the Jews in Ezra 4:8, not builders in 5:2.
Sanballat and Tobiah
Sanballat and Tobiah opposed Nehemiah’s wall building (Nehemiah 4:1, 3), not the temple rebuilding in 5:2.
In the temple-rebuilding account in Ezra 5, who came to Jerusalem to question the Jews about who had authorized the rebuilding?
Tattenai the governor of the region west of the Euphrates, Shethar-bozenai and their associates questioned the Jews about who authorized the rebuilding (5:3).
Ezra 5:3
Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe, with their associates in Samaria
Rehum and Shimshai wrote to Artaxerxes (Ezra 4:8), a different letter in a different reign.
Tattenai governor of Trans-Euphrates, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates
Sanballat the Horonite and Geshem the Arab, with their allies from Samaria
Sanballat and Geshem opposed Nehemiah’s wall building (Nehemiah 6:1), not the temple work in 5:3.
Cyrus king of Persia and his advisers, who had come from Babylon
Cyrus issued the original decree (5:13); he was not the questioner in 5:3.
Mordecai and Esther, who had come up from the citadel of Susa
Mordecai and Esther lived in the Persian capital, and are not in this account.
When Persian officials inspected the temple work in Judah in Ezra 5, what additional information did they ask the Jewish builders to provide?
The officials also asked, “What are the names of the men who are constructing this building?” (5:4).
Ezra 5:4, 10
The amount of gold collected for the temple
The amount of gold collected is not what they asked for in 5:4.
The names of the men constructing the building
The genealogy of Aaron’s priests
The genealogy of Aaron’s priests is not what they asked for in 5:4.
The date of the Passover
The date of Passover is not what they asked for in 5:4.
The dimensions of Solomon’s palace
Solomon’s palace dimensions are not what they asked for in 5:4.
In Ezra 5, why were the elders of the Jews not forced to stop rebuilding the house of God in Jerusalem immediately?
The eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews, so they were not stopped until a report was sent to Darius and written instructions returned (5:5).
Ezra 5:5
Because Darius personally visited Judah and ordered the work to continue
Darius did not visit Judah; a report was sent to him (5:5).
Because the city wall was already completed and the officials were satisfied
The wall of Jerusalem is not mentioned in 5:5; the temple was the project.
Because the eye of their God was upon them until a report could go to Darius and a written reply return
Because the Samaritans joined the work and shared in building the house
The Samaritans are not mentioned as joining the work in 5:5.
Because the ark of the covenant was found and brought back into the house
The ark is not mentioned in 5:5.
In the letter sent to King Darius in Ezra 5, how did Tattenai and the officials describe the rebuilding of the temple in the province of Judah?
The letter reported that the people were rebuilding with large stones and placing timbers in the walls, and that the work was carried out diligently and was prospering in their hands (5:8).
Ezra 5:8
It was abandoned, with burned gates and broken stones scattered across the site
The report said the work was prospering, not abandoned (5:8).
It was being built with large stones, timber was being laid in the walls, and the work was progressing diligently
It was being decorated with ivory and cedar from Lebanon as in Solomon’s day
Ivory and cedar from Lebanon are not mentioned in the report (5:8).
It was only a foundation, with no workers present and the site left empty
The report described active building with workers, not a bare foundation (5:8).
It had already been fully completed and dedicated with offerings and feasting
The report said the building was under construction, not completed and dedicated (5:8, 16).
In the reply quoted in Ezra 5, how did the Jewish elders identify themselves before the Persian officials while explaining the rebuilding in Jerusalem?
The elders answered, “We are servants of the God of heaven and earth” (5:11).
Ezra 5:11
We are the sons of Levi only
The sons of Levi are not the group they named in 5:11.
We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth
We are the nobles of Judah and Benjamin
Nobles of Judah and Benjamin is not how they identified themselves in 5:11.
We are the guardians of the royal treasury
Guardians of the royal treasury is not how they identified themselves in 5:11.
We are the descendants of David’s mighty men
David’s mighty men is not how they identified themselves in 5:11.
According to the elders’ explanation in Ezra 5, which king destroyed the former temple in Jerusalem and carried the people away to Babylon after their fathers angered the God of heaven?
The elders said God delivered their fathers into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who destroyed the temple and carried the people to Babylon (5:12).
Ezra 5:12
Pharaoh Necho
Pharaoh Necho killed Josiah (2 Kings 23:29), but 5:12 names Nebuchadnezzar as the destroyer of the temple.
Sennacherib king of Assyria
Sennacherib threatened Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:13), but 5:12 names Nebuchadnezzar as the destroyer of the temple.
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon
Artaxerxes king of Persia
Artaxerxes lived long after the temple’s destruction; 5:12 names Nebuchadnezzar.
Belshazzar king of Babylon
Belshazzar was a later king of Babylon (Daniel 5:1), and 5:12 names Nebuchadnezzar.
In the history retold in Ezra 5, what did Cyrus king of Babylon do with the gold and silver articles that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple in Jerusalem?
Cyrus gave the articles Nebuchadnezzar had taken to Sheshbazzar, whom he appointed governor, and told him to put them in the temple in Jerusalem (5:14–15).
He melted them down and used the silver to pay the Persian taxes owed
Cyrus did not melt them down; he returned them (5:14–15).
He sent them to Egypt as tribute to secure peace on the border
Cyrus did not send them to Egypt; he gave them to Sheshbazzar (5:14).
He gave them to Sheshbazzar, whom he appointed governor, to take back to Jerusalem
He placed them in the temple of Dagon as spoils for the gods of Babylon
Cyrus did not place them in the temple of Dagon; he gave them to Sheshbazzar (5:14).
He gave them to Zerubbabel to sell for lumber and stone for the work
Cyrus gave the articles to Sheshbazzar, not Zerubbabel, and for the temple, not for sale (5:14–15).
At the end of the letter in Ezra 5, what specific investigation did Tattenai ask King Darius to make in the royal archives at Babylon concerning the house of God in Jerusalem?
Tattenai asked that a search be made of the royal archives in Babylon to see if King Cyrus had issued a decree to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem (5:17).
Ezra 5:17
Whether Solomon had taxed Tyre for cedar wood
Tyre and cedar wood are not what Tattenai asked about in 5:17.
Whether Nebuchadnezzar had dedicated the temple vessels to Marduk
Marduk dedication is not what Tattenai asked about in 5:17.
Whether Cyrus had issued a decree to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem
Whether David had chosen Jerusalem as the capital
David’s choice of Jerusalem is not what Tattenai asked about in 5:17.
Whether Nehemiah had permission to rebuild the city wall
Nehemiah’s permission to rebuild the wall belongs to a later period (Nehemiah 2:8); it is not what Tattenai asked about in 5:17.
In Ezra 6, which Persian king ordered a search of the royal archives concerning the house of God in Jerusalem?
“King Darius ordered a search of the archives stored in the treasury of Babylon” (6:1).
Ezra 6:1
Cyrus
Cyrus issued the original decree (6:3), but Darius ordered the search.
Darius
Xerxes
Xerxes ruled later, in the story of Esther; Ezra 6:1 names Darius.
Artaxerxes
Artaxerxes appears later in Ezra (Ezra 7:1) and is named among the kings of 6:14, not as the one who ordered the search.
Nebuchadnezzar
Nebuchadnezzar took the temple articles to Babylon (6:5); he did not order the search.
In the record about the Jerusalem temple in Ezra 6, where was the scroll containing Cyrus’s decree found?
A scroll “was found in the fortress of Ecbatana, in the province of Media” (6:2).
Ezra 6:2
Babylon in Chaldea
Darius ordered the search in the archives in Babylon (6:1), but the scroll was found at Ecbatana.
Susa in Elam
Susa appears in Nehemiah and Esther (Nehemiah 1:1), not in Ezra’s account of the scroll.
Ecbatana in Media
Nineveh in Assyria
Nineveh was the Assyrian capital (Jonah 1:2); Ezra 6:2 names Ecbatana in Media.
Jerusalem in Judah
The decree concerned Jerusalem, but the scroll was found at Ecbatana (6:2).
According to Cyrus’s decree cited in Ezra 6, what was to happen at the house of God in Jerusalem?
Cyrus decreed, “Let the house be rebuilt as a place for offering sacrifices” (6:3).
Ezra 6:3
It was to be converted into a royal palace
The decree ordered the house of God rebuilt, not made into a palace (6:3).
It was to be rebuilt as a place to present sacrifices
It was to be moved to Samaria
The house was to be rebuilt in Jerusalem on its original site (6:3, 6:7), not moved to Samaria.
It was to be left in ruins until peace came
Cyrus ordered the rebuilding, with costs from the royal treasury (6:4).
It was to become a fortress for Persia
Costs were paid by the royal treasury (6:4); the house was not a Persian fortress.
In Ezra 6, what did the decree say should be done with the gold and silver articles that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple in Jerusalem?
The decree said the gold and silver articles Nebuchadnezzar took “must also be returned to the temple in Jerusalem” (6:5).
Ezra 6:5
Melt them down for tax payments
The articles were to be returned, not melted down (6:5).
Keep them in Babylon permanently
They were not to stay in Babylon; 6:5 orders their return to Jerusalem.
Return them to the temple in Jerusalem
Divide them among the priests in Persia
They were deposited in the house of God (6:5), not shared out among Persian priests.
Send them to Egypt for safekeeping
Egypt plays no role here; the decree sends them back to the temple in Jerusalem (6:5).
When Darius gave orders about the rebuilding work in Jerusalem, from where were the Jewish elders’ expenses to be paid?
Darius ordered that the cost be “paid in full to these men from the royal treasury out of the taxes of the provinces west of the Euphrates” (6:8).
Ezra 6:8
From offerings collected in Judah
The cost came from the royal treasury (6:8), not offerings collected in Judah.
From the royal treasury, out of the taxes of the provinces west of the Euphrates
From the private wealth of Zerubbabel
Zerubbabel is not named in this decree; the cost came from the royal treasury (6:8).
From the treasury of Egypt
Egypt is not mentioned; the money came from provinces west of the Euphrates (6:8).
From the sale of temple vessels
The temple articles were to be returned (6:5), not sold to pay for the work.
In Darius’s decree in Ezra 6, why were bulls, rams, lambs, wheat, salt, wine, and oil to be supplied daily to the priests in Jerusalem?
The supplies were given daily so “they will be able to offer sacrifices of a sweet aroma to the God of heaven and to pray for the lives of the king and his sons” (6:9–10).
Ezra 6:9-10
So they could feed the Persian army
The supplies were for the temple offerings, not for feeding the army (6:9–10).
So they could trade with Tyre and Sidon
Trade with Tyre and Sidon is not the aim; the goods were to be given daily to the priests for sacrifices (6:9–10).
So they could offer pleasing sacrifices to God and pray for the king and his sons
So they could celebrate only the New Moon festivals
They were given daily without fail (6:9), not limited to New Moon festivals.
So they could store them for a future famine
They were supplied daily for sacrifice (6:9–10), not stored against famine.
During the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem, which two prophets are named in Ezra 6 as helping the elders prosper?
“The Jewish elders built and prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah son of Iddo” (6:14).
Ezra 6:14
Elijah and Elisha son of Shaphat
Elijah and Elisha prophesied in the northern kingdom centuries earlier (1 Kings 17:1).
Isaiah son of Amoz and Jeremiah of Anathoth
Isaiah and Jeremiah prophesied before the exile (Jeremiah 1:1), not during the temple’s rebuilding.
Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo
Amos of Tekoa and Hosea son of Beeri
Amos and Hosea prophesied in the eighth century (Hosea 1:1); Ezra 6 names Haggai and Zechariah.
Nathan the prophet and Gad the seer
Nathan and Gad served David (2 Samuel 24:11), long before this rebuilding.
In the royal warning attached to the temple decree in Ezra 6, what punishment was declared for anyone who altered the edict?
Darius decreed that if anyone interfered, “a beam is to be torn from his house and raised up, and he is to be impaled on it,” and his house made “a pile of rubble” (6:11).
Ezra 6:11
Exile to Egypt for the man, his family, and all of his household
The penalty in 6:11 is impalement and ruin of his house, not exile to Egypt.
Loss of all his farmland for seven years and a heavy fine of silver
Loss of farmland is not mentioned; Darius prescribed a far more severe penalty (6:11).
A beam would be pulled from his house, he would be impaled on it, and his house made a pile of rubble
He would be forced to rebuild the city wall of Jerusalem by himself
Rebuilding the wall alone is not the penalty; 6:11 describes impalement and rubble.
He would be thrown into a den of lions before the royal court
The lions’ den belongs to Daniel 6:16; Ezra 6:11 describes impalement on a beam.
Ezra 6 says the house of God in Jerusalem was finished according to whose command and whose decrees?
“They finished building according to the command of the God of Israel and the decrees of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes, kings of Persia” (6:14).
Ezra 6:14
According to the command of Moses and the decrees of Saul, David, and Solomon
Moses and Israel’s early kings are not credited; 6:14 names the God of Israel and Persian kings.
According to the command of the God of Israel and the decrees of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes king of Persia
According to the command of Joshua and the decrees of the judges of Israel
Joshua and the judges are not named in 6:14; the Persian kings are.
According to the command of Ezra and the decrees of the priests and Levites
Ezra and the priests are not named as the source of the decrees in 6:14.
According to the command of Nehemiah and the decrees of Darius alone
Nehemiah is not named in 6:14, and the decrees came from Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes.
At the end of Ezra 6, after Passover and during the Feast of Unleavened Bread, what royal title is used when saying the LORD turned the king’s heart toward the returned exiles?
The LORD “turned the heart of the king of Assyria toward them to strengthen their hands in the work” (6:22).
Ezra 6:22
King of Babylon
Babylon’s kings had destroyed the temple, but 6:22 names the king of Assyria.
King of Persia
Persian kings are named elsewhere in the chapter (6:14), but 6:22 uses the title king of Assyria.
King of Assyria
King of Media
Media is mentioned only as the place the scroll was found (6:2), not as the king’s title.
King of Judah
Judah’s monarchy had ended; 6:22 names the king of Assyria.
In Ezra 7, which Persian king was reigning when Ezra went up from Babylon to Jerusalem?
Ezra 7:1 dates his coming “during the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia,” and 7:7 places it in the king’s seventh year.
Ezra 7:1, 7
Cyrus
Cyrus issued the first return decree (Ezra 1) decades before Ezra’s journey.
Darius
Darius reigned in the time of the temple’s completion (Ezra 6), before Ezra’s trip.
Artaxerxes
Xerxes
Xerxes is not the king named for Ezra’s journey; the king is Artaxerxes.
Nebuchadnezzar
Nebuchadnezzar was a Babylonian king who destroyed Jerusalem, long before Ezra.
When Ezra 7 introduces Ezra’s journey, from which city did he travel up to Jerusalem?
“This Ezra came up from Babylon” (7:6).
Ezra 7:6
Susa
Susa was a Persian royal city, but Ezra is said to have come up from Babylon.
Nineveh
Nineveh was Assyria’s capital and is not named as Ezra’s starting point.
Babylon
Samaria
Samaria is in the land of Israel, not where Ezra’s journey began.
Jericho
Jericho is in the land of Israel and not Ezra’s starting point.
In the account of Ezra chapter 7, how is Ezra described in relation to God’s Law?
Ezra “was a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses, which the LORD, the God of Israel, had given” (7:6).
Ezra 7:6
A military commander skilled with the sword
Ezra’s skill was in the Law, not in warfare.
A skilled scribe in the Law of Moses
A temple singer with a harp
Singers are listed among those who went up with him (7:7), but Ezra himself was a scribe.
A mason rebuilding the wall
Wall rebuilding is Nehemiah’s work (Nehemiah 2–6), not how Ezra is described.
A prophet interpreting dreams
Interpreting dreams describes figures like Daniel, not Ezra, who was a scribe of the Law.
Ezra 7:1–5 traces Ezra’s priestly line all the way back to which chief priest, the earliest ancestor it names?
Ezra’s genealogy ends “the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the chief priest” (7:5).
Ezra 7:1-5
Eli
Eli was a priest at Shiloh in Samuel’s day and is not named in Ezra’s list.
Zadok
Zadok is in Ezra’s line (7:2), but the line runs back further, to Aaron the chief priest.
Aaron
Abiathar
Abiathar is not named in Ezra’s genealogy.
Jehoiada
Jehoiada is not named in Ezra’s genealogy.
According to Ezra 7, in which year of King Artaxerxes did Ezra arrive in Jerusalem?
“In the seventh year of King Artaxerxes, he went up to Jerusalem” (7:7).
Ezra 7:7-8
Third year
The third year is not the year given; it was the seventh.
Fifth year
The fifth year is not the year given; the fifth month is when he arrived (7:8).
Seventh year
Tenth year
The tenth year is not the year given; it was the seventh.
Twelfth year

Jericho and watching the eastern road are not mentioned in 4:22.

In the night-warning section of Job 33, when does Elihu say God may open a person’s ears?
Elihu says God speaks “in a dream, in a vision in the night, when deep sleep falls upon men as they slumber on their beds,” and opens their ears (33:15–16).
At noon in the marketplace, when the merchants are all gathered there
Elihu speaks of night dreams, not midday public places (33:15).
In a dream, in a vision in the night, when deep sleep falls upon men
During the Feast of Booths, when the people dwell in shelters
The Feast of Booths is a festival of living in booths (Leviticus 23:42); Elihu’s warning comes at night.
On the battlefield, when the armies are about to meet in war
No battlefield is mentioned; the warning comes in a dream while men sleep (33:15).
At the city gate at dawn, when the elders sit down to judge
Job sat at the city gate in better days (Job 29:7); Elihu’s warning comes in sleep, not at the gate.
According to Job 33, what is one purpose of God’s warnings in dreams?
God warns people “to turn a man from wrongdoing and keep him from pride” (33:17).
To reveal hidden treasure buried in the fields of his fathers
Elihu names turning from wrongdoing, not revealing hidden treasure (33:17).
To turn a man from wrongdoing and keep him from pride
To make him ruler over nations and give him a great name
Joseph’s dreams did foretell his rule (Genesis 37:7–8), but Elihu says God’s warnings aim to restrain wrongdoing and pride (33:17).
To teach him a new song of praise for the temple choirs
A new song of praise is mentioned in Psalm 33:3, but Elihu’s warnings aim to turn a man from wrongdoing (33:17).
To show him the exact date of his death so he can prepare
Elihu does not say God shows a man the date of his death; the warnings turn him from wrongdoing (33:17).
In Elihu’s explanation to Job, from what does God preserve a person through such warnings?
Elihu says God’s warnings “preserve his soul from the Pit and his life from perishing by the sword” (33:18).

Floods and hail are not in Elihu’s list; he names the Pit and the sword (33:18).

Prison and exile are not mentioned; God preserves a man from the Pit and the sword (33:18).
From the Pit and from perishing by the sword
From old age and from the gray hair of the elderly
Elihu speaks of preserving life, not preventing old age (33:18).
From famine alone and from every kind of drought
Famine is not mentioned here; Elihu says God preserves from the Pit and the sword (33:18).
Besides dreams, what other form of correction does Elihu describe in Job 33?

Chastening by shipwreck on the sea and the loss of his goods
Shipwreck is not mentioned; the chastening is bodily pain (33:19).
Chastening by public shame at the city gate before the elders
Public shame is not mentioned; Elihu describes pain and distress in the bones (33:19).
Chastening by loss of speech so that he can no longer complain
Loss of speech is not mentioned; the sufferer loses his appetite and wastes away (33:20–21).

He detests his bread, and his soul loathes his favorite food
He asks only for wine and refuses everything else
Wine is not mentioned in the description (33:20).
He refuses water but cries out for honey instead
Honey is not mentioned; he loathes even his favorite food (33:20).

A vow is not mentioned; the reason is that a ransom has been found (33:24).

What confession does the restored man sing before others in Job 33?

He confesses sin; the claim of innocence is the one Elihu quotes from Job in 33:9.
“I have sinned and perverted what was right, yet I did not get what I deserved”

Near the end of Job 33, how often does Elihu say God does such things for a man, and for what purpose?
Elihu says God does all these things “two or even three times, to bring back his soul from the Pit, that he may be enlightened with the light of life” (33:29–30).

Elihu says two or even three times, not once, and the purpose is to rescue a man’s soul, not display power (33:29–30).

Two or even three times, to bring back his soul from the Pit and enlighten him with the light of life

Seven times is not what Elihu says; he says two or even three times (33:29).
Forty times, to prepare him for battle against his enemies on the field
Forty days is a number tied to Moses (Exodus 24:18), not Elihu’s count; he says two or even three times (33:29).
