Hear my prayer, O LORD
“Hear my prayer, O LORD” opens a plea in Psalm 102:1, not Psalm 13.
How long, O LORD?
Why do the nations rage?
“Why do the nations rage” begins Psalm 2:1, not this lament.
Bless the LORD, O my soul
“Bless the LORD, O my soul” is the opening of Psalm 103:1, a psalm of praise.
Create in me a clean heart
“Create in me a clean heart” is David’s prayer of repentance in Psalm 51:10.
In David’s opening complaint in Psalm 13, what does he ask if the LORD will do to him forever?
David asks, “Will You forget me forever?” (13:1).
Psalm 13:1
Judge him forever
David asks about being forgotten, not judged, in 13:1.
Forget him forever
Test him forever
David does not ask whether the LORD will test him forever in this verse; he asks whether he will be forgotten (13:1).
Exalt him forever
David feels forgotten, not exalted; exalting him is not what he asks about (13:1).
Scatter him forever
Scattering is not mentioned in 13:1; David’s question is “Will You forget me forever?”
In the first verse of Psalm 13, what does David say the LORD may be doing besides forgetting him?
David asks, “How long will You hide Your face from me?” (13:1).
Psalm 13:1
Hiding His face from him
Taking away his crown
Taking away his crown is not mentioned anywhere in Psalm 13.
Removing his lampstand
A lampstand is a tabernacle and temple furnishing, not something David mentions in Psalm 13.
Breaking his bow
Breaking his bow is not part of the complaint in Psalm 13:1; he fears God is hiding His face.
Closing the temple doors
Closing the temple doors is not mentioned in Psalm 13; the complaint is that God hides His face (13:1).
In Psalm 13, what inner struggle does David describe before mentioning sorrow in his heart day after day?
David asks, “How long must I wrestle in my soul, with sorrow in my heart each day?” (13:2).
Psalm 13:2
Wrestling in his soul
Forgetting the law
Forgetting the law is not mentioned in Psalm 13; he says he wrestles in his soul (13:2).
Fasting in the wilderness
Fasting in the wilderness is not named in Psalm 13:2; the struggle is within his soul.
Bearing the ark alone
Carrying the ark is not part of David’s complaint in Psalm 13:2.
Climbing the hill of Zion
Climbing Zion’s hill is not in Psalm 13; verse 2 speaks of wrestling in his soul.
Who does David say is dominating him in Psalm 13:2?
David asks, “How long will my enemy dominate me?” (13:2).
Psalm 13:2
His neighbor
A neighbor is not mentioned in Psalm 13; the one who dominates him is his enemy (13:2).
His servant
A servant is not mentioned in Psalm 13:2; David names his enemy.
His enemy
A foreign king
A foreign king is not named in Psalm 13; David simply says “my enemy” (13:2).
The elders at the gate
The elders at the gate are not mentioned in Psalm 13; the one dominating him is his enemy (13:2).
In Psalm 13, after saying, “Consider me and respond, O LORD my God,” what specific request does David make?
David prays, “Consider me and respond, O LORD my God. Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep in death” (13:3).
Psalm 13:3
Teach me Your statutes
“Teach me Your statutes” is a prayer from Psalm 119:12.
Give light to my eyes
Establish the work of my hands
Asking God to establish the work of our hands is the prayer of Psalm 90:17.
Let justice roll on like a river
“Let justice roll on like a river” is from Amos 5:24, not Psalm 13.
Open my lips to declare Your praise
“O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare Your praise” is David’s prayer in Psalm 51:15.
In Psalm 13, what does David fear will happen if the LORD does not give light to his eyes?
David prays, “Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep in death” (13:3).
Psalm 13:3
He will be taken captive
Captivity is not mentioned in Psalm 13; David fears death (13:3).
He will sleep in death
He will lose the throne
Losing the throne is not his fear in Psalm 13:3; he fears sleeping in death.
He will wander among the nations
Wandering among the nations is not mentioned in Psalm 13; the fear is death (13:3).
He will forget the covenant
Forgetting the covenant is not his concern in Psalm 13:3; he asks for light to his eyes lest he sleep in death.
In Psalm 13, if God does not answer, what boast does David fear his enemy will make?
David fears his enemy will say, “I have overcome him,” and his foes will rejoice when he falls (13:4).
Psalm 13:4
“The LORD has abandoned him.”
The enemy’s boast in Psalm 13:4 is “I have overcome him,” not that the LORD has abandoned him.
“I have overcome him.”
“He has fled to the mountains.”
Fleeing to the mountains is not what the enemy boasts in Psalm 13:4.
“His shield has failed him.”
A failed shield is not mentioned in Psalm 13; the enemy says “I have overcome him” (13:4).
“He trusted in horses and chariots.”
Trusting in horses and chariots is not part of the boast in Psalm 13:4.
Near the end of Psalm 13, which pair correctly describes David’s renewed confidence in God?
David says, “I have trusted in Your loving devotion; my heart will rejoice in Your salvation” (13:5).
Psalm 13:5
“I have trusted in my sword; my heart will rejoice in battle.”
David does not trust in a sword; he trusts in God’s loving devotion (13:5).
“I have trusted in Your loving devotion; my heart will rejoice in Your salvation.”
“I have trusted in the sanctuary; my heart will rejoice in Jerusalem.”
The sanctuary and Jerusalem are not what David names in 13:5; he trusts God’s loving devotion and rejoices in His salvation.
“I have trusted in my innocence; my heart will rejoice in vindication.”
David does not claim his innocence as his ground in Psalm 13:5; he trusts God’s loving devotion.
“I have trusted in the prophets; my heart will rejoice in wisdom.”
The prophets and wisdom are not named in Psalm 13:5; the verse speaks of loving devotion and salvation.
At the close of Psalm 13, which option correctly gives David’s full response of faith after his distress?
Psalm 13 ends, “I will sing to the LORD, for He has been good to me” (13:6).
Psalm 13:6
“I will wait for the dawn, for my help comes from the hills.”
“I lift up my eyes to the hills” is from Psalm 121:1, not Psalm 13:6.
“I will offer sacrifices in the tent, and fire will answer from heaven.”
Fire from heaven answering sacrifice is not in Psalm 13; the psalm ends with singing to the LORD (13:6).
“I will sing to the LORD, for He has been good to me.”
“I will lift up my cup, for the city is secure around me.”
A secure city is not mentioned in Psalm 13; David’s closing words are about singing to the LORD (13:6).
“I will lie down in peace, for my barns are filled with grain.”
Barns filled with grain are not in Psalm 13; the closing words are “I will sing to the LORD” (13:6).
In Psalm 14, what does the fool say in his heart?
“The fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Psalm 14:1).
Psalm 14:1
There is no God
The LORD has forgotten
Complaining that the LORD has forgotten is a complaint psalmists make elsewhere, but Psalm 14:1 says the fool denies God.
I will never be shaken
Feeling unshakable is not what the fool says in Psalm 14:1; he says there is no God.
Peace will save us
Peace saving us is not what the fool says in Psalm 14:1; he says there is no God.
Wisdom is greater than God
The fool does not rank wisdom above God here; he says there is no God (Psalm 14:1).
In David’s Psalm 14, from where does the LORD look down to examine mankind?
“The LORD looks down from heaven upon the sons of men to see if any understand, if any seek God” (Psalm 14:2).
Psalm 14:2
Mount Zion
Zion is mentioned at the end of the psalm as the source of salvation (Psalm 14:7), not where the LORD looks down from.
The temple courts
The temple courts are not mentioned; the LORD looks down from heaven (Psalm 14:2).
Heaven
The wilderness
The wilderness is not mentioned; the LORD looks down from heaven (Psalm 14:2).
The deep
The deep is not mentioned; the LORD looks down from heaven (Psalm 14:2).
In Psalm 14, what is the LORD looking to see among the sons of men?
The LORD looks “to see if any understand, if any seek God” (Psalm 14:2).
Psalm 14:2
If any understand and seek God
If any bring lambs for sacrifice
Bringing lambs is not what He looks for in Psalm 14:2; He looks for understanding and seeking God.
If any rebuild the altar
Rebuilding the altar is not what He looks for in Psalm 14:2.
If any defeat their enemies
Defeating enemies is not what He looks for in Psalm 14:2; He looks for those who understand and seek God.
If any can interpret dreams
Interpreting dreams is not what He looks for in Psalm 14:2.
According to Psalm 14, how many people do good after all have turned away?
“There is no one who does good, not even one” (Psalm 14:3).
Psalm 14:3
Many
The psalm says not many, but none, do good (Psalm 14:3).
A faithful few
A faithful few are not mentioned; the verse says no one does good, not even one (Psalm 14:3).
Only kings
Only kings is not said; the verse says no one does good, not even one (Psalm 14:3).
No one, not even one
Only the poor
Only the poor is not said; the verse says no one does good, not even one (Psalm 14:3).
In the psalm that says evildoers “never learn,” how do they treat God’s people?
“They devour my people like bread” (Psalm 14:4).
Psalm 14:4
They drive them into Egypt
Driving God’s people into Egypt is not mentioned; they devour them like bread (Psalm 14:4).
They consume them like bread
They clothe them in sackcloth
Clothing them in sackcloth is not mentioned; they devour them like bread (Psalm 14:4).
They hide them in caves
Hiding them in caves is not mentioned; they devour them like bread (Psalm 14:4).
They divide them by tribes
Dividing them by tribes is not mentioned; they devour them like bread (Psalm 14:4).
In Psalm 14, whom do the evildoers fail to call upon?
They “refuse to call upon the LORD” (Psalm 14:4).
Psalm 14:4
David
David wrote the psalm, but the evildoers are said to refuse to call on the LORD (Psalm 14:4).
Moses
Moses is not named in Psalm 14; the evildoers refuse to call upon the LORD (Psalm 14:4).
The LORD
Aaron
Aaron is not named in Psalm 14; the evildoers refuse to call upon the LORD (Psalm 14:4).
Zion
Zion is named only as the source of salvation (Psalm 14:7); the evildoers refuse to call upon the LORD (14:4).
In Psalm 14, why are the wicked overwhelmed with dread?
“There they are, overwhelmed with dread, for God is in the company of the righteous” (Psalm 14:5).
Psalm 14:5
Because the Philistines surround them
The Philistines are not mentioned in Psalm 14; the dread is because God is with the righteous (Psalm 14:5).
Because famine strikes the land
Famine is not mentioned in Psalm 14; the dread is because God is with the righteous (Psalm 14:5).
Because God is in the company of the righteous
Because the sun is darkened
A darkened sun is not mentioned in Psalm 14; the dread is because God is with the righteous (Psalm 14:5).
Because Jerusalem falls
Jerusalem’s fall is not mentioned in Psalm 14; the dread is because God is with the righteous (Psalm 14:5).
In Psalm 14:6, whose plans do sinners frustrate, even though the LORD is that group’s shelter?
“You sinners frustrate the plans of the oppressed, yet the LORD is their shelter” (Psalm 14:6).
Psalm 14:6
The mighty
The mighty are not the ones whose plans are frustrated; the oppressed are (Psalm 14:6).
The oppressed
The priests
Priests are not named in Psalm 14:6; the oppressed are.
The merchants
Merchants are not named in Psalm 14:6; the oppressed are.
The nations
Nations are not named in Psalm 14:6; the oppressed are.
In the closing prayer of Psalm 14, from what place does the psalmist long for the salvation of Israel to come?
“Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion!” (Psalm 14:7).
Psalm 14:7
Bethlehem
Bethlehem is not named in Psalm 14; the salvation of Israel is longed for from Zion (Psalm 14:7).
Sinai
Sinai is not named in Psalm 14; the salvation of Israel is longed for from Zion (Psalm 14:7).
Hebron
Hebron is not named in Psalm 14; the salvation of Israel is longed for from Zion (Psalm 14:7).
Zion
Babylon
Babylon is not named in Psalm 14; the salvation of Israel is longed for from Zion (Psalm 14:7).
In Psalm 14, when the LORD restores His captive people, which pair is specifically called to respond with joy?
“When the LORD restores His captive people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad!” (Psalm 14:7).
Psalm 14:7
Judah and Benjamin
Judah and Benjamin are not named in Psalm 14:7; Jacob and Israel are.
Jacob and Israel
Moses and Aaron
Moses and Aaron are not named in Psalm 14:7; Jacob and Israel are.
Ephraim and Manasseh
Ephraim and Manasseh are not named in Psalm 14:7; Jacob and Israel are.
David and Solomon
David and Solomon are not named in Psalm 14:7; Jacob and Israel are.
In Psalm 15, David asks, “O LORD, who may abide in Your tent? Who may dwell” in what place?
Psalm 15:1 asks, “O LORD, who may abide in Your tent? Who may dwell on Your holy mountain?” The place of dwelling with the LORD is His holy mountain.
Psalm 15:1
Beside still waters
Quiet waters belong to the shepherd psalm (Psalm 23:2); Psalm 15:1 names the LORD’s holy mountain as the place of dwelling.
On Your holy mountain
In the king’s palace
David asks who may dwell with the LORD, and the place he names is God’s holy mountain, not any royal palace.
By the rivers of Babylon
The rivers of Babylon belong to the exiles’ lament in Psalm 137:1, not to this psalm of David.
In the Valley of Elah
The Valley of Elah is where David met Goliath (1 Samuel 17:2); it is not the place named in Psalm 15:1.
In David’s Psalm 15, what kind of person is first described as fit to dwell with the LORD?
Psalm 15:2 begins the answer with the one “who walks with integrity and practices righteousness.”
Psalm 15:2
One who walks with integrity and practices righteousness
One who offers the most sacrifices at the temple altar
Psalm 15 names upright conduct and honest speech, not sacrifices; Samuel told Saul that obedience matters more than sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:22).
One who wins great battles for the king of Israel
Winning battles is not a requirement in Psalm 15; the psalm lists honest, fair and faithful living (15:2–5).
One who fasts publicly where all the people can see
Fasting is not mentioned in Psalm 15; Isaiah 58:6–7 says the fast God wants is justice and kindness to others.
One who speaks in clever riddles to the elders and judges
Riddles do not appear in Psalm 15, which asks for a person who speaks the truth from his heart (15:2).
In the psalm that asks who may abide in the LORD’s tent, what does the upright person speak “from his heart”?
Psalm 15:2 describes the person “who speaks the truth from his heart.”
Psalm 15:2
Flattery
Flattery is the opposite of the heartfelt truth Psalm 15:2 requires of the one who may dwell with the LORD.
Parables
Parables are a teaching form (Psalm 78:2), but Psalm 15:2 says the upright speak truth from the heart.
Truth
Secrets
Psalm 15 does not praise secrets; the upright person speaks the truth openly from his heart (15:2).
Complaints
Complaints are poured out to God in some psalms (Psalm 142:2), but Psalm 15:2 names truth as what the upright speak.
According to Psalm 15, what must not be found “on his tongue”?
Psalm 15:3 describes the person “who has no slander on his tongue.”
Psalm 15:3
Prophecy
Prophecy is not what Psalm 15:3 mentions; it names slander as the fault that must be absent from the tongue.
Thanksgiving
Thanksgiving is welcome before the LORD (Psalm 100:4); it is not what Psalm 15:3 says must be absent.
Wisdom
Wisdom on the tongue is praised (Proverbs 15:2); Psalm 15:3 names slander as what must not be there.
Slander
Singing
Singing to the LORD is encouraged (Psalm 96:1); Psalm 15:3 names slander as what must be absent.
In Psalm 15, where David asks who may dwell on the LORD’s holy mountain, how does the righteous person treat others close to him?
Psalm 15:3 says the one who may dwell with the LORD is “who does no harm to his neighbor, who casts no scorn on his friend.”
Psalm 15:3
He does no harm to his neighbor and casts no scorn on his friend
He rebukes his neighbor daily and avoids his friend
Psalm 15:3 says nothing about daily rebukes or avoiding a friend; it says he does no harm to his neighbor and casts no scorn on his friend.
He honors his neighbor but mocks his friend
Mocking a friend is exactly what Psalm 15:3 rules out when it says he casts no scorn on his friend.
He pays back his neighbor and tests his friend
Paying a neighbor back is the opposite of doing him no harm; Proverbs 24:29 also warns against repaying someone for what he has done.
He ignores his neighbor and flatters his friend
Ignoring a neighbor and flattering a friend is not what Psalm 15:3 describes; it speaks of no harm and no scorn.
In David’s description in Psalm 15 of the person who may dwell on the LORD’s holy mountain, whom does he honor?
Psalm 15:4 says he “honors those who fear the LORD,” while despising the vile.
Psalm 15:4
The wealthy
The wealthy are not singled out for honor in Psalm 15:4; the honor goes to those who fear the LORD.
Those who fear the LORD
Military leaders
Psalm 15:4 does not name military leaders; it names those who fear the LORD.
Royal officials
Royal officials are not mentioned in Psalm 15:4; he honors those who fear the LORD.
His own relatives only
Psalm 15:4 does not limit his honor to relatives; it goes to all who fear the LORD.
Psalm 15 says the upright person “does not revise a costly oath.” What does that mean?
Psalm 15:4 says he “does not revise a costly oath,” meaning he keeps his sworn word even when it costs him.
Psalm 15:4
He cancels promises that become expensive
Cancelling promises when they become expensive is the opposite of not revising a costly oath (Psalm 15:4).
He keeps his promise even when it costs him
He swears only in public worship
Psalm 15:4 does not limit oaths to public worship; it says he keeps even a costly oath.
He changes his words to protect himself
Changing his words to protect himself is exactly what Psalm 15:4 says the upright person does not do.
He avoids making commitments at all
Psalm 15:4 praises keeping an oath that has been made, not avoiding commitments altogether.
In the psalm that begins, “O LORD, who may abide in Your tent?”, which financial conduct matches the person fit for the LORD’s presence?
Psalm 15:5 describes the one “who lends his money without interest and refuses a bribe against the innocent.”
Psalm 15:5
He lends at interest and avoids witnesses
Lending at interest is the opposite of Psalm 15:5; Exodus 22:25 also forbids charging interest to a poor fellow Israelite.
He lends without interest and refuses a bribe against the innocent
He stores up silver and withholds payment
Withholding payment is not what Psalm 15:5 praises; Deuteronomy 24:15 commands paying a hired worker his wages each day.
He accepts gifts in court but gives alms in public
Accepting gifts in court is a bribe, which Psalm 15:5 refuses and Exodus 23:8 forbids.
He lends only to the rich and ignores the poor
Psalm 15:5 praises lending without interest and refusing a bribe, not lending only to the rich.
In David’s Psalm 15, which person best fits the description of one who may dwell on the LORD’s holy mountain?
Psalm 15:2–5 describes one who speaks truth from his heart, honors those who fear the LORD, and refuses a bribe against the innocent, as this choice does.
Psalm 15:2-5
A man who flatters with his lips, praises the wicked, and changes his oath when it hurts
Flattery, praising the wicked and changing an oath are the opposite of Psalm 15:2–4, which has the upright despise the vile and not revise a costly oath.
A woman who speaks truth from her heart, honors those who fear the LORD, and refuses a bribe against the innocent
A judge who avoids slander but takes payment to condemn the innocent
Taking payment to condemn the innocent is the very bribe Psalm 15:5 says the upright refuse.
A merchant who keeps his oath but mocks his friend and lends at interest
Lending at interest and mocking a friend break Psalm 15:5 and 15:3, even if he keeps his oath.
A leader who gives gifts to the poor but secretly harms his neighbor
Secretly harming a neighbor contradicts Psalm 15:3, which says he does no harm to his neighbor.
According to Psalm 15, which full statement best matches both the character and the outcome David gives for the one who may abide in the LORD’s tent?
Psalm 15:2–5 describes integrity, righteousness, truth from the heart and refusing a bribe, and ends, “He who does these things will never be shaken.”
Psalm 15:2-5
He offers many burnt offerings, defeats his enemies, and will gain a throne
Burnt offerings, victory over enemies and a throne are not named in Psalm 15, which promises that the upright will never be shaken (15:5).
He walks with integrity, practices righteousness, speaks truth from his heart, refuses corruption, and will never be shaken
He sings loudly in the sanctuary, keeps the feasts, and will be praised by nations
Loud singing, keeping feasts and praise from nations are not in Psalm 15; its promise is that he will never be shaken (15:5).
He hides in the wilderness, waits for battle, and will inherit cities
Hiding in the wilderness, waiting for battle and inheriting cities do not appear in Psalm 15.
He gains wisdom with age, builds a house, and will sleep without fear
Wisdom with age, a house and fearless sleep are not in Psalm 15; the closing promise is that he will never be shaken (15:5).
In Psalm 16, what does the psalmist ask God to do for him because he takes refuge in God?
The psalm opens, “Preserve me, O God, for in You I take refuge” (Psalm 16:1).
Psalm 16:1
Vindicate him
The psalmist asks God to preserve him, not to vindicate him (Psalm 16:1).
Preserve him
Enrich him
The psalm opens with a plea for protection, not riches (Psalm 16:1).
Exalt him
He asks to be kept safe, not exalted (Psalm 16:1).
Avenge him
He prays for preservation, not for vengeance on enemies (Psalm 16:1).
In David’s confession in Psalm 16, what does he say he has apart from the LORD?
David says, “You are my Lord; apart from You I have no good thing” (Psalm 16:2).
Psalm 16:2
No wisdom
The psalmist does not say he lacks wisdom; he says he has no good thing apart from the LORD (Psalm 16:2).
No shelter
Shelter is not what he says is lacking; he takes refuge in God (Psalm 16:1) and has no good thing apart from Him (16:2).
No good thing
No inheritance
He calls the LORD his chosen portion and says his inheritance is delightful (Psalm 16:5–6).
No song
He does not mention song in verse 2; he says he has no good thing apart from the LORD.
In the prayer of Psalm 16, how are the “saints in the land” described?
David calls the saints in the land “the excellence in whom all my delight resides” (Psalm 16:3).
Psalm 16:3
As the excellence in whom all his delight resides
As mighty warriors of Judah
The psalm does not describe the saints as warriors of Judah; they are excellent ones in whom he delights (Psalm 16:3).
As priests serving at Shiloh
Shiloh is not mentioned in the psalm; the saints are called the excellence in whom all his delight resides (Psalm 16:3).
As rulers seated on thrones
Rulers on thrones are not mentioned; the saints are those in whom he delights (Psalm 16:3).
As exiles by the rivers of Babylon
Exiles by Babylon’s rivers are in a different psalm; Psalm 16:3 speaks of saints in the land.
In Psalm 16, what does the psalmist say about those who chase other gods, and how does he respond?
“Sorrows will multiply to those who chase other gods. I will not pour out their libations of blood, or speak their names with my lips” (Psalm 16:4).
Psalm 16:4
Their sorrows multiply, and he refuses their blood libations and their names on his lips
Their strength increases, and he joins their feasts and speaks the names of their gods
The psalm says sorrows multiply for idolaters, not that their strength increases; David refuses to join them (Psalm 16:4).
Their cities prosper, and he records their names in a book and offers them his praise
The psalm does not say their cities prosper; it says sorrows multiply, and David will not speak their names (Psalm 16:4).
Their enemies flee, and he builds their altars and pours out their libations of wine
The psalm does not say their enemies flee; David refuses to pour out their blood libations (Psalm 16:4).
Their children are blessed, and he sings their praises and carries their idols home
Their children are not said to be blessed; sorrows multiply, and David will not speak their names (Psalm 16:4).
In Psalm 16, how does David describe the LORD when speaking of his inheritance?
David says, “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; You have made my lot secure” (Psalm 16:5).
Psalm 16:5
The LORD is his shepherd and tower
The LORD is called a shepherd in Psalm 23:1, but Psalm 16:5 calls Him David’s chosen portion and cup.
The LORD is his chosen portion and his cup
The LORD is his sword and shield
The LORD is called a rock and shield in Psalm 18:2, but Psalm 16:5 speaks of a portion and a cup.
The LORD is his altar and sacrifice
Psalm 16:5 does not call the LORD an altar or sacrifice; He is David’s chosen portion and cup.
The LORD is his judge and king
Judge and king are not the images in Psalm 16:5, which speaks of a portion, a cup, and a secure lot.
In Psalm 16, what does the psalmist say has fallen to him in pleasant places?
David says, “The lines of my boundary have fallen in pleasant places” (Psalm 16:6).
Psalm 16:6
The dew of Hermon
Hermon’s dew is not mentioned in Psalm 16; it is the lines of his boundary that fell in pleasant places (Psalm 16:6).
The tents of Jacob
The tents of Jacob are not part of Psalm 16; the lines of his boundary fell in pleasant places (Psalm 16:6).
The lines of his boundary
The gates of Zion
The gates of Zion are not mentioned in this psalm; verse 6 speaks of boundary lines.
The cedars of Lebanon
The cedars of Lebanon are not in Psalm 16; the pleasant places are the lines of his boundary (Psalm 16:6).
In Psalm 16, where does the psalmist say the LORD is, and what is the result?
David says, “Because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken” (Psalm 16:8).
Psalm 16:8
In the sanctuary, so he brings offerings
The LORD is not placed in the sanctuary and offerings are not mentioned; He is at David’s right hand (Psalm 16:8).
At his right hand, so he will not be shaken
On the mountain, so he climbs upward
The mountain and climbing are not in Psalm 16:8, which says the LORD is at his right hand.
In the storm, so he hides in fear
Psalm 16:8 describes steadiness, not fear; because the LORD is at his right hand, he will not be shaken.
Among the nations, so he goes to war
War among the nations is not mentioned; the psalmist says the LORD’s nearness keeps him from being shaken (Psalm 16:8).
In David’s words near the end of Psalm 16, what does he trust God will not do?
David says, “You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay” (Psalm 16:10).
Psalm 16:10
Forget his prayer or let his enemies triumph
The verse is about not being abandoned to Sheol and decay, not about enemies triumphing (Psalm 16:10).
Abandon his soul to Sheol or let His Holy One see decay
Remove his crown or scatter his army
Removing a crown and scattering an army are not in Psalm 16:10, which speaks of Sheol and decay.
Close the heavens or dry up the sea
Closing the heavens and drying up the sea are not in this verse; it speaks of Sheol and decay (Psalm 16:10).
Break His covenant or forsake Jerusalem
God’s covenant and Jerusalem are not mentioned in this verse; it promises that His Holy One will not see decay (Psalm 16:10).
In the closing verse of Psalm 16, what does God make known, and what is found in His presence and at His right hand?
Psalm 16:11 says, “You have made known to me the path of life; You will fill me with joy in Your presence, with eternal pleasures at Your right hand.”
Psalm 16:11
The path of life, joy in His presence, and eternal pleasures at His right hand
The way of wisdom, hidden manna in His presence, and crowns at His right hand
