Solomon sacrificed at Gibeon (1 Kings 3:4); Psalm 52:6 mentions no sacrifices there.
Mock the evildoer
Call for Samuel
Saul called for Samuel through a medium (1 Samuel 28:11); nobody calls for him in Psalm 52:6.
Flee to Egypt
Jeroboam fled to Egypt (1 Kings 11:40), but in Psalm 52:6 the righteous do not flee; they mock the evildoer.
In the words quoted by the righteous in Psalm 52, which description best fits the man they mock?
The righteous say of him, “Look at the man who did not make God his refuge, but trusted in the abundance of his wealth and strengthened himself by destruction” (Psalm 52:7).
Psalm 52:7
He honored God with his lips but trusted in the strength of his armies and fortresses
The mockers charge him with not making God his refuge and trusting wealth, not with trusting armies and fortresses.
He did not make God his refuge, but trusted in the abundance of his wealth and strengthened himself by destruction
He trusted in horses and chariots instead of prayer and boasted in the size of his army
Horses and chariots are not mentioned in Psalm 52:7; the man trusted in the abundance of his wealth.
He sought help from Egypt rather than from the LORD and relied on foreign alliances
Psalm 52:7 never mentions Egypt or alliances; the man trusted in the abundance of his wealth instead of making God his refuge.
He built strong walls around his city and trusted in them rather than in the LORD
Walls are not mentioned in Psalm 52:7; the man trusted in his wealth and strengthened himself by destruction.
At the close of Psalm 52, which two responses does David promise before God and His people?
David says, “I will praise You forever” and “I will wait on Your name” in the presence of God’s saints (Psalm 52:9).
Psalm 52:9
To fast and mourn
Fasting and mourning are not promised in Psalm 52:9; David resolves to praise God forever and wait on His name.
To praise forever and wait on God’s name
To sing and dance before the ark
David danced before the LORD when the ark was brought up (2 Samuel 6:14), but Psalm 52:9 promises praise and waiting.
To build an altar and call fire from heaven
Elijah called down the fire of the LORD on his altar (1 Kings 18:38); David’s promise here is praise and waiting.
To flee and hide until danger passes
David did flee from Saul (1 Samuel 21:10), but Psalm 52:9 ends in praise and waiting on God’s name, not hiding.
In the historical note connected with Psalm 52, who told King Saul that David had gone to the house of Ahimelech?
The heading of Psalm 52 says Doeg the Edomite went to Saul and told him, “David has gone to the house of Ahimelech”; see also 1 Samuel 22:9.
Psalm 52 title; 1 Samuel 22:9
Abner
Abner was the commander of Saul’s army (1 Samuel 14:50), not the one who reported David to Saul.
Doeg the Edomite
Joab
Joab was David’s commander, not the Edomite who informed Saul about David’s visit to Ahimelech.
Abiathar
Abiathar was a son of Ahimelech who escaped the slaughter and fled to David (1 Samuel 22:20); he did not inform on him.
Achish of Gath
Achish was the king of Gath, where David fled from Saul (1 Samuel 21:10), not Saul’s informer.
In the setting behind Psalm 52, David had gone to the house of which priest, later identified in 1 Samuel as being at Nob?
Psalm 52’s heading says David “has gone to the house of Ahimelech,” the priest at Nob (1 Samuel 21:1; 22:9).
Psalm 52 title; 1 Samuel 21:1; 22:9
Zadok
Zadok served as a priest in David’s later reign (2 Samuel 8:17), not at Nob in this episode.
Eli
Eli served at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:3), long before David’s visit to Nob.
Ahimelech
Jehoiada
Jehoiada was the priest who protected young Joash (2 Kings 11:4), generations after David.
Eleazar
Eleazar was Aaron’s son and successor (Numbers 20:28), centuries before David.
In David’s Psalm 53, what does the fool say in his heart?
Psalm 53:1 says, “The fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God.’” The psalm opens by naming practical atheism as folly.
Psalm 53:1
“The LORD is my shepherd.”
Psalm 23:1 declares the LORD as the believer’s shepherd; the fool in Psalm 53:1 denies God rather than trusting Him.
“There is no God.”
“I shall not be shaken.”
Not being shaken is the confidence of the righteous who keep the LORD before them (Psalm 16:8); the fool of Psalm 53 has no such trust.
“Peace, peace.”
“Peace, peace” was the false reassurance of leaders who dressed the people’s wound lightly (Jeremiah 6:14), not the fool’s words in Psalm 53.
“My help comes from the hills.”
Looking to the hills for help is the pilgrim’s question in Psalm 121:1; it is not what the fool says in Psalm 53:1.
In Psalm 53, from where does God look down to examine humanity?
Psalm 53:2 says, “God looks down from heaven upon the sons of men to see if any understand, if any seek God.”
Psalm 53:2
Mount Sinai
Sinai is where God gave the law to Israel (Exodus 19–20); Psalm 53:2 places His searching gaze in heaven.
Jerusalem
Zion and Jerusalem are where salvation is hoped for (53:6), but God’s looking down is from heaven, not a city.
Heaven
The wilderness
The wilderness was Israel’s wandering place, not where God surveys humanity; Psalm 53:2 says He looks down from heaven.
The sea
The sea is never named in Psalm 53; God looks down from heaven upon mankind.
According to Psalm 53, what is God looking to find among mankind?
Psalm 53:2 says God looks down “to see if any understand, if any seek God.” He is searching for understanding and a seeking heart.
Psalm 53:2
Singers for the temple
Temple singers are not mentioned in Psalm 53; God looks for those who understand and seek Him (53:2).
Kings with power
God is not scanning for powerful kings in 53:2; He wants to find anyone who understands and seeks Him.
Men of war
Warriors are not the object of God’s search here; the psalm asks only whether any understand and seek God.
Any who understand and seek God
Builders of altars
Altar-building belongs to the patriarchs (e.g. Genesis 8:20), not to Psalm 53:2, where God seeks those who understand and seek Him.
In Psalm 53’s assessment of humanity, what has happened to everyone?
Psalm 53:3 says, “All have turned away, they have together become corrupt; there is no one who does good, not even one.”
Psalm 53:3
All have turned away and become corrupt
All have returned to the covenant
Psalm 53:3 says the opposite: all have turned away, not returned to the covenant.
All have learned wisdom
Wisdom is what God looks for in 53:2, but verse 3 reports that no one has it: all have turned away and become corrupt.
All have entered God’s courts
Entering God’s courts is the pilgrim’s joy elsewhere in the Psalms; Psalm 53:3 says all have turned away.
All have humbled themselves
Psalm 53:3 describes universal corruption, not humility; no one does good, not even one.
In the rebuke found in Psalm 53, how are the workers of iniquity said to consume God’s people?
Psalm 53:4 says, “They devour my people like bread,” picturing the wicked consuming God’s people as casually as eating a meal.
Psalm 53:4
Like wolves
Wolves appear as a picture of ravenous enemies elsewhere, but Psalm 53:4 uses the image of eating bread.
Like fire
Fire is not the image in Psalm 53:4; the wicked devour God’s people like bread.
Like bread
Like locusts
Locusts are a plague image (Exodus 10:14), not used in Psalm 53:4, where the comparison is to bread.
Like floodwaters
Floodwaters sweep away in other psalms, but Psalm 53:4 compares the workers of iniquity to people eating bread.
In Psalm 53:5, what suddenly overwhelms the wicked where there was nothing to fear?
Psalm 53:5 says, “There they are, overwhelmed with dread, where there was nothing to fear.” God’s judgment strikes them with sudden terror.
Psalm 53:5
Laughter
Laughter is not mentioned in Psalm 53:5; the wicked are overwhelmed with dread.
Hunger
Hunger is not what overwhelms them in 53:5; the psalm speaks of dread where there was nothing to fear.
Sleep
Sleep does not appear in Psalm 53:5; the wicked are overwhelmed with dread.
Dread
Silence
Silence is not named in 53:5; what seizes them is dread.
In Psalm 53’s warning against enemies of God’s people, what does God scatter?
Psalm 53:5 says, “For God has scattered the bones of those who besieged you,” a picture of complete defeat for Israel’s attackers.
Psalm 53:5
The chariots and horses of their armies
The chariots and horses of their armies are not named in Psalm 53:5; God scatters the bones of those who besieged His people.
The treasures stored up in their cities
Stored-up treasures are not mentioned in 53:5; the verse says God has scattered the bones of those who besieged you.
The bones of those who besiege you
The idols they set up on the high places
Idols on the high places are not in Psalm 53:5; what God scatters is the bones of the besiegers.
The harvest of their fields and vineyards
Harvests of fields and vineyards are not mentioned in 53:5; God scatters the bones of those who besieged you.
In the closing hope of Psalm 53, what act of God would bring rejoicing when salvation comes from Zion?
Psalm 53:6 says, “When God restores His captive people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad!”
Psalm 53:6
When God restores His captive people
When David builds the temple
David’s temple plans (1 Chronicles 28) are not the cause of rejoicing in Psalm 53:6; it is God restoring His captive people.
When the Jordan dries up
The Jordan drying up recalls Joshua 3, not Psalm 53:6, where rejoicing follows God’s restoring of His captive people.
When Solomon is crowned
Solomon’s coronation is not mentioned in Psalm 53; the rejoicing is for God restoring His captive people.
When the ark is hidden
The ark’s being hidden is not in Psalm 53; the hope of verse 6 is God restoring His captive people.
In the final line of Psalm 53, which two names are called to celebrate after God restores His people?
Psalm 53:6 ends, “let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad!”
Psalm 53:6
Judah and Benjamin
Judah and Benjamin are not named in Psalm 53; the closing call is for Jacob and Israel.
Moses and Aaron
Moses and Aaron are not mentioned in Psalm 53:6; the people called to rejoice are Jacob and Israel.
Zion and Jerusalem
Zion is the place salvation comes from in 53:6, but those told to rejoice are Jacob and Israel, not Zion and Jerusalem.
Jacob and Israel
Ephraim and Manasseh
Ephraim and Manasseh are not named in Psalm 53; the verse calls Jacob and Israel to be glad.
In Psalm 53:4, besides devouring God’s people, what do the workers of iniquity refuse to do?
Psalm 53:4 says, “they refuse to call upon God”; the matching Psalm 14:4 says, “they refuse to call upon the LORD.”
Psalm 53:4
Call upon God
Keep the Sabbath
Sabbath-breaking greed is condemned in Amos 8:5, but Psalm 53:4 says the wicked refuse to call upon God.
Listen to the prophets
Zechariah 7:11 says the people “refused to pay attention”; Psalm 53:4 says they refuse to call upon God.
Bring their tithes
Withholding tithes is the charge of Malachi 3:8; Psalm 53:4 says they refuse to call upon God.
Tear down their idols
Idols are not mentioned in Psalm 53; verse 4 says the wicked refuse to call upon God.
In the historical setting connected with Psalm 54, which people told Saul where David was hiding?
The superscription of Psalm 54 names the Ziphites, who told Saul that David was hiding among them (1 Samuel 23:19).
1 Samuel 23:19; Psalm 54 superscription
Ziphites
Gibeonites
The Gibeonites tricked Joshua into a treaty (Joshua 9) and had no part in betraying David to Saul.
Amalekites
The Amalekites were Israel’s old enemies whom Saul fought (1 Samuel 15); they did not report David’s hiding place.
Men of Keilah
God warned David that the men of Keilah would surrender him to Saul (1 Samuel 23:12), but it was the Ziphites who actually informed Saul.
Philistines
The Philistines were Israel’s foes; David even sheltered among them for a time, but they did not betray him to Saul here.
In Psalm 54, David begins by asking, “Save me, O God, by Your ____.”
Psalm 54:1 opens, “Save me, O God, by Your name,” appealing to God’s name as the ground of rescue.
Psalm 54:1
Temple
David never asks to be saved by the temple, which did not yet exist in his day.
Covenant
God’s covenant matters throughout Scripture, but Psalm 54:1 asks for salvation by His name.
Name
Prophet
No prophet is named as David’s saviour in Psalm 54; he looks to God Himself.
Altar
David does not ask to be saved by an altar; he calls on God’s name (Psalm 54:1).
In the opening line of Psalm 54, by what does David ask God to vindicate him?
Psalm 54:1 continues, “and vindicate me by Your might!”
Psalm 54:1
Your wisdom
Wisdom is praised elsewhere, as in Proverbs 8, but Psalm 54:1 asks for vindication by God’s might.
Your law
God’s law is celebrated in Psalm 119, but it is not what David names for vindication in Psalm 54:1.
Your angels
Angels are not mentioned anywhere in Psalm 54.
Your might
Your throne
God’s throne appears in other psalms, but Psalm 54:1 does not mention it; David asks for vindication by His might.
In David’s prayer in Psalm 54, what does he ask God to hear and listen to?
In Psalm 54:2 David prays, “Hear my prayer, O God; listen to the words of my mouth.”
Psalm 54:2
My song and the music of my harp
David often plays the harp (1 Samuel 16:23), but in Psalm 54:2 he asks God to hear his prayer, not his music.
My prayer and the words of my mouth
My vows and the offerings I bring
Vows and offerings come up in verse 6 as David’s promised response, not as what he asks God to hear in verse 2.
My tears and the fasting of my soul
Tears and fasting are not mentioned in Psalm 54; David asks God to listen to his prayer and the words of his mouth.
My battle plans and the strategy of my army
David asks God to hear his prayer, not to take up military plans; he trusts God as his helper (Psalm 54:4).
In Psalm 54, how does David describe the people who are attacking him?
Psalm 54:3 says, “strangers rise up against me, and ruthless men seek my life.”
Psalm 54:3
Kings and priests
Kings and priests are not named as David’s attackers in Psalm 54; the enemies are strangers and ruthless men.
Shepherds and merchants
Shepherds and merchants are not mentioned in this psalm; David describes his enemies as strangers and ruthless men.
Strangers and ruthless men
Scribes and elders
Scribes and elders are not David’s attackers here; Psalm 54:3 speaks of strangers and ruthless men.
Prophets and warriors
Psalm 54:3 does not call his enemies prophets and warriors; they are strangers and ruthless men with no regard for God.
According to Psalm 54, what is true of the men seeking David’s life?
Psalm 54:3 says the ruthless men seeking David’s life are “men with no regard for God.”
Psalm 54:3
They trust in chariots
Trusting in chariots is warned against in Psalm 20:7, but Psalm 54:3 says these men have no regard for God.
They have no regard for God
They live by the sword
Living by the sword is Esau’s fate in Genesis 27:40, not a description given in Psalm 54:3.
They mock the law of Moses
Psalm 54 never accuses the enemies of mocking the law of Moses; it says they have no regard for God.
They fear the Philistines
The Philistines are not mentioned in Psalm 54, and the verse says these men have no regard for God.
In Psalm 54:4, which pair of descriptions does David use for God?
Psalm 54:4 says, “Surely God is my helper; the Lord is the sustainer of my soul.”
Psalm 54:4
My rock and my fortress
“My rock and my fortress” is how David speaks of the LORD in Psalm 18:2, not in Psalm 54:4.
My shepherd and my light
The LORD as David’s shepherd is Psalm 23:1; Psalm 54:4 calls God his helper and the sustainer of his soul.
My helper and the sustainer of my soul
My judge and my king
God is the judge and king in other psalms, but Psalm 54:4 calls Him helper and sustainer of the soul.
My shield and my song
“My shield” appears in Psalm 28:7 and “my song” in Exodus 15:2, but Psalm 54:4 says helper and sustainer of my soul.
In the confidence statement of Psalm 54, what does David say God will do to his enemies?
Psalm 54:5 says, “He will reward my enemies with evil. In Your faithfulness, destroy them.”
Psalm 54:5
Teach them wisdom and spare them from judgment
In Psalm 54:5 David asks for his enemies to be destroyed, not taught wisdom and spared judgment.
Reward them with evil and destroy them in faithfulness
Scatter them among the nations and drive them out
Scattering the nations is not what Psalm 54:5 says; David trusts God to repay his enemies with evil and destroy them.
Make peace with them at once and reward them with good
David does not ask God to make peace with his enemies in Psalm 54:5; he asks Him to destroy them.
Hide them in caves and shelter them from the storm
Hiding in caves describes David’s own flight (1 Samuel 22:1), not what he asks for his enemies in Psalm 54:5.
Near the end of Psalm 54, what response does David promise to make to God?
Psalm 54:6 says, “Freely I will sacrifice to You; I will praise Your name, O LORD, for it is good.”
Psalm 54:6
I will fast in sackcloth and ashes and mourn before You
Fasting in sackcloth is a sign of mourning, not what David promises in Psalm 54:6; he promises a willing sacrifice and praise.
I will offer a freewill sacrifice and praise Your name, for it is good
I will build a palace in Jerusalem and dedicate it to You
Building a palace in Jerusalem is not David’s promise in Psalm 54:6; he promises a freewill sacrifice and praise.
I will anoint a new priest and consecrate him at the altar
Anointing a priest is not part of David’s promise in Psalm 54:6; he vows a willing sacrifice and praise of God’s name.
I will sound the trumpet in Zion and call a holy assembly
Blowing a trumpet in Zion for a sacred assembly is from Joel 2:15, not Psalm 54:6.
How does Psalm 54 close David’s testimony about God’s deliverance?
Psalm 54:7 closes with, “For He has delivered me from every trouble, and my eyes have looked in triumph on my foes.”
Psalm 54:7
He has led me beside quiet waters and given me green pastures
Being led beside quiet waters is from Psalm 23:2, not the closing verse of Psalm 54.
He has delivered me from every trouble, and my eyes have looked in triumph on my foes
He restores my soul and guides me in the paths of righteousness
“He restores my soul” is from Psalm 23:3; it is not how Psalm 54 ends.
He has made my feet like those of a deer and set me on the heights
Feet like those of a deer is from Psalm 18:33, not from the end of Psalm 54.
He has set my feet upon a rock and made my footsteps firm
Setting David’s feet upon a rock is from Psalm 40:2; Psalm 54:7 speaks of deliverance from every trouble and triumph over foes.
In Psalm 55, as David begins his prayer to God, what does he ask God not to ignore?
David opens by asking God to “Listen to my prayer, O God, and do not ignore my plea” (Psalm 55:1).
Psalm 55:1
His song
David does not mention a song here; his opening request is that God not ignore his plea (55:1).
His plea
His sacrifice
No sacrifice is mentioned in this prayer; sacrifices belong to the offerings of Leviticus 1–7, not David’s opening plea (55:1).
His vow
David makes no vow in Psalm 55:1; he simply pleads for a hearing and asks that God not ignore his plea.
His fasting
Fasting is not mentioned in Psalm 55; David asks God not to ignore his plea (55:1).
In David’s lament in Psalm 55, what bird does he mention when he wishes he could fly away and find rest?
David cries, “Oh, that I had wings like a dove! I would fly away and find rest” (Psalm 55:6).
Psalm 55:6
Eagle
Eagles appear in Isaiah 40:31 as a picture of renewed strength, but David’s wish in 55:6 is for wings like a dove.
Raven
Ravens fed Elijah in 1 Kings 17:6, but David wishes for wings like a dove, not a raven (55:6).
Dove
Sparrow
Sparrows are not mentioned in Psalm 55; David longs for wings like a dove to fly away and rest (55:6).
Stork
Storks are not in this psalm; David’s wish to escape is for wings like a dove (55:6).
According to Psalm 55, if David could flee, where does he say he would remain?
David says, “How far away I would flee! In the wilderness I would remain” (Psalm 55:7).
Psalm 55:7
On Mount Zion
Zion is not where David wishes to hide; he longs to flee to the wilderness (55:7).
In the wilderness
Beside still waters
Quiet waters belong to Psalm 23:2; in 55:7 David pictures remaining in the wilderness.
In the king’s house
David longs to escape the city, not to find refuge in the king’s house; he would remain in the wilderness (55:7).
Among the cedars of Lebanon
The cedars of Lebanon are not mentioned in Psalm 55; David would flee to the wilderness (55:7).
In the prayer of Psalm 55, what does David ask the Lord to confuse and confound in the city?
Seeing “violence and strife in the city,” David prays, “O Lord, confuse and confound their speech” (Psalm 55:9).
Psalm 55:9
Their speech
Their chariots
Chariots are not mentioned in Psalm 55; David asks God to confuse their speech (55:9).
Their harvest
Harvests are not in view in this psalm; the confusion David requests is of their speech (55:9).
Their idols
Idols are not mentioned in Psalm 55; what David asks God to confound is their speech (55:9).
Their gates
Gates are not the target of David’s prayer in 55:9; he asks God to confuse and confound their speech.
When David describes the city in Psalm 55, what two conditions does he say he sees there?
David says, “I see violence and strife in the city” (Psalm 55:9).
Psalm 55:9
Peace and justice
Peace and justice are the opposite of what David sees; he sees violence and strife (55:9).
Singing and thanksgiving
Singing and thanksgiving are not part of David’s picture of the city; he sees violence and strife (55:9).
Violence and strife
Famine and drought
Famine and drought are not named in Psalm 55; the city is marked by violence and strife (55:9).
Wisdom and understanding
Wisdom and understanding are not what David finds in the city; he sees violence and strife (55:9).
In Psalm 55, whose betrayal does David say is especially painful?
David says an enemy’s insult he could endure, “But it is you, a man like myself, my companion and close friend” (Psalm 55:12–13).
A Philistine commander
A Philistine commander would be a foe David could face or hide from; the painful betrayal comes from a close friend (55:12–13).
A distant stranger
David says an enemy’s insult he could endure and a foe he could hide from; the hurt is from someone close (55:12–13).
An enemy king
David says it is not an enemy who insults him, so an enemy king is not the one he mourns (55:12).
A man like himself, his companion and close friend
A corrupt judge from another city
A corrupt judge from another city is nowhere in the psalm; the betrayer is a man like David, his companion (55:13).
In David’s words from Psalm 55, what had he and this close companion done together?
David recalls, “We shared sweet fellowship together; we walked with the crowd into the house of God” (Psalm 55:14).
Psalm 55:14
Built an altar at Bethel and offered sacrifices there together
Jacob built an altar at Bethel (Genesis 35:7), but Psalm 55:14 recalls sweet fellowship, not building an altar and offering sacrifices there.
Shared sweet fellowship and walked with the crowd into the house of God
Crossed the Jordan with the priests and carried the ark together
Crossing the Jordan with the priests and the ark is from Joshua 3, not David’s memory of walking with his friend to God’s house (55:14).
Guarded the city gates at night and kept watch on the walls
Guarding the gates is not mentioned; enemies are the ones who encircle the walls (55:10), and the friends walked to God’s house (55:14).
Anointed a new king in Hebron and feasted with the elders
David was anointed king at Hebron (2 Samuel 2:4), but 55:14 recalls sweet fellowship with a friend, not anointing a king or feasting with elders.
In Psalm 55, when does David say he cries out in distress and God hears his voice?
David says, “Morning, noon, and night, I cry out in distress, and He hears my voice” (Psalm 55:17).
Psalm 55:17
Only at dawn
David does not limit his crying out to dawn; he prays morning, noon, and night (55:17).
Morning, noon, and night
Every third watch
Watches of the night are not mentioned in Psalm 55; David prays morning, noon, and night (55:17).
At Passover and Tabernacles
Passover and Tabernacles are annual feasts (Leviticus 23), but David describes a daily rhythm of prayer (55:17).
Only in the night season
David’s prayer is not limited to the night; he cries out morning, noon, and night (55:17).
According to Psalm 55, what does God do for David’s soul even though many oppose him?
David says, “He redeems my soul in peace from the battle waged against me, even though many oppose me” (Psalm 55:18).
Psalm 55:18
Hides it in a cave until the enemy has passed by
David hid in a cave from Saul (1 Samuel 24:3), but Psalm 55:18 says God redeems his soul in peace, not that He hides it until the enemy passes.
Makes it forget the battle and the sorrows of the years
God does not make David forget the battle and the sorrows of the years; He redeems his soul in peace from it (55:18).
Redeems it in peace from the battle waged against him
Sends it into exile far from the city and its walls
Exile is not God’s answer in 55:18; David wishes to flee himself (55:6–7), but God redeems his soul in peace from the battle.
Crowns it with wealth and honor among the nations
Wealth and honor are not the reward in Psalm 55:18; God redeems David’s soul in peace from the battle waged against him.
In Psalm 55, why does David say God will hear and humiliate his opponents?
David says God will humiliate them “because they do not change and they have no fear of God” (Psalm 55:19).
Psalm 55:19
Because they are poor and weak
Poverty and weakness are not the reason given; David says they do not change and have no fear of God (55:19).
Because they do not change and have no fear of God
Because they have lost their king
Losing a king is not mentioned in Psalm 55; the reason is that they do not change and do not fear God (55:19).
Because they forgot the feast days
Forgetting the feast days is not the charge; David says they do not change and have no fear of God (55:19).
Because they abandoned Jerusalem’s walls
Abandoning Jerusalem’s walls is not the charge; the walls are where malice and trouble prowl (55:10), and the reason is no fear of God (55:19).
In the later part of Psalm 55, how is the treacherous companion described in relation to his friends and covenant?
David says, “My companion attacks his friends; he violates his covenant” (Psalm 55:20).
Psalm 55:20
He blesses his friends and keeps his covenant
This is the opposite of 55:20, which says the companion attacks his friends and violates his covenant.
He avoids his friends and ignores his oath
The companion does not avoid his friends; he attacks them and violates his covenant (55:20).
He attacks his friends and violates his covenant
He deceives strangers and forgets his family
Strangers and family are not in view; the companion attacks his friends and violates his covenant (55:20).
He fears his enemies and abandons his city
The companion is not described as fearing enemies; he attacks his friends and violates his covenant (55:20).
Which description best matches Psalm 55’s portrayal of the betrayer’s speech and heart?
David says of the betrayer, “His speech is smooth as butter, but war is in his heart. His words are softer than oil, yet they are swords unsheathed” (Psalm 55:21).
Psalm 55:21
His speech is rough as stone and hard to bear, yet his heart is tender toward his friends
Rough speech hiding a tender heart is the reverse of 55:21, where smooth words cover war in the heart.
His speech is smooth as butter and softer than oil, yet war is in his heart and his words are drawn swords
His speech is loud as thunder and shakes the city, yet his heart is quiet and at peace
Thunderous speech and a quiet heart are not in the verse; the betrayer’s words are smooth as butter and softer than oil (55:21).
His speech is sweet as honey and pleasing to all, yet his hands are empty and his house is poor
The verse likens his speech to butter and oil, not honey, and his heart holds war, not empty hands (55:21).
His speech is brief and honest and never flatters, yet his plans fail and come to nothing
Brief, honest speech is the opposite of 55:21, where soft flattering words conceal war in his heart.
In Psalm 55, what instruction and promise are given about burdens and the righteous?
The verse says, “Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you; He will never let the righteous be shaken” (Psalm 55:22).
Psalm 55:22
Hide your burden within yourself and wait for other men to help you carry it
Hiding a burden and waiting for others is the opposite of 55:22, which says to cast it upon the LORD.
Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you; He will never let the righteous be shaken
Give your burden to the priest and your house will prosper and stand secure
Psalm 55:22 sends the burden to the LORD, not to a priest, and promises He will sustain you.
Carry your burden in silence and God will test you until you are found faithful
Carrying a burden in silence is not the instruction; 55:22 says to cast it upon the LORD, who will sustain you.
Lay your burden before the king and he will defend you from all your enemies
Psalm 55:22 says to cast the burden upon the LORD, not to lay it before a king.
Near the end of Psalm 55, what does David say God will do to men of bloodshed and deceit?
David says, “You, O God, will bring them down to the Pit of destruction; men of bloodshed and deceit will not live out half their days” (Psalm 55:23).
Psalm 55:23
Give them long life and honor
Long life and honor are the opposite of 55:23, where men of bloodshed and deceit will not live out half their days.
Scatter them among the nations but preserve their days
Scattering among the nations is not what David says; the wicked are brought down to the Pit and their days cut short (55:23).
Bring them down to the Pit of destruction, and they will not live out half their days
Forgive them immediately and restore their strength
David does not say God forgives them; he says they will be brought down to the Pit of destruction (55:23).
Make them rulers over the city
Ruling the city is the reverse of 55:23, where men of bloodshed and deceit are brought down to the Pit.
In one of the strongest judgments spoken in Psalm 55, what does David ask to happen to the wicked?
David prays, “Let death seize them by surprise; let them go down to Sheol alive, for evil is with them in their homes” (Psalm 55:15).
Psalm 55:15
Let them be driven into the wilderness for forty days
Forty days in the wilderness recalls Israel’s wanderings and Jesus’ temptation, not David’s prayer in 55:15 for death to seize the wicked.
Let their lamps be put out at noon
Lamps put out at noon are not in Psalm 55; David asks that death seize them by surprise (55:15).
Let death seize them by surprise and let them go down to Sheol alive
Let their harvest fail for seven years
Seven years of failed harvest echo Genesis 41, not 55:15, where David asks that the wicked go down to Sheol alive.
Let them be carried away to Egypt
Being carried away to Egypt is not in this psalm; David asks that the wicked go down to Sheol alive (55:15).
In Psalm 56, what does David say he does when he is afraid?
David says, “When I am afraid, I put my trust in You” (56:3), and repeats his trust in God in 56:4 and 56:11.
Psalm 56:3
He hides in the wilderness
David is pursued by enemies, but in this psalm he never retreats to the wilderness; he answers fear with trust in God.
He puts his trust in God
He calls for a chariot
No chariot appears in Psalm 56; David’s refuge is God Himself, in whom he says he trusts and is not afraid.
He returns to Bethlehem
The psalm is set when the Philistines seized David in Gath (56:1), and it never mentions a return to Bethlehem.
He asks to die
David never asks to die; he thanks God for delivering his soul from death (56:13).
At the beginning of Psalm 56, how often does David say men and enemies pursue or attack him?
The attacks are constant: “all day they press their attack” (56:1) and “My enemies pursue me all day long” (56:2).
Psalm 56:1-2
Only at night
David says the pressure is “all day,” not merely at night, though he later notes that his enemies lurk and watch his steps (56:6).
All day long
Once each week
No weekly rhythm is mentioned; David describes pursuit as continual, “all day long” (56:2).
During harvest only
Harvest is never mentioned in Psalm 56; the attack is described as unceasing, all day long.
For forty days
Forty days belongs to other stories, such as the flood or Moses on Sinai; here the attack is “all day long” (56:2).
In David’s words in Psalm 56, after praising God’s word and declaring trust, what question does he ask about man?
David says, “In God, whose word I praise—in God I trust. I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?” (56:4).
Psalm 56:4
What can man do to me?
Why does man return to dust?
David does not ask why man returns to dust; he asks what man can do to him, since he trusts in God (56:4).
Who will cleanse the heart of man?
No question about cleansing the heart appears here; David’s concern is the threat from men who hound him (56:1).
When will man be renewed?
David does not ask when man will be renewed; he declares that he will not be afraid (56:4).
Can man enter heaven?
Heaven is not the subject; David is asking what mere men can do to him (56:4).
In Psalm 56, what does David say his enemies do to his words all day long?
David complains, “All day long they twist my words” (56:5); his enemies distort what he says.
Psalm 56:5
They memorize them
His enemies do not memorize his words; they twist them, and all their thoughts are on his demise (56:5).
They sing them
Singing is not what the enemies do; David is the one who praises God’s word (56:4, 56:10).
They twist them
They bury them
Nothing is said about burying his words; they twist them (56:5).
They bless them
His enemies do not bless his words; they twist them, intending harm (56:5).
In Psalm 56, while David’s enemies wait to take his life, what does he say they do?
“They conspire, they lurk, they watch my steps while they wait to take my life” (56:6).
Psalm 56:6
They conspire, lurk, and watch his steps
They fast, mourn, and repent
Fasting and repentance are not what David’s enemies do; they plot and lurk to take his life (56:6).
They build altars and pray
They are not worshipers; they conspire against David and watch his steps (56:6).
They flee to the mountains
They do not flee; they lurk and watch his steps, waiting to take his life (56:6), and David asks that they retreat (56:9).
They ask for peace
They seek his life, not peace; David asks God to cast down the nations in anger (56:7).
In Psalm 56, what does David ask God to do with his tears, and where does he say they are recorded?
David prays, “Put my tears in Your bottle—are they not in Your book?” (56:8), picturing God recording his sorrow.
Psalm 56:8
Put them in Your bottle, and they are in Your book
Burn them on the altar, and they are in the smoke
David mentions no altar or smoke; his tears are kept in God’s bottle and book (56:8).
Scatter them on the sea, and they are in the waves
The tears are not scattered on the sea; David asks that they be put in God’s bottle (56:8).
Hide them in the earth, and they are in the dust
Nothing is hidden in the earth; David asks God to keep his tears in His bottle (56:8).
Give them to angels, and they are in the heavens
Angels are not mentioned in Psalm 56; David appeals directly to God, who records his tears (56:8).
In Psalm 56, after asking whether the wicked will escape, what does David ask God to do in anger?
David asks, “In spite of such sin, will they escape? In Your anger, O God, cast down the nations” (56:7).
Psalm 56:7
Strike the shepherd
Striking the shepherd is not in Psalm 56; David prays for God to cast down the nations (56:7).
Dry up the river
No river is mentioned in this psalm; David asks God to cast down the nations in anger (56:7).
Cast down the nations
Shatter the temple doors
Temple doors are never mentioned in Psalm 56; his plea is that God cast down the nations (56:7).
Silence the trumpets
Trumpets do not appear in the psalm; the plea is for God to cast down the nations (56:7).
According to Psalm 56, when David calls out, what does he say will happen, and what will he know?
David says, “Then my enemies will retreat on the day I cry for help. By this I will know that God is on my side” (56:9).
Psalm 56:9
His enemies will retreat, and he will know God is on his side
Saul will repent, and he will know the kingdom is near
Saul is not named in Psalm 56, and David expects his enemies to retreat, not for a kingdom to draw near (56:9).
The Philistines will feast, and he will know peace has come
The Philistines seized David in Gath (56:1), but he does not say they will feast; he says his enemies will retreat (56:9).
The heavens will open, and he will know Elijah has returned
Elijah does not appear in Psalm 56; David’s sign is that his enemies retreat when he cries for help (56:9).
His army will grow, and he will know victory is certain
David boasts of no army; his certainty is that God is on his side when his enemies retreat (56:9).
Near the end of Psalm 56, what does David say he will render to God because his vows are upon him?
David says, “Your vows are upon me, O God; I will render thank offerings to You” (56:12).
Psalm 56:12
Burnt offerings only
The psalm mentions no burnt offerings; David promises thank offerings (56:12).
A royal crown
David speaks of no crown; his response to God’s rescue is thank offerings (56:12).
Thank offerings
A cedar palace
No palace is mentioned; David’s vows lead him to render thank offerings (56:12).
Silver trumpets
Silver trumpets are not mentioned in Psalm 56; he will render thank offerings (56:12).
In the closing verse of Psalm 56, what does David say God has delivered, and for what purpose?
“For You have delivered my soul from death, and my feet from stumbling, that I may walk before God in the light of life” (56:13).
Psalm 56:13
His house from ruin and his city from siege, so he may reign in Jerusalem
David’s house and city are not mentioned; God delivered his soul and feet so he could walk before God (56:13).
His soul from death and his feet from stumbling, so he may walk before God in the light of life
His ships from storms and his nets from breaking, so he may feed the poor
No ships or nets appear in Psalm 56; God delivered his soul from death and his feet from stumbling (56:13).
His crops from locusts and his wells from drought, so he may bless the land
Crops, locusts and wells are not in the psalm; the deliverance in 56:13 concerns his soul and feet.
His throne from rebels and his sword from rust, so he may judge the nations
Thrones, rebels and swords are not mentioned in 56:13; he is delivered so that he may walk in the light of life.
In the heading of Psalm 57, whom was David fleeing when he wrote this psalm?
The heading of Psalm 57 says it is a Miktam of David, “when he fled from Saul into the cave.”
Psalm 57:title
Absalom
Absalom drove David out of Jerusalem much later (2 Samuel 15), and Psalm 3 is the one linked to that flight.
Saul
Goliath
Goliath was killed by David in the Valley of Elah (1 Samuel 17); he was not a pursuer David fled from.
Nebuchadnezzar
Nebuchadnezzar ruled Babylon centuries after David and has no part in the heading of Psalm 57.
The Philistines
David did flee to the Philistines at other times, but the heading of Psalm 57 names Saul.
In the superscription of Psalm 57, where had David gone while fleeing from Saul?
The heading says David wrote this Miktam “when he fled from Saul into the cave.”
Psalm 57:title
Into the cave
Into the temple
The temple was built by Solomon after David’s death, so David could not have fled into it.
Into the palace
David fled from Saul’s palace rather than into one; the heading names a cave as his hiding place.
Into the city gate
The heading does not mention a city gate; David was hiding from Saul in a cave.
Into the camp of Israel
Saul led the army of Israel, so its camp was no refuge for David; the heading says a cave.
In Psalm 57, where does David say he will take shelter until the danger has passed?
David says, “In the shadow of Your wings I will take shelter until the danger has passed” (57:1).
Psalm 57:1
In the courts of the LORD
The courts of the LORD appear in other psalms (for example Psalm 84:2), but not as David’s shelter here.
Beside still waters
Quiet waters belong to the shepherd psalm (Psalm 23:2), not to this prayer for refuge from danger.
In the shadow of Your wings
On Mount Zion
Mount Zion is not mentioned in Psalm 57; David’s shelter is God’s own wings.
In a fortified city
David pictures God’s wings as his shelter, not a fortified city, though Psalm 59:9 does call God his fortress.
In David’s prayer in Psalm 57, to whom does he cry out?
David says, “I cry out to God Most High,” and adds that God fulfills His purpose for him (57:2).
Psalm 57:2
The God of Jacob
God of Jacob is a title used in other psalms (for example Psalm 46:11), but not in Psalm 57.
The LORD of Hosts
LORD of Hosts appears in other psalms (for example Psalm 46:11), but David cries to God Most High here.
God Most High
The Holy One of Israel
Holy One of Israel is a favorite title in Isaiah (Isaiah 45:11), not in Psalm 57.
The Angel of the LORD
The Angel of the LORD is not addressed in Psalm 57; David prays directly to God.
In Psalm 57, when David says God reaches down from heaven and saves him, what two things does God send forth?
God sends forth “His loving devotion and His truth” (57:3).
Psalm 57:3
Wisdom and understanding
Wisdom and understanding are not what God sends forth here; the verse names His loving devotion and truth.
Loving devotion and truth
Fire and consuming wrath
Fire and consuming wrath fall on the wicked elsewhere, but here God sends loving devotion and truth to save David.
Peace and lasting prosperity
Peace and lasting prosperity are not mentioned in Psalm 57:3; God reaches down from heaven to save David.
Manna and fresh water
Manna and fresh water came to Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16), not in this verse.
In Psalm 57, David says he lies among ravenous beasts. How does he describe the tongues of these men?
David says the men around him have tongues that are “sharp swords” (57:4), picturing cutting, destructive speech.
Psalm 57:4
Like honey
Honey suggests sweet speech, but David compares the tongues of these men to sharp swords.
Like poisoned arrows
Arrows are what he says their teeth are like (57:4); their tongues are compared to swords.
Like sharp swords
Like roaring thunder
Roaring thunder is not an image in Psalm 57; the beasts and men are pictured with teeth and tongues.
Like burning coals
Burning coals are called down on evil men in Psalm 140:10, not used for tongues in this psalm.
In the repeated refrain of Psalm 57, what does David ask to cover all the earth?
Twice David prays, “may Your glory cover all the earth” (57:5, 11).
Psalm 57:5, 11
Your law
God’s law is not what David asks to cover the earth in this refrain; it is His glory.
Your peace
Peace is not named in the refrain of Psalm 57, which asks that God be exalted above the heavens.
Your righteousness
Righteousness is not the thing David asks to cover the earth here; it is God’s glory.
Your glory
Your judgment
Judgment is not named in the refrain; David asks that God’s glory cover the earth.
In Psalm 57, what happened to the pit David’s enemies dug before him?
David says his enemies “dug a pit before me, but they themselves have fallen into it” (57:6).
Psalm 57:6
David escaped by climbing a wall
David does not say he climbed a wall to escape; the trap fell on the ones who set it.
It was filled with water
The pit being filled with water is not mentioned; the enemies fell into it themselves.
They fell into it themselves
Saul covered it with stones
Saul covering the pit with stones is not in the psalm; the enemies fell into their own pit.
It was destroyed by fire
Fire is not part of this image; the pit trapped those who dug it.
In Psalm 57, after calling on the harp and lyre to awake, what does David say he will awaken?
After calling on the harp and lyre to awake, David says, “I will awaken the dawn” (57:8).
Psalm 57:8
Jerusalem
Jerusalem is not named in Psalm 57; David says he will awaken the dawn.
The dawn
The watchmen
Watchmen are not mentioned in the psalm; David vows to wake the dawn with music.
The nations
David says he will praise God among the nations (57:9), not awaken them.
The evening sacrifice
The evening sacrifice is not mentioned; David looks to the dawn.
In the superscription to Psalm 57, to what tune is this psalm assigned?
The heading of Psalm 57 reads, “To the tune of ‘Do Not Destroy,’” a tune name shared with Psalms 58, 59 and 75.
Psalm 57:title
Lilies
Lilies is the tune named in the headings of Psalm 45 and Psalm 69 (“The Lilies” and “Lilies”).
The Doe of the Dawn
The Doe of the Dawn is the tune named in the heading of Psalm 22.
Do Not Destroy
Alamoth
Alamoth appears in the heading of Psalm 46, not Psalm 57.
Mahalath
Mahalath appears in the heading of Psalm 53, not Psalm 57.
In Psalm 58, David opens by challenging what group about whether they speak justly and judge fairly?
David opens by asking, “Do you indeed speak justly, O rulers? Do you judge uprightly, O sons of men?” (58:1).
Psalm 58:1
Rulers
Shepherds
Shepherds are not the group David challenges; he addresses rulers who are supposed to judge justly.
Priests
Priests are not named in Psalm 58; David confronts rulers about justice.
Merchants
Merchants are not addressed; the opening question is aimed at rulers and judges.
Exiles
Exiles are not mentioned in Psalm 58; David challenges rulers.
In David’s Psalm 58, he says the hearts of the wicked devise injustice, and their hands mete out what on the earth?
David says, “in your hearts you devise injustice; with your hands you mete out violence on the earth” (58:2).
Psalm 58:2
Mercy
Mercy is the opposite of what these rulers deal out; David says they mete out violence.
Violence
Wisdom
Wisdom is not what their hands mete out; the verse says violence.
Harvest
Harvest is not mentioned in Psalm 58:2; their hands deal out violence.
Peace
Peace is not what they bring; they mete out violence on the earth.
In the psalm about corrupt judgment, when are the wicked said to go astray?
Psalm 58:3 says, “The wicked are estranged from the womb; the liars go astray from birth.”
Psalm 58:3
From youth
Youth is not the starting point David names; he says they go astray from birth.
From old age
Old age is not mentioned; the verse says they go astray from birth.
From birth
From exile
Exile is not part of this verse; the wicked are estranged from the womb.
From battle
Battle is not mentioned in 58:3; the liars go astray from birth.
Psalm 58 compares the wicked to the venom of which creature that shuts its ears and refuses the charmer’s tune?
David says their venom is “like a cobra that shuts its ears, refusing to hear the tune of the charmer” (58:4–5).
Psalm 58:4-5
Viper
A viper is the creature of Isaiah 59:5, but in Psalm 58:4 it is the cobra that shuts its ears.
Eagle
An eagle is not an image in Psalm 58; David speaks of snake venom and a cobra.
Cobra
Scorpion
A scorpion is not mentioned in this psalm; the image is a cobra that will not hear the charmer.
Wolf
A wolf is not part of this comparison; the verses name a snake and a cobra.
In his prayer in Psalm 58, what does David ask God to shatter in the mouths of the wicked?
David prays, “O God, shatter their teeth in their mouths” (58:6).
Psalm 58:6
Shields
Shields are not what he asks God to shatter; it is their teeth.
Teeth
Idols
Idols are not mentioned in Psalm 58; David prays about teeth and fangs.
Arrows
He asks that their arrows be blunted (58:7), not shattered in their mouths.
Chains
Chains are not mentioned in this psalm; the prayer concerns teeth and fangs.
Later in Psalm 58, when the wicked draw the bow, David prays that their arrows may be what?
David prays, “when they draw the bow, may their arrows be blunted” (58:7).
Psalm 58:7
Gilded
Gilded arrows are not mentioned; David asks that they be blunted.
Blunted
Hidden
He does not ask that the arrows be hidden but that they lose their point.
Multiplied
Multiplied arrows would help the wicked; David prays that their arrows be blunted.
Fiery
Fiery arrows are a New Testament image (Ephesians 6:16), not what Psalm 58:7 says.
In one striking image from Psalm 58, the wicked are compared to a slug that does what?
David pictures the wicked “like a slug that dissolves in its slime” (58:8).
Psalm 58:8
Climbs a rock
Climbing a rock is not part of the image; the slug dissolves in its slime.
Hides under leaves
Hiding under leaves is not mentioned in the verse.
Dissolves in its slime
Seeks water
Seeking water is not said of the slug; it dissolves in its slime.
Leaves a silver trail
Leaving a silver trail is not in the verse; the slug dissolves in its slime.
Psalm 58 also says the wicked may never see the sun like what?
The psalm says, “Like a slug that dissolves in its slime, like a woman’s stillborn child, may they never see the sun” (58:8).
Psalm 58:8
A dried branch
A dried branch is not the image used here; the comparison is a stillborn child.
A broken lamp
A broken lamp is not mentioned in Psalm 58.
A woman’s stillborn child
A lost lamb
A lost lamb is not part of this psalm; the image is a woman’s stillborn child.
A shattered jar
A shattered jar is not mentioned in 58:8; the child never sees the sun.
In the line about pots and burning thorns in Psalm 58, what does David say will happen before the pots can feel the heat?
David says, “Before your pots can feel the burning thorns—whether green or dry—He will sweep them away” (58:9).
Psalm 58:9
Rain will quench the fire
Rain quenching the fire is not in the verse; God sweeps them away.
He will sweep them away
The thorns will blossom
The thorns blossoming is not mentioned; the thorns are burning.
The pots will crack in the flame
The pots cracking in the flame is not what the verse says; God sweeps them away first.
The fire will turn to smoke
The fire turning to smoke is not in the verse; God sweeps them away before they feel the heat.
At the close of Psalm 58, what conclusion will people reach when they see God’s judgment?
The psalm ends, “There is surely a reward for the righteous! There is surely a God who judges the earth!” (58:11).
Psalm 58:11
There is surely wisdom for the humble and a king over Israel
The closing words are about reward for the righteous and a God who judges; they do not mention a king over Israel.
There is surely mercy for the poor and a priest in Zion
Mercy for the poor and a priest in Zion is not what 58:11 says; it speaks of a reward and a God who judges.
There is surely strength for the warrior and justice in the gate
Strength for the warrior and justice in the gate is not the conclusion men reach in 58:11.
There is surely a reward for the righteous and surely a God who judges the earth
There is surely refuge for the remnant and a shepherd for Judah
Refuge for the remnant and a shepherd for Judah is not in 58:11; the verse speaks of a reward and judgment.
In the historical setting behind Psalm 59, who sent men to watch David’s house in order to kill him?
The heading of Psalm 59 says it is a Miktam of David, “when Saul sent men to watch David’s house in order to kill him” (see 1 Samuel 19:11).
1 Samuel 19:11
Absalom
Absalom rebelled against David much later (2 Samuel 15), and Psalm 3 is the psalm tied to that flight.
Saul
Achish
Achish was the Philistine king of Gath (1 Samuel 21:10), not the one who sent men to David’s house.
Joab
Joab was David’s commander, not the one who sent men to watch his house.
Doeg
Doeg the Edomite informed against David to Saul (1 Samuel 22:9), but he did not send the men in this heading.
In the opening plea of Psalm 59, what does David ask God to do for him from his enemies?
David opens, “Deliver me from my enemies, O my God; protect me from those who rise against me” (59:1).
Psalm 59:1
Teach me
Teaching is not the plea here; David asks for deliverance.
Deliver me
Reward me
Rewarding is not what David asks in the opening plea.
Test me
Testing is not his request; he asks to be delivered.
Rebuke me
He does not ask God to rebuke him; he asks to be delivered and protected.
In Psalm 59, at what time of day does David say his enemies return?
David says, “They return in the evening, snarling like dogs and prowling around the city” (59:6).
Psalm 59:6
At dawn
Dawn is not when they return; the verse says evening.
At noon
Noon is not named in 59:6; they return in the evening.
In the evening
At midnight
Midnight is not named in the verse.
At sunrise
Sunrise is not when they return; Psalm 59:16 uses the morning for David’s song instead.
In David’s description in Psalm 59, what animal are the enemies compared to as they prowl around the city?
David says they return in the evening, “snarling like dogs and prowling around the city” (59:6).
Psalm 59:6
Lions
Lions are the image in Psalm 57:4, but here the enemies are compared to dogs.
Serpents
Serpents are used for the wicked in Psalm 58:4, but Psalm 59:6 says dogs.
Dogs
Ravens
Ravens are not part of this image; the enemies snarl like dogs.
Bears
Bears are not named in this psalm; the enemies snarl like dogs.
According to Psalm 59, what do David’s enemies spew from their mouths?
David says, “See what they spew from their mouths—sharp words from their lips” (59:7).
Psalm 59:7
Blessings
Blessings are the opposite of what they speak; their mouths spew sharp words.
Sharp words
Songs
Songs are not what they spew; David is the one who sings (59:16).
Wisdom
Wisdom is not what comes from their mouths; the verse says sharp words.
Parables
Parables are not mentioned in Psalm 59.
In Psalm 59, what does David say about his own guilt in the attack against him?
David says the enemies conspire “for no transgression or sin of my own” and attack “for no fault of my own” (59:3–4).
Psalm 59:3-4
He admits a secret sin that he hopes God will forgive
David does not admit to a secret sin in this psalm; he says he has done nothing wrong.
He says he broke a vow and deserves the punishment he faces
Breaking a vow is not claimed here; David says there is no fault of his own.
He says there is no transgression, sin, or fault of his own
He says he forgot the Law and has been rightly rebuked
Forgetting the Law is not mentioned; David says the attack is undeserved.
He says he acted rashly and brought the trouble on himself
Acting rashly is not mentioned in Psalm 59; he says he has no fault in the matter.
In the repeated lines of Psalm 59, what title does David use for God as his place of safety?
David says, “You, O God, are my fortress” (59:9, 17), and calls God his fortress again in 59:16.
Shepherd
Shepherd is the title of Psalm 23, not the title used in the repeated lines of Psalm 59.
Fortress
Scribe
A scribe is not a title of God in this psalm.
Vine
A vine is not used for God in Psalm 59; David calls Him his fortress.
Lamp
A lamp is not the title David repeats here; it is fortress.
In Psalm 59, how does the LORD respond to the hostile nations and enemies?
David says, “But You, O LORD, laugh at them; You scoff at all the nations” (59:8).
Psalm 59:8
He hides from them
The LORD does not hide from them; He laughs at them.
He negotiates with them
The LORD does not negotiate; David says He laughs and scoffs.
He laughs at them
He fears them
The LORD does not fear them; He laughs at them.
He joins them
The LORD does not join them; He scoffs at all the nations.
When David appeals to God in Psalm 59:5, which titles does he use?
David calls out, “O LORD God of Hosts, the God of Israel” (59:5).
Psalm 59:5
LORD God of Hosts, the God of Israel
God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is the title God gives Moses (Exodus 3:6), not the one David uses in 59:5.
King of Salem, Holy One of Sinai
King of Salem and Holy One of Sinai are not the titles David uses in 59:5.
Shepherd of Bethlehem, Rock of Judah
Shepherd of Bethlehem and Rock of Judah are not the titles David uses in 59:5.
Ancient of Days, Prince of Peace

No battle is mentioned in 63:6; David thinks of God on his bed through the night watches.
