His mouth is not what is kept from closing; the psalmist says he is too troubled to speak (77:4).
His eyes
The heavens
The heavens are mentioned in the storm imagery (77:17), but God does not keep them from closing in this verse.
The city gates
City gates are not mentioned in Psalm 77.
The temple doors
Temple doors are not mentioned in Psalm 77; the verse concerns the psalmist’s eyes.
In Psalm 77, when the writer reflected on earlier times, what did he consider?
Psalm 77:5 says, “I considered the days of old, the years long in the past.”
Psalm 77:5
The conquest of Canaan
The conquest of Canaan is not named in Psalm 77; the psalmist recalls the past in general terms and then the exodus (77:15–20).
The days of old and years long past
The building of the temple
The building of the temple is not mentioned in Psalm 77.
The reign of Solomon
Solomon is not mentioned in Psalm 77; the psalm is attributed to Asaph.
The exile in Babylon
The exile in Babylon is not mentioned in Psalm 77; the psalm looks back to the redemption of Jacob and Joseph’s sons.
In the searching questions of Psalm 77, what did Asaph wonder had vanished forever?
Psalm 77:8 asks, “Is His loving devotion gone forever?”
Psalm 77:8
The priesthood
The priesthood is not mentioned in Psalm 77; the questions in 77:7–9 are about God’s favor, devotion and promise.
The ark
The ark is not mentioned in Psalm 77.
God’s loving devotion
The morning sacrifice
No sacrifice is mentioned in Psalm 77; the questions concern God’s own devotion and compassion.
The throne of David
David’s throne is not mentioned in Psalm 77; what Asaph fears is gone is God’s loving devotion.
In Psalm 77, which quality of God did the psalmist ask whether God had forgotten?
Psalm 77:9 asks, “Has God forgotten to be gracious?”
Psalm 77:9
To judge
Asaph does not ask whether God has forgotten to judge; he asks whether God has forgotten to be gracious (77:9).
To save
Saving is not what 77:9 names; the question is whether God has forgotten to be gracious.
To be gracious
To reign
Reigning is not named in 77:9; the question is whether God has forgotten to be gracious.
To speak
Speaking is not named in 77:9; Asaph asks whether God has forgotten to be gracious.
After his grief in Psalm 77, what did the psalmist resolve to remember?
In Psalm 77:11 the psalmist says, “I will remember the works of the LORD; yes, I will remember Your wonders of old.”
Psalm 77:11
His own victories in battle and the triumphs of his youth
The psalmist does not boast of his own victories in battle; he turns to the works of the LORD (77:11).
The works of the LORD and His wonders of old
The songs of the Levites and the praises of the temple choir
He recalls “my song” at night (77:6), but what he resolves to remember is the LORD’s works and wonders, not the Levites’ songs.
The wisdom of Solomon and the proverbs of earlier kings
Solomon’s wisdom is not mentioned in Psalm 77; the psalmist remembers God’s works of old.
The walls of Jerusalem and the gates of the holy city
Jerusalem’s walls and gates are not mentioned in Psalm 77; he remembers what God has done.
In Asaph’s meditation in Psalm 77, how is God’s way described?
Psalm 77:13 says, “Your way, O God, is holy.”
Psalm 77:13
Hidden
God’s footprints were hard to trace (77:19), but Psalm 77 never calls His way hidden; it calls it holy.
Holy
Harsh
Nothing in Psalm 77 calls God’s way harsh; it is holy (77:13).
Ancient
God’s works are “of old” (77:11), but 77:13 describes His way as holy, not ancient.
Narrow
Psalm 77 does not call God’s way narrow; it calls it holy (77:13).
According to Psalm 77, what does God display among the peoples?
Psalm 77:14 says, “You are the God who works wonders; You display Your strength among the peoples.”
Psalm 77:14
Wealth
Wealth is not mentioned in Psalm 77; God displays His strength.
Strength
Silence
The psalmist fears God may be silent, but God’s strength, not silence, is displayed among the peoples (77:14).
Fear alone
Fear is not what 77:14 says God displays; it is His strength.
Harvests
Harvests are not mentioned in Psalm 77; God displays His strength among the peoples.
In Psalm 77, which people are said to have been redeemed with power?
Psalm 77:15 says, “With power You redeemed Your people, the sons of Jacob and Joseph.”
Psalm 77:15
The sons of Jacob and Joseph
The house of Aaron only
Aaron is named only as one of the leaders (77:20); the redeemed are the sons of Jacob and Joseph, not just his house.
The tribe of Judah alone
Judah is not named in Psalm 77; the redeemed are the sons of Jacob and Joseph.
The sons of Korah
The sons of Korah appear in other psalm titles, not here; Psalm 77 names the sons of Jacob and Joseph (77:15).
The people of Nineveh
Nineveh is not mentioned in Psalm 77; the people redeemed are Israel, the sons of Jacob and Joseph.
In the water imagery of Psalm 77, what happened when the waters saw God?
Psalm 77:16 says, “The waters saw You, O God; the waters saw You and swirled; even the depths were shaken.”
Psalm 77:16
They dried up at once and left the seabed bare
The waters do not dry up in this verse; they swirl and the depths shake (77:16).
They turned bitter and could not be drunk
Waters turning bitter happened at Marah (Exodus 15:23), not here; in Psalm 77:16 the waters swirl.
They swirled, and even the depths were shaken
They became calm as glass and lay perfectly still
Far from calm, the waters swirled and the depths were shaken (77:16).
They froze solid and stopped moving altogether
Waters freezing solid is not in Psalm 77; the waters swirled and the depths shook.
In the storm scene of Psalm 77, what resounded in the whirlwind?
Psalm 77:18 says, “Your thunder resounded in the whirlwind.”
Psalm 77:18
A trumpet
A trumpet is not mentioned in Psalm 77; it is thunder that resounds in the whirlwind.
Thunder
Singing
Singing is not part of the storm scene in 77:16–18; thunder resounds in the whirlwind.
Chariots
Chariots are not mentioned in Psalm 77; the storm imagery has thunder, lightning and arrows.
Weeping
Weeping is not part of the storm scene; thunder resounds in the whirlwind (77:18).
In Psalm 77, where did God’s path lead, even though His footprints could not be found?
Psalm 77:19 says, “Your path led through the sea, Your way through the mighty waters, but Your footprints were not to be found.”
Psalm 77:19
Through the desert and over the hills
The desert and hills are not in this verse; God’s path led through the sea and mighty waters (77:19).
Through the temple courts
The temple courts are not mentioned in Psalm 77.
Through the sea and through the mighty waters
Through Babylon and back to Zion
Babylon and Zion are not mentioned in Psalm 77; God’s path led through the sea.
Through the valley and into the city
The valley and the city are not mentioned in 77:19; God’s way was through the mighty waters.
At the close of Psalm 77, by whose hand did God lead His people like a flock?
Psalm 77:20 says, “You led Your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron.”
Psalm 77:20
Joshua and Caleb
Joshua and Caleb are not mentioned in Psalm 77; Moses and Aaron led the flock (77:20).
Samuel and David
Samuel and David later led Israel, but Psalm 77:20 names Moses and Aaron.
Moses and Aaron
Elijah and Elisha
Elijah and Elisha were prophets in a later age, not the leaders named in 77:20.
Ezra and Nehemiah
Ezra and Nehemiah led the return from exile centuries later, not the exodus recalled in 77:20.
In Psalm 78, who is told to “give ear” and listen to the psalmist’s instruction?
Psalm 78:1 opens, “Give ear, O my people, to my instruction; listen to the words of my mouth.”
Psalm 78:1
The kings of Judah
The kings of Judah are not addressed; the psalm calls on “my people” as a whole (78:1).
My people
The priests of Levi
The priests of Levi are not singled out; the whole people are told to listen (78:1).
The nations
The nations are not addressed here; the instruction is for the psalmist’s own people (78:1).
The elders of Ephraim
Ephraim is named later, as a tribe that turned back in battle (78:9), not as the audience of the opening call.
At the start of Psalm 78, what does the psalmist say he will open his mouth in?
Psalm 78:2 says, “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the beginning.”
Psalm 78:2
Laments
Laments are not what the psalmist promises here; Psalm 78 is a Maskil of Asaph that teaches through parables (78:1–2).
Proverbs of Solomon
The proverbs of Solomon are a separate collection (Proverbs 1:1); this psalm is attributed to Asaph.
Parables
Songs of ascent
Songs of ascent are the psalms such as Psalm 120, headed “A song of ascents” (Psalm 120:1), not the form promised in 78:2.
Blessings
Blessings are not named in 78:2; the psalmist says he will open his mouth in parables.
In Psalm 78, to whom were God’s praiseworthy deeds and wonders to be told?

Psalm 78:4 says, “We will not hide them from their children but will declare to the next generation the praises of the LORD and His might,” and 78:6 adds that even children yet to be born are to tell their own children.
Psalm 78:4-6
Only the priests who served at the sanctuary
The psalm is not for the priests alone; the fathers are to teach their children, and the next generation after them (78:5–6).
Foreign nations who had never heard of Israel’s God
Foreign nations are not the audience here; the telling is passed from fathers to children within Israel (78:4–6).
The next generation and their children
The kings of Israel and the princes of their courts
Kings are not singled out; the praises of the LORD are for the next generation and their children (78:4–6).
The army of Judah gathered for the day of battle
Judah’s army is not the audience; the command is to teach children so they put their confidence in God (78:5–7).
While recounting God’s wonders in Egypt in Psalm 78, what named region is mentioned?
Psalm 78:12 says God worked wonders “in the land of Egypt, in the region of Zoan,” and 78:43 repeats “the fields of Zoan.”
Goshen
Goshen was where the Israelites settled in Egypt (Genesis 47:27), but Psalm 78 names Zoan.
Zoan
Sinai
Sinai is where God gave the law (Exodus 19:11), not the region of the wonders in Egypt.
Jericho
Jericho is in Canaan, where the wall fell (Joshua 6:20); it is not named in Psalm 78.
Hebron
Hebron is in Canaan, where Abraham buried Sarah (Genesis 23:19); it is not in this psalm.
During Israel’s wilderness journey in Psalm 78, how did God lead His people by day and by night?
Psalm 78:14 says, “He led them with a cloud by day and with a light of fire all night.”
Psalm 78:14
By a dove in the day and thunder at night
A dove is not part of Israel’s wilderness guidance; a dove appears at Jesus’ baptism (Matthew 3:16).
By priests in the day and angels at night
Priests and angels did not guide them; the LORD led them with a cloud by day and fire by night (78:14).
By a cloud in the day and a light of fire at night
By wind in the day and stars at night
Wind and stars were not their guide; Psalm 78:14 names a cloud and a light of fire.
By Moses in the day and Joshua at night
Moses led the people as God’s servant, but 78:14 says God Himself led them with a cloud and fire, as in Exodus 13:21.
In Psalm 78, what did God split in the wilderness to give Israel abundant drink?
Psalm 78:15 says, “He split the rocks in the wilderness and gave them drink as abundant as the seas.”
Cedars
Cedars are not mentioned in Psalm 78; God split rocks in the wilderness (78:15).
Mountains
God did not split mountains for water; the psalm says He split the rocks (78:15) and brought streams from the stone (78:16).
Rocks
Wells
Wells are not mentioned; the water came from split rocks and streams from the stone (78:15–16).
Tents
Tents were where Israel lived (78:55), not what God split to give them water.
In Psalm 78, what skeptical question did the Israelites ask when they spoke against God in the wilderness?
Psalm 78:19 records them saying, “Can God really prepare a table in the wilderness?”
Psalm 78:19
“Can God part the Jordan again?”
Parting the Jordan belongs to Joshua 3, not to the complaint in Psalm 78:19.
“Can God really prepare a table in the wilderness?”
“Can God send another flood?”
The flood is not mentioned in Psalm 78; the people doubted God could prepare a table in the wilderness.
“Can God make the sun stand still?”
The sun standing still happened under Joshua (Joshua 10:13), not in the wilderness complaint.
“Can God raise up judges for us?”
Judges were raised up later (Judges 2:16); the wilderness question was about a table.
According to Psalm 78, what food did God rain down from heaven for Israel to eat?
Psalm 78:24 says, “He rained down manna for them to eat; He gave them grain from heaven.”
Figs
Figs were part of the spies’ report from Canaan (Numbers 13:23), not rained from heaven.
Grapes
Grapes were carried back by the spies (Numbers 13:23); God rained down manna.
Manna
Barley loaves
Barley loaves appear in the boy’s lunch in John 6:9; Psalm 78 speaks of manna.
Lentils
Lentils appear in Jacob’s stew for Esau (Genesis 25:34); the food from heaven was manna.
In Psalm 78, which winds did God use when He brought meat to the camp?
Psalm 78:26 says, “He stirred the east wind from the heavens and drove the south wind by His might.”
North and west
The north and west winds are not named; the psalm names the east and south winds (78:26).
East and south
South and west
The west wind is not named; the winds are the east and the south (78:26).
East and north
The north wind is not named; the winds are the east and the south (78:26).
A whirlwind only
Two winds are named, not a whirlwind only; He stirred the east wind and drove the south wind (78:26).
In Psalm 78, which tribe’s armed bowmen turned back on the day of battle?
Psalm 78:9 says, “The archers of Ephraim turned back on the day of battle.”
Psalm 78:9
Judah
Judah is the tribe God chose in the end (78:68), not the one whose archers turned back.
Levi
Levi is not named in Psalm 78; the archers who turned back were from Ephraim (78:9).
Ephraim
Benjamin
Benjamin is not named in Psalm 78; the archers were from Ephraim (78:9).
Simeon
Simeon is not named in Psalm 78; the archers were from Ephraim (78:9).
In Psalm 78, when God slew some of the people, how did they respond?
Psalm 78:34 says, “When He slew them, they would seek Him; they repented and searched for God.”
Psalm 78:34
They crowned a new king to lead them back to the land
No king is crowned in this passage; when God slew them they sought Him and repented (78:34).
They sought Him, repented, and searched for God
They returned to Egypt to seek help from Pharaoh
They sought God, not Egypt; returning to Egypt is what Israel often wished for, but Psalm 78:34 says they repented and searched for God.
They built the temple to atone for their sins
No temple is built in this passage; building the temple is not part of their response in 78:34.
They crossed the Jordan to begin the conquest
Crossing the Jordan is not mentioned in 78:34; their response was to seek and search for God.
In Psalm 78, when the people remembered God after judgment, what did they remember Him to be?
Psalm 78:35 says they remembered “that God was their Rock, that God Most High was their Redeemer.”
Psalm 78:35
Their Rock and the Most High their Redeemer
Their Priest and their Sacrifice
Priest and Sacrifice are not titles of God in Psalm 78; the people remembered Him as their Rock and Redeemer (78:35).
Their Vineyard and their Watchman
The vineyard is an image of Israel itself (Isaiah 5:7), not a title Psalm 78:35 gives to God.
Their Scribe and their Judge
God is called Judge in Isaiah 33:22, but Psalm 78:35 names Him their Rock and Redeemer.
Their Captain and their Banner
The LORD is called a Banner in Exodus 17:15, but Psalm 78:35 names Him their Rock and Redeemer.
According to Psalm 78, why did God often restrain His anger and not destroy Israel completely?
Psalm 78:38–39 says He often restrained His anger, for “He remembered that they were but flesh, a passing breeze that does not return.”
Because Egypt feared Him
Egypt’s fear of God plays no part in this passage; God held back because He remembered they were but flesh (78:39).
Because they offered enough sacrifices
Sacrifices are not given as the reason; God was compassionate and forgave their iniquity (78:38).
Because He remembered they were but flesh, a passing breeze
Because Joshua interceded for them
No intercession by Joshua is mentioned here; it was Moses who pleaded for the people (Exodus 32:11), and Psalm 78:39 gives God’s own reason.
Because the Philistines withdrew
The Philistines are not mentioned in Psalm 78; God’s restraint came from His compassion (78:38–39).
In Psalm 78’s retelling of the plagues on Egypt, what did God unleash in His fury?
Psalm 78:49 says, “He unleashed His fury against them, wrath, indignation, and calamity—a band of destroying angels.”
Psalm 78:49
A band of destroying angels
Chariots of fire
A chariot of fire carried Elijah to heaven (2 Kings 2:11); it is not among the plagues of Psalm 78.
Lions from the desert
Lions were sent among settlers in Samaria (2 Kings 17:25), not against Egypt in Psalm 78.
Ravens from the sky
Ravens fed Elijah (1 Kings 17:6); they are not among the plagues of Psalm 78.
A troop of archers
Archers appear in 78:9, where the archers of Ephraim turn back, not among the plagues on Egypt.
In Psalm 78, whom did God strike in Egypt, described as “the virility in the tents of Ham”?
Psalm 78:51 says, “He struck all the firstborn of Egypt, the virility in the tents of Ham.”
Psalm 78:51
The magicians of Pharaoh
Pharaoh’s magicians copied some early signs (Exodus 7:11), but Psalm 78:51 says the firstborn were struck.
The charioteers at the sea
Pharaoh’s chariots were drowned in the sea (Exodus 14:28), not struck in this verse.
All the firstborn in Egypt
The priests of Ra
Priests of Ra are not mentioned in Psalm 78; the verse is about the firstborn of Egypt.
The builders of Pithom
The Israelites built Pithom and Rameses under forced labor (Exodus 1:11); the builders are not struck in Psalm 78:51.
After bringing Israel to His holy land in Psalm 78, what did God do before them?
Psalm 78:55 says, “He drove out nations before them and apportioned their inheritance; He settled the tribes of Israel in their tents.”
He sent them back into the wilderness
After bringing them to His holy land (78:54), God did not send them back to the wilderness; He settled them in the land.
He drove out nations and allotted their inheritance
He made them serve Moab
Serving Moab is not mentioned in Psalm 78; God drove out nations before Israel (78:55).
He hid the land from them for forty years
Forty years in the wilderness came before the land; here God brought them to His holy land and gave it to them (78:54–55).
He moved the tabernacle to Egypt
The tabernacle was not moved to Egypt; Psalm 78:60 says He abandoned the tabernacle of Shiloh.
In Psalm 78, what did Israel use to provoke God’s jealousy and anger after entering the land?
Psalm 78:58 says, “They enraged Him with their high places and provoked His jealousy with their idols.”
High places and idols
Unclean food and torn garments
Unclean food and torn garments are not given as the cause in 78:58; it was high places and idols.
Trumpets and festivals
Trumpets and festivals are not named; the offense in 78:58 was high places and idols.
Foreign language and trade
Foreign language and trade are not mentioned in Psalm 78; the offense was high places and idols (78:58).
Wells and vineyards
Wells and vineyards are not what provoked God; high places and idols did (78:58).
In Psalm 78, after Israel’s rebellion, which sanctuary did God abandon, and what did He deliver into the enemy’s hand?
Psalm 78:60–61 says, “He abandoned the tabernacle of Shiloh… He delivered His strength to captivity, and His splendor to the hand of the adversary.”
The tent at Bethel, and the bronze serpent
Bethel and the bronze serpent are not in this passage; the bronze snake was later destroyed by Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:4).
The tabernacle at Shiloh, and His strength and splendor
The altar on Carmel, and Elijah’s cloak
Carmel and Elijah’s cloak are not in Psalm 78; the sanctuary abandoned was at Shiloh (78:60).
The temple in Jerusalem, and the lampstand
The temple in Jerusalem is not what God abandoned here; Psalm 78:60 names the tabernacle of Shiloh.
The tent at Gilgal, and the book of the law
Gilgal was a camp by Jericho (Joshua 4:19); Psalm 78:60 names Shiloh, not Gilgal.
Near the end of Psalm 78, which tribe and mountain did God choose after rejecting Joseph and not choosing Ephraim?
Psalm 78:67–68 says, “He rejected the tent of Joseph and refused the tribe of Ephraim. But He chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which He loved.”
Levi and Sinai
Levi and Sinai are not named here; God chose Judah and Mount Zion (78:68).
Benjamin and Gibeah
Benjamin and Gibeah are not named; Saul was a Benjamite (1 Samuel 9:21), but the psalm chooses Judah and Mount Zion.
Judah and Mount Zion
Dan and Hermon
Dan and Hermon are not named; the tribe and mountain chosen were Judah and Mount Zion (78:68).
Issachar and Tabor
Issachar and Tabor are not named; Tabor appears in Judges 4:6, but Psalm 78:68 chooses Judah and Mount Zion.
In Psalm 78’s closing lines, from where did God take David, and how did David shepherd Israel?
Psalm 78:70–72 says He “took him from the sheepfolds” and that “David shepherded them with integrity of heart and guided them with skillful hands.”
From the battlefield, with power and fear
David was taken from tending sheep (78:70–71), not the battlefield, and he led with integrity, not fear.
From the palace, with wisdom and wealth
God took David from the sheepfolds, not a palace, and the psalm praises his integrity of heart rather than wealth (78:70–72).
From the sheepfolds, with integrity of heart and skillful hands
From the wilderness cave, with boldness and secrecy
David is taken from the sheepfolds, not a wilderness cave, and he shepherded openly with integrity and skill (78:70–72).
From the school of the prophets, with visions and songs
The psalm says nothing of a school of prophets; David came from the sheepfolds and led with integrity and skill (78:70–72).
In Asaph’s lament in Psalm 79, after the nations invaded God’s inheritance, which city is said to have been reduced to rubble?
Psalm 79:1 says the nations “have defiled Your holy temple and reduced Jerusalem to rubble.”
Psalm 79:1
Hebron
Hebron is where Abraham buried Sarah (Genesis 23:19); it is not named in Psalm 79.
Jerusalem
Samaria
Samaria was the capital Omri built in the north (1 Kings 16:24); Psalm 79:1 names Jerusalem.
Bethlehem
Bethlehem is the town from which Micah foretold a ruler (Micah 5:2); it is not mentioned in Psalm 79.
Jericho
Jericho’s wall fell in Joshua’s day (Joshua 6:20); Psalm 79:1 says Jerusalem was reduced to rubble.
According to Psalm 79, what sacred place did the invading nations defile when they entered God’s inheritance?
Psalm 79:1 says the nations “have defiled Your holy temple.”
Psalm 79:1
The Ark of the Covenant
The Ark of the Covenant is not mentioned in Psalm 79; the nations defiled the holy temple (79:1).
The holy temple
The tabernacle in Shiloh
The tabernacle at Shiloh is recalled in Psalm 78:60, but the sanctuary defiled in Psalm 79:1 is the holy temple.
The altar on Mount Carmel
The altar on Mount Carmel was repaired by Elijah (1 Kings 18:30); it is not named in Psalm 79.
The city gates of Zion
The gates of Zion are not mentioned in Psalm 79; the nations defiled the holy temple (79:1).
In the description of Jerusalem’s devastation in Psalm 79, the corpses of God’s servants were given as food to which creatures?
Psalm 79:2 says, “They have given the corpses of Your servants as food to the birds of the air, the flesh of Your saints to the beasts of the earth.”
Psalm 79:2
Fish of the sea
Fish are not mentioned in Psalm 79:2; the corpses were given to the birds of the air.
Birds of the air
Sheep of the field
Sheep appear in 79:13 as the image of God’s people, not as the creatures that devoured the dead.
Horses of war
Horses of war are not mentioned in Psalm 79; the corpses were given to the birds of the air (79:2).
Swarms of locusts
Locusts came upon Egypt by an east wind (Exodus 10:13); they are not in Psalm 79:2.
In Psalm 79, how does Asaph describe the blood of the slain being poured out around Jerusalem?
Psalm 79:3 says, “They have poured out their blood like water all around Jerusalem, and there is no one to bury the dead.”
Psalm 79:3
Like oil
Oil is not the comparison in 79:3; the blood was poured out like water.
Like dew
Dew is not the comparison in 79:3; the blood was poured out like water.
Like water
Like wine
Wine is not the comparison in 79:3; the blood was poured out like water.
Like sand
Sand is not the comparison in 79:3; the blood was poured out like water.
When Psalm 79 cries, “How long, O LORD?”, what does the psalmist say may burn like fire?
Psalm 79:5 asks, “How long, O LORD? Will You be angry forever? Will Your jealousy burn like fire?”
Psalm 79:5
His covenant
The covenant is not what burns in 79:5; the psalmist asks whether God’s jealousy will burn like fire.
His jealousy
His mercy
Mercy is not what burns in 79:5; Asaph instead pleads for God’s compassion to come quickly (79:8).
His patience
Patience is not what burns in 79:5; the question is whether God’s jealousy will burn like fire.
His throne
The throne is not mentioned in Psalm 79; it is God’s jealousy that may burn like fire (79:5).
In the prayer of Psalm 79, upon whom does Asaph ask God to pour out His wrath?
Psalm 79:6 prays, “Pour out Your wrath on the nations that do not acknowledge You, on the kingdoms that refuse to call on Your name.”
Psalm 79:6
The priests who offered blemished sacrifices and neglected the service of the temple
The psalm does not target Israel’s priests; the prayer is against the nations that do not acknowledge God (79:6).
The kings of Judah who trusted in Egypt and turned from the covenant
Judah’s kings are not named in Psalm 79; the wrath is asked for the nations that do not acknowledge God (79:6).
The nations that do not acknowledge You and the kingdoms that refuse to call on Your name
The remnant returning from exile who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem
A returning remnant is not mentioned in Psalm 79; the wrath is asked for the nations that refuse to call on God’s name (79:6).
The merchants who cheated the poor and sold grain with false measures
Merchants are not mentioned in Psalm 79; the prayer is directed at the nations that devoured Jacob (79:6–7).
In Psalm 79, what name does the psalmist use for the people whose homeland had been devoured and devastated?
Psalm 79:7 says, “they have devoured Jacob and devastated his homeland.”
Psalm 79:7
Ephraim
Ephraim is named in Psalm 80:2, not in Psalm 79:7, where the people are called Jacob.
Benjamin
Benjamin is named in Psalm 80:2, not in Psalm 79:7, where the people are called Jacob.
Jacob
Levi
Levi is not named in Psalm 79; the people devoured are called Jacob (79:7).
Manasseh
Manasseh is named in Psalm 80:2, not in Psalm 79:7, where the people are called Jacob.
In the plea to the “God of our salvation” in Psalm 79, what two things does Asaph ask God to do for the sake of His name?
Psalm 79:9 prays, “Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of Your name; deliver us and atone for our sins, for the sake of Your name.”
Psalm 79:9
Gather us and restore our borders
Gathering the people and restoring borders is not requested in 79:9; Asaph asks for deliverance and atonement.
Heal us and multiply our flocks
Healing and multiplied flocks are not requested in 79:9; Asaph asks for deliverance and atonement.
Deliver us and atone for our sins
Teach us and establish our king
Teaching and establishing a king are not requested in 79:9; Asaph asks for deliverance and atonement.
Clothe us and satisfy us with bread

In David's prayer recorded in Psalm 86, what reason does he give when asking the LORD to hear and answer him?

Psalm 86:1
He is poor and needy
He is mighty in battle
David was a warrior, but in this prayer he pleads from weakness and need, not from military might (86:1).
He is young and inexperienced
David never claims to be young or inexperienced here; he calls himself poor, needy, and godly (86:1–2).
He is exiled in a foreign land
Psalm 86 gives no exile setting; David rests his plea on his need and on trusting God as his helper (86:1–2, 17).
He is sick with fever

Once each morning

Three times a day

All day long
Only at night

Loving devotion

David
Hezekiah

Jacob

Proverbs 1:1
Israel
Judah
Judah became a separate kingdom only after Solomon (1 Kings 12:20); Hezekiah was “king of Judah” (Proverbs 25:1).
Edom
Edom had its own line of kings (Genesis 36:31); Solomon was king of Israel (1:1).
Egypt
Solomon married Pharaoh’s daughter (1 Kings 3:1), but he was king of Israel, not Egypt.
Tyre
Tyre’s king was Hiram, Solomon’s ally (1 Kings 5:1).

Lemuel’s mother warns him against destructive excess and urges him to defend the voiceless (31:1–9), and the poem then praises “a wife of noble character” (31:10).

Green pastures and still waters belong to Psalm 23, not Proverbs 31.

Hezekiah did not display the letter publicly; he spread it out before the LORD in the temple (37:14).
In Hezekiah’s prayer during Jerusalem’s crisis, how did he describe the LORD God of Israel?
Hezekiah prayed, “O LORD of Hosts, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth” (37:16).
Isaiah 37:16
The God of thunder and fire who spoke only at Sinai
Hezekiah called Him God of all kingdoms and Maker of heaven and earth (37:16), not a god of one mountain.
Enthroned above the cherubim, God over all the kingdoms of the earth
The god of harvest and rain who blesses Israel’s fields
Hezekiah spoke of the God who made the heavens and the earth (37:16), not a local harvest god like the idols he mentioned (37:19).
King only over Judah and Benjamin, the tribes of his realm
Hezekiah said the LORD is God over all the kingdoms of the earth (37:16), not only over his own realm.
A distant God who neither sees nor hears Judah’s plight
Hezekiah begged the LORD to incline His ear and open His eyes (37:17), so he believed God sees and hears.
While praying about Assyria, why did Hezekiah say the nations’ gods had been destroyed?
Hezekiah said the Assyrians “cast their gods into the fire and destroyed them, for they were not gods, but only wood and stone—the work of human hands” (37:19).

They had abandoned their temples

The priests had hidden them
No priests are mentioned; the Assyrians threw the idols into the fire (37:19).
They were not gods, but wood and stone made by human hands
Fire from heaven judged them
Fire did not fall from heaven; the Assyrians themselves cast the idols into the fire (37:19).
Their worshipers melted them into coins
Nothing is said of coins; the idols were burned because they were wood and stone (37:19).
In Hezekiah’s prayer for deliverance in Isaiah 37, what result did he ask God to bring about?
Hezekiah asked God to save them “so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone, O LORD, are God” (37:20).

So Judah could conquer Egypt

The prayer does not touch prophets; God was already answering through Isaiah (37:21).
In the oracle against Sennacherib, how is Jerusalem personified in response to the Assyrian king?
The LORD said, “The Virgin Daughter of Zion despises you and mocks you; the Daughter of Jerusalem shakes her head behind you” (37:22).
Isaiah 37:22
As a grieving widow of Hebron

In the boast quoted by the LORD against Sennacherib, what place did the king of Assyria claim he had reached with his many chariots?
Sennacherib boasted, “With my many chariots I have ascended to the heights of the mountains, to the remote peaks of Lebanon” (37:24).
Isaiah 37:24
The plains of Jericho
The plains of Jericho are not in the boast; he claimed the heights of the mountains and Lebanon (37:24).
The valleys of Jezreel
The valleys of Jezreel are not named in the boast (37:24).
The remotest heights of Lebanon
The wilderness of Zin
The wilderness of Zin is not named; the boast speaks of Lebanon’s remote peaks and cedars (37:24).
The coastlands of Tarshish
Tarshish is not in the boast; Sennacherib spoke of Lebanon and the streams of Egypt (37:24–25).
In God’s reply to Sennacherib, which statement shows the LORD’s complete knowledge of the Assyrian king?
The LORD told Sennacherib, “I know your sitting down, your going out and coming in, and your raging against Me” (37:28).
Isaiah 37:28
I know your fathers and your sons and all your household
God did not speak of the king’s family; He named his sitting, his going out and coming in, and his raging (37:28).
I know your secret treaties with Egypt and your hidden plans
No treaty with Egypt is mentioned here; the verse covers all the king’s movements and his rage against God (37:28).
I know your sitting down, your going out and coming in, and your raging against Me
I know the number of your horses and the strength of your army
The number of his horses is not mentioned; God knew his daily movements and his rage (37:28).
I know the walls of Nineveh and the gates of your palace
Nineveh’s walls are not mentioned; Sennacherib did return to Nineveh (37:37), but this verse speaks of his sitting, going out, coming in and raging.
In Isaiah 37, what vivid image did God use to describe how He would force Sennacherib to return?
The LORD said, “I will put My hook in your nose and My bit in your mouth; I will send you back the way you came” (37:29).
Isaiah 37:29
A chain on his ankles and ashes on his head
A chain on the ankles and ashes on the head are not the image; the LORD spoke of a hook and a bit (37:29).
A hook in his nose and a bit in his mouth
A yoke on his neck and dust in his eyes
A yoke and dust in the eyes are not the image used here; God spoke of a hook and a bit (37:29).
A sword at his back and fire before him
The sword is part of the promise that he would fall by it in his own land (37:7), but the image for turning him back is a hook and a bit.
A net over his camp and famine in his land
A net and famine are not mentioned; the LORD would turn him back like a beast with a hook and bit (37:29).
What sign did Isaiah give King Hezekiah concerning food and farming over the next three years?

Isaiah 37:30
First year famine, second year exile in Babylon, third year war in the land again
Famine, exile and war are not the sign; it promised survival and then ordinary farming (37:30).
First year manna from heaven, second year quail from the sea, third year a full harvest
Manna and quail were God’s provision in the wilderness (Exodus 16:13–14), not part of this sign about self-sown crops.
First year eat what grows on its own, second year what springs from that, third year sow, reap, and plant vineyards
First year buy grain from Egypt, second year trade oil for wheat, third year store the wine
The sign does not involve buying or trading; the first two years the land would feed them with what grew on its own (37:30).
First year harvest the wheat, second year gather the barley, third year pick only the grapes
The sign does not list wheat, barley and grapes by year; it names self-sown growth, then sowing, reaping and vineyards (37:30).
In the promise to Judah after the Assyrian threat, from what place would a remnant and survivors go out?
God promised, “a remnant will go forth from Jerusalem, and survivors from Mount Zion” (37:32).
Isaiah 37:32
Bethel and Shiloh
Bethel and Shiloh are not named; the remnant comes from Jerusalem and Mount Zion (37:32).
Jerusalem and Mount Zion
Lachish and Libnah
Lachish and Libnah are the Assyrian battlegrounds (37:8), not the source of the remnant.
Nineveh and Calah
Nineveh and Calah were Assyrian cities (Genesis 10:11); Sennacherib returned to Nineveh (37:37), but the remnant comes from Jerusalem.
Hebron and Beersheba
Hebron and Beersheba are not named in this promise; the verse speaks of Jerusalem and Mount Zion (37:32).
According to the LORD’s word about Jerusalem, which outcome was specifically denied to the king of Assyria?
The LORD said of the Assyrian king, “He will not enter this city or shoot an arrow into it” (37:33).
Isaiah 37:33
He would capture the temple and burn it
He would not capture the temple; the LORD promised to defend the city (37:33–35).
He would enter the city and divide the spoil
The king would not enter the city at all (37:33–34), so there was no spoil.
He would not enter the city or shoot an arrow there
He would make Jerusalem his winter palace
The king would never enter Jerusalem, so it would not be his palace (37:34).
He would appoint Hezekiah as his governor
The LORD promised Jerusalem’s safety (37:35); Hezekiah would not become an Assyrian governor.
In the night of divine deliverance described in Isaiah 37, who struck down 185,000 in the camp of Assyria?
“The angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians” (37:36).
Isaiah 37:36
Hezekiah’s elite guard
Hezekiah’s guard did not fight; the LORD defended the city Himself (37:35–36).
An angel of the LORD
Tirhakah’s army
Tirhakah’s army had been reported as marching against Sennacherib (37:9), but the slaughter was by the angel of the LORD (37:36).
A plague sent by Egypt
No plague from Egypt is mentioned; the angel of the LORD struck the camp (37:36).
The elders of Judah
The elders of Judah are not mentioned; the LORD said He would defend the city for His own sake and for David’s (37:35).
In the closing scene of Isaiah 37, while Sennacherib was worshiping in the temple of Nisroch his god, who killed him and where did they flee?
“His sons Adrammelech and Sharezer put him to the sword and escaped to the land of Ararat” (37:38), while he worshiped in the temple of Nisroch.
Isaiah 37:38
Joab and Abishai; to Moab
Joab and Abishai served King David (2 Samuel 20:10), centuries earlier, and had nothing to do with Sennacherib.
Adrammelech and Sharezer; to the land of Ararat
Eliakim and Shebna; to Egypt
Eliakim and Shebna were Hezekiah’s officials, sent to Isaiah (37:2).
Merodach-baladan’s men; to Babylon
Merodach-baladan’s men are tied to his letters to Hezekiah (Isaiah 39:1), not to Sennacherib’s death.
Pekah and Rezin; to Damascus
Pekah and Rezin marched against Jerusalem in Ahaz’s time (Isaiah 7:1), well before Sennacherib’s death.
In Isaiah 38, which king of Judah became mortally ill?
Isaiah 38:1 says Hezekiah became mortally ill.
Isaiah 38:1
Ahaz
Ahaz was Hezekiah’s father, and the stairway in 38:8 is named for him; he is not the king who fell ill.
Hezekiah
Josiah
Josiah is not mentioned in Isaiah 38; Hezekiah was the king who became ill (38:1).
Jehoiakim
Jehoiakim is not mentioned in Isaiah 38; Hezekiah was the king who became ill (38:1).
Zedekiah
Zedekiah is not mentioned in Isaiah 38; Hezekiah was the king who became ill (38:1).
In the account of Hezekiah’s illness, which prophet came to him with a message from the LORD?
Isaiah 38:1 says the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz came to Hezekiah.
Isaiah 38:1
Jeremiah son of Hilkiah
Jeremiah is not mentioned in Isaiah 38; the prophet who came was Isaiah son of Amoz (38:1).
Elijah the Tishbite
Elijah is not mentioned in Isaiah 38; Isaiah son of Amoz came to Hezekiah (38:1).
Isaiah son of Amoz
Elisha son of Shaphat
Elisha is not mentioned in Isaiah 38; Isaiah son of Amoz came to Hezekiah (38:1).
Ezekiel son of Buzi
Ezekiel is not mentioned in Isaiah 38; Isaiah son of Amoz came to Hezekiah (38:1).
When Isaiah spoke to King Hezekiah during his sickness, what did he tell the king to do because he was about to die?
Isaiah told Hezekiah, “Put your house in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover” (38:1).
Isaiah 38:1
Flee to Egypt
Fleeing to Egypt is not part of the message; Isaiah said to put his house in order (38:1).
Build an altar
Building an altar is not in the message; Isaiah said to put his house in order (38:1).
Put his house in order
Gather the elders
Gathering the elders is not in the message; Isaiah said to put his house in order (38:1).
Appoint a new commander
Appointing a new commander is not in the message; Isaiah said to put his house in order (38:1).
After hearing the announcement that he was about to die, what did King Hezekiah do in Isaiah 38?
Isaiah 38:2 says Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD.
Isaiah 38:2
He sent tribute to Assyria
Sending tribute to Assyria is not mentioned here; Hezekiah turned to the wall and prayed (38:2).
He turned his face to the wall and prayed
He went to battle
Going to battle is not mentioned here; Hezekiah prayed to the LORD (38:2).
He called for the priests to blow trumpets
Calling for priests to blow trumpets is not mentioned here; he prayed (38:2).
He tore down the high places
Tearing down the high places is not mentioned in Isaiah 38; Hezekiah turned to the wall and prayed (38:2).
In Hezekiah’s prayer during his illness, how did he say he had walked before the LORD?
Hezekiah prayed, “remember how I have walked before You faithfully and with wholehearted devotion” (38:3).
Isaiah 38:3
In power and victory
Power and victory are not what he cites in 38:3; he cites faithfulness and wholehearted devotion.
Faithfully and with wholehearted devotion
In fasting and silence
Fasting and silence are not mentioned in 38:3; he cites faithfulness and wholehearted devotion.
In wisdom and wealth
Wisdom and wealth are not mentioned in 38:3; he cites faithfulness and wholehearted devotion.
In fear and trembling only
Fear and trembling are not mentioned in 38:3; he cites faithfulness and wholehearted devotion.
When God answered Hezekiah through Isaiah, how many years did He promise to add to the king’s life?
The LORD said, “I will add fifteen years to your life” (38:5).
Isaiah 38:5
7 years
Seven years is not the number given in 38:5; the LORD promised fifteen years.
10 years
Ten steps is the distance the shadow moved back (38:8), not the years added to his life.
12 years
Twelve years is not the number given in 38:5; the LORD promised fifteen years.
15 years
20 years
Twenty years is not the number given in 38:5; the LORD promised fifteen years.
As a sign to King Hezekiah in Isaiah 38, what happened to the sun’s shadow on the stairway of Ahaz in Jerusalem?
As a sign, the LORD made the sun’s shadow go back ten steps on the stairway of Ahaz (38:8).
Isaiah 38:7-8
It moved forward five steps
The shadow did not move forward five steps; it went back ten steps (38:8).
It disappeared at noon
The shadow did not disappear at noon; it went back ten steps (38:8).
It went back ten steps
It stood still until evening
The shadow did not stand still until evening; it went back ten steps (38:8).
It darkened the whole city
The city is not said to have darkened; the shadow went back ten steps (38:8).
In the writing Hezekiah composed after recovering, through what gates did he think he must go in the prime of life?
Hezekiah wrote, “In the prime of my life I must go through the gates of Sheol” (38:10).
Isaiah 38:10
The gates of Jerusalem
The gates of Jerusalem are not named in 38:10; he spoke of the gates of Sheol.
The gates of the temple
The gates of the temple are not named in 38:10; he spoke of the gates of Sheol.
The gates of Babylon
The gates of Babylon are not named in 38:10; he spoke of the gates of Sheol.
The gates of Sheol
The gates of bronze
Gates of bronze are not named in 38:10; he spoke of the gates of Sheol.
In Hezekiah’s reflection on his near death, what did he compare his dwelling to?
Hezekiah said, “My dwelling has been picked up and removed from me like a shepherd’s tent” (38:12).
Isaiah 38:12
A fortified tower
A fortified tower is not the comparison in 38:12; his dwelling was like a shepherd’s tent.
A shepherd’s tent
A cedar palace
A cedar palace is not the comparison in 38:12; his dwelling was like a shepherd’s tent.
A ship at sea
A ship at sea is not the comparison in 38:12; his dwelling was like a shepherd’s tent.
A threshing floor
A threshing floor is not the comparison in 38:12; his dwelling was like a shepherd’s tent.
Describing his weakness in his lament, what bird sounds did Hezekiah say he made?
Hezekiah said, “I chirp like a swallow or crane; I moan like a dove” (38:14).
Isaiah 38:14
He sang like a lark and cried like a raven
Singing like a lark and crying like a raven is not what Hezekiah says in 38:14.
He chirped like a swallow or crane and moaned like a dove
He called like a rooster and wailed like an owl
Calling like a rooster and wailing like an owl is not what Hezekiah says in 38:14.
He hummed like a bee and shrieked like a hawk
Humming like a bee and shrieking like a hawk is not what Hezekiah says in 38:14.
He whispered like a sparrow and roared like an eagle
Whispering like a sparrow and roaring like an eagle is not what Hezekiah says in 38:14.
In Hezekiah’s thanksgiving after recovery, what did he say God had done with all his sins?
Hezekiah said, “You have cast all my sins behind Your back” (38:17).
Isaiah 38:17
Written them in the dust
Writing sins in the dust is not what Hezekiah says in 38:17; God cast them behind His back.
Burned them with fire
Burning sins with fire is not what Hezekiah says in 38:17; God cast them behind His back.
Remembered them forever
Remembering sins forever is the opposite of 38:17, which says God cast them behind His back.
Cast them behind His back
Sent them into exile
Sending sins into exile is not what Hezekiah says in 38:17; God cast them behind His back.
According to Hezekiah’s song in Isaiah 38, who can thank the LORD?
Hezekiah said, “The living, only the living, can thank You” (38:19).
Isaiah 38:19
The dead in Sheol
The dead in Sheol cannot thank the LORD (38:18); only the living can (38:19).
Those in the Pit
Those who descend to the Pit cannot hope for God’s faithfulness (38:18); only the living can thank Him (38:19).
The living, only the living
The kings of the nations
The kings of the nations are not mentioned in 38:19; the living can thank the LORD.
The angels only
Angels are not mentioned in 38:19; the living, only the living, can thank the LORD.
In Hezekiah’s closing praise after being saved, what did he say they would play in the house of the LORD all the days of their lives?
Hezekiah said, “we will play songs on stringed instruments all the days of our lives in the house of the LORD” (38:20).
Isaiah 38:20
Trumpet blasts at every feast
Trumpet blasts at every feast are not mentioned in 38:20; the songs are on stringed instruments.
Songs on stringed instruments
Cymbals before the altar
Cymbals before the altar are not mentioned in 38:20; the songs are on stringed instruments.
Tambourines and dancing songs
Tambourines and dancing songs are not mentioned in 38:20; the songs are on stringed instruments.
Silent prayers only
Silent prayers are not mentioned in 38:20; they will play songs on stringed instruments.
In Isaiah 39, after King Hezekiah of Judah recovered from illness, who sent him letters and a gift in Jerusalem?
Isaiah 39:1 says “Merodach-baladan son of Baladan king of Babylon sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah” after hearing of his illness and recovery.
Isaiah 39:1
Sennacherib king of Assyria, ruling from Nineveh
Sennacherib king of Assyria threatened Jerusalem in Hezekiah’s day (Isaiah 36:1) but did not send this gift after the king’s recovery.
Merodach-baladan son of Baladan, king of Babylon
Pharaoh king of Egypt, ruling from Memphis
Pharaoh king of Egypt is not part of this visit; the envoys came from Babylon (39:1–3).
Hiram king of Tyre, Solomon’s old ally
Hiram king of Tyre was Solomon’s ally (1 Kings 5:1), long before Hezekiah.
Rezin king of Aram, ruling from Damascus
Rezin king of Aram opposed Judah in the days of Ahaz (Isaiah 7:1), not Hezekiah’s recovery.
In the account of Hezekiah and the Babylonian envoys in Isaiah 39, why did the king of Babylon send this message to Hezekiah?

He wanted cedar from Lebanon

He heard that Hezekiah had been ill and had recovered
He demanded tribute from Judah
Babylon demanded no tribute; it sent letters and a gift (39:1).
He invited Hezekiah to Babylon for a feast
No invitation to a feast in Babylon is mentioned; the message was prompted by Hezekiah’s illness and recovery (39:1).

No request about rebuilding Nineveh appears; the king sent letters because he heard of Hezekiah’s recovery (39:1).
In Isaiah 39, how did King Hezekiah respond when the Babylonian envoys arrived at his palace?

He sent them away without a meeting

He welcomed them gladly and showed them his treasures
He hid his wealth and spoke only through servants

He asked Isaiah to question them first
Isaiah came to him only afterward and asked about the visit (39:3).
He imprisoned them as spies

When the prophet Isaiah questioned King Hezekiah in chapter 39, from what place did Hezekiah say the visitors had come?

Isaiah 39:3
From Nineveh in Assyria
Nineveh was the Assyrian capital; the envoys came from Babylon (39:3).
From Memphis in Egypt
Memphis in Egypt is not named; the visitors came from Babylon (39:3).
From a distant land, from Babylon
From Damascus in Aram
Damascus was the capital of Aram; Hezekiah said the visitors came from Babylon (39:3).
From Samaria in Israel
Samaria is not named in Isaiah 39; Hezekiah said the visitors came from Babylon (39:3).
In the visit recorded in Isaiah 39, which group of items was specifically named among the things Hezekiah showed the men from Babylon?

Isaiah 39:2
Silver, gold, spices, and precious oil
Manna, Aaron’s staff, and the tablets of the covenant

Cedar beams, altar stones, and bronze pillars

Fishing nets, grain stores, and vineyard tools

Harps, trumpets, and priestly garments

Everything in his palace, with nothing among his treasures withheld

They would be buried beneath Jerusalem

Isaiah 47:1
Mighty and terrible
The title taken from her is tender and delicate, a picture of her pampered life, not might.
Tender and delicate
Righteous and faithful
The oracle exposes Babylon’s wickedness (47:10); she is never called righteous.
Beloved and chosen
Beloved and chosen describes Israel, not Babylon.
Ancient and honored
Babylon showed no honor even to the elderly (47:6); the lost title is tender and delicate.
In Isaiah’s prophecy against Babylon in chapter 47, what task is the fallen city told to do with millstones?
God tells her, “Take millstones and grind flour” (47:2), the work of a slave.
Isaiah 47:2
Build a wall
Wall-building is not mentioned; the millstones are for grinding flour.
Grind flour
Crush grapes
Crushing grapes is not mentioned; she is told to grind flour with millstones.
Carve idols
Carving idols is not mentioned in this verse; she is to grind flour.
Draw water
Drawing water is not mentioned; the task is grinding flour with millstones.

Her treasure

Her army
Her army is not mentioned in the verse; her nakedness and shame are exposed.
Her nakedness
Her palace
Her palace is not mentioned; the verse speaks of her nakedness and shame.
Her counsel
Her counsel is not the thing uncovered; her counselors are mocked later in 47:13.

Isaiah 47:5
Queen of kingdoms
Lady of Zion

Mistress of the seas

Crown of the East
Crown of the East is not in the chapter; the lost title is queen of kingdoms.
Mother of nations
Mother of nations is not in the chapter; the lost title is queen of kingdoms.
In the middle of Isaiah 47’s judgment speech, how is Israel’s Redeemer identified?

In Isaiah 47, why does God say He placed His people under Babylon’s power?

Because He was angry with His people
Because Assyria defeated Judah first
Assyria is not mentioned in the chapter; the reason is God’s anger with His people.
Because Jerusalem requested Babylon’s help
Jerusalem did not ask for Babylon’s help; God Himself placed His people under her control.
Because Babylon showed mercy
The verse says the opposite: Babylon showed them no mercy.
According to Isaiah 47, on whom did Babylon lay a very heavy yoke when she showed no mercy?

Priests
Priests are not mentioned; the heavy yoke fell on the elderly.
Children

Farmers
Farmers are not mentioned; the verse names the elderly.
The elderly
Foreign merchants
Foreign merchants are not mentioned; the heavy yoke was laid on the elderly.
In Isaiah chapter 47, what boast did Babylon make about her future rule?
Babylon said, ‘I will be queen forever’ (47:7).
Isaiah 47:7
“I will never be conquered”

“I will be queen forever”
“I will reign from Zion”

“I will outlive the stars”

“I will rule every sea”

“The temple of the LORD”

“My strength is my god”

Isaiah 47:8-9
Famine and drought
Famine and drought are not mentioned; the two losses are loss of children and widowhood.
Exile and sword
Exile and sword are not named in this verse; the two losses are loss of children and widowhood.
Widowhood and loss of children
Fire and flood
Fire and flood are not named; the two losses are loss of children and widowhood.
Pestilence and locusts
Pestilence and locusts are not mentioned; the two losses are widowhood and loss of children.
According to Isaiah 47, what had led Babylon astray?

Her armies and chariots
Her armies and chariots are not mentioned; wisdom and knowledge led her astray.

Her treaties with Egypt
Treaties with Egypt are not mentioned; wisdom and knowledge led her astray.

Isaiah 47:13
Levites who lead the singing in the temple at Jerusalem
Temple singers are not mentioned; the challenged group is her astrologers.
Her astrologers, who observe the stars and predict her fate each month
Scribes who keep the royal records of Babylon’s kings
Scribes are not mentioned; the challenged group is her astrologers.
Warriors who guard her walls with horses and chariots
Horsemen are not mentioned; the challenged group is her astrologers.
Craftsmen who build her city walls and gates
Stonecutters are not mentioned; the challenged group is her astrologers.

“each one strays in his own direction; not one of them can save you” (47:15).

They secretly carry her treasures out to safety

Isaiah 48:1
The house of Jacob
The sons of Korah
The sons of Korah are named in the title of Psalm 48, not in Isaiah 48:1.
The tribe of Dan

The people of Tyre
Tyre is not addressed in Isaiah 48; the chapter speaks to the house of Jacob (48:1).

Song and sacrifice

The holy city
The daughter of Babylon

The city of palms
The “City of Palms” is Jericho (Deuteronomy 34:3), not the holy city of Isaiah 48:2.

When the LORD describes Israel’s stubbornness in Isaiah chapter 48, what are their neck and forehead compared to?

Cedar and clay

Iron and bronze
Stone and silver

Brass and gold
Brass and gold are not named in verse 4; the comparison is iron and bronze.
Flint and dust
Flint and dust are not named in verse 4; the comparison is iron and bronze.

Babylon

Sarah

Eden

Rahab
