In Isaiah 61’s promise about places long devastated, what will happen to the ancient ruins and ruined cities?
“They will rebuild the ancient ruins; they will restore the places long devastated; they will renew the ruined cities” (Isaiah 61:4).
Isaiah 61:4
They will be hidden beneath the sand
Isaiah 61:4 promises rebuilding, not burial under sand.
They will be rebuilt, restored, and renewed
They will become foreign capitals
Becoming foreign capitals is not mentioned in Isaiah 61:4; the ruins will be rebuilt, restored and renewed.
They will remain desolate forever
Isaiah 61:4 says the opposite: the devastated places will be restored.
They will be turned into wilderness pasture
Isaiah 61:4 promises restored cities, not wilderness pasture.
In Isaiah 61, who will stand and feed the flocks and serve as plowmen and vinedressers for the restored people?
“Strangers will stand and feed your flocks, and foreigners will be your plowmen and vinedressers” (Isaiah 61:5).
Isaiah 61:5
Levites and singers
Levites and singers are not mentioned in Isaiah 61:5; strangers and foreigners do the work.
Kings and commanders
Kings serve Zion in Isaiah 60:10, but Isaiah 61:5 names strangers and foreigners as plowmen and vinedressers.
Strangers and foreigners
Widows and orphans
Widows and orphans are not mentioned in Isaiah 61:5; strangers and foreigners do the work.
Prophets and scribes
Prophets and scribes are not mentioned in Isaiah 61:5; strangers and foreigners do the work.
In Isaiah 61, what titles will the restored people receive before others?
“You will be called the priests of the LORD; they will speak of you as ministers of our God” (Isaiah 61:6).
Isaiah 61:6
Shepherds of Israel and princes of Judah
Shepherds of Israel and princes of Judah are not the titles in Isaiah 61:6.
Priests of the LORD and ministers of our God
Builders of Zion and guards of Jerusalem
Builders of Zion and guards of Jerusalem are not the titles in Isaiah 61:6, though the people do rebuild ruins in 61:4.
Sons of Abraham and heirs of Jacob
Sons of Abraham and heirs of Jacob are not the titles in Isaiah 61:6; the titles are priests of the LORD and ministers of our God.
Prophets of fire and servants of Elijah
Prophets of fire and servants of Elijah are not titles in Isaiah 61:6.
When the LORD speaks in Isaiah 61 about reward and covenant, what does He say He loves and hates?
“I, the LORD, love justice; I hate robbery and iniquity; in My faithfulness I will give them their recompense and make an everlasting covenant with them” (Isaiah 61:8).
Isaiah 61:8
He loves mercy and hates the sacrifices of Israel
The LORD says in Hosea 6:6, “I desire mercy, not sacrifice,” but Isaiah 61:8 says He loves justice and hates robbery and iniquity.
He loves justice and hates robbery and iniquity
He loves fasting and hates feasting and revelry
Fasting and feasting are not mentioned in Isaiah 61:8, which says He loves justice and hates robbery and iniquity.
He loves silence and hates all songs of praise
Praise is a garment God gives in Isaiah 61:3, so He does not hate singing; Isaiah 61:8 says He loves justice and hates robbery and iniquity.
He loves wisdom and hates the rule of kings
Isaiah 61:8 says nothing against kings or in favor of wisdom; He loves justice and hates robbery and iniquity.
In the closing celebration of Isaiah 61, how does the speaker describe God’s saving work using clothing and wedding imagery?
“He has clothed me with garments of salvation and wrapped me in a robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom wears a priestly headdress, as a bride adorns herself with her jewels” (Isaiah 61:10).
Isaiah 61:10
He covered me with sackcloth and ashes, like a mourner who weeps beside a grave and refuses every comfort
Sackcloth and ashes are what God replaces with a crown of beauty in Isaiah 61:3; Isaiah 61:10 speaks of garments of salvation.
He clothed me with garments of salvation and wrapped me in a robe of righteousness, like a bridegroom and bride adorned for joy
He armed me with bronze and iron, like a soldier marching out to battle against the enemies of the nations
God puts on a breastplate of righteousness and a helmet of salvation as a warrior in Isaiah 59:17, but Isaiah 61:10 is wedding clothing worn by the speaker.
He crowned me with cedar and gold, like a king who sits in splendor on his throne in the royal palace
A crown of glory is Zion’s picture in Isaiah 62:3; Isaiah 61:10 describes garments of salvation and a robe of righteousness.
He veiled me with clouds and fire, like Israel wandering through the wilderness at night beneath the mountain
Cloud and fire led Israel in Exodus 13:21; Isaiah 61:10 uses garments of salvation and a robe of righteousness.
At the opening of Isaiah 62, for whose sake does the speaker say he will not keep silent or remain quiet?
“For Zion’s sake I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not keep still” (Isaiah 62:1).
Isaiah 62:1
Babylon and Chaldea
Babylon is foretold to be overthrown in Isaiah 13:19, not the city for whose sake the speaker keeps speaking in Isaiah 62:1.
Zion and Jerusalem
Tyre and Sidon
Tyre and Sidon are not named in Isaiah 62:1; the speaker will not be silent for Zion and Jerusalem.
Samaria and Ephraim
Samaria and Ephraim are not named in Isaiah 62:1; the speaker will not be silent for Zion and Jerusalem.
Moab and Ammon
Moab and Ammon are not named in Isaiah 62:1; the speaker will not be silent for Zion and Jerusalem.
In Isaiah 62, who is said to see Jerusalem’s righteousness and glory?
“Nations will see your righteousness, and all kings your glory” (Isaiah 62:2).
Isaiah 62:2
Only the priests of Judah
Priests are not mentioned in Isaiah 62:2; nations and kings see her righteousness and glory.
The poor and the widows
The poor and widows are not mentioned in Isaiah 62:2; nations and kings see her righteousness and glory.
The nations and all kings
The tribes east of the Jordan
The tribes east of the Jordan are not mentioned in Isaiah 62:2; nations and kings see her righteousness and glory.
The sailors of Tarshish
Sailors of Tarshish appear in Isaiah 60:9, not in Isaiah 62:2, where nations and kings see her glory.
In the promise given to Jerusalem in Isaiah 62, what will she be in the hand of the LORD?
“You will be a crown of glory in the hand of the LORD, a royal diadem in the palm of your God” (Isaiah 62:3).
Isaiah 62:3
A sharpened sword and a polished arrow
The sharp sword and polished arrow describe the LORD’s servant in Isaiah 49:2, not what Jerusalem is in Isaiah 62:3.
A sealed scroll and a golden censer
Words sealed in a scroll appear in Isaiah 29:11, not in Isaiah 62:3, where Jerusalem is a crown and diadem.
A lampstand of fire and a bowl of oil
A lampstand with a bowl of oil is Zechariah’s vision (Zechariah 4:2), not the picture of Jerusalem in Isaiah 62:3.
A crown of glory and a royal diadem
A trumpet of silver and a ram’s horn
Silver trumpets were for calling the congregation (Numbers 10:2), not the picture of Jerusalem in Isaiah 62:3.
When Isaiah 62 describes God’s joy over restored Jerusalem, what comparison does it use?
“As a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you” (Isaiah 62:5).
Isaiah 62:5
As a shepherd rejoices over a rescued lamb
The shepherd gathering lambs in his arms is Isaiah 40:11’s picture, not the comparison in Isaiah 62:5.
As a king rejoices over conquered nations
Isaiah 62:5 compares God’s joy to a bridegroom’s, not a king’s over conquered nations.
As a bridegroom rejoices over his bride
As an eagle stirs up its nest
The eagle stirring its nest is in Deuteronomy 32:11, not in Isaiah 62:5.
As a farmer rejoices at harvest
Harvest joy is not the comparison in Isaiah 62:5; the comparison is a bridegroom rejoicing over his bride.
In Isaiah 62, Jerusalem is told she will no longer be called “Forsaken,” and her land will no longer be called “Desolate.” What new names are given instead?

“No longer will you be called Forsaken, nor your land named Desolate; but you will be called Hephzibah, and your land Beulah; for the LORD will take delight in you, and your land will be His bride” (Isaiah 62:4).
Isaiah 62:4
Ariel and Jeshurun
Ariel is a name for Jerusalem in Isaiah 29:1 and Jeshurun is a name for Israel in Isaiah 44:2, but neither is the new name in Isaiah 62:4.
Hephzibah and Beulah
Salem and Shiloh
Shiloh is mentioned in Genesis 49:10, and neither it nor Salem is given as a new name in Isaiah 62:4.
Tirzah and Carmel
Tirzah and Carmel are not named in Isaiah 62:4; the new names are Hephzibah and Beulah.
Naomi and Ephraim
Naomi is a name Ruth 1:20 says she rejected for Mara, and Ephraim is not a new name in Isaiah 62:4.
Regarding the walls of Jerusalem in Isaiah 62, whom has the LORD posted there?
“On your walls, O Jerusalem, I have posted watchmen; they will never be silent day or night” (Isaiah 62:6).
Isaiah 62:6
Levites with harps
Levites with harps are not mentioned in Isaiah 62:6; the LORD posts watchmen.
Watchmen who never keep silent
Elders judging at the gate
Elders judging at the gate are not mentioned in Isaiah 62:6; the LORD posts watchmen on the walls.
Horsemen from Judah
Horsemen from Judah are not mentioned in Isaiah 62:6; the LORD posts watchmen on the walls.
Stonecutters and masons
Stonecutters and masons are not mentioned in Isaiah 62:6; the LORD posts watchmen on the walls.
In Isaiah 62, those who call on the LORD are told to give themselves no rest and give Him no rest until what happens?
“You who call on the LORD shall take no rest… nor give Him any rest until He establishes Jerusalem and makes her the praise of the earth” (Isaiah 62:6–7).
Isaiah 62:6-7
Until Babylon is rebuilt and its gates stand open again
Babylon’s rebuilding is not mentioned; Isaiah 13:19 says Babylon will be overthrown, and the prayer in Isaiah 62:7 is for Jerusalem.
Until the ark of the covenant is found and carried home
The ark is not mentioned in Isaiah 62:6–7; the prayer continues until Jerusalem is established.
Until Jerusalem is established and made the praise of the earth
Until Egypt and Cush send tribute to her king every year
Egypt’s tribute is not mentioned in Isaiah 62:7; the prayer continues until Jerusalem is established and made the praise of the earth.
Until every mountain is leveled and every valley filled
Leveling mountains is Isaiah 40:4’s picture of preparing the LORD’s way, not the goal of the prayer in Isaiah 62:7.
In the oath spoken over Jerusalem in Isaiah 62, what does the LORD swear by His right hand and mighty arm He will never again allow?
The LORD swears, “Never again will I give your grain to your enemies for food, nor will foreigners drink the new wine for which you have toiled” (Isaiah 62:8).
Isaiah 62:8-9
Her temple to be burned by fire and her walls to be torn down
The temple was burned in 2 Kings 25:9, but that is not the content of the oath in Isaiah 62:8–9, which concerns her grain and new wine.
Her children to be led away into Egypt as slaves and servants
Being led into Egypt is not the subject of the oath in Isaiah 62:8–9; it concerns her grain and new wine.
Her grain to feed enemies and her new wine to be drunk by foreigners
Her priests to forget the Law and neglect the daily sacrifices
Priests forgetting the Law is not in the oath of Isaiah 62:8–9; it concerns her grain and new wine.
Her king to sit on an ivory throne and rule over the nations
Solomon’s ivory throne is in 1 Kings 10:18, not in the oath of Isaiah 62:8–9, which concerns her grain and new wine.
In the call to prepare the way in Isaiah 62, which set of actions is commanded for the people and the nations?
“Go out, go out through the gates; prepare the way for the people! Build it up, build up the highway; clear away the stones; raise a banner for the nations!” (Isaiah 62:10).
Isaiah 62:10
Mend the nets, launch the boats, cast the hooks, and gather the fish
Mending nets and launching boats is the work of fishermen (Luke 5:4), not the commands of Isaiah 62:10.
Go through the gates, prepare the way, build up the highway, clear the stones, and raise a banner
Measure the temple, anoint the altar, light the lamps, and sound the trumpet
Measuring the temple and lighting lamps are not the commands of Isaiah 62:10, which is about preparing the way.
Flee to the hills, hide in caves, cover the wells, and bar the doors
Fleeing to the mountains is Matthew 24:16’s warning, the opposite of Isaiah 62:10’s call to go out through the gates and build the highway.
Count the tribes, divide the land, appoint the judges, and write the law
Counting tribes is the census of Numbers 1:2, not the commands of Isaiah 62:10.
At the close of Isaiah 62, what titles are given to the restored people and to Jerusalem herself?
“They will be called the Holy People, the Redeemed of The LORD; and you will be called Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken” (Isaiah 62:12).
Isaiah 62:12
The Mighty Remnant, the Chosen of Jacob; Fortress of David, Stronghold of Zion
The Mighty Remnant and Fortress of David are not names in Isaiah 62:12; the people are the Holy People and the city is Sought Out.
Priests of Fire, the Servants of the Altar; Mountain of the Covenant
Priests of Fire and Mountain of the Covenant are not names in Isaiah 62:12; the people are the Holy People and the city is Sought Out.
Holy People, the Redeemed of the LORD; Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken
Sons of Jacob, the Beloved Flock; City of Palms, Gate of the Tribes
City of Palms is Jericho (Deuteronomy 34:3), not a name for Jerusalem in Isaiah 62:12.
Servants of Elijah, the Faithful of Carmel; Pride of Carmel, Crown of the Hills
Servants of Elijah and Joy of Carmel are not names in Isaiah 62:12; the people are the Holy People and the city is Sought Out.
In Isaiah 63’s opening scene, from which land does the majestic figure with crimson-stained garments come?
Isaiah 63 opens, “Who is this coming from Edom, from Bozrah with crimson-stained garments?” (63:1).
Isaiah 63:1
Moab
Moab is the subject of an oracle in Isaiah 15:1, but the figure of Isaiah 63:1 comes from Edom.
Edom
Egypt
Egypt is where Israel was once enslaved, but 63:1 names Edom as the land this figure comes from.
Assyria
Assyria is a power Isaiah mentions elsewhere, but it is not the land named in this scene; the figure comes from Edom.
Phoenicia
Phoenicia, the land of Tyre and Sidon, is not named in this scene; the figure comes from Edom and Bozrah.
At the start of Isaiah 63, which specific city is named along with Edom as the place from which the figure comes?
The figure comes “from Edom, from Bozrah with crimson-stained garments” (63:1), so Bozrah is the city named with Edom.
Isaiah 63:1
Hebron
Hebron is the city where the men of Judah anointed David king (2 Samuel 2:4), not the city named in 63:1.
Samaria
Samaria was the northern kingdom’s capital, but 63:1 names the Edomite city of Bozrah.
Bozrah
Jericho
Jericho is the city whose wall collapsed for Joshua (Joshua 6:20); it is not named in Isaiah 63.
Damascus
Damascus is the capital of Aram and is not named in this scene; the figure comes from Bozrah in Edom.
In the dialogue that opens Isaiah 63, how does the majestic figure identify Himself?
Asked who He is, the figure answers, “It is I, proclaiming vindication, mighty to save” (63:1).
Isaiah 63:1
“I am the LORD of Hosts, seated between the cherubim”
The LORD of Hosts is described as enthroned between the cherubim in 1 Samuel 4:4, but that is not how the figure answers in 63:1.
“It is I, proclaiming vindication, mighty to save”
“I am the light of the world”
Jesus says “I am the light of the world” in John 8:12; the figure in Isaiah 63:1 gives a different answer.
“I am a voice of one calling in the wilderness”
John the Baptist says this of himself in John 1:23; it is not the figure’s reply in Isaiah 63:1.
“I am the Good Shepherd”
Jesus says “I am the good shepherd” in John 10:11; it is not the figure’s reply in Isaiah 63:1.
According to Isaiah 63, why are the coming one’s garments red, like someone stained at work?
The figure says, “I have trodden the winepress alone” (63:3), so His clothes are red like those of someone who treads the winepress (63:2).
Isaiah 63:2-3
He had been anointed with scarlet oil
Anointing was done with sacred oil (Exodus 30:25), but the stains here come from treading the winepress.
He had fought with wild beasts
Wild beasts are not mentioned; the red comes from the winepress and the blood of the nations (63:3).
He had trodden the winepress
He wore royal red linen
His garments are stained, not woven red; verse 3 says their blood spattered His garments from the winepress.
He had passed through fire
Passing through fire is a different image (Isaiah 43:2); in 63:2–3 the red comes from treading the winepress.
In Isaiah 63, what two time expressions are joined in the statement about judgment and deliverance?
The LORD says, “the day of vengeance was in My heart, and the year of My redemption had come” (63:4).
Isaiah 63:4
The day of vengeance and the year of My redemption
The hour of testing and the month of peace
A time of testing and a month of peace are not named here; verse 4 pairs vengeance with redemption.
The day of sacrifice and the year of release
A day of sacrifice and a year of release are not named here; verse 4 pairs the day of vengeance with the year of redemption.
The night of weeping and the morning of joy
Weeping that lasts the night and joy in the morning is the image of Psalm 30:5, not of Isaiah 63:4.
The season of sowing and the day of harvest
Seedtime and harvest are the earth’s seasons (Genesis 8:22); Isaiah 63:4 speaks of a day of vengeance and a year of redemption.
In the judgment speech of Isaiah 63, what happened when the speaker looked for help?
The LORD says, “I looked, but there was no one to help,” and so “My arm brought Me salvation” (63:5).
Isaiah 63:5
The kings of Judah came to assist
No kings of Judah are mentioned; verse 5 says there was no one to help.
The priests offered counsel
Priests are not mentioned either; the LORD says no one assisted Him (63:5).
The nations joined Him
The nations did not join Him; 63:3 says no one from the nations was with Him, and He trampled them.
No one helped, so His own arm brought salvation
Angels descended to fight
Angels are not said to descend; verse 5 says His own arm brought salvation and His wrath upheld Him.
Later in Isaiah 63, when the prophet begins recounting God’s goodness to Israel, what does he say he will make known?
The prophet says, “I will make known the LORD’s loving devotion and His praiseworthy acts” (63:7).
Isaiah 63:7
The measurements of the sanctuary
Measurements of the sanctuary belong to Ezekiel’s temple vision (Ezekiel 40:5), not to Isaiah 63:7.
The kings of David’s line
Kings of David’s line are not the subject; the prophet recounts the LORD’s loving devotion and praiseworthy acts (63:7).
The LORD’s loving devotion and praiseworthy acts
The laws of ritual cleansing
Laws of ritual cleansing are not the topic here; the prophet recounts the LORD’s kindness to Israel (63:7).
The visions of the night
Visions of the night are not what he promises; he will make known the LORD’s loving devotion and acts (63:7).
In Isaiah 63:8, what did the LORD say about His people before becoming their Savior?
The LORD says, “They are surely My people, sons who will not be disloyal.” So He became their Savior (63:8).
Isaiah 63:8
“My people have forgotten Me for days without number”
This charge, that My people have forgotten Me, comes from Jeremiah 2:32; in Isaiah 63:8 the LORD affirms His people instead.
“They are surely My people, sons who will not be disloyal”
“My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge”
Hosea 4:6 speaks of ruin for lack of knowledge; in Isaiah 63:8 the LORD says the people are surely His.
“Israel does not know; My people do not understand”
Israel’s failure to understand is the rebuke of Isaiah 1:3; in 63:8 the LORD calls them sons who will not be disloyal.
“My people will go into exile for their lack of understanding”
Exile for lack of understanding is the warning of Isaiah 5:13; in 63:8 the LORD calls them His people and becomes their Savior.
In Isaiah 63’s review of God’s past mercy, who is said to have saved Israel in all their distress?
Isaiah says “the Angel of His Presence saved them” in all their distress (63:9).
Isaiah 63:9
Moses
Moses led Israel, but 63:9 credits the Angel of His Presence with saving them; Moses is named in 63:11–12.
The Angel of His Presence
Aaron
Aaron is not named anywhere in this chapter.
Joshua
Joshua is not mentioned in this chapter, which recalls the days of Moses (63:11).
Michael
Michael is named as a chief prince in Daniel 10:13, but he is not named in Isaiah 63.
In Isaiah 63, what did the people do that caused God to turn and become their enemy?
The people “rebelled and grieved His Holy Spirit,” so He “turned and became their enemy” (63:10).
Isaiah 63:10
They neglected the feasts
Neglected feasts are not mentioned; 63:10 names rebellion and grieving His Holy Spirit.
They rebelled and grieved His Holy Spirit
They demanded a king
Demanding a king was Israel’s sin in 1 Samuel 8:5, not what 63:10 names.
They forgot to build an altar
Forgetting to build an altar is not mentioned; the cause in 63:10 is rebelling and grieving His Holy Spirit.
They refused to cross the Jordan
Refusing to cross the Jordan is not mentioned here; 63:10 names rebellion and grieving His Holy Spirit.
When Isaiah 63 recalls the days of Moses and the Exodus, what had God put among His flock?
The people ask, “Where is the One who set His Holy Spirit among them” (63:11).
Isaiah 63:11
A bronze serpent
The bronze snake was mounted on a pole (Numbers 21:9); it is not what God set among His flock in 63:11.
A pillar of cloud
A pillar of cloud guided Israel (Exodus 13:21), but 63:11 says God set His Holy Spirit among them.
His Holy Spirit
The Urim and Thummim
The Urim and Thummim were kept in the high priest’s breastpiece (Exodus 28:30) and are not named here.
A new covenant scroll
A new covenant is promised in Jeremiah 31:31, but a covenant scroll is not mentioned in Isaiah 63:11.
In the Exodus remembrance of Isaiah 63, at whose right hand was God’s glorious arm?
God “sent His glorious arm to lead them by the right hand of Moses” (63:12).
Isaiah 63:12
Aaron
Aaron is not named anywhere in this chapter; verse 12 names Moses.
Joshua
Joshua succeeded Moses (Joshua 1:2), but 63:12 names Moses at whose right hand the arm of God went.
Moses
Caleb
Caleb is not mentioned in this chapter, which names Moses (63:11–12).
Samuel
Samuel lived long after the Exodus; verse 12 recalls the days of Moses.
In Isaiah 63, when God led His people through the depths “like a horse in the wilderness,” what did not happen to them?
God led them through the depths like a horse in the wilderness, “so that they did not stumble” (63:13).
Isaiah 63:13
They did not hunger
Israel did hunger in the wilderness and God gave manna (Exodus 16:4), so hunger is not what the horse comparison says.
They did not stumble
They did not age
Not aging is never mentioned; verse 13 only says they did not stumble.
They did not sleep
Sleep is not mentioned in 63:13; the point is that they did not stumble.
They did not speak
Speaking is not mentioned in 63:13; the point is that they did not stumble.
In the prayer near the end of Isaiah 63, even though Abraham does not know us and Israel ignores us, who is still addressed as Father?
The prayer says, “You, O LORD, are our Father; our Redeemer from Everlasting is Your name” (63:16).
Isaiah 63:16
Moses
Moses is named in 63:11–12 as Israel’s leader, but he is not the one addressed as Father.
The LORD
Jacob
Jacob, also called Israel, is said not to acknowledge them; he is not the one addressed as Father.
Zion
Zion is not addressed as Father in this chapter; the prayer is to the LORD (63:16).
David
David is not mentioned in this chapter; the prayer calls the LORD their Father (63:16).
In the closing lament of Isaiah 63, after the enemies have trampled God’s sanctuary, how do the people say they have become?
The people lament, “We have become like those You never ruled, like those not called by Your name” (63:19), after enemies trampled the sanctuary (63:18).
Isaiah 63:18-19
Like dry bones scattered across a lifeless valley
Dry bones scattered in a valley are Ezekiel’s vision (Ezekiel 37:1), not the image in Isaiah 63:19.
Like sheep that have no shepherd to lead them
Sheep without a shepherd appear in Numbers 27:17 and Matthew 9:36, not in this lament.
Like those You never ruled, like those not called by Your name
Like captives weeping beside the rivers of Babylon
Weeping beside the rivers of Babylon is the scene of Psalm 137:1; Isaiah 63:19 uses a different comparison.
Like a withered vine burned with fire in the field
A burned vine is not the comparison here; 63:19 says they are like those God never ruled.
In Isaiah 64, when the prophet pleads for God to intervene for His people, what does he ask the LORD to rend and come down from?
The prophet pleads, “If only You would rend the heavens and come down” (64:1).
Isaiah 64:1
The earth
He asks God to come down to the earth, not to tear it open; what is to be rent is the heavens (64:1).
The heavens
Mount Zion
Mount Zion is not what is torn open; in 64:1 the mountains would quake when God comes down.
The sea
The sea is not mentioned in 64:1; the prophet asks God to rend the heavens.
The temple
The temple is mentioned in 64:11 as burned with fire, not as what God would rend in 64:1.
In Isaiah’s opening cry in chapter 64, what does he say the mountains would do at the LORD’s presence?
Isaiah longs for God to come down “so that mountains would quake at Your presence” (64:1).
Isaiah 64:1
Clap their hands
Clapping hands belongs to the trees in Isaiah 55:12; in 64:1 the mountains quake at God’s presence.
Bloom with flowers
Blooming with flowers is not mentioned; in 64:1 the mountains quake at God’s presence.
Quake
Turn into rivers
Turning into rivers is not mentioned; in 64:1 the mountains quake and in 64:3 they tremble.
Stand perfectly still
Standing still is the opposite of the image; the mountains quake at God’s presence (64:1).
In the prayer of Isaiah 64, God’s coming is compared to fire; what does the fire specifically cause water to do?
God’s coming is pictured “as fire kindles the brushwood and causes the water to boil” (64:2).
Isaiah 64:2
Freeze
Freezing is the opposite of what fire does; 64:2 says fire causes the water to boil.
Divide
Water was divided at the sea in Exodus 14:21, but in 64:2 the fire makes the water boil.
Rise into clouds
Rising into clouds is not mentioned; in 64:2 fire causes the water to boil.
Boil
Turn to blood
Water turned to blood in Exodus 7:20, but in 64:2 the fire makes the water boil.
In Isaiah’s confession of sin in chapter 64, what does he say all human righteous acts are like?
Isaiah confesses, “all our righteous acts are like filthy rags” (64:6).
Isaiah 64:6
Polished silver
Refined silver is how Psalm 12:6 describes the LORD’s flawless words, not how Isaiah 64:6 describes human righteousness.
Morning dew
Morning dew is not mentioned; 64:6 compares our righteous acts to filthy rags and ourselves to a withering leaf.
Filthy rags
A strong tower
A strong tower is the name of the LORD in Proverbs 18:10, not a picture of human righteousness in 64:6.
A crown of gold
A crown of gold is not mentioned; 64:6 says all our righteous acts are like filthy rags.
When Isaiah appeals to the LORD as Father in chapter 64, what picture does he use for God’s relationship to His people?
Isaiah says, “You are our Father; we are the clay, and You are the potter” (64:8).
Isaiah 64:8
Sheep and shepherd
Sheep and shepherd is the picture of Psalm 23:1, not the image Isaiah uses in 64:8.
Vine and branches
Vine and branches is the picture Jesus uses in John 15:5, not the image in Isaiah 64:8.
Clay and potter
Soldiers and king
Soldiers and king is not the picture here; Isaiah 64:8 speaks of a Father, clay and a potter.
Children and teacher
Children and teacher is not the picture here; Isaiah 64:8 speaks of a Father, clay and a potter.
In Isaiah 64’s declaration about the LORD’s uniqueness, for whom does God act?
No one has seen any God besides the LORD, “who acts on behalf of those who wait for Him” (64:4).
Isaiah 64:4
Those who trust in horses
Trusting in horses is condemned in Isaiah 31:1; in 64:4 God acts for those who wait for Him.
Those who offer the most sacrifices
The most sacrifices are not mentioned; 64:4 says God acts for those who wait for Him.
Those who rule nations
Ruling nations is not the condition; 64:4 says God acts for those who wait for Him.
Those who hide in fear
Hiding in fear is not the condition; 64:4 says God acts for those who wait for Him.
Those who wait for Him
In Isaiah 64, whom does the LORD welcome?
Isaiah says, “You welcome those who gladly do right, who remember Your ways” (64:5).
Isaiah 64:5
Those who make alliances with Egypt
Making alliances with Egypt is condemned in Isaiah 31:1; in 64:5 God welcomes those who gladly do right.

Jeremiah’s eyes are tested in the visions that follow (1:11, 1:13), but the LORD touched his mouth (1:9).
Ears
Ears are not touched in Jeremiah 1; the LORD touched his mouth (1:9).
Hands
It was the LORD’s hand that reached out; He touched Jeremiah’s mouth (1:9).
Mouth
Feet
Feet are not mentioned in 1:9; the LORD touched Jeremiah’s mouth.
After touching Jeremiah’s mouth, what did the LORD say He had put there?
Touching his mouth, the LORD said, “Behold, I have put My words in your mouth” (1:9).
Jeremiah 1:9
Fire
Fire is not put in his mouth in 1:9, though God’s message later becomes “a fire burning in my heart” (Jeremiah 20:9).
A song
A song is not mentioned in 1:9; God put His words in Jeremiah’s mouth.
Wisdom only
The LORD did not say wisdom; He said, “I have put My words in your mouth” (1:9).
My words
A seal
A seal is not mentioned in 1:9; Isaiah’s mouth was touched with a glowing coal (Isaiah 6:6–7), Jeremiah’s with God’s words.
In the first vision of Jeremiah chapter 1, what did Jeremiah say he saw?
“I see a branch of an almond tree,” Jeremiah replied (1:11).
Jeremiah 1:11
A lampstand of gold
The solid gold lampstand is Zechariah’s vision (Zechariah 4:2).
A basket of figs
Baskets of figs came to Jeremiah later (Jeremiah 24:1), not in chapter 1.
A branch of an almond tree
A flying scroll
The flying scroll is Zechariah’s vision (Zechariah 5:1).
A valley of dry bones
The valley full of bones is Ezekiel’s vision (Ezekiel 37:1).
What did the LORD say the almond-branch vision showed about His word in Jeremiah’s first chapter?
“You have observed correctly,” said the LORD, “for I am watching over My word to accomplish it” (1:12).
Jeremiah 1:12
He would let it fall to the ground unfulfilled
The opposite: God was watching over His word to accomplish it (1:12).
He was hiding it from Judah until a later day
God was not hiding His word; He was watching over it to fulfill it (1:12).
He was watching over it to accomplish it
He would soon withdraw it from the prophets
God was not withdrawing His word; He had just put His words in Jeremiah’s mouth (1:9).
He had sealed it up until the time of the end
Sealing words “until the time of the end” is Daniel 12:4; in 1:12 God watches over His word to accomplish it.
In Jeremiah’s second vision in chapter 1, what object did he see?

A plumb line
The plumb line was Amos’s vision (Amos 7:7).
A boiling pot
A scroll eaten by the prophet
Ezekiel was told to eat a scroll (Ezekiel 3:1); Jeremiah saw a boiling pot (1:13).
A golden calf
Aaron fashioned a molten calf at Sinai (Exodus 32:4); Jeremiah’s second vision was a boiling pot.
A valley full of bones
The valley full of bones was Ezekiel’s vision (Ezekiel 37:1).
In the LORD’s explanation of Jeremiah’s boiling-pot vision, from which direction would disaster be poured out on the land?
“Disaster from the north will be poured out on all who live in the land” (1:14).
Jeremiah 1:14
From the south
The pot was tilting from the north (1:13), not the south.
From the east
East is not mentioned in Jeremiah 1; disaster comes from the north (1:14).
From the west
West is not mentioned in Jeremiah 1; the boiling pot tilts from the north (1:13–14).
From the north
From the sea
The sea is not mentioned in Jeremiah 1; disaster comes from the north (1:14).
In the warning vision given to Jeremiah, what did the LORD say He was about to summon from the north?
“For I am about to summon all the clans and kingdoms of the north” (1:15).

The tribes of the south

All the clans and kingdoms of the north

Jeremiah 1:15
In the courts of the house of the LORD

At the entrance to the gates of Jerusalem

On the banks of the Jordan River
The Jordan is not mentioned in Jeremiah 1; the kings set up thrones at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem (1:15).
In Jeremiah’s first chapter, the invading forces from the north were also said to attack all the other cities of which region?

Jeremiah 1:15
Samaria
Samaria was the northern capital; Jeremiah 1:15 speaks of the cities of Judah.
Galilee
Galilee is not mentioned in Jeremiah 1; the invaders attack the cities of Judah (1:15).
Edom
Edom is not mentioned in Jeremiah 1; the attack falls on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah (1:15).
Judah
Moab
Moab is not in Jeremiah 1; the attacked cities are Judah’s (1:15).
In Jeremiah 1, what central sin did the LORD name as a reason for pronouncing judgment on His people?
God pronounces judgment “because they have forsaken Me” (1:16).
Jeremiah 1:16
They had forsaken Him

The ark was captured by the Philistines in Eli’s day (1 Samuel 4:11); Jeremiah 1 does not mention it.
They had failed to build walls
Walls are not the charge; the northern kings will attack Jerusalem’s walls (1:15). The sin was forsaking God (1:16).
They had not gathered manna
Israel ate manna in the wilderness for forty years (Exodus 16:35); Jeremiah 1:16 charges Judah with forsaking God.
They had forgotten Passover entirely
Passover is not mentioned in Jeremiah 1; the sins named are forsaking God, burning incense to other gods, and idolatry (1:16).
What specific act of idolatry is mentioned in Jeremiah 1 as part of Judah’s wickedness?
“They have burned incense to other gods and worshiped the works of their own hands” (1:16).
Jeremiah 1:16
They sacrificed on Mount Carmel
Mount Carmel was the site of Elijah’s contest (1 Kings 18:20), not mentioned in Jeremiah 1.
They burned incense to other gods
They worshiped the Nile
The Nile is not mentioned in Jeremiah 1; they burned incense to other gods (1:16).
They bowed to Pharaoh
Pharaoh is not mentioned in Jeremiah 1; the idolatry was burning incense to other gods (1:16).
They swore by Dagon alone
Dagon was the Philistine god (1 Samuel 5:2); Jeremiah 1:16 speaks of incense to other gods.
Besides burning incense to other gods, what else had the people worshiped in Jeremiah 1?
They “worshiped the works of their own hands” (1:16).
Jeremiah 1:16
The stars of heaven only
Worship of the host of heaven is condemned in Jeremiah 8:2, not in 1:16.
Foreign armies
Foreign armies are the instruments of judgment in 1:15, not objects of worship.
The works of their own hands
The bronze serpent
Hezekiah destroyed the bronze snake to which Israel burned incense (2 Kings 18:4); Jeremiah 1 does not mention it.
The cedars of Lebanon
Cedars of Lebanon are not mentioned in Jeremiah 1; the people worshiped the works of their own hands (1:16).
When sending Jeremiah to speak, what did the LORD first tell him to do in Jeremiah chapter 1?
“Get yourself ready. Stand up and tell them everything that I command you” (1:17).
Jeremiah 1:17
Hide in the temple
God sent Jeremiah to stand up and speak, not to hide (1:17).
Get yourself ready
Return to Egypt
Egypt is not mentioned in Jeremiah 1; he was told to get ready and speak.
Fast for forty days
No fast is commanded in Jeremiah 1; the first command in 1:17 is to get ready.
Write the vision on stone
Jeremiah is told to speak, not write; tablets of stone belong to Moses at Sinai (Exodus 31:18).
What warning did the LORD give Jeremiah if he became intimidated by those he had to address?
“Do not be intimidated by them, or I will terrify you before them” (1:17).
Jeremiah 1:17
He would lose his voice
Being made silent was Ezekiel’s experience (Ezekiel 3:26); the warning in 1:17 is that God would terrify Jeremiah.
He would be sent to exile
Exile is not threatened against Jeremiah in 1:17; God warns He would terrify him before them.
God would terrify him before them
The temple would be closed
The temple is not mentioned in Jeremiah 1; God warns He would terrify Jeremiah before them (1:17).
His visions would cease
The visions do not cease; God warns that He would terrify him before them (1:17).
In God’s promise of strength to Jeremiah, what kind of city did He say He had made the prophet?
“This day I have made you like a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls” (1:18).

A ruined city
Jeremiah is made strong, not ruined: he is “like a fortified city” (1:18).
A hidden city
Jeremiah is not hidden; he is set as a fortified city against the whole land (1:18).
A fortified city
A holy city
1:18 says fortified, not holy; God makes him an iron pillar and bronze walls.
A desert city
No desert city appears; God made Jeremiah a fortified city (1:18).
In Jeremiah 1, against which four groups in Judah was the prophet made strong?
He stands “against the kings of Judah, its officials, its priests, and the people of the land” (1:18).
Jeremiah 1:18
Prophets, merchants, widows, and soldiers

Kings of Judah, officials, priests, and the people of the land
Judges, singers, Levites, and foreigners
Judges, singers, Levites, and foreigners are not listed; the four groups are kings, officials, priests, and the people (1:18).
Elders, scribes, captains, and farmers
Elders, scribes, captains, and farmers are not in 1:18; the list begins with the kings of Judah.
Kings of Israel, princes of Tyre, priests of Dan, and exiles
The list concerns Judah, not Israel, Tyre, or Dan: the kings of Judah, its officials, its priests, and the people (1:18).
What did the LORD say Jeremiah’s opponents would do, but fail to accomplish, in the close of Jeremiah chapter 1?
“They will fight against you but will never overcome you” (1:19).
Jeremiah 1:19
They would praise him but never follow him
1:19 promises opposition, not praise; they will fight against him.
They would imprison him but never accuse him
Jeremiah was later beaten and jailed (Jeremiah 37:15), but 1:19 says they will fight against him and not overcome him.
They would fight against him but never overcome him
They would ignore him but never hear him
1:19 speaks of fighting, not ignoring; his enemies will fight but never overcome him.
They would flee from him but never return
His enemies do not flee in 1:19; they fight against him but cannot overcome him.
Why, according to Jeremiah 1:19, would those who fought Jeremiah not overcome him?
“They will fight against you but will never overcome you, since I am with you to deliver you” (1:19).
Jeremiah 1:19
He had a large army
Jeremiah had no army; his protection was the LORD’s presence (1:19).
Jerusalem’s walls were strong
The walls in 1:18 are Jeremiah himself, made “bronze walls” by God; his safety lay in God’s presence (1:19).
The priests would protect him
The priests are among those he is set against (1:18), not his protectors.
The LORD was with him to deliver him
Babylon feared him
Babylon is not named in Jeremiah 1; the LORD promises, “I am with you to deliver you” (1:19).
In the opening dating statement of Jeremiah, in which month of the eleventh year of King Zedekiah did the people of Jerusalem go into exile?
The ministry ran “until the fifth month of the eleventh year of Zedekiah” (1:3).
Jeremiah 1:3
First month
The first month is not mentioned; 1:3 names the fifth month of Zedekiah’s eleventh year.
Third month
1:3 names the fifth month, not the third.
Fifth month
Seventh month
The seventh month is not in 1:3; Jerusalem went into exile in the fifth month.
Tenth month
The tenth month is when Babylon’s siege began, in Zedekiah’s ninth year (2 Kings 25:1); the exile came in the fifth month (1:3).
In Jeremiah’s commission over nations and kingdoms, which ordered sequence of actions is correct?
God appointed him “to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant” (1:10).
Jeremiah 1:10
Uproot and tear down, destroy and overthrow, build and plant
Build and plant, uproot and tear down, destroy and overthrow
Building and planting come last in 1:10, after the four verbs of destruction.
Destroy and overthrow, build and plant, uproot and tear down
Destroy and overthrow come second in 1:10, after uproot and tear down.
Tear down and uproot, plant and build, destroy and overthrow
This reverses each pair; 1:10 begins “uproot and tear down” and ends “build and plant.”
Overthrow and build, uproot and plant, destroy and tear down
These pairs are scrambled; the order in 1:10 is uproot and tear down, destroy and overthrow, build and plant.

Jeremiah 2:2
Her victories over Canaan
Victories over Canaan are not mentioned; He remembers her devotion and love (2:2).
Her devotion and love as a young bride
Her building of Solomon’s temple
Solomon’s temple is not mentioned; He remembers her devotion and love (2:2).
Her wisdom under Moses
Wisdom under Moses is not mentioned; He remembers her devotion and love (2:2).
Her wealth in the land
Wealth in the land is not mentioned; He remembers her following Him in the wilderness (2:2).
In the opening of Jeremiah chapter 2, Israel is called holy to the LORD and the firstfruits of what?
“Israel was holy to the LORD, the firstfruits of His harvest” (2:3).
Jeremiah 2:3
The vineyard
The vineyard image appears later in 2:21; here Israel is the firstfruits of His harvest.
The covenant
The covenant is not the thing named; Israel is the firstfruits of His harvest (2:3).
The nations
The nations are not the thing named; Israel is the firstfruits of His harvest (2:3).
His harvest
The altar
The altar is not the thing named; Israel is the firstfruits of His harvest (2:3).
Recounting the exodus in Jeremiah 2, through what kind of region did the LORD say He led Israel after bringing them out of Egypt?
The people did not ask about the LORD, “who led us through the wilderness, through a land of deserts and pits, a land of drought and darkness” (2:6).
Jeremiah 2:6
A land of deserts and pits, drought and darkness
A land of cedar forests and rivers

A land of snow and mountains
Snow and mountains are not described; the land is one of deserts and pits (2:6).
A land of fortified cities and vineyards

A land of islands and harbors
Islands and harbors are not described; the land is one of deserts and pits (2:6).
In the LORD’s complaint in Jeremiah 2, what happened when Israel went after worthless idols?
“They followed worthless idols, and became worthless themselves” (2:5).
Jeremiah 2:5
They became stronger than their enemies
They did not grow stronger; they became worthless themselves (2:5).
They learned the Law more carefully
They did not learn the Law more carefully; they followed worthless idols (2:5).
They became worthless themselves
They found rest for their souls
They found no rest; they became worthless themselves (2:5).
They inherited new land
New land was not their result; they became worthless themselves (2:5).
In Jeremiah 2, after the LORD brought His people into a fertile land to eat its fruit and bounty, what did they do?
“You came and defiled My land and made My inheritance detestable” (2:7).
Jeremiah 2:7
They rebuilt the tabernacle there
Rebuilding the tabernacle is not mentioned; they defiled the land (2:7).
They asked for a king there
Asking for a king is not mentioned here; they defiled the land (2:7).
They divided it among the tribes again
Dividing the land again is not mentioned; they defiled the land (2:7).
They offered pure worship there
The opposite happened: they defiled the land rather than worshiping purely (2:7).
They defiled His land and made His inheritance detestable

Prophets
Levites
Levites are not named in this verse; the prophets prophesied by Baal (2:8).
Judges
Judges are not named in this verse; the prophets prophesied by Baal (2:8).
Elders
Elders are not named in this verse; the prophets prophesied by Baal (2:8).

“My people have exchanged their Glory for useless idols” (2:11).
Jeremiah 2:11
Chariots from Egypt
Chariots from Egypt are not mentioned; they exchanged their Glory for useless idols (2:11).
Silver and gold
Silver and gold are not mentioned; they exchanged their Glory for useless idols (2:11).
Cedar idols
Cedar idols are not mentioned; they exchanged their Glory for useless idols (2:11).
Useless idols
Foreign wives
Foreign wives are not mentioned; they exchanged their Glory for useless idols (2:11).

They trusted in kings and fortified cities rather than in God

They married foreign wives and ate unclean food at their feasts
Marrying foreigners and eating unclean food are not the two evils named in 2:13.
They rejected the prophets and despised the Law of their fathers
Rejecting prophets and despising the Law are not the two evils named in 2:13.
They forsook the spring of living water and dug broken cisterns that could not hold water

Jeremiah 2:10
Bethel and Dan
Bethel and Dan are not named in 2:10; the places are Cyprus and Kedar.
Tyre and Sidon
Tyre and Sidon are not named in 2:10; the places are Cyprus and Kedar.
Egypt and Assyria
Egypt and Assyria are named later (2:18), not in 2:10; the places here are Cyprus and Kedar.
Tarshish and Sheba
Tarshish and Sheba are not named in 2:10; the places are Cyprus and Kedar.
Cyprus and Kedar

Jeremiah 2:14-15
Locusts stripping a field
Locusts are not mentioned; the image is young lions (2:15).
Eagles circling prey
Eagles are not mentioned; the image is young lions (2:15).
Young lions roaring and laying waste the land
Bears prowling vineyards
Bears are not mentioned; the image is young lions (2:15).
Floodwaters sweeping cities away
Floodwaters are not mentioned; the image is young lions (2:15).
In Jeremiah chapter 2, which two Egyptian cities are named as having shaved the crown of Israel’s head?

Memphis and Tahpanhes
Zoan and Thebes

Gaza and Ashkelon

Hebron and Beersheba

The Jordan and the Jabbok

Abana and Pharpar

The Kishon and the Litani

The Nile and the Euphrates

In the LORD’s charge in Jeremiah 2, what did His people do on every high hill and under every green tree?

Jeremiah 2:20
They lay down as a prostitute
They built cities of refuge

They gathered manna
Gathering manna is not mentioned; the charge is spiritual prostitution (2:20).
They read the Book of the Law
Reading the Book of the Law is not mentioned; the charge is spiritual prostitution (2:20).

Burying the ark is not mentioned; the charge is spiritual prostitution (2:20).

As a choice vine from the very best seed

Her kings falling in battle is not mentioned here; the stain of her guilt remains before Him (2:22).

A heifer treading grain

Jeremiah 14:17
They were to look toward the temple
Looking toward the temple is not mentioned; his eyes overflow with tears (14:17).
They were to search for rain clouds
Searching for rain clouds is not mentioned in this verse; the eyes overflow with tears (14:17).
They were to overflow with tears without ceasing
They were to be covered with ashes
Being covered with ashes is not mentioned; the farmers and nobles cover their heads (14:3–4).
They were to watch the city gates
Watching the city gates is not mentioned; the eyes overflow day and night (14:17).
In Jeremiah’s closing appeal about rain and hope, who alone could truly give showers to Judah?
Jeremiah 14:22 asks, “Is this not by You, O LORD our God?” and says the idols of the nations cannot bring rain.
Jeremiah 14:22
The false gods of the nations
The verse asks, “Can the worthless idols of the nations bring rain?” and implies they cannot (14:22).
The heavens by themselves
Jeremiah asks, “Do the skies alone send showers?” implying that rain comes from the LORD (14:22).
The priests of Jerusalem
Priests are not credited with sending rain; the LORD is (14:22).
The LORD our God
The king of David’s line
The king of David’s line is not mentioned; the verse credits the LORD our God (14:22).
In Jeremiah 15, the LORD says that even if two famous intercessors stood before Him, He would still not turn toward Judah. Who were they?
Jeremiah 15:1 says, “Even if Moses and Samuel should stand before Me, My heart would not go out to this people.”
Jeremiah 15:1
Abraham and Isaac
Abraham pleaded for Sodom (Genesis 18:23), but Jeremiah 15:1 names Moses and Samuel.
Moses and Samuel
David and Solomon
David and Solomon were kings, not the intercessors named in Jeremiah 15:1.
Elijah and Elisha
Elijah and Elisha were prophets, but Jeremiah 15:1 names Moses and Samuel.
Ezra and Nehemiah
Ezra and Nehemiah lived after the exile and are not named in Jeremiah 15:1.
When the people in Jeremiah 15 ask, “Where shall we go?” which four outcomes does the LORD tell Jeremiah to announce?
Jeremiah 15:2 lists “Those destined for death, to death; those destined for the sword, to the sword; those destined for famine, to famine; and those destined for captivity, to captivity.”
Jeremiah 15:2
Plague, drought, exile, and tribute

Death, sword, famine, and captivity
Fire, flood, pestilence, and exile
Fire, flood and pestilence are not the four outcomes of Jeremiah 15:2.
Sword, plague, locusts, and shame
Locusts and shame are not among the outcomes of Jeremiah 15:2.
Bondage, flight, hunger, and mourning
Bondage, flight, hunger and mourning are not the wording of Jeremiah 15:2.
In the judgment against Judah in Jeremiah 15, which set correctly names the four kinds of destroyers the LORD appointed?
Jeremiah 15:3 names “the sword to kill, the dogs to drag away, and the birds of the air and beasts of the earth to devour and destroy.”
Jeremiah 15:3
Plague, hail, drought, and fire
Plague, hail, drought and fire are not the four destroyers of Jeremiah 15:3.
Sword, dogs, birds of the sky, and beasts of the earth
Chariots, horsemen, archers, and spearmen
Chariots, horsemen, archers and spearmen are human armies, not the four destroyers of Jeremiah 15:3.
Lions, bears, wolves, and serpents
Lions, bears, wolves and serpents are not the list in Jeremiah 15:3; Jeremiah 5:6 names a lion, wolf and leopard elsewhere.
Flood, wind, famine, and earthquake
Flood, wind, famine and earthquake are not the four destroyers of Jeremiah 15:3.
In Jeremiah 15, because of whose actions would the people of Jerusalem become a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth?
Jeremiah 15:4 says Judah would be a horror “because of what Manasseh son of Hezekiah king of Judah did in Jerusalem.”
Jeremiah 15:4
Ahaz son of Jotham, king of Judah
Ahaz son of Jotham was a Judean king (2 Kings 16:1), but Jeremiah 15:4 names Manasseh.
Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah
Jehoiakim son of Josiah ruled in Jeremiah’s time, but Jeremiah 15:4 names Manasseh.
Manasseh son of Hezekiah, king of Judah
Jeroboam son of Nebat, king of Israel
Jeroboam son of Nebat led the northern kingdom into sin (1 Kings 12:28–30), not the king named in Jeremiah 15:4.
Omri, father of Ahab and king of Israel
Omri ruled the northern kingdom of Israel (1 Kings 16:23), not the Judean king named in Jeremiah 15:4.
In Jeremiah 15, to what did the LORD say He would make Judah’s widows more numerous?

The stars in the heavens

The dust of the earth

The sand of the seas
The cedars of Lebanon
Cedars of Lebanon are not mentioned in Jeremiah 15:8, which compares the widows to the sand of the sea.
The fish of the sea
Fish of the sea are not mentioned in Jeremiah 15:8, which compares the widows to the sand of the sea.
In Jeremiah’s lament in chapter 15, what ordinary cause of disputes did he say he had not been involved in, though everyone still cursed him?
Jeremiah 15:10 says, “I have neither lent nor borrowed, yet everyone curses me.”
Jeremiah 15:10
Buying and selling
Buying and selling are not mentioned in Jeremiah 15:10; he says he has neither lent nor borrowed.
Planting and harvesting
Planting and harvesting are not mentioned in Jeremiah 15:10; he says he has neither lent nor borrowed.
Lending and borrowing
Marrying and divorcing
Marrying and divorcing are not mentioned in Jeremiah 15:10; he says he has neither lent nor borrowed.
Judging and testifying
Judging and testifying are not mentioned in Jeremiah 15:10; he says he has neither lent nor borrowed.
In Jeremiah 15, what did Jeremiah say he did when he found the LORD’s words?
Jeremiah 15:16 says, “Your words were found, and I ate them. Your words became my joy and my heart’s delight.”

A jar was used to keep deeds of purchase (Jeremiah 32:14), not the LORD’s words found in Jeremiah 15:16.
He wrote them on a scroll and read them to the king
Baruch wrote the scroll at Jeremiah’s dictation later (Jeremiah 36:4); Jeremiah 15:16 says he ate the words.
He taught them to the priests, who rejoiced in them
Teaching the priests is not mentioned in Jeremiah 15:16, which says he ate the words.
He ate them, and they became his joy and heart’s delight
He buried them in the field until the day of judgment
Burying the words is not mentioned in Jeremiah 15:16, which says he ate them and found them his delight.
Because the LORD’s hand was upon him in Jeremiah 15, with what group did Jeremiah say he never sat or celebrated?
Jeremiah 15:17 says, “I never sat with the band of revelers, nor did I celebrate with them.”
Jeremiah 15:17
The merchants at the gate
Merchants at the gate are not mentioned in Jeremiah 15:17; he sat apart from the band of revelers.
The soldiers on the wall
Soldiers on the wall are not mentioned in Jeremiah 15:17; he sat apart from the band of revelers.
The band of revelers
The elders in the court
Elders in the court are not mentioned in Jeremiah 15:17; he sat apart from the band of revelers.
The singers in the temple
Singers in the temple are not mentioned in Jeremiah 15:17; he sat apart from the band of revelers.
In Jeremiah’s prayer for justice in chapter 15, what did he ask the LORD to do against his persecutors?
Jeremiah 15:15 says, “Avenge me against my persecutors.”
Jeremiah 15:15
Hide him from them
Jeremiah does not ask to be hidden in 15:15; he asks the LORD to avenge him against his persecutors.
Avenge him
Promote him above them
Promotion is not what Jeremiah asks in 15:15; he asks the LORD to avenge him.
Send them into exile at once
Jeremiah 15:15 does not ask for immediate exile; he asks the LORD to avenge him.
Make them forget his words
Making them forget his words is not asked in Jeremiah 15:15; he asks the LORD to avenge him.
In Jeremiah 15:18, to what unreliable source of water did Jeremiah compare the LORD in his unending pain?
Jeremiah 15:18 says, “You have indeed become like a mirage to me—water that is not there.”
Jeremiah 15:18
A broken cistern that cannot hold water
A broken cistern is Jeremiah 2:13’s image of Israel’s own idolatry, not the image of Jeremiah 15:18.
A dried-up well in the desert wilderness
A dried-up well is not the image of Jeremiah 15:18, which says a mirage, water that is not there.
A mirage, like water that is not there
A muddy spring fouled by animals
A muddy spring is not the image of Jeremiah 15:18, which says a mirage, water that is not there.
A flooded river that sweeps all away
A flooded river is the opposite of the failing water in Jeremiah 15:18, where the LORD is like water that is not there.
In the LORD’s rhetorical question in Jeremiah 15, from what direction was the iron said to come?
Jeremiah 15:12 asks, “Can anyone smash iron—iron from the north—or bronze?”
Jeremiah 15:12
East
East is not the direction named in Jeremiah 15:12; the iron is from the north.
West
West is not the direction named in Jeremiah 15:12; the iron is from the north.
South
South is not the direction named in Jeremiah 15:12; the iron is from the north.
North
Sea
The sea is not a direction named in Jeremiah 15:12; the iron is from the north.
In Jeremiah 15, what did the LORD promise to do regarding Jeremiah’s enemy in his time of trouble?
Jeremiah 15:11 says, “surely I will intercede with your enemy in your time of trouble, in your time of distress.”
Jeremiah 15:11
Destroy the enemy immediately

Turn the enemy into a servant
Making the enemy a servant is not promised in Jeremiah 15:11; the LORD says He will intercede.
Intercede with the enemy
Blind the enemy
Blinding the enemy is not promised in Jeremiah 15:11; the LORD says He will intercede.
Scatter the enemy into the wilderness
Scattering the enemy into the wilderness is not promised in Jeremiah 15:11; the LORD says He will intercede.
In God’s reply to Jeremiah in chapter 15, what kind of speech must Jeremiah offer if he is to be God’s spokesman?
Jeremiah 15:19 says, “if you speak words that are noble instead of worthless, you will be My spokesman.”
Jeremiah 15:19
Lofty and poetic words
Lofty poetry is not what Jeremiah 15:19 requires; it asks for noble words instead of worthless ones.
Worthy, not worthless, words
Secret and hidden words
Secret words are not required by Jeremiah 15:19; it asks for noble words instead of worthless ones.
Harsh and terrifying words
Harsh, terrifying words are not required by Jeremiah 15:19; it asks for noble words instead of worthless ones.
New and strange words
New and strange words are not required by Jeremiah 15:19; it asks for noble words instead of worthless ones.
According to the LORD’s answer to Jeremiah in chapter 15, what was Jeremiah’s proper relationship to the people, and what protection would God give him?
Jeremiah 15:19–20 says, “It is they who must turn to you, but you must not turn to them,” and promises “a fortified wall of bronze.”
Jeremiah 15:19-20
He must turn to them, and God would make him a reed in the wind
Jeremiah is told not to turn to the people (15:19), and the protection is a bronze wall (15:20), not a reed in the wind.
They must turn to him, and God would make him a fortified wall of bronze
He must flee from them, and God would hide him in caves
Jeremiah is not told to flee in Jeremiah 15:19–20; God promises a fortified wall of bronze.
He must flatter them, and God would make him a golden crown
Jeremiah is not told to flatter the people in Jeremiah 15:19–20; God promises a fortified wall of bronze.
He must join them, and God would make him a chariot of fire
Jeremiah is not told to join the people in Jeremiah 15:19–20; God promises a fortified wall of bronze.
When the word of the LORD came to the prophet Jeremiah in the land of Judah, what personal command did he receive about family life?
The LORD told Jeremiah, “You must not marry or have sons or daughters in this place” (16:2), a personal sign of the coming judgment on families in Judah.
Jeremiah 16:1-2
He had to leave Jerusalem and settle in Egypt
Jeremiah was later carried to Egypt against the LORD’s word by the remnant (Jeremiah 43:6–7), but the command in 16:1–2 was about family life, not moving.
He was not to marry or have sons or daughters in that place
He had to shave his head and wear sackcloth every day
Shaving the head was an ordinary mourning custom, and 16:6 says the dead would go unmourned with no one shaving his head; it was not Jeremiah’s command.
He was to buy land in Anathoth immediately
Jeremiah did buy a field in Anathoth, but that was a later, separate act (Jeremiah 32:8–9), not the command of 16:2.
He had to live in the temple courts
Nothing in 16:1–2 sends Jeremiah to live in the temple courts; the command was to stay unmarried and childless in that place.
In Jeremiah’s message about children born among the people of Judah, what did the LORD say would happen to them?
The LORD said the sons and daughters born in that place “will die from deadly diseases” and would not be mourned or buried (16:4), then be finished off by sword and famine.
Jeremiah 16:3-4
They would be honored as priests serving in the Jerusalem temple
The children are doomed, not honored: 16:4 says they die of disease, sword and famine, so there is no priestly service awaiting them.
They would be carried safely to Egypt and live there in peace
Egypt is not their refuge; 16:4 describes death at home, and the exile in 16:13 is to a land they have not known.
They would inherit the throne of David and rule over the land
The throne of David is not promised to them in this passage; 16:4 describes death, unburied corpses and food for birds and beasts.
They would die from deadly diseases and go unlamented and unburied
They would rebuild the ruined cities and restore the nation
Rebuilding is not in view here; 16:4 says they die unburied, and the ruin of the land comes first.
As a sign of coming judgment in Jeremiah 16, what kind of house was Jeremiah forbidden to enter to mourn or show sympathy?
The LORD said, “Do not enter a house where there is a funeral meal” (16:5), because He had removed His peace, loving devotion and compassion from the people.
Jeremiah 16:5
A house where there is a funeral meal
The king’s palace
The king’s palace is not mentioned in 16:5; the ban concerned mourning houses, and in 16:8 also houses of feasting.
The house of the high priest
Nothing in 16:5 mentions the high priest’s house; the forbidden place was a house holding a funeral meal.
A foreign embassy
A foreign embassy does not appear in this chapter; Jeremiah was told to avoid a house of mourning.
A city gate guardhouse
A city gate guardhouse is not mentioned; 16:5 speaks of a house with a funeral meal.
Speaking about Judah’s near future, what everyday sounds did the LORD say He would silence from the land?
The LORD said He would remove “the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of the bride and bridegroom” from the place, before their eyes and in their days (16:9).
Jeremiah 16:9
Trumpets, harps, and cymbals from the temple
Trumpets, harps and cymbals are not named in 16:9; the sounds silenced were joy and gladness and the voices of bride and bridegroom.
The cries of merchants in the marketplace
The marketplace cries of merchants are not mentioned in this verse, which names joyful celebration and weddings.
The songs of Levites at Passover
Levites’ Passover songs are not mentioned in 16:9; the silenced sounds are those of joy, gladness and the wedding couple.
The marching orders of the army
Military marching orders are not in 16:9, which speaks of festive, domestic sounds.
The sounds of joy and gladness and the voices of bride and bridegroom
When Judah asked why such a great disaster had been announced, what answer did Jeremiah 16 say he was to give first?
Jeremiah was to say, “It is because your fathers have forsaken Me, declares the LORD, and followed other gods, and served and worshiped them” (16:11).
Jeremiah 16:10-11
Because they had failed to rebuild the city walls and gates of Jerusalem
Rebuilding city walls is never given as the reason; 16:11 names forsaking the LORD and following other gods.
Because they had refused to pay the temple tax and the yearly tithes
The Sabbath year is not mentioned in 16:11; the answer was idolatry and abandoning the LORD’s instruction.
Because their fathers had forsaken the LORD, followed other gods, and did not keep His law
Because Egypt had broken a treaty with Judah and betrayed its king
Egypt’s treaty-breaking is not in the answer; 16:11 blames the people’s own fathers for forsaking the LORD.
Because the temple treasures had been stolen and carried off to Egypt
Missing temple treasures are not given as a reason; 16:11 points to idolatry and disobedience.
Addressing Jeremiah’s generation rather than their ancestors, how did the LORD describe the people’s conduct?
The LORD said, “you have done more evil than your fathers,” with each following “the stubbornness of his evil heart instead of obeying Me” (16:12).
Jeremiah 16:12
They were less violent than their fathers, but more fearful of Babylon
The people are not described as less violent; 16:12 says they did more evil than their fathers.
They were exactly the same as their fathers, no better and no worse
They were not the same as their fathers; 16:12 says they had done more evil than their fathers.
They were more righteous than their fathers, but poorly taught by the priests
They were not more righteous; 16:12 says they had done more evil and refused to obey the LORD.
They had done more evil, each following the stubbornness of his evil heart
They were innocent victims of foreign nations that had attacked them
They are not innocent victims; 16:12 puts the blame on their own stubborn, evil hearts.
In the exile warning given through Jeremiah, what sort of land would the people be driven into?
The LORD said, “I will cast you out of this land into a land that neither you nor your fathers have known. There you will serve other gods day and night” (16:13).
Jeremiah 16:13
A rich land flowing with milk and honey, as in the days of Joshua
A land flowing with milk and honey was the promised land they were leaving; 16:13 sends them to an unknown land with no favor.
A land ruled by David’s descendants, where they would be safe and at peace
Nothing in 16:13 mentions David’s descendants ruling there; it is a land they and their fathers had never known.
A land reserved for priests and Levites, where they would offer sacrifices
A land set apart for priests and Levites is not what 16:13 describes; they serve other gods there.
A land neither they nor their fathers had known, where they would serve other gods day and night
A land beside the Jordan where they would rest and worship in peace
The LORD says He will show them no favor (16:13), so rest beside the Jordan is not the picture.
Jeremiah 16 looks beyond judgment. What deliverance would one day replace the exodus from Egypt as the great confession about the LORD?
The LORD said people would no longer swear by the God who brought Israel out of Egypt but by the One “who brought the Israelites up out of the land of the north and all the other lands” (16:14–15).
Jeremiah 16:14-15
The LORD bringing the Israelites up from the land of the north and from all the lands where they had been banished
The LORD sending fire from heaven on Mount Carmel to consume the sacrifice
Fire on Mount Carmel was a past deliverance in the days of Elijah (1 Kings 18:38), not the new confession of 16:15.
The LORD opening the Jordan so Joshua and Israel crossed on dry ground
Opening the Jordan for Joshua was a past wonder (Joshua 3:17), not the future return from the north that 16:15 describes.
The LORD rescuing David from the hand of Saul and from all his enemies
David’s rescue from Saul (2 Samuel 22:1) is not the great confession of 16:14–15, which looks to Israel’s return from exile.
The LORD feeding Elijah with the bread and meat the ravens brought him
Elijah being fed by ravens (1 Kings 17:6) was a private provision, not the national return promised in 16:15.
Using vivid judgment imagery, whom did the LORD say He would send to capture the people?
The LORD said, “I will send for many fishermen,” and after that “many hunters” (16:16), a picture of an inescapable search.
Jeremiah 16:16
Shepherds and watchmen
Shepherds and watchmen are not the figures used here; 16:16 names fishermen and hunters.
Fishermen and hunters
Prophets and priests
Prophets and priests are not the ones sent to capture them in 16:16, which names fishermen and hunters.
Sowers and reapers
Sowers and reapers are farming images, not in 16:16, where the LORD sends fishermen and hunters.
Kings and scribes
Kings and scribes are not sent in 16:16; the image is fishing, then hunting.
According to that prophecy in Jeremiah 16, where would these hunters search for the people?
The hunters would “hunt them down on every mountain and hill, even from the clefts of the rocks” (16:16), and the LORD’s eyes are on all their ways (16:17).
Jeremiah 16:16-17
Only in the cities of the plain and the valleys below them
The search is not limited to the cities of the plain; 16:16 says every mountain and hill and the clefts of the rocks.
Only in the temple courts and the streets of Jerusalem itself
The temple courts are not the only place; 16:16 names every mountain, hill and cleft of the rocks.
On every mountain and hill and out of the clefts of the rocks
Only in the lands beyond the Euphrates River in distant Babylon
The Euphrates is not named in 16:16; the hunting is on every mountain and hill.
In the ships of Tyre and Sidon sailing across the Great Sea
Tyre and Sidon’s ships do not appear in 16:16; the hunters search the mountains, hills and rock clefts.
Why did the LORD say He would repay the people of Judah double for their sin?
The LORD said He would repay them double “because they have defiled My land with the carcasses of their detestable idols, and they have filled My inheritance with their abominations” (16:18).
Jeremiah 16:18
Because they refused to rebuild the altar of the LORD after returning from exile
Refusing to rebuild the altar after exile is not the reason; 16:18 blames idols and abominations that defiled the land.
Because they taxed the poor too heavily and seized the fields of widows
Taxing the poor is not mentioned in 16:18; the cause is the defiling of the land with detestable idols.
Because they made alliances with Assyria and Egypt instead of trusting the LORD
Alliances with Assyria and Egypt are not the stated cause in 16:18, which names detestable idols and abominations.
Because they had defiled His land with the carcasses of their detestable idols and filled His inheritance with abominations
Because they had crowned a foreign king in Jerusalem against the LORD’s command
Crowning a foreign king is not mentioned in 16:18; the double repayment is for idolatry.
In Jeremiah’s prayer near the end of the chapter, which three titles did he give the LORD?
Jeremiah prays, “O LORD, my strength and my fortress, my refuge in the day of distress” (16:19), three titles for the LORD as his protection.
Jeremiah 16:19
My strength, my fortress, and my refuge in time of distress
My shepherd, my vineyard, and my song
The LORD is called a shepherd elsewhere, but 16:19 names strength, fortress and refuge.
My king, my chariot, and my banner
King, chariot and banner are not the titles in 16:19; Jeremiah calls Him strength, fortress and refuge.
My judge, my scribe, and my witness
Judge, scribe and witness are not given in 16:19; the titles speak of protection in distress.
My bread, my light, and my wisdom
Bread, light and wisdom are not in 16:19; the three titles are strength, fortress and refuge.
What confession would the nations from the ends of the earth make when they came to the LORD, according to Jeremiah 16?
The nations from the ends of the earth would say, “Our fathers inherited nothing but lies, worthless idols of no benefit at all” (16:19).
Jeremiah 16:19
They inherited mighty cities and lasting peace
The nations admit they inherited nothing of value; 16:19 says their fathers inherited nothing but lies.
They inherited secret wisdom from the stars
Secret wisdom from the stars is not in 16:19; they confess an inheritance of lies and worthless idols.
They inherited only lies, worthless idols of no benefit
They inherited the priesthood of Aaron
The priesthood of Aaron belonged to Israel, and 16:19 has the nations confess lies and worthless idols instead.
They inherited victory over Babylon
Victory over Babylon is not in the nations’ confession in 16:19, which admits their idols were worthless.
The chapter closes with a challenge to idolatry. Which statement matches Jeremiah 16?
Jeremiah 16:20 asks, “Can man make gods for himself? Such are not gods!”, pointing out that man-made idols are not real gods.
Jeremiah 16:20
Can stone images speak, and if so, who teaches them?
The idea of images that cannot teach appears in Habakkuk 2:18–19, not in the closing challenge of Jeremiah 16.
Can man make gods for himself? Such are not gods!
Can the dead praise the LORD from Sheol?
The dead praising the LORD from Sheol is raised in Psalm 6:5, not in Jeremiah 16.
Can a king save himself by a great army?
A king not being saved by a great army is a thought from Psalm 33:16, not Jeremiah 16:20.
Can the sun stand still over Gibeon?
The sun standing still happened at Gibeon in Joshua 10:12–13, not in Jeremiah 16.
In the final verse of Jeremiah 16, what did the LORD say He would make people know?

Jeremiah 16:21
The hidden name of the coming king who would rule Judah in righteousness

The exact date of Jerusalem’s rebuilding and the return of the exiles
No date for Jerusalem’s rebuilding is given in 16:21; the LORD promises to make them know His power and might.
The number of nations under heaven and the names of all their rulers
The number of nations is not mentioned in 16:21; they will know the LORD’s power and might.
The exact borders of restored Israel and the portions of each tribe
No borders of restored Israel are given in 16:21; the verse is about knowing the LORD’s power, might and name.
His power and His might, so they would know that His name is the LORD

Diamond point

Jeremiah 17:1
Steps of the altars
Steps of the altars are not mentioned in Jeremiah 17:1; the sin is engraved on the horns.
Horns of the altars

In Jeremiah 17, what do Judah’s children remember beside the green trees and on the high hills?

Jeremiah 17:2
Wells and vineyards
Wells and vineyards are not mentioned in Jeremiah 17:2; the children remember altars and Asherah poles.
Altars and Asherah poles
Priests and Levites
Priests and Levites are not mentioned in Jeremiah 17:2; the children remember altars and Asherah poles.
Scrolls and songs
Scrolls and songs are not mentioned in Jeremiah 17:2; the children remember altars and Asherah poles.
Tents and banners
Tents and banners are not mentioned in Jeremiah 17:2; the children remember altars and Asherah poles.
