Jeremiah 22:10-12
Josiah son of Amon
Josiah is the dead one, for whom the people are told not to weep (22:10); the one to weep over is the exile.
Shallum son of Josiah
Hezekiah son of Ahaz
Hezekiah is not mentioned in this passage; the exile named is Shallum.
Jehoiakim son of Josiah
Jehoiakim son of Josiah is addressed in 22:18–19 and would be buried outside Jerusalem’s gates, not exiled.
Gedaliah son of Ahikam
Gedaliah was governor after Jerusalem fell (2 Kings 25:22), not named in this chapter.
In the “woe” pronounced in Jeremiah 22, what abuse did the condemned ruler commit while building his house?
Jeremiah 22:13 pronounces woe on the ruler “who makes his countrymen serve without pay, and fails to pay their wages.”
Jeremiah 22:13
He taxed the priests twice each year to pay for it
Taxing priests is not mentioned; the abuse was unpaid labor.
He seized gold from the temple treasury
Seizing temple gold is not mentioned; he built his palace with unpaid work.
He made his countrymen serve without pay and gave them no wages
He forced the foreigners to leave the city
Expelling foreigners is not the charge; verse 3 actually forbids wronging the foreigner.
He burned the city records of the poor
Burning records is not mentioned; his sin was not paying his countrymen’s wages.
In Jeremiah 22, which description matches the self-indulgent palace the unjust king wanted to build?
Jeremiah 22:14 quotes the king’s plan, “a great palace, with spacious upper rooms,” and says he cuts windows, “panels it with cedar, and paints it with vermilion.”
Jeremiah 22:14
A house of hewn stone with blue banners and bronze gates
Hewn stone and blue banners are not mentioned; the palace was paneled with cedar and painted with vermilion.
A great palace with spacious upper rooms, windows, cedar paneling, and bright red paint
A fortress with iron doors, thick walls, and a tall watchtower
A fortress with iron doors is not described; the king wanted a palace with spacious upper rooms.
A tent of goat hair held up with bronze pins and cords
A goat-hair tent is the opposite of the grand palace described.
A shrine of carved olive wood overlaid with pure gold
A shrine of olive wood is not mentioned; the palace was paneled with cedar.
In Jeremiah 22, Jeremiah contrasted King Jehoiakim with his father Josiah. What action of Josiah showed what it meant to know the LORD?
Jeremiah 22:16 says, “He took up the cause of the poor and needy,” and asks, “Is this not what it means to know Me?”
Jeremiah 22:15-16
He expanded the army
Expanding the army is not mentioned; Josiah’s record was justice for the poor.
He built cedar palaces
Verse 15 asks whether excelling in cedar makes a king; building cedar palaces is not what it means to know the LORD.
He took up the cause of the poor and needy
He stored up silver and gold
Storing up silver and gold is not what knowing the LORD means; it is taking up the cause of the poor.
He made treaties with Tyre
Treaties with Tyre are not mentioned in this passage.
In Jeremiah’s oracle in Jeremiah 22, which king was specifically told that people would not mourn for him with cries like “Alas, my brother!” or “Alas, his splendor!”?
Jeremiah 22:18 says, “concerning Jehoiakim son of Josiah king of Judah: ‘They will not mourn for him,’” and that no one will cry for him.
Jeremiah 22:18
Ahaz
Ahaz is not named in Jeremiah 22; the oracle concerns the sons of Josiah.
Jehoiakim son of Josiah
Uzziah
Uzziah is not named in this oracle; the king addressed is Jehoiakim.
Manasseh
Manasseh is not named in Jeremiah 22; the oracle concerns Jehoiakim.
Jehoahaz son of Jehu
Jehoahaz son of Jehu was a northern king (2 Kings 13:1), not the king in this oracle.
According to Jeremiah 22, how would Jehoiakim be buried?
Jeremiah 22:19 says, “He will be buried like a donkey, dragged away and thrown outside the gates of Jerusalem.”
Jeremiah 22:19
In the royal tombs of David’s city with fragrant spices
Royal tombs and spices are the opposite of the shameful burial foretold.
In a ship at sea with full royal honors paid
Burial at sea is not mentioned; he is dragged away and thrown outside the gates of Jerusalem.
Like a donkey, dragged away and thrown outside the gates of Jerusalem
In Bethel beside the altar of the old shrine
Bethel is not mentioned; his body would be thrown outside Jerusalem’s gates.
In Egypt among the princes who welcomed him
Egypt is not mentioned in this prophecy; the burial is outside Jerusalem.
In the lament of Jeremiah 22, from which three places was Jerusalem told to cry out because all her lovers were crushed?
Jeremiah 22:20 says, “Go up to Lebanon and cry out; raise your voice in Bashan; cry out from Abarim.”
Jeremiah 22:20
Zion, Moriah, and Tekoa
Zion, Moriah, and Tekoa are not the places named; the cry goes out from Lebanon, Bashan, and Abarim.
Dan, Bethel, and Gilgal
Dan, Bethel, and Gilgal are not named in this lament.
Lebanon, Bashan, and Abarim
Carmel, Tabor, and Hermon
Carmel, Tabor, and Hermon are not named; the places are Lebanon, Bashan, and Abarim.
Jericho, Ai, and Gibeon
Jericho, Ai, and Gibeon are not named in this verse.
In Jeremiah 22, how did Judah answer the LORD when He warned her while she was secure?
Jeremiah 22:21 records Judah’s answer when warned while secure: “I will not listen.”
Jeremiah 22:21
“We will repent at once.”
Repenting at once is the opposite of what Judah said; the LORD says she answered, “I will not listen.”
“We will ask the priests.”
Asking the priests is not mentioned; Judah’s answer was a refusal to listen.
“We will listen after the feast.”
Listening after the feast is not what Judah said; she flatly refused.
“I will not listen.”
“Send us a sign.”
Asking for a sign is not mentioned; the LORD records a refusal to listen.
In the word spoken against Coniah son of Jehoiakim in Jeremiah 22, what object did the LORD say He would pull off His right hand even if Coniah were like it?
Jeremiah 22:24 says, “even if you, Coniah son of Jehoiakim king of Judah, were a signet ring on My right hand, I would pull you off.”
Jeremiah 22:24
A sword
A sword is not named in the image; the LORD speaks of a signet ring.
A bracelet
A bracelet is not mentioned; the object is a signet ring on His right hand.
A signet ring
A lampstand
A lampstand is not mentioned in this verse.
A crown
A crown is not named; the picture is a signet ring on His right hand.
In the final decree over Coniah in Jeremiah 22, what was to be recorded about him and his line?
Jeremiah 22:30 says, “Enroll this man as childless,” and “None of his descendants will prosper to sit on the throne of David or to rule again in Judah.”
Jeremiah 22:30
He would rebuild the temple through his sons and grandsons, and the kingdom would prosper
No rebuilding through his sons is promised; he is to be enrolled as childless and none of his line will prosper.
He would become a priest in exile and found a new line of priests
Priesthood in exile is not mentioned; the decree ends his line’s royal success.
He was to be recorded as childless, and none of his descendants would prosper sitting on David’s throne in Judah
His descendants would rule both Judah and Israel for many generations
His descendants would not rule; none would sit on the throne of David or rule again in Judah.
His mother alone would return from Babylon and reign over Judah
His mother would not return; 22:26–27 says they would both die in another land and never return.
In Jeremiah 23, whom does the LORD rebuke for destroying and scattering the sheep of His pasture?
“Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of My pasture!” declares the LORD (23:1); these are the leaders who tend His people (23:2).
Jeremiah 23:1-2
The shepherds over His people
The sailors of Tarshish
The ships of Tarshish belong to the oracle on Tyre in Isaiah 23:1, not to Jeremiah’s woe on Israel’s shepherds.
The archers of Elam
The bow of Elam is broken in a separate oracle (Jeremiah 49:35), not in this rebuke of Israel’s leaders.
The elders of Midian
The elders of Midian appear in Numbers 22:4, not in this woe on the shepherds of God’s people.
The craftsmen of Sidon
Sidon is mentioned elsewhere in Jeremiah, but this woe targets Israel’s own shepherds who scattered the flock.
In the restoration promise of Jeremiah 23, what does the LORD say He Himself will do for the remnant of His flock?
“I Myself will gather the remnant of My flock from all the lands to which I have banished them, and I will return them to their pasture” (23:3).
Jeremiah 23:3
Leave them in exile as a witness
God promises the opposite: He will gather them back, not leave them in exile (23:3).
Gather them from all countries and bring them back to their pasture
Send them to Egypt for safety
Egypt is where the remnant fled against Jeremiah’s word (Jeremiah 43:7), not the safety God promises here.
Divide them among the tribes of Edom
Edom is judged in Jeremiah 49; the flock is returned to its own pasture, not divided among Edom’s tribes.
Hide them in the wilderness for forty years
Forty years in the wilderness belongs to the exodus generation (Numbers 14:33); here God returns the flock to be fruitful (23:3).
According to Jeremiah 23, what additional care will the LORD provide after bringing His flock back?
“I will raise up shepherds over them who will tend them, and they will no longer be afraid or dismayed, nor will any go missing” (23:4).
Jeremiah 23:4
He will build a stone temple for every tribe
No stone temples for the tribes are promised; the care is shepherds who tend the flock (23:4).
He will appoint judges at every gate
Judges at the gates is a different arrangement (Deuteronomy 16:18), not the promise of this verse.
He will raise up shepherds over them who will tend them
He will make them nomads again
The flock is returned to pasture to be fruitful (23:3), not made into nomads again.
He will place them under foreign kings
Foreign kings ruled them in exile; the promise is shepherds who tend them so none go missing (23:4).
In Jeremiah 23’s royal promise, from whose line will the “righteous Branch” come?
“I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and He will reign wisely as King” (23:5).
Jeremiah 23:5
Levi
Levi was the priestly tribe; the promise here is for a king from David’s line.
Saul
Aaron’s line supplied the high priests, but this Branch is raised up for David.
Aaron
Saul’s dynasty was rejected (1 Samuel 13:14), so the royal promise does not run through him.
David
Ephraim
Ephraim was the leading northern tribe, but the promise is made to David.
What name will the coming king in Jeremiah 23 be called?
“this is His name by which He will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness” (23:6).
Jeremiah 23:6
The LORD Is Peace
“The LORD Is Peace” is the name Gideon gave his altar (Judges 6:24), not the coming king’s title.
The LORD Our Righteousness
The LORD My Shepherd
“The LORD is my shepherd” is David’s opening line in Psalm 23:1, not the name given the Branch.
The LORD of Sinai
No title “The LORD of Sinai” appears; Sinai is where the law was given, not a name for the king.
The LORD of Carmel
No title “The LORD of Carmel” appears; Carmel is where Elijah faced Baal’s prophets, not a name for the king.
According to Jeremiah 23:7–8, a day is coming when people will no longer swear by the LORD who brought Israel out of Egypt. What deliverance will they mention instead?

People will say, “As surely as the LORD lives, who brought and led the descendants of the house of Israel up out of the land of the north and all the other lands to which He had banished them” (23:8).
Jeremiah 23:7-8
Israel crossing the Jordan River into the land under Joshua’s leadership
Crossing the Jordan under Joshua is past history, not the new deliverance from the north and all banishment (23:8).
Judah returning home from captivity among the Philistines on the coast
Philistia is not named; the people come back from the land of the north and all the other lands (23:8).
The descendants of the house of Israel brought up from the land of the north and all the countries of banishment
The walls of Jericho falling before the army of Israel after its march
Jericho fell at the start of the conquest (Joshua 6:20), long before this promised return.
David escaping from King Saul and hiding in the caves of the wilderness
David’s escape from Saul (1 Samuel 19:10) is not the deliverance named in 23:8.
In Jeremiah’s words about the prophets in chapter 23, what did the holy words of the LORD make him feel like?
“I have become like a drunkard, like a man overcome by wine, because of the LORD, because of His holy words” (23:9).
Jeremiah 23:9
A watchman on the wall
A watchman is Ezekiel’s role (Ezekiel 3:17); Jeremiah says his heart is broken and his bones tremble (23:9).
A warrior ready for battle
Jeremiah describes himself as broken and trembling, not as a warrior ready for battle (23:9).
A drunken man overcome by wine
An eagle rising on the wind
Rising like an eagle is the image of renewed strength in Isaiah 40:31, not Jeremiah’s reaction to God’s words.
A shepherd calling sheep
Jeremiah condemns shepherds (23:1); he does not compare himself to one calling sheep.
In Jeremiah 23, which two groups are specifically called ungodly, with wickedness found even in the LORD’s house?
“For both prophet and priest are ungodly; even in My house I have found their wickedness” (23:11).
Jeremiah 23:11
Kings and merchants
Kings are rebuked in Jeremiah 22, but 23:11 names the prophet and the priest.
Prophet and priest
Judge and scribe
Judges and scribes are not named in this verse; it indicts the prophet and priest.
Father and son
Fathers and sons are not named; the charge falls on religious leaders found wicked in God’s house.
Prince and soldier
Princes and soldiers are not named; the wickedness found even in the LORD’s house is that of prophet and priest.
When Jeremiah 23 compares northern and southern prophetic corruption, what had the prophets of Samaria done?
“Among the prophets of Samaria I saw an offensive thing: They prophesied by Baal and led My people Israel astray” (23:13).
Jeremiah 23:13
Prophesied by Baal and led Israel astray
Rebuilt Jericho for profit
Rebuilding Jericho for profit is Hiel’s story (1 Kings 16:34), not the charge against Samaria’s prophets.
Worshiped the queen of heaven in Egypt
Worshiping the queen of heaven in Egypt is described in Jeremiah 44:17, not here.
Sold the temple vessels to Tyre
Nothing in this chapter mentions selling temple vessels; Samaria’s prophets are charged with prophesying by Baal.
Made a golden calf in Jerusalem
Golden calves were set up at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28–29), not in Jerusalem, and not in this charge.
In Jeremiah 23, to which two cities are the prophets and people of Jerusalem compared because of adultery and lies?
“They are all like Sodom to Me; the people of Jerusalem are like Gomorrah” (23:14).
Jeremiah 23:14
Tyre and Sidon
Tyre and Sidon are the Phoenician trading cities of Isaiah 23, not the cities Jeremiah names for Jerusalem’s sin.
Nineveh and Babylon
Nineveh and Babylon were foreign capitals; Jeremiah compares Jerusalem to Sodom and Gomorrah.
Sodom and Gomorrah
Bethel and Dan
Bethel and Dan housed Jeroboam’s golden calves (1 Kings 12:29), but they are not the comparison in 23:14.
Ashdod and Gaza
Ashdod and Gaza are Philistine cities and are not named in this verse.
What bitter judgment does the LORD announce for the prophets of Jerusalem in Jeremiah 23?
“I will feed them wormwood and give them poisoned water to drink” (23:15).
Jeremiah 23:15
Ashes and dust
Ashes and dust are not named; the judgment is bitter food and poisoned water (23:15).
Thorns and briars
Thorns and briars are not part of this judgment; the LORD announces wormwood and poisoned water (23:15).
Wormwood and poisoned water
Chains and iron
Chains and iron are not named; the bitter judgment is wormwood and poisoned water.
Hail and brimstone
Brimstone fell on Sodom (Genesis 19:24), but Jeremiah’s judgment on the prophets is wormwood and poisoned water.
In Jeremiah 23, what reassuring message did false prophets keep giving to those who despised the LORD and walked in stubbornness?
They told those who despised the LORD, “The LORD says that you will have peace,” and everyone stubborn, “No harm will come to you” (23:17).
Jeremiah 23:16-17
“The temple will never fall”
“The temple will never fall” is the false trust Jeremiah attacks in Jeremiah 7:4, not the promise quoted here.
“you will have peace” and “No harm will come to you”
“Babylon will be your eternal refuge”
Babylon is never called an eternal refuge; the false message is peace and no harm (23:17).
“Your sacrifices have removed all guilt”
Sacrifices removing all guilt is not the claim here; the prophets promised peace and safety (23:17).
“The ark will return this year”
The ark’s return is not mentioned here; Jeremiah 3:16 says the ark will no longer be remembered.
Which image does Jeremiah 23 use for the LORD’s judgment rushing upon the wicked?
“The storm of the LORD has gone out with fury, a whirlwind swirling down upon the heads of the wicked” (23:19).
Jeremiah 23:19-20
A flood rising up from the Nile over the land
A rising Nile flood is the image for Egypt’s advance in Jeremiah 46:7–8, not for this storm.
A lion bounding up out of the thicket on its prey
A lion coming up from the thicket is used in Jeremiah 4:7, not in this passage about a whirlwind.
A whirlwind swirling down on the heads of the wicked
A plague of locusts stripping the fields of the land
A plague of locusts is Joel’s image (Joel 1:4), not the one used here.
Fire falling from heaven on the top of Mount Carmel
Fire from Carmel recalls Elijah (1 Kings 18:38), not the whirlwind of Jeremiah 23:19.
According to Jeremiah 23, what would true prophets have done if they had stood in the council of the LORD?
“If they had stood in My council, they would have proclaimed My words to My people and turned them back from their evil ways and deeds” (23:22).
Jeremiah 23:21-22
Crowned a new king in Jerusalem to rule over the people
No coronation is mentioned; true prophets would have proclaimed God’s words and turned the people back (23:22).
Proclaimed His words and turned the people from their evil ways and deeds
Hidden the scroll of the covenant in the temple court
Hiding a scroll is not mentioned; the prophets would have proclaimed God’s words (23:22).
Called down fire from heaven on the armies of Babylon
Calling down fire on Babylon is not what the verse says; they would have turned the people from evil ways (23:22).
Rebuilt the altar at Shiloh where the tabernacle once stood
Shiloh was where the Tent of Meeting once stood (Joshua 18:1); rebuilding its altar is not the point of 23:22.
In Jeremiah 23, how does the LORD describe His presence?
He asks, “Am I only a God nearby” and “Do I not fill the heavens and the earth?” (23:23–24).
Jeremiah 23:23-24
He is present only in Jerusalem, in the temple He chose
He is not confined to Jerusalem; no one can hide in secret places where He cannot see (23:24).
He is present only in the wilderness, away from the cities
He is not confined to the wilderness; He fills the heavens and the earth (23:24).
He is a God nearby and also far away, filling heaven and earth
He dwells only above the cherubim in the inner sanctuary
His throne is above the cherubim (Exodus 25:22), but He also fills heaven and earth (23:24).
He departs from the people and their land whenever they sin
The LORD sees every hidden place and speaks against the lying prophets; He does not depart whenever the people sin (23:24).
In the section against lying prophets in Jeremiah 23, what repeated claim does the LORD say He has heard from them?
The LORD says, “I have heard the sayings of the prophets who prophesy lies in My name: ‘I had a dream! I had a dream!’” (23:25).
Jeremiah 23:25-27
“I have seen a sign!”
The false prophets claimed dreams, not signs (23:25).
“I had a dream! I had a dream!”
“I have found the lost ark!”
Finding the lost ark is not claimed here; Jeremiah 3:16 says the ark will no longer even be remembered.
“I have spoken with Elijah!”
Speaking with Elijah is not claimed; their repeated claim was “I had a dream!” (23:25).
“I have measured the temple!”
Measuring the temple is Ezekiel’s vision (Ezekiel 40), not the false prophets’ claim in Jeremiah 23.
Jeremiah 23 contrasts dreams with the true word of God. What should the one who has God’s word do?
“Let him who has My word speak it truthfully. For what is straw compared to grain?” (23:28).
Jeremiah 23:28
Seal it up until the exile ends
Sealing up words until the end is Daniel’s charge (Daniel 12:4), not the instruction here.
Sing it only in the temple
The word is to be spoken truthfully to the people (23:22, 23:28), not sung only in the temple.
Speak God’s word faithfully
Trade it for silver
Selling God’s word is never commended; the one who has it must speak it truthfully (23:28).
Hide it from the nations
Hiding God’s word is the opposite of the command to speak it truthfully (23:28).
In Jeremiah 23, what two objects are used to describe the power of God’s word?
“Is not My word like fire,” declares the LORD, “and like a hammer that smashes a rock?” (23:29).
Jeremiah 23:29
Oil and wine poured out as offerings
Oil and wine are not the images used for God’s word in this verse; Jeremiah uses fire and a hammer.
A sword and a shield for battle
Ephesians 6:17 calls God’s word the sword of the Spirit, but Jeremiah 23:29 uses fire and a hammer.
Fire and a hammer that shatters rock
A lamp and a trumpet sounding alarm
Psalm 119:105 calls God’s word a lamp, but Jeremiah pairs fire with a hammer, not a lamp and trumpet.
Dew and cedar, refreshing and strong
Dew and cedar are not used here; the word is like fire and a hammer that smashes a rock (23:29).
In Jeremiah 23, what practice made the LORD say He was against certain prophets?
“I am against the prophets who steal from one another words they attribute to Me” (23:30).
Jeremiah 23:30
They fasted too long at Mizpah
Fasting at Mizpah is Samuel’s story (1 Samuel 7:6), not the charge against these prophets.
They stole from one another words supposedly from Him
They refused to wear sackcloth
Refusing sackcloth is not charged; the LORD is against prophets who steal words from one another (23:30).
They hid the Book of the Law
The Book of the Law was found in the temple in Josiah’s time (2 Kings 22:8); hiding it is not the charge here.
They moved the boundary stones of Benjamin
Moving boundary stones is forbidden in Deuteronomy 19:14, not the offense named in 23:30.
When people in Jeremiah 23 asked, “What is the burden of the LORD?” what answer was Jeremiah told to give?
He was to say, “What burden? I will forsake you, declares the LORD” (23:33).
Jeremiah 23:33
“The burden is Babylon for seventy years”
Seventy years of Babylon is the word of Jeremiah 25:11, not the answer in 23:33.
“The burden is famine in the land”
Famine is threatened elsewhere (Jeremiah 14:12), but it is not the answer given here.
“What burden? I will forsake you”
“The burden is the rebuilding of Zion”
Zion’s rebuilding is promised elsewhere (Jeremiah 30:18), not in this answer about the burden.
“The burden is the fall of Nineveh”
The fall of Nineveh is Nahum’s theme (Nahum 3:7), not Jeremiah’s answer in 23:33.
In Jeremiah 24, what fruit did the prophet Jeremiah see in two baskets in his vision in Jerusalem?
Jeremiah 24:1 says, “the LORD showed me two baskets of figs placed in front of the temple of the LORD.”
Jeremiah 24:1-3
Grapes
Grapes are not in the vision; Jeremiah saw two baskets of figs (24:1).
Figs
Olives
Olives are not in the vision; Jeremiah saw two baskets of figs (24:1).
Pomegranates
Pomegranates are not in the vision; Jeremiah saw two baskets of figs (24:1).
Dates
Dates are not in the vision; Jeremiah saw two baskets of figs (24:1).
According to the vision in Jeremiah 24, where were the two baskets of figs placed?
Jeremiah 24:1 says the LORD showed him “two baskets of figs placed in front of the temple of the LORD.”
Jeremiah 24:1
At the city gate of Jerusalem
The city gate is not named in 24:1; the baskets were in front of the temple of the LORD.
In the palace of the king of Judah
The king’s palace is not named in 24:1; the baskets were in front of the temple of the LORD.
In front of the temple of the LORD
By the Jordan River
The Jordan River is not named in 24:1; the baskets were in front of the temple of the LORD.
On the Mount of Olives
The Mount of Olives is not named in 24:1; the baskets were in front of the temple of the LORD.
In Jeremiah’s description in chapter 24, what were the good figs like?
Jeremiah 24:2 says, “One basket had very good figs, like those that ripen early.”
Jeremiah 24:2
Like figs that ripen early
Like dried figs for winter
Dried winter figs are not the comparison in 24:2; the good figs are like those that ripen early.
Like grapes from a vineyard
Grapes are not the comparison in 24:2; the good figs are like figs that ripen early.
Like olives ready for pressing
Olives are not the comparison in 24:2; the good figs are like figs that ripen early.
Like almonds in blossom
Almond blossom is not the comparison in 24:2; the good figs are like figs that ripen early.
In the setting of Jeremiah 24, which king had deported Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim from Judah before Jeremiah saw the vision?
Jeremiah 24:1 says Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon “had carried away Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim king of Judah” and brought him to Babylon.
Jeremiah 24:1
Sennacherib king of Assyria
Sennacherib of Assyria attacked Judah’s fortified cities in Hezekiah’s day (2 Kings 18:13), long before Jeconiah’s exile.
Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt
Pharaoh Neco imprisoned Jehoahaz at Riblah (2 Kings 23:33); Jeconiah was carried away to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar.
Cyrus king of Persia
Cyrus of Persia later allowed the exiles to return (Ezra 1:1); he did not deport Jeconiah.
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon
Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria
Tiglath-pileser of Assyria captured northern towns in Pekah’s day (2 Kings 15:29), not Jeconiah of Judah.
In Jeremiah 24, which people from Jerusalem are specifically named as being taken into exile along with Jeconiah king of Judah?
Jeremiah 24:1 says Nebuchadnezzar carried away Jeconiah “as well as the officials of Judah and the craftsmen and metalsmiths from Jerusalem.”
Jeremiah 24:1
The officials of Judah, the craftsmen, and the metalsmiths
The singers of the temple and the gatekeepers
Temple singers and gatekeepers are not named in 24:1; the exiles were officials, craftsmen and metalsmiths.
The shepherds of Bethlehem and the elders of Hebron
Shepherds of Bethlehem and elders of Hebron are not named in 24:1; the exiles were officials, craftsmen and metalsmiths from Jerusalem.
The priests of Shiloh and the judges of Beersheba
Priests of Shiloh and judges of Beersheba are not named in 24:1; the exiles were officials, craftsmen and metalsmiths from Jerusalem.
The merchants of Joppa and the sailors of Tyre
Merchants of Joppa and sailors of Tyre are not named in 24:1; the exiles were officials, craftsmen and metalsmiths from Jerusalem.
When the LORD explained the good figs in Jeremiah 24, whom did they represent?
Jeremiah 24:5 says, “Like these good figs, so I regard as good the exiles from Judah, whom I have sent away from this place to the land of the Chaldeans.”
Jeremiah 24:5
The remnant that stayed in Jerusalem under Zedekiah
Zedekiah and the remnant in Jerusalem are compared to the bad figs (24:8), not the good ones.
The people of Moab who feared Babylon
Moab is not mentioned in Jeremiah 24; the good figs are the exiles from Judah (24:5).
The prophets serving in the temple courts
Prophets in the temple courts are not mentioned in Jeremiah 24; the good figs are the exiles from Judah (24:5).
The Egyptians living near the border of Judah
The Egyptians are not the figs; Judeans living in Egypt are counted among the bad figs (24:8).
The exiles from Judah whom God had sent to the land of the Chaldeans
In Jeremiah 24, what did God promise to do for the exiles symbolized by the good figs?
Jeremiah 24:6 says, “I will build them up and not tear them down; I will plant them and not uproot them.”
Jeremiah 24:6
Make them a taunt and a curse among the nations
Being a disgrace and an object of scorn and cursing is the fate of the bad figs (24:9), not the good ones.
Build them up and not tear them down, and plant them and not uproot them
Leave them in Babylon forever with no return
God promises to return the good figs to this land (24:6), not leave them in Babylon forever.
Scatter them to Egypt and Cush

A crown of thorns was placed on Jesus’ head (Matthew 27:29), not Jonah’s; Jonah describes seaweed.
In Jonah 2, to what place did Jonah say he descended before the LORD raised his life from the pit?
Jonah 2:6 says, “To the roots of the mountains I descended,” and then he adds, “But You raised my life from the pit, O LORD my God!”
Jonah 2:6
The plains of Moab
The plains of Moab were where Israel camped before entering Canaan; Jonah mentions neither them nor any land journey.
The roots of the mountains
The courts of the temple
Jonah only looked toward the temple (2:4, 2:7); he did not descend to its courts.
The camp of Assyria
Assyria is where Nineveh was, the city Jonah tried to avoid; his descent in 2:6 was to the roots of the mountains.
The cedars of Lebanon
The cedars of Lebanon are not mentioned in Jonah 2; he describes sinking to the mountains’ roots.
In Jonah chapter 2, when Jonah said his life was fading away, what did he do?
Jonah 2:7 says, “As my life was fading away, I remembered the LORD. My prayer went up to You, to Your holy temple.”
Jonah 2:7
He built a raft from the floating wreckage of the ship
Jonah makes no raft; the ship’s crew had already thrown him into the sea (Jonah 1:15), and he cries out for rescue instead.
He cursed the sailors who had thrown him overboard
Jonah never cursed the sailors; they feared the LORD and offered sacrifices after the storm calmed (Jonah 1:16).
He remembered the LORD, and his prayer went up to God’s holy temple
He fell asleep again as he had done in the ship
Jonah had fallen asleep in the ship during the storm (Jonah 1:5), but in the fish he remembered the LORD and prayed.
He called out to the king of Nineveh for rescue
The king of Nineveh appears only in Jonah 3:6, and Jonah makes no appeal to him from the fish.
In Jonah 2, what did Jonah say those who cling to worthless idols forsake?
Jonah 2:8 says, “Those who cling to worthless idols forsake His loving devotion.”
Jonah 2:8
Their earthly inheritance
The verse says nothing about an earthly inheritance; the loss in view is God’s loving devotion.
Wisdom and instruction
Proverbs 1:7 says fools despise wisdom and discipline, but Jonah 2:8 names loving devotion as what idol worshipers forsake.
Peace with their neighbors
Peace with neighbors is not mentioned; Jonah says idol worshipers forsake God’s loving devotion.
His loving devotion
The fear of the LORD
Proverbs 1:7 calls the fear of the LORD the beginning of knowledge, but Jonah 2:8 speaks of forsaking His loving devotion.
In Jonah’s vow of thanksgiving in chapter 2, which statement did he make?
Jonah 2:9 says, “But I, with the voice of thanksgiving, will sacrifice to You. I will fulfill what I have vowed. Salvation is from the LORD!”
Jonah 2:9
“I will return to Tarshish with a song of praise, for the storm has finally ceased.”
Jonah went to Tarshish in flight (Jonah 1:3); his prayer in 2:9 promises sacrifice and thanksgiving, not a return there.
“I, with the voice of thanksgiving, will sacrifice to You. I will fulfill what I have vowed. Salvation is from the LORD!”
“I will rebuild the temple in Jerusalem, for the land will surely prosper again.”
Rebuilding the temple belongs to the later work of Haggai (Haggai 1:8); Jonah promises thanksgiving and sacrifice.
“I will fast for forty days in repentance, and then Nineveh will surely fall.”
Nineveh fasted in repentance (Jonah 3:5), but Jonah’s vow in 2:9 is about thanksgiving and sacrifice, not Nineveh’s fall.
“I will offer incense on the high places, for the LORD’s mercy has found me.”
Jonah promises to sacrifice with thanksgiving to the LORD, not to burn incense on the high places.
In Jonah 3, when the word of the LORD came to Jonah a second time, which city was he told to go to and preach?
The LORD told Jonah to go to “the great city of Nineveh” and proclaim the message He would give him (3:2).
Jonah 3:1-2
Jerusalem
Jerusalem was Judah’s capital; the LORD sent Jonah to the pagan city of Nineveh, not to his own people (3:2).
Nineveh
Tarshish
Tarshish was the far-off place Jonah sailed toward when he tried to flee the LORD (Jonah 1:3), not where he was sent.
Joppa
Joppa was the port where Jonah boarded a ship to run away (Jonah 1:3); the second command sent him to Nineveh.
Babylon
Babylon is never named in Jonah; the second command (3:2) sent him to Assyria’s great city, Nineveh.
In the account of Jonah preaching in Nineveh, what warning did Jonah announce on the first day he entered the city?
Jonah proclaimed, “Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned!” on the first day of his journey into the city (3:4).
Jonah 3:4
“Seven more days and Nineveh will be flooded!”
Seven days is the warning before the flood in Noah’s day (Genesis 7:4); Jonah announced forty days and an overturning (3:4).
“Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned!”
“Three more days and Nineveh will fall by the sword!”
Three days is the length of the journey across Nineveh (3:3), not Jonah’s warning, and he did not speak of the sword.
“Forty more days and Assyria will be divided!”
The forty days is right, but Jonah said Nineveh would be overturned, not that Assyria would be divided (3:4).
“One more day and Nineveh will burn!”
Jonah gave forty days, not one, and said Nineveh would be overturned, not burned (3:4).
In Jonah chapter 3, how did the people of Nineveh respond when they heard Jonah’s message from God?
The Ninevites “believed God,” proclaimed a fast, and dressed in sackcloth, “from the greatest of them to the least” (3:5).
Jonah 3:5
They arrested Jonah and questioned him
No one arrested Jonah; the whole city, from the greatest to the least, believed God (3:5).
They ignored him and continued feasting
Instead of feasting, they proclaimed a fast (3:5), and even the animals were kept from food and water (3:7).
They believed God, proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth
They fled from Nineveh to the mountains
Nobody fled; they stayed in the city and repented, and the king himself sat in ashes there (3:6).
They went to Jerusalem to offer sacrifices
Nineveh’s repentance happened at home; the chapter never mentions Jerusalem or sacrifices (3:5–9).
In Jonah 3, how is the size of the city of Nineveh described?
Nineveh was “an exceedingly great city, requiring a three-day journey” (3:3).
Jonah 3:3
A small walled village by the sea
Nineveh was exceedingly great, not a small village; it took three days to journey through it (3:3).
A royal city with twelve gates
Twelve gates describe the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:12); Jonah 3:3 measures Nineveh by a three-day journey instead.
An exceedingly great city requiring a three-day journey
A mountain fortress in the wilderness
Nineveh was a vast city, not a mountain fortress; Jonah “set out into the city” and preached there (3:4).
A city built beside the Jordan River
No river is named in Jonah’s description; the Jordan is in Israel, while Nineveh was a great city far away in Assyria (3:3).
When the message about Jonah’s preaching reached the king of Nineveh in Jonah 3, what did the king do?
On hearing the news, the king “got up from his throne, took off his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes” (3:6).
Jonah 3:6
He put on his armor, gathered his soldiers, and prepared to defend the city
The king did not prepare for war; he humbled himself in sackcloth and ashes (3:6).
He rose from his throne, removed his robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes
He sent Jonah away on a ship, ordering him to leave the city at once
He did not expel the prophet; his response was repentance, and the only ship in Jonah is the one bound for Tarshish (Jonah 1:3).
He ordered a great feast for his nobles to celebrate Jonah’s message
A feast is the opposite of his decree, which forbade everyone to eat or drink (3:7).
He went to the temple of Dagon to ask the idol for protection from judgment
Dagon was a Philistine god (1 Samuel 5:2); Nineveh’s king instead hoped that the true God might relent (3:9).
In the decree proclaimed in Nineveh in Jonah 3, who was forbidden to taste anything or drink during the fast?
The decree said, “Let no man or beast, herd or flock, taste anything at all,” so animals fasted along with people (3:7).
Jonah 3:7
Only the priests and the nobles of Nineveh
The decree came from the king and his nobles and covered everyone, not just priests and nobles: “man or beast” (3:7).
Only the adult men who were able to fight
It was not limited to adult men; “no man or beast, herd or flock” was to taste anything (3:7).
Only the poor people living in the city
The poor were not singled out; the whole city and even its animals were to fast (3:7).
Only the soldiers guarding the city walls
Soldiers were not singled out; the ban covered every person and animal in Nineveh (3:7).
Both people and animals, including herd and flock
According to the proclamation in Jonah chapter 3, besides fasting and sackcloth, what was everyone in Nineveh told to do?
The king’s decree told everyone to “call out earnestly to God” and to “turn from his evil ways and from the violence in his hands” (3:8).
Jonah 3:8
Build an altar of stone
The decree called for no altar; it called for earnest prayer and a change of conduct (3:8).
Call out earnestly to God and turn from evil ways and violence
March around the city walls seven times
Marching around walls seven times is Jericho’s story (Joshua 6:15), not Nineveh’s decree.
Bring Jonah into the palace
The decree did not involve Jonah at all; it called for prayer and turning from evil and violence (3:8).
Wash in the Jordan River
Washing in the Jordan recalls Naaman’s healing (2 Kings 5:14), not the Ninevites’ repentance.
In the wording of the proclamation in Jonah 3, who was named alongside the king as sharing authority for the decree in Nineveh?
The proclamation began “By the decree of the king and his nobles” (3:7).
Jonah 3:7
The priests
The priests are not mentioned in Jonah 3; the decree came from the king and his nobles (3:7).
The judges of Israel
Israel’s judges had no role in a decree issued in Nineveh (3:7).
The king’s nobles
The sailors from the ship
The sailors appear only in Jonah 1 (Jonah 1:5) and had no part in Nineveh’s decree.
The elders of Bethlehem
Bethlehem is in Judah; the decree was issued by Nineveh’s own king and nobles (3:7).
In Jonah 3, what hope did the king of Nineveh express after calling the city to repent?
The king said, “Who knows? God may turn and relent; He may turn from His fierce anger, so that we will not perish” (3:9).
Jonah 3:9
God would bless Nineveh with great wealth and make its armies victorious
The king’s hope was to avoid perishing, not to gain wealth or victory (3:9).
God would destroy Tarshish instead of Nineveh and spare the Assyrian city
Tarshish was the place Jonah fled toward (Jonah 1:3); the king hoped God would spare Nineveh, not destroy another place.
God might turn and relent, turning from His fierce anger so they would not perish
God would immediately make them His chosen nation and send a prophet to rule
No one claimed chosen-nation status; the king hoped only that God might relent from His anger (3:9).
God would send manna from heaven to feed the people during their long fast
Manna fed Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16:35); Nineveh sought mercy, not food, and was fasting (3:7).
At the end of Jonah 3, what does the text specifically say God saw that led Him to relent from the disaster He had threatened against Nineveh?
“When God saw their actions—that they had turned from their evil ways—He relented from the disaster He had threatened” (3:10).
Jonah 3:10
Their costly offerings
Offerings are not mentioned in Nineveh’s repentance; God responded to their turning from evil (3:10).
Their tears before the throne
The text mentions no tears; what God saw was their actions of repentance (3:10).
Their actions, that they had turned from their evil ways
Their military surrender
Nineveh made no military surrender; its change was moral, a turning from evil ways (3:10).
Their promise to honor Jonah as a prophet
No promise to honor Jonah is recorded; God saw that they had turned from their evil ways (3:10).
In Jonah 4, after God spared the people of Nineveh from disaster, how did the prophet Jonah react?
Jonah “was greatly displeased, and he became angry” (4:1).
Jonah 4:1
With anger
With rejoicing
He did not rejoice; he was greatly displeased.
With fear
He was not afraid; he became angry.
With indifference
He was not indifferent; he was greatly displeased and angry.
With gratitude
He was not grateful; he resented God’s mercy to Nineveh.
In Jonah’s prayer after Nineveh was spared, to what place did he say he had fled at first to avoid his mission?
Jonah says, “This is why I was so quick to flee toward Tarshish” (4:2).
Jonah 4:2
Joppa
Joppa was the port where he boarded a ship (Jonah 1:3), not the destination he names in his prayer.
Tarshish
Jerusalem
Jerusalem is not mentioned as the place he fled to.
Damascus
Damascus is not mentioned.
Bethel
Bethel is not mentioned.
After the LORD showed mercy to Nineveh, what did Jonah ask God to do for him?
Jonah prayed, “please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live” (4:3).
Jonah 4:3
Send him home
He did not ask to be sent home.
Give him food
He did not ask for food.
Take his life from him
Make him king
He did not ask to be made king.
Hide him from the Assyrians
He did not ask to be hidden from the Assyrians; he asked to die.
In Jonah 4, which description of God did Jonah give as the reason he had fled from his calling?
Jonah says, “I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion—One who relents from sending disaster” (4:2).
Jonah 4:2
Gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion, One who relents from sending disaster
Jealous and consuming, swift to destroy, and never willing to relent once He has spoken in anger
God is not described as swift to destroy or never relenting; Jonah says He relents from sending disaster.
Hidden and distant, refusing to hear prayer, and unwilling to answer those who call on Him
Jonah does not call God distant or deaf to prayer; he is praying to Him.
Mighty in war but weak in mercy, quick to punish and slow to forgive any who repent
Jonah says God abounds in loving devotion, not that He is weak in mercy.
Concerned only for Israel and no one else, a God who has no care for foreign nations
Jonah’s point is that God cares for Nineveh too; 4:11 shows His concern for the great city.
After leaving Nineveh to watch what would happen, where did Jonah sit?
“Jonah left the city and sat down east of it” (4:5).
Jonah 4:5
North of the city
The text says east, not north.
South of the city
The text says east, not south.
West of the city
The text says east, not west.
East of the city
In the city gate
He left the city and sat east of it; he did not sit in the gate.
While Jonah sat outside Nineveh, what did the LORD God appoint to grow over him and shade his head?
“The LORD God appointed a vine, and it grew up to provide shade over Jonah’s head” (4:6); verse 6 also calls it “the plant.”
Jonah 4:6
A cedar tree
A cedar tree is not mentioned; the shade came from a fast-growing vine (the plant).
A plant
A cloud
A cloud is not mentioned.
A fig orchard
A fig orchard is not mentioned.
A vine-covered wall
A vine-covered wall is not what God appointed; the vine itself grew over Jonah.
At dawn the next day in Jonah 4, what did God appoint to attack the plant that had shaded Jonah?
“When dawn came the next day, God appointed a worm that attacked the plant so that it withered” (4:7).
Jonah 4:7
A locust swarm
A locust swarm is not mentioned in Jonah 4; the worm did it.
A worm
A goat
A goat is not mentioned.
A fire from heaven
Fire from heaven is not mentioned.
A hailstorm
A hailstorm is not mentioned.
As the sun was rising over Jonah outside Nineveh, what additional hardship did God appoint?
“As the sun was rising, God appointed a scorching east wind” (4:8).
Jonah 4:8
A heavy rain
Heavy rain is not mentioned; the hardship was heat.
A deep darkness
Darkness is not mentioned; the hardship was a scorching wind and sun.
A scorching east wind
An earthquake
An earthquake is not mentioned.
A cold night frost
Frost is not mentioned; the sun beat down on his head.
In the LORD’s final rebuke to Jonah, which contrast did God use to teach him mercy?

The LORD said, “You cared about the plant, which you neither tended nor made grow… So should I not care about the great city of Nineveh, which has more than 120,000 people… and many cattle as well?” (4:10–11).
Jonah 4:10-11
Jonah cared about a plant he neither tended nor made grow, but God cared about Nineveh with more than 120,000 people who could not tell their right hand from their left, and also many animals
Jonah cared about a boat he built with his own hands, but God cared about the sailors who sailed from Joppa with their cargo
A boat and the sailors from Joppa are not part of God’s final rebuke.
Jonah cared about a vineyard he planted by his house, but God cared about Jerusalem’s temple and the priests who served in it
A vineyard and Jerusalem’s temple are not part of the contrast in 4:10–11.
Jonah cared about a lamb he raised from birth, but God cared about Bethlehem’s shepherds and the flocks they kept by night
A lamb and Bethlehem’s shepherds are not part of the contrast in 4:10–11.
Jonah cared about a fig tree beside his home, but God cared about the king of Tyre and the merchants of that great port
A fig tree and the king of Tyre are not part of the contrast in 4:10–11.
In Jonah 4:9, when God asks, “Have you any right to be angry about the plant?” what does Jonah say after replying “I do”?
Jonah answers, “I do,” and then, “I am angry enough to die!” (4:9).
Jonah 4:9
“I am angry enough to die!”
“I have sinned against the LORD”
David said, “I have sinned against the LORD” to Nathan in 2 Samuel 12:13; Jonah did not repent here.
“Here am I. Send me!”
“Here am I. Send me!” is Isaiah’s answer in Isaiah 6:8, not Jonah’s.
“Speak, for Your servant is listening”
“Speak, for Your servant is listening” is Samuel’s reply in 1 Samuel 3:10.
“Woe is me, for I am ruined”
“Woe is me, for I am ruined” is Isaiah’s cry in Isaiah 6:5; Jonah stays angry in 4:9.
33: In the opening verse of Micah, which prophet from Moresheth received the word of the LORD concerning Samaria and Jerusalem?
1:1 names “Micah the Moreshite,” to whom the word came about “Samaria and Jerusalem.”
Micah 1:1
Amos
Amos was “among the sheepherders of Tekoa” (Amos 1:1), not from Moresheth.
Micah
Hosea
Hosea son of Beeri prophesied in the same era (Hosea 1:1), but he was not from Moresheth.
Joel
Joel was the son of Pethuel (Joel 1:1); Moresheth is Micah’s town.
Nahum
Nahum was the Elkoshite (Nahum 1:1), and his burden was against Nineveh.
At the start of Micah’s prophecy, which two cities are specifically named as the focus of his vision?
The word came to Micah concerning “what he saw regarding Samaria and Jerusalem” (1:1).
Micah 1:1
Bethlehem and Hebron
Bethlehem appears later in Micah 5:2; 1:1 names Samaria and Jerusalem.
Jericho and Ai
Jericho and Ai were conquered by Joshua (Joshua 6:24; 8:28), centuries before Micah.
Samaria and Jerusalem
Tyre and Sidon
Tyre and Sidon were Phoenician cities; Micah’s vision concerned Samaria and Jerusalem (1:1).
Dan and Beersheba
“From Dan to Beersheba” describes the length of Israel (Judges 20:1), not Micah’s focus.
In Micah 1, when all peoples and the earth are called to listen, from where is the Lord said to bear witness?
“May the Lord GOD bear witness against you, the Lord from His holy temple” (1:2).
Micah 1:2
Mount Sinai
Mount Sinai is where the Law was given; Micah speaks of the Lord’s witness from His holy temple (1:2).
The tabernacle in Shiloh
Shiloh housed the Tent of Meeting in Joshua’s day (Joshua 18:1); Micah says “His holy temple” (1:2).
The palace in Jerusalem
No palace is named; the witness comes from His holy temple (1:2).
His holy temple
The Jordan River
The Jordan is not mentioned in 1:2; the Lord bears witness from His holy temple.
When Micah identifies the time of his ministry in chapter 1, during whose reigns in Judah did the word of the LORD come to him?
The word came to Micah “in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah” (1:1).
Micah 1:1
Saul, David, and Solomon
Saul, David, and Solomon ruled the united kingdom centuries earlier.
Uzziah, Jotham, and Ahaz
Uzziah begins the lists in Isaiah 1:1 and Hosea 1:1; Micah’s list begins with Jotham (1:1).
Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah
Hezekiah, Manasseh, and Josiah
Manasseh and Josiah came after Hezekiah; Zephaniah prophesied under Josiah (Zephaniah 1:1).
Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, and Zedekiah
These were Judah’s last kings, in Jeremiah’s day (Jeremiah 1:3).
In Micah’s description of the LORD coming forth from His dwelling place, what happens to the mountains and valleys?
“The mountains will melt beneath Him, and the valleys will split apart, like wax before the fire” (1:4).
Micah 1:3-4
The mountains are lifted higher and the valleys are filled with grain
Lifted mountains and filled valleys are not Micah’s picture; here they melt and split (1:4).
The mountains melt beneath Him and the valleys split apart
The mountains are covered with snow and the valleys with mist
Snow and mist are not mentioned; the mountains melt like wax (1:4).
The mountains quake but the valleys remain still
The valleys do not stay still; they “split apart” (1:4).
The mountains become bronze and the valleys become iron
Bronze and iron are not mentioned; the mountains melt like wax before the fire (1:4).
In Micah’s indictment of Israel and Judah, what does he identify as the transgression of Jacob and the high place of Judah?
“What is the transgression of Jacob? Is it not Samaria? And what is the high place of Judah? Is it not Jerusalem?” (1:5).
Micah 1:5
Bethel and Gilgal
Bethel and Gilgal are paired in Amos 4:4; Micah names Samaria and Jerusalem (1:5).
Nineveh and Babylon
Nineveh and Babylon were foreign capitals; Micah blames Israel’s and Judah’s own capitals (1:5).
Samaria and Jerusalem
Dan and Bethel
Dan and Bethel held Jeroboam’s golden calves (1 Kings 12:29), but Micah names Samaria and Jerusalem.
Shechem and Shiloh
Shechem and Shiloh are not named in Micah 1; the answer is Samaria and Jerusalem (1:5).
Regarding coming judgment in Micah 1, what did the LORD say He would make of Samaria?
“I will make Samaria a heap of rubble in the open field, a planting area for a vineyard” (1:6).
Micah 1:6
A royal fortress guarded by gates of iron and bronze
Samaria would be ruined, not fortified: her stones poured into the valley (1:6).
A heap in the open field, a place for planting vineyards
A busy harbor for the merchant ships of the sea
Samaria was a hill city, not a port; the LORD would make it a heap of rubble (1:6).
A walled city stronger than it had ever been before
The LORD would expose her foundations (1:6), the opposite of strengthening her walls.
A holy sanctuary where all the nations would worship
Nations streaming to the LORD’s house is said of Zion (Isaiah 2:3); Samaria would become a heap (1:6).
Concerning Samaria’s idols in chapter 1, what judgment is announced against her carved images and idol wealth?
“All her carved images will be smashed to pieces; all her wages will be burned in the fire, and I will destroy all her idols” (1:7).
Micah 1:7
They will be hidden in caves for safety
The idols would not be preserved; they would be smashed and burned (1:7).
They will be dedicated to the temple in Jerusalem
None of Samaria’s idols go to Jerusalem’s temple; they will be destroyed (1:7).
They will be sold to Egypt for horses
Sending to Egypt for horses was forbidden to Israel’s kings (Deuteronomy 17:16); Micah says the idols will be destroyed.
They will be smashed to pieces and burned in the fire
They will be covered in gold again after the invasion
Rather than regilded, her idols would be destroyed (1:7).
When Micah responds to the incurable wound that has reached Judah and even Jerusalem, how does he say he will lament?
“I will walk barefoot and naked. I will howl like a jackal and mourn like an ostrich” (1:8).
Micah 1:8-9
By sitting in sackcloth at the city gate only
Sackcloth at the gate is not Micah’s image; he walks barefoot and naked (1:8).
By fasting forty days in the wilderness
No forty-day fast appears; Micah howls like a jackal and mourns like an ostrich (1:8).
By walking barefoot and naked, howling like a jackal and mourning like an ostrich
By tearing the temple veil and blowing silver trumpets
The temple veil and silver trumpets are not mentioned; Micah laments barefoot and naked (1:8).
By hiding in a cave until peace returns
Micah does not hide; he laments openly and loudly (1:8).
In Micah 1’s oracle against the towns of Judah, which place is told, “Harness your chariot horses,” because it was the beginning of sin to the Daughter of Zion?
“Harness your chariot horses, O dweller of Lachish. You were the beginning of sin to the Daughter of Zion” (1:13).
Micah 1:13
Lachish
Bethlehem
Bethlehem’s word in Micah is hope: a ruler will come from it (Micah 5:2).
Tekoa
Tekoa was Amos’s hometown (Amos 1:1) and is not in Micah 1’s list.
Hebron
Hebron does not appear in Micah 1; the chariot command is for Lachish (1:13).
Mizpah
Mizpah is where Israel assembled in Judges 20:1; Micah 1:13 names Lachish.
In the opening woe of Micah chapter 2, when do the people who “devise iniquity and plot evil on their beds” carry out their plans?
Micah 2:1 says, “At morning’s light they accomplish it because the power is in their hands.”
Micah 2:1
At midnight
Micah says they plot on their beds, but the evil is carried out in the morning, not at midnight.
At morning light
At the evening sacrifice
The evening sacrifice is not mentioned in Micah 2; the verse names morning’s light.
On the Sabbath
The Sabbath is not mentioned in Micah 2:1; the plans are carried out at morning’s light.
At harvest time
Harvest time is not named in Micah 2:1; they act at morning’s light.
In Micah’s rebuke of greedy people in Israel, what do they covet and seize?
Micah 2:2 says, “They covet fields and seize them; they take away houses.”
Micah 2:2
Silver and gold
Silver and gold are not named in Micah 2:2; the verse speaks of fields and houses.
Vineyards and wells
Vineyards and wells are not named in Micah 2:2; they covet fields and houses.
Fields and houses
Flocks and herds
Flocks and herds are not mentioned in the verse; the people covet fields and take houses.
Cities and towers
Cities and towers are not mentioned; Micah 2:2 names fields and houses.
When Micah addresses the house of Jacob in chapter 2, for whom does he say the LORD’s words bring good?
Micah 2:7 asks, “Do not My words bring good to him who walks uprightly?”
Micah 2:7
The one who walks uprightly
The one who offers many sacrifices
Many sacrifices are not the standard here; Micah 2:7 says God’s words bring good to the one who walks uprightly.
The one who wins battles
Winning battles is not the condition; the verse says the one who walks uprightly receives good.
The one who fasts in sackcloth
Fasting in sackcloth is not mentioned in Micah 2:7; upright living is.
The one who lives in Jerusalem
Living in Jerusalem is not the qualification in Micah 2:7; walking uprightly is.
In the disaster the LORD plans against the nation in Micah 2, what will the people no longer do?
In Micah 2:3 the LORD says, “you cannot free your necks. Then you will not walk so proudly, for it will be a time of calamity.”
Micah 2:3
Build altars
Building altars is not mentioned in Micah 2:3; the people will no longer walk so proudly.
Walk proudly
Speak in parables
Micah 2:4 says they will take up a proverb in mockery, but 2:3 says they will no longer walk proudly.
Enter Samaria
Entering Samaria is not mentioned in Micah 2:3; it speaks of walking proudly.

Peter

Michael is “one of the chief princes” in Daniel 10:13 and “the archangel” who disputed with the devil (Jude 1:9); he never appears to Mary.
Raphael
Raphael is not named anywhere in the BSB; he comes from the apocryphal book of Tobit. Luke 1:26 names Gabriel.
Gabriel
Uriel
Uriel is never an angel in the BSB; the name belongs to Levites such as Uriel the Kohathite chief (1 Chronicles 15:5). Luke 1:26 names Gabriel.
Apollyon
Apollyon (Hebrew Abaddon) is “the angel of the Abyss” who rules the locusts in Revelation 9:11, not the messenger sent to Mary.
In Luke 1, to what town in Galilee was Gabriel sent to visit Mary?
God sent Gabriel “to a town in Galilee called Nazareth” (1:26).
Luke 1:26
Bethlehem
Bethlehem in Judea is “the city of David,” where Joseph and Mary went for the census (Luke 2:4), not the Galilean town Gabriel visited.
Capernaum
Capernaum is a town in Galilee where Jesus later taught on the Sabbath (Luke 4:31), but Gabriel was sent to Nazareth.
Cana
Cana in Galilee is where Jesus attended a wedding (John 2:1); Mary lived in Nazareth when Gabriel came.
Nazareth
Nain
Nain is the town where Jesus raised a widow’s son (Luke 7:11); Gabriel’s visit was to Nazareth.
In the angel’s message to Mary in Luke 1, what name was she told to give her son?
Gabriel told Mary, “You will conceive and give birth to a son, and you are to give Him the name Jesus” (1:31).
Luke 1:31
Immanuel
Immanuel is the name from Isaiah’s prophecy, “they will call Him Immanuel” (Matthew 1:23; Isaiah 7:14), not the name Mary was told to give.
Jesus
John
John was the name given for Zechariah and Elizabeth’s son (1:13), not Mary’s son.
Joseph
Joseph was the name of Mary’s betrothed (1:27), not the name given for her son.
David
David is named as the child’s royal father, whose throne He would receive (1:32), not as His name.
In Luke 1, what name was Zechariah and Elizabeth’s child commanded to receive?
The angel told Zechariah, “Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you are to give him the name John” (1:13).
Luke 1:13
Samuel
Samuel was the name Hannah gave her long-prayed-for son (1 Samuel 1:20), not Zechariah’s son.
Elijah
John would go before the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (1:17), but he was not to be named Elijah.
John
Aaron
Aaron was Elizabeth’s ancestor (1:5); the child’s name was to be John.
Judah
Judah was Jacob’s fourth son by Leah (Genesis 35:23), a tribal name, not the name commanded in 1:13.
In Luke 1, who was Mary pledged to be married to?
Gabriel came “to a virgin pledged in marriage to a man named Joseph, who was of the house of David” (1:27).
Luke 1:27
Zechariah
Zechariah was Elizabeth’s husband, a priest of the division of Abijah (1:5), not Mary’s betrothed.
Boaz
Boaz was the man who married Ruth (Ruth 4:13), generations before Mary.
Joseph
Cleopas
Cleopas was one of the two disciples on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:18).
Nathanael
Nathanael was the disciple Philip brought to Jesus (John 1:45).
In the visit described in Luke 1, what happened in Elizabeth’s womb when Mary greeted her?
“When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the baby leaped in her womb” (1:41); Elizabeth said he “leaped for joy” (1:44).
The baby became still
The opposite happened: the baby moved, leaping in Elizabeth’s womb at Mary’s greeting (1:41).
The baby cried aloud
No sound from the unborn child is mentioned; it was Elizabeth who exclaimed “in a loud voice” (1:42).
The baby leaped
The baby was born
John was not born until later, “when the time came for Elizabeth to have her child” (1:57), after Mary’s three-month stay.
Elizabeth fainted
Elizabeth did not faint; she was filled with the Holy Spirit and blessed Mary (1:41–42).
In Luke 1, during whose reign did the events surrounding Zechariah and Elizabeth begin?
Luke dates the story “in the time of Herod king of Judea” (1:5).
Luke 1:5
Caesar Augustus
Caesar Augustus is named in Luke 2:1 for the census decree before Jesus’ birth, not in 1:5.
Herod king of Judea
Pontius Pilate
Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea when John began preaching (Luke 3:1), some thirty years later.
Archelaus
Archelaus reigned in Judea after his father Herod died (Matthew 2:22), after these events.
Claudius
Claudius was a later emperor who expelled the Jews from Rome (Acts 18:2).
In Luke chapter 1, what was Zechariah’s occupation?
Zechariah was “a priest” of the division of Abijah (1:5), serving “as priest before God” when the angel came (1:8).
Luke 1:5, 8
Shepherd
Shepherds appear in Luke 2:8, keeping watch over their flocks by night; Zechariah was a priest.
Fisherman
Simon Peter and Andrew were fishermen (Matthew 4:18); Zechariah served in the temple as a priest.
Scribe
Scribes like Ezra were skilled in the Law (Ezra 7:6); Zechariah is introduced as a priest (1:5).
Priest
Carpenter
Jesus was called “the carpenter” (Mark 6:3); Zechariah was a priest.
In Luke 1, from what priestly division was Zechariah?
Zechariah “belonged to the priestly division of Abijah” (1:5), the eighth of David’s priestly divisions (1 Chronicles 24:10).
Luke 1:5
Levi
Levi is the tribe from which all priests came, not a priestly division; Zechariah’s division was Abijah’s (1:5).
Zadok
Zadok son of Ahitub was a priest under David (2 Samuel 8:17); Luke names Zechariah’s division as Abijah.
Abijah
Gershon
Gershon was a son of Levi (Numbers 3:17), heading a Levite clan, not a priestly division.
Kohath
Kohath was a son of Levi (Numbers 3:17), ancestor of a Levite clan; Zechariah’s division was Abijah.
In the description of Elizabeth in Luke 1, from whom was she descended?
Luke says Elizabeth “was a descendant of Aaron” (1:5), so both she and her husband came from priestly lines.
Luke 1:5
Judah
Judah was the royal tribe from which our Lord descended (Hebrews 7:14); Elizabeth is traced to Aaron.
Benjamin
Benjamin was Rachel’s last son (Genesis 35:18); Luke 1:5 links Elizabeth to Aaron.
Aaron
Ephraim
Ephraim was Joseph’s second son (Genesis 41:52); Elizabeth was a descendant of Aaron.
David
Joseph, not Elizabeth, is linked to the house of David (1:27).
In Luke 1, why had Zechariah and Elizabeth remained childless?
“They had no children, because Elizabeth was barren, and they were both well along in years” (1:7).
Luke 1:7
Zechariah had taken a vow
No vow is mentioned; the reason given is that Elizabeth was barren (1:7).
They lived apart
They were together; when Zechariah’s service ended he “returned home” and Elizabeth became pregnant (1:23–24).
Elizabeth was barren
They were too poor
Poverty is never mentioned; both were righteous and blameless (1:6), and the reason for childlessness was barrenness.
They were foreigners
They were not foreigners: Zechariah was a priest and Elizabeth a descendant of Aaron (1:5).
In Luke 1, what temple duty was assigned to Zechariah by lot?
Zechariah “was chosen by lot, according to the custom of the priesthood, to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense” (1:9).
Luke 1:9
Reading the Law
Reading the Law is not mentioned in 1:9; the lot fell to Zechariah to burn incense.
Lighting the menorah
Tending the lamps was a priestly task (Exodus 27:21), but Zechariah’s lot was to burn incense (1:9).
Burning incense
Offering the Passover lamb
The Passover lamb was slaughtered by the whole assembly at twilight (Exodus 12:6), not a duty chosen by lot here.
Sweeping the court
No sweeping is mentioned; Zechariah entered the temple to burn incense (1:9).
In the temple scene of Luke 1, what were the people doing outside while Zechariah offered incense?
“At the hour of the incense offering, the whole congregation was praying outside” (1:10).
Luke 1:10
Singing psalms
No psalm-singing is mentioned; the congregation was praying (1:10).
Sleeping
No one was sleeping; at the hour of the incense offering the whole congregation was praying outside (1:10).
Praying
Selling doves
Selling doves in the temple courts is what Jesus later drove out (Mark 11:15), not what the people did in 1:10.
Studying scrolls
No scroll study is mentioned; the people were praying outside (1:10).
In Luke 1, where did the angel stand when appearing to Zechariah in the temple?
The angel appeared “standing at the right side of the altar of incense” (1:11).
Luke 1:11
At the entrance gate
Luke places the angel inside, by the altar of incense (1:11), not at an entrance gate.
Above the ark
The LORD promised to meet Moses above the mercy seat between the cherubim (Exodus 25:22); the angel stood by the incense altar.
On the left side of the altar
Luke specifies the right side of the altar of incense (1:11), not the left.
At the right side of the altar of incense
In the outer court
The congregation was outside (1:10); the angel appeared inside the temple, by the altar of incense.
In Luke 1, how did Zechariah react when he saw the angel in the temple?
“When Zechariah saw him, he was startled and gripped with fear” (1:12).
Luke 1:12
He laughed in disbelief at the sight
Laughing in disbelief was Sarah’s reaction to the promise of a son (Genesis 18:12), not Zechariah’s at the angel’s appearance.
He rejoiced aloud and praised God
Zechariah did not rejoice; he was startled and gripped with fear (1:12), and later doubted the message (1:18).
He was troubled and fear fell upon him
He fled from the altar in terror
Zechariah did not flee; he stayed and questioned the angel, “How can I be sure of this?” (1:18).
He bowed low and worshiped the angel
Falling down to worship an angel was John’s reaction in Revelation 19:10; Zechariah was gripped with fear (1:12).
In Luke 1:13, what did the angel say Elizabeth would bear for Zechariah?
The angel promised Zechariah a son and instructed him to name the child John.
Luke 1:13
A daughter named Mary
Mary was Elizabeth’s relative, not her daughter (Luke 1:36).
A son named James
The angel instructed Zechariah to name his son John (Luke 1:13).
A son named John
A son named Zechariah
Those present at his circumcision wanted to name him after his father, but the angel had specified John (Luke 1:13, 59).
A son named Elijah
John would serve “in the spirit and power of Elijah,” but his name would be John (Luke 1:13, 17).
In Luke 1, what effect did the angel say John’s birth would have on many people?
The angel said John “will be a joy and delight to you, and many will rejoice at his birth” (1:14).
Luke 1:14
Many would mourn
Mourning is not foretold; the angel promised “many will rejoice at his birth” (1:14).
Many would rejoice
Many would doubt
Doubt came from Zechariah himself (1:18–20), not from the many who would rejoice at John’s birth.
Many would flee
No fleeing is foretold; the angel spoke of joy and rejoicing (1:14).
Many would oppose him
Opposition is not mentioned at his birth; instead many would rejoice (1:14) and his neighbors did rejoice (1:58).
In Luke 1, what did Gabriel say John must never drink?
Gabriel said John “shall never take wine or strong drink” (1:15), like a Nazirite (Numbers 6:3).
Luke 1:15
Water and milk
Water and milk are not mentioned; the prohibition was wine and strong drink (1:15).
Vinegar and oil
Vinegar made from wine was forbidden to Nazirites (Numbers 6:3), but Gabriel named wine and strong drink for John.
Tea and honey
John actually ate wild honey with locusts in the wilderness (Matthew 3:4); the ban was on wine and strong drink.
Wine and strong drink
Fruit juice and broth
Neither fruit juice nor broth is named; John was never to take wine or strong drink (1:15).
According to Luke 1, when would John be filled with the Holy Spirit?
Gabriel said John “will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb” (1:15); he leaped when Mary arrived (1:41).
Luke 1:15
At his circumcision
John’s circumcision on the eighth day (1:59) is when he was named, but the Spirit filled him before birth (1:15).
At age twelve
Age twelve is when Jesus went with His parents to the Passover feast (Luke 2:42), not when John received the Spirit.
When Jesus was baptized
At Jesus’ baptism the Spirit descended on Jesus like a dove (Luke 3:22); John was filled from the womb (1:15).
Even from his mother’s womb
After preaching in the wilderness
John lived in the wilderness until his public appearance (1:80), but he was filled with the Spirit from the womb (1:15).
In Luke 1, many of the sons of Israel would be turned back to whom through John’s ministry?
“Many of the sons of Israel he will turn back to the Lord their God” (1:16).
Luke 1:16
Moses
Moses is not named in 1:16; John would turn many back to the Lord their God.
David
David appears in Luke 1 as Jesus’ royal father (1:32), not as the one Israel would turn back to.
The Lord their God
Abraham
Abraham is named in Mary’s and Zechariah’s songs (1:55, 1:73), but John would turn people to the Lord their God.
Elijah
John would go in Elijah’s spirit and power (1:17), but people would be turned back to the Lord, not to Elijah.
In the prophecy of Luke 1, in whose spirit and power would John go before the Lord?
John would “go on before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah” (1:17), echoing Malachi 4:5–6.
Luke 1:17
Moses
Moses spoke of “a prophet like me” (Deuteronomy 18:15), but Gabriel tied John to Elijah (1:17).
Elisha
Elisha asked for a double portion of Elijah’s spirit (2 Kings 2:9); John came in the spirit and power of Elijah himself.
Elijah
Samuel
Samuel is not named in Luke 1; John’s ministry is linked to Elijah (1:17).
Isaiah
Isaiah wrote of “a voice of one calling in the wilderness” fulfilled in John (Luke 3:4), but 1:17 names Elijah’s spirit and power.
In Luke 1, what did Gabriel say John would help make ready for the Lord?
John would go before the Lord “to make ready a people prepared for the Lord” (1:17).
Luke 1:17
A rebuilt temple
No rebuilt temple is mentioned; John would make ready a people prepared for the Lord (1:17).
A new priesthood
Though a priest’s son, John was not sent to found a priesthood; he would prepare a people (1:17).
A people prepared
A royal army
No army is in view; John’s task was to prepare a people for the Lord (1:17).
A written gospel
Luke himself wrote an orderly account (1:3); John’s task was to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.
In Luke 1, what reason did Zechariah give for doubting the angel’s message?
Zechariah asked, “How can I be sure of this? … I am an old man, and my wife is well along in years” (1:18).
Luke 1:18
He was poor
Poverty is never mentioned; Zechariah pointed to his and Elizabeth’s age (1:18).
He was in exile
Zechariah was not in exile; he was serving in the temple in Jerusalem (1:8–9).
He and his wife were old
He had no priestly authority
He was a serving priest, chosen by lot to burn incense (1:9); his doubt rested on old age (1:18).
He had already named a son
He had no children at all (1:7); he doubted because he and his wife were old (1:18).
In Luke 1, how did the angel identify himself to Zechariah?
“I am Gabriel,” replied the angel. “I stand in the presence of God, and I have been sent to speak to you” (1:19).
Luke 1:19
“I am Michael, captain of heaven”
Michael is called “one of the chief princes” (Daniel 10:13) and “the archangel” (Jude 1:9); the angel here was Gabriel.
“I am Gabriel” and “I stand in the presence of God”
“I am the angel of the covenant”
Malachi foretold “the Messenger of the covenant” (Malachi 3:1), but the angel in 1:19 named himself Gabriel.
“I am Elijah returned”
Jesus said John was “the Elijah who was to come” (Matthew 11:14); the angel identified himself as Gabriel.
“I am the messenger of Zion”
No such title appears; the angel named himself Gabriel and said, “I stand in the presence of God” (1:19).
In Luke 1, what sign was given to Zechariah because he did not believe the angel’s words?
Gabriel said, “You will be silent and unable to speak until the day this comes to pass, because you did not believe my words” (1:20).
Luke 1:20
He became blind
Saul of Tarsus was struck blind on the Damascus road (Acts 9:8–9); Zechariah was struck silent (1:20).
He became lame
Lameness is not mentioned; Zechariah’s sign was being unable to speak (1:20).
He became silent
He lost his priesthood
He kept his priesthood and finished his days of service (1:23) despite being silent.
He was sent into exile
He was not exiled; he returned home after his service (1:23).
In Luke 1, why were the people outside the temple wondering about Zechariah?
“The people were waiting for Zechariah and wondering why he took so long in the temple” (1:21).
Luke 1:21
He had fainted
Zechariah did not faint; he came out and made signs to the people (1:22).
He delayed inside
He left without incense
Nothing says he left without offering incense; the people wondered why he took so long (1:21).
He broke the lampstand
No damage to the lampstand is mentioned; the people wondered at his delay (1:21).
He brought out a scroll
He brought out no scroll; he came out unable to speak and made signs (1:22).
In the temple account of Luke 1, what did the people realize when Zechariah came out unable to speak?
When he came out unable to speak, “they realized he had seen a vision in the temple” (1:22).
Luke 1:22
He had become ill
The people did not conclude he was ill; they realized he had seen a vision (1:22).
He had forgotten the blessing
Nothing about forgetting a blessing is mentioned; they understood he had seen a vision (1:22).
He had seen a vision in the temple
He had fallen asleep
Sleep is not mentioned; the people realized he had seen a vision in the temple (1:22).
He had quarreled with the priests
There is no quarrel in the account; his silence and signs showed he had seen a vision (1:22).
In Luke 1, after Zechariah finished his days of service, where did he go?
“When the days of his service were complete, he returned home” (1:23), to a town in the hill country of Judah (1:39–40).
Luke 1:23
To Jerusalem’s upper room
The upper room appears at the Last Supper (Luke 22:12) and after the ascension (Acts 1:13); Zechariah simply returned home (1:23).
To the Jordan River
The Jordan is where John later preached a baptism of repentance (Luke 3:3); Zechariah went home (1:23).
To the wilderness
John, not Zechariah, later lived in the wilderness (1:80); Zechariah returned home (1:23).
To his home
To Nazareth
Nazareth was Mary’s town (1:26–27); Zechariah’s home was in the hill country of Judah (1:39–40).
In Luke 1, for how long did Elizabeth remain in seclusion after conceiving?
Elizabeth became pregnant “and for five months remained in seclusion” (1:24).
Luke 1:24
Three days
Three days is not mentioned; Elizabeth stayed in seclusion five months (1:24).
Forty days
Forty days recalls Jesus’ fast in the wilderness (Matthew 4:2); Elizabeth’s seclusion lasted five months (1:24).
Five months
Six months
The sixth month is when Gabriel visited Mary (1:26, 1:36), after Elizabeth’s five months of seclusion.
One year
No year-long seclusion is described; it was five months (1:24).
In Luke 1, what did Elizabeth say the Lord had taken away from her among the people?
Elizabeth said the Lord “has shown me favor and taken away my disgrace among the people” (1:25), the reproach of childlessness.
Luke 1:25
Her sickness
Elizabeth was not sick but barren (1:7); the Lord removed her disgrace (1:25).
Her poverty
Poverty is not mentioned; she rejoiced that her disgrace was taken away (1:25).
Her fear
Fear is not what she named; she spoke of her disgrace among the people (1:25).
Her disgrace
Her loneliness
Loneliness is not mentioned; she said the Lord took away her disgrace (1:25), much as Rachel spoke of her shame (Genesis 30:23).
In the sixth month mentioned in Luke 1, to whom was Gabriel sent?
“In the sixth month, God sent the angel Gabriel” to a virgin pledged to Joseph, whose name was Mary (1:26–27).
Elizabeth
Elizabeth was the one in her sixth month (1:36); Gabriel was sent to Mary.
Anna
Anna the prophetess met the infant Jesus in the temple (Luke 2:36–38), not Gabriel.
Mary
Martha
Martha welcomed Jesus into her home years later (Luke 10:38); Gabriel was sent to Mary.
Salome
Salome is not named in Luke 1; Gabriel was sent to the virgin Mary (1:27).
In Luke 1, to what royal house did Joseph belong?
Joseph “was of the house of David” (1:27), and Luke later says he was “from the house and line of David” (Luke 2:4).
Luke 1:27
The house of Saul
Saul was Israel’s first king from Benjamin (1 Samuel 9:2); Joseph belonged to the house of David.
The house of Levi
Levi was the priestly tribe of Zechariah and Elizabeth (1:5); Joseph was of the house of David.
The house of Herod
Herod was the reigning king of Judea (1:5), not Joseph’s family line.
The house of David
The house of Omri
Omri was a king of the northern kingdom of Israel (1 Kings 16:23); Joseph was of David’s house.
In Luke 1, how did Gabriel greet Mary?
Gabriel said to Mary, “Greetings, you who are highly favored! The Lord is with you” (1:28).
Luke 1:28
“Peace to you, daughter of Zion! Your King is coming”

“Greetings, you who are highly favored! The Lord is with you”
“Rise up, maiden of Israel! The Lord has chosen you”
