“Hail, mother of the King! The Most High is near you”
Gabriel did not call Mary the King’s mother; Elizabeth later called her “the mother of my Lord” (1:43).
“Arise, shine, for your light has come, O virgin!”
“Arise, shine, for your light has come” is Isaiah’s call to Zion (Isaiah 60:1), not Gabriel’s greeting.
In Luke 1, how did Mary respond inwardly to Gabriel’s greeting?
“Mary was greatly troubled at his words and wondered what kind of greeting this might be” (1:29).
Luke 1:29
She grew angry and demanded his name
Mary showed no anger and did not ask the angel’s name; she was troubled and wondered (1:29).
She was deeply troubled and wondered about the greeting
She burst at once into a song of praise
Mary’s song of praise came later, at Elizabeth’s home (1:46–55), not as her first reaction.
She fainted and fell to the ground in fear
Mary did not faint; she listened and asked, “How can this be?” (1:34).
She ran at once to tell Joseph the news
Luke records no trip to Joseph; Mary hurried to Elizabeth in the hill country of Judah (1:39).
In Luke 1, what title did Gabriel say Jesus would be called?
Gabriel said, “He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High” (1:32).
Luke 1:32
Son of Aaron
Sons of Aaron were the priests (Exodus 28:1); Jesus would be called the Son of the Most High (1:32).
Son of Moses
No one is called a son of Moses in Luke 1; Gabriel’s title for Jesus was Son of the Most High (1:32).
Son of the Most High
Son of Caesar
Caesar Augustus appears in Luke 2:1; Jesus would be called Son of the Most High, not son of any emperor.
Son of Elijah
Elijah is linked to John, who would come in his spirit and power (1:17); Jesus is the Son of the Most High (1:32).
In Luke 1, whose throne would the Lord God give to Jesus?
“The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David” (1:32), fulfilling the oath of Psalm 132:11.
Luke 1:32
Solomon’s throne only
Solomon is not named in Luke 1; Gabriel spoke of “the throne of His father David” (1:32).
Herod’s throne
Herod was king of Judea when the story began (1:5), but Jesus would receive David’s throne (1:32).
David’s throne
Caesar’s throne
Caesar’s throne is not in view; the promise was the throne of His father David (1:32).
Zechariah’s throne
Zechariah was a priest (1:5), not a king, and had no throne to give.
In Luke 1, over whose house would Jesus reign forever?
Gabriel said, “He will reign over the house of Jacob forever” (1:33), Jacob being Israel (Genesis 32:28).
Luke 1:33
The house of Levi
Levi was the priestly tribe of Zechariah and Elizabeth (1:5); Jesus would reign over the house of Jacob.
The house of Joseph
Joseph was of the house of David (1:27); the kingdom promised was over the house of Jacob (1:33).
The house of Jacob
The house of Judah only
Judah is only one of Jacob’s sons; Gabriel promised a reign over the whole house of Jacob (1:33).
The house of Aaron
Aaron’s house is the priestly line (1:5), not the realm of Jesus’ reign (1:33).
In Luke 1, what did Gabriel say about the end of Jesus’ kingdom?
Gabriel declared, “His kingdom will never end!” (1:33).
Luke 1:33
It would end after forty years
David reigned over Israel forty years (1 Kings 2:11), but Jesus’ kingdom “will never end” (1:33).
It would end at the judgment
Gabriel set no end at the judgment or anywhere else: “His kingdom will never end!” (1:33).
It would be hidden
Nothing is said about hiddenness; Gabriel promised an everlasting kingdom (1:33).
It would have no end
It would be divided
David’s kingdom split under Rehoboam (1 Kings 12:19), but Jesus’ kingdom would never end (1:33).
In Luke 1, what question did Mary ask in response to the announcement that she would bear a son?
Mary asked the angel, “How can this be… since I am a virgin?” (1:34).
Luke 1:34
“Why me?”
Mary did not ask “Why me?”; her question concerned how it could happen, since she was a virgin (1:34).
“When will this happen?”
Mary asked how, not when; she said, “How can this be” (1:34).
“How can this be, since I am a virgin?”
“What shall I name Him?”
Gabriel had already given the name Jesus (1:31); Mary asked how it would happen (1:34).
“Must I go to Bethlehem?”
Bethlehem comes in Luke 2:4 with the census; Mary’s question was about her virginity (1:34).
In Gabriel’s answer to Mary in Luke 1, who would come upon her?
Gabriel answered, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you” (1:35).
Luke 1:35
An angelic host
An angelic host appeared to the shepherds at Jesus’ birth (Luke 2:13), not upon Mary.
The Spirit of Elijah
The spirit and power of Elijah were promised for John (1:17), not for Mary.
The Holy Spirit
A cherub
Cherubim guarded the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24); Gabriel said the Holy Spirit would come upon Mary.
The hand of Moses
No “hand of Moses” is mentioned; the Holy Spirit would come upon Mary (1:35).
In Luke 1, what would overshadow Mary according to Gabriel?
“The power of the Most High will overshadow you” (1:35).
Luke 1:35
The temple cloud
The cloud filled the tabernacle with glory (Exodus 40:34), but Gabriel said the power of the Most High would overshadow Mary.
The power of the Most High
The wings of seraphim
Seraphim with six wings appear in Isaiah 6:2; Gabriel spoke of the power of the Most High (1:35).
The glory of David
David’s glory is not mentioned; it was the power of the Most High that would overshadow Mary (1:35).
The fire of Sinai

In Luke 1, because of His miraculous conception, what would the child born to Mary be called?
Gabriel said, “The Holy One to be born will be called the Son of God” (1:35).

In Acts 2, what did the Spirit enable the believers to begin speaking?
Acts 2:4 says they “began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit enabled them.”
Acts 2:4
Parables
Parables were a teaching style of Jesus; at Pentecost the Spirit enabled them to speak in other tongues.
Other tongues
Latin only
Acts 2:6 says each hearer heard his own language, so they were not limited to one language such as Latin.
Secret codes
Nothing in Acts 2 suggests secret codes; the crowd understood “the wonders of God” in their own languages (2:11).
Songs of ascent
Songs of ascent are the psalms pilgrims sang on the way to Jerusalem (such as Psalm 120); the Spirit enabled other tongues.
In Acts 2, who were staying in Jerusalem and heard about the Pentecost event?
Acts 2:5 says there were “God-fearing Jews from every nation under heaven” dwelling in Jerusalem.
Acts 2:5
Roman soldiers from Caesar’s house
Acts 2:5 names God-fearing Jews, not Roman soldiers, as the people dwelling in Jerusalem.
God-fearing Jews from every nation under heaven

Samaritan villagers
Samaritans are not mentioned in Acts 2 (Samaria comes up later, in Acts 8).
Greek philosophers from Athens
Acts 2:5 speaks of Jews gathered in Jerusalem, not Greek philosophers from Athens.

The sun stood still in Joshua 10:13; it is not part of the Pentecost scene.
In the Jerusalem crowd of Acts 2, what region were the speakers said to be from?

Galilee
Judea
Judea is where the crowd was gathered, but the speakers were identified as Galileans (2:7).
Samaria
Samaria is not mentioned in Acts 2; the amazed crowd called the speakers Galileans.
Idumea
Idumea (Edom) is not mentioned in Acts 2; the speakers were called Galileans.
Decapolis
The Decapolis is not mentioned in Acts 2; the speakers were called Galileans.
In Acts 2, what did the foreign hearers say they were hearing in their own tongues?

Acts 2:11
The law of Moses only
The crowd did not say they heard only the law of Moses; they heard the wonders of God.
Warnings about famine
Famine is not mentioned in Acts 2; the hearers heard the wonders of God in their own languages.
The wonders of God

The rebuilding of the temple is not the subject; they heard the wonders of God declared (2:11).

No call to overthrow Rome appears in Acts 2; the message was about the wonders of God.

Stealing temple money is not mentioned; the mockers said they were drunk on new wine.

Plotting rebellion is not the accusation here; Acts 2:13 says they were mocked as drunk.

The Pharisees are not part of the scene; Peter stood up with the Eleven.

The third hour

Sunset
Peter’s argument is that it is still morning, not sunset.

Joel

Sons and daughters

Chariots of fire

Visions

Saul’s throne is not mentioned in the quotation; David saw the Lord always before him.

Acts 2:25 quotes David: “because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken.”

The names of all nations are not in the quotation; God made known the paths of life.

The measure of the temple is not in the quotation; God made known the paths of life.

His crown
David’s crown is not mentioned; Peter points to his tomb.
His harp
David’s harp is not mentioned; Peter says his tomb is with them to this day.
His palace

His tomb

The birth of John the Baptist

Nehemiah’s rebuilding is not the subject; David spoke about the resurrection of the Christ.

Acts 3:26
First to the Gentiles, to enlighten them with Greek philosophy and wisdom
Greek philosophy is not mentioned in Acts 3:26; God sent Him first to Israel, not to the Gentiles.
First to Samaria, to rebuild their rival worship on Mount Gerizim
Samaria hears the gospel later (Acts 8); Acts 3:26 says He was sent first to Israel.
First to Rome, to establish justice and peace under Caesar’s rule
Rome is not mentioned in Acts 3:26; He was sent first to Israel, to bless them.
First to Israel, to bless them by turning each of them from wicked ways
First to Egypt, to bring plagues on Pharaoh and free the captives
Plagues on Egypt belong to Exodus; Acts 3:26 says He was sent first to Israel to bless them.

Acts 4:1-3
Peter and John
Peter and James
James, John’s brother, was put to death by Herod later (Acts 12:2); he is not among those seized here.

Andrew is not mentioned in Acts 3–4; the two men seized are Peter and John (4:3).
James and Jude
Neither James nor Jude is named in this scene; Acts 4:3 says Peter and John were seized.
Paul and Barnabas
Paul was not yet a believer, and Barnabas first appears at the end of this chapter (4:36).
Why were the temple authorities upset with Peter and John in this Jerusalem scene?
Acts 4:2 says the authorities were greatly disturbed that Peter and John were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection of the dead.
Acts 4:2

Acts 4:2 never mentions refusing to leave the courts; the offense was the message about the resurrection of the dead.

No Sabbath charge is made in this scene; Acts 4:2 names the teaching of the resurrection as the cause of their anger.
They were disputing with Roman soldiers and urging the people to refuse Caesar’s taxes
No dispute with Roman soldiers is recorded; the priests and Sadducees were upset about the message (4:2).

No feast is mentioned in Acts 4:3; the reason given is that it was evening.
It was evening

Witnesses are not mentioned in the arrest; the healed man was in fact standing with them the next day (4:14).

The healed man was not missing; he stood with Peter and John at the hearing (4:14).

Ten thousand is never given in Acts 4; Luke says the number of men grew to about five thousand.

Annas

Caiaphas

Luke calls Lystra and Derbe “the Lycaonian cities” (14:6).
Acts 14:6
Decapolis
Decapolis was the ten-city region east of the Sea of Galilee (Mark 5:20), not Lystra and Derbe.
Lycaonia
Samaria
Samaria is in Palestine (Acts 8:5), far from Lystra and Derbe.
Achaia
Achaia is in Greece (Acts 18:12), not near Lystra and Derbe.
Idumea
Idumea is south of Judea (Mark 3:8), not near Lystra and Derbe.
In the Lystra healing account, what did Paul notice about the crippled man before commanding him to stand?
Paul “saw that he had faith to be healed” (14:9).
Acts 14:9
He had faith to be healed
He was a priest of Zeus
The priest of Zeus appears later (14:13); the man had faith.
He had followed them from Iconium
Nothing says he followed them from Iconium; he was listening in Lystra (14:9).
He had brought an offering
He brought no offering; Paul saw that he had faith (14:9).
He had seen a vision the night before
No vision is mentioned; he listened to Paul and Paul saw his faith (14:9).
In the protest speech at Lystra, which full description best matches the evidence Paul gave that God had not left Himself without testimony?
“He gives you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness” (14:17).
Acts 14:17
He gave the Law, the priesthood, and the temple sacrifices so that all nations could worship Him
The Law, priesthood and sacrifices were given to Israel; Paul told the pagans of Lystra that God gives rain from heaven and fruitful seasons (14:17).
He sent judges, kings, and prophets to every nation so that none could claim ignorance of Him
Judges, kings and prophets were sent to Israel, not to every nation; Paul’s evidence was rain and fruitful seasons (14:17).
He showed kindness by giving rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling hearts with food and gladness
He destroyed idols with fire from heaven in every city, proving that He alone was God
Luke records no idols destroyed by fire from heaven; Paul’s evidence was rain, fruitful seasons, food and gladness (14:17).
He wrote His name in the clouds above Lycaonia and set signs in the stars to point to Him
Nothing is written in the clouds or stars in Paul’s speech; his evidence was rain, fruitful seasons, food and gladness (14:17).
Which sequence best matches the closing return route of Paul and Barnabas in Acts 14 after they revisited Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch in Pisidia?
They passed through Pisidia to Pamphylia, spoke in Perga, went down to Attalia and sailed to Antioch (14:24–26).
Perga → Lystra → Attalia → Antioch in Syria
Lystra was visited earlier (14:8); after Pisidia the route went to Perga, then Attalia (14:24–26).
Attalia → Perga → Pamphylia → Jerusalem
The route ends at Antioch (14:26), not Jerusalem, and Attalia is the port, not the start.
Pamphylia → Pisidia → Derbe → Antioch in Syria
Pamphylia comes after Pisidia (14:24), and Derbe was earlier (14:20–21).
Antioch in Syria → Perga → Attalia → Iconium
The route leaves Antioch only at the beginning of the journey; the return runs the other way (14:24–26).
Pisidia → Pamphylia → Perga → Attalia → Antioch in Syria
In the Antioch dispute recorded in Acts 15, what were certain men from Judea teaching?
Luke records that men from Judea taught, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved” (15:1), which set off the dispute.
Acts 15:1
That Gentile converts had to move to Jerusalem to be saved
Nothing in the chapter requires Gentiles to relocate; the dispute is about circumcision, and the church replies with a letter sent to them (15:22–23).
That unless men were circumcised according to the custom of Moses, they could not be saved
That only Levites were permitted to preach the gospel
Preaching is not restricted to Levites in Acts 15; the debate concerns circumcision, and Paul, Barnabas, Judas and Silas all teach (15:32, 15:35).
That believers had to rebuild the temple before baptism
No one in Acts 15 asks for the temple to be rebuilt; the only rebuilding mentioned is David’s fallen tent in James’s prophecy (15:16).
That Samaritans could not be admitted into the church
Samaritans are not the issue here; Acts 15:3 says the news of Gentile conversions brought great joy to believers in Samaria.
In Acts 15, the men who stirred the debate in Antioch came down from which region?
Acts 15:1 says some men “came down from Judea” to Antioch and began teaching the brothers.
Acts 15:1
Galilee
Galilee is not mentioned in Acts 15; the troublemakers came from Judea, the region around Jerusalem (15:1).
Samaria
Paul and Barnabas passed through Samaria with good news (15:3), but the men who caused the dispute came from Judea.
Judea
Macedonia
Macedonia comes into the story later, when Paul sees a vision of a man from there (Acts 16:9), not in this dispute.
Pamphylia
Pamphylia is where John Mark deserted Paul and Barnabas (15:38), not where the teachers of circumcision came from.
When this teaching arose in Antioch in Acts 15, which two missionaries had a sharp dispute with the men from Judea?
Acts 15:2 says Paul and Barnabas were in sharp debate with the men from Judea and were then appointed to go to Jerusalem.
Acts 15:2
Peter and John
Peter and John were in Jerusalem; Peter only speaks after the delegation arrives (15:7).
Paul and Barnabas
Silas and Judas Barsabbas
Judas Barsabbas and Silas are chosen later in Jerusalem to accompany Paul and Barnabas to Antioch (15:22).
Philip and Stephen
Philip and Stephen belong to the earlier Jerusalem and Samaria story in Acts 6–8, not this dispute.
James and Andrew
James speaks at the Jerusalem meeting (15:13), and Andrew is not mentioned in Acts 15.
In response to the circumcision controversy in Acts 15, to what city were Paul and Barnabas appointed to go?
Acts 15:2 says Paul and Barnabas were appointed “to go up to Jerusalem to see the apostles and elders about this question.”
Acts 15:2
Antioch
The dispute broke out in Antioch, so they left from there rather than traveling to it (15:1–2).
Damascus
Damascus is where Paul first preached after his conversion (Acts 9:19–20), not their destination here.
Jerusalem
Ephesus
Ephesus plays no part in Acts 15; the question was settled in Jerusalem.
Tarsus
Tarsus is Paul’s hometown (Acts 9:30), but the dispute was taken to Jerusalem.
According to Acts 15, Paul and Barnabas went to Jerusalem to consult with whom about the dispute?
Acts 15:2 says they were to go up to Jerusalem “to see the apostles and elders about this question.”
Acts 15:2
The scribes and tax collectors
Scribes and tax collectors are not mentioned in Acts 15; the leaders consulted were the apostles and elders (15:2).
The apostles and elders
The Roman governor and soldiers
Roman officials had no role in the council; the matter was a dispute within the church, handled by its own leaders (15:6).
The synagogue rulers only
Synagogue rulers are not named in the chapter, and the consultation was with the apostles and elders, not a group “only.”
The Pharisees only
A Pharisee party did press for circumcision (15:5), but they were not the ones Paul and Barnabas were sent to see.
On the way to Jerusalem in Acts 15, who sent Paul and Barnabas on their journey?
Acts 15:3 says that Paul and Barnabas were “sent on their way by the church.”
Acts 15:3
The Sanhedrin
The Sanhedrin was the Jewish high court in Jerusalem and had no part in sending the Antioch delegates (15:3).
The church
Cornelius
Cornelius was the Gentile centurion converted in Acts 10, long before this journey.
Lydia
Lydia was a believer in Philippi (Acts 16:14), a later episode and a different city.
The chief priest
The chief priest opposed the church in Acts and did not send Paul and Barnabas on their way.
During the journey described in Acts 15, through which two regions did the delegation pass?
Acts 15:3 says they “passed through Phoenicia and Samaria, recounting the conversion of the Gentiles.”
Acts 15:3
Judea and Galilee
Judea and Galilee are not named on this trip; Luke names Phoenicia and Samaria (15:3).
Syria and Cilicia
Syria and Cilicia are addressed in the Jerusalem letter (15:23) and visited by Paul at the chapter’s end (15:41), not on this outward journey.
Phoenicia and Samaria
Asia and Bithynia
Asia and Bithynia come up in Acts 16 when the Spirit redirects Paul, after this chapter.
Cyprus and Crete
Cyprus is where Barnabas and Mark sail afterward (15:39), and Crete is not part of this account.
As Paul and Barnabas traveled in Acts 15, what report brought great joy to the believers in Phoenicia and Samaria?
Acts 15:3 says they were “recounting the conversion of the Gentiles and bringing great joy to all the brothers.”
Acts 15:3
The rebuilding of Jerusalem’s walls
Rebuilding Jerusalem’s walls is an Old Testament story (Nehemiah 3); it has nothing to do with Acts 15.
The conversion of the Gentiles
The defeat of Herod
Herod’s defeat is not reported here; his death is recorded earlier in Acts 12:23.
The release of Peter from prison
Peter’s release from prison happened in Acts 12 and was not the news that brought joy on this trip.
The appointment of deacons
The appointment of the first deacons is in Acts 6, not part of the report in 15:3.
When Paul and Barnabas arrived in Jerusalem in Acts 15, who welcomed them?
Acts 15:4 says they “were welcomed by the church and apostles and elders.”
Acts 15:4
Only James

The church, the apostles, and the elders
Only the Pharisees

The Roman garrison
No Roman soldiers took part in the welcome; the reception was from the church and its leaders (15:4).

In the Jerusalem discussion of Acts 15, which group of believers insisted that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses?

Acts 15:5
Believers from the party of the Pharisees
The Hellenists
The Hellenists appear in Acts 6:1 as Greek-speaking Jewish believers, and they are not named as the circumcision party here.
The Sadducees who had believed
Sadducees are not mentioned in Acts 15; the group in 15:5 is from the party of the Pharisees.
The Samaritans
Samaritans were not among those demanding circumcision; Samaria rejoiced at the news of Gentile conversions (15:3).
The disciples from Emmaus
The Emmaus disciples belong to the resurrection story in Luke 24 and have no role in this council.
In the Jerusalem council scene of Acts 15, who gathered to examine the matter?
Acts 15:6 says that “the apostles and elders met to look into this matter.”
Acts 15:6
The widows and deacons
Widows and deacons appear in Acts 6; Acts 15:6 names the apostles and elders as the ones who met.
The prophets and teachers

The apostles and elders
The Roman officials
Roman officials had no place in the church’s council on circumcision.
The temple guards
Temple guards are never mentioned in Acts 15.
After much discussion in Acts 15, which apostle stood up to address the assembly?
Acts 15:7 says that after much discussion, Peter got up and addressed the assembly.
Acts 15:7
Thomas
Thomas is not mentioned anywhere in Acts 15; Peter is the apostle who speaks (15:7).
Peter
Matthew

Bartholomew
Bartholomew is also only listed in Acts 1:13 and does not speak at the council.
Judas son of James

John Mark’s
John Mark is mentioned only in connection with the later dispute (15:37–39), not as a preacher to the Gentiles here.
Silas’s
Silas is chosen later to go to Antioch (15:22), after Peter’s speech.

The temple tax exemption
A temple tax exemption is never mentioned in Acts 15.
The Holy Spirit
A written covenant on stone

The priesthood
The priesthood is not given to Gentiles in this chapter; the sign Peter cites is the Spirit (15:8).
In Peter’s argument at the council in Acts 15, between whom did God make no distinction?
Acts 15:9 says God “made no distinction between us and them, for He cleansed their hearts by faith.”
Acts 15:9
Priests and Levites
Priests and Levites are not the groups in view; Peter compares Jewish believers (“us”) with Gentile believers (“them”).
Jews and Samaritans
Samaritans are not the point of comparison in Peter’s speech; the contrast is Jew and Gentile.
Us and them
Men and women
Men and women are not contrasted in this passage; the dispute concerns Jews and Gentiles.
Rich and poor
Rich and poor are not discussed in Peter’s argument at the council.

Peter says in Acts 15:9 that God “cleansed their hearts by faith.”
Acts 15:9
Their houses
Houses are not cleansed in the passage; Peter speaks of the Gentiles’ hearts (15:9).
Their hands
Hands are not in view; the cleansing Peter describes is inward, of the heart by faith.
Their hearts
Their garments
Garments are not mentioned in Peter’s speech; the cleansing is inward (15:9).
Their altars
Altars are not cleansed in Acts 15; Peter says God cleansed hearts.
At the Jerusalem meeting in Acts 15, Peter said some were trying to place what on the disciples’ necks?

Acts 15:10
A crown

A chain

A yoke
A sword
A sword has no place in the image; Peter uses a yoke to describe the law’s burden on Gentile converts (15:10).
A veil
A veil is not used in Peter’s speech; the picture is a heavy yoke.

In the Jerusalem council account of Acts 15, who described the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles?

James and Peter

Barnabas and Paul
Judas and Silas

Philip and Timothy
Philip and Timothy are not mentioned in Acts 15; the reporters are Barnabas and Paul.
John and Andrew
John and Andrew are not named in Acts 15.

Peter

James
John Mark

Silas

Judas Barsabbas

Simon

David’s

The Lord said, “Hurry! Leave Jerusalem quickly” (22:18).
Acts 22:18

The Lord said to hurry away because the people would not accept his testimony, not to stay and debate (22:18).
Hurry and leave Jerusalem at once
Return immediately to Tarsus
Paul was told to leave Jerusalem; the Lord did not name Tarsus here (22:18).
Go first to Samaria
Samaria is not named; the Lord later said He would send Paul to the Gentiles (22:21).
Build an altar on the Mount of Olives
Building an altar is not in the vision; the Lord told him to leave Jerusalem quickly (22:18).
Why did the Lord tell Paul to leave Jerusalem quickly in Acts 22?
The Lord said, “the people here will not accept your testimony about Me” (22:18).
Acts 22:18
A famine was coming
No famine is mentioned; the stated reason is rejection of Paul’s testimony (22:18).
The Romans would destroy the city that night

The apostles are not mentioned in the vision; the reason was that the people would not accept his testimony (22:18).

Which martyr’s death did Paul mention in his Jerusalem vision report in Acts 22?

James the son of Zebedee

Stephen

The Gentiles

Athens is not mentioned in this speech; the word that provoked them was “Gentiles” (22:21–22).

Babylon’s exiles are not named; the crowd erupted at the mention of the Gentiles (22:21–22).

Moses

The church does not decide his travel; Paul prays to come by God’s will (1:10).
God’s will
The apostles’ will
Paul places his plans under God’s will, not the apostles’ (1:10).
His own will alone
Not his own will alone; he hopes to come “by God’s will” (Romans 15:32; 1:10).
In Romans 1, Paul says one reason for coming to Rome was to have what among them?
Paul planned to come “in order that I might have a harvest among you” (1:13).
Romans 1:13
A new law
Paul did not seek to bring a law; he hoped for a harvest among them (1:13).
A harvest
A throne
No throne is in view; Paul hoped for a harvest of ministry among them (1:13).
A census
A census is not mentioned; Paul wanted a harvest among them (1:13).
A temple choir
No choir is mentioned; Paul wanted a harvest among them, as among the other Gentiles (1:13).
In Romans 1, Paul says he wanted a harvest among the believers in Rome just as he had among whom?
Paul wanted a harvest among them “just as I have had among the other Gentiles” (1:13).
Romans 1:13
The priests of Judea
Paul does not compare Rome with priests; his comparison is “the other Gentiles” (1:13).
The kings of Israel
Israel’s kings are not mentioned; Paul compares Rome with the other Gentiles (1:13).
The other Gentiles
The desert hermits
Hermits are not mentioned; Paul compares Rome with the other Gentiles (1:13).
The Roman soldiers
A Roman soldier later guarded Paul in Rome (Acts 28:16); 1:13 compares Rome with the other Gentiles.
In Romans 1, which pair correctly completes Paul’s statement of obligation?
“I am obligated both to Greeks and non-Greeks” (1:14).
Romans 1:14
Jews and priests
Jews and priests are not Paul’s pair; he names Greeks and non-Greeks (1:14).
Greeks and non-Greeks
Kings and slaves
Kings and slaves are not named; the first pair is Greeks and non-Greeks (1:14).
Men and women
“Male nor female” appears in Galatians 3:28; Romans 1:14 names Greeks and non-Greeks.
Rich and poor
Rich and poor are not named in 1:14; the pairs are Greeks and non-Greeks, wise and foolish.
In Romans 1, which second pair also appears in Paul’s statement of obligation?
Paul is obligated “both to the wise and the foolish” (1:14).
Romans 1:14
Wise and foolish
Strong and weak
Paul writes about the strong and the weak in Romans 15:1, not in his statement of obligation.
Old and young
Old and young are paired in Acts 2:17, not in Romans 1:14.
Free and enslaved
Slave and free are paired in Galatians 3:28; Romans 1:14 pairs the wise and the foolish.
Holy and unholy
Holy and unholy are not named in 1:14; the second pair is the wise and the foolish.
In Romans 1, which phrase best completes Paul’s thought: “I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is…”?
“I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes” (1:16).
Romans 1:16
The glory of David for Israel
David is named only as Jesus’ ancestor (1:3); the gospel is the power of God for salvation.
The power of God for salvation
The wisdom of Greece for rulers
“Greeks search for wisdom” (1 Corinthians 1:22), but the gospel is the power of God for salvation.
The burden of the law for sinners
The gospel reveals righteousness “apart from the law” (Romans 3:21); it is not a burden but God’s power for salvation.
The mystery of angels for prophets
Angels are not mentioned; the gospel is the power of God for salvation (1:16).
In Romans 1, which ordered description of Jesus is correct?
Jesus was “a descendant of David according to the flesh” and “declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead” (1:3–4).
Romans 1:3-4
Descendant of Moses according to the flesh, then declared high priest by the temple
Jesus descended from David, not Moses (1:3), and was declared Son of God by His resurrection, not by the temple.
Descendant of David according to the flesh, then declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead
Born in Rome, then made king by Caesar
Jesus was born in Bethlehem, the city of David (Luke 2:4), and was declared Son of God by His resurrection (1:4).
Son of Aaron according to the flesh, then declared prophet by John
Jesus descended from Judah, not Aaron (Hebrews 7:14); 1:3–4 names David and the resurrection.
Descendant of Solomon only, then declared judge by Israel
Paul names David, not Solomon (1:3), and Jesus was declared Son of God by His resurrection (1:4).
In Romans 1, which statement best matches Paul’s purpose in wanting to see the Roman believers?
Paul wants to “impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you” and adds, “that you and I may be mutually encouraged by each other’s faith” (1:11–12).
Romans 1:11-12
To demand payment from them for his apostolic labors
Paul says preachers may live from the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14), but in 1:11–12 he seeks to give, not collect.
To impart some spiritual gift and to be mutually encouraged by faith
To crown a new ruler over the city of Rome
Paul teaches that authorities are appointed by God (Romans 13:1); he came to strengthen believers, not crown rulers.
To settle a property dispute among the believers
No dispute is mentioned; Paul wanted to impart a spiritual gift and be mutually encouraged (1:11–12).
To appoint musicians for worship in the temple
The temple is not in view; Paul wanted to strengthen the believers and be encouraged by their faith (1:11–12).
In Romans 1, which statement best reflects Paul’s travel history regarding Rome?
Paul “planned to come to you (but have been prevented from visiting until now)” (1:13).
Romans 1:13
He had never intended to visit the believers in Rome
Paul says he had “longed for many years to visit you” (Romans 15:23).
He had already visited Rome many times on his journeys
Paul had been prevented “until now” (1:13); he reached Rome only later (Acts 28:16).
He had planned many times to come but had been prevented until now
He had been forbidden by the emperor ever to go there
Claudius had once ordered the Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2), but Paul says only that he had been prevented.
He had chosen to stay in Athens instead of going to Rome
Paul did preach in Athens (Acts 17:22), but 1:13 says he often planned to come to Rome.
In Romans 1, which full set names the two pairs Paul says he is obligated to?
“I am obligated both to Greeks and non-Greeks, both to the wise and the foolish” (1:14).
Romans 1:14
Jews and priests; kings and judges
Paul names neither priests nor judges; his pairs are Greeks and non-Greeks, wise and foolish (1:14).
Greeks and non-Greeks; wise and foolish
Rich and poor; young and old
Rich and poor, young and old are not Paul’s pairs in 1:14.
Men and women; slave and free
Slave and free, male and female appear in Galatians 3:28, not Romans 1:14.
Circumcised and uncircumcised; strong and weak
Circumcised and uncircumcised appear in Colossians 3:11; Romans 1:14 names Greeks and non-Greeks, wise and foolish.
In Romans 1, which statement correctly compares what is being revealed?
The gospel “reveals the righteousness of God” (1:17), and “the wrath of God is being revealed from heaven” (1:18).
Romans 1:17-18
Only mercy is revealed, not wrath
Paul says God’s wrath is being revealed from heaven (1:18), so not only mercy.
Wrath is revealed from heaven, and righteousness is revealed in the gospel
Only law is revealed through Moses
God’s righteousness has been revealed “apart from the law” (Romans 3:21), and wrath is revealed from heaven.
Wrath is revealed in the temple, and righteousness in Rome
Wrath is revealed from heaven, not the temple, and righteousness in the gospel, not Rome (1:17–18).
Neither wrath nor righteousness is revealed
Both are revealed: righteousness in the gospel and wrath from heaven (1:17–18).
In Romans 1, which contrast appears in Paul’s description of salvation?
Salvation comes “first to the Jew, then to the Greek” (1:16).
Romans 1:16
First to the Greek, then to the Jew
This reverses Paul’s order; it is the Jew first (1:16), as again in Romans 2:9–10.
First to the Jew, then to the Greek
First to Rome, then to Jerusalem
No cities are ranked; the order is the Jew first, then the Greek (1:16).
First to the rich, then to the poor
Rich and poor are not ranked; the order is the Jew first, then the Greek (1:16).
First to the wise, then to the strong
The wise appear in 1:14, but the order of salvation in 1:16 is the Jew, then the Greek.
In Romans 1, which contrast appears in Paul’s description of false worship?
They “worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (1:25).
Romans 1:25
Prophets rather than kings
Prophets and kings are not contrasted in 1:25; the contrast is the creature and the Creator.
Created things rather than the Creator
Mercy rather than justice
Mercy and justice are not contrasted here; false worship served the creature rather than the Creator (1:25).
Faith rather than sight
The contrast in 1:25 is the creature versus the Creator, not faith versus sight.
Jerusalem rather than Babylon
Neither city is named; the contrast is the creature rather than the Creator (1:25).
In Romans 1, which two failures come before people become futile in their thinking?
“Although they knew God, they neither glorified Him as God nor gave thanks to Him” (1:21).
Romans 1:21
They neither glorified God as God nor gave thanks to Him
They neither built altars nor offered incense
Altars and incense are not mentioned; the failures were not glorifying God and not giving thanks (1:21).
They neither fasted nor prayed
Fasting and prayer are not mentioned; the failures were not glorifying God and not giving thanks (1:21).
They neither read Moses nor heard Isaiah
These people knew God through creation (1:20), not through Moses or Isaiah; their failure was ingratitude.
They neither traveled to Zion nor brought offerings
Pilgrimage and offerings are not in view; the failures were not glorifying God and not giving thanks (1:21).
In Romans 1, why are people without excuse?
God’s invisible qualities “have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship, so that men are without excuse” (1:20).
Romans 1:20
Because an apostle had been sent to every nation on earth
Creation, not apostles, is the witness; Paul still aimed to preach “where Christ was not known” (Romans 15:20).
Because God’s invisible qualities have been clearly seen in creation
Because Rome enforced the true worship of God everywhere
Rome did not enforce true worship; people are without excuse because of creation’s witness (1:20).
Because the temple in Jerusalem stayed open to all nations
The temple is not mentioned; God’s qualities are seen in His workmanship (1:20).
Because all men had learned Hebrew and read the Law
Gentiles “do not have the law” (Romans 2:14); creation, not Hebrew learning, leaves them without excuse.
In Romans 1, which phrase shows Paul’s dependence on God for his travel plans?
Paul prays “that now at last by God’s will I may succeed in coming to you” (1:10).
Romans 1:10
“I have already arrived”
Paul had not yet arrived; he had been prevented from visiting until now (1:13).
“By God’s will I may succeed in coming to you”
“Caesar has commanded my visit”
No command of Caesar is mentioned; Paul hoped to come by God’s will (1:10).
“I will come whether God wills or not”
This contradicts Paul’s submission to God’s will in 1:10 and Romans 15:32.
“The sea will guide me”
Paul trusts God’s will, not the sea; later a storm nearly wrecked his voyage (Acts 27:20).
In Romans 1, which phrase explains why creation gives knowledge about God?
God’s invisible qualities are “understood from His workmanship” (1:20).
Romans 1:20
“His workmanship”
“The traditions of the elders”
The tradition of the elders belonged to the Pharisees (Mark 7:3); Paul points to God’s workmanship.
“The temple sacrifices”
Temple sacrifices are not mentioned; God is known from His workmanship (1:20).
“The decrees of Rome”
Rome’s decrees are not mentioned; God is known from His workmanship (1:20).
“The wisdom of the Greeks”
“Greeks search for wisdom” (1 Corinthians 1:22), but 1:20 points to God’s workmanship.
In Romans 1, which phrase identifies the source of the gospel promise before Christ’s coming?
The gospel was “promised beforehand through His prophets in the Holy Scriptures” (1:2).
Romans 1:2
Through His prophets in the Holy Scriptures
Through Caesar in the imperial courts
Caesar has no part; the promise came through the prophets in Scripture (1:2).
Through priests in the temple treasury
Priests and the treasury are not mentioned; the promise came through His prophets (1:2).
Through angels in the desert
Angels are not mentioned; the promise came through His prophets in the Holy Scriptures (1:2).
Through philosophers in Athens
Paul debated philosophers in Athens (Acts 17:18), but the gospel was promised through the prophets.
In Romans 1, which phrase identifies the resurrection’s role in Jesus’ identity?
Jesus “was declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead” (1:4).
Romans 1:4
It made Him a descendant of David by birth
Jesus’ descent from David was “according to the flesh” (1:3), by birth, not by the resurrection.
It declared with power that He is the Son of God
It replaced the Holy Scriptures with a new message
The gospel was promised beforehand in the Holy Scriptures (1:2); the resurrection fulfills them, not replaces them.
It removed His lordship over His own people
The opposite: 1:4 ends by naming Him “Jesus Christ our Lord.”
It made Him a king over the city of Rome
Rome is not in view; the resurrection declared Him the Son of God (1:4).
In Romans 1, which phrase introduces Paul’s solemn assurance that he remembers the believers in Rome?
Paul writes, “God, whom I serve with my spirit… is my witness how constantly I remember you” (1:9).
Romans 1:9
“Moses is my witness”
Moses is not mentioned in Romans 1; Paul calls God as his witness (1:9).
“God, whom I serve with my spirit… is my witness”
“The church in Antioch is my witness”
The church in Antioch is not mentioned; Paul appeals to God as witness (1:9).
“My conscience alone is witness”
Paul speaks of conscience bearing witness in Romans 2:15, but in 1:9 his witness is God.
“Caesar himself is witness”
Caesar is not his witness; Paul calls God as witness, as also in 2 Corinthians 1:23.
In Romans 1, which sequence of human rebellion and God’s response is presented in the correct order?
Paul’s three “gave them over” steps: images led to impurity (1:23–24), the lie to dishonorable passions (1:25–26), and refusing to acknowledge God to a depraved mind (1:28).
Romans 1:23-28

They did not see fit to acknowledge God, so He gave them over to impurity; they exchanged the truth of God for a lie, so He gave them over to a depraved mind; they exchanged His glory for images, so He gave them over to dishonorable passions
The pairings are scrambled: idolatry led to impurity (1:23–24), the lie to dishonorable passions (1:25–26), and refusing God to a depraved mind (1:28).

They exchanged the glory of God for images, so God gave them over to impurity; they exchanged the truth of God for a lie, so God gave them over to dishonorable passions; they did not see fit to acknowledge God, so He gave them over to a depraved mind

They exchanged the glory of God for images, so God sent famine on their land; they exchanged the truth of God for a lie, so He sent them into exile; they did not acknowledge Him, so He struck them with plague
Paul names no famine, exile, or plague; God gave them over to impurity, dishonorable passions, and a depraved mind (1:24–28).
They exchanged the truth of God for a lie, so God gave them over to a depraved mind; then they exchanged the glory of God for images, so He gave them over to impurity and dishonorable passions
The order is reversed: idolatry and impurity come first (1:23–24), then the lie (1:25), and the depraved mind last (1:28).
They glorified God and gave thanks to Him, so He gave them wisdom; they worshiped the Creator rather than the creature, so He gave them peace; they acknowledged God, so He gave them a sound mind
The opposite: they neither glorified God nor gave thanks (1:21), and they worshiped the creature rather than the Creator (1:25).
In Romans 2, when Paul addresses the person who judges others, who does he say has “no excuse”?
Paul says in 2:1, “You, therefore, have no excuse, you who pass judgment on another,” because the judge does the same things and so condemns himself.
Romans 2:1
People who have never heard any part of the law
Paul argues in 2:14–15 that even people without the law show its work written on their hearts, so lacking the law is not what he means here.
Gentile idolaters who worship carved images alone
Paul’s target in 2:1 is the person who judges others, not only idolaters; the idolatry of the Gentiles was his subject earlier in the letter.
Anyone who judges another while doing the same things
Only the teachers who instruct others in Jerusalem
Paul does not limit the charge to teachers or to Jerusalem; it falls on anyone who judges another while doing the same things.
Only those who rob pagan temples in the night
Robbing temples comes up in 2:22 as one example of hypocrisy; it is not the group addressed in 2:1.
According to Romans chapter 2, what is God’s judgment against those who do evil based on?
Romans 2:2 says, “we know that God’s judgment against those who do such things is based on truth.”
Romans 2:2
Truth
Tradition
Tradition is what people hand down, but Paul says God’s verdict rests on truth, and 2:6 says He repays according to deeds.
Public opinion
God does not follow popular opinion; 2:11 says He does not show favoritism, so no crowd can sway Him.
The number of sacrifices offered
Sacrifices are never the measure in this chapter; God’s repayment is according to each one’s deeds (2:6).
National identity
National identity does not decide God’s judgment; He deals with Jew and Greek by the same standard (2:9–10).
In Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter 2, God’s kindness is meant to lead a person to what?
Romans 2:4 asks whether you disregard His kindness, “not realizing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance.”
Romans 2:4
Prosperity
Prosperity is not what Paul says kindness is for; he says it leads to repentance (2:4).
Knowledge
Knowledge is not named; the purpose Paul gives for God’s kindness, tolerance, and patience is repentance.
Power
Power belongs to God’s own character, but Paul does not say His kindness hands power to people; it leads them to repent.
Repentance
Long life
Long life is not promised in this verse; Paul says eternal life goes to those who persevere in doing good (2:7).
In the second chapter of Romans, what does Paul say God will do for each person?
Paul quotes the standard in 2:6: God “will repay each one according to his deeds,” echoing Psalm 62:12.
Romans 2:6
Overlook every secret thing that people hide
Paul says the opposite: God will judge men’s secrets through Christ Jesus (2:16), so nothing hidden is ignored.
Repay each one according to his deeds
Judge only the words that people speak aloud
Words are not the only measure; the standard in 2:6 is each one’s deeds, and 2:16 adds that God judges even secrets.
Save everyone in the same way without any distinction
Paul says there will be wrath for the wicked and eternal life for those who do good (2:7–8), so not everyone is treated equally.
Reward people according to the family they came from
Ancestry earns nothing with God, because He does not show favoritism (2:11) and repays according to deeds.
In Romans 2, what does God give to those who by perseverance in doing good seek glory, honor, and immortality?
Romans 2:7 says that to those who by perseverance in doing good seek glory, honor, and immortality, “He will give eternal life.”
Romans 2:7
Earthly wealth
Earthly wealth is not what Paul promises; those who seek glory, honor, and immortality receive eternal life (2:7).
Political peace
Peace is promised in 2:10 to everyone who does good, but political peace is not what 2:7 says God gives.
Long life in Canaan
Canaan and long life belong to the old covenant promises to Israel; Paul’s reward here is eternal life.
Prophetic visions
Prophetic visions are not mentioned in this chapter; the reward for persevering in good is eternal life.
Eternal life
According to Romans 2, what awaits those who are self-seeking, reject the truth, and follow wickedness?
Romans 2:8 says that for the self-seeking, who reject the truth and follow wickedness, “there will be wrath and anger.”
Romans 2:8
Wrath and anger
A second chance after death
Paul gives no hint of a second chance after death; he speaks of wrath and anger, and a day of judgment (2:5, 2:16).
Temporary discipline only
Paul speaks of wrath and anger, not mild or temporary discipline, for those who reject the truth (2:8).
Material loss
Material loss is not the outcome Paul names; the outcome is wrath and anger (2:8).
Silence from God
Silence from God is not Paul’s picture here; God’s righteous judgment will be revealed on the day of wrath (2:5).
In Romans 2, what does Paul say comes upon every human being who does evil, first for the Jew, then for the Greek?
Romans 2:9 says, “There will be trouble and distress for every human being who does evil, first for the Jew, then for the Greek.”
Romans 2:9
Famine and exile
Famine and exile are judgments from Israel’s history, but the pair Paul names in 2:9 is trouble and distress.
Shame and nakedness
Shame and nakedness recall the fall in Genesis 3, but they are not the pair in 2:9.
Trouble and distress
Sword and captivity
Sword and captivity describe national disasters in the prophets, not the pair in 2:9, which is trouble and distress.
Sorrow and sleep
Sorrow and sleep are not what Paul names; he says trouble and distress will come on every human being who does evil (2:9).
In Romans chapter 2, what does Paul say comes to everyone who does good, first for the Jew, then for the Greek?
Romans 2:10 promises “glory, honor, and peace for everyone who does good, first for the Jew, then for the Greek.”
Romans 2:10
Grace, mercy, and help
Grace, mercy, and help are real gifts of God, but Paul’s trio in 2:10 is glory, honor, and peace.
Wisdom, faith, and love
Wisdom, faith, and love are not the reward listed in 2:10, which is glory, honor, and peace.
Rest, safety, and joy
Rest, safety, and joy sound comforting, but they are not the words Paul uses in 2:10.
Glory, honor, and peace
Bread, shelter, and health
Bread, shelter, and health are earthly needs; Paul’s promise to those who do good is glory, honor, and peace (2:10).
In Romans 2, what does Paul plainly say God does not show?
Romans 2:11 says, “For God does not show favoritism.”
Romans 2:11
Mercy
Mercy is shown by God, as 2:4 stresses His kindness, tolerance, and patience; it is favoritism that He does not show.
Favoritism
Power
God does show power; Paul speaks of His judgment and wrath, and what He does not show is favoritism (2:11).
Justice
God shows perfect justice, since His righteous judgment will be revealed (2:5); the thing He does not show is favoritism.
Patience
God does show patience (2:4); Paul says plainly that He does not show favoritism (2:11).
In the discussion of the law in Romans 2, who will be declared righteous before God?
Romans 2:13 says, “it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but it is the doers of the law who will be declared righteous.”
Romans 2:13
The hearers of the law only
Paul says the opposite: merely hearing the law does not make anyone righteous before God (2:13).
The scribes
Scribes are not named in this chapter; Paul says it is the doers of the law who will be declared righteous (2:13).
The circumcised only
Paul argues that circumcision has value only if you observe the law (2:25), so being circumcised alone does not make one righteous.
The oldest believers
Age or seniority in the faith is not the test; God does not show favoritism (2:11) and declares the doers of the law righteous.
The doers of the law
According to Romans 2, what happens to those who sin apart from the law?
Romans 2:12 says, “All who sin apart from the law will also perish apart from the law.”
Romans 2:12
They perish apart from the law
They are excused automatically
Paul does not excuse them; he says they will perish apart from the law (2:12), and God’s judgment is based on truth (2:2).
They inherit the kingdom immediately
Inheriting the kingdom is not what Paul says of those who sin; they will perish, while eternal life goes to those who persevere in doing good (2:7).
They are judged only by angels
Angels are not named as judges; Paul says God will judge men’s secrets through Christ Jesus (2:16).
They return to dust without judgment
Paul does not describe them as simply returning to dust; he says they will perish apart from the law, and judgment is real (2:12, 2:16).
In Romans 2, when Gentiles who do not have the law do by nature what the law requires, what are they said to be?
Romans 2:14 says that Gentiles who do not have the law but do by nature what it requires “are a law to themselves.”
Romans 2:14
Sons of Abraham by blood
Being sons of Abraham by blood is not the point; Paul says these Gentiles are a law to themselves, though they lack the law (2:14).
Priests to the nations
Priests to the nations is a title for Israel in Exodus 19:6, not what Paul says about these Gentiles.
A law to themselves
Free from all judgment
They are not free from judgment; God will judge men’s secrets through Christ Jesus (2:16).
Equal to apostles
Apostles are not mentioned here; the Gentiles are called a law to themselves (2:14).
In Romans chapter 2, what do such Gentiles show is written on their hearts?
Romans 2:15 says these Gentiles “show that the work of the law is written on their hearts.”
Romans 2:15
The prophets
The prophets’ writings are not what Paul says is on their hearts; it is the work of the law (2:15).
The work of the law
The names of the tribes
Tribal names are not in view; Paul says the work of the law is written on their hearts (2:15).
The covenant sign of circumcision
Circumcision is the outward sign Paul contrasts with the heart (2:28–29), not what is written on these Gentiles’ hearts.
The psalms of David
David’s psalms are not mentioned; the work of the law is what is written on their hearts (2:15).
In Romans 2, what do people’s thoughts do as their consciences bear witness?
Romans 2:15 says their consciences bear witness, “their thoughts either accusing or defending them.”
Romans 2:15
They sing or lament
Singing and lamenting are responses in the Psalms, but Paul’s verse says thoughts accuse or defend (2:15).
They remember or forget
Remembering and forgetting are not what Paul says the thoughts do; they accuse or defend (2:15).
They rise or fall
Rising and falling describe people in other passages, not the thoughts in 2:15, which accuse or defend.
They bless or curse
Blessing and cursing are speech acts toward others; Paul says thoughts accuse or defend (2:15).
They accuse or defend
In Paul’s teaching in Romans 2, what does God judge on that coming day?
Romans 2:16 speaks of “the day when God will judge men’s secrets through Christ Jesus.”
Romans 2:16
Only public deeds
Paul says more than public deeds will be judged; God will judge men’s secrets (2:16).
Only spoken vows
Spoken vows are not singled out; the object of judgment in 2:16 is men’s secrets.
The works of angels
The works of angels are not the subject; Paul says God will judge men’s secrets (2:16).
Men’s secrets
The borders of nations
National borders are not what Paul has in mind; the verse speaks of men’s secrets being judged (2:16).
According to Romans 2, through whom will God judge men’s secrets?
Romans 2:16 says God will judge men’s secrets “through Christ Jesus, as proclaimed by my gospel.”
Romans 2:16
Christ Jesus
Moses
Moses gave the law, but Paul names Christ Jesus as the one through whom God judges men’s secrets (2:16).
Michael the archangel
Michael the archangel appears in Jude 1:9 and Daniel, but Paul does not name him as the agent of judgment here.
The church in Rome
The church in Rome receives the letter, but God’s judgment is through Christ Jesus (2:16).
Abraham
Abraham is a figure of faith elsewhere in Romans, not the agent of judgment; Paul names Christ Jesus (2:16).
In Romans 2:16, Paul says this message about judgment is proclaimed by what?
Romans 2:16 closes the thought about judgment “through Christ Jesus, as proclaimed by my gospel.”
Romans 2:16
The temple liturgy
The temple liturgy is not mentioned; Paul says the judgment is proclaimed by his gospel (2:16).
The wisdom of Solomon
Solomon’s wisdom does not appear in Romans 2; Paul points to his gospel (2:16).
My gospel
The law of Sinai alone
Sinai’s law is part of Paul’s argument, but the phrase in 2:16 is “my gospel.”
The Roman church elders
Paul does not cite the elders of Rome as the source; the message is proclaimed by his gospel (2:16).
In Romans 2, when Paul addresses someone who calls himself a Jew, what two things does he say that person does?
Romans 2:17 says, “if you call yourself a Jew; if you rely on the law and boast in God.”
Romans 2:17
Rejects the prophets and fears Caesar
Rejecting the prophets and fearing Caesar are not part of the description; the Jew relies on the law and boasts in God (2:17).

In Romans 8, through whom are believers more than conquerors?
Paul says we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us (8:37).
Romans 8:37
Through Moses who taught us

Through the law that guides us
The law cannot give this victory; 8:3 says it was powerless, and 8:37 says through Him who loved us.
Through angels who watch us
Angels watch over believers (Hebrews 1:14), but 8:37 says victory comes through Him who loved us.
Through Him who loved us
Through kings who defend us
Kings who defend are not the source; 8:37 says through Him who loved us.
In Romans 8:38, which pair does Paul say cannot separate believers from God’s love?
Paul says that neither death nor life can separate us from the love of God (8:38).
Romans 8:38
Seedtime and harvest
Seedtime and harvest (Genesis 8:22) are not in Paul’s list in 8:38.
Death and life
Sun and moon
Sun and moon are not in Paul’s list in 8:38.
North and south
North and south are not in Paul’s list in 8:38.
Youth and old age
Youth and old age are not in Paul’s list in 8:38.
In Romans 8:38, after mentioning the present and the future, what else does Paul say cannot separate us?
Paul says that neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, can separate us from the love of God (8:38).
Romans 8:38
Rivers
Rivers are not in Paul’s list in 8:38.
Mountains
Mountains are not in Paul’s list in 8:38.
Chariots
Chariots are not in Paul’s list in 8:38.
Powers
Merchants
Merchants are not in Paul’s list in 8:38.
In Romans 8:39, which pair of spatial extremes does Paul name?
Paul says neither height nor depth can separate us from the love of God (8:39).
Romans 8:39
East and west
East and west are not the pair named in 8:39.
Height and depth
Valley and hill
Valley and hill are not the pair named in 8:39.
Field and vineyard
Field and vineyard are not the pair named in 8:39.
Sea and shore
Sea and shore are not the pair named in 8:39.
In the closing assurance of Romans 8, what broader phrase follows height and depth?
Paul continues: neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God (8:39).
Romans 8:39
Nor anything else in all creation
Nor any tribe of Israel
Any tribe of Israel is not in 8:39; the phrase is nor anything else in all creation.
Nor any ship at sea
Any ship at sea is not in 8:39; the phrase is nor anything else in all creation.
Nor any feast in Judea
Any feast in Judea is not in 8:39; the phrase is nor anything else in all creation.
Nor any gate in Rome
Any gate in Rome is not in 8:39; the phrase is nor anything else in all creation.
In Romans 8:39, from what specifically can nothing separate believers?
Paul closes by saying nothing will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord (8:39).
Romans 8:39
The love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord
The wisdom of Solomon in Jerusalem
Solomon’s wisdom (1 Kings 4:29–34) is not what 8:39 says cannot be taken from believers.
The mercy seat in the tabernacle
The mercy seat (Exodus 25:17–22) is not what 8:39 names.
The promises to Noah alone
The promises to Noah (Genesis 9:11) are not what Paul closes with.
The songs of the temple choirs
The songs of the temple choirs are not what Paul closes with.
In Romans 8:4, whose righteous standard is fulfilled in believers who walk according to the Spirit?
Paul says God sent His Son so that the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk according to the Spirit (8:4).
Romans 8:4
The Sanhedrin’s
The Sanhedrin’s standard is not what Paul means; 8:4 speaks of the law’s righteous standard.
Caesar’s
Caesar’s standard is not in view; 8:4 names the righteous standard of the law.
The law’s
Rome’s
Rome’s standard is not in view; 8:4 names the righteous standard of the law.
The philosophers’
The philosophers’ standard is not in view; 8:4 names the righteous standard of the law.
In Romans 8:10, which combination matches Paul’s teaching if Christ is in you?
Paul says that if Christ is in you, your body is dead because of sin, yet your spirit is alive because of righteousness (8:10).
Romans 8:10
Body alive because of law, spirit dead because of fear
This reverses Paul: the body, not the spirit, is dead because of sin, and the spirit is alive because of righteousness (8:10).
Body hidden because of glory, spirit sleeping because of sorrow
Paul does not say the body is hidden because of glory or the spirit sleeping; 8:10 says the body is dead because of sin.
Body dead because of sin, spirit alive because of righteousness
Body glorified because of works, spirit justified because of birth
Paul does not credit works or birth; he says the spirit is alive because of righteousness (8:10).
Body strong because of zeal, spirit weak because of grief
Paul does not say the body is strong or the spirit weak; 8:10 says the body is dead because of sin, the spirit alive.
In Romans 8:15-16, which combined work of the Spirit is described?
Paul describes the Spirit of adoption by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!” (8:15) and who testifies that we are God’s children (8:16).
Romans 8:15-16
Sonship and witness
Sacrifice and cleansing
Sacrifice and cleansing are not the Spirit’s work in 8:15–16, which describe sonship and testimony.
Law and judgment
Law and judgment are not what 8:15–16 describe; the Spirit gives sonship and testifies.
Battle and victory
Battle and victory appear in 8:37, but 8:15–16 describe sonship and testimony.
Exile and return
Exile and return are not in 8:15–16; the Spirit gives sonship and testifies.
In Romans 8:17, which statement exactly matches Paul’s teaching on inheritance?
Paul says we are heirs: heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ (8:17).
Romans 8:17
Heirs of the earth and servants of the law
Paul does not call believers heirs of the earth and servants of the law; they are heirs of God (8:17).
Heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ
Heirs of Moses and sons of Levi
Moses and Levi are not the source of the inheritance; 8:17 says heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ.
Heirs of Rome and citizens of heaven
Rome is not the source of the inheritance; 8:17 says heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ.
Heirs of David and builders of the temple
David and the temple are not the source of the inheritance in 8:17; believers are heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ.
In Romans 8:20-21, what word shows that creation’s subjection to futility was not the end of the story?
Paul says creation was subjected to futility in hope that it will be set free from its bondage to decay (8:20–21).
Romans 8:20-21
Today
Today is not the word of hope; 8:20 says in hope.
In hope
By chance
By chance contradicts 8:20, which says creation was subjected by the One who subjected it, in hope.
At once
At once is not in 8:20–21; creation was subjected in hope of future freedom.
In secret
In secret is not in 8:20–21; the phrase that gives hope is in hope.
In Romans 8:23, which two expressions refer to the future hope believers still await?
Paul says believers groan as they wait eagerly for their adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies (8:23).
Romans 8:23
Adoption as sons and the redemption of our bodies
The ark of the covenant and the priesthood of Aaron
The ark and the priesthood are Old Testament institutions (Exodus 25:10; 28:1), not the future hope of 8:23.
Circumcision of the flesh and the offering of sacrifices
Circumcision and sacrifice belong to the law (Genesis 17:10; Leviticus 1:3) and are not the hope of 8:23.
The throne of David and the scepter of Judah
A throne and scepter are signs of kingship (Genesis 49:10), not the two expressions in 8:23.
The pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire by night
The pillar of cloud and fire led Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21), not the hope of 8:23.
In Romans 8:24, what does Paul say no one hopes for?
Paul asks, “Who hopes for what he can already see?” (8:24), meaning hope concerns what is not yet seen.
Romans 8:24
What he can already see
What God has promised
God’s promises are exactly what believers hope for; Paul’s point is that no one hopes for what is already seen (8:24).
What the prophets wrote
The prophets’ writings pointed to hope, but 8:24 says no one hopes for what he already sees.
What the temple displayed
What the temple displayed is not in view; 8:24 says no one hopes for what he can already see.
What Israel remembered
What Israel remembered is not in view; 8:24 says no one hopes for what is already seen.
In Romans 8:26-27, which description correctly combines the Spirit’s help in prayer?
Paul says the Spirit helps us in weakness, intercedes with groans too deep for words, and intercedes for the saints according to the will of God (8:26–27).
Romans 8:26-27
He teaches believers the right words and the grammar of prayer
Paul says nothing about teaching grammar and memory; the Spirit intercedes when we do not know how to pray (8:26).
He intercedes with groans too deep for words and according to God’s will
He removes every weakness from believers at once and for all time
The Spirit helps us in our weakness (8:26); He does not remove all weakness at once.
He prays only for the apostles gathered in Jerusalem
The Spirit intercedes for the saints (8:27), not only for apostles in Jerusalem.
He speaks to believers only through thunder and fire
The Spirit intercedes with groans too deep for words (8:26), not with thunder.
In Romans 8:28, the promise that God works all things together for good is limited to which people?
Paul limits the promise to those who love God and are called according to His purpose (8:28).
Romans 8:28
Everyone without exception regardless of response
The promise is limited to those who love Him and are called (8:28), not to everyone regardless of response.
Only residents of Rome
Residents of Rome are not singled out; 8:28 names those who love God and are called.
Those who love God and are called according to His purpose
Only the sons of Aaron
The sons of Aaron are not singled out; 8:28 names those who love God and are called.
Only kings of Judah
The kings of Judah are not singled out; 8:28 names those who love God and are called.
In Romans 8:29, why are the predestined conformed to the image of God’s Son?
Paul says God predestined believers to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers (8:29).
Romans 8:29
So they can judge the twelve tribes
Judging the twelve tribes is promised to the apostles (Matthew 19:28), not stated as the purpose in 8:29.
So He would be the firstborn among many brothers
So they can rebuild Jerusalem
Rebuilding Jerusalem is not the purpose given in 8:29; it is that the Son be the firstborn among many brothers.
So they can avoid suffering entirely
Avoiding suffering entirely is not the purpose; 8:17 says believers suffer with Christ.
So they can replace the angels
Replacing the angels is not the purpose given in 8:29.
In Romans 8:33-34, which legal-style pair of questions does Paul raise to stress the believer’s security?
Paul asks, “Who will bring any charge against God’s elect?” (8:33) and, “Who is there to condemn us?” (8:34).
Romans 8:33-34
Who will teach us and who will feed us
Teaching and feeding are not the questions Paul asks in 8:33–34.
Who will accuse and who will condemn
Who will buy us and who will sell us
Buying and selling are not the questions Paul asks in 8:33–34.
Who will house us and who will clothe us
Housing and clothing are not the questions Paul asks in 8:33–34.
Who will crown us and who will praise us
Crowning and praising are not the questions Paul asks in 8:33–34.
In Romans 8, which three are all described with groaning in this section?
Creation groans (8:22), believers groan inwardly (8:23), and the Spirit intercedes with groans too deep for words (8:26).
Kings, priests, and prophets
Kings, priests and prophets are not said to groan in 8:22–26.
Jews, Greeks, and Romans
Jews, Greeks and Romans are not the three groaning in 8:22–26.
Creation, believers, and the Spirit
Heaven, earth, and sea only
Heaven, earth and sea are not said to groan in 8:22–26; creation, believers and the Spirit do.
Peter, James, and John
Peter, James and John are not named in Romans 8.
In Romans 8:29-30, which sequence matches Paul’s order of God’s saving actions?
Paul’s chain in 8:29–30 begins with those God foreknew, then predestined, called, justified and glorified.
Romans 8:29-30
Called, glorified, foreknew, justified
This puts called and glorified before foreknew; Paul begins with foreknew (8:29).
Justified, predestined, called, foreknew
This ends with foreknew; Paul begins with it (8:29).
Foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified
Glorified, called, foreknew, predestined
This begins with glorified; Paul ends with it (8:30).
Predestined, glorified, called, justified
This puts glorified before called and justified; Paul puts glorified last (8:30).
In Romans 8:35, which of these is not one of the hardships Paul names as unable to separate believers from the love of Christ?
Paul lists trouble, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger and sword (8:35); shipwreck is not among them.
Romans 8:35
Distress
Distress is named in 8:35.
Persecution
Persecution is named in 8:35.
Famine
Famine is named in 8:35.
Shipwreck
Sword
Sword is named in 8:35.
In Romans 8:38-39, which of these is not specifically named in Paul’s list of things that cannot separate believers from God’s love?
Paul’s list in 8:38–39 includes death, life, angels, principalities, the present, the future, powers, height and depth; sickness is not named.
Romans 8:38-39
Death
Death is named in 8:38.
Future
The future is named in 8:38.
Height
Height is named in 8:39.
Sickness
Depth
Depth is named in 8:39.
In Romans 8, which pairing correctly reflects Paul’s two love expressions near the chapter’s end?
Paul speaks of the love of Christ in 8:35 and closes with the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord (8:39).
Romans 8:35, 39
The love of Moses and the love of David
Moses and David are not named in Romans 8:35–39.
The love of Christ and the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord
The love of angels and the love of prophets

The love of the temple and the love of the law

The love of Rome and the love of Jerusalem
Rome and Jerusalem are not the loves Paul names in 8:35–39.
In Romans 8:34, which full set of truths about Christ Jesus is used to answer the question of condemnation?
Paul answers the question of condemnation by saying Christ Jesus died, was raised to life, is at the right hand of God, and is interceding for us (8:34).
Romans 8:34
He taught in Galilee, fed the crowds, walked on water, and entered Jerusalem

He died, was raised to life, is at the right hand of God, and intercedes for us
He was born in Bethlehem, fled to Egypt, worked in Nazareth, and called twelve disciples
Birth in Bethlehem, flight to Egypt, work in Nazareth and calling twelve disciples are Gospel events, not Paul’s four truths in 8:34.
He was transfigured, silenced demons, healed lepers, and multiplied loaves
Transfiguration, silencing demons, healing lepers and multiplying loaves are Gospel events, not Paul’s four truths in 8:34.
He fasted forty days, quoted Moses, rode a donkey, and slept in a boat
Fasting forty days, quoting Moses, riding a donkey and sleeping in a boat are Gospel events, not Paul’s four truths in 8:34.
At the opening of Romans 9, Paul says he is speaking the truth in whom?
Paul opens with “I speak the truth in Christ; I am not lying” (9:1), grounding his claim in his union with Christ.
Romans 9:1
Abraham
Abraham appears later in the chapter (9:7) as the father of Israel, but Paul does not say he speaks the truth in him.
Christ
Moses
Moses is named in 9:15 as the man to whom God spoke about mercy, not as the one in whom Paul speaks the truth.
David
David is not mentioned anywhere in Romans 9; Paul’s oath is “in Christ.”
Israel

In Romans 9, Paul says his conscience is confirmed by whom?
Paul says his conscience confirms his truthfulness “in the Holy Spirit” (9:1).
Romans 9:1
The apostles
Paul appeals to no other apostles here; his conscience is confirmed by the Holy Spirit (9:1).
The Law
The Law is listed among Israel’s privileges (9:4), but it is not what confirms Paul’s conscience.
The Holy Spirit

At the start of Romans chapter 9, what does Paul say fills his heart regarding Israel?
Paul writes, “I have deep sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart” (9:2), grieving over his fellow Israelites.
Romans 9:2
Quiet joy and settled contentment
Paul’s heart is heavy over Israel’s unbelief; he speaks of sorrow, not joy or contentment (9:2).
Peace and complete confidence
Paul is confident that God’s word has not failed (9:6), but over his own people he feels anguish, not peace.
Fear and lasting confusion

Deep sorrow and unceasing anguish
Anger and a desire for revenge

In Romans 9, what does Paul say he could wish for himself for the sake of his brothers, the Israelites?
Paul says he “could wish that I myself were cursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers” (9:3), showing the depth of his love for Israel.
Romans 9:3
To become a king
Paul seeks no honor; his wish is to be cursed for his people’s sake (9:3), not to gain a throne.
To be sent to Rome

To be cursed and cut off from Christ
To return to Tarsus
Tarsus was Paul’s hometown (Acts 21:39), but returning there is not the wish he states in 9:3.
To offer more sacrifices
Paul’s wish is a costly, self-giving love for Israel (9:3), not an offer of more sacrifices.
In Paul’s words in Romans 9, who are the “brothers” for whom he feels such anguish?
Paul calls them “my brothers, my own flesh and blood, the people of Israel” (9:3–4).
Romans 9:3-4
The believers in the church at Corinth
Paul wrote to the Corinthians in other letters, but here the “brothers” are his Israelite kinsmen (9:3–4).
The Christians living in the city of Rome
The Roman believers are his readers; the “brothers” he grieves for are his own people, the people of Israel (9:3–4).
The churches he had planted in Galatia
The Galatians were churches Paul wrote to elsewhere; in 9:3–4 the brothers are “the people of Israel.”
Only the priests from the tribe of Levi
The Levites were only one tribe; Paul’s anguish is for all Israel, “my own flesh and blood” (9:3–4).
His own flesh and blood, the Israelites

Among Israel’s privileges Paul lists “the adoption as sons” (9:4).
Romans 9:4
Adoption as sons
Rebuilding the temple walls
Rebuilding the temple walls was Nehemiah’s work (Nehemiah 2–6), not an item in Paul’s list in 9:4.
The exile to Babylon
The exile to Babylon was a judgment on Judah (2 Kings 25), not one of the privileges Paul lists.
The Day of Pentecost
Pentecost is the coming of the Spirit on the church (Acts 2), not a privilege in Paul’s list for Israel.
The office of deacon
Deacons appear in the church (Philippians 1:1), not in Paul’s list of Israel’s privileges in 9:4.
According to Paul’s list in Romans 9, what else belongs to Israel?
Paul lists “the divine glory” among Israel’s privileges (9:4).
Romans 9:4
The ministry of reconciliation
The ministry of reconciliation was given to believers in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:18); it is not in Paul’s list for Israel.
The divine glory
The island of Patmos
Patmos is the island where John received Revelation (Revelation 1:9), not a privilege of Israel.
The ark’s recovery from Philistia
The ark’s return from Philistia is told in 1 Samuel 5–6, but Paul does not include it in 9:4.
The mission to Nineveh
Jonah’s mission to Nineveh (Jonah 1–3) is not among the privileges Paul names in 9:4.
In Romans chapter 9, which of these is named as belonging to Israel?
Paul says “theirs are… the covenants” (9:4).
Romans 9:4
The seven churches
The seven churches are addressed in Revelation 2–3, not named as Israel’s possession in 9:4.
The covenants
The walls of Jericho
The walls of Jericho fell in Joshua 6; they are not one of the privileges in Paul’s list.
The throne of Caesar
Caesar’s throne belonged to Rome, not to Israel; Paul’s list in 9:4 names spiritual privileges.
The Areopagus
The Areopagus is where Paul spoke in Athens (Acts 17), not a privilege of Israel in 9:4.
In Paul’s summary of Israel’s blessings in Romans 9, what was given to them?
Paul includes “the giving of the law” among Israel’s privileges (9:4).
Romans 9:4
The crown of thorns
The crown of thorns was pressed on Jesus by soldiers (John 19:2); it is not one of Israel’s privileges.
The keys of the kingdom
Jesus promised the keys of the kingdom to Peter (Matthew 16:19), not to Israel in Paul’s list.
The giving of the Law
The new tongues of fire
Tongues of fire came at Pentecost (Acts 2:3), not in Paul’s list of Israel’s privileges.
The lot of Matthias
The lot fell to Matthias in Acts 1:26 to replace Judas; it is not in Paul’s list in 9:4.
In Romans 9, what form of worship does Paul say belongs to Israel?
Paul lists “the temple worship” among the privileges of Israel (9:4).
Romans 9:4
Temple worship
House-church worship
House churches existed among believers (Romans 16:5), but they are not an item in Paul’s list of Israel’s privileges.
Mountain worship in Samaria
Mountain worship in Samaria was a Samaritan practice (John 4:20), not one of Israel’s privileges in 9:4.
Worship before the golden calf
Worship before the golden calf was Israel’s sin (Exodus 32), not a blessing in Paul’s list.
Worship in Athens
Athens is where Paul preached to Greeks (Acts 17); worship there is not in his list for Israel.
In Romans 9, Paul says, “Theirs are the” what?
Paul says, “Theirs are the patriarchs” (9:5), naming Israel’s forefathers among its privileges.
Romans 9:5
Apostles
Apostles were Christ’s messengers; Paul’s list names Israel’s forefathers, the patriarchs (9:5).
Kings of the Gentiles
Kings of the Gentiles are not part of Paul’s list; he names Israel’s own ancestors (9:5).
Patriarchs
Temple guards
Temple guards are not in Paul’s list; the temple worship he names in 9:4 is a different thing.
Fishermen
Some of Jesus’ disciples were fishermen (Matthew 4:18), but fishermen are not in Paul’s list in 9:5.
In Romans 9:5, Paul says the human descent of which person proceeds from Israel’s patriarchs, and calls Him “God over all”?
Paul says “from them proceeds the human descent of Christ, who is God over all” (9:5).
Romans 9:5
John the Baptist
John the Baptist was a man sent from God (John 1:6), but Paul calls only Christ “God over all” (9:5).
Moses
Moses was Israel’s lawgiver, but he is not called “God over all.”
Elijah
Elijah was a prophet, but 9:5 is about the one who is “God over all.”
Christ
Paul
Paul was himself an Israelite, but the one called “God over all” in 9:5 is Christ.
In Romans 9:5, how does Paul describe Christ after mentioning His human descent from Israel?
Paul calls Christ “God over all, forever worthy of praise! Amen” (9:5).
Romans 9:5
The first and greatest of created beings

A faithful servant of God and nothing more

A great prophet raised up in Galilee
Many people called Jesus a prophet, but Romans 9:5 describes Him as God over all, not merely a prophet.
A king who ranks below the angels
Hebrews 2:9 says Jesus was made a little lower than the angels for a time, but Romans 9:5 calls Him “God over all.”
God over all, forever worthy of praise
Early in Romans 9, what does Paul say has not failed?

Romans 9:6
The temple curtain
The temple curtain was torn at Jesus’ death (Matthew 27:51); Paul says God’s word has not failed.
God’s word
Abraham’s memory

Israel’s language
Israel’s language is not discussed in Romans 9; the point is that God’s word has not failed (9:6).
Moses’ staff
Moses’ staff is not mentioned in Romans 9; Moses appears only as the one God spoke to about mercy (9:15).
In Romans 9, what statement does Paul make about those descended from Israel?

Every one of them speaks as a prophet of God
Paul does not call all Israel’s descendants prophets; he says not all of them are truly Israel (9:6).
Not all who are descended from Israel are Israel

Yes, every descendant without exception

Yes, but only after circumcision

No, not all are counted as his children
No, because Abraham had no children

Only the Egyptians were counted

In Romans 9, through whom does God say Abraham’s offspring will be reckoned?
God said, “Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned” (9:7; Genesis 21:12).
Romans 9:7
Ishmael

Isaac
Esau

Jacob

Lot

According to Romans 9, who are regarded as Abraham’s offspring in the fullest sense?
Paul says “it is the children of the promise who are regarded as offspring” (9:8).
Romans 9:8
The children of the flesh
Paul says the opposite: “it is not the children of the flesh who are God’s children” (9:8).
The oldest sons only

The children of the promise
The kings of Judah
The kings of Judah are not mentioned in Romans 9; the offspring are the children of the promise (9:8).
