Paul says in 2:6–7, “not the wisdom of this age,” but “the mysterious and hidden wisdom of God.”
1 Corinthians 2:6-7
Not the wisdom of this age, but God’s hidden wisdom
Not Hebrew wisdom, but Roman wisdom
Paul’s contrast is not between Hebrew and Roman wisdom; it is between the wisdom of this age and God’s hidden wisdom (2:6–7).
Not prophetic wisdom, but priestly wisdom
Prophetic versus priestly wisdom is not the contrast; Paul sets this age’s wisdom against God’s hidden wisdom (2:6–7).
Not written wisdom, but oral wisdom
Written versus oral wisdom is not Paul’s contrast in 2:6–7.
Not ancient wisdom, but modern wisdom
Ancient versus modern is not the point; Paul says the wisdom was destined before time began (2:7).
In chapter 2 of 1 Corinthians, which person cannot welcome the things of the Spirit, and for what combined reason?

Paul says in 2:14, “The natural man does not accept the things that come from the Spirit of God. For they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned.”
1 Corinthians 2:14
The mature believer, because they are too deep
The mature believer is the one among whom Paul speaks wisdom (2:6); he is not the one who rejects the Spirit’s things.
The natural man, because they seem foolish and are spiritually discerned
The apostle, because he trembles
The apostle’s trembling (2:3) is about how Paul came, not the reason anyone rejects the Spirit’s things.
The ruler, because he lacks a title
Titles are not mentioned; the natural man rejects spiritual things because they seem foolish and are spiritually discerned (2:14).
The teacher, because he lacks scrolls
Scrolls are not mentioned; the reason is that the things are foolishness to him and spiritually discerned (2:14).
In Paul’s statement about what the rulers did to Jesus, which title for Jesus sharpens the seriousness of their blindness?
Paul says in 2:8 that the rulers would not have crucified “the Lord of glory.”
1 Corinthians 2:8
Bread of Life
“Bread of Life” is Jesus’ self-description in John 6:35, not Paul’s title in 2:8.
Son of Man
“Son of Man” is Jesus’ favorite self-designation in the Gospels, but Paul’s title in 2:8 is the Lord of glory.
Lord of glory
Good Shepherd
“Good Shepherd” is from John 10:11, not 1 Corinthians 2:8.
Morning Star
“Morning Star” is from Revelation 22:16, not 1 Corinthians 2:8.
Paul uses a comparison in 1 Corinthians 2 between human self-knowledge and divine knowledge. Which statement matches his analogy?
Paul asks in 2:11, “who among men knows the thoughts of man except his own spirit within him? So too, no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God.”
1 Corinthians 2:11
As kings know the nations they rule, so prophets know God
Kings and nations are not part of Paul’s comparison; it is a man’s own spirit and the Spirit of God (2:11).
As a person’s own spirit knows that person’s thoughts, so the Spirit of God knows God’s thoughts
As priests know the sacrifices they offer, so angels know God
Priests and sacrifices are not part of the analogy; Paul compares a man’s spirit with God’s Spirit (2:11).
As parents know their children, so rulers know the Lord
Parents and children are not part of Paul’s comparison; the analogy is the spirit within a man and the Spirit of God (2:11).
As scribes know the Law they copy, so philosophers know God
Scribes and the Law are not part of the comparison; Paul says only the Spirit of God knows God’s thoughts (2:11).
In Paul’s quotation about what God has prepared, which three human capacities are said to be insufficient to discover it?
Paul quotes in 2:9, “No eye has seen, no ear has heard, no heart has imagined, what God has prepared for those who love Him.”
1 Corinthians 2:9
Eye, ear, and heart
Hand, mouth, and strength
Hand, mouth, and strength are not the capacities in the quotation, which names eye, ear, and heart (2:9).
Law, altar, and priesthood
Law, altar, and priesthood are not part of the quotation, which names eye, ear, and heart (2:9).
Youth, age, and memory
Youth, age, and memory are not in the quotation (2:9).
Faith, hope, and love
Faith, hope, and love appear in 1 Corinthians 13:13, not in 2:9, which names eye, ear, and heart.
When Paul explains how he communicates spiritual truth in chapter 2, which wording best matches his claim?
Paul says in 2:13, “in words taught by the Spirit, expressing spiritual truths in spiritual words.”
1 Corinthians 2:13
In words taught by famous rabbis
Famous rabbis are not mentioned; Paul says his words were taught by the Spirit (2:13).
In words taught by human wisdom, polished by debate
Paul says his words were not taught by human wisdom (2:13), and he says nothing of polish by debate.
In words taught by the Spirit, expressing spiritual truths in spiritual words
In secret sayings for rulers only
Secret sayings for rulers are the opposite; the rulers did not understand God’s wisdom (2:8).
In songs that cannot be understood
Songs that cannot be understood are not what Paul describes; he says spiritual truths in spiritual words (2:13).
Which summary best reflects the full movement of 1 Corinthians 2 in Paul’s message to the church in Corinth?
Chapter 2 moves from Christ crucified (2:2) and the Spirit’s power instead of human wisdom (2:4–5) to God’s hidden wisdom, revealed by the Spirit (2:10) and spiritually discerned (2:14).
1 Corinthians 2:1-16
Paul praises eloquence, celebrates worldly rulers, and says natural minds grasp God’s truth without help
Paul rejects eloquence (2:1), says the rulers are coming to nothing (2:6), and says the natural man cannot accept spiritual truth (2:14).
Paul centers on Christ crucified, rejects reliance on human wisdom, and teaches that God’s hidden wisdom is revealed by the Spirit and discerned spiritually
Paul replaces the gospel with philosophy, and says that faith should rest on clever argument and learning
Paul does not replace the gospel with philosophy; he says faith should rest on God’s power, not men’s wisdom (2:5).
Paul teaches that only political power and royal authority can spread God’s kingdom across the nations
Political power is not what Paul relies on; he came in weakness and fear (2:3) and his message rests on the Spirit’s power (2:4).
Paul says spiritual truth belongs only to rulers and scholars, who alone are able to understand God’s wisdom
Spiritual truth is not limited to rulers and scholars; the rulers did not understand it (2:8), and God reveals it by the Spirit (2:10).
In Paul’s correction to the church in Corinth in 1 Corinthians 3, how did he say he had to address them?
Paul says he “could not address you as spiritual, but as worldly—as infants in Christ” (3:1), because they were spiritually immature.
1 Corinthians 3:1
As mature saints
Paul says the opposite: he could not address them as spiritual, let alone mature (3:1).
As worldly—as infants in Christ
As prophets of the Spirit
Paul could not even call them spiritual, so he certainly did not treat them as Spirit-led prophets (3:1).
As blameless elders
Paul does not call them blameless elders; he rebukes their jealousy and dissension (3:3).
As strangers to grace
Paul never calls them strangers to grace; he calls them infants in Christ (3:1), who still belong to Christ (3:23).
In 1 Corinthians 3, what kind of spiritual food did Paul say he had given the believers in Corinth?
Paul says, “I gave you milk, not solid food,” because they were not yet ready for solid food (3:2); milk pictures basic teaching.
1 Corinthians 3:2
Bread and wine
Bread belongs to the Lord’s Supper (Luke 22:19), but Paul’s food picture here is milk versus solid food (3:2).
Solid food, not milk
This reverses the verse: Paul gave milk, not solid food, because they could not yet handle more (3:2).
Milk, not solid food
Meat and herbs
Meat and herbs are not mentioned; Paul’s food image is milk and solid food (3:2).
Honey and curds
Curds and honey appear in Isaiah 7:15, but Paul’s food picture here is milk versus solid food (3:2).
Why did Paul say the Corinthians were still not ready for solid food in 1 Corinthians 3?
Paul says they were not ready for solid food because “you are still worldly” (3:3), shown by their jealousy and dissension.
1 Corinthians 3:2-3
They lacked teachers
Lack of teachers was not the problem; Paul and Apollos had both served them (3:5–6).
They were still worldly
They were under persecution
Persecution is not mentioned; the problem was their own jealousy and dissension (3:3).
They had forgotten the Law
Forgetting the Law is not the issue; Paul rebukes their worldly factions (3:3–4).
They were fasting
No fasting is mentioned; Paul’s feeding picture is spiritual milk and solid food (3:2).
In Paul’s words to Corinth, what behavior showed that they were still worldly?
Paul asks, “since there is jealousy and dissension among you, are you not worldly?” (3:3).
1 Corinthians 3:3
Silence and solitude
Corinth’s trouble was noisy rivalry, not silence; they were quarreling over leaders (3:3–4).
Jealousy and dissension
Generosity and prayer
Generosity and prayer are not the evidence Paul cites; he points to jealousy and dissension (3:3).
Travel and trade
Travel and trade are not mentioned; Paul points to jealousy and dissension (3:3).
Visions and dreams
Visions and dreams are not what Paul names here; the sign of worldliness was jealousy and dissension (3:3).
In the passage about divisions in Corinth, what did Paul call Apollos and himself?
Paul asks, “What then is Apollos? And what is Paul?” and answers that they are “servants through whom you believed” (3:5).
1 Corinthians 3:5
Rulers over the church
Paul claims no ruling status; he and Apollos are servants whom the Lord assigned (3:5).
Servants through whom you believed
Judges of the saints
Paul gives himself and Apollos no judicial role; they are servants assigned by the Lord (3:5).
Founders of separate churches
Separate churches is the opposite of Paul’s point; the planter and the waterer are one in purpose (3:8).
Keepers of the temple
Paul says the church itself is God’s temple (3:16); he and Apollos are servants, not temple keepers (3:5).
In Paul’s farming illustration for the church at Corinth, who said, “I planted the seed”?
Paul writes, “I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow” (3:6).
1 Corinthians 3:6
Cephas
Cephas is named only later, among the things that belong to the believers (3:22), not as the planter.
Apollos
Apollos is the one who watered the seed, not the one who planted it (3:6).
Paul
Timothy
Timothy is not mentioned in this chapter; the planter was Paul (3:6).
Barnabas
Barnabas is not mentioned in this chapter; Paul says he himself planted (3:6).
According to 1 Corinthians 3, who made the seed grow in the work at Corinth?
Paul says “God made it grow” (3:6), and that neither planter nor waterer is anything, “but only God, who makes things grow” (3:7).
1 Corinthians 3:6-7
Paul
Paul planted, but he says neither the planter nor the waterer is anything (3:7).
Apollos
Apollos watered the seed, but the growth came from God (3:6).
The Corinthians
The Corinthians are God’s field (3:9), not the source of the growth.
God
The elders
Elders are not mentioned in the farming picture; the growth comes from God alone (3:7).
In 1 Corinthians 3:9, what two images did Paul use for the believers in Corinth?
Paul says, “you are God’s field, God’s building” (3:9), moving from farming imagery to construction imagery.
1 Corinthians 3:9
God’s vineyard and God’s army
Paul’s images in 3:9 are a field and a building, not a vineyard or an army.
God’s flock and God’s lampstand
A flock and a lampstand are not the images in this verse; Paul says field and building (3:9).
God’s field and God’s building
God’s family and God’s bride
Paul’s images in 3:9 are a field and a building, not a family and a bride.
God’s priesthood and God’s nation
A priesthood and a nation are not the images in 3:9; Paul says field and building.
In the building metaphor addressed to Corinth, what kind of builder did Paul say he was?
Paul says, “By the grace God has given me, I laid a foundation as an expert builder” (3:10).
1 Corinthians 3:10
A careless laborer
Paul says he laid the foundation “as an expert builder,” the opposite of careless (3:10).
An expert builder
A temple priest
Paul does not call himself a temple priest; the church is the temple (3:16), and he is an expert builder (3:10).
A wandering mason
A wandering mason is not Paul’s description; he calls himself an expert builder (3:10).
A royal architect
Paul claims no royal title; he calls himself an expert builder by God’s grace (3:10).
By what did Paul say he laid the foundation in Corinth?
Paul says, “By the grace God has given me, I laid a foundation” (3:10); his work was credited to God’s grace, not personal merit.
1 Corinthians 3:10
By human wisdom
Paul rejects human wisdom as a basis; the wisdom of this world is foolishness in God’s sight (3:19).
By inherited authority
Paul credits God’s grace, not inherited authority; he says the Lord assigned each one’s role (3:5).
By the grace God had given him
By signs alone
Paul does not rest his work on signs alone; he credits the grace God gave him (3:10).
By Roman protection
Roman protection is not mentioned; Paul credits God’s grace (3:10).
In 1 Corinthians 3, what warning did Paul give to anyone building on the foundation?
Paul warns, “each one must be careful how he builds” (3:10), since the Day will test the work (3:13).
1 Corinthians 3:10
Build quickly
Paul urges care, not speed, since the Day will test every work (3:13).
Build privately
Privacy is not the point; the Day will bring each person’s work to light (3:13).
Be careful how he builds
Build with cedar only
Cedar is not mentioned; the materials are gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay or straw (3:12).
Avoid all testing
Paul says the opposite: the fire will prove the quality of each man’s work (3:13).
In Paul’s construction analogy for the Corinthian church, what is the only foundation that can be laid?
Paul says, “no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ” (3:11).
1 Corinthians 3:11
The Law of Moses
The Law is not the foundation Paul names; he says the foundation is Jesus Christ (3:11).
The apostles
Ephesians 2:20 mentions the foundation of the apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone, but here Paul names Christ alone (3:11).
The church in Jerusalem
The Jerusalem church is not named; Paul says the one foundation is Jesus Christ (3:11).
Jesus Christ
Spiritual gifts
Spiritual gifts are not the foundation; Paul names Jesus Christ (3:11).
In the list of building materials in 1 Corinthians 3, which set contains only materials Paul actually named?
Paul lists “gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw” (3:12), contrasting lasting and perishable materials.
1 Corinthians 3:12
Gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw
Iron, bronze, cedar, clay, lime, reeds
This set shares nothing with Paul’s list of gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay and straw (3:12).
Marble, pearl, cedar, wool, flax, brick
This mixes items Paul never names; his six materials are gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay and straw (3:12).
Gold, silver, oil, wine, grain, salt
Gold and silver are named, but oil, wine, grain and salt are not (3:12).
Stone, pitch, gopher wood, bronze, scarlet, linen
Gopher wood is from Noah’s ark (Genesis 6:14), and none of these items is in Paul’s list (3:12).
In the Corinth passage about building on Christ, what will make each person’s workmanship evident?
Paul says each man’s workmanship “will be evident, because the Day will bring it to light” (3:13).
1 Corinthians 3:13
The applause of the church
Church applause is not the test; the Day and its fire are (3:13).
The passage of years
The passing of years is not the test; Paul points to the Day (3:13).
The Day that brings it to light
The city magistrates
City magistrates are not mentioned; the Day brings the work to light (3:13).
Dreams and visions
Dreams and visions are not mentioned; the Day reveals the work by fire (3:13).
In 1 Corinthians 3, what does the fire test or prove?
Paul says “the fire will prove the quality of each man’s work” (3:13).
1 Corinthians 3:13
The number of workers
The fire does not count workers; it tests the quality of each man’s work (3:13).
The age of the builder
The builder’s age is irrelevant; the fire proves the quality of his work (3:13).
The quality of each person’s work
The size of the church
Size is not the test; the fire proves quality (3:13).
The eloquence of the preacher
Eloquence is not tested; the fire proves the quality of each man’s work (3:13).
According to Paul’s teaching in 1 Corinthians 3, what happens if a person’s work survives the testing?
Paul says, “If what he has built survives, he will receive a reward” (3:14).
1 Corinthians 3:14
He becomes an apostle
The reward is not apostleship; Paul says only that the builder will receive a reward (3:14).
He receives a reward
He avoids all suffering
Paul does not promise freedom from suffering; the reward is for work that survives the fire (3:14).
He is made ruler of Corinth
Paul gives no rulership over Corinth; he tells them to stop boasting in men (3:21).
He no longer needs faith
Nothing in the passage makes faith unnecessary; the reward is for work that lasts (3:14).
In Paul’s warning to the believers in Corinth, what did he say they collectively are?
Paul asks, “Do you not know that you yourselves are God’s temple,” using temple language for the whole church (3:16).
1 Corinthians 3:16
God’s mountain
Paul calls them God’s field, building and temple (3:9, 16), not a mountain.
God’s temple
God’s courtroom
Paul does not call them a courtroom; they are God’s temple (3:16).
God’s ship
A ship is not among Paul’s images; they are God’s field, building and temple (3:9, 16).
God’s vineyard wall
A vineyard wall is not Paul’s image; he says they are God’s temple (3:16).
According to 1 Corinthians 3:16, who dwells in the believers in Corinth?
Paul says, “God’s Spirit dwells in you” (3:16), which is why the church is holy.
1 Corinthians 3:16
The spirit of Elijah
Elijah’s spirit is not mentioned; Paul says God’s Spirit dwells in them (3:16).
An angelic host
An angelic host is not said to dwell in them; it is God’s Spirit (3:16).
God’s Spirit
The souls of the apostles
The apostles’ souls are not the indwelling presence; Paul says God’s Spirit dwells in them (3:16).
The wisdom of Solomon
Solomon’s wisdom is not mentioned; Paul says worldly wisdom is foolishness in God’s sight (3:19).
In the temple warning given to Corinth, what does Paul say God will do to anyone who destroys God’s temple?
Paul warns, “If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him; for God’s temple is holy” (3:17).
1 Corinthians 3:17
Ignore him
Ignoring him is far too mild; Paul warns that God will destroy him (3:17).
Exile him
Exile is not the penalty; Paul says God will destroy the one who destroys His temple (3:17).
God will destroy him
Crown him
Paul gives no crown to a temple destroyer; the penalty is destruction (3:17).
Test him a second time
A second test is not mentioned; the warning is that God will destroy him (3:17).
In 1 Corinthians 3, what should a person do if he thinks he is wise in this age?
Paul says that anyone who thinks he is wise in this age “should become a fool, so that he may become wise” (3:18).
1 Corinthians 3:18
Teach others what he knows right away
Paul does not tell the self-confident to start teaching; he tells them to become fools in order to be wise (3:18).
Become a fool so that he may become wise
Seek a higher office in the church
Paul warns against boasting in men (3:21), not seeking rank; the wise must become fools (3:18).
Withdraw from the church altogether
Paul never tells the wise to leave the church; he calls them to humility (3:18).
Write a new law for the church
Paul says nothing about writing a new law; the wise in this age must become fools (3:18).
How does Paul describe the wisdom of this world in God’s sight in 1 Corinthians 3?
Paul says, “the wisdom of this world is foolishness in God’s sight” (3:19).
1 Corinthians 3:19
Powerful
Paul says the opposite: worldly wisdom is foolishness in God’s sight (3:19).
Hidden treasure
Worldly wisdom is not a hidden treasure; Paul calls it foolishness (3:19).
Foolishness
Perfect righteousness
Perfect righteousness is not what Paul calls worldly wisdom; he calls it foolishness (3:19).
The key to salvation
Salvation does not come through worldly wisdom; the only foundation is Jesus Christ (3:11).
In Paul’s rebuke about worldly wisdom in Corinth, which quoted line appears first?

“The righteous will live by faith”

“He catches the wise in their craftiness”
“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom”

“Wisdom is vindicated by all her children”

“The fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God’”

In the second quotation about wisdom in 1 Corinthians 3, what does the Lord know about the thoughts of the wise?
Paul quotes Scripture: “The Lord knows that the thoughts of the wise are futile” (3:20).
1 Corinthians 3:20
They are eternal
The wise person’s thoughts are not eternal; the Lord knows they are futile (3:20).
They are hidden from men
The thoughts of the wise are not hidden from men; the Lord knows they are futile (3:20).
They are futile
They are stronger than faith
Paul does not compare their thoughts with faith; the Lord knows they are futile (3:20).
They are the path to glory
Futile thoughts are no path to glory; Paul says the wisdom of this world is foolishness in God’s sight (3:19).
After speaking about worldly wisdom, what command does Paul give the Corinthians concerning human leaders?
Paul commands, “Therefore, stop boasting in men” (3:21).
1 Corinthians 3:21
Honor them above all
Paul tells them to stop boasting in men, not to honor them above all (3:21).
Stop boasting in men
Appoint more of them
Paul calls for no more leaders; he says stop boasting in men (3:21).
Compare their gifts

Divide into schools under them
Dividing into schools under leaders is the problem Paul is correcting (3:4, 21).
Near the end of 1 Corinthians 3, which three named leaders does Paul include in the statement that all things are yours?
Paul says all things are theirs, “whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death” (3:21–22).
1 Corinthians 3:21-22
Moses, Elijah, and Elisha

Paul, Apollos, and Cephas (Peter)
Peter, James, and John
Peter is Cephas, but James and John are not named in Paul’s list (3:22).
Barnabas, Silas, and Timothy
Barnabas, Silas and Timothy are not named in this chapter’s list (3:22).
Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are not named in the list (3:22).
In the list Paul gives to the church in Corinth, which pair of realities is explicitly said to belong to them?
Paul lists “life or death” among the things that belong to the believers (3:22).
1 Corinthians 3:22
Law and grace
Law and grace are not in Paul’s list of what belongs to them (3:22).
Circumcision and uncircumcision
Circumcision and uncircumcision are not in the list (3:22).
Life and death
Famine and plenty
Famine and plenty are not in the list; the list includes the world, life, death, the present and the future (3:22).
Kings and nations

According to Paul’s conclusion in 1 Corinthians 3, to whom do the believers belong?

To Apollos

To Cephas
Believers do not belong to Cephas; Cephas is among the things that are theirs (3:22).
To Christ
To the angels
Angels are not mentioned; believers belong to Christ (3:23).

1 Corinthians 3:23
To the church in Corinth
The Corinthians belong to Christ, not the other way round (3:23).
To Israel only

To God
To the apostles

In 1 Corinthians 3:8, how are “he who plants” and “he who waters” described?

1 Corinthians 3:8
Rivals in rank

One in purpose
Enemies in doctrine

Equal in authority to Christ

Rulers over the harvest

On what basis does Paul say each worker will be rewarded in 1 Corinthians 3?

According to his popularity

According to his own labor
According to his birthplace

According to his eloquence

According to his visions

In the statement about Paul and Apollos being servants, who assigned to each his role?

1 Corinthians 3:5
The congregation
The congregation did not assign their roles; the Lord did (3:5).
The Roman governor
The Roman governor is not mentioned; the Lord assigned each role (3:5).
The Lord

An angel

The waterer
The waterer is nothing by himself; only God makes things grow (3:7).
The field itself

God

1 Corinthians 3:4

Faithful stewards

Mere men

Perfect disciples

After mentioning jealousy and dissension among the Corinthians, what further question did Paul ask about their conduct?

1 Corinthians 3:3

Partly

Wisely

Everything
Secretly

Me only

Us
Jerusalem

The Romans

To the elders

To the widows

To the brothers
To the magistrates

To the travelers

Ephesians 6:23
God of Abraham

God Most High
God Most High is not the title in 6:23.
God the Father
Lord of Hosts
Lord of Hosts is not the title in 6:23.
Ancient of Days

The saints of Asia
The saints of Asia are not the object of love in 6:24.
The household of faith

What quality of love closes the letter to the Ephesians in chapter 6?

A hidden love

An undying love
A first love

A cautious love
A cautious love is not the phrase in 6:24.
A youthful love
A youthful love is not the phrase in 6:24.
In the promise quoted in Ephesians 6 about honoring parents, which result is named first?

Ephesians 6:3
Long life
Long life is the second result, after it may go well with you (6:3).
Many children
Many children are not mentioned in 6:3.
Peace in the land
Peace in the land is not mentioned in 6:3.
Well-being
Victory over enemies
Victory over enemies is not mentioned in 6:3.

Hide the full armor of God and then polish it well

Paul and Silas

Paul and Timothy
Peter and John

Corinth

Philippi

Along with the saints in Philippi, which two church leadership groups are specifically mentioned in Philippians 1?

Philippians 1:1
Apostles and prophets

Elders and widows
Paul gives instructions about elders and widows in 1 Timothy 5, not in the Philippian greeting.
Pastors and teachers
“Pastors and teachers” appear in the list of Christ’s gifts in Ephesians 4:11.
Overseers and deacons
Priests and Levites
Priests and Levites were sent from Jerusalem to question John the Baptist (John 1:19).
In Philippians 1, from whom does Paul say grace and peace come?
Paul writes, “Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:2).
Philippians 1:2
Abraham and David
Abraham and David are patriarch and king of Israel, never named as sources of grace in Paul’s greetings.
Moses and Elijah

God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ

In his opening remarks in Philippians 1, what does Paul say he does every time he remembers the believers in Philippi?

Fasts
Paul mentions no fasting in Philippians 1; his remembering leads to thanksgiving.
Thanks God
Writes another letter
Paul does not mention writing more letters; remembering them leads him to thank God.

Paul’s prayers for the Philippians are joyful, not sorrowful (1:4).
Fear

Joy

Paul planted the church, but he credits the good work in them to “He who began” it, that is, God (1:6).
Timothy
Timothy co-sends the letter (1:1), but God is the One who began the good work (1:6).

The Jerusalem church is not mentioned in Philippians 1; God began the work in them (1:6).
God

The palace guard heard of Paul’s chains (1:13); they did not begin a work in the Philippians.

Paul is confident that God “will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus” (1:6).

In his heart

Goodwill

Family pressure is not mentioned; Paul names goodwill (1:15).
Curiosity
