Paul calls Epaphras “our beloved fellow servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ on our behalf” (1:7).
Colossians 1:7
A prophet who came down from Judea
The prophet who came down from Judea was Agabus (Acts 21:10), not Epaphras.
A ruler of the synagogue at Corinth
Crispus was the synagogue leader at Corinth who believed (Acts 18:8); Epaphras was a minister of Christ.
A faithful minister of Christ on our behalf
An evangelist who preached in Samaria
Philip preached Christ in a city of Samaria (Acts 8:5); Epaphras taught the Colossians.
One of the seven chosen at Jerusalem
The seven chosen at Jerusalem included Stephen and Philip (Acts 6:5); Epaphras was not among them.
What did Epaphras report to Paul about the believers in Colossae?
Epaphras “also informed us of your love in the Spirit” (1:8).
Colossians 1:8
Their fasting in secret
Jesus taught that fasting should be done in secret (Matthew 6:18); Epaphras reported their love in the Spirit.
Their gifts to Jerusalem
Macedonia and Achaia sent gifts for the poor in Jerusalem (Romans 15:26); Epaphras reported the Colossians’ love.
Their love in the Spirit
Their knowledge of Hebrew
Nothing is said about language; Epaphras told Paul of their love in the Spirit (1:8).
Their persecution by Rome
Colossians 1 mentions no persecution by Rome; Epaphras’s report concerned their love in the Spirit (1:8).
In his prayer for the church at Colossae, what does Paul ask God to fill them with?
Paul asks God “to fill you with the knowledge of His will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding” (1:9).
Colossians 1:9
Visions and dreams
Joel foretold dreams and visions (Joel 2:28); Paul’s prayer asks for the knowledge of God’s will.
The knowledge of His will
Earthly riches
Paul speaks of “the glorious riches of this mystery” (1:27), not earthly wealth.
Authority over nations
Authority over the nations is promised to the overcomer in Revelation 2:26; Paul prays for knowledge of God’s will.
Long life
Long life is promised to those who honor their parents (Ephesians 6:3); Paul’s prayer asks for knowledge of His will.
In Colossians 1:9, the knowledge of God’s will is linked with what?
Paul prays for “the knowledge of His will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding” (1:9).
Colossians 1:9
All spiritual wisdom and understanding
Signs and wonders
Signs and wonders accompanied Paul’s preaching (Romans 15:19), but they are not part of this prayer.
Fasting and mourning
“Fasting, weeping, and mourning” is Joel’s call to return to the LORD (Joel 2:12), not Paul’s prayer.
Law and sacrifice
Law and sacrifice belong to the Mosaic system; Paul links God’s will with spiritual wisdom and understanding.
Tongues and prophecy only
Tongues and prophecy are discussed in 1 Corinthians 14:5, not in Colossians 1:9.
Paul prays that the Colossians may walk in a manner worthy of whom?
Paul prays “that you may walk in a manner worthy of the Lord and may please Him in every way” (1:10).
Colossians 1:10
Abraham
Abraham is never mentioned in Colossians; the worthy walk is in reference to the Lord (1:10).
Caesar
Caesar is not mentioned in Colossians; Paul urges a walk worthy of the Lord.
The Lord
Moses
Moses does not appear in Colossians; the standard for their walk is the Lord (1:10).
Timothy
Timothy is Paul’s co-sender (1:1), not the one whose worthiness they are to match.
In Colossians 1, believers are to bear fruit in what?
Paul prays they will be “bearing fruit in every good work” (1:10).
Colossians 1:10
Every good work
Every debate
Paul later warns against being deceived “by smooth rhetoric” (Colossians 2:4); fruit is borne in every good work.
Every ceremony
Paul later tells them not to be judged over feasts or Sabbaths (Colossians 2:16); fruit is borne in good works.
Every hardship
Hardship calls for “full endurance and patience” (1:11); the fruit-bearing of 1:10 is in every good work.
Every journey
Paul prays for fruit “in every good work” (1:10); journeys are not part of the prayer.
Besides bearing fruit, in what are the Colossians to grow?
Paul prays they will be “growing in the knowledge of God” (1:10).
Colossians 1:10
Political influence
Paul’s prayer seeks spiritual growth, not political power; they are to grow in the knowledge of God (1:10).
The knowledge of God
Temple offerings
Temple offerings are never mentioned in Colossians; growth is in the knowledge of God.
Military strength
The strength in 1:11 is God’s “glorious might,” not military power; growth is in the knowledge of God.
Ritual purity alone
Paul later criticizes rules like “Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch!” (Colossians 2:21); growth is in knowing God.
In Paul’s prayer for Colossae, believers are to be strengthened with what?
Believers are “being strengthened with all power according to His glorious might” (1:11).
Colossians 1:11
Riches stored up in earthly treasuries
Jesus warned against storing up treasures on earth (Matthew 6:19); Paul prays for strength from God’s glorious might.
The might of the angels around the throne
Colossians later warns against “the worship of angels” (Colossians 2:18); the strength comes from God’s own might.
All power according to His glorious might
The wisdom and learning of this world
“The wisdom of this world is foolishness in God’s sight” (1 Corinthians 3:19); the strengthening is by God’s power.
The strength of horses and chariots
“Some trust in chariots and others in horses” (Psalm 20:7); Paul’s readers are strengthened by God’s glorious might.
According to Colossians 1:11, this strengthening is for what?
They are strengthened “so that you may have full endurance and patience” (1:11).
Colossians 1:11
Conquest and fame
Paul’s prayer seeks endurance and patience, not worldly conquest or fame.
Visions and ecstasy
Paul later criticizes one who dwells on “what he has seen” (Colossians 2:18); the strengthening is for endurance and patience.
Full endurance and patience
Wealth and peace
Peace is made through the blood of His cross (1:20); the strengthening of 1:11 is for endurance, not wealth.
Silence and solitude
Silence and solitude are not mentioned; the purpose given is “full endurance and patience” (1:11).
In the prayer section of Colossians 1, what are believers to do joyfully?
Paul prays they will “joyfully” be “giving thanks to the Father” (1:11–12).
Colossians 1:11-12
Sing before kings
The psalmist vows to speak of God’s testimonies before kings (Psalm 119:46); Paul’s prayer is for joyful thanks to the Father.
Give thanks to the Father
Build altars
Altar-building marks the patriarchs, as when Abram built an altar (Genesis 12:7); here believers give thanks to the Father.
Judge the nations
Paul prays for joyful thanksgiving to the Father (1:12), not for believers to judge the nations.
Speak in parables
Jesus spoke to the crowds in parables (Matthew 13:34); the joyful act in 1:12 is giving thanks.
Who has qualified believers to share in the inheritance mentioned in Colossians 1?
Believers give thanks “to the Father, who has qualified you to share in the inheritance” (1:12).
Colossians 1:12
The apostles
The apostles proclaim and teach (1:28), but 1:12 credits the Father with qualifying believers.
The church
The church is Christ’s body (1:18), not the source of qualification; the Father qualifies.
The Father
The Son only
The Son is the one in whom we have redemption (1:14), but 1:12 says the Father has qualified believers.
The law
No one is justified by works of the law (Romans 3:20); the Father is the one who qualifies.
In Colossians 1, believers share in the inheritance of whom?
The Father qualified believers “to share in the inheritance of the saints in the light” (1:12).
Colossians 1:12
The prophets in exile
Ezekiel prophesied among the exiles by the River Kebar (Ezekiel 1:1); Paul speaks of the inheritance of the saints in the light.
The saints in the light
The priests in Jerusalem
The LORD told Aaron he would have no land inheritance, but “I am your portion” (Numbers 18:20); 1:12 names the saints in the light.
The kings of Judah
The kings of Judah are not mentioned in Colossians; the inheritance belongs to the saints in the light.
The martyrs only
The inheritance belongs to all the saints in the light (1:12), not to a select group of martyrs.
From what has God rescued believers, according to Colossians 1?
“He has rescued us from the dominion of darkness” (1:13).
Colossians 1:13
The sea of chaos
Paul describes a spiritual rescue from the dominion of darkness (1:13), not from the sea.
The dominion of darkness
The curse of Egypt
God brought Israel “out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2); Paul describes rescue from darkness.
The armies of Assyria
God struck down the Assyrian army besieging Jerusalem (2 Kings 19:35); 1:13 speaks of the dominion of darkness.
The wilderness
Israel wandered forty years in the wilderness (Numbers 14:33); Paul speaks of rescue from the dominion of darkness.
Into what has God brought believers in Colossians 1:13?
God “brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son” (1:13).
Colossians 1:13
The courts of David
David’s courts are not mentioned; believers are brought into the kingdom of God’s beloved Son (1:13).
The kingdom of His beloved Son
The mountain of the Lord
Isaiah foresaw nations going up to “the mountain of the LORD” (Isaiah 2:3); 1:13 speaks of the Son’s kingdom.
The land flowing with milk and honey
“A land flowing with milk and honey” was promised to Israel (Exodus 3:8); believers are brought into the Son’s kingdom.
The city of Rome
Rome is not mentioned in Colossians; believers are transferred into the kingdom of His beloved Son.
In whom do believers have redemption, according to Paul’s words to Colossae?
Paul speaks of “His beloved Son, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins” (1:13–14).
Colossians 1:14
In Moses
Moses led Israel out of Egypt, but Paul locates redemption in God’s beloved Son (1:13–14).
In David
David is not mentioned in Colossians; redemption is in the beloved Son.
In His beloved Son
In the temple
The temple is never mentioned in Colossians; redemption is found in a person, the Son.
In the covenant at Sinai
The covenant at Sinai called Israel to keep God’s covenant (Exodus 19:5); redemption is in the Son (1:14).
What is named alongside redemption in Colossians 1:14?
“In whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins” (1:14).
Colossians 1:14
Adoption
Adoption to sonship is spoken of in Romans 8:15, not in Colossians 1:14.
Healing
Healing is not mentioned in 1:14; redemption is paired with the forgiveness of sins.
Forgiveness of sins
Resurrection power
Christ’s resurrection appears in 1:18 (“firstborn from among the dead”), not in 1:14.
The gift of prophecy
Prophecy is listed among the Spirit’s gifts in 1 Corinthians 12:10; 1:14 pairs redemption with forgiveness.
In Paul’s description of Christ in Colossians 1, the Son is the image of whom?
“The Son is the image of the invisible God” (1:15).
Colossians 1:15
Adam
Adam was created in God’s image (Genesis 1:27); the Son is the image of the invisible God.
The invisible God
The heavenly host
Angelic powers are among the things created in Him (1:16); the Son is the image of God Himself.
The patriarchs
The patriarchs are not mentioned; Paul calls the Son the image of the invisible God.
The saints
The saints share an inheritance (1:12), but the Son is the image of the invisible God.
Over what is the Son called the firstborn in Colossians 1?
The Son is “the firstborn over all creation” (1:15).
Colossians 1:15
Israel
God called Israel “My firstborn son” (Exodus 4:22), but 1:15 makes the Son firstborn over all creation.
The church
Christ is head of the church (1:18), but 1:15 calls Him firstborn over all creation.
All creation
The nations
The nations are not named here; the Son is firstborn over all creation.
The dead only
He is also “firstborn from among the dead” (1:18), but 1:15 says over all creation.
In Colossians 1:16, where were all things created in Christ?
“In Him all things were created, things in heaven and on earth” (1:16).
Colossians 1:16
In the sea and desert
Paul speaks of heaven and earth (1:16), the whole created order, not merely sea and desert.
In heaven and on earth
In Zion and Samaria
Zion and Samaria are places in Israel; Paul’s scope is all things in heaven and on earth.
In the heart and mind
Paul describes the whole created order, in heaven and on earth, not the inner life.
In Judea and Galilee
Judea and Galilee were the regions of Jesus’ earthly ministry; creation in Him spans heaven and earth.
What contrast does Paul use in Colossians 1 to describe the created order?
All things were created in Him, “visible and invisible” (1:16).
Colossians 1:16
Young and old
Joel pairs old men and young men in his prophecy (Joel 2:28); Paul contrasts visible and invisible.
Jew and Greek
“There is neither Jew nor Greek” comes in Galatians 3:28 (compare Colossians 3:11); 1:16 contrasts visible and invisible.
Visible and invisible
Rich and poor
“The rich and the poor have this in common” (Proverbs 22:2); 1:16 contrasts visible and invisible.
Wise and foolish
Jesus contrasts wise and foolish virgins in a parable (Matthew 25:2); Paul contrasts visible and invisible.
Which set of powers is specifically listed as created through Christ in Colossians 1?
Paul lists “thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities” among the things created in Him (1:16).
Colossians 1:16
Kings, judges, elders, scribes
Kings, judges, elders, and scribes are human offices found throughout Scripture, not Paul’s list in 1:16.
Seraphim, cherubim, archangels, hosts
Seraphim appear in Isaiah 6:2; Paul’s list is thrones, dominions, rulers, and authorities.
Thrones, dominions, rulers, authorities
Priests, prophets, apostles, teachers
Apostles, prophets, and teachers are Christ’s gifts to the church (Ephesians 4:11), not the powers of 1:16.
Mountains, rivers, stars, seas
Mountains, rivers, stars, and seas are physical creation; Paul’s list names powers.
According to Colossians 1, all things were created through Christ and for whom?
“All things were created through Him and for Him” (1:16).
Colossians 1:16
For Adam
Adam was given rule over creatures (Genesis 1:28), but 1:16 says all things were created for Christ.
For Israel
Israel is not mentioned here; all things were created for Christ.
For Him
For the church alone
The church is Christ’s body (1:18), but 1:16 says all things were created for Him.
For the nations
The nations are not mentioned in 1:16; creation exists for Christ.
What does Paul say about Christ before saying that all things hold together in Him?
“He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together” (1:17).
Colossians 1:17
He is before all things
He is the last Adam
Paul calls Christ “the last Adam” in 1 Corinthians 15:45, not in Colossians 1:17.
He is the wisdom of Solomon
Jesus said “One greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42); 1:17 says He is before all things.
He is the angel of the covenant
“The Messenger of the covenant” is Malachi’s title (Malachi 3:1); 1:17 says He is before all things.
He is seated with Elijah
Elijah appeared with Moses at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:3); Christ is seated at God’s right hand (Colossians 3:1).
In Colossians 1:17, what happens in Christ regarding all things?
“In Him all things hold together” (1:17).
Colossians 1:17
They disappear
Paul says the opposite: all things are held together, not dissolved, in Christ (1:17).
They are judged
Judgment is not the subject of 1:17; Paul says all things hold together in Him.
They hold together
They sleep
Paul describes Christ sustaining creation; all things hold together in Him.
They become spiritual only
Paul says things visible and invisible were created in Him (1:16) and all things hold together in Him (1:17).
In Paul’s teaching to the Colossians, Christ is the head of what?
“He is the head of the body, the church” (1:18).
Colossians 1:18
Israel
Israel is not mentioned in Colossians 1; Christ is head of the body, the church.
The priesthood
Hebrews calls Jesus “a great high priest” (Hebrews 4:14); Colossians 1:18 calls Him head of the church.
The body, the church
The nations
The nations are not named in 1:18; Christ is head of the body, the church.
The heavenly army
Heavenly powers were created through Him (1:16), but 1:18 names Him head of the church.
In Colossians 1:18, from among what is Christ called the firstborn?
He is “the beginning and firstborn from among the dead” (1:18).
Colossians 1:18
The prophets
The prophets are not mentioned here; the firstborn title refers to His resurrection from the dead.
The angels
God commands the angels to worship His firstborn (Hebrews 1:6); Christ is not called firstborn among angels.
The dead
The patriarchs
The patriarchs are not mentioned; Christ is firstborn from among the dead.
The Gentiles
The Gentiles appear in 1:27; in 1:18 Christ is firstborn from among the dead.
Why does Colossians 1 say Christ is firstborn from among the dead?
He is “the beginning and firstborn from among the dead, so that in all things He may have preeminence” (1:18).
Colossians 1:18
So that the law may continue
The law is not mentioned in 1:18; the purpose is Christ’s preeminence.
So that in all things He may have preeminence
So that Israel alone may rule
Paul’s concern is Christ’s preeminence in all things, not any rule by Israel alone.
So that the temple may be rebuilt
The temple is never mentioned in Colossians; the purpose is Christ’s preeminence.
So that angels may worship men
When John fell before an angel, he was told “Worship God!” (Revelation 22:9); 1:18 is about Christ’s preeminence.
Through Christ, what does God reconcile to Himself in Colossians 1?
God was pleased “through Him to reconcile to Himself all things” (1:20).
Colossians 1:20
Israel only
The reconciliation in 1:20 is of all things, not Israel alone.
The church only
The church is reconciled, but 1:20 extends reconciliation to all things.
All things
The angels only
Angels are not singled out; God reconciles all things, on earth and in heaven.
The Gentiles only
The Gentiles are included (1:27), but 1:20 says all things.
Colossians 1 says reconciliation includes things on earth and where else?
God reconciles all things, “whether things on earth or things in heaven” (1:20).
Colossians 1:20
Under the sea
Paul’s pairing is earth and heaven (1:20), not the sea.
In the wilderness
The wilderness is not mentioned; the pair is things on earth and things in heaven.
In heaven
In Sheol
Sheol is not named in Colossians; reconciliation reaches things on earth and in heaven.
In Eden
Eden was the garden God planted in the east (Genesis 2:8); 1:20 speaks of earth and heaven.
By what means is peace made in Colossians 1:20?
God makes peace “through the blood of His cross” (1:20).
Colossians 1:20
The water of baptism
Baptism appears later as being buried with Him (Colossians 2:12), but peace is made through the blood of His cross.
The blood of His cross
The prayers of the saints
The prayers of the saints rise like incense in Revelation 5:8; peace is made through the blood of the cross.
The fire from heaven
Fire fell from heaven on Elijah’s sacrifice (1 Kings 18:38); peace in 1:20 comes through the cross.
The ark of the covenant
The ark held the tablets of the covenant (Hebrews 9:4); peace is made through the blood of His cross.
Before reconciliation, what were the Colossian believers once said to be in relation to God?
“Once you were alienated from God and were hostile in your minds” (1:21).
Colossians 1:21
Anointed
Being anointed is not mentioned; Paul describes their former state as alienated from God.
Alienated
Sanctified
Sanctification describes believers’ new state, not their former one; once they were alienated (1:21).
Justified
“Those He called, He also justified” (Romans 8:30) describes the new life; formerly they were alienated.
Glorified
Glorification is the final stage of salvation (Romans 8:30), not their former condition.
According to Colossians 1:21, where were these believers hostile?
They “were hostile in your minds, engaging in evil deeds” (1:21).
Colossians 1:21
In the temple
The temple is never mentioned in Colossians; their hostility was in their minds.
In their minds
In their homes
Their hostility is located in their minds (1:21), not in their homes.
In the marketplace
The marketplace is not mentioned; Paul says they were hostile in their minds.
In the synagogues
Synagogues are not mentioned in Colossians; the hostility was inward, in their minds.
What kind of deeds were associated with the Colossians’ former life?
Paul says they were “engaging in evil deeds” (1:21).
Colossians 1:21
Evil deeds
Priestly duties
Priestly duties are not mentioned; their former life was marked by evil deeds.
Works of mercy
Works of mercy would be good deeds; Paul says their former deeds were evil (1:21).
Fasting rites
Fasting rites are not mentioned; their former life involved evil deeds.
Military campaigns
Military campaigns are not mentioned; Paul describes evil deeds.
By what has Christ now reconciled believers, according to Colossians 1:22?
“He has reconciled you by Christ’s physical body through death” (1:22).
Colossians 1:22
His parables through teaching
Jesus taught the crowds in parables (Matthew 13:34), but reconciliation came through His physical body in death.
His physical body through death
His miracles through compassion
Jesus healed out of compassion (Matthew 14:14), but 1:22 says reconciliation came through His death.
His Spirit through visions
Visions are not mentioned in 1:22; reconciliation came by Christ’s physical body through death.
His angels through messages
Angels are not mentioned in 1:22; reconciliation is through Christ’s bodily death.
In Colossians 1:22, believers are to be presented as what?
He reconciled them “to present you holy, unblemished, and blameless in His presence” (1:22).
Colossians 1:22
Holy, unblemished, and blameless
Rich, honored, and strong
Paul’s goal is moral and spiritual purity, not wealth, honor, or strength.
Wise, eloquent, and bold
Eloquence and boldness are not mentioned; believers are presented holy, unblemished, and blameless.
Humble, poor, and wandering
The triad in 1:22 is holy, unblemished, and blameless, not humble, poor, and wandering.
Joyful, singing, and free
Joy appears in 1:11, but 1:22 describes believers as holy, unblemished, and blameless.
What must the Colossians continue in, according to Paul?
“If indeed you continue in your faith, established and firm” (1:23).
Colossians 1:23
The traditions of men
Paul later warns against teaching “based on human tradition” (Colossians 2:8); they must continue in their faith.
Their faith
The ceremonies of Moses
The ceremonies of Moses are not what Paul urges; they must continue in their faith (1:23).
Fasting every week
The Pharisee in Jesus’ parable boasted of fasting twice a week (Luke 18:12); Paul urges continuing in faith.
Speaking in mysteries
Uttering “mysteries in the Spirit” is linked with tongues in 1 Corinthians 14:2; Paul urges continuing in faith.
How does Paul describe the Colossians’ faith in Colossians 1:23?
Paul urges them to continue in their faith, “established and firm” (1:23).
Colossians 1:23
Ancient and secret
Paul’s gospel is openly proclaimed (1:23), not secret; their faith is to be established and firm.
Established and firm
Emotional and changing
Paul calls for steadfast faith, the opposite of changeable emotion.
Hidden and private
The gospel has been proclaimed to every creature under heaven (1:23); their faith is not described as hidden.
Tested and failing
Paul calls them to be established and firm, not failing.
In Colossians 1:23, believers must not be moved from what?
They must be “not moved from the hope of the gospel you heard” (1:23).
Colossians 1:23
The hope of the gospel
The city of David
The City of David was the fortress of Zion (2 Samuel 5:7); Paul speaks of the hope of the gospel.
The temple courts
The temple is never mentioned in Colossians; they must hold to the hope of the gospel.
The traditions of the elders
“The tradition of the elders” was the Pharisees’ concern (Mark 7:5); Paul speaks of the hope of the gospel.
The hope of earthly peace
The hope is “the hope of the gospel” (1:23), stored up in heaven (1:5), not earthly peace.
What had Paul become in relation to the gospel, according to Colossians 1:23?
“Of which I, Paul, have become a servant” (1:23).
Colossians 1:23
Its judge
Paul does not claim to judge the gospel; he became its servant (1:23).
Its servant
Its owner
Paul calls himself the gospel’s servant (1:23), not its owner.
Its guardian angel
Paul calls himself a servant of the gospel (1:23), not an angel.
Its scribe only
Tertius wrote down Romans for Paul (Romans 16:22); Paul calls himself the gospel’s servant.
In Colossians 1:24, what does Paul say he rejoices in?
“Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you” (1:24).
Colossians 1:24
His visions
Paul boasts of “visions and revelations” in 2 Corinthians 12:1; in 1:24 he rejoices in his sufferings.
His sufferings for you
His status as an apostle
Paul mentions his apostleship in 1:1, but in 1:24 he rejoices in his sufferings for them.
His travel plans
Travel plans are not mentioned in Colossians 1; Paul rejoices in his sufferings for them.
His Roman citizenship
Paul appealed to his Roman citizenship in Acts 22:25; in 1:24 he rejoices in his sufferings.
What does Paul say he fills up in his flesh in Colossians 1:24?
Paul fills up in his flesh “what is lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions for the sake of His body” (1:24).
Colossians 1:24
What remains of the promises made to Abraham
“The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed” (Galatians 3:16); Paul fills up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions.
What is lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions
What was lacking in the sufferings of the prophets
Jesus noted that the prophets were persecuted (Matthew 5:12); Paul speaks of Christ’s afflictions.
What remains of the punishment due to Israel
Isaiah announced that Jerusalem’s “iniquity has been pardoned” (Isaiah 40:2); Paul speaks of Christ’s afflictions.
What is still owed in taxes to Caesar
“Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s” (Matthew 22:21) concerns taxes; Paul speaks of Christ’s afflictions.
For the sake of what does Paul say he suffers in Colossians 1:24?
Paul suffers “for the sake of His body, which is the church” (1:24).
Colossians 1:24
The temple
The temple is never mentioned in Colossians; Paul suffers for Christ’s body, the church.
The synagogue
The synagogue is not mentioned; Paul suffers for the church, Christ’s body.
His body, which is the church
The empire
The empire is not mentioned; Paul suffers for Christ’s body, the church.
The law of Moses
The law of Moses is not mentioned in 1:24; Paul suffers for the church.
In Colossians 1:25, by what did Paul become a servant of the church?
“I became its servant by the commission God gave me” (1:25).
Colossians 1:25
The vote of the elders
Matthias was added to the apostles by lot (Acts 1:26); Paul’s service rests on God’s commission.
The commission God gave me
A dream from Joseph
Joseph dreamed dreams that his brothers hated (Genesis 37:5); Paul’s service rests on God’s commission.
His studies under Gamaliel
Paul was educated at the feet of Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), but his ministry rests on God’s commission.
A royal decree
Cyrus issued a royal proclamation (Ezra 1:1); Paul’s ministry rests on God’s commission.
What was the purpose of Paul’s commission to the Colossians?
God commissioned Paul “to fully proclaim to you the word of God” (1:25).
Colossians 1:25
To collect alms for the poor in Jerusalem
Paul did gather gifts for Jerusalem’s poor (Romans 15:26), but 1:25 states his commission was to proclaim God’s word.
To fully proclaim to you the word of God
To appoint judges in every town of the land
Moses commanded Israel to appoint judges in every town (Deuteronomy 16:18); Paul’s commission was to proclaim God’s word.
To rebuild the walls of the city of Jerusalem
Nehemiah led the rebuilding of Jerusalem’s wall (Nehemiah 2:17); Paul’s commission was to proclaim God’s word.
To teach them the laws and customs of Rome
Paul was accused of promoting customs unlawful for Romans (Acts 16:21); he never taught Roman law.
For how long had the mystery been hidden, according to Colossians 1?
“The mystery that was hidden for ages and generations” (1:26).
Colossians 1:26
Forty days and nights
Forty days and nights recalls the flood rains (Genesis 7:12) and Jesus’ fast (Matthew 4:2), not the hidden mystery.
Seven generations only
Paul says “ages and generations” (1:26), with no specific count of seven.
Ages and generations
From David to Christ
Matthew counts fourteen generations from David to the exile (Matthew 1:17); Paul says the mystery was hidden for ages and generations.
Until the exile
The exile is not mentioned in Colossians; the mystery was hidden for ages and generations.
To whom has the mystery now been revealed?
The mystery “is now revealed to His saints” (1:26).
Colossians 1:26
Kings of the earth
Kings of the earth are not the recipients; the mystery is revealed to His saints (1:26).
Philosophers
Epicurean and Stoic philosophers debated Paul in Athens (Acts 17:18); the mystery is revealed to His saints.
His saints
Scribes and Pharisees
Jesus said such things were hidden “from the wise and learned” (Matthew 11:25); the mystery is revealed to His saints.
Roman rulers
Roman rulers are not mentioned; the mystery is revealed to His saints.
Among whom has God chosen to make known the glorious riches of this mystery?
God chose “to make known among the Gentiles the glorious riches of this mystery” (1:27).
Colossians 1:27
The Levites
The Levites are not mentioned; the mystery is made known among the Gentiles.
The Gentiles
The Sadducees
The Sadducees denied resurrection and angels (Acts 23:8); the mystery is made known among the Gentiles.
The twelve tribes only
Paul stresses the mystery’s reach to the Gentiles (1:27), not the twelve tribes only.
The Samaritans only
Jesus spoke with a Samaritan woman (John 4:9), but 1:27 says the mystery is made known among the Gentiles.
What is the mystery described in Colossians 1:27?
The mystery “is Christ in you, the hope of glory” (1:27).
Colossians 1:27
The rebuilding of Zion
Isaiah speaks of the law going forth from Zion (Isaiah 2:3); Paul defines the mystery as Christ in you.
Christ in you, the hope of glory
The return of Elijah
Malachi foretold the sending of Elijah (Malachi 4:5); the mystery is Christ in you, the hope of glory.
The hidden manna
“The hidden manna” is promised to the overcomer in Revelation 2:17; the mystery is Christ in you.
The wisdom of Solomon
God gave Solomon great wisdom (1 Kings 4:29); the mystery is Christ in you, the hope of glory.
Whom does Paul say “we proclaim” in Colossians 1:28?
“We proclaim Him” (1:28) — Christ, the hope of glory just named in 1:27.
Colossians 1:28
Moses
Moses is never mentioned in Colossians; Paul proclaims Christ.
John the Baptist
John the Baptist preached in the wilderness of Judea (Matthew 3:1); Paul proclaims Christ (1:28).
Him
The prophets
The prophets are not mentioned in Colossians; Paul proclaims Christ.
The law
Paul proclaims a person, Christ (1:28), not the law.
What two activities accompany Paul’s proclamation of Christ?
“We proclaim Him, admonishing and teaching everyone with all wisdom” (1:28).
Colossians 1:28
Healing the sick and feeding the hungry crowds
Jesus healed the sick and fed the crowds (Matthew 14:14); Paul’s proclamation is with admonishing and teaching.
Building houses and planting gardens in exile
Jeremiah told the exiles to build houses and plant gardens (Jeremiah 29:5); Paul admonishes and teaches.
Admonishing and teaching everyone with all wisdom
Judging and correcting the rulers of this age
Paul speaks of “the rulers of this age” in 1 Corinthians 2:6, but here he admonishes and teaches everyone.
Fasting and waiting in prayer for many days
The church at Antioch fasted and prayed before sending Paul out (Acts 13:3); 1:28 names admonishing and teaching.
What is the goal of Paul’s ministry in Colossians 1:28?
His aim is “that we may present everyone perfect in Christ” (1:28).
Colossians 1:28
To make everyone wealthy
Paul’s goal is spiritual maturity in Christ, not wealth.
To present everyone perfect in Christ
To establish a new nation
Founding a nation is not Paul’s aim; he seeks to present everyone perfect in Christ.
To appoint bishops in every city
Titus was told to appoint elders in every town (Titus 1:5); Paul’s aim in 1:28 is to present everyone perfect in Christ.
To silence all critics
Paul’s goal is not silencing critics but presenting everyone perfect in Christ.
In Colossians 1:29, how does Paul pursue this goal?
“To this end I also labor, striving with all His energy working powerfully within me” (1:29).
Colossians 1:29
By resting in old traditions
Paul warns against teaching “based on human tradition” (Colossians 2:8); he labors and strives.
By laboring and striving with all His energy
By avoiding hardship
Paul does not avoid hardship; he rejoices in his sufferings (1:24) and labors and strives.
By seeking political influence
Political influence is not mentioned; Paul labors with God’s energy at work in him.
By writing only to rulers
Paul writes to “the saints and faithful brothers” (1:2), not to rulers; he labors and strives.
In Colossians 1:4-5, the Colossians’ faith in Christ Jesus and love for all the saints are said to spring from what?
Their faith and love are “proceeding from the hope stored up for you in heaven” (1:5).
Colossians 1:4-5
Zeal for the temple
“Zeal for Your house will consume Me” is said of Jesus (John 2:17); the Colossians’ faith and love spring from hope.
Hope stored up in heaven
Fear of judgment alone
Paul roots their faith and love in a heavenly hope (1:5), not fear of judgment.
The wisdom of Greece
“Greeks search for wisdom” (1 Corinthians 1:22), but the Colossians’ faith and love proceed from hope in heaven.
The traditions of the fathers
Paul was once zealous “for the traditions of my fathers” (Galatians 1:14); their faith and love spring from hope.
According to Colossians 1:6, since when had the gospel been bearing fruit among the Colossians?
The gospel had been bearing fruit among them “since the day you heard it and truly understood the grace of God” (1:6).
Colossians 1:6
Since the day Paul first visited and preached to them in person
Many in the region had not met Paul “face to face” (Colossians 2:1); they learned the gospel from Epaphras (1:7).
Since the day they heard it and truly understood the grace of God
Since the apostles and elders in Jerusalem formally approved them
The Jerusalem apostles and elders wrote to Gentiles in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia (Acts 15:23), not to approve Colossae.
Since the day they were circumcised according to the law of Moses
Paul says they were circumcised “by Christ and not by human hands” (Colossians 2:11); fruit began when they heard the gospel.
Since the day Epaphras returned to them from his time in Rome
Epaphras was still with Paul, sending greetings (Colossians 4:12); the fruit began when they first heard the gospel.
What did the Colossians truly understand when the gospel came to them?
The gospel bore fruit since they “truly understood the grace of God” (1:6).
Colossians 1:6
The mysteries of angels
“Even angels long to look into these things” (1 Peter 1:12); the Colossians understood the grace of God.
The grace of God
The calendar of feasts
Paul tells them not to be judged over feasts and Sabbaths (Colossians 2:16); they understood the grace of God.
The law of sacrifices
The law of sacrifices is not mentioned; what they understood was the grace of God.
The politics of Rome
The politics of Rome are not mentioned; they understood the grace of God (1:6).
Before calling Epaphras a faithful minister of Christ, what affectionate title does Paul use for him?
Paul calls Epaphras “our beloved fellow servant” before calling him “a faithful minister of Christ” (1:7).
Colossians 1:7
Our fellow prisoner
Paul calls Epaphras “my fellow prisoner” in Philemon 1:23, but in 1:7 he is a beloved fellow servant.
Our beloved fellow servant
Our beloved physician
“The beloved physician” is Luke (Colossians 4:14), not Epaphras.
Our chosen elder
Epaphras is not called an elder; Paul calls him a beloved fellow servant (1:7).
Our brother of Jerusalem
Epaphras was “one of you,” a Colossian (Colossians 4:12), not from Jerusalem.
In Colossians 1:7, Epaphras is a faithful minister of Christ on whose behalf?
Epaphras is “a faithful minister of Christ on our behalf” (1:7).
Colossians 1:7
On Caesar’s behalf
Caesar is not mentioned; Epaphras served on Paul’s behalf.
On his own behalf
Paul says Epaphras ministered “on our behalf” (1:7), not his own.
On our behalf
On Jerusalem’s behalf
Jerusalem is not mentioned; Epaphras served on Paul’s behalf.
On the angels’ behalf
Angels are not mentioned in 1:7; Epaphras served on Paul’s behalf.
Which pair in Colossians 1:10 describes a worthy walk before the Lord?
The worthy walk means “bearing fruit in every good work, growing in the knowledge of God” (1:10).
Colossians 1:10
Fasting in secret and mourning over sin in sackcloth and ashes
Daniel sought God “with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes” (Daniel 9:3); 1:10 describes fruit-bearing and growth.
Bearing fruit in every good work and growing in the knowledge of God
Offering sacrifices on the altar and singing psalms in the temple
Sacrifice and temple song are not part of 1:10; the worthy walk bears fruit and grows in the knowledge of God.
Debating in the synagogues and persuading Jews and Greeks every Sabbath
Paul reasoned every Sabbath in the synagogue at Corinth (Acts 18:4), but 1:10 describes fruit and growth.
Ruling over the nations and judging the twelve tribes of Israel
Jesus promised the Twelve thrones “judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28); 1:10 describes fruit and growth.
According to Colossians 1:11-12, believers are strengthened for “full endurance and patience,” and then are to do what?
After “full endurance and patience,” Paul continues, “and joyfully giving thanks to the Father” (1:11–12).
Colossians 1:11-12
Rebuild the temple
The temple is never mentioned in Colossians; believers joyfully give thanks to the Father.
Joyfully give thanks to the Father
Seek signs from heaven
Seeking signs is what “Jews demand” (1 Corinthians 1:22); 1:12 calls for joyful thanks to the Father.
Appoint new kings
Appointing kings is not mentioned; believers give thanks to the Father.
Return to Jerusalem
Returning to Jerusalem is not mentioned; believers joyfully give thanks to the Father.
In Colossians 1:12, the inheritance shared by believers belongs to “the saints” in what sphere?
Believers share “in the inheritance of the saints in the light” (1:12).
Colossians 1:12
In the wilderness
Israel wandered in the wilderness (Numbers 14:33), but the inheritance belongs to the saints in the light.
In the light
In the sea
The sea is not mentioned; the phrase is “the saints in the light” (1:12).
In the temple courts
The temple courts are not mentioned in Colossians; the phrase is “the saints in the light.”
In the age to come only
The phrase is “the saints in the light” (1:12), not “the age to come.”
Which statement best matches Colossians 1:13?
“He has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son” (1:13).
Colossians 1:13
God called us out of the land of Egypt and brought us into the land of Canaan
God brought Israel out of Egypt toward Canaan (Exodus 3:8); 1:13 describes rescue from darkness into the Son’s kingdom.
God rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son
God sent fire down from heaven to purify us and brought us into His holy temple
Fire fell from heaven on Elijah’s altar (1 Kings 18:38); 1:13 speaks of rescue from darkness.
God gave His angels charge over us and brought us safely into His holy mountain
God “will command His angels concerning you” (Psalm 91:11); 1:13 is about transfer into the Son’s kingdom.
God hid us in the wilderness for safety and brought us into the cleft of the rock
God hid Moses in “a cleft of the rock” (Exodus 33:22); 1:13 speaks of rescue from the dominion of darkness.
Which two blessings are joined together in the Son in Colossians 1:14?
“In whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins” (1:14).
Colossians 1:14
Wisdom and the power of God
Christ is called “the power of God and the wisdom of God” in 1 Corinthians 1:24, not in Colossians 1:14.
Redemption and forgiveness of sins
Glory and power forever and ever
“The glory and power forever and ever” is ascribed to Christ in Revelation 1:6, not in Colossians 1:14.
Grace and the gift of apostleship
Paul speaks of receiving “grace and apostleship” in Romans 1:5; 1:14 joins redemption and forgiveness.
Prophecy and the gifts of healing
Prophecy and gifts of healing are among the Spirit’s gifts (1 Corinthians 12:9–10), not the blessings of 1:14.
In Colossians 1:16, what is the broad spatial contrast used to describe creation’s extent?
“In Him all things were created, things in heaven and on earth” (1:16).
Colossians 1:16
East and west
East and west are not mentioned; Paul’s pair is heaven and earth.
Land and sea
Land and sea are not Paul’s pair; he says heaven and earth (1:16).
Heaven and earth
North and south
North and south are not mentioned; the pair is heaven and earth.
Day and night
Day and night are not mentioned; Paul’s second pair is visible and invisible.
Which exact conclusion follows Paul’s list of thrones, dominions, rulers, and authorities?
After the list of powers Paul writes, “All things were created through Him and for Him” (1:16).
Colossians 1:16
All things will pass away in Him
Jesus said heaven and earth will pass away (Matthew 24:35); 1:16 concludes that all things were created through Him.
All things were created through Him and for Him
All things were judged by Him already
1:16 is about creation, not judgment; all things were created through Him and for Him.
All things bow to Israel
Isaiah foresees oppressors bowing to Zion (Isaiah 60:14); 1:16 says all things were created for Christ.
All things are hidden from Him
“Nothing in all creation is hidden from God’s sight” (Hebrews 4:13); 1:16 says all things were made through Him.
In Colossians 1:17, which statement comes before “in Him all things hold together”?
“He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together” (1:17).
Colossians 1:17
He emptied Himself
Christ “emptied Himself” in Philippians 2:7, not in Colossians 1:17.
He is before all things
He learned obedience
“He learned obedience from what He suffered” is in Hebrews 5:8, not Colossians 1:17.
He was tempted in every way
Christ “was tempted in every way” according to Hebrews 4:15, not Colossians 1:17.
He sat at the right hand of David
Christ sat down “at the right hand of the Majesty on high” (Hebrews 1:3), not of David.
In Colossians 1:18, what two titles are joined before the phrase about preeminence?
“He is the beginning and firstborn from among the dead, so that in all things He may have preeminence” (1:18).
Colossians 1:18
Shepherd and bishop
Christ is called “the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” in 1 Peter 2:25, not in Colossians 1:18.
King and priest
Believers are made “a kingdom, priests” in Revelation 1:6; 1:18 calls Christ the beginning and firstborn from the dead.
The beginning and firstborn from among the dead
Son of David and son of Abraham
Matthew 1:1 calls Jesus “the son of David, the son of Abraham”; 1:18 uses different titles.
Lamb and lion
Christ is the Lion of Judah and the Lamb in Revelation 5:5–6, not in Colossians 1:18.
What was God pleased to do in relation to Christ, according to Colossians 1:19?
“God was pleased to have all His fullness dwell in Him” (1:19).
Colossians 1:19
Hide His name for a time
Nothing about hiding His name appears; God’s fullness dwells in Christ (1:19).
Have all His fullness dwell in Him
Make Him lower than angels forever
Jesus was made “a little lower than the angels” only for a time, now crowned with glory (Hebrews 2:9).
Send Him only to Israel
Jesus said He was sent to Israel’s lost sheep (Matthew 15:24), but 1:19 speaks of God’s fullness dwelling in Him.
Entrust Him with the law alone
“The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17).
In Colossians 1:21, the believers’ alienation from God was joined to hostility in what place?
“Once you were alienated from God and were hostile in your minds” (1:21).
Colossians 1:21
Their cities
Their hostility was inward, in their minds (1:21), not in their cities.
Their minds
Their bodies
Their hostility was in their minds; reconciliation came by Christ’s body (1:22).
Their assemblies
Assemblies are not mentioned; the hostility was in their minds.
Their households
Households are not mentioned; the hostility was in their minds.
In Colossians 1:22, reconciliation by Christ’s physical body through death has what purpose?
He reconciled them “to present you holy, unblemished, and blameless in His presence” (1:22).
Colossians 1:22
To make believers rulers over angels
Paul writes “we will judge angels” in 1 Corinthians 6:3, but 1:22 is about being presented holy.
To present believers holy, unblemished, and blameless
To restore the Levitical priesthood
Hebrews says perfection could not come through the Levitical priesthood (Hebrews 7:11).
To reveal the dates of the end
Jesus said it is not for us “to know times or seasons” (Acts 1:7); 1:22 is about being presented holy.
To establish an earthly throne
No earthly throne is mentioned; the goal is to present believers holy and blameless.
What condition follows Paul’s statement about being presented holy, unblemished, and blameless?
“If indeed you continue in your faith, established and firm” (1:23).
Colossians 1:23
If indeed you continue in your faith
If you move to Jerusalem
Moving to Jerusalem is not mentioned; the condition is continuing in faith.
If you keep the food laws
Paul tells them not to be judged by what they eat or drink (Colossians 2:16); the condition is continuing in faith.
If you sell all possessions
Jesus told the rich ruler to sell everything (Luke 18:22); Paul’s condition is continuing in faith.
If you never suffer
Paul rejoices in his own sufferings (1:24); avoiding suffering is not the condition.
Which full description of steadfastness appears in Colossians 1:23?
Paul urges them to continue “established and firm, not moved from the hope of the gospel” (1:23).
Colossians 1:23
Humble and poor, waiting in silence
“It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD” (Lamentations 3:26); 1:23 urges being established and firm.
Established and firm, not moved from the hope of the gospel
Fervent in fasting, careful in speech
Fasting and speech are not mentioned in 1:23; the call is to be established and firm.
Zealous for the temple, loyal to the law
Temple zeal and loyalty to the law are not Paul’s call; he urges firmness in the hope of the gospel.
Joyful in trials, bold before kings
“Consider it pure joy … when you encounter trials” is James 1:2; Colossians 1:23 calls for firmness in the gospel’s hope.
What scope of proclamation does Paul give the gospel in Colossians 1:23?
The gospel “has been proclaimed to every creature under heaven” (1:23).
Colossians 1:23
Every synagogue in Judea
Paul’s scope is every creature under heaven, far wider than Judea’s synagogues.
Every creature under heaven
Every city of Asia only
Paul’s scope is universal, not limited to the cities of Asia.
Every disciple in Jerusalem
Paul says every creature under heaven, not only disciples in Jerusalem.
Every house in Colossae
The gospel reached Colossae, but Paul says it was proclaimed to every creature under heaven.
In Colossians 1:24, for whose sake does Paul say he fills up in his flesh what is lacking regarding Christ’s afflictions?
Paul suffers “for the sake of His body, which is the church” (1:24).
Colossians 1:24
For the sake of Caesar’s peace
Caesar is not mentioned in Colossians; Paul suffers for the church.
For the sake of His body, which is the church
For the sake of the temple tax
Collectors of the temple tax approached Peter in Matthew 17:24; Paul suffers for Christ’s body, the church.
For the sake of the elders in Jerusalem
The Jerusalem elders are not mentioned; Paul suffers for the church.
For the sake of his own salvation
Salvation is “by grace … through faith” (Ephesians 2:8); Paul suffers for the church, not to earn salvation.
What was Paul commissioned to do with the word of God for the Colossians?
Paul’s commission was “to fully proclaim to you the word of God” (1:25).
Colossians 1:25
Hide it until the right time
The mystery was hidden in the past but is now revealed (1:26); Paul was to proclaim it fully.
Fully proclaim it to them
Translate it into Latin only
Latin is not mentioned; Paul was to fully proclaim God’s word.
Reserve it for elders
Paul teaches “everyone with all wisdom” (1:28), not elders only.
Debate it in the synagogues only
Paul was to fully proclaim God’s word to the Colossians, not only in synagogues.
In Colossians 1:26, the mystery hidden for ages and generations is now revealed to whom?
The mystery “is now revealed to His saints” (1:26).
Colossians 1:26
Kings and rulers
Kings and rulers are not mentioned; the mystery is revealed to His saints.
His saints
Philosophers of Athens
Philosophers in Athens debated with Paul (Acts 17:18), but 1:26 says the mystery is revealed to His saints.
The sons of Aaron
The sons of Aaron were ordained as priests (Exodus 28:41); the mystery is revealed to His saints.
Roman judges
Roman judges are not mentioned; the mystery is revealed to His saints.
What exactly has God chosen to make known among the Gentiles in Colossians 1:27?
God chose “to make known among the Gentiles the glorious riches of this mystery” (1:27).
Colossians 1:27
The rebuilding of David’s tent
Rebuilding David’s fallen tent is quoted by James in Acts 15:16, not in Colossians 1:27.
The glorious riches of this mystery
The names of the archangels
Scripture names the archangel Michael (Jude 1:9), but 1:27 is about the riches of the mystery.
The sequence of empires
Daniel interpreted a dream of successive kingdoms (Daniel 2:39); 1:27 is about the glorious riches of the mystery.
The hidden code of the law
No hidden code is mentioned; God makes known the glorious riches of this mystery.
In Colossians 1:28, everyone is admonished and taught with what?
“Admonishing and teaching everyone with all wisdom” (1:28).
Colossians 1:28
Strict severity
Paul teaches “with all wisdom” (1:28), not with severity.
All wisdom
Miraculous signs
Signs accompanied Paul’s preaching (Romans 15:19), but 1:28 says teaching is with all wisdom.
Secret traditions
Paul warns against “human tradition” (Colossians 2:8); he teaches with all wisdom.
Temple authority
The temple is never mentioned in Colossians; Paul teaches with all wisdom.
In Colossians 1:28, who is the repeated object of Paul’s admonishing, teaching, and presenting?
“Admonishing and teaching everyone … so that we may present everyone perfect in Christ” (1:28).
Colossians 1:28
Israel
Israel is not mentioned; Paul repeats “everyone.”
The elders
Elders are not singled out; Paul’s ministry is to everyone.
Everyone
The poor only
Paul’s ministry is to everyone, not the poor only.
New converts only
Paul aims to present everyone perfect in Christ, not only new converts.
How does Paul describe the power behind his labor in Colossians 1:29?
Paul labors, “striving with all His energy working powerfully within me” (1:29).
Colossians 1:29
My determination working secretly within me
Paul credits “His energy,” not his own determination (1:29).
His energy working powerfully within me
The strength of my companions
Paul’s companions are not credited; he relies on His energy.
The authority of Rome within me
Rome is not mentioned; the power is His energy working within Paul.
The memory of the law within me
The law is not mentioned; Paul relies on His energy.
Which sequence best matches the flow of Colossians 1?
Colossians 1 moves from thanksgiving (1:3–8) and prayer (1:9–14) to Christ’s supremacy (1:15–20), a call to continue in faith (1:21–23), and Paul’s ministry of the mystery (1:24–29).
Colossians 1:3-29
Warning against hollow philosophy, rules for wives and husbands, greetings from Aristarchus, request for the cloak left at Troas, shipwreck on Malta
These come from later in Colossians (Colossians 2:8; 3:18; 4:10), 2 Timothy 4:13, and Acts 28:1, not chapter 1.
Thanksgiving for faith and love, prayer for spiritual growth, Christ’s supremacy in creation and reconciliation, call to continue in faith, Paul’s ministry of the mystery
Genealogy of Jesus from Abraham, birth in Bethlehem of Judea, Sermon on the Mount, crucifixion at Golgotha, resurrection on the first day
This outline follows Matthew’s Gospel (Matthew 1:1; 2:1; 27:33; 28:1), not Colossians 1.
Dedication of Solomon’s temple, division of the kingdom under Rehoboam, exile to Babylon, return under Ezra, rebuilding of Jerusalem’s wall
This traces Israel’s history in Kings, Ezra, and Nehemiah (Nehemiah 2:17), not Colossians 1.
Parables beside the Sea of Galilee, feeding of the five thousand, transfiguration on the mountain, triumphal entry, ascension into heaven
These are events in Jesus’ ministry recorded in the Gospels (Matthew 13:34; 17:1), not Colossians 1.
In Paul’s letter to the believers in Colossae, which nearby city did he mention alongside them when describing the people for whom he was struggling?
Paul says he is struggling for the Colossians “and for those at Laodicea” (2:1), a neighboring city in the Lycus valley.
Colossians 2:1
Laodicea
Philippi
Philippi was a Macedonian church Paul wrote to separately (Philippians 1:1), not the neighbor named in 2:1.
Berea
Berea was a Macedonian city where Paul preached (Acts 17:10), not one mentioned in Colossians 2:1.
Troas
Troas was a port where Paul stayed on his journeys (Acts 20:6), not the city named alongside Colossae here.
Antioch
Antioch was the Syrian city that sent Paul out (Acts 13:1–3); Colossians 2:1 names Laodicea instead.
In Colossians chapter 2, Paul also said he was struggling for what other group besides the believers in Colossae and Laodicea?
Paul says he is struggling for the Colossians, for those at Laodicea, “and for all who have not met me face to face” (2:1).
Colossians 2:1
Those under Roman guard
Paul was in custody himself, but 2:1 names no group under Roman guard.
Traveling teachers
No traveling teachers are mentioned in 2:1; the group is people who had never met Paul.
All who had not met him face to face
The elders in Jerusalem
The elders in Jerusalem are not named in Colossians 2:1.
The church in Corinth
Corinth had its own letters from Paul (1 Corinthians 1:2); Colossians 2:1 names Laodicea and those who never met him.
In the opening of Colossians 2, what did Paul want for the believers’ inner lives?
Paul wants “that they may be encouraged in heart” (2:2), so that their inner lives are strengthened.
Colossians 2:2
That their hands be strengthened
Strengthening hands is an Old Testament idea (Nehemiah 2:18), not Paul’s wish in 2:2.
That their wealth increase
Paul asks for encouraged hearts, not increased wealth.
That their enemies be scattered
Scattering enemies is a psalm theme (Psalm 68:1), not what Paul asks for in 2:2.
That their hearts be encouraged
That their names be honored
Paul does not mention honored names; he wants their hearts encouraged.
According to Colossians 2, in what did Paul want the believers to be knit together?
Paul wants them “knit together in love” (2:2).
Colossians 2:2
Fear
Fear does not knit believers together; Paul names love.
Love
Fasting
Fasting is not what unites them in 2:2; the bond is love.
Silence
Silence is not the bond Paul describes; it is love.
Ritual
Ritual is exactly what Paul argues against later in the chapter (2:16–23); love is the bond.
In Paul’s message to the Colossian church, knowing “the mystery of God” points to whom?
Paul wants them to know “the mystery of God, namely Christ” (2:2).
Colossians 2:2
Moses
Moses is not the mystery; Paul says it is Christ.
The Law
The Law is later called a shadow, with Christ as the reality (2:17).
The temple
The temple is not named in this passage; the mystery is Christ.
The apostles
The apostles are messengers, not the mystery of God; Paul says it is Christ.
Christ
In Colossians 2, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge?
Paul says Christ is the one “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (2:3).
Colossians 2:3
Christ
Solomon
Solomon was famous for wisdom (1 Kings 4:30), but 2:3 locates all wisdom and knowledge in Christ.
Abraham
Abraham is a patriarch of faith, not the one in whom wisdom is hidden according to 2:3.
The prophets
The prophets spoke for God, but all the treasures of wisdom are in Christ (2:3).

Paul says, “admonish the unruly, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with everyone” (5:14).
1 Thessalonians 5:14
Warn the weak, comfort the unruly, honor the fainthearted, and judge everyone
This option scrambles the objects: the unruly are admonished, the fainthearted encouraged, and the weak helped (5:14).
Admonish the unruly, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with everyone
Rebuke the elders, help the wealthy, honor the widows, and separate from all
Rebuking elders, honoring widows, and separating from all are not the actions of 5:14.
Instruct the prophets, comfort the strong, discipline the weak, and test everyone
Instructing prophets, comforting the strong, and disciplining the weak are not the actions of 5:14.
Appoint the idle, comfort the rulers, aid the teachers, and be patient with friends
Appointing the idle, aiding teachers, and patience only with friends are not the actions of 5:14, which says patient with everyone.
In the closing prayer of 1 Thessalonians 5, what comprehensive work does Paul ask the God of peace to do?
Paul prays, “may the God of peace Himself sanctify you completely, and may your entire spirit, soul, and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (5:23).
1 Thessalonians 5:23
Gather believers from every nation into one great kingdom before the Lord returns
Gathering all nations into one empire is not what Paul asks in 5:23.
Remove all suffering and persecution from the church before Christ comes again
Removing all suffering is not what Paul asks in 5:23; he asks for sanctification and blamelessness.
Sanctify believers completely and keep their spirit, soul, and body blameless at the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ
Reveal the exact day of the Lord to the church so that they can prepare for it
Revealing the exact day is not Paul’s request in 5:23; in 5:1–2 he says they need no writing about times and seasons.
Appoint new apostles in every city to guard the church until the Lord Jesus returns
Appointing new apostles is not Paul’s request in 5:23.
53: In the opening of Paul’s second letter to the believers in Thessalonica, which three men are named as the senders?
The letter opens, “Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians” (1:1), the same trio named in 1 Thessalonians 1:1.
2 Thessalonians 1:1
Paul, Barnabas, and Mark
Barnabas and Mark traveled together to Cyprus after parting from Paul (Acts 15:39); 2 Thessalonians is sent by Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy.
Peter, James, and John
Peter, James, and John are the three Jesus took up the mountain of the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1), not the senders of this letter.
Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy
Paul, Titus, and Luke
Titus and Luke were Paul’s coworkers elsewhere (Titus 1:4; Colossians 4:14), but 1:1 names Silvanus and Timothy with Paul.
Silvanus, Apollos, and Titus
Apollos was an eloquent Alexandrian teacher (Acts 18:24); neither he nor Titus is named in 1:1, and Paul himself heads the list.
At the start of 2 Thessalonians chapter 1, to whom in the city of Thessalonica is the letter addressed?
Paul writes “To the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:1), addressing the believers as a church belonging to God.
2 Thessalonians 1:1
The rulers of the synagogue that Paul first visited in Thessalonica
Paul did first preach in the Jewish synagogue at Thessalonica (Acts 17:1), but this letter is addressed to the church, not synagogue rulers.
The church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ
The city officials of Thessalonica who had dragged Jason before them
The city officials of Thessalonica were the ones Jason was dragged before (Acts 17:6); the letter is written to the church.
The church in Berea, whose people examined the Scriptures every day
The Bereans examined the Scriptures every day (Acts 17:11), but 1:1 addresses the church of the Thessalonians, not Berea.
The apostles and elders of the church in Jerusalem and all Judea
Paul and Barnabas went up to see the apostles and elders in Jerusalem (Acts 15:2); this letter is sent to the Thessalonian church.
In the greeting of 2 Thessalonians 1 to the believers in Thessalonica, what two blessings are spoken over them?
Paul writes, “Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:2).
2 Thessalonians 1:2
Mercy and truth
“Loving devotion and faithfulness have joined together” in Psalm 85:10; Paul’s greeting in 1:2 is grace and peace.
Hope and patience
Hope and perseverance belong to Paul’s teaching on suffering (Romans 5:3–4), not the greeting of 1:2.
Joy and endurance
Joy is a fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22), but the blessing Paul speaks in 1:2 is grace and peace.
Grace and peace
Wisdom and power
Christ is called “the power of God and the wisdom of God” in 1 Corinthians 1:24; the greeting in 1:2 is grace and peace.
In Paul’s thanksgiving for the Christians in Thessalonica, what does he say is growing more and more?
Paul thanks God “because your faith is growing more and more, and your love for one another is increasing” (1:3).
2 Thessalonians 1:3
Their numbers
Acts 17:4 records many Thessalonians joining Paul, but in 1:3 it is their faith that is growing more and more.
Their faith
Their wealth
The Macedonian churches were marked by “deep poverty” (2 Corinthians 8:2), and 1:3 praises growing faith, not wealth.
Their knowledge of the Law
Paul says nothing in 1:3 about knowledge of the Law; he thanks God for their growing faith and increasing love.
Their influence in Rome
Their faith became known “to every place” (1 Thessalonians 1:8), but 1:3 speaks of growing faith, not influence in Rome.
In 2 Thessalonians chapter 1, among whom does Paul say he boasts about the believers in Thessalonica?
Paul writes, “That is why we boast among God’s churches about your perseverance and faith” (1:4).
2 Thessalonians 1:4
Among Roman officials
Paul did stand before Roman officials elsewhere (Acts 16:37), but in 1:4 he boasts about the Thessalonians among God’s churches.
Among the philosophers of Athens
Paul debated Epicurean and Stoic philosophers in Athens (Acts 17:18); his boasting in 1:4 is among God’s churches.
Among God’s churches
Among the priests in Jerusalem
Paul never boasts to the Jerusalem priests here; 1:4 says he boasts “among God’s churches.”
Among traveling merchants
Traveling merchants play no part in 1:4; Paul’s boasting about the Thessalonians is done among God’s churches.
When Paul boasts about the Thessalonian believers, which two qualities does he highlight in the middle of their suffering?
Paul boasts “about your perseverance and faith in the face of all the persecution and affliction you are enduring” (1:4).
2 Thessalonians 1:4
Wisdom and bold speech
Bold speech marked Paul’s own preaching at Thessalonica (1 Thessalonians 2:2); in 1:4 he praises their perseverance and faith.
Patience and charity
Patience is a fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22), but the pair Paul names in 1:4 is perseverance and faith.
Perseverance and faith
Fasting and prayer
Fasting and prayer accompanied the sending of Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:3); 1:4 highlights perseverance and faith.
Zeal and knowledge
Zeal and knowledge are not the qualities named in 1:4, where Paul boasts of their perseverance and faith under persecution.
In describing the hardships faced by the Christians in Thessalonica, what two kinds of troubles are mentioned?
Paul speaks of “all the persecution and affliction you are enduring” (1:4).
2 Thessalonians 1:4
Famine and shipwrecks
Famine and shipwreck were among the hardships Paul knew (Romans 8:35; 2 Corinthians 11:25), not those named for the Thessalonians in 1:4.
Wars and plagues
Wars and famines are signs Jesus foretold (Matthew 24:7); 1:4 names persecution and affliction.
Imprisonments and exile
Paul and Silas were imprisoned at Philippi (Acts 16:23), but 1:4 speaks of the Thessalonians’ persecution and affliction.
Persecution and affliction
Hunger and nakedness
Famine and nakedness appear in Paul’s list in Romans 8:35, but 1:4 names persecution and affliction.
According to 2 Thessalonians 1, what are the Thessalonian believers’ endurance and suffering a clear proof of?
Paul says, “All this is clear evidence of God’s righteous judgment” (1:5), so that they will be counted worthy of the kingdom.
2 Thessalonians 1:5
Human injustice only
Paul does not reduce their suffering to human injustice; he calls it “clear evidence of God’s righteous judgment” (1:5).
Satan’s victory
Far from showing Satan’s victory, their endurance is evidence of God’s righteous judgment (1:5), and God will repay their afflictors (1:6).
God’s righteous judgment
The fall of the Roman Empire
The Roman Empire is not mentioned in the chapter; 1:5 calls their endurance evidence of God’s righteous judgment.
The end of prayer
Prayer continues in this very chapter: “we always pray for you” (1:11); their suffering is evidence of God’s righteous judgment (1:5).
In Paul’s words to the church in Thessalonica, they are to be counted worthy of what?
Paul writes, “And so you will be counted worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are suffering” (1:5).
2 Thessalonians 1:5
The temple in Jerusalem
The rebuilt temple was completed under Darius (Ezra 6:15); in 1:5 they are counted worthy of the kingdom of God.
The kingdom of God
The throne of David
The throne of David is promised to Jesus Himself (Luke 1:32); 1:5 speaks of being counted worthy of the kingdom of God.
The priesthood of Aaron
The priesthood belonged to Aaron and his sons (Exodus 28:1); 1:5 says they will be counted worthy of the kingdom of God.
The courts of Caesar
Paul appealed to Caesar for his own trial (Acts 25:11), but 1:5 concerns being counted worthy of the kingdom of God.
In 2 Thessalonians 1, what does Paul say God will rightly repay to those who afflict the believers in Thessalonica?
Paul writes, “it is only right for God to repay with affliction those who afflict you” (1:6).
2 Thessalonians 1:6
Mercy
Mercy is what Paul himself received as a former persecutor (1 Timothy 1:13), but 1:6 says God will repay the afflicters with affliction.
Silence
God is not silent toward them; 1:6 says it is right for Him “to repay with affliction those who afflict you.”
Honor
Honor is not their reward; 1:6 says God will repay with affliction, and 1:9 speaks of eternal destruction.
Affliction
Riches
Riches are not their reward; God will repay the afflicters with affliction (1:6), echoing “I will repay, says the Lord” (Romans 12:19).
In 2 Thessalonians chapter 1, who besides the oppressed Thessalonian believers does Paul say will also receive relief?
God will grant relief “to you who are oppressed and to us as well” (1:7), that is, to Paul and his companions too.
2 Thessalonians 1:7
Only the apostles in Jerusalem
Relief is not limited to the apostles in Jerusalem; 1:7 promises it to the Thessalonians “and to us as well,” meaning Paul’s team.
The churches in Galatia only
Galatia is not mentioned in the chapter; 1:7 says relief comes to the Thessalonians and to Paul and his companions.
The Roman soldiers
Roman soldiers are not named in the chapter; the relief in 1:7 is for the oppressed believers and Paul’s group.
Paul and his companions as well
The rulers of Thessalonica
The rulers of Thessalonica are not promised relief; 1:6 says God repays those who afflict the believers.
According to Paul’s message to Thessalonica, when will relief come to the oppressed believers?
Relief will come “when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with His mighty angels” (1:7).
2 Thessalonians 1:7
When the temple is rebuilt
The temple was rebuilt after the exile (Ezra 6:15); 1:7 ties relief to the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven.
When the harvest is gathered
No harvest timing appears here; 1:7 says relief comes “when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven.”
When the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven
When Paul returns to Macedonia
Paul’s travel plans are not the trigger; 1:7 links relief to the Lord Jesus being revealed from heaven.
When Caesar changes the law
Caesar’s laws play no role; relief comes when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven (1:7).
In Paul’s description of the Lord’s return in 2 Thessalonians 1, with whom will Jesus be revealed from heaven?
Jesus will be “revealed from heaven with His mighty angels in blazing fire” (1:7–8).
2 Thessalonians 1:7
With the twelve tribes
The twelve tribes are judged by the apostles in Matthew 19:28; in 1:7 Jesus is revealed with His mighty angels.
With His mighty angels
With the elders of Israel
The elders of Israel are not mentioned here; 1:7 says Jesus will be revealed with His mighty angels.
With Moses and Elijah only
Moses and Elijah appeared with Jesus at the Transfiguration, not at His return; 1:7 says He comes with His mighty angels.
With the armies of Rome
The armies following Christ in Revelation 19:14 are “the armies of heaven,” not Rome; 1:7 names His mighty angels.
In the section of 2 Thessalonians 1 about Christ’s return, what fiery setting is mentioned?
Jesus is “revealed from heaven with His mighty angels in blazing fire” (1:7–8).
2 Thessalonians 1:8
A burning bush
The burning bush was where the angel of the LORD appeared to Moses “in a blazing fire” (Exodus 3:2), not Christ’s return.
A pillar of fire
The pillar of fire led Israel by night in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21), not part of 1:8.
A lake of fire
The lake of fire appears in Revelation 20:14 as the second death; 1:8 describes Jesus revealed in blazing fire.
Tongues of fire
Tongues like flames of fire rested on the disciples at Pentecost (Acts 2:3), not at the Lord’s return.
Blazing fire
In 2 Thessalonians chapter 1, on whom is vengeance said to fall when the Lord Jesus is revealed?
Jesus comes “inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus” (1:8).
2 Thessalonians 1:8
Those who do not know God
Those who travel by sea
Sea travel is irrelevant here; 1:8 says vengeance falls on those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel.
Those who speak Greek
Language has nothing to do with it; the gospel is for the Jew “then to the Greek” (Romans 1:16). 1:8 targets those who do not know God.
Those who live in Macedonia
Macedonia was home to the Thessalonian believers themselves; 1:8 targets those who do not know God, not a region.
Those who are unmarried
Paul commends remaining unmarried (1 Corinthians 7:8); 1:8 aims vengeance at those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel.
In Paul’s warning to Thessalonica, which full description identifies the people who face vengeance at Christ’s return?
Vengeance falls “on those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus” (1:8), both conditions together.
2 Thessalonians 1:8
Those who are rich and powerful and who trust in their own wealth
Wealth and power are not the charge here; 1:8 names those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel.
Those who oppose Rome’s rulers and refuse to pay taxes to Caesar
Paul taught submission to the governing authorities (Romans 13:1); 1:8 condemns those who do not know God or obey the gospel.
Those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus
Those who fail to keep the Jewish feast days and the Sabbath rest
Feast days are not the issue; 1:8 names those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus.
Those who abandon Macedonia and refuse to return to Thessalonica
Leaving a region is not the issue; vengeance falls on those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel (1:8).
What penalty does 2 Thessalonians 1 say awaits those who reject God and the gospel?
Paul writes, “They will suffer the penalty of eternal destruction” (1:9).
2 Thessalonians 1:9
Seven years of famine
Seven years of famine came on Egypt in Joseph’s day (Genesis 41:30); 1:9 names eternal destruction.
Temporary exile
The penalty is not temporary; 1:9 calls it “eternal destruction,” like the “eternal punishment” of Matthew 25:46.
Loss of property
Loss of property was something the faithful themselves endured (Hebrews 10:34); the penalty in 1:9 is eternal destruction.
Eternal destruction
Sickness only
The penalty is far more than sickness; 1:9 says “eternal destruction, separated from the presence of the Lord.”
In 2 Thessalonians chapter 1, from what are the condemned said to be separated?
The condemned are “separated from the presence of the Lord and the glory of His might” (1:9).
2 Thessalonians 1:9
The land of Israel and the city of David
Separation from the land was Israel’s exile; 1:9 speaks of separation from the presence of the Lord.
The presence of the Lord and the glory of His might
Their families and their fields
Families and fields are not mentioned; 1:9 says they are separated from the presence of the Lord and the glory of His might.
The sea and the mountains
In Revelation 21:1 “the sea was no more,” but 1:9 speaks of separation from the presence of the Lord.
Angels and prophets
Angels come with Christ in 1:7, but 1:9 says the condemned are separated from the presence of the Lord and the glory of His might.
On the day Christ returns, what does Paul say will happen in His saints?
Paul says it is “the day He comes to be glorified in His saints and regarded with wonder by all who have believed” (1:10).
2 Thessalonians 1:10
They will appoint judges
Saints given authority to judge appear in Revelation 20:4, but 1:10 says Christ comes to be glorified in His saints.
They will hide in caves
Hiding in caves is what the kings of the earth do in Revelation 6:15; in 1:10 Christ is glorified in His saints.
He will be glorified in them
They will rebuild the temple
Rebuilding the temple is not mentioned; 1:10 says Christ comes to be glorified in His saints.
They will rule from Thessalonica immediately
No reign from Thessalonica is promised; 1:10 says Christ will be glorified in His saints and admired by believers.
Why does Paul tell the Christians in Thessalonica that they are included among those who will admire Christ at His coming?
Christ will be regarded with wonder by all who have believed, “including you who have believed our testimony” (1:10).
2 Thessalonians 1:10
Because they gave money to Jerusalem
Gifts to Jerusalem are mentioned elsewhere (Romans 15:26), but 1:10 includes them because they believed Paul’s testimony.
Because they saw Jesus in person
They had not seen Jesus; “blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (John 20:29). 1:10 cites their belief.
Because they believed the testimony given to them
Because they kept the Law of Moses perfectly
No one is justified by works of the law (Galatians 2:16); 1:10 includes them because they believed the testimony.
Because they escaped persecution
They had not escaped persecution but were enduring it (1:4); 1:10 includes them because they believed Paul’s testimony.
Near the end of 2 Thessalonians 1, what does Paul say he and his companions always do for the believers in Thessalonica?
Paul writes, “To this end, we always pray for you” (1:11).
2 Thessalonians 1:11
Send them money
Money gifts appear elsewhere, such as the Macedonian contribution (Romans 15:26); in 1:11 Paul says “we always pray for you.”
Write to Caesar
Paul appealed to Caesar only for his own case (Acts 25:11); in 1:11 he says “we always pray for you.”
Pray for them
Visit them every year
Paul longed to see them (1 Thessalonians 3:6) but promises no yearly visits; 1:11 says they always pray for them.
Appoint kings over them
Paul and Barnabas appointed elders in churches (Acts 14:23), never kings; 1:11 says “we always pray for you.”
In Paul’s prayer for the church in Thessalonica, of what does he ask God to count them worthy?
Paul prays “that our God will count you worthy of His calling” (1:11).
2 Thessalonians 1:11
His calling
The throne of Israel
The apostles are promised thrones judging Israel’s tribes (Matthew 19:28); in 1:11 Paul prays they be counted worthy of His calling.
The office of apostle
The apostolic office is not in view; 1:11 asks that God count them worthy of His calling.
The city of Rome
Rome is not mentioned in the chapter; Paul prays that God will count them worthy of His calling (1:11).
The treasures of the temple
Temple treasures are not in view; 1:11 prays that God will count them worthy of His calling.
By whose power does Paul ask for those good desires and works of faith to be fulfilled in Thessalonica?
Paul prays that God “will powerfully fulfill your every good desire and work of faith” (1:11), so the power is God’s.
2 Thessalonians 1:11
By the power of angels
Angels accompany Christ at His return (1:7), but in 1:11 it is God who powerfully fulfills their good desires.
By the power of the Law
The law brings awareness of sin (Romans 3:20), not fulfillment; 1:11 says God powerfully fulfills their work of faith.
By human effort
Human effort is not the source; “it is God who works in you to will and to act” (Philippians 2:13), as 1:11 also says.
By Caesar’s authority
Caesar has no part here; 1:11 says “our God” will powerfully fulfill their every good desire and work of faith.
By God’s power
According to Paul’s prayer at the close of 2 Thessalonians chapter 1, what is to be glorified in the believers?
Paul prays “so that the name of our Lord Jesus will be glorified in you, and you in Him” (1:12).
2 Thessalonians 1:12
The city of Thessalonica
The city itself is not glorified; 1:12 says “the name of our Lord Jesus will be glorified in you.”
The name of our Lord Jesus
The name of Paul
Paul seeks no glory for his own name; 1:12 asks that the name of the Lord Jesus be glorified in them.
The temple of Solomon
Solomon’s temple is not mentioned in the chapter; 1:12 speaks of the name of the Lord Jesus being glorified.
The empire of Rome
Rome’s empire is not mentioned; 1:12 says the name of our Lord Jesus will be glorified in the believers.
Which summary best matches Paul’s teaching in 2 Thessalonians 1 about the suffering church in Thessalonica and the return of Jesus?

Their endurance is “clear evidence of God’s righteous judgment” (1:5); God will “repay with affliction those who afflict you” (1:6) and grant relief “when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven” (1:7).
2 Thessalonians 1:5-8
Their suffering shows God has abandoned them, and relief will come only when the rulers of Thessalonica change their policies
Paul says the opposite: their suffering is evidence of God’s righteous judgment (1:5), and relief comes when Jesus is revealed (1:7).
Their trials prove God’s righteous judgment, God will repay affliction to their afflictors, and the oppressed will receive relief when Jesus is revealed from heaven
Their persecution proves they have believed a false gospel, so they should turn back to their former way of life before it is too late
