Their reward will come only through wealth and safety in this life, since God repays faithful servants with earthly prosperity now
Their reward is the kingdom of God, “for which you are suffering” (1:5), and relief at Jesus’ return (1:7), not earthly wealth.
Jesus will return quietly and unseen, without His angels or blazing fire, and will bring no judgment on those who afflict His people

In Paul's second letter to the believers in Thessalonica, what two events does he mention together at the start of chapter 2?
Paul begins, “Now concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered together to Him” (2:1).
2 Thessalonians 2:1
The fall of Jerusalem and the deportation of its people to Babylon
The fall of Jerusalem is not mentioned in 2:1; Paul speaks of Christ’s coming and the gathering.
The coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered together to Him
The calling of Abraham and the giving of the Law at Mount Sinai
The calling of Abraham and the giving of the Law are not the events of 2:1.
The breaking of bread and baptism in water for all new believers
The breaking of bread and baptism are not the events of 2:1.
The judgment of the angels and the creation of a new earth
The judgment of angels and the new earth are not the events of 2:1.
In 2 Thessalonians 2, how does Paul tell the church in Thessalonica not to react to disturbing claims?
Paul asks them “not to be easily disconcerted or alarmed” (2:2).
2 Thessalonians 2:2
Do not be quickly angered or revengeful
Being quickly angered is not what Paul warns against in 2:2; it is being disconcerted or alarmed.
Do not be easily disconcerted or alarmed
Do not be silent or ashamed
Being silent or ashamed is not what Paul warns against in 2:2.
Do not be doubtful or double-minded
Being doubtful or double-minded echoes James 1:8, not 2:2.
Do not be weary or idle
Being weary or idle is not what Paul warns against in 2:2.
In the second chapter of 2 Thessalonians, by which three possible channels did Paul say the false claim might seem to come?
Paul warns against “any spirit or message or letter seeming to be from us” (2:2).
2 Thessalonians 2:2
A prophet, a priest, or a king speaking in God’s name
A prophet, a priest, or a king are not the three channels of 2:2.
A dream, a vision, or a parable seeming to be from God
A dream, a vision, or a parable are not the three channels of 2:2.
A spirit, a message, or a letter seeming to be from us
A psalm, a proverb, or a law seeming to be from Moses
A psalm, a proverb, or a law are not the three channels of 2:2.
A trumpet, a seal, or a bowl seeming to be from heaven
A trumpet, a seal, or a bowl are images from Revelation, not the channels of 2:2.
In Paul's warning to the Thessalonians, what false report was troubling some believers?
Some were “alleging that the Day of the Lord has already come” (2:2).
2 Thessalonians 2:2
That the resurrection had never happened
The resurrection not having happened is not the false report in 2:2.
That the kingdom had been taken from Israel
The kingdom being taken from Israel is not the false report in 2:2.
That the Day of the Lord had already come
That Christ would never return
Paul affirms Christ’s coming (2:1); the false report was that the Day had already come.
That the temple in Thessalonica would be rebuilt
A rebuilt temple in Thessalonica is not mentioned in 2:2.
In 2 Thessalonians chapter 2, what event does Paul say must come first before that day?
Paul says that day “will not come until the rebellion occurs” (2:3).
2 Thessalonians 2:3
A worldwide famine
A worldwide famine is not the event Paul names in 2:3.
The rebellion
The rebuilding of the ark
Rebuilding the ark is not the event Paul names in 2:3.
A Roman census
A Roman census is not the event Paul names in 2:3; Luke 2:1 mentions one at Jesus’ birth.
The conversion of Nineveh
The conversion of Nineveh (Jonah 3:5) is not the event Paul names in 2:3.
In 2 Thessalonians 2, what second title is given to the man of lawlessness?
Paul calls him “the man of lawlessness—the son of destruction” (2:3).
2 Thessalonians 2:3
The son of encouragement
Son of Encouragement is the meaning of Barnabas’ name (Acts 4:36), not this title.
The son of thunder

The son of destruction
The son of Zadok
The son of Zadok is not a title used in 2:3.
The son of David

In the Thessalonian passage about the lawless one, what attitude will he have toward every so-called god or object of worship?

2 Thessalonians 2:4
He will protect and honor them
The lawless one will not honor them; he will exalt himself above them (2:4).
He will ignore and dismiss them
He will not ignore them; 2:4 says he will oppose and exalt himself above them.
He will oppose and exalt himself above them
He will destroy only pagan idols

He will serve in their temples
He will not serve in their temples; he will seat himself in the temple of God (2:4).
In 2 Thessalonians chapter 2, where does Paul say the lawless one will seat himself?
Paul says “he will seat himself in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God” (2:4).
2 Thessalonians 2:4
In the synagogue at Capernaum
Capernaum’s synagogue is not mentioned in 2:4.
On Mount Carmel
Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:19) is not mentioned in 2:4.
In the palace of Caesar
Caesar’s palace is not mentioned in 2:4; the place is the temple of God.
In the temple of God
At the gate of Samaria

Paul wrote to “the churches of Galatia” (Galatians 1:2), but 1:3 says he was departing to Macedonia.
Cyprus
Barnabas and Saul sailed to Cyprus on their first journey (Acts 13:4); 1:3 names Macedonia.
In Paul’s charge to Timothy in Ephesus in 1 Timothy 1, what were certain men to stop teaching?
Timothy was to “instruct certain men not to teach false doctrines” (1:3).
1 Timothy 1:3
Parables
Parables were Jesus’ own way of teaching (Matthew 13:3), not the problem in 1:3, which is false doctrines.
False doctrines
The Psalms
The Psalms are Scripture, not the problem; 1:3 says certain men were teaching false doctrines.
The resurrection
Teaching the resurrection was the apostles’ message (Acts 4:2); denying it was the error of Hymenaeus in 2 Timothy 2:18.
Repentance
Repentance was central to apostolic preaching (Acts 2:38); in 1:3 Timothy is to stop false doctrines.
According to 1 Timothy 1, what two things were some people devoting themselves to instead of sound instruction?
Paul warns against those who “devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies” (1:4).
1 Timothy 1:4
Dreams and visions
Dreams and visions are promised when the Spirit is poured out (Acts 2:17); 1:4 warns against myths and endless genealogies.
Signs and wonders
Signs and wonders are performed by false prophets in Matthew 24:24; 1:4 names myths and endless genealogies.
Myths and endless genealogies
Fasting and vows
Fasting and vows are not the distraction here; 1:4 names “myths and endless genealogies.”
Trade and travel
Trade and travel are not mentioned; 1:4 warns against devotion to myths and endless genealogies.
In 1 Timothy chapter 1, myths and endless genealogies are said to promote what?
Myths and genealogies “promote speculation rather than the stewardship of God’s work, which is by faith” (1:4).
1 Timothy 1:4
Unity
They promote speculation, not unity; Titus 3:9 likewise calls genealogies and quarrels “pointless and worthless.”
Speculation
Generosity
Generosity is not their fruit; 1:4 says myths and endless genealogies “promote speculation.”
Courage
Courage is not what they produce; 1:4 says they promote speculation.
Revival
Revival is not their result; Paul says they lead to speculation rather than God’s work by faith (1:4).
In the first chapter of 1 Timothy, what is the goal of Paul’s instruction?
Paul writes, “The goal of our instruction is the love that comes from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith” (1:5).
1 Timothy 1:5
Power
The kingdom of God is “not a matter of talk but of power” (1 Corinthians 4:20), but 1:5 names love as the goal of instruction.
Wealth
Wealth is not the aim; 1:5 says “The goal of our instruction is the love.”
Love
Ritual purity
Ritual washing was the Pharisees’ concern (Mark 7:3); Paul’s goal in 1:5 is love from a pure heart.
Political peace
Political peace is not mentioned; the goal of Paul’s instruction is love (1:5).
In 1 Timothy 1, Paul says love comes from which three sources?
Love “comes from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith” (1:5).
1 Timothy 1:5
Prayer, fasting, and giving
Prayer, fasting, and giving appear in Jesus’ teaching (Matthew 6:16), but 1:5 names a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith.
Wisdom, knowledge, and strength
Wisdom and knowledge are not the sources named; 1:5 lists a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith.
A pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith
Obedience, sacrifice, and praise
Obedience and sacrifice are not listed; love comes from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith (1:5).
Patience, kindness, and self-control
Patience, kindness, and self-control are fruits of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23), not the sources of love in 1:5.
In Paul’s warning to Timothy in chapter 1, some people strayed from these things and turned aside to what?
Paul writes, “Some have strayed from these ways and turned aside to empty talk” (1:6).
1 Timothy 1:6
Prophecy
Prophecy is not what they turned to; 1:6 says they “turned aside to empty talk.”
Empty talk
Dreams
Dreams are not mentioned; they turned aside to empty talk (1:6).
Silence
Silence is the opposite of their fault; 1:6 says they turned aside to empty talk.
Philosophy
Paul warns of “philosophy and empty deception” in Colossians 2:8, but 1:6 says they turned aside to empty talk.
According to 1 Timothy 1, what did these misguided people want to be?
Paul says, “They want to be teachers of the law, but they do not understand what they are saying” (1:7).
1 Timothy 1:7
Kings
Kingship is not their aim; 1:7 says they want to be teachers of the law.
Apostles
False apostles appear in 2 Corinthians 11:13, but these men in 1:7 want to be teachers of the law.
Teachers of the law
High priests
The high priesthood is not in view; 1:7 says they want to be teachers of the law.
Judges
Judges are not mentioned; their ambition in 1:7 is to be teachers of the law.
In 1 Timothy chapter 1, what problem did Paul identify with those who wanted to be teachers of the law?
Paul says “they do not understand what they are saying or that which they so confidently assert” (1:7).
1 Timothy 1:7
They were too young to teach and had not yet been appointed as elders
Youth was Timothy’s own concern (1 Timothy 4:12), not these men’s; 1:7 faults them for not understanding what they so confidently assert.
They refused to travel with Paul and abandoned the work in Macedonia
Travel is not the issue; 1:7 says they do not understand what they are saying.
They did not understand what they were saying or what they so confidently asserted
They lacked Roman citizenship and so were barred from teaching publicly
Paul himself was a Roman citizen (Acts 22:25), but citizenship is not the issue; 1:7 faults their lack of understanding.
They could not read Hebrew and so misread the Scriptures they quoted
Language skill is not the charge; 1:7 says they do not understand what they say or confidently assert.
In 1 Timothy 1, Paul says the law is good if it is used how?
Paul writes, “Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it legitimately” (1:8).
1 Timothy 1:8
Publicly
Public use is not the condition; 1:8 says the law is good “if one uses it legitimately.”
Strictly
Strictness is not the point; Paul says the law is good if used legitimately (1:8).
Legitimately
Ceremonially
Ceremonial use is not the condition; 1:8 says the law is good if one uses it legitimately.
Occasionally
Occasional use is not the point; the law is good if one uses it legitimately (1:8).
According to 1 Timothy chapter 1, the law is not enacted for whom?
Paul writes, “law is not enacted for the righteous, but for the lawless and rebellious” (1:9).
1 Timothy 1:9
Travelers
Travelers are not mentioned; 1:9 says the law is not enacted for the righteous.
Rulers
Rulers are not named; 1:9 says the law is not for the righteous but for the lawless and rebellious.
The righteous
The poor
The poor are not singled out; 1:9 says the law is not enacted for the righteous.
Widows
Widows receive care elsewhere (James 1:27); 1:9 says the law is not enacted for the righteous.
In Paul’s list in 1 Timothy 1, which pair appears first as those for whom the law is enacted?
The list begins, “for the lawless and rebellious, for the ungodly and sinful” (1:9).
1 Timothy 1:9
Saints and prophets
Saints and prophets are not lawbreakers; the list in 1:9 opens with the lawless and rebellious.
Lawless and rebellious
Elders and deacons
Elders and deacons are church offices (1 Timothy 3); the list in 1:9 opens with the lawless and rebellious.
Husbands and wives
Husbands and wives are not in the list; 1:9 begins with the lawless and rebellious.
Slaves and masters
Slaves and masters are addressed elsewhere; the list in 1:9 opens with the lawless and rebellious.
In the sin list of 1 Timothy chapter 1, which people are specifically mentioned in connection with harming parents?
The law is enacted “for killers of father or mother, for murderers” (1:9).
1 Timothy 1:9
Kidnappers of children
Kidnapping is a capital crime in Exodus 21:16, and “slave traders” appear in 1:10, but the parent-related group in 1:9 is killers of father or mother.
Killers of father or mother
Rebellious sons only
The stubborn and rebellious son is in Deuteronomy 21:18; 1:9 names killers of father or mother.
Mockers of elders
Respect for the elderly is commanded in Leviticus 19:32, but 1:9 names killers of father or mother.
Neglecters of widows
Caring for widows is commanded in James 1:27; the parent-related group in 1:9 is killers of father or mother.
In 1 Timothy 1:10, which group is specifically named among those contrary to sound teaching?
Paul lists “for slave traders and liars and perjurers” among those for whom the law is enacted (1:10).
1 Timothy 1:10
Nazarites
Nazirites took a vow to separate themselves to the LORD (Numbers 6:2); they are not in the list in 1:10.
Slave traders
Levites
Levites served at the sanctuary; they are not in the sin list of 1:10.
Scribes
Scribes sat “in Moses’ seat” (Matthew 23:2), but 1:10 names slave traders, liars, and perjurers.
Tax collectors
Tax collectors ate with Jesus (Matthew 9:10); they are not in the list in 1:10, which names slave traders.
Closing the list in 1 Timothy chapter 1, how does Paul describe “anyone else” for whom the law is enacted?
The list ends “for anyone else who is averse to sound teaching” (1:10).
1 Timothy 1:10
As someone whose faith is being tested
Testing of faith develops perseverance (James 1:3), but 1:10 describes anyone else as averse to sound teaching.
As someone averse to sound teaching
As someone learning patience
Building patience is not what Paul says; 1:10 describes anyone else who is averse to sound teaching.
As someone weak in the faith
Paul does not call them weak; 1:10 says the law is for anyone else averse to sound teaching.
As someone the church should ignore
Paul does not say to ignore them; the law is enacted for anyone averse to sound teaching (1:10).
In 1 Timothy 1, sound teaching is said to agree with what?
Sound teaching is that which “agrees with the glorious gospel of the blessed God, with which I have been entrusted” (1:10–11).
1 Timothy 1:11
The traditions of the elders
The tradition of the elders was the Pharisees’ standard (Mark 7:5); 1:11 measures sound teaching by the glorious gospel.
The glorious gospel of the blessed God
The wisdom of Greece
Paul warns against “philosophy and empty deception” (Colossians 2:8); sound teaching agrees with the glorious gospel (1:11).
The decrees of Caesar
Caesar’s decree ordered a census (Luke 2:1); sound teaching agrees with the glorious gospel of the blessed God (1:11).
The genealogies of Israel
Endless genealogies are what Paul warns against in 1:4, not the standard of sound teaching in 1:11.
According to 1 Timothy chapter 1, with what had Paul been entrusted?
Paul speaks of “the glorious gospel of the blessed God, with which I have been entrusted” (1:11).
1 Timothy 1:11
The treasury of the temple in Jerusalem
Temple treasure was entrusted to priests in Ezra 8:33; Paul was entrusted with the glorious gospel (1:11).
The priesthood of Aaron and his sons
The priesthood was given to Aaron and his sons (Exodus 28:1); Paul was entrusted with the gospel (1:11).
The glorious gospel of the blessed God
A royal crown and the throne of David
David’s throne is promised to Jesus (Luke 1:32); Paul was entrusted with the glorious gospel of the blessed God (1:11).
The land of Canaan as an inheritance
Canaan was Israel’s inheritance, not Paul’s trust; 1:11 says he was entrusted with the glorious gospel.
In Paul’s testimony in 1 Timothy 1, whom does he thank for strengthening him?
Paul writes, “I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who has strengthened me” (1:12).
1 Timothy 1:12
God our Father only
Paul does give glory to God in 1:17, but in 1:12 he thanks Christ Jesus our Lord for strengthening him.
Timothy his child
Timothy is the letter’s recipient (1:2), not the one who strengthened Paul; 1:12 thanks Christ Jesus.
Christ Jesus our Lord
The church in Ephesus
The Ephesian church is where Timothy served (1:3); Paul thanks Christ Jesus for strengthening him (1:12).
Barnabas his friend
Barnabas was Paul’s early partner (Acts 13:2), but 1:12 thanks Christ Jesus our Lord.
In 1 Timothy chapter 1, why does Paul say Christ appointed him to service?
Paul thanks Christ Jesus “that He considered me faithful and appointed me to service” (1:12).
1 Timothy 1:12
Because he was born in Tarsus
Paul was born in Tarsus (Acts 22:3), but 1:12 says Christ appointed him because He considered him faithful.
Because he had studied under Gamaliel
Paul was educated under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), but in 1:12 his appointment rests on Christ considering him faithful.
Because Christ considered him faithful
Because the apostles voted for him
No vote of the apostles is mentioned; Matthias was chosen by lot (Acts 1:26). 1:12 credits Christ’s judgment.
Because he was the eldest disciple
Paul calls himself “the least of the apostles” (1 Corinthians 15:9), not the eldest; 1:12 says Christ considered him faithful.
In his personal history in 1 Timothy 1, which three descriptions does Paul apply to his former life?
Paul writes, “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a violent man” (1:13).
1 Timothy 1:13
Doubter, wanderer, prisoner
Paul was later a prisoner for Christ (Philemon 1:1), but 1:13 describes his former life as blasphemer, persecutor, and violent man.
Blasphemer, persecutor, and violent man
Tax collector, zealot, and fisherman
These fit others: “Matthew the tax collector” (Matthew 10:3). Paul’s own words in 1:13 are blasphemer, persecutor, violent man.
Idolater, sorcerer, and adulterer
Paul does not use these terms of himself; 1:13 says he was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a violent man.
Shepherd, soldier, and judge
Paul was a tentmaker by trade (Acts 18:3); in 1:13 his former life is that of a blasphemer, persecutor, and violent man.
In 1 Timothy chapter 1, why does Paul say he was shown mercy despite his former violence?
Paul says, “because I had acted in ignorance and unbelief, I was shown mercy” (1:13).
1 Timothy 1:13
Because he fasted often
Fasting is not the reason given; 1:13 says he was shown mercy because he acted in ignorance and unbelief.
Because he acted in ignorance and unbelief
Because Ananias defended him
Ananias laid hands on Saul to restore his sight (Acts 9:17), but 1:13 grounds mercy in his ignorance and unbelief.
Because he was from Benjamin
Paul was of the tribe of Benjamin (Philippians 3:5), but that is not why he was shown mercy (1:13).
Because he kept feast days
Keeping feasts is not the reason; 1:13 says he acted in ignorance and unbelief.
According to 1 Timothy 1, what overflowed to Paul after mercy was shown to him?
Paul writes, “And the grace of our Lord overflowed to me” (1:14).
1 Timothy 1:14
Authority from Jerusalem
Paul once acted “with authority from the chief priests” (Acts 26:10), but in 1:14 it is the grace of our Lord that overflowed.
The grace of our Lord
Gold from Macedonia
Macedonian generosity is praised in 2 Corinthians 8:2; 1:14 says the grace of our Lord overflowed to Paul.
Wisdom from Egypt
Egypt’s wisdom is not mentioned; the grace of our Lord overflowed to Paul (1:14).
Favor from Caesar
Caesar’s favor is not in view; 1:14 says the grace of our Lord overflowed to him.
In 1 Timothy chapter 1, what accompanied the overflowing grace of the Lord in Paul’s life?
Grace overflowed to Paul, “along with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus” (1:14).
1 Timothy 1:14
Visions and dreams of the heavenly realms
Visions and dreams are promised in Acts 2:17, but 1:14 says faith and love accompanied grace.
Faith and love that are in Christ Jesus
Riches and influence among the Gentiles
Riches and influence did not accompany grace here; 1:14 names faith and love in Christ Jesus.
Law and sacrifice at the temple in Jerusalem
Law and sacrifice are not mentioned; grace came “along with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus” (1:14).
Signs and healings wherever he traveled
Gifts of healing are listed in 1 Corinthians 12:9, but 1:14 says grace came with faith and love.
In the middle of 1 Timothy chapter 1, which statement does Paul call trustworthy and deserving full acceptance?
Paul writes, “This is a trustworthy saying, worthy of full acceptance: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (1:15).
1 Timothy 1:15
The law was abolished forever
Paul affirms “the law is good, if one uses it legitimately” (1:8); the trustworthy saying in 1:15 is about Christ saving sinners.
Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners
Wisdom is proved right by her children
Jesus said “wisdom is vindicated by all her children” (Luke 7:35); the trustworthy saying in 1:15 is about Christ saving sinners.
All Israel will be saved immediately
Paul writes “all Israel will be saved” in Romans 11:26, but the trustworthy saying in 1:15 is that Christ came to save sinners.
The dead are already raised
Saying the resurrection has already occurred was Hymenaeus’s error (2 Timothy 2:18), not the trustworthy saying.
In 1 Timothy 1, of whom does Paul say he is the worst?
Paul says Christ came “to save sinners, of whom I am the worst” (1:15).
1 Timothy 1:15
Pharisees
Paul was a Pharisee (Philippians 3:5), but in 1:15 he calls himself the worst of sinners.
The lost sheep of Israel
“The lost sheep of Israel” is Jesus’ phrase in Matthew 10:6; Paul calls himself the worst of sinners (1:15).
Sinners
False apostles
Paul warns about false apostles in 2 Corinthians 11:13; in 1:15 he calls himself the worst of sinners.
Roman officials
Roman officials are not mentioned; Paul says he is the worst of sinners (1:15).
In Paul’s explanation in 1 Timothy chapter 1, why was mercy shown to him as the worst of sinners?
Paul says he was shown mercy “so that in me, the worst of sinners, Christ Jesus might display His perfect patience” (1:16).
1 Timothy 1:16
So he could rebuild the temple in Jerusalem for Israel
The temple was rebuilt in Ezra’s day (Ezra 6:15); Paul was shown mercy so Christ might display His patience (1:16).
So Christ Jesus might display His perfect patience in him
So he could serve as high priest in the order of Aaron
Paul was never a priest of Aaron’s line; mercy was shown so Christ might display His perfect patience (1:16).
So that Rome would honor the church and stop persecuting it
Roman honor is not the reason; 1:16 says Christ displayed His perfect patience in Paul as an example.
So Timothy would move to Jerusalem to lead the church there
Timothy was told to stay in Ephesus (1:3); mercy was shown so Christ might display His patience (1:16).
In 1 Timothy 1, Paul says his own mercy serves as an example to whom?
Christ displayed His patience in Paul “as an example to those who would believe in Him for eternal life” (1:16).
1 Timothy 1:16
Those who would believe in Christ Jesus for eternal life
The rulers of the synagogues throughout Asia and Macedonia
Synagogue rulers are not in view; Paul is an example “to those who would believe in Him for eternal life” (1:16).
The priests who served in the temple at Jerusalem
Temple priests are not mentioned; Paul’s mercy is an example to future believers (1:16).
The tribes of Israel returning from exile in Babylon
The return from exile is not in view; 1:16 says Paul is an example to those who would believe for eternal life.
All who seek earthly power and honor among the nations
Earthly power is not the focus; Paul’s mercy is an example to those who would believe in Christ for eternal life (1:16).
In the doxology of 1 Timothy chapter 1, what title does Paul use first for God?
The doxology begins, “Now to the King eternal, immortal, and invisible, the only God” (1:17).
1 Timothy 1:17
King eternal
Lord of armies
God is called “The LORD of Hosts” in Psalm 24:10, but Paul’s doxology in 1:17 begins with “the King eternal.”
Shepherd of Israel
“Shepherd of Israel” is from Psalm 80:1; Paul’s first title in 1:17 is “the King eternal.”
Ancient of Days
“The Ancient of Days” is Daniel’s title (Daniel 7:9); 1:17 begins “Now to the King eternal.”
Father of mercies
Paul calls God “the Father of compassion” in 2 Corinthians 1:3; 1:17 opens with “the King eternal.”
In 1 Timothy chapter 1, besides being eternal, immortal, and invisible, God is called what?
Paul praises “the King eternal, immortal, and invisible, the only God” (1:17).
1 Timothy 1:17
The firstborn of creation
“The firstborn over all creation” describes the Son (Colossians 1:15), not the title in 1:17.
The only God
The God of thunder
No such title appears; 1:17 calls Him “the only God.”
The Lord of hosts only
God is “The LORD of Hosts” in Psalm 24:10, but 1:17 calls Him “the only God.”
The judge of Jerusalem only
This title is not found here; 1:17 calls Him “the only God.”
In Paul’s doxology in 1 Timothy 1, what does he ascribe to the only God forever and ever?
Paul writes, “to the King eternal… the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen” (1:17).
1 Timothy 1:17
Gold and incense
Gold and incense were among the magi’s gifts (Matthew 2:11); Paul ascribes honor and glory to God (1:17).
Fear and silence
“Let all the earth be silent before Him” is Habakkuk 2:20; Paul ascribes honor and glory in 1:17.
Honor and glory
Law and judgment
Law and judgment are not ascribed here; 1:17 says “be honor and glory forever and ever.”
Wisdom and power only
Wisdom and power appear with honor and glory in Revelation 7:12, but 1:17 names only honor and glory.
Near the end of 1 Timothy chapter 1, how does Paul address Timothy when renewing his charge?
Paul writes, “Timothy, my child, I entrust you with this command” (1:18).
1 Timothy 1:18
My coworker
Timothy is called “my fellow worker” in Romans 16:21, but in 1:18 Paul says “my child.”
My child
My cousin
Timothy is never called Paul’s cousin; 1:18 says “Timothy, my child.”
My brother by blood
Timothy was not Paul’s blood brother; his father was Greek (Acts 16:1). 1:18 says “my child.”
My servant
Paul does not call Timothy his servant here; 1:18 says “Timothy, my child.”
In 1 Timothy 1, Paul’s instruction to Timothy is said to be in keeping with what?
Paul gives the charge “in keeping with the previous prophecies about you” (1:18).
1 Timothy 1:18
The decision of the Jerusalem council
The Jerusalem council is in Acts 15; Paul’s charge in 1:18 accords with previous prophecies about Timothy.
Previous prophecies about Timothy
The customs of Ephesus
Ephesian customs are not mentioned; the charge is in keeping with previous prophecies about Timothy (1:18).
A Roman decree
No Roman decree is in view; 1:18 links the charge to prophecies about Timothy, like the one in 1 Timothy 4:14.
The songs of David
David’s songs are not mentioned; the charge accords with previous prophecies about Timothy (1:18).
According to 1 Timothy chapter 1, what was Timothy to do by means of those previous prophecies?
Paul says the prophecies were given “so that by them you may fight the good fight” (1:18).
1 Timothy 1:18
Collect an offering
Paul gathered a collection for the saints (1 Corinthians 16:1), but 1:18 says Timothy was to fight the good fight.
Build a synagogue
Building a synagogue is not in view; 1:18 says Timothy is to fight the good fight.
Fight the good fight
Seek a wife
Marriage is not the subject; Timothy is to fight the good fight (1:18).
Travel to Spain
Paul himself hoped to go to Spain (Romans 15:24); Timothy was to fight the good fight (1:18).
In the closing instruction of 1 Timothy 1, which two things must Timothy hold on to?
Timothy is to fight the good fight “holding on to faith and a good conscience” (1:19).
1 Timothy 1:19
Fasting and prayer
Fasting and prayer accompanied the sending of missionaries (Acts 13:3); 1:19 says hold on to faith and a good conscience.
Faith and a good conscience
Wisdom and power
Wisdom and power are not named; Timothy must hold on to faith and a good conscience (1:19).
Zeal and knowledge
Zeal and knowledge are not the pair; 1:19 says “faith and a good conscience.”
Hope and endurance
Hope and endurance are not named here; 1:19 says “holding on to faith and a good conscience.”
In 1 Timothy chapter 1, what happened to some people who rejected faith and a good conscience?
Paul writes that some “have rejected and thereby shipwrecked their faith” (1:19).
1 Timothy 1:19
They became kings
They did not become kings; 1:19 says they shipwrecked their faith.
They shipwrecked their faith
They returned to Jerusalem
No return to Jerusalem is mentioned; 1:19 says they shipwrecked their faith.
They saw angels
Seeing angels is not mentioned; those who rejected faith and conscience shipwrecked their faith (1:19).
They became wealthy
Wealth is not their outcome; 1:19 says they shipwrecked their faith.
In the final verse of 1 Timothy chapter 1, which two men are named as examples of such failure?
Paul writes, “Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander” (1:20).
1 Timothy 1:20
Demas and Crescens
Demas deserted Paul and Crescens went to Galatia (2 Timothy 4:10); 1:20 names Hymenaeus and Alexander.
Hymenaeus and Alexander
Silas and Titus
Silas and Titus were faithful coworkers of Paul; 1:20 names Hymenaeus and Alexander.
Jason and Sosipater
Jason and Sosipater sent greetings as Paul’s countrymen (Romans 16:21); 1:20 names Hymenaeus and Alexander.
Ananias and Sapphira
Ananias and Sapphira lied about a property sale (Acts 5:1); 1:20 names Hymenaeus and Alexander.
According to 1 Timothy 1, what did Paul say he had done with Hymenaeus and Alexander?
Paul says, “whom I have handed over to Satan to be taught not to blaspheme” (1:20).
1 Timothy 1:20
Sent them to Crete
Titus, not these men, was left in Crete (Titus 1:5); Paul handed Hymenaeus and Alexander over to Satan (1:20).
Appointed them as elders
Far from being appointed elders, they were handed over to Satan (1:20).
Handed them over to Satan
Forgiven them publicly
They were not publicly forgiven; Paul handed them over to Satan to be taught not to blaspheme (1:20).
Entrusted them with the offering
They were not entrusted with an offering; Paul handed them over to Satan (1:20).
In 1 Timothy chapter 1, for what purpose were Hymenaeus and Alexander handed over to Satan?
They were handed over to Satan “to be taught not to blaspheme” (1:20), a corrective aim.
1 Timothy 1:20
To make them wealthy
Wealth is not the purpose; 1:20 says they were handed over “to be taught not to blaspheme.”
To teach them not to blaspheme
To prepare them for martyrdom
Martyrdom is not in view; the purpose in 1:20 is that they be taught not to blaspheme.
To send them to Rome
Rome is not mentioned; they were handed over to Satan to be taught not to blaspheme (1:20).
To test Timothy
Testing Timothy is not the goal; 1:20 says the aim was that they be taught not to blaspheme.
In 1 Timothy 1, which of the following is not one of the three sources from which love is said to come?
Love comes “from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith” (1:5); a spiritual gift is not one of the three.
1 Timothy 1:5
A pure heart
A pure heart is the first source of love named in 1:5.
A clear conscience
A clear conscience is the second source of love named in 1:5.
A sincere faith
A sincere faith is the third source of love named in 1:5.
A spiritual gift
None of the above
One choice does fit: a spiritual gift is not among the three sources in 1:5, so “none of the above” is wrong.
According to the contrast in 1 Timothy chapter 1, myths and endless genealogies promote speculation rather than what?
Myths and genealogies “promote speculation rather than the stewardship of God’s work, which is by faith” (1:4).
1 Timothy 1:4
The rebuilding of God’s temple in Jerusalem
The temple was rebuilt in Ezra’s day (Ezra 6:15); 1:4 contrasts speculation with the stewardship of God’s work.
The stewardship of God’s work, which is by faith
The defense of Caesar’s rule throughout the empire
Caesar is not mentioned; 1:4 contrasts speculation with “the stewardship of God’s work, which is by faith.”
The spread of Greek learning among the churches
Greek learning is not the contrast; 1:4 sets speculation against the stewardship of God’s work by faith.
The increase of sacrifices offered at the altar
Sacrifices are not mentioned; 1:4 contrasts speculation with the stewardship of God’s work.
In 1 Timothy 1, which description best captures the irony Paul sees in certain men at Ephesus?
Paul says, “They want to be teachers of the law, but they do not understand what they are saying or that which they so confidently assert” (1:7).
1 Timothy 1:7
They wanted to be kings over Israel but were afraid to lead the people into battle

Paul tells Titus to teach plain, sound doctrine for everyone, not secret mysteries for a few; he warns against myths in Titus 1:14.
Things consistent with sound doctrine
New ceremonial regulations
Titus is told to teach what fits sound doctrine; ceremonial rules are not what Paul commands here, and Titus 1:14 warns against human commands.
Endless genealogies
Paul warns against genealogies in Titus 3:9 as pointless and worthless, so they are not what Titus is to speak.
Political reforms
Nothing in Titus 2 calls for political reform; Paul’s concern is godly living grounded in sound doctrine.
In Paul’s instructions for church life on Crete, which group was specifically told to be temperate?
Titus 2:2 says “Older men are to be temperate, dignified, self-controlled, and sound in faith, love, and perseverance.”
Titus 2:2
Younger women
Titus 2:4–5 gives younger women other instructions, such as loving their husbands and children; temperance is not their line in this chapter.
Deacons
Deacons are not mentioned in Titus 2; Paul’s qualifications for deacons are in 1 Timothy 3:8–13.
Older men
Children
Children are not addressed in Titus 2; Paul speaks to older men, older women, young women, younger men and slaves.
Travelers
Travelers are not addressed anywhere in Titus 2; the groups named are older and younger men and women, and slaves.
In Paul’s household teaching to Titus, older women were to teach what is good so they could train whom?
Titus 2:4 says the older women can “train the young women to love their husbands and children.”
Titus 2:3-4
Young women
Older men
Older men receive their own instructions in Titus 2:2; the older women are charged with training the young women.
New elders
Elders are discussed in Titus 1:5–9; in Titus 2:3–4 the older women train the young women, not new elders.
Merchants
Merchants are not mentioned in Titus 2; the women’s training is directed at the young women.
Children only
The training is for young women, not children only; Titus 2:4 mentions children only as people the young women are to love.
In Titus 2, young women were to be trained to love which two groups of people?
Titus 2:4 says the young women are trained “to love their husbands and children.”
Titus 2:4
Parents and siblings
Parents and siblings are not named in Titus 2:4; the young women are to love their husbands and children.
Neighbors and strangers
Loving neighbors is taught elsewhere (Mark 12:31), but Titus 2:4 names husbands and children specifically.
Husbands and children
Elders and deacons
Elders and deacons are not the object of this love in Titus 2:4; Paul names husbands and children.
The poor and widows
Care for the poor and widows appears elsewhere (1 Timothy 5:3), but Titus 2:4 names husbands and children.
In Paul’s direct instruction to Titus, what quality was younger men urged to have?

Wealth
Wealth is never urged on younger men in Titus 2; Paul asks for self-control, and warns about love of money in 1 Timothy 6:10.
Self-control
Eloquence
Eloquence is not what Paul asks of younger men in Titus 2:6; he asks for self-control.
Political skill
Titus 2:6 does not ask younger men for political skill; the quality named is self-control.
Pilgrimage zeal
Pilgrimage zeal is not a Christian requirement in Titus 2; the younger men are urged to be self-controlled.
In the section where Paul tells Titus how to lead, Titus was to show himself as an example by doing what?

Good works
Settling lawsuits
Settling lawsuits is not part of Titus 2:7; Paul wants Titus to be an example by doing good works.
Fasting publicly

In Titus 2, whose conduct was meant to make the teaching about God our Savior attractive?

Roman governors
Roman governors are not addressed in Titus 2; the passage speaks to slaves about adorning the teaching.
Slaves
Older widows
Older widows are not addressed in Titus 2; Paul speaks to older women, who are to teach what is good.
Temple singers
Temple singers are not mentioned in Titus 2; the group addressed in verses 9–10 is slaves.
Shepherds
Shepherds are not mentioned in Titus 2; verses 9–10 speak to slaves.

The grace of God
A new priesthood
A new priesthood is not mentioned in Titus 2:11; what appeared is the grace of God.
The ark of the covenant
The ark of the covenant is not part of Titus 2:11; the verse says the grace of God has appeared.
In Titus 2, believers are said to await what future reality?

In Paul’s instructions to Titus, older men were to be sound in which three areas?

Vision, prophecy, and dreams
Vision, prophecy and dreams are not the older men’s areas in Titus 2:2; Paul names faith, love and perseverance.

Managers of their households
Scribes
Scribes are not named in Titus 2:5; young women are to be managers of their households.
Tax collectors
Tax collectors are not named in Titus 2:5; young women are to be managers of their households.

Humor and flexibility are not asked of Titus in 2:7; he is to show integrity, dignity and wholesome speech.
Integrity and dignity

Mystery and symbolism
Mystery and symbolism are not requested in Titus 2:7; Paul wants integrity and dignity.
Wealth and status
Wealth and status are not qualities Paul asks Titus to show in his teaching.

Their own masters in everything

The priests in Jerusalem

Singing is not forbidden in Titus 2:9; slaves are told not to be argumentative.
Traveling
Traveling is not mentioned in Titus 2:9; slaves are told not to be argumentative.
Arguing
Farming
Farming is not mentioned in Titus 2:9; the warning to slaves is against being argumentative and stealing.
Marriage
Marriage is not forbidden to slaves in Titus 2:9; the warning is against being argumentative.

Titus 2:11 says, “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone.”

Judgment on Jerusalem alone

Language and learning are not what Titus 2:12 says to renounce; the verse names ungodliness and worldly passions.

Sensible, upright, and godly
Isolated, silent, and hidden

Titus 2:14 says Christ gave Himself “to redeem us from all lawlessness.”

Hunger and drought

Physical weakness

Foreign languages

Debates

Good deeds
Ceremonial washings

Military victory

Pilgrimages to Jerusalem
Pilgrimages to Jerusalem are not named in Titus 2:14; the people are zealous for good deeds.

Sing and fast

Younger women

Jewish teachers

Shepherds

Escaping slavery and gaining their freedom at once

Greek philosophy

In Paul’s re-framing of Onesimus’s status, Philemon should receive him no longer merely as what?
Paul says to receive him “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (1:16).
Philemon 1:16
A traveler
Paul’s contrast is slave versus beloved brother (1:16); traveler is not mentioned.
A debtor
Paul does mention possible debts (1:18), but the contrast in 1:16 is slave versus brother.
A stranger
Paul contrasts slave and beloved brother (1:16), not stranger and friend.
A slave
A tax collector
“A pagan or a tax collector” is Jesus’ phrase in Matthew 18:17; in 1:16 Paul speaks of a slave.
In Paul’s appeal, Onesimus is described as a beloved brother especially to whom, and even more so to whom else?
Paul writes, “He is especially beloved to me, but even more so to you” (1:16), that is, to Paul and to Philemon.
Philemon 1:16
Especially to Timothy, even more to Luke
Timothy and Luke appear in the greeting (1:1) and the closing (1:24), not in this statement.
Especially to Paul, even more to Philemon
Especially to Apphia, even more to Archippus
Apphia and Archippus are greeted in 1:2; the beloved-brother statement concerns Paul and Philemon (1:16).
Especially to Epaphras, even more to Mark
Epaphras and Mark send greetings (1:23–24); they are not part of the statement in 1:16.
Especially to the saints, even more to the elders
Paul says “to me” and “to you” (1:16), meaning himself and Philemon, not groups of saints or elders.
In Paul’s request to Philemon, if Philemon considers Paul a partner, how should he receive Onesimus?
Paul writes, “So if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me” (1:17).
Philemon 1:17
As he would receive Paul himself
As he would receive a servant
Paul says the opposite: receive him “no longer as a slave” (1:16).
As he would receive a judge
No judge is mentioned; Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul himself (1:17).
As he would receive a stranger
Paul calls Onesimus a beloved brother (1:16), not a stranger.
As he would receive a child
Paul calls Onesimus “my child” (1:10), but he asks Philemon to receive him as he would receive Paul (1:17).
In the letter concerning any wrong done by Onesimus, what does Paul tell Philemon to do if Onesimus owes anything?
Paul says, “if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account” (1:18).
Philemon 1:18
Forgive the debt silently
Paul does not ask Philemon to absorb the loss silently; he asks that any debt be charged to his account (1:18).
Demand payment from Timothy
Timothy is not involved; Paul takes the debt on himself (1:18–19).
Charge it to Paul’s account
Take it before the church
Telling it to the church is Jesus’ instruction in Matthew 18:17; here Paul says “charge it to my account” (1:18).
Send Onesimus to Jerusalem
Jerusalem is not mentioned; Paul is sending Onesimus back to Philemon (1:12).
In a line Paul says he writes with his own hand, what promise does he make to Philemon?
Paul writes, “I, Paul, write this with my own hand. I will repay it” (1:19).
Philemon 1:19
I will visit soon
Paul does hope to visit (1:22), but the promise written in his own hand is to repay (1:19).
I will send Mark
Mark is only named among those sending greetings (1:24).
I will pray daily
Paul already remembers Philemon in his prayers (1:4); his handwritten promise is to repay (1:19).
I will repay it
I will tell the church
Paul makes no promise to tell the church; he pledges to repay any debt himself (1:19).
After offering to repay any debt, what pointed reminder does Paul add to Philemon?
After promising to repay, Paul adds, “not to mention that you owe me your very self” (1:19).
Philemon 1:19
You owe me your very self
You owe the church a tithe
No tithe is mentioned; Paul reminds Philemon that he owes Paul his very self (1:19).
You owe Caesar tribute
Paying taxes to Caesar was the question put to Jesus (Matthew 22:17); it is not in Philemon.
You owe Onesimus an apology
Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as a brother (1:16), not to apologize to him.
You owe Timothy a welcome
Timothy is only a co-sender (1:1); the debt Paul names is Philemon’s very self (1:19).
In Paul’s request near the end of the letter, what does he ask Philemon to do for him in Christ?
Paul writes, “Yes, brother, let me have some benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ” (1:20).
Philemon 1:20
Defend my ministry
Paul asks for benefit and refreshment (1:20), not for a defense of his ministry.
Refresh my heart
Deliver my letters
Tychicus carried Paul’s news to Colossae (Colossians 4:7); Paul asks Philemon to refresh his heart (1:20).
Hide me from soldiers
Paul asks for a guest room (1:22), not a hiding place from soldiers.
Appoint new elders
Appointing elders was the task Paul gave Titus (Titus 1:5); Philemon is asked to refresh Paul’s heart (1:20).
In his confidence about Philemon’s response, what does Paul say Philemon will do?
Paul writes, “Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I ask” (1:21).
Philemon 1:21
Refuse politely
Paul expects the opposite: obedience and even more (1:21).
Ask for more witnesses
No witnesses are mentioned; Paul is confident of Philemon’s obedience (1:21).
Obey and do even more than Paul asks
Wait until winter
“Come to me before winter” is Paul’s request to Timothy (2 Timothy 4:21), not a delay Paul expects from Philemon.
Send Onesimus elsewhere
Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as he would Paul (1:17), not to send him elsewhere.
In the final practical request of Philemon, what does Paul ask to be prepared for him?
Paul writes, “In the meantime, prepare a guest room for me” (1:22), hoping to be restored to them.
Philemon 1:22
A feast
No feast is requested; Paul asks for lodging because he hopes to be restored to them (1:22).
A scroll
Paul asks Timothy to bring his scrolls (2 Timothy 4:13); Philemon is to prepare a guest room (1:22).
A ship
Paul sailed as a prisoner on an Adramyttian ship (Acts 27:2); here he asks for a guest room (1:22).
A guest room
A robe
The best robe is brought for the returning son in Luke 15:22; Paul asks for a guest room (1:22).
In the closing greetings of Philemon, who is singled out as Paul’s “fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus”?
The closing reads, “Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings” (1:23).
Philemon 1:23
Demas
Demas is listed among the fellow workers (1:24) and later deserted Paul (2 Timothy 4:10).
Luke
Luke is one of the fellow workers (1:24) and is called “the beloved physician” in Colossians 4:14.
Epaphras
Archippus
Archippus is called “our fellow soldier” (1:2), not a fellow prisoner.
Tychicus
Tychicus is not named in Philemon; he is the “faithful minister” of Colossians 4:7.
In the farewell section of Philemon, which group is named as Paul’s fellow workers?
Paul sends greetings from “Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers” (1:24).
Philemon 1:24
Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke
Peter, James, John, and Andrew
Peter, James, John, and Andrew are among the twelve apostles (Matthew 10:2); none appears in Philemon.
Barnabas, Silas, Titus, and Timothy
Barnabas, Silas, and Titus are not in Philemon; Timothy appears only as co-sender (1:1).
Aquila, Priscilla, Apollos, and Sosthenes
Aquila, Priscilla, and Apollos appear in Acts 18:2, 24, not in Philemon’s closing greetings.
Philip, Stephen, Nicanor, and Parmenas
Philip, Stephen, Nicanor, and Parmenas were among the seven chosen in Jerusalem (Acts 6:5).
In the order of names in Philemon’s closing greetings, who is listed immediately before Luke?
The list reads “Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke” (1:24), so Demas comes just before Luke.
Philemon 1:24
Mark
Mark is listed first, not just before Luke (1:24).
Demas
Aristarchus
Aristarchus is second in the list, before Demas (1:24).
Epaphras
Epaphras is named separately in 1:23 as Paul’s fellow prisoner.
Timothy
Timothy appears in the opening as co-sender (1:1), not in the closing list.
In the opening and appeal of Philemon, which description best matches how Paul presents himself instead of using his usual title “apostle”?
Paul calls himself “a prisoner of Christ Jesus” (1:1) and says he is “now aged” (1:9).
Philemon 1:1, 9
Shepherd and teacher
Paul uses neither title here; he calls himself a prisoner (1:1) and aged (1:9).
Elder and prophet
Peter calls himself “a fellow elder” (1 Peter 5:1); in Philemon Paul is aged and a prisoner (1:9).
Prisoner of Christ Jesus and aged
Servant of the temple and rabbi
Paul calls himself “a servant of Christ Jesus” in Romans 1:1, but in Philemon he is a prisoner (1:1).
Ruler and judge
Paul deliberately sets authority aside, preferring to appeal on the basis of love (1:8–9).
In Paul’s prayer for Philemon, what does he want to become effective?
Paul prays “that your partnership in the faith may become effective” (1:6).
Philemon 1:6
Your preaching in public
Paul does not mention Philemon’s preaching; he prays for his partnership in the faith (1:6).
Your partnership in the faith
Your giving to Jerusalem
The gift for Jerusalem was the collection of Romans 15:26, unrelated to this prayer (1:6).
Your fasting in secret
Fasting in secret is Jesus’ teaching in Matthew 6:18, not Paul’s prayer for Philemon.
Your knowledge of the Law
Paul prays for full acknowledgment of “every good thing that is ours in Christ” (1:6), not knowledge of the Law.
In Paul’s words about Philemon’s love, what two responses does Paul say he himself has experienced?
Paul writes, “I take great joy and encouragement in your love” (1:7).
Philemon 1:7
Fear and trembling
“With fear and trembling” is Paul’s phrase in Philippians 2:12, not his response to Philemon’s love.
Sorrow and shame
Philemon’s love brought Paul joy, not sorrow or shame (1:7).
Joy and encouragement
Patience and silence
Paul speaks of joy and encouragement (1:7), not patience and silence.
Zeal and anger
Paul felt no anger; he took great joy and encouragement in Philemon’s love (1:7).
In the rhetorical contrast Paul makes before pleading for Onesimus, what does he say he is bold enough to do, yet chooses not to do?
Paul writes, “although in Christ I am bold enough to order you to do what is proper, I prefer to appeal” (1:8–9).
Philemon 1:8-9
Baptize Philemon again
Baptism is not mentioned; Paul says he could order Philemon to do what is proper (1:8).
Order Philemon to do what is proper
Send Onesimus to another city
Paul is sending Onesimus back to Philemon (1:12), not to another city.
Discipline Archippus publicly
Archippus is greeted warmly as a fellow soldier (1:2); no discipline is mentioned.
Close the house church
Paul greets the church that meets at Philemon’s house (1:2); closing it is never suggested.
In the hardest part of Paul’s appeal about Onesimus, how does he redefine Onesimus’s relationship to Philemon?
Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (1:16).
Philemon 1:16
No longer as a messenger, but greater than a messenger, as a prophet
Paul’s contrast is slave versus beloved brother (1:16); Onesimus is never called a messenger or prophet.
No longer as a debtor, but freed from his debt, as a creditor
Paul offers to cover any debt Onesimus owes (1:18), but he never calls Onesimus a creditor.
No longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother
No longer as a visitor, but more than a visitor, as a ruler
Onesimus is not made a ruler; he is to be received as a beloved brother (1:16).
No longer as a servant, but above a servant, as an apostle
Onesimus is not made an apostle; Paul says he is to be received as a beloved brother (1:16).
58: In the opening of Hebrews chapter 1, who spoke long ago to the fathers through the prophets?
Hebrews opens, “On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets” (1:1).
Hebrews 1:1
Moses
Moses was one of God’s spokesmen, “faithful as a servant in all God’s house” (Hebrews 3:5); in 1:1 God is the one who spoke.
God
David
David wrote psalms quoted later in the chapter (Psalm 110:1 in 1:13), but 1:1 names God as the speaker.
Gabriel
Gabriel is the angel sent to Zechariah (Luke 1:19); Hebrews 1 goes on to set the Son above all angels.
Paul
Paul is not named in Hebrews 1; the verse says God spoke to the fathers through the prophets (1:1).
According to the first verse of Hebrews 1, through whom did God speak long ago?
The verse says God “spoke to our fathers through the prophets” (1:1).
Hebrews 1:1
Kings
Kings are not named in 1:1; the channel of God’s past speaking was the prophets.
Priests
Hebrews treats priesthood later (Hebrews 5:6), but 1:1 says God spoke through the prophets.
Apostles
Apostles belong to the new era; 1:1 describes God’s past speaking through the prophets.
Prophets
Judges
Judges led Israel before the kings, but 1:1 names the prophets as God’s spokesmen.
In Hebrews 1:1, to whom had God spoken long ago through the prophets?
God “spoke to our fathers through the prophets” (1:1), that is, to Israel’s forefathers.
Hebrews 1:1
The Egyptians
The Egyptians are not in view; God’s word through the prophets came to “our fathers” (1:1).
The nations
The verse names the fathers of Israel, not the nations, as those God spoke to (1:1).
The fathers
The Romans
Rome is not mentioned; 1:1 speaks of the fathers.
The disciples
The disciples belong to “these last days,” when God has spoken by His Son (1:2).
In the first chapter of Hebrews, how is God’s earlier speaking through the prophets described?
Hebrews 1:1 says, “On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets.”
Hebrews 1:1
Once and for all in one place
“Once for all” describes Christ entering the Most Holy Place (Hebrews 9:12); God’s past speaking came on many occasions (1:1).
Secretly and silently
God spoke openly through the prophets (1:1), not secretly or silently.
On many past occasions and in many different ways
Only through dreams
God did speak in dreams (Numbers 12:6), but 1:1 stresses “many different ways,” not dreams only.
Only through angels
The law was “spoken by angels” (Hebrews 2:2), but 1:1 names the prophets and many different ways.
In Hebrews chapter 1, in what time period has God spoken to us by His Son?
The verse says, “But in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son” (1:2).
Hebrews 1:2
In the days of Noah
The days of Noah long preceded even the prophets; God spoke by His Son “in these last days” (1:2).
In the wilderness years
The wilderness years were when God spoke to Moses at Sinai (Acts 7:38), part of the past era (1:1).
In these last days
At the exile
The exile belongs to the time when God spoke through the prophets (1:1), not by His Son.
In the millennium only
The thousand-year reign appears in Revelation 20:4; Hebrews says the Son has spoken in these last days (1:2).
According to Hebrews 1:2, what did God appoint His Son to be?
God appointed the Son “heir of all things” (1:2).
Hebrews 1:2
Priest of Levi
Jesus “descended from Judah,” not Levi (Hebrews 7:14).
Ruler of Israel only
The Son’s inheritance is “all things” (1:2), not Israel only.
Judge of angels only
The Son is heir of all things (1:2); angels are servants sent for the heirs of salvation (1:14).
Heir of all things
Keeper of the Law
The Son is appointed heir (1:2); the Law is not mentioned in Hebrews 1.
In the opening description of the Son in Hebrews 1, through whom did God make the universe?
The Son is the one “through whom He made the universe” (1:2).
Hebrews 1:2
Through Moses
Moses was a servant in God’s house (Hebrews 3:5), not the agent of creation.
Through the prophets
The prophets were God’s past messengers (1:1), not the agents of creation.
Through the Son
Through Michael
Michael is an archangel (Jude 1:9); Hebrews 1 sets the Son far above the angels (1:4).
Through David
David wrote psalms but did not create; all things were created through the Son (1:2; Colossians 1:16).
In Hebrews 1:3, the Son is called the radiance of whose glory?
The verse says, “The Son is the radiance of God’s glory” (1:3).
Hebrews 1:3
Abraham’s glory
Abraham is not mentioned in Hebrews 1; the Son radiates God’s glory (1:3).
Israel’s glory
The text says God’s glory, not Israel’s (1:3).
The angels’ glory
Angels are inferior to the Son (1:4); He radiates God’s glory, not theirs.
God’s glory
Creation’s glory
Creation is the work of the Lord’s hands (1:10); the Son is the radiance of God’s glory (1:3).
According to Hebrews chapter 1, what does the Son uphold?
The Son is described as “upholding all things by His powerful word” (1:3).
Hebrews 1:3
Israel by the Law
The Son upholds all things, not Israel by the Law (1:3).
The temple by priests
Temple and priests are not in 1:3; the Son upholds all things by His word.
All things by His powerful word
The heavens by angels
Angels are ministering spirits (1:14), not the means by which the Son upholds the heavens.
The church by apostles
The Son upholds all things by His powerful word (1:3), not the church through apostles.
In Hebrews 1:3, what did the Son provide before He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high?
The verse says, “After He had provided purification for sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high” (1:3).
Hebrews 1:3
A new temple
Christ did not build a temple; He entered heaven itself, not “a man-made copy of the true sanctuary” (Hebrews 9:24).
Purification for sins
The Ten Commandments
The Ten Commandments were the stone tablets given to Moses on Sinai (Exodus 31:18).
A kingdom for David
The promise to David’s son lies behind 2 Samuel 7:14, quoted in 1:5, but 1:3 speaks of purification for sins.
Manna in the wilderness
Manna was Israel’s bread in the wilderness (Exodus 16:15), not something the Son provided in 1:3.
In the first chapter of Hebrews, where did the Son sit after providing purification for sins?
“He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high” (1:3).
Hebrews 1:3
On David’s throne in Jerusalem
The Son is enthroned in heaven, “on high” (1:3), not on an earthly throne in Jerusalem.
At the right hand of the Majesty on high
Between the cherubim
Between the cherubim above the mercy seat is where God met Moses (Exodus 25:22).
In the temple court
Christ entered heaven itself, not an earthly sanctuary (Hebrews 9:24).
On the Mount of Olives
The disciples returned from the Mount of Olives after the ascension (Acts 1:12); the Son sat down on high (1:3).
In Hebrews 1:4, what is said to be more excellent than that of the angels?
The Son became superior to the angels “as the name He has inherited is excellent beyond theirs” (1:4).
Hebrews 1:4
The Son’s robe
No robe is mentioned; the comparison in 1:4 is about His inherited name.
The Son’s sacrifice
His sacrifice is the theme of Hebrews 10:12, but 1:4 compares His name with the angels’.
The Son’s throne
His throne appears in 1:8; 1:4 compares the name He has inherited.
The name the Son has inherited
The Son’s birthplace
Hebrews 1 does not mention His birthplace; 1:4 compares His name with the angels’.
In Hebrews 1, to which beings did God never say, “You are My Son; today I have become Your Father”?
The writer asks, “For to which of the angels did God ever say” these words from Psalm 2:7 (1:5).
Hebrews 1:5
Prophets
Prophets appear in 1:1 as God’s past spokesmen; the contrast in 1:5 is with angels.
Kings
The psalm was first spoken of God’s anointed king (Psalm 2:7), but Hebrews 1:5 contrasts the Son with angels.
Priests
Hebrews 5:5 applies the same words to Christ as high priest, but 1:5 contrasts Him with angels.
Apostles
Apostles do not appear in Hebrews 1; the contrast in 1:5 is with angels.
Angels
In the comparison between the Son and angels in Hebrews chapter 1, which second statement is also quoted about the Son?
The second quotation is “I will be His Father, and He will be My Son” (1:5), from 2 Samuel 7:14.
Hebrews 1:5
“I will make Him a prophet to the nations”
“A light for the nations” is spoken of the Servant in Isaiah 49:6; it is not quoted in Hebrews 1.
“I will be His Father, and He will be My Son”
“I will send Him to Egypt”
An angel told Joseph to flee to Egypt with the Child (Matthew 2:13), but that is not quoted in Hebrews 1.
“I will build Him a city”
No promise to build a city is quoted; the second quotation in 1:5 is a father-son promise.
“I will hide Him in the wilderness”
Jesus was led into the wilderness to be tempted (Matthew 4:1); that is not quoted in Hebrews 1.
In Hebrews 1:6, when God brings His firstborn into the world, what does He say?
God says, “Let all God’s angels worship Him” (1:6), words found in Deuteronomy 32:43.
Hebrews 1:6
“Let all nations fear Him”
The command in 1:6 is addressed to God’s angels, not to the nations.
“Let Israel receive Him”
The command in 1:6 is to angels, not to Israel.
“Let all God’s angels worship Him”
“Let the priests anoint Him”
Anointing appears in 1:9, where God anoints the Son with the oil of joy, not priests.
“Let the heavens be opened”
The heavens were opened at Jesus’ baptism (Matthew 3:16); 1:6 is a call for angels to worship.
In the verse about angels in Hebrews 1:7, what does God make His angels?
The quotation says, “He makes His angels winds, His servants flames of fire” (1:7).
Hebrews 1:7
Stars
Stars are not mentioned in 1:7; God makes His angels winds.
Winds
Pillars of fire
Fire appears as “flames of fire” for His servants (1:7); a pillar of fire led Israel by night (Exodus 13:21).
Trumpets
Angels sound trumpets in Revelation 11:15, but 1:7 says God makes His angels winds.
Chariots of bronze
Chariots of fire surrounded Elisha (2 Kings 6:17); they are not in Hebrews 1:7.
In the quotation addressed to the Son in Hebrews 1, how long does His throne endure?
“Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever” (1:8), quoting Psalm 45:6.
Hebrews 1:8
For a generation
The throne endures “forever and ever” (1:8), not for a generation.
Until the exile
The exile is not mentioned; the Son’s throne endures forever and ever (1:8).
A thousand years only
The thousand years appear in Revelation 20:4; the Son’s throne endures forever and ever (1:8).
Forever and ever
Until the temple falls
The temple is not mentioned; the Son’s throne endures forever and ever (1:8).
According to Hebrews 1:8, what is the scepter of the Son’s kingdom?
The verse says, “justice is the scepter of Your kingdom” (1:8).
Hebrews 1:8
Mercy
Mercy is not named as the scepter; 1:8 says justice.
Peace
Righteousness and peace kiss in Psalm 85:10, but the scepter in 1:8 is justice.
Justice
Wrath
Wrath is not mentioned; the scepter of the Son’s kingdom is justice (1:8).
Wisdom
Wisdom is not named as the scepter; 1:8 says justice.
In Hebrews 1:9, what has the Son loved?
“You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness” (1:9), quoting Psalm 45:7.
Hebrews 1:9
Sacrifice
The Son did offer “one sacrifice for sins” (Hebrews 10:12), but 1:9 says He loved righteousness.
Riches
Jesus warns against storing up treasures on earth (Matthew 6:19); 1:9 says the Son loved righteousness.
Righteousness
Secrecy
Secrecy is not mentioned; the Son loved righteousness and hated wickedness (1:9).
Power
Power is not what 1:9 names; the Son loved righteousness.
Because the Son loved righteousness and hated wickedness, what did God do for Him in Hebrews 1?
“Therefore God, Your God, has anointed You above Your companions with the oil of joy” (1:9).
Hebrews 1:9
Set Him over all the land of Egypt with Pharaoh’s ring
Pharaoh set Joseph over all the land of Egypt (Genesis 41:41); in 1:9 God anoints the Son with the oil of joy.
Gave Him the two stone tablets of the Testimony at Sinai
The stone tablets were given to Moses on Sinai (Exodus 31:18), not to the Son in 1:9.
Anointed Him above His companions with the oil of joy
Sent Him to wander forty years in the wilderness
The forty years in the wilderness were Israel’s; in 1:9 God anoints the Son above His companions.
Built Him a house of cedar in the city of Jerusalem
No house is built in 1:9; God anoints the Son above His companions with the oil of joy.
In the creation quotation found in Hebrews chapter 1, what did the Lord lay in the beginning?
“In the beginning, O Lord, You laid the foundations of the earth” (1:10), quoting Psalm 102:25.
Hebrews 1:10
The gates of Jerusalem
The gates of Jerusalem are not in 1:10; the Lord laid the foundations of the earth.
The foundations of the earth
The altar of incense
Moses was told to make an altar for burning incense (Exodus 30:1); 1:10 speaks of the earth’s foundations.
The walls of Jericho
The wall of Jericho collapsed (Joshua 6:20); it is not in Hebrews 1:10.
The riverbeds of Eden
A river flowed out of Eden (Genesis 2:10); 1:10 speaks of the foundations of the earth.
In Hebrews 1:10, what are the heavens called?
“The heavens are the work of Your hands” (1:10).
Hebrews 1:10
The host of Israel
The heavens are not called a host of Israel; they are “the work of Your hands” (1:10).
The chambers of glory
This phrase is not in 1:10; the heavens are the work of the Lord’s hands.
The work of Your hands
The footstool of heaven
The earth is God’s footstool (Isaiah 66:1); the heavens are the work of His hands (1:10).
The crown of creation
The heavens are not called a crown; they are the work of the Lord’s hands (1:10).
In contrast to creation perishing in Hebrews 1:11, what is said about the Lord?
“They will perish, but You remain” (1:11), and again, “You remain the same” (1:12).
Hebrews 1:12
You sleep
The Lord does not sleep; in contrast with perishing creation, He remains (1:11).
You return
The text says the Lord remains (1:11), not that He returns.
You remain
You ascend
Ascending is not the point; creation perishes but the Lord remains (1:11).
You hide
The Lord does not hide; He remains while creation perishes (1:11).
In Hebrews chapter 1, like what will creation wear out?
“They will all wear out like a garment” (1:11), quoting Psalm 102:26.
Hebrews 1:11
Like smoke
“My days vanish like smoke” is earlier in the same psalm (Psalm 102:3), not Hebrews 1:11.
Like a garment
Like dust in the wind
Dust in the wind is not the image; creation wears out like a garment (1:11).
Like grass in summer
Withering grass is Isaiah’s image (Isaiah 40:7); Hebrews 1:11 says like a garment.
Like a broken jar
A broken jar is not the image here; creation wears out like a garment (1:11).
In the imagery of Hebrews 1:12, like what will the Lord roll up the heavens and earth?
“You will roll them up like a robe” (1:12).

Which sequence matches the order of Hebrews 1:2-3 in describing the Son?

Hebrews 1:2–3 runs in this order: “heir of all things,” “through whom He made the universe,” “upholding all things by His powerful word,” “provided purification for sins,” then “sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high.”
Hebrews 1:2-3
Appointed heir of all things → through whom God made the universe → upholding all things by His powerful word → provided purification for sins → sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high
Provided purification for sins → appointed heir of all things → sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high → upheld all things by His powerful word → made the universe
These are the right items in the wrong order; 1:2 begins with the appointment as heir, and purification comes just before He sat down (1:3).
Sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high → upheld all things by His powerful word → made the universe → provided purification for sins → appointed heir of all things
This runs the order backward; 1:2–3 starts with the heir of all things and ends with sitting down at the right hand.
Brought as firstborn into the world → made His angels winds → laid the foundations of the earth → anointed with the oil of joy → sat down at the right hand of God
These items come from later quotations in the chapter (1:6–13), not from the description of the Son in 1:2–3.
Loved righteousness → hated wickedness → anointed above His companions with the oil of joy → made His enemies a footstool → served those who will inherit salvation
These phrases come from 1:9 and 1:13–14, and the last describes what angels do, not the Son.

Hebrews 7:11
Melchizedek’s priesthood

The Levitical priesthood
Samuel’s priesthood
Samuel is not mentioned in Hebrews 7; the priesthood named in 7:11 is the Levitical one.
David’s priesthood
David came from Judah, a tribe Moses said nothing about for priests (7:14).
Ezra’s priesthood
Ezra was a priest from Aaron’s line (Ezra 7:5), so he belongs to the Levitical priesthood itself.
In Hebrews 7, another priest was to appear according to which order?
Hebrews 7:11 speaks of “another priest to appear—one in the order of Melchizedek and not in the order of Aaron.”
Hebrews 7:11
The order of Moses
Moses is not given a priestly order in Hebrews 7; he was Aaron’s brother.
The order of Aaron

The order of Zadok
Zadok served as priest in David’s and Solomon’s time (1 Kings 2:35), but Hebrews 7 does not name his order.
The order of Melchizedek
The order of Phinehas
Phinehas was Aaron’s grandson (Exodus 6:25), so his line belongs to Aaron’s order.
According to Hebrews 7, the needed priest would be in the order of Melchizedek and not in the order of whom?
Hebrews 7:11 says the needed priest would be “in the order of Melchizedek and not in the order of Aaron.”
Hebrews 7:11
Eli
Eli was a priest at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:9), but Hebrews 7:11 names Aaron as head of the order contrasted with Melchizedek’s.
Aaron
Joshua son of Nun
Joshua son of Nun was Israel’s military leader, not the priestly figure contrasted in Hebrews 7.
Samuel
Samuel is not named in Hebrews 7; the verse contrasts Melchizedek with Aaron.
Eleazar
Eleazar was Aaron’s son and successor (Numbers 20:28), so he belongs to Aaron’s order rather than naming it.

Hebrews 7:12

The throne

The law

Hebrews 7:13
The city gate
Hebrews 7:13 speaks of priestly service at the altar, not at the city gate.
The altar
The ark

The battlefield

In Hebrews 7, from which tribe did the Lord Jesus descend?

Levi

Benjamin

Ephraim
Ephraim, Joseph’s son, is not named in Hebrews 7.
Judah
Naphtali

“You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek”

“The scepter will not depart from Judah”

According to Hebrews 7, why was the former commandment set aside?

Because it was weak and useless

Galatians 3:21 says the law is not opposed to the promises of God; it is set aside as weak and useless (7:18).

Nothing

The king’s sins
The king’s sins are not mentioned in Hebrews 7:27.
Their own sins
Abraham’s sins
Abraham’s sins are not mentioned in Hebrews 7:27.

Jesus is a temporary priest from the tribe of Levi who, like the other priests, must keep offering sacrifices every day for sin
