Fast twice a week
The Pharisee boasted, “I fast twice a week” (Luke 18:12); James’s test is bridling the tongue.
Bridle his tongue
Memorize the Psalms
Memorizing Scripture is good, but James’s test in 1:26 is bridling the tongue.
Visit Jerusalem
James does not mention pilgrimage; the test of religion is bridling the tongue (1:26).
Give public testimony
James’s concern is restraining speech, not adding public testimony (1:26).
What does the unbridled speaker deceive, according to James?
The one who does not bridle his tongue “deceives his heart” (1:26).
James 1:26
The church
James says he deceives his own heart (1:26), not the church.
His enemies
His enemies are not the ones deceived; “he deceives his heart” (1:26).
His heart
The poor
James later rebukes dishonoring the poor (2:6), but in 1:26 the unbridled speaker deceives his heart.
His family
James says the deceived one is the speaker himself: “he deceives his heart” (1:26).
How does James describe that person’s religion?
James says of the man who does not bridle his tongue, “his religion is worthless” (1:26).
James 1:26
Incomplete
James’s word is stronger than incomplete: his religion is “worthless” (1:26).
Immature
James does not call it immature; he calls it worthless (1:26).
Worthless
Traditional
James is not describing tradition; he calls such religion worthless (1:26).
Difficult
James calls such religion “worthless” (1:26), not difficult.
In the closing verse of James 1, pure and undefiled religion is described before whom?
James says “Pure and undefiled religion before our God and Father is this” (1:27).
James 1:27
The angels of heaven
James measures religion before God, not before angels (1:27).
Our God and Father
The elders of Israel
Moses assembled the elders of Israel (Exodus 3:16); James defines religion “before our God and Father” (1:27).
The nations
The standard is God’s, not the nations’: “before our God and Father” (1:27).
The temple priests
Temple priests are not the judges here; religion is pure “before our God and Father” (1:27).
According to James 1, pure religion includes caring for whom?
Pure religion is “to care for orphans and widows in their distress” (1:27).
James 1:27
Kings and rulers
Paul urges submission to governing authorities (Romans 13:1), but James names orphans and widows.
Merchants and travelers
James later rebukes merchants who boast of their plans (4:13); pure religion cares for orphans and widows.
Orphans and widows in their distress
Soldiers and tax collectors
Tax collectors and soldiers asked John the Baptist what to do (Luke 3:12–14); James names orphans and widows.
Scribes and Pharisees
Scribes and Pharisees are rebuked in Matthew 23:23; James calls for care of orphans and widows.
What second mark of pure religion does James give besides caring for the vulnerable?
Pure religion includes “to keep oneself from being polluted by the world” (1:27).
James 1:27
Keeping every feast day and new moon festival
God appointed feasts for Israel (Leviticus 23:2), but James names keeping oneself unpolluted by the world.
Keeping oneself from being polluted by the world
Learning foreign languages to spread the faith
James says nothing about learning languages; the second mark is keeping oneself unpolluted by the world (1:27).
Building altars wherever the Lord appears
Noah built an altar to the LORD (Genesis 8:20); James’s second mark is purity from the world’s pollution.
Avoiding marriage to serve without distraction
Paul discussed singleness for “undivided devotion” (1 Corinthians 7:35); James’s mark is keeping unpolluted by the world.
Which sequence matches James 1’s teaching about trials and growth?
Testing of faith develops perseverance (1:3), and perseverance makes believers “mature and complete” (1:4).
James 1:3-4
Trials, wealth, honor, and a long life of rest
James warns that wealth fades (1:10–11); his sequence runs from tested faith to perseverance to maturity (1:3–4).
Testing of faith, perseverance, maturity and completeness
Anger, bold speech, worldly wisdom, and reward
James says anger does not bring about God’s righteousness (1:20); it is no step toward maturity.
Fasting, sacrifice, night visions, and lasting peace
Fasting and visions are not in James 1; the sequence is testing, perseverance, maturity (1:3–4).
Sorrow, revenge, victory, and earthly comfort
James forbids revenge-like anger (1:20); the true sequence is testing, perseverance, maturity (1:3–4).
Which sequence matches James 1’s teaching about temptation?
Desire “gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death” (1:15).
James 1:14-15
Law, fear, punishment, exile
James traces temptation from inner desire, not from law and fear (1:14–15).
Desire, sin, death
Doubt, prayer, wealth, reward
Doubt hinders prayer (1:6–7), but James’s chain of temptation is desire, sin, death (1:15).
Anger, jealousy, war
James later says quarrels come from passions at war within (4:1), but 1:15 traces desire, sin, death.
Pride, famine, captivity
Pride goes before destruction (Proverbs 16:18), but James’s sequence is desire, sin, death (1:15).
In James’s teaching about wisdom, which combination is correct?
James says to “ask God, who gives generously to all” (1:5), and “he must ask in faith, without doubting” (1:6).
James 1:5-6
Ask a prophet in secret and wait for a sign
James says to ask God directly (1:5), not a prophet, and not to wait for a sign.
Ask God, who gives generously, and ask in faith without doubting
Buy wisdom with offerings
God gives wisdom generously (1:5); it is not bought with offerings.
Ask only after the trial has ended
James says to ask now if lacking wisdom (1:5); trials are the very setting for asking.
Learn wisdom from the rich alone
James never sends anyone to the rich for wisdom; he says ask God (1:5).
Which contrast about social status appears in James 1?
James says the humble brother “should exult in his high position” and the rich man “in his low position” (1:9–10).
James 1:9-10
The strong should boast in their strength, and the weak should boast in their weakness alone
God says the strong man must not boast in his strength (Jeremiah 9:23); James contrasts humble and rich (1:9–10).
The brother in humble circumstances should exult in his high position, and the rich in his low position
The old should rule over the assembly, and the young should keep silent before them
James does not speak of age in 1:9–10; his contrast is between the humble brother and the rich man.
The Jew should boast in the Law, and the Greek should boast in his wisdom and learning
Paul contrasts Jews seeking signs and Greeks seeking wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:22); James contrasts humble and rich.
The poor should seek riches with diligence, and the rich should seek the applause of men
James tells neither group to chase riches or applause; each is to exult in a reversal of status (1:9–10).
Which pair of images does James use for instability and passing wealth?
The doubter is “like a wave of the sea” (1:6), and the rich man “will pass away like a flower of the field” (1:10).
James 1:6, 10
A broken wall and a dry brook
A broken wall pictures a man without self-control (Proverbs 25:28); James uses a wave and a flower.
A wave of the sea and a flower of the field
A moth and rust
Moth and rust destroy earthly treasure in Matthew 6:19; James uses a wave of the sea and a flower of the field.
A lost sheep and a barren fig tree
The lost sheep (Luke 15:4) and barren fig tree (Luke 13:6) are Jesus’ parables, not James’s images.
A chariot wheel and a falling star
James does not use chariots or falling stars; his images are a sea wave and a field flower (1:6, 10).
What is the correct order of James’s instruction about everyday conduct?
James says, “Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (1:19).
James 1:19
Slow to anger, quick to listen, slow to speak
James begins with listening, not anger: quick to listen, slow to speak, slow to anger (1:19).
Quick to listen, slow to speak, slow to anger
Slow to speak, quick to anger, quick to listen
James says slow to anger and quick to listen (1:19); this choice reverses the anger instruction.
Quick to speak, slow to listen, slow to anger
This reverses James: he says quick to listen and slow to speak (1:19).
Quick to listen, quick to speak, slow to anger
James says slow to speak, not quick to speak (1:19).
Which two people are explicitly connected with blessing in James 1?
James says “Blessed is the man who perseveres under trial” (1:12) and the effective doer “will be blessed in what he does” (1:25).
James 1:12, 25
The rich man who gives alms and the teacher of the Law
James warns that the rich man will fade away (1:11); neither the rich nor teachers are called blessed in James 1.
The man who perseveres under trial and the effective doer of the word
The widow in distress and the orphan who is cared for
Orphans and widows are to be cared for (1:27), but James does not pronounce them blessed.
The prophet who sees visions and the elder who prays
Prophets and elders are not mentioned in James 1; the blessed are the persevering and the doer (1:12, 25).
The merchant who travels to a city and the trader who makes a profit
James later rebukes merchants who boast of going to a city to make a profit (4:13); they are not called blessed.
According to James 1, who should not expect to receive anything from the Lord?
The one who doubts “should not expect to receive anything from the Lord”; he is “a double-minded man” (1:7–8).
James 1:6-8
The poor believer
James says the humble brother should exult in his high position (1:9); he is not the one denied.
The rich landowner
James warns the rich they will fade (1:10–11), but 1:7 concerns the doubter.
The doubting, double-minded man
The widow in distress
Widows in distress are to be cared for (1:27), not denied God’s help.
The one who speaks little
Speaking little is commended: be slow to speak (1:19).
In James 1, what should come after getting rid of moral filth and evil?
After getting rid of moral filth, believers are to “humbly accept the word planted in you” (1:21).
James 1:21
Public mourning
Public mourning is not mentioned in 1:21; the next step is humbly accepting the word.
Humbly accepting the word planted in you
Taking a Nazarite vow
The Nazirite vow is described in Numbers 6:2; James calls for accepting the word planted in you.
Retreating to the wilderness
James does not call believers to the wilderness; he calls them to accept the implanted word (1:21).
Seeking revenge on oppressors
Revenge is excluded, since man’s anger does not bring about God’s righteousness (1:20).
Which combination best matches James’s description of pure religion?
Pure religion is “to care for orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world” (1:27).
James 1:27
Attending the temple faithfully and tithing mint, dill, and cumin
Jesus rebuked those who tithed mint, dill, and cumin but neglected justice and mercy (Matthew 23:23).
Caring for orphans and widows, and keeping oneself from worldly pollution
Speaking in tongues often and seeing visions in the night
Speaking in tongues happened at Pentecost (Acts 2:4), but James defines pure religion by compassion and purity.
Fasting twice a week and wearing sackcloth and ashes
The Pharisee boasted of fasting twice a week (Luke 18:12); James’s definition is care for the needy and purity (1:27).
Studying the genealogies and charting the prophecies of the end
Paul warned against devotion to “endless genealogies” (1 Timothy 1:4); James defines religion by compassion and purity.
In James 1, the title “Father of the heavenly lights” is used in connection with what theme?
“Every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights” (1:17).
James 1:17
Military victory
James does not speak of military victory in 1:17; the title is tied to God’s good and perfect gifts.
Every good and perfect gift
End-time judgment
End-time judgment is not the theme of 1:17; the title introduces every good and perfect gift.
Temple rebuilding
The temple foundation was relaid in Ezra 3:10; James’s title concerns God’s gifts.
The crossing of the Jordan
Israel crossed the Jordan on dry ground (Joshua 3:17); James’s title concerns God’s good and perfect gifts.
What quality of God does James emphasize by saying there is no change or shifting shadow with Him?
James says the Father of lights is One “with whom there is no change or shifting shadow” (1:17), as the LORD says, “I, the LORD, do not change” (Malachi 3:6).
James 1:17
His hiddenness
James stresses that God does not change, not that He is hidden; He gives generously to all (1:5).
His unchangeableness
His anger
James says nothing about God’s anger here; his point is that God does not change (1:17).
His silence
God’s silence is not the point; James says there is “no change or shifting shadow” with Him (1:17).
His distance
James describes God giving gifts “from above” (1:17); his point is constancy, not distance.
James says believers were brought forth to be a kind of what?
God gave us birth “that we would be a kind of firstfruits of His creation” (1:18).
James 1:18
Kingdom over the nations
James says believers are firstfruits (1:18), not a kingdom over the nations.
Firstfruits of His creation
Wall around Jerusalem
The wall of Jerusalem is not James’s image; believers are a kind of firstfruits (1:18).
Lamp to the temple
James does not call believers a lamp; he calls them firstfruits of His creation (1:18).
Branch from Jesse
“A Branch from his roots” of Jesse is Isaiah’s messianic prophecy (Isaiah 11:1), not James’s word for believers.
What object in James 1 illustrates hearing without doing?
The hearer who does not act “is like a man who looks at his face in a mirror” and then forgets (1:23–24).
James 1:23-24
A trumpet
Paul uses a trumpet with a muffled call to picture unclear speech (1 Corinthians 14:8), not James.
A mirror
A net
The kingdom is like a net cast into the sea (Matthew 13:47); James’s image is a mirror.
A lampstand
The golden lampstand stood in the tabernacle (Exodus 25:31); James uses a mirror (1:23).
A vineyard
Jesus told a parable of a fig tree in a vineyard (Luke 13:6); James’s illustration is a mirror.
According to James’s mirror illustration, what is forgotten?
The man “goes away and immediately forgets what he looks like” (1:24).
James 1:24
The law itself
In the illustration he forgets his own face; the law is what the blessed person keeps looking into (1:25).
A friend’s advice
No friend gives advice in James’s mirror picture; he forgets what he looks like (1:24).
What one looks like
The name of the Lord
James’s mirror illustration says nothing about forgetting the Lord’s name; it is his own appearance (1:24).
The place of worship
The place of worship is not in view; he forgets what he looks like (1:24).
What must a person bridle, according to James 1, if he would not have worthless religion?
James says the religious man who “does not bridle his tongue” has worthless religion (1:26).
James 1:26
His appetite
James names the tongue, not the appetite, as what must be bridled (1:26).
His feet
James’s test concerns speech: “does not bridle his tongue” (1:26).
His tongue
His hands
Hands are not mentioned in 1:26; it is the tongue that must be bridled.
His eyes
James names the tongue (1:26); controlling speech is the test of real religion.
Which statement about God in James 1 is true?
God “gives generously to all” (1:5), “nor does He tempt anyone” (1:13), and with Him there is “no change or shifting shadow” (1:17).
He gives wisdom reluctantly and tests by evil
James says God gives generously (1:5) and tempts no one (1:13).
He gives generously, tempts no one, and does not change
He favors the rich and neglects the poor
James says God gives generously to all (1:5) and gives the humble brother a high position (1:9).
He withholds gifts until people deserve them
God gives “without finding fault” (1:5), not only to the deserving.
He is like shifting shadows
James says the opposite: with God there is “no change or shifting shadow” (1:17).
Which command-and-promise pair fits James 1?
“Blessed is the man who perseveres under trial, because when he has stood the test, he will receive the crown of life” (1:12).
James 1:12
Store treasure, and you will escape death
Jesus warned against storing up treasure on earth (Matthew 6:19); James promises the crown of life for perseverance.
Persevere under trial, and you will receive the crown of life
Build an altar, and fire will fall
Fire fell on Elijah’s altar on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:38), not in James 1.
Fast forty days, and angels will feed you
After Jesus fasted forty days, “angels came and ministered to Him” (Matthew 4:11); that is not James’s promise.
Flee the city, and you will find peace
Jesus told those in Judea to flee to the mountains (Matthew 24:16); James’s promise is the crown of life.
In James’s teaching on prayer for wisdom, “without doubting” is attached to what action?
“He should ask God” (1:5), “But he must ask in faith, without doubting” (1:6).
James 1:5-6
Giving alms
Almsgiving is taught in Matthew 6:2; in James 1:6 “without doubting” goes with asking God.
Asking God
Visiting widows
Visiting orphans and widows comes in 1:27; “without doubting” is attached to asking (1:6).
Bridling the tongue
Bridling the tongue comes in 1:26; “without doubting” governs the request for wisdom (1:6).
Counting trials as joy
Counting trials as joy comes in 1:2; “without doubting” describes how to ask God (1:6).
Which phrase in James 1 describes the doubter?
The doubter is “like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind” (1:6).
James 1:6
Rooted and grounded
Paul prays believers will be “rooted and grounded in love” (Ephesians 3:17), the opposite of the doubter.
Blown and tossed by the wind
Clothed in white garments
White garments are promised to the overcomer (Revelation 3:5), not used of the doubter.
Guarded by angels
James does not describe the doubter as guarded by angels; he is blown and tossed by the wind (1:6).
Burning with holy zeal
Holy zeal is not James’s description; the doubter is unstable, blown and tossed by the wind (1:6).
Which phrase in James 1 describes the wealthy person’s earthly future?
James writes, “the rich man will fade away in the midst of his pursuits” (1:11).
James 1:11
Shining like the stars forever and ever
It is the wise who “will shine like the stars forever and ever” (Daniel 12:3), not the rich man of James 1.
Seated with the elders at the city gate
Boaz sat at the city gate (Ruth 4:1), but James says the rich man fades away amid his pursuits (1:11).
Fading away in the midst of his pursuits
Flourishing like a cedar in Lebanon
It is the righteous who “grow like a cedar in Lebanon” (Psalm 92:12); James says the rich man fades.
Dwelling secure in his house forever
“The righteous will inherit the land and dwell in it forever” (Psalm 37:29); James says the rich man fades away.
Which phrase in James 1 describes the saving power of God’s word?
James calls it “the word planted in you, which can save your souls” (1:21).
James 1:21
“Written on stone”
The tablets of the Testimony were “tablets of stone” (Exodus 31:18); James speaks of the word planted in you.
“Hidden in heaven”
The psalmist hid God’s word in his heart (Psalm 119:11), but James does not call it hidden in heaven.
“Which can save your souls”
“Sealed in the ark”
Moses placed the Testimony in the ark (Exodus 40:20); James does not use that phrase.
“Spoken through thunder”
Thunder sounded at Sinai (Exodus 19:16), but James describes the word as able to save souls (1:21).
Which description in James 1 belongs to pure and undefiled religion?
Pure religion is “to care for orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world” (1:27).
James 1:27
Performing public signs and wonders before the whole assembly
The apostles performed signs and wonders (Acts 5:12), but James defines pure religion by care and purity (1:27).
Keeping careful ritual washings before every meal and prayer
The Pharisees held to ritual hand-washing (Mark 7:3); James’s pure religion is caring for the needy and staying unpolluted.
Caring for orphans and widows in distress and keeping oneself from the world
Debating daily with the philosophers in the marketplace
Paul debated with philosophers in the marketplace at Athens (Acts 17:17–18); that is not James’s definition.
Multiplying sacrifices and burnt offerings at the altar
“What good to Me is your multitude of sacrifices?” the LORD asks (Isaiah 1:11); James defines religion by compassion and purity.
James 1 mentions two forms of self-deception. Which pair is correct?
Hearers only are “deceiving yourselves” (1:22), and the religious man who does not bridle his tongue “deceives his heart” (1:26).
James 1:22, 26
Seeking signs from heaven, and fearing the storms that toss the sea
Jesus rebuked a generation that “demands a sign” (Matthew 12:39), but James’s self-deceptions concern the word and the tongue.
Hearing the word without doing it, and thinking oneself religious while not bridling the tongue
Eating with tax collectors and sinners, and neglecting the incense offering
Jesus was criticized for eating with tax collectors and sinners, but James names hearing without doing and an unbridled tongue (1:22, 26).
Leaving Jerusalem for a far country, and crossing the sea to Tarshish
Jonah fled toward Tarshish by sea, but James’s two self-deceptions are hearing without doing and an unbridled tongue.
Marrying foreign wives, and neglecting to keep the Sabbath day holy
Nehemiah rebuked Israel for “marrying foreign women” (Nehemiah 13:27); James names hearing without doing and an unbridled tongue.
Which summary of temptation matches James 1?
Each one is tempted “by his own evil desires” (1:14); desire “gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death” (1:15).
James 1:14-15
Temptation comes from God Himself, who uses evil to teach His people lessons
James says the opposite: “God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone” (1:13).
Temptation starts in one’s own evil desire, which conceives sin, and sin brings forth death
Temptation is harmless as long as no one else sees it or knows about it
James says sin full-grown gives birth to death (1:15); temptation is deadly whether or not others see it.
Temptation is only outward pressure from enemies, never from one’s own heart
James locates temptation within: “by his own evil desires he is lured away and enticed” (1:14).
Temptation, if tolerated long enough, ends in wisdom and peace of mind
Tolerated temptation leads to sin and death (1:15); wisdom comes from asking God (1:5).
Which summary of wisdom matches James 1?
James says the one lacking wisdom “should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault” (1:5).
James 1:5
Wisdom belongs only to kings and rulers, who receive it at their anointing
Solomon asked God for an understanding heart (1 Kings 3:9), but James says God gives wisdom to all who ask (1:5).
Wisdom is gained by age alone, as many years teach a man understanding
Elihu thought “many years should teach wisdom” (Job 32:7); James says wisdom is asked of God (1:5).
Wisdom should be asked of God, who gives generously and without finding fault
Wisdom comes by keeping silent under the stars and waiting for a vision
James says to ask God for wisdom (1:5), not to wait silently for a vision.
Wisdom must be purchased at the temple with offerings of silver and gold
God gives wisdom generously (1:5); it is not purchased with offerings.
Which summary of God’s gifts matches James 1?
James writes, “Every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights” (1:17).
James 1:17
Some good gifts are from above, but trials are always evil gifts from God
James says every good gift is from above (1:17) and that God tempts no one (1:13).
Every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights
Gifts descend from angels who change like shadows
Gifts come from the Father, with whom there is “no change or shifting shadow” (1:17), not from changing angels.
Only material gifts are from God
James counts wisdom (1:5) and new birth (1:18) among God’s gifts, not only material things.
God’s gifts depend on rank and status
God gives “generously to all without finding fault” (1:5), not by rank.
Which summary of how to face trials matches James 1?
“Consider it pure joy … when you encounter trials of many kinds, because you know that the testing of your faith develops perseverance” (1:2–3).
James 1:2-3
Escape them at all costs, because trials only weaken a person’s faith
James tells believers to let perseverance finish its work (1:4), not to escape trials at all costs.
Blame God for them, because He is the One who tempts people with evil
James forbids this: “no one should say, ‘God is tempting me’” (1:13).
Consider them pure joy because the testing of faith develops perseverance
Answer them with anger, because man’s anger brings about righteousness
James says “man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires” (1:20).
Deny that they exist, because believers should never face any hardship
James assumes believers will “encounter trials of many kinds” (1:2).
Which summary of the believer’s response to the word matches James 1?
James says to “humbly accept the word planted in you” (1:21) and “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only” (1:22).
James 1:21-22
Hear it once and move on
Hearing once and moving on is the forgetful hearer of 1:23–24, who deceives himself.
Debate it but do not practice it
James condemns hearing without practicing as self-deception (1:22).
Accept the word planted in you and be a doer of it
Reserve it for teachers only
James addresses all believers: “Be doers of the word” (1:22), not teachers only.
Use it only in public worship
James calls for doing the word in daily life, including caring for orphans and widows (1:27).
Which comparison in James 1 involves seeing but not retaining?
The hearer who does not act is like a man who looks in a mirror, “goes away and immediately forgets what he looks like” (1:23–24).
James 1:23-24
A flower of the field fading in the sun
The fading flower pictures the passing rich man (1:10–11), not seeing and forgetting.
A wave of the sea tossed by the wind
The tossed wave pictures the doubter (1:6), not one who sees and forgets.
A man looking in a mirror and forgetting
A lamp set on a stand to light a house
A lamp set on a stand is from Matthew 5:15, about letting light shine, not forgetting.
A seed sown on shallow, rocky soil
Seed on rocky ground is from the parable of the sower (Matthew 13:5), not James 1.
Which comparison in James 1 involves motion and instability?
The doubter is “like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind” (1:6).
James 1:6
The wandering sheep
“We all like sheep have gone astray” is Isaiah 53:6, not James 1.
The wave of the sea
The withered grass
James does mention a withering plant (1:11), but it pictures fading wealth, not instability in motion.
The broken cistern
Broken cisterns that cannot hold water are from Jeremiah 2:13.
The falling tower
The tower of Siloam that collapsed is mentioned by Jesus in Luke 13:4, not James.
Which comparison in James 1 involves beauty that quickly disappears?
The rich man “will pass away like a flower of the field”; “its flower falls and its beauty is lost” (1:10–11).
James 1:10-11
A flower of the field
A pearl before swine
“Do not throw your pearls before swine” is from Matthew 7:6, not James.
A vine in Egypt
God brought a vine from Egypt (Psalm 80:8); James uses a flower of the field.
A mustard seed
The mustard seed is Jesus’ parable of growth (Matthew 13:31), not of fading beauty.
A silver cord
The silver cord snapping pictures death in Ecclesiastes 12:6, not James 1.
Which summary best fits the message of James chapter 1?
James says to count trials as joy (1:2), ask God for wisdom in faith (1:5–6), be doers of the word (1:22), and care for orphans and widows while keeping unpolluted by the world (1:27).
Avoid every trial, seek wealth as God’s favor, be quick to speak and answer, and trust outward ritual to make religion pure
James calls trials joy (1:2), warns that wealth fades (1:11), and says be slow to speak (1:19).
Count trials as joy, ask God for wisdom in faith, be doers of the word, and care for the vulnerable while staying unstained by the world
Wait for signs before believing, blame God when tempted, hear the word without doing it, and measure religion by appearance
James forbids blaming God for temptation (1:13) and calls hearing without doing self-deception (1:22).
Pursue riches while they last, answer offenders in anger, glance once into the word, and listen only to yourself
James says the rich fade away (1:11), anger misses God’s righteousness (1:20), and the forgetful hearer deceives himself (1:24).
Seek honor from the world, favor the rich over the poor, keep wisdom to yourself, and leave orphans and widows to others
James calls believers to care for orphans and widows and keep unpolluted by the world (1:27).
In James 2, as believers hold to faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, what are they told not to show?
James 2:1 tells believers who hold their faith in Jesus Christ not to show favoritism, which sets up the whole chapter.
James 2:1
Envy
Envy is condemned in James 3:14–16, but 2:1 specifically forbids favoritism.
Impatience
Patience is urged in James 5:7–8, but the command here is about favoritism.
Favoritism
Fear
Verse 1 says nothing about fear; it forbids treating people differently according to status.
Secrecy
Nothing in verse 1 concerns secrecy; James forbids favoritism within the believers’ gathering.
In the opening verse of James 2, faith is centered in whom?
James 2:1 speaks of holding faith in “our glorious Lord Jesus Christ.”
James 2:1
Moses the lawgiver
Moses gave the law, but James 2:1 centers faith in Jesus Christ, not in Moses.
Our glorious Lord Jesus Christ
King David
David is not mentioned in James; faith here is placed in the Lord Jesus Christ.
Abraham our father
Abraham is James’s later example of faith (2:21–23), not the One in whom faith is held.
John the Baptist
John the Baptist prepared the way for Christ (Mark 1:4), but he is not mentioned in James.
In James 2, what is the wealthy visitor wearing when he enters the meeting?
James 2:2 pictures a man coming into the meeting “wearing a gold ring and fine clothes.”
James 2:2
Sackcloth and ashes
Sackcloth and ashes signal mourning or repentance (Jonah 3:6); James describes a rich man in fine clothes.
A priestly robe
No priestly robe appears here; the visitor’s wealth shows in his gold ring and fine clothing.
A gold ring and fine clothes
Armor and a sword
Armor and a sword belong to soldiers (1 Samuel 17:38–39); the visitor in 2:2 is simply well dressed.
Traveler’s sandals only
Sandals alone would not mark a man as wealthy; James points to a gold ring and fine clothes.
In James 2, what is said to the richly dressed man?
In 2:3 the believers say to the man in fine clothes, “Here is a seat of honor,” which is the favoritism James condemns.
James 2:3
“Wait outside”
Being told to wait outside is not James’s picture; the rich man is offered a seat of honor (2:3).
“Kneel here”
Nothing about kneeling is said; the rich man is simply given a seat of honor (2:3).
“Here is a seat of honor”
“Bring an offering first”
No offering is required of the rich man; James describes him being welcomed to a seat of honor.
“Wash before entering”
No washing is mentioned; the rich man is welcomed straight to a seat of honor (2:3).
In James’s illustration about the poor visitor, what lower treatment is he given?
In 2:3 the poor man is told, “You must stand” or “Sit at my feet,” in sharp contrast to the seat of honor given the rich man.
James 2:3
“Lead the prayer for everyone here”
Leading prayer would be an honor; James says the poor man is pushed aside, told to stand or sit at someone’s feet (2:3).
“Take the front seat by the leaders”
The good seat goes to the rich man in fine clothes, not to the poor man (2:3).
“You must stand” or “Sit at my feet”
“Receive the offering for the poor”
James mentions no offering role for the poor man; he is told to stand or sit at someone’s feet.
“Teach the assembly this morning”
Teaching the assembly would be a place of honor, not the humiliation James describes in 2:3.
According to James 2, what have believers become if they treat rich and poor visitors differently?
James 2:4 says that treating people this way makes believers “judges with evil thoughts.”
James 2:4
Peacemakers without wisdom
Peacemakers are called blessed in Matthew 5:9; James says partiality makes believers judges with evil thoughts.
Judges with evil thoughts
Prophets without honor
A prophet without honor is Jesus’ saying in Matthew 13:57, unrelated to James’s warning about partiality.
Servants of two masters
Serving two masters is Jesus’ teaching in Matthew 6:24, not James’s description of favoritism.
Blind guides
“Blind guides” is Jesus’ charge against the Pharisees (Matthew 23:16), not James’s wording here.
In James 2, whom has God chosen to be rich in faith?
James 2:5 asks, “Has not God chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith” and heirs of the kingdom?
James 2:5
The rulers of the nations
God does not typically choose rulers; Paul notes that not many of the powerful were called (1 Corinthians 1:26).
The scribes
James does not mention scribes; the ones God chose to be rich in faith are the poor.
The poor of this world
The strong in body
God’s choice is about faith, not strength; 1 Corinthians 1:27 says He chose the weak to shame the strong.
The firstborn sons
Firstborn sons held inheritance rights in Israel, but James says God chose the poor of this world.
In James 2, who are said to oppress believers and drag them into court?
James 2:6 asks, “Is it not the rich who oppress you and drag you into court?”
James 2:6
The poor
The believers had dishonored the poor (2:6); the poor are not the oppressors.
The prophets
Prophets were more often the ones who suffered (James 5:10) than the oppressors in this verse.
The Gentiles
James names no Gentiles here; he points to wealthy oppressors.
The rich
The widows
Widows are among those believers should care for (James 1:27), not those who oppress.
In James 2, who blaspheme the noble name by which believers have been called?
James 2:7 asks, “Are they not the ones who blaspheme the noble name by which you have been called?” referring to the rich of verse 6.
James 2:7
The poor
The poor are the ones God has chosen (2:5), not the blasphemers.
The rich
The apostles
The apostles proclaimed that name; James does not accuse them of blaspheming it.
The judges of Israel
The judges of Israel belong to an earlier era; James speaks of present oppressors, the rich.
The tax collectors
Tax collectors are not mentioned in James; the rich are in view in 2:6–7.
In James 2, which command is called the royal law?
James 2:8 calls “Love your neighbor as yourself” the royal law, a command taken from Scripture (Leviticus 19:18).
James 2:8
“Honor your father and mother”
Honoring father and mother is the fifth commandment (Exodus 20:12), but James calls neighbor-love the royal law.
“Pray without ceasing”
“Pray without ceasing” is Paul’s exhortation in 1 Thessalonians 5:17, not the law James calls royal.
“Love your neighbor as yourself”
“Remember the Sabbath day”
Remembering the Sabbath day is the fourth commandment (Exodus 20:8), not the law James calls royal.
“Go into all the world”
Going into all the world is Jesus’ commission in Mark 16:15, not the royal law of James 2:8.
According to James 2, if a believer truly fulfills the royal law, how is that described?
James 2:8 says that if you really fulfill the royal law, “you are doing well.”
James 2:8
“You are doing well”
“You have earned salvation”
James never says keeping the royal law earns salvation; he says you are doing well.
“You need no mercy”
Mercy is still needed; 2:13 says judgment without mercy awaits the unmerciful.
“You have surpassed the law”
James does not say believers surpass the law; they are to fulfill it.
“You have become perfect”
James says nothing here about becoming perfect; the verse simply commends doing well.
In James 2, what does James say happens if someone shows favoritism?
James 2:9 says, “But if you show favoritism, you sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors.”
James 2:9
He loses the respect of the whole assembly
James names no loss of respect; he says favoritism is sin and the law convicts the one who shows it.
He sins and is convicted by the law as a transgressor
He becomes poor and loses his seat of honor
Favoritism toward the rich does not make a person poor; James says it makes him a transgressor.
He is praised by men for being generous
Favoritism is not praised; James says the law convicts those who show it (2:9).
He fulfills the law and is rewarded by God
Showing favoritism breaks the royal law of neighbor-love rather than fulfilling it (2:8–9).
In James 2, what is true of a person who keeps the whole law but stumbles at one point?
James 2:10 says whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles at just one point “is guilty of breaking all of it.”
James 2:10
He is excused by intentions
Good intentions do not excuse the failure; James says the person is guilty of breaking all of it.
He is guilty of breaking all of it
He needs only a sacrifice of grain
A grain offering (Leviticus 2:1) was a voluntary gift, not James’s answer to the guilt of breaking the whole law.
He has broken no command
James says the opposite: stumbling at one point means a command has been broken, and the whole law is violated.
He is judged only by men
Judgment here comes from the law that gives freedom (2:12), not from the opinion of men alone.
Which two commandments does James 2 use to show that the same Lawgiver gave them both?
James 2:11 says the One who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.”
James 2:11
Do not steal and do not lie
Not stealing and not lying are also commandments (Exodus 20:15–16), but they are not the pair James cites.
Do not covet and do not swear
Not coveting is in Exodus 20:17, but James’s pair is adultery and murder.
Do not commit adultery and do not murder
Honor your parents and do not bow to idols
Honoring parents and avoiding idols appear in Exodus 20:4–5 and 20:12, but James cites adultery and murder.
Keep the feast and bring tithes
Feasts and tithes are ceremonial laws (Leviticus 23:4; Malachi 3:10), not James’s illustration.
In James 2, believers are told to speak and act as those who will be judged by what?
James 2:12 says to “Speak and act as those who are going to be judged by the law that gives freedom.”
James 2:12
The customs of the elders
The customs of the elders are not the standard James names; he points to the law that gives freedom.
The law that gives freedom
The decree of Caesar
Caesar’s decrees (Luke 2:1) govern earthly matters, but believers answer to God’s law.
The traditions of men
Mark 7:8 contrasts human traditions with God’s commands; James points to God’s law of freedom.
The opinion of the crowd
The crowd’s opinion is no standard of judgment; James names the law that gives freedom (2:12).
According to James 2, judgment without mercy will be shown to whom?
James 2:13 says, “judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful.”
James 2:13
Anyone who has not been merciful
Anyone who is poor
The verse is about the unmerciful, not the poor, who are God’s chosen (2:5).
Anyone who is unlearned
Being unlearned is not the issue; mercy is.
Anyone who fasts too little
Fasting is not mentioned; the issue is showing mercy.
Anyone who lives far away
Distance has nothing to do with it; James speaks of anyone who has not been merciful.
What short statement closes James’s warning about mercy and judgment?
James 2:13 ends with the line “Mercy triumphs over judgment.”
James 2:13
Love covers a multitude of sins
That thought comes from 1 Peter 4:8, which says love covers over a multitude of sins.
Wisdom is proved by deeds
James speaks of wisdom shown by good deeds in James 3:13, not in this closing line.
Mercy triumphs over judgment
Faith comes by hearing
Faith comes by hearing is Paul’s statement in Romans 10:17, not James’s line here.
Truth sets you free
The truth will set you free is Jesus’ saying in John 8:32, not James’s closing line.
In James 2, what need does James describe for a brother or sister?
James 2:15 supposes “a brother or sister is without clothes and daily food.”
James 2:15
Imprisonment and chains
Visiting prisoners is a theme in Matthew 25:36, but James 2:15 describes lack of clothes and food.
Sickness and fever
Sickness is the subject of James 5:14, not this example.
Without clothes and daily food
Loneliness and grief
Loneliness and grief are not mentioned; the need is clothing and food.
Blindness and lameness
Blindness and lameness are not mentioned; the example is a lack of clothing and daily food.
In James’s example of empty compassion, what words are spoken to the needy person?
James 2:16 pictures someone saying, “Go in peace; stay warm and well fed,” while giving no practical help.
James 2:16
“Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven”
Jesus said this to a paralytic in Matthew 9:2, and it is not part of James’s example.
“Go in peace; stay warm and well fed”
“Silver or gold I do not have”
Peter said this to a lame beggar in Acts 3:6, and then actually healed him, the opposite of empty words.
“Be still!”
Jesus spoke to the storm this way in Mark 4:39; it is not James’s example of empty compassion.
“Get up and walk”
Peter spoke this healing command in Acts 3:6; James’s example is words without any action.
According to James 2, what is missing when someone offers kind words but does nothing for a needy believer’s physical needs?
James 2:16 asks of empty kind words, “what good is that?”, meaning they are useless without practical help.
James 2:16
Prophecy
James does not say prophecy is missing; he asks what good empty kind words are.
Ceremony
Ceremony is not the issue; the missing element is practical help that benefits the needy.
Usefulness
Music
Music is never mentioned; the point is that words without action do no good.
Leadership
Leadership is not James’s concern here; the words are simply of no use.
In James 2, what is faith by itself if it does not result in action?
James 2:17 says, “faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead.”
James 2:17
Growing
Faith without action is not growing; James calls it dead.
Mysterious
James does not call it mysterious; he says it is dead.
Dead
Hidden
Faith without action is not hidden but lifeless, says James.
Ceremonial
Ceremony is not James’s word; he says faith that produces no action is dead.
In James 2, how does James say he will show his faith?
James 2:18 has him say, “I will show you my faith by my deeds.”
James 2:18
By silence
Silence cannot show faith; James says he shows it by deeds.
By visions
Visions are not James’s proof of faith; deeds are.
By his deeds
By his ancestry
Ancestry proves nothing about faith, and James appeals to deeds.
By his knowledge alone
Knowledge alone is the kind of faith he challenges; he shows his faith by deeds.
In James 2, who also believe that God is one—and shudder?
James 2:19 says, “Even the demons believe that—and shudder.”
James 2:19
Angels
James names demons, not angels, as believing that God is one and shuddering.
Kings
Kings are not mentioned; James names demons.
Demons
Shepherds
Shepherds are not mentioned; James says the demons believe and shudder.
Priests
Priests are not mentioned in this verse; the demons believe and shudder.
Before giving examples from Abraham and Rahab, what does James 2 call faith without deeds?
James 2:20 asks, “do you want evidence that faith without deeds is worthless?”
James 2:20
Precious
Faith without deeds is not precious; James calls it worthless.
Hidden
James does not call it hidden; he calls it worthless.
Worthless
Mature
Faith without deeds is not mature; James calls it worthless.
Perfect
Faith without deeds is not perfect; James says Abraham’s faith was perfected by what he did (2:22).
In James 2, which Old Testament man is used as the first example of active faith?
James 2:21 asks, “Was not our father Abraham justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar?”
James 2:21
Joseph
Joseph is not mentioned in James; the first example is Abraham.
Abraham
Samuel
Samuel is not cited in James 2; the first example is Abraham.
Elijah
Elijah appears in James 5:17 as an example of prayer, not here.
Daniel
Daniel is not mentioned in James; the first example is Abraham.
According to James 2, what act of Abraham is highlighted?
James 2:21 points to Abraham offering “his son Isaac on the altar” (Genesis 22:9).
James 2:21
Leaving his homeland at God’s call
Abraham left his homeland in obedience to God (Genesis 12:1), but James cites the offering of Isaac.
Digging a well at Beersheba
Abraham dug a well at Beersheba (Genesis 21:30), but James does not cite it.
Offering his son Isaac on the altar
Buying a burial field for Sarah
Abraham bought a burial field for Sarah (Genesis 23:20), but James does not cite it.
Entertaining three visitors at Mamre
Abraham welcomed three visitors at Mamre (Genesis 18:2), but James cites the offering of Isaac.
In James 2, what was Abraham’s faith doing together with his actions?
James 2:22 says, “his faith was working with his actions.”
James 2:22
Hiding from them
Faith did not hide from his actions; it worked with them (2:22).
Working with them
Replacing them
Faith did not replace actions; it worked together with them.
Denying them
Faith did not deny his actions; it worked with them.
Delaying them
Faith did not delay his actions; James says it was working with them.
In James 2, what Scripture about Abraham was fulfilled?
James 2:23 says, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness,” quoting Genesis 15:6.
James 2:23
“Abram built an altar there to the LORD, who had appeared to him”
Genesis 12:7 records Abram building an altar, but that is not the Scripture James says was fulfilled.
“Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness”
“Abraham planted a tamarisk tree in Beersheba”
Genesis 21:33 records the tamarisk tree at Beersheba, but James does not cite it.
“Abram had become extremely wealthy in livestock and silver and gold”
Genesis 13:2 describes Abram’s wealth, but James does not cite it as fulfilled Scripture.
“Abraham looked up and saw three men standing nearby”
Genesis 18:2 describes three visitors, but James does not cite it as fulfilled Scripture.
In James 2, what title was Abraham given?
James 2:23 adds that “he was called a friend of God” (see also 2 Chronicles 20:7).
James 2:23
Servant of Pharaoh
Abraham is called God’s friend (Isaiah 41:8), not Pharaoh’s servant.
Prince of peace
“Prince of Peace” is a Messianic title in Isaiah 9:6, not Abraham’s.
Friend of God
Scribe of the law
Scribe of the law is not a title given to Abraham.
Son of thunder
“Sons of Thunder” was the nickname for James and John in Mark 3:17, not Abraham’s title.
What conclusion does James 2 state after the example of Abraham?
James 2:24 concludes, “a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone.”
James 2:24
A man is justified by fasting
Fasting is not James’s basis; he says deeds, together with faith.
A man is justified by deeds and not by faith alone
A man is justified by birthright
Birthright is not James’s basis for justification.
A man is justified by circumcision only
Circumcision is debated in Romans 4:9–12; James names deeds and not faith alone.
A man is justified by dreams
Dreams have nothing to do with James’s conclusion.
In James 2, which woman is used as another example of active faith?
James 2:25 asks, “was not even Rahab the prostitute justified by her actions” when she welcomed the spies?
James 2:25
Deborah
Deborah was a judge in Israel (Judges 4:4), but James does not use her.
Ruth
Ruth showed loyalty (Ruth 1:16), but James does not use her.
Rahab the prostitute
Esther
Esther’s courage is told in Esther 4:16, but James does not use her.
Hannah
Hannah’s prayer is in 1 Samuel 1:10, but James does not use her.
According to James 2, what did Rahab do?
James 2:25 says Rahab “welcomed the spies and sent them off on another route” (Joshua 2:4, 2:15).
James 2:25
Hid a hundred prophets in a cave and fed them
Obadiah hid a hundred prophets in caves (1 Kings 18:4); that is not what Rahab did.
Welcomed the spies and sent them off on another route
Anointed a young shepherd as king with oil
Samuel anointed David as king with oil (1 Samuel 16:13), which is not Rahab’s deed.
Judged Israel while sitting under a palm tree
Deborah judged Israel under a palm tree (Judges 4:5), not Rahab.
Sang a victory song beside the Red Sea
Moses and the Israelites sang at the Red Sea (Exodus 15:1), not Rahab.
What final comparison closes James 2?
James 2:26 closes, “As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead.”
James 2:26
As a lamp without oil is dark, so hope without prayer is dark
James does not use a lamp analogy; he compares a body without the spirit.
As a tree without fruit is cut down, so speech without wisdom is cut down
James does not use a tree analogy here; he compares a body without the spirit.
As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead
As a city without walls is weak, so love without truth is weak
James does not use a city analogy here; he compares a body without the spirit.
As water without a spring dries up, so zeal without knowledge dries up
James does not use a spring analogy here; he compares a body without the spirit.
In the opening illustration of James 2, what is the setting when the rich man and poor man arrive?
James 2:2 begins, “Suppose a man comes into your meeting,” placing the test of favoritism in the believers’ gathering.
James 2:2
A battlefield
A battlefield is not the setting; the men enter the believers’ meeting.
A wedding feast
A wedding feast is not mentioned; the setting is the believers’ meeting.
Your meeting
The temple treasury
The temple treasury is not mentioned; the setting is the believers’ meeting.
A royal court
A royal court is not the setting; the court in 2:6 is where the rich drag believers.
In James 2, what visible detail especially marks the rich visitor as wealthy?
James 2:2 describes a man “wearing a gold ring and fine clothes.”
James 2:2
A gold ring
A crown of thorns
A crown of thorns was placed on Jesus (John 19:2); it is not James’s picture of a rich man.
A shepherd’s staff
A shepherd’s staff suggests a shepherd, not a wealthy man; James names a gold ring.
A scroll of the law
A scroll of the law is not mentioned in the scene; the rich man wears a gold ring.
A bronze shield
A bronze shield suggests a soldier, not a wealthy visitor; James names a gold ring.
In the scene about rich and poor visitors, what behavior makes the believers “judges with evil thoughts”?

James 2:3-4
Praying earnestly for both men at once

Refusing to let either man come in

Honoring the rich and humiliating the poor
Collecting an offering from both men
Collecting an offering is not part of the scene; the sin is unequal treatment.
Asking both men to serve in the meeting
Asking both men to serve would be equal treatment; James condemns honoring the rich and humiliating the poor.
In James 2, what does God promise to those who love Him?
James 2:5 says God chose the poor “to inherit the kingdom He promised those who love Him.”
James 2:5
Long life in Canaan
Long life in Canaan was an Old Testament promise; James speaks of the kingdom.
The kingdom
Earthly riches
Earthly riches are not what God promises; He chose the poor to be rich in faith.
Freedom from trials

Immediate victory over enemies
Immediate victory over enemies is not promised; James says the kingdom is promised to those who love Him.
According to James 2, how are the poor whom God has chosen described?
James 2:5 says God chose the poor “to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom.”
James 2:5
Slow to anger and mighty in battle

Rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom
Filled with wine and song
Being filled with wine and song is not what James says of the poor.
Pure in speech and strong in body
Strength of body is not what James says; he says they are rich in faith.
Learned in the law and respected by kings
Being learned in the law and respected by kings is not James’s description; they are rich in faith.
Besides oppressing believers, what do the rich do in James 2?
James 2:6 asks, “Is it not the rich who oppress you and drag you into court?”
James 2:6

Drag them into court
Exile them from Jerusalem
Exile from Jerusalem is not mentioned; he says the rich drag believers into court.
Take away their fields by force
Seizing fields by force is not mentioned in James 2:6.
Stone them at the gate
Stoning at the gate is not mentioned; the rich drag believers into court.

James 2:8

The law of Moses
James does not call it the law of Moses; he calls it the royal law.
The royal law
The first covenant
The first covenant is not James’s title for it; he calls it the royal law.
The law of sacrifice
The law of sacrifice is not a title for this command; James calls it the royal law.

James 2:11

Someone who avoids adultery but commits murder

Tithing and singing are not mentioned; James cites adultery and murder.
Someone who studies but does not travel
Studying and travel are not mentioned; James cites adultery and murder.
Someone who sacrifices but does not wash
Sacrificing and washing are not James’s example; he cites adultery and murder.

James 2:13
Knowledge

Sacrifice
Sacrifice is not what triumphs; mercy does.
Mercy
Fasting
Fasting is not mentioned; mercy triumphs over judgment.
Zeal
Zeal is not mentioned; mercy triumphs over judgment.
In the practical example of need in James 2, what daily necessity is mentioned along with clothing?

James 2:15

Shelter

Land

Asking elders to visit is not James’s example of a rejected response here.
Fasting for three days
Fasting for three days is not mentioned in James 2.
According to James 2, how can faith be shown?
James 2:18 says, “I will show you my faith by my deeds.”
James 2:18

Heritage is not how faith is shown; James says deeds show it.

Temple attendance is not named; James points to deeds.

The harvest will fail

In James 5, the prophets are examples of patience in what?

James 5:10
Prosperity
Prosperity is the opposite of the affliction named in 5:10.
Affliction
Kingship
Kingship is not what the prophets are examples of in 5:10; it is affliction.
Military victory
Military victory is not what the prophets are examples of in 5:10; it is affliction.
Rebuilding walls
Rebuilding walls is Nehemiah’s work, not the affliction named in 5:10.
According to James 5, what have believers heard of regarding Job?
James 5:11 says, “You have heard of Job’s perseverance.”
James 5:11
Job’s wealth
Job’s wealth is not what 5:11 says believers have heard; it is his perseverance.
Job’s friends
Job’s friends appear in the Book of Job but are not mentioned in 5:11.
Job’s perseverance
Job’s homeland
Job’s homeland is not mentioned in 5:11; it is his perseverance.
Job’s genealogy
Job’s genealogy is not mentioned in 5:11; it is his perseverance.
In James chapter 5, what have believers seen in connection with Job’s story?
James 5:11 says, “have seen the outcome from the Lord.”
James 5:11
The outcome from the Lord
The chariots of fire
Chariots of fire belong to Elijah’s departure (2 Kings 2:11), not Job’s story in 5:11.
The rebuilding of Jerusalem
Rebuilding Jerusalem is not mentioned in 5:11.
The tablets of stone
The tablets of stone belong to Sinai, not to Job’s story in 5:11.
The ark’s return
The ark’s return is not mentioned in 5:11.
In James 5:11, which pair of qualities describes the Lord after the mention of Job?
James 5:11 says, “The Lord is full of compassion and mercy.”
James 5:11
Righteous and mighty
Righteous and mighty are not the qualities named in 5:11.
Compassionate and merciful
Jealous and holy
Jealous and holy are not the qualities named in 5:11.
Faithful and true
Faithful and true are not the qualities named in 5:11.
Eternal and glorious
Eternal and glorious are not the qualities named in 5:11.
According to James 5:12, which statement about swearing by heaven, by earth, or by any other oath is correct?
James 5:12 says, “do not swear, not by heaven or earth or by any other oath.”
James 5:12
Only oaths by heaven are forbidden
Heaven is not the only one; James also forbids swearing by earth or by any other oath (5:12).
Only oaths by earth are forbidden
Earth is not the only one; James also forbids swearing by heaven or by any other oath (5:12).
Only oaths by other things are forbidden
James forbids oaths by heaven and earth too, not only by other things (5:12).
Oaths by heaven, earth, or anything else are forbidden
Such oaths are allowed if the speaker is truthful
James allows no exception; he says, “do not swear” and to let your “Yes” be yes (5:12).
In James chapter 5, what simple pattern of speech is commanded instead of oath-taking?
James 5:12 says, “Simply let your “Yes” be yes, and your “No,” no.”
James 5:12
“Perhaps” and “possibly”
“Perhaps” and “possibly” are the hedging 5:12 rules out.
“Peace” and “war”
“Peace” and “war” are not the pattern in 5:12.
“Yes” be yes and “No” be no
“Soon” and “later”
“Soon” and “later” are not the pattern in 5:12.
“Mine” and “yours”
“Mine” and “yours” are not the pattern in 5:12.
According to James 5, what is the proper response for someone who is suffering, and what is the response for someone who is cheerful?
James 5:13 says, “Is any one of you suffering? He should pray. Is anyone cheerful? He should sing praises.”
James 5:13
Fast / stay silent
Fasting and silence are not what 5:13 prescribes.
Pray / sing praises
Call elders / confess sins
Calling elders is for the sick (5:14) and confessing sins is in 5:16, not 5:13.
Mourn / give alms
Mourning and almsgiving are not what 5:13 prescribes.
Flee / rejoice in secret
Fleeing and secret rejoicing are not what 5:13 prescribes.
In James 5, which person is instructed to initiate help by calling the elders of the church?
James 5:14 says, “Is any one of you sick? He should call the elders of the church.”
James 5:14
The cheerful person
The cheerful person is told to sing praises in 5:13, not to call the elders.
The suffering person
The suffering person is told to pray in 5:13; it is the sick person who calls the elders.
The sick person
The rich person
The rich person is addressed in 5:1–6, not in the instruction of 5:14.
The prophet
The prophet is not told to call the elders in 5:14; the sick person is.
In James chapter 5, which action accompanies the elders’ prayer over the sick?
James 5:14 says the elders are to “pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord.”
James 5:14
Laying gold on his forehead
Gold on the forehead is not in 5:14; the elders anoint with oil.
Washing his feet in the river
Washing in a river is not in 5:14; the elders anoint with oil.
Anointing him with oil
Shaving his head
Shaving the head is not in 5:14; the elders anoint with oil.
Clothing him in sackcloth
Sackcloth is not in 5:14; the elders anoint with oil.
According to James 5, what two outcomes may follow the prayer offered in faith for the sick person?
James 5:15 says the prayer “will restore the one who is sick” and “If he has sinned, he will be forgiven.”
James 5:15
Riches and honor
Riches and honor are not promised in 5:15; restoration and forgiveness are.
Restoration and forgiveness
Travel and freedom
Travel and freedom are not promised in 5:15; restoration and forgiveness are.
Silence and secrecy
Silence and secrecy are not promised in 5:15; restoration and forgiveness are.
Exile and fear
Exile and fear are the opposite of what 5:15 promises.
In James 5, who is the one that ultimately raises up the sick person?
James 5:15 says, “The Lord will raise him up.”
James 5:15
The righteous man
The righteous man’s prayer has power (5:16), but 5:15 says the Lord raises him up.
Elijah
Elijah is the example of prayer in 5:17–18, not the one who raises the sick in 5:15.
The Lord
The church treasurer
A church treasurer is not mentioned in 5:15; the Lord raises him up.
The farmer
The farmer appears in 5:7, not in 5:15.
According to James 5, what is said about the prayer of a righteous man?
James 5:16 says, “The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail.”
James 5:16
It is heard only in the temple
5:16 does not limit such prayer to the temple.
It has great power to prevail
It must be repeated seven times
Seven repetitions are not required in 5:16.
It belongs only to prophets
5:16 speaks of any righteous man, not only prophets.
It ends all suffering instantly
5:16 says the prayer has great power to prevail, not that it ends all suffering instantly.
In James 5, which Old Testament man is used as an example that effective prayer can come from someone with a nature like ours?
James 5:17 says, “Elijah was a man just like us.”
James 5:17
Noah
Noah is not the figure in 5:17; it is Elijah.
Elijah
Gideon
Gideon is not the figure in 5:17; it is Elijah.
Hezekiah
Hezekiah is not the figure in 5:17; it is Elijah.
Ezra
Ezra is not the figure in 5:17; it is Elijah.
In James chapter 5, what exactly did Elijah pray about in his first example?
James 5:17 says, “He prayed earnestly that it would not rain.”
James 5:17
That fire would fall
Fire falling came in a different event (1 Kings 18:38), not the prayer in 5:17.
That a child would rise
Raising a child came in another event (1 Kings 17:21), not the prayer in 5:17.
That it would not rain
That a wall would stand
A standing wall is not what Elijah prayed about in 5:17.
That a king would repent
A king’s repentance is not what Elijah prayed about in 5:17.
According to James 5, where did the drought described in Elijah’s story take effect?
James 5:17 says, “it did not rain on the land for three and a half years.”
James 5:17
In the sea
The sea is not the place named in 5:17; it did not rain on the land.
On the land
In the temple
The temple is not the place named in 5:17; it did not rain on the land.
Above Jerusalem only
5:17 says the land, not Jerusalem only.
In Egypt
Egypt is not named in 5:17; it did not rain on the land.
In James 5, after Elijah prayed again, which two things responded?
James 5:18 says, “the heavens gave rain, and the earth yielded its crops.”
James 5:18
The priests and the king
Priests and the king are not the two responders in 5:18; the heavens and earth are.
The mountains and the valleys
Mountains and valleys are not the two responders in 5:18; the heavens and earth are.
The heavens and the earth
The sea and the wind
The sea and the wind are not the two responders in 5:18; the heavens and earth are.
The temple and the altar
The temple and altar are not the two responders in 5:18; the heavens and earth are.
In the last two verses of James 5, what has one person done if he strays and then is rescued?
James 5:19 begins, “if one of you should wander from the truth.”
James 5:19
Wandered from the truth
Missed the feast
Missing a feast is not what 5:19 describes; the wandering is from the truth.
Forgotten a proverb
Forgetting a proverb is not what 5:19 describes; the wandering is from the truth.
Broken a fast
Breaking a fast is not what 5:19 describes; the wandering is from the truth.
Lost a field
Losing a field is not what 5:19 describes; the wandering is from the truth.
According to James 5, what does someone do when he helps a wandering sinner rightly?
James 5:20 says, “Whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way.”
James 5:20
Turns him from the error of his way
Crowns him with oil
Crowning him with oil is not in 5:20; the helper turns him from error.
Sends him to the judge
Sending him to the judge is not in 5:20; the helper turns him from error.
Hides him from the church
Hiding him from the church is not in 5:20; the helper turns him from error.
Teaches him to swear truthfully
Teaching him to swear truthfully is not in 5:20, and 5:12 forbids swearing.
In James chapter 5, what exact phrase describes the mistaken path of the sinner who is restored?
James 5:20 refers to “the error of his way.”
James 5:20
The path of darkness
The path of darkness is not the phrase used in 5:20; it is the error of his way.
The snare of the devil
The snare of the devil is not the phrase used in 5:20; it is the error of his way.
The error of his way
The broad road of ruin
The broad road to destruction is in Matthew 7:13, not the phrase used in 5:20.
The valley of trouble
The valley of trouble is not the phrase used in 5:20; it is the error of his way.
According to James 5, what is saved from death when a sinner is turned back?
James 5:20 says he “will save his soul from death.”
James 5:20
His body
His body is not what 5:20 says is saved from death; it is his soul.
His name
His name is not what 5:20 says is saved from death; it is his soul.
His house
His house is not what 5:20 says is saved from death; it is his soul.
His soul
His memory
His memory is not what 5:20 says is saved from death; it is his soul.
In James 5, what is covered over by turning a sinner back?
James 5:20 says he will “cover over a multitude of sins.”
James 5:20
A hidden treasure
Hidden treasure is not what 5:20 says is covered; it is a multitude of sins.
A multitude of sins
A field of weeds
A field of weeds is not what 5:20 says is covered; it is a multitude of sins.
The elder’s weakness
The elder’s weakness is not what 5:20 says is covered; it is a multitude of sins.
The clouds of heaven
The clouds of heaven are not what 5:20 says is covered; it is a multitude of sins.
In James chapter 5, which statement exactly matches the chapter’s teaching about the rich?
James 5:3 says, “Your gold and silver are corroded.”
James 5:3
Their barns are full and their names are honored
Full barns and honored names are not what 5:2–3 says of the rich.
Their gold and silver are corroded
Their vineyards sing with joy
Singing vineyards are not what 5:2–3 says of the rich.
Their children rise and bless them
Children who rise and bless them are not what 5:2–3 says of the rich.
Their ships bring in wealth from afar
Ships bringing wealth are not what 5:2–3 says of the rich.
In the patience section of James 5, which statement exactly matches the chapter?
James 5:7 says, “See how the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the soil.”
James 5:7
The farmer waits for summer winds
Summer winds are not what the farmer awaits in 5:7.
The farmer awaits the precious fruit of the soil
The shepherd waits for spotless lambs
The shepherd and spotless lambs are not in 5:7.
The merchant waits for favorable tides
The merchant and favorable tides are not in 5:7.
The watchman waits for the morning star
The watchman and the morning star are not in 5:7.
In James 5, which statement about community behavior is correct?
James 5:9 says, “Do not complain about one another, brothers, so that you will not be judged.”
James 5:9
Complain about one another so your grief is known
5:9 forbids complaining about one another, not complaining so that grief is known.
Do not complain about one another, so that you will not be judged
Accuse one another before the elders
5:9 does not tell them to accuse one another before the elders.
Isolate the suffering from the cheerful
5:9 does not tell them to isolate the suffering from the cheerful; 5:13 tells each to pray or sing.
Let only prophets pray for the sick

In James chapter 5, which statement accurately combines the lesson from Job?
James 5:11 says, “You have heard of Job’s perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord.”
James 5:11
You have heard of Job’s riches and seen his palace
Job’s riches and palace are not what 5:11 mentions.
You have heard of Job’s perseverance and seen the outcome from the Lord
You have heard of Job’s sons and seen his long journeys
Job’s sons and long journeys are not what 5:11 mentions.
You have heard of Job’s wisdom and seen his books
Job’s wisdom and books are not what 5:11 mentions.
You have heard of Job’s victories and seen his throne
Job’s victories and throne are not what 5:11 mentions.
In James 5, which option gives the exact threefold warning about oaths?
James 5:12 says, “do not swear, not by heaven or earth or by any other oath.”
James 5:12
Not by altar, temple, or Jerusalem
The altar, temple and Jerusalem are not the oaths named in 5:12.
Not by heaven or earth or by any other oath
Not by Moses, Aaron, or David
Moses, Aaron and David are not the oaths named in 5:12.
Not by sun, moon, or stars
The sun, moon and stars are not the oaths named in 5:12.
Not by city, gate, or court
The city, gate and court are not the oaths named in 5:12.
According to James 5, which exact pair of responses is assigned to different circumstances?
James 5:13 says, “Is any one of you suffering? He should pray. Is anyone cheerful? He should sing praises.”
James 5:13
Sick—sing praises; cheerful—call the elders
The sick person calls the elders (5:14), and the cheerful sing praises, so this swaps the pairs.
Suffering—pray; cheerful—sing praises
Wandering—weep; rich—anoint with oil
Wandering, weeping, the rich and anointing are not the pairs in 5:13.
Prophets—swear oaths; elders—mow fields
Prophets swearing oaths contradicts 5:12, and mowing fields is not in 5:13.
Patient—store treasure; righteous—complain
