In James chapter 5, which sequence best reflects the care of a sick believer?

James 5:14–15 says the sick person “should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil,” the prayer offered in faith “will restore the one who is sick,” and “The Lord will raise him up.”
James 5:14-15
Call elders, prayer and anointing, prayer of faith restores, the Lord raises up
Sell possessions, travel to Jerusalem, offer incense, recover slowly
Selling possessions, traveling to Jerusalem and offering incense are not in 5:14–15.
Swear an oath, confess to a priest, fast seven days, be healed
Swearing, confessing to a priest and fasting seven days are not in 5:14–15.
Wait alone, hide the sickness, repay wages, rejoice
Waiting alone and hiding the sickness is the opposite of calling the elders in 5:14.
Ask a farmer, gather rainwater, sing loudly, return to work
Asking a farmer and gathering rainwater are not in 5:14–15.
In James 5, which exact statement about Elijah appears in the chapter?
James 5:17 says, “Elijah was a man just like us.”
James 5:17
Elijah was an angel among men
Elijah is not called an angel in 5:17; he was a man just like us.
Elijah was a man just like us
Elijah never suffered weakness
5:17 says he was a man just like us, so he did suffer weakness as we do.
Elijah prayed only once in his life
5:17 says he prayed and the rain stopped, and 5:18 says he prayed again; he did not pray only once.
Elijah ruled as king in Israel
Elijah was a prophet, not a king of Israel; 5:17 calls him a man just like us.
According to James 5, which full result followed Elijah’s second prayer?
James 5:18 says, “Again he prayed, and the heavens gave rain, and the earth yielded its crops.”
James 5:18
Fire fell, and the altar was consumed
Fire consuming the altar happened at Carmel (1 Kings 18:38), not in the result named in 5:18.
The heavens gave rain, and the earth yielded its crops
The sea opened, and Israel crossed through
The sea opening is the Exodus (Exodus 14:21), not the result named in 5:18.
The sun stood still, and the battle was won
The sun standing still is from Joshua’s battle, not the result named in 5:18.
Manna fell, and the camp was fed
Manna feeding the camp belongs to the wilderness, not the result named in 5:18.
In the final chapter of James, which option correctly combines one warning from the opening and one promise from the closing?
James 5:3 says hoarded wealth “will testify against you,” and 5:20 says turning a sinner back “will save his soul from death.”
James 5:3, 20
Hoarded treasure brings crowns, and restoring a sinner brings wealth
Hoarded treasure brings testimony against the rich, not crowns, and restoring a sinner saves his soul, not brings wealth.
Corroded gold proves earthly blessing, and restoring a sinner hides his name
Corroded gold does not prove blessing, and restoring a sinner covers his sins rather than hiding his name.
Hoarded treasure stands as testimony against the rich, and turning a sinner back saves his soul from death
Withheld wages are forgotten, and wandering from truth has no danger
Withheld wages cry out and are not forgotten (5:4), and wandering from truth is dangerous (5:20).
Luxury on earth earns mercy, and covering sins removes the need for repentance
Luxury on earth leads to slaughter (5:5), not mercy, and covering sins does not remove the need for repentance.
60: In the opening line of 1 Peter chapter 1, who identifies himself as the sender of the letter?
The letter opens, “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1), naming Peter as its sender.
1 Peter 1:1
Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ
Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus
Paul opens Romans as “a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle” (Romans 1:1); he is not the author of 1 Peter.
James, a servant of God
“James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” opens the letter of James (James 1:1), not 1 Peter.
John, the elder
“The elder” is how the writer of 2 and 3 John introduces himself (2 John 1:1; 3 John 1:1).
Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ
Jude calls himself “a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James” in his own short letter (Jude 1:1).
In Peter’s greeting in 1 Peter 1, how are the recipients described?
Peter writes “To the elect who are exiles of the Dispersion” scattered through five provinces of Asia Minor (1:1).
1 Peter 1:1
The saints loved by God in Rome
Paul wrote “To all in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints” (Romans 1:7); Peter’s readers lived in Asia Minor.
The elders of the church in Ephesus
Paul summoned “the elders of the church” of Ephesus to Miletus (Acts 20:17); Peter addresses scattered exiles, not one church’s elders.
The elect, exiles of the Dispersion
The churches throughout Macedonia
Paul praised “the churches of Macedonia” for their generosity (2 Corinthians 8:1); Macedonia is not among Peter’s regions.
The children of Abraham by faith
Paul says “those who have faith are sons of Abraham” (Galatians 3:7); Peter’s greeting calls his readers elect exiles instead.
In the address of 1 Peter 1, which place is named among the regions where the scattered believers lived?
Peter addresses exiles “throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1).
1 Peter 1:1
Egypt
Visitors from Egypt were in the Pentecost crowd (Acts 2:10), but Egypt is not among the regions Peter names.
Judea
Judea is listed with Cappadocia and Pontus in the Pentecost crowd (Acts 2:9), but Peter’s greeting does not include it.
Crete
Paul left Titus in Crete to appoint elders (Titus 1:5); Crete is not among the regions in 1 Peter.
Cappadocia
Achaia
Achaia was the province around Corinth (2 Corinthians 1:1); Peter’s list stays in Asia Minor.
In the list of regions in 1 Peter chapter 1, which location is not named?
Peter’s list is “Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1); Jerusalem is not among them.
1 Peter 1:1
Pontus
Pontus is the first region Peter names in his greeting (1:1).
Jerusalem
Galatia
Galatia is the second region in Peter’s list (1:1).
Asia
Asia is named fourth, just before Bithynia (1:1).
Bithynia
Bithynia closes Peter’s list of regions (1:1).
According to the opening greeting of 1 Peter 1, the elect are chosen according to whose foreknowledge?
The elect are chosen “according to the foreknowledge of God the Father” (1:2).
1 Peter 1:2
The prophets’
The prophets foretold the coming grace (1:10), but election rests on the Father’s foreknowledge, not theirs.
The apostles’
Peter is himself an apostle (1:1), yet he grounds election in God the Father’s foreknowledge, not the apostles’.
The elders’
Peter later appeals to “the elders among you” (1 Peter 5:1) but never ties election to their knowledge.
The angels’
Angels “long to look into these things” (1:12); they do not foreknow or choose the elect.
God the Father’s
In 1 Peter chapter 1, by whose sanctifying work are believers set apart?
The elect are chosen and “sanctified by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus Christ” (1:2).
1 Peter 1:2
The law’s
Hebrews says “the law made nothing perfect” (Hebrews 7:19); Peter credits sanctification to the Spirit.
The Spirit’s
Moses’
Moses received the tablets on Mount Sinai (Exodus 31:18), but Peter credits sanctification to the Spirit, not to Moses.
The temple’s
Peter later calls believers living stones built into “a spiritual house” (1 Peter 2:5), but here sanctification is the Spirit’s work.
The church’s
The church does not sanctify itself here; Peter says believers are “sanctified by the Spirit” (1:2).
In Peter’s greeting, believers are chosen for obedience to whom?
The elect are chosen “for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling by His blood” (1:2).
1 Peter 1:2
Abraham
Paul calls Abraham “the father of all who believe” (Romans 4:11), but Peter’s readers are chosen for obedience to Christ.
David
David is not mentioned in 1 Peter 1; obedience here is owed to Jesus Christ (1:2).
Jesus Christ
Moses
Moses was “the servant of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 34:5), but Peter directs obedience to Jesus Christ.
The high priest
Hebrews calls Jesus Himself “a great high priest” (Hebrews 4:14); Peter’s readers obey Jesus Christ, not an earthly high priest.
At the end of his opening greeting in 1 Peter 1, what does Peter wish his readers to have in abundance?
Peter closes the greeting, “Grace and peace be yours in abundance” (1:2).
1 Peter 1:2
Faith and hope
Faith and hope come later, when Peter says “your faith and hope are in God” (1:21), not in the greeting.
Mercy and truth
Mercy appears in the next verse, “By His great mercy” (1:3), but the greeting itself wishes grace and peace.
Wisdom and strength
Daniel blesses God, “for wisdom and power belong to Him” (Daniel 2:20); Peter’s greeting wishes grace and peace.
Grace and peace
Gifts and callings
Paul writes that “God’s gifts and His call are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29); Peter’s greeting wishes grace and peace.
In the blessing at the start of 1 Peter 1, by what has God given believers new birth?
Peter blesses God because “By His great mercy He has given us new birth into a living hope” (1:3).
1 Peter 1:3
His great mercy
Their good works
Paul says God saved us “not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy” (Titus 3:5).
Temple sacrifices
Hebrews says “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4); new birth comes by mercy.
Angelic help
Angels only “long to look into these things” (1:12); they are not the source of new birth.
Earthly wisdom
Paul says God “made foolish the wisdom of the world” (1 Corinthians 1:20); new birth comes by God’s great mercy.
According to 1 Peter chapter 1, new birth brings believers into what?
God “has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ” (1:3).
1 Peter 1:3
An earthly kingdom
The disciples asked Jesus, “will You at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” (Acts 1:6); Peter speaks of a living hope.
A restored temple
No temple is mentioned; new birth leads into “a living hope” and a heavenly inheritance (1:3–4).
A hidden mystery
Paul speaks of “the mystery that was hidden for ages” (Colossians 1:26); Peter says new birth is into a living hope.
A priestly office
Peter later calls believers “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9), but in 1:3 new birth is into a living hope.
A living hope
In 1 Peter 1, through what event does this living hope come?
The living hope comes “through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1:3).
1 Peter 1:3
The giving of the law at Mount Sinai
The LORD gave Moses the tablets on Mount Sinai (Exodus 31:18); Peter grounds hope in Christ’s resurrection instead.
The resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead
The conquest of Canaan under Joshua
Joshua led Israel into Canaan, and Jericho’s wall collapsed (Joshua 6:20); Peter’s living hope rests on the resurrection.
The building of the temple by Solomon
Solomon began building the house of the LORD in his fourth year (1 Kings 6:1); Peter ties hope to Christ rising from the dead.
The anointing of David as king of Israel
Samuel anointed David with the horn of oil (1 Samuel 16:13), but Peter’s hope comes through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
In Peter’s opening blessing, where is the believers’ inheritance reserved?
The inheritance is “reserved in heaven for you” (1:4).
1 Peter 1:4
In Zion
God installed His King “on Zion, upon My holy mountain” (Psalm 2:6), but Peter places the inheritance in heaven.
In the temple
The inheritance is not kept in the temple; Paul likewise speaks of “an eternal house in heaven” (2 Corinthians 5:1).
In heaven
In the wilderness
Israel ate manna forty years in the wilderness (Exodus 16:35); the believers’ inheritance is kept in heaven.
In the sea
Nothing is stored in the sea; Peter says the inheritance is “reserved in heaven for you” (1:4).
In 1 Peter 1:4, which word is one of the terms used to describe the inheritance?
Peter calls the inheritance “imperishable, undefiled, and unfading” (1:4).
1 Peter 1:4
Visible

God gave Solomon great wisdom (1 Kings 4:29), but Peter says new birth comes through God’s word.
The sign of circumcision
Abraham “received the sign of circumcision” (Romans 4:11); Peter names God’s living word as the means of new birth.
The living and enduring word of God
The fire on the altar
The fire of the LORD consumed Elijah’s sacrifice (1 Kings 18:38); new birth comes through God’s word.
In Peter’s quotation near the end of chapter 1, all flesh is like what?
Peter quotes, “All flesh is like grass” (1:24), from Isaiah 40:6.
1 Peter 1:24
Dust
God told Adam, “For dust you are, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19); Peter’s quotation compares flesh to grass.
Grass
Iron
Iron is not mentioned; the quotation says flesh is like grass (1:24).
Smoke
The psalmist says “my days vanish like smoke” (Psalm 102:3), but Peter compares flesh to grass.
Dew
Hosea likens Israel’s loyalty to “the early dew that vanishes” (Hosea 6:4); Peter compares flesh to grass.
According to 1 Peter 1:24, what happens to the grass?
“The grass withers and the flowers fall” (1:24), quoting Isaiah 40:7–8.
1 Peter 1:24
It blooms
The psalmist says man “blooms like a flower of the field” (Psalm 103:15), but Peter’s quotation stresses withering.
It is gathered
Gathering is not mentioned; the grass withers (1:24).
It withers
It is planted
Planting is not in the quotation; the grass withers (1:24).
It is burned immediately
Jesus speaks of grass “thrown into the furnace” (Matthew 6:30), but Peter’s quotation says the grass withers.
In the closing quotation of 1 Peter chapter 1, what happens to the flowers?
“The grass withers and the flowers fall” (1:24).
1 Peter 1:24
They fall
They spread
Spreading is not mentioned; the flowers fall (1:24).
They remain
The flowers do not remain; only “the word of the Lord stands forever” (1:25).
They are crowned
Peter speaks of “the crown of glory that will never fade away” (1 Peter 5:4), but here the flowers fall.
They bear fruit
Bearing fruit is not in the quotation; the flowers fall (1:24).
In the final sentence of 1 Peter 1, this enduring word is said to be the word that was what to the readers?
Peter ends, “And this is the word that was proclaimed to you” (1:25).
1 Peter 1:25
Hidden from you
Paul speaks of “the mystery that was hidden for ages” (Colossians 1:26), but Peter says this word was proclaimed.
Proclaimed to you
Sealed from you
Daniel was told to “seal the book until the time of the end” (Daniel 12:4); Peter’s word has been proclaimed.
Copied by you
Copying is not mentioned; the word “was proclaimed to you” (1:25).
Lost to you
The word is not lost; it “stands forever” and was proclaimed to them (1:25).
In the greeting of 1 Peter 1, which list of Roman provinces is correct?
Peter writes to exiles “throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1).
1 Peter 1:1
Judea, Samaria, Galilee, Decapolis, and Perea
Judea, Galilee, and Samaria are where the church grew in Acts 9:31; Peter’s list is of provinces in Asia Minor.
Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia
Rome, Corinth, Ephesus, Philippi, and Thessalonica
Rome, Corinth, Ephesus, Philippi, and Thessalonica are cities that received Paul’s letters, not regions in Peter’s greeting.
Syria, Cilicia, Lycaonia, Pamphylia, and Crete
Paul traveled “through Syria and Cilicia” (Acts 15:41); none of these regions is in Peter’s list.
Egypt, Libya, Cyrene, Cyprus, and Malta
Egypt, Libya, and Cyrene appear in the Pentecost crowd (Acts 2:10), not in Peter’s greeting.
In Peter’s first chapter, which description exactly matches the inheritance kept for believers?
The inheritance is “imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven” (1:4).
1 Peter 1:4
Perishable, honored, and expanding
Perishable is the opposite of Peter’s first term, imperishable (1:4).
Glorious, earthly, and secure
The inheritance is “reserved in heaven,” so it is not earthly (1:4).
Imperishable, undefiled, and unfading
Hidden, mysterious, and temporary
The inheritance is not hidden or temporary; it is unfading and reserved in heaven (1:4).
Rich, visible, and increasing
Peter’s inheritance is kept in heaven and not yet seen (1:4), not rich, visible, and increasing.
In the part of 1 Peter 1 about suffering, which phrase tells how long the grief lasts?
Peter writes that “for a little while you may have had to suffer grief in various trials” (1:6).
1 Peter 1:6
For many generations
The grief lasts “for a little while” (1:6), not for generations.
For a little while
Until evening
The psalm says “Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning” (Psalm 30:5); Peter says “for a little while.”
For forty days
Jesus fasted forty days and forty nights (Matthew 4:2); Peter’s phrase is “for a little while.”
Forever
Grief is not forever; it lasts “for a little while” (1:6), while “the word of the Lord stands forever” (1:25).
According to 1 Peter 1:7, what is being proven through trials?
Trials come “so that the proven character of your faith” may result in praise, glory, and honor (1:7).
1 Peter 1:7
The greatness of wealth
Peter says gold “perishes” (1:7), so trials do not prove the greatness of wealth.
The power of rulers
Rulers are not mentioned; trials prove the character of faith (1:7).
The character of faith
The length of prayer
Jesus condemned those who “for a show make lengthy prayers” (Mark 12:40); trials prove faith, not prayer length.
The wisdom of the law
The law is not mentioned in 1 Peter 1; trials prove the character of faith (1:7).
In 1 Peter 1:8, which pair of actions toward Jesus is stated even though He is unseen?
Peter writes, “Though you have not seen Him, you love Him” and “you believe in Him” (1:8).
1 Peter 1:8
Fear and flee
Fear and flight are not mentioned; the readers love and believe in Christ (1:8).
Love and believe
Follow and touch
Jesus invited Thomas to touch His wounds (John 20:27), but Peter’s readers have not seen Him.
Question and test
Questioning and testing are not mentioned; they love Him and believe in Him (1:8).
Praise and anoint
A woman anointed Jesus in Bethany (Mark 14:3), but Peter’s readers love and believe without seeing.
In 1 Peter 1:11, which sequence is predicted by the Spirit of Christ?
The Spirit “predicted the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow” (1:11).
1 Peter 1:11
The kingdom of David and the exile to Babylon
The exile to Babylon (2 Kings 25:11) is Old Testament history; Peter’s prophecy concerns Christ’s sufferings and glories.
The sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow
The birth of John and the ministry of Elijah
Gabriel announced John’s birth (Luke 1:13) and said he would go “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17), not Peter’s subject.
The fall of Jerusalem and the rebuilding of the temple
Jesus foretold Jerusalem “surrounded by armies” (Luke 21:20), but 1:11 speaks of Christ’s sufferings and glories.
The signs of Moses and the plagues of Egypt
Moses’ signs and the plagues fill Exodus 7–12; Peter speaks of Christ’s sufferings and the glories to follow.
In 1 Peter 1:12, who is said to long to look into the truths of salvation?
“Even angels long to look into these things” (1:12).
1 Peter 1:12
Kings
Jesus said “many prophets and kings desired to see what you see” (Luke 10:24), but 1:12 names angels.
Prophets
The prophets searched carefully (1:10), but the longing to look in 1:12 is the angels’.
Priests
Priests are not mentioned in 1:10–12; angels long to look into these things.
Angels
Shepherds
Shepherds watched their flocks the night Jesus was born (Luke 2:8), but 1:12 says angels long to look into salvation.
Which statement best matches Peter’s call to holiness in 1 Peter 1:15-16?
Peter quotes, “Be holy, because I am holy” (1:16), from Leviticus 11:44–45.
Be humble, because I was humble
Peter later says “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5:5), but 1:16 calls for holiness.
Be just, because the law is just
Paul calls the law “holy, righteous, and good” (Romans 7:12), but Peter quotes God: “Be holy, because I am holy.”
Be merciful, because judgment is near
Jesus said, “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36); Peter quotes the call to be holy.
Be strong, because the battle is fierce
Joshua was told “to be strong and courageous” (Joshua 1:9); Peter quotes the call to holiness.
Be holy, because I am holy
In 1 Peter 1:17, what is the basis for reverent fear during believers’ stay as foreigners?
Believers call on “a Father who judges each one’s work impartially,” so they live in reverent fear (1:17).
1 Peter 1:17
The Father judges each one’s work impartially
Satan roams like a lion
Peter warns that the devil prowls “like a roaring lion” in 1 Peter 5:8, not as the basis given in 1:17.
The law condemns every sinner
Peter grounds reverent fear in the Father’s impartial judgment, not in the law’s condemnation (1:17).
The nations hate the righteous
Jesus warned, “you will be hated by all nations” (Matthew 24:9), but 1:17 grounds fear in God’s judgment.
Death comes like a thief
“The Day of the Lord will come like a thief” (1 Thessalonians 5:2) concerns that Day, and is not Peter’s reason in 1:17.
In Peter’s teaching on redemption, which contrast is explicitly made?
Believers were redeemed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold” but “with the precious blood of Christ” (1:18–19).
Bread and wine versus body and blood
Bread and wine as Christ’s body and blood belong to the Last Supper (Matthew 26:26–28), not this passage.
Silver and gold versus the precious blood of Christ
Goats and calves versus incense and oil
Hebrews contrasts “the blood of goats and calves” with Christ’s own blood (Hebrews 9:12), not incense and oil.
Stone tablets versus living letters
Paul contrasts “tablets of stone” with “tablets of human hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:3), not Peter.
Tents and temples versus houses and fields
Tents, temples, houses, and fields are not mentioned; the contrast is silver and gold versus Christ’s blood (1:18–19).
In 1 Peter 1:21, what two acts of God toward Jesus are named?
God “raised Him from the dead and glorified Him” (1:21).
1 Peter 1:21
Anointed Him and sent Him
God “anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 10:38), but 1:21 names raising and glorifying.
Healed Him and strengthened Him
An angel strengthened Jesus in Gethsemane (Luke 22:43), but 1:21 names God raising and glorifying Him.
Raised Him from the dead and glorified Him
Concealed Him and revealed Him
Peter says Christ was known before the world and revealed in the last times (1:20); the acts in 1:21 are raising and glorifying.
Tempted Him and vindicated Him
Jesus was led into the wilderness “to be tempted by the devil” (Matthew 4:1); 1:21 names His resurrection and glorification.
Near the end of 1 Peter 1, what did obedience to the truth produce?
Purified by obedience to the truth, believers have “a genuine love for your brothers” (1:22).
1 Peter 1:22
Authority over nations
Christ promises “authority over the nations” to the overcomer (Revelation 2:26); 1:22 speaks of genuine love.
A genuine love for brothers
Freedom from all suffering
Peter says they may still suffer grief in trials (1:6), so obedience did not end all suffering.
Knowledge of every mystery
Paul says one who can “fathom all mysteries” but lacks love is nothing (1 Corinthians 13:2); Peter names genuine love.
Mastery of the law
Mastery of the law is not in view; obedience to the truth produced genuine brotherly love (1:22).
In the new birth language of 1 Peter 1:23, what contrast is used?
Believers are born again “not of perishable seed, but of imperishable” (1:23).
1 Peter 1:23
Old covenant and new covenant
Hebrews contrasts the first covenant with the new (Hebrews 8:13), but 1:23 contrasts perishable and imperishable seed.
Earthly tent and heavenly house
Paul contrasts “the earthly tent” with “an eternal house in heaven” (2 Corinthians 5:1), not Peter in 1:23.
Darkness and light
Peter speaks of darkness and light in 1 Peter 2:9, not in the new-birth language of 1:23.
Perishable seed and imperishable seed
Milk and solid food
Hebrews contrasts milk and solid food (Hebrews 5:12); Peter mentions milk in 1 Peter 2:2, not in 1:23.
According to the same quotation in 1 Peter 1:24, what is human glory like?
The quotation says “all its glory like the flowers of the field” (1:24).
1 Peter 1:24
The flowers of the field
Waves of the sea
James likens the doubter to “a wave of the sea” (James 1:6); Peter compares glory to flowers of the field.
Stars of heaven
God promised to multiply Abraham’s descendants “like the stars in the sky” (Genesis 22:17), a different image.
Oil in a lamp
Oil for lamps appears in the parable of the ten virgins (Matthew 25:4), not in Peter’s quotation.
Branches of a vine
Jesus says, “I am the vine and you are the branches” (John 15:5), a different image.
Which paired outcome appears in 1 Peter 1:24?
Peter quotes, “the grass withers and the flowers fall” (1:24), from Isaiah 40:7–8.
1 Peter 1:24
The stone breaks and the wall falls
Jericho’s wall collapsed (Joshua 6:20), but that is not the paired image in 1:24.
The grass withers and the flowers fall
The sea rages and the hills melt
The psalmist speaks of waters that “roar and foam” and mountains that quake (Psalm 46:3); Peter’s pair is grass and flowers.
The lamp dims and the oil fails
The foolish virgins said “our lamps are going out” (Matthew 25:8); Peter’s pair is grass withering and flowers falling.
The cloud passes and the dew dries
Hosea speaks of “the early dew that vanishes” (Hosea 6:4); Peter quotes grass and flowers.
In contrast to fading flesh in 1 Peter 1:25, what stands forever?
“But the word of the Lord stands forever” (1:25), quoting Isaiah 40:8.
1 Peter 1:25
The temple of the Lord
Jesus foretold that not one stone of the temple would be left on another (Matthew 24:2); the word of the Lord stands forever.
The throne of David
God promised David, “your throne will be established forever” (2 Samuel 7:16), but 1:25 speaks of the word of the Lord.
The church in Jerusalem
The church in Jerusalem is not mentioned; Peter says the word of the Lord stands forever (1:25).
The covenant of Sinai
Hebrews calls the first covenant obsolete and soon to “disappear” (Hebrews 8:13); the word of the Lord stands forever.
The word of the Lord
In 1 Peter 1:2, which arrangement of divine action is stated correctly?
The elect are chosen “according to the foreknowledge of God the Father and sanctified by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling by His blood” (1:2).
1 Peter 1:2
Chosen according to Christ’s foreknowledge, by the angels’ sanctifying work, for obedience to Moses and sprinkling by the blood of bulls
Peter assigns foreknowledge to the Father and sanctification to the Spirit (1:2); the blood of bulls cannot take away sins (Hebrews 10:4).
Chosen according to the Father’s foreknowledge, by the Spirit’s sanctifying work, for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling by His blood
Chosen according to the law’s demands, by the priests’ purifying work, for obedience to the prophets and washing with water
Peter mentions neither the law nor priests here; the elect are sanctified by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus Christ (1:2).
Chosen according to the apostles’ foreknowledge, by the temple’s cleansing work, for service in Jerusalem and sprinkling with oil
Election rests on God the Father’s foreknowledge, not the apostles’, and the sprinkling is by Christ’s blood (1:2).
Chosen according to the Spirit’s foreknowledge, by the Father’s sanctifying work, for obedience to the elders and sprinkling with ashes
This swaps the roles: the foreknowledge is the Father’s and the sanctifying work the Spirit’s (1:2); obedience is to Jesus Christ.
In 1 Peter 1:3-5, which chain of blessings matches Peter’s wording?
God gave “new birth into a living hope” (1:3) and “an inheritance that is imperishable” (1:4) to those “shielded by God’s power” through faith (1:5).
1 Peter 1:3-5
New birth into a living hope, into an imperishable inheritance, shielded by God’s power through faith
Repentance into peace, into earthly abundance, guarded by human wisdom
Repentance and human wisdom are not in 1:3–5; Peter speaks of new birth, an inheritance, and God’s power.
Baptism into service, into temple worship, strengthened by priestly sacrifices
Baptism, temple worship, and sacrifices are not in 1:3–5; believers are shielded by God’s power through faith.
Sorrow into patience, into prosperity, upheld by angels
Peter mentions grief in trials (1:6), but 1:3–5 describe a living hope and heavenly inheritance, not prosperity or angels.
Adoption into Israel, into land possession, preserved by the law
The inheritance is not land in Israel; it is “reserved in heaven for you” (1:4).
In 1 Peter 1:10-12, which statement best summarizes the prophets’ role?
The prophets “searched and investigated carefully” (1:10), and “It was revealed to them that they were not serving themselves, but you” (1:12).
They created the message of salvation by their own insight
The message was not their own insight; “the Spirit of Christ in them” predicted it (1:11).
They served themselves by hiding the message from future generations
The prophets were “not serving themselves, but you” (1:12), and they foretold the message rather than hiding it.
They searched carefully about the coming grace and served later believers with what they foretold
They replaced the gospel preachers and finished the work of angels
The prophets did not replace the gospel preachers; the message was later announced by those who preached the gospel (1:12).
They denied the sufferings of Christ and taught only earthly triumph
The Spirit in the prophets “predicted the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow” (1:11).
In the full flow of 1 Peter 1:22-25, which statement best captures Peter’s concluding argument?
Born again “of imperishable” seed (1:23), believers must “love one another deeply” (1:22), for flesh is like grass but “the word of the Lord stands forever” (1:24–25).
Because believers know the law, they must defend the temple, since the nations fade but the covenant of Sinai stands forever
The law and the temple are not mentioned in 1:22–25; the word of the Lord, not the Sinai covenant, stands forever (1:25).
Because believers have been born again through imperishable seed, they should love deeply, since human life fades but the word of the Lord endures forever
Because believers suffer trials, they should withdraw from society, since the world fades but quiet patience will be rewarded at the end
Peter commands deep love for one another (1:22), not withdrawal; trials were addressed earlier in 1:6.
Because believers are redeemed by silver and gold, they must honor their forefathers’ customs, since tradition endures from age to age
Peter says believers were redeemed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold” and from their forefathers’ empty ways (1:18).
Because angels long to look into salvation, believers should seek visions above all, since the flesh fades but heavenly sights remain forever
Angels long to look into salvation (1:12), but 1:22–25 calls for love grounded in God’s enduring word, not visions.
In 1 Peter 2, what is the first sinful attitude believers are told to rid themselves of?
1 Peter 2:1 begins, “Rid yourselves, therefore, of all malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander,” and malice comes first.
1 Peter 2:1
Doubt
Doubt is not in Peter’s list in 2:1; he names malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander.
Malice
Greed
Greed is not among the five sins listed in 2:1, and it is certainly not the first.
Fear
Fear is not in this list; Peter later tells believers to “fear God” (2:17) as a good thing.
Laziness
Laziness does not appear in 2:1; the verse lists malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander.
In Peter’s teaching to Christians, what are believers to crave like newborn babies?
Peter writes, “Like newborn babies, crave pure spiritual milk, so that by it you may grow up in your salvation” (2:2).
1 Peter 2:2
Hidden manna
Hidden manna is a promise to the overcomer in Revelation 2:17, not what Peter tells believers to crave like infants.
Pure spiritual milk
Wine and oil
Wine and oil are not what newborns crave; Peter’s image is milk, the first food of a baby.
Meat from the altar
Meat from the altar belongs to the priests’ share of sacrifices; Peter’s image for newborns is milk.
Honey from the comb
Honey from the comb is not mentioned here; Peter’s picture of a baby’s craving is pure spiritual milk.
In the opening of 1 Peter 2, believers have “tasted” that the Lord is what?
Peter says believers have “tasted that the Lord is good” (2:3), echoing Psalm 34:8, “Taste and see that the LORD is good.”
1 Peter 2:3
Mighty
Mighty is true of God elsewhere, but 2:3 says believers have tasted that the Lord is good.
Near
Near is not the word in 2:3; the verse says believers have tasted that the Lord is good.
Good
Holy
The Lord is holy in Scripture, but 2:3 names His goodness as what believers have tasted.
Jealous
Jealous is not the word in 2:3; what believers have tasted is that the Lord is good.
In the part of 1 Peter 2 about stones and building, who is called “the living stone”?
1 Peter 2:4 says, “As you come to Him, the living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious in God’s sight,” referring to Jesus Christ (2:5).
1 Peter 2:4
Peter
Peter is not the living stone; he is the writer who calls believers “living stones” (2:5) through Christ.
Moses
Moses is not the living stone; this stone is rejected by men yet chosen and precious to God, which Peter applies to Christ.
David
David is not the living stone here; the stone is the One to whom believers come (2:4), Jesus Christ.
Jesus Christ
John the Baptist
John the Baptist pointed to Jesus (John 1:29) but is not the living stone of 1 Peter 2:4.
In 1 Peter 2, believers are like living stones being built into what?
Peter says believers “are being built into a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood” (2:5).
1 Peter 2:5
A royal palace
A royal palace is not the image; 2:5 says a spiritual house, with “royal” appearing later in “royal priesthood” (2:9).
A spiritual house
An earthly temple
Peter calls it a spiritual house, not an earthly temple; the sacrifices are “spiritual sacrifices” (2:5).
A fortified city
A fortified city is not Peter’s picture; the living stones are built into a spiritual house.
A vineyard wall
A vineyard wall is not mentioned; the stones in 2:5 form a spiritual house and a holy priesthood.
According to 1 Peter 2, believers are being formed into what kind of priesthood?
1 Peter 2:5 says believers are built into “a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.”
1 Peter 2:5
Levitical priesthood
Levitical priests came from Levi’s tribe, but Peter calls believers a holy priesthood.
Earthly priesthood
“Earthly” is not Peter’s word; he stresses spiritual sacrifices, and the priesthood is called holy.
Holy priesthood
Temporary priesthood
Temporary is never used; the priesthood is called holy and, in 2:9, royal.
Prophetic priesthood
A prophetic priesthood is not named in the chapter; Peter says holy priesthood (2:5) and royal priesthood (2:9).
In the Scripture quotation used in 1 Peter 2, where does God lay the chosen and precious cornerstone?
Peter quotes Scripture: “See, I lay in Zion a stone, a chosen and precious cornerstone” (2:6), drawing on Isaiah 28:16.
1 Peter 2:6
Jerusalem
Jerusalem is where Zion lay, but the quotation in 2:6 names Zion as the place the stone is laid.
Bethel
Bethel is where Jacob met God (Genesis 28:19), not where the cornerstone is laid in 2:6.
Zion
Hebron
Hebron is associated with the patriarchs, but the stone in 2:6 is laid in Zion.
Samaria
Samaria was the capital of the northern kingdom; the quotation in 2:6 speaks of Zion.
In Peter’s citation about the cornerstone, who will never be put to shame?
The quotation ends, “the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame” (2:6).
1 Peter 2:6
The one who suffers in silence
Suffering in silence is praised elsewhere in the chapter (2:19–20), but the promise of no shame is for the one who believes in Him.
The one who gives alms
Giving alms is not mentioned in 2:6; the promise is tied to belief in the cornerstone.
The one who believes in Him
The one who keeps the Law
Keeping the Law is not the condition in 2:6; the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame.
The one who fasts often
Fasting is not mentioned in the chapter; the promise in 2:6 belongs to the one who believes.
In 1 Peter 2, what has the stone rejected by the builders become?
Peter quotes “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (2:7), from Psalm 118:22.
1 Peter 2:7
A millstone
A millstone is a grinding stone, not the image here; the rejected stone became the cornerstone.
A capstone of bronze
A bronze capstone is not in the verse; the rejected stone “has become the cornerstone.”
A stumbling wall
“Stumbling” is what the stone is to unbelievers (2:8), but the rejected stone itself became the cornerstone.
The cornerstone
A broken idol
A broken idol is not part of the image; the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone (2:7).
For those who do not believe, what is Christ called in 1 Peter 2?
For those who do not believe, Peter says, “A stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” (2:8), echoing Isaiah 8:14.
1 Peter 2:8
A hidden treasure and pearl
Hidden treasure and pearl are Jesus’ images of the kingdom (Matthew 13), not what Peter calls Christ for unbelievers.
A stone of stumbling and a rock of offense
A consuming fire and sword
A consuming fire is said of God elsewhere, but 2:8 calls the stone a stumbling stone and rock of offense.
A lamp and a banner
A lamp and banner are not Peter’s words here; for unbelievers the stone is one of stumbling and offense.
A gate and a ladder
A gate and ladder come from other passages (Genesis 28:12; John 10:9), not from 2:8.
In 1 Peter 2:9, believers are first described as what?
1 Peter 2:9 begins, “But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession.”
1 Peter 2:9
A chosen people
A remnant only
A remnant only is not Peter’s description; he calls them a chosen people.
A wandering tribe
A wandering tribe is not the phrase; Peter calls them foreigners and exiles in 2:11, but in 2:9 a chosen people.
A house of prophets
A house of prophets is not in 2:9; the first description is a chosen people.
A nation of judges
A nation of judges is not in the verse; the nation is called holy, and the first title is a chosen people.
In 1 Peter 2, believers are also called what kind of nation?
1 Peter 2:9 calls believers “a holy nation,” recalling Exodus 19:6, “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.”
1 Peter 2:9
A divided nation
Divided is not the word; Peter calls believers a holy nation.
A restored nation
Restored is not used in 2:9; the nation is called holy.
A holy nation
A desert nation
Desert nation is not in the text; Peter says a holy nation.
A hidden nation
Hidden nation is not in the text; believers are to proclaim God’s virtues publicly (2:9), and the nation is holy.
In 1 Peter 2:9, believers are a people for whose possession?
Believers are “a people for God’s own possession” (2:9), as Israel was His prized possession in Deuteronomy 7:6.
1 Peter 2:9
The apostles’ possession
Believers belong to God, not to the apostles; 2:9 says “a people for God’s own possession.”
Israel’s possession
Israel’s possession is not the phrase; Peter says God’s own possession.
God’s own possession
The temple’s possession
The temple does not own the people; 2:9 says God’s own possession.
The king’s possession
The king is to be honored (2:17), but he does not own God’s people; they are God’s own possession.
According to 1 Peter 2, God called believers out of darkness into what?
God “called you out of darkness into His marvelous light” (2:9).
1 Peter 2:9
A fiery furnace
A fiery furnace is not the destination; Peter says God called them into His marvelous light.
His marvelous light
The courts of Zion
The courts of Zion are not named; the verse says His marvelous light.
A hidden chamber
A hidden chamber is the opposite of the image; God calls believers into marvelous light.
A cloud by day

2 Peter 1:3
Only wisdom for leaders
The provision is for “us” all, not only for leaders, and covers everything needed for life and godliness (1:3).
Everything we need for life and godliness
A temporary kingdom
Peter speaks of “the eternal kingdom” (1:11), not a temporary one.
Freedom from all suffering
Freedom from suffering is not promised; His power gives what is needed for life and godliness (1:3).
Secret knowledge for a few
The knowledge is “of Him who called us,” shared by all believers, not secret (1:3).
According to 2 Peter 1:3, the One who called us did so by what two qualities?
God “called us by His own glory and excellence” (1:3).
2 Peter 1:3
Wrath and fire
Wrath and fire are not mentioned; Peter says God called us by His glory and excellence (1:3).
Justice and law
Justice and law are not Peter’s words; the call is “by His own glory and excellence” (1:3).
Mercy and peace
“Mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you” is Jude’s greeting (Jude 1:2); 1:3 names glory and excellence.
His own glory and excellence
Wisdom and age
Wisdom and age are not mentioned; God called us “by His own glory and excellence” (1:3).
In the chapter where Peter speaks of sharing in the divine nature, what has God given?
“He has given us His precious and magnificent promises” (1:4).
2 Peter 1:4
Tablets of stone
God gave Moses tablets of stone on Sinai (Exodus 31:18); 2 Peter 1:4 speaks of precious and magnificent promises.
Precious and magnificent promises
The ark of the covenant
The priests carried “the ark of the covenant” across the Jordan (Joshua 3:17); it is not what 1:4 says God gave.
Manna for the wilderness
Israel ate manna forty years in the wilderness (Exodus 16:35); Peter speaks of promises.
An earthly throne
No earthly throne is given; believers look to “the eternal kingdom” (1:11).
According to 2 Peter 1:4, what can believers become through God’s promises?
Through the promises “you may become partakers of the divine nature” (1:4).
2 Peter 1:4
Rulers of nations now
Christ promises “authority over the nations” to the overcomer (Revelation 2:26), not in 2 Peter 1:4.
Authors of Scripture
Peter says prophets “spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (1:21); believers do not become authors of Scripture.
Partakers of the divine nature
Sinless judges on earth
The promise is a share in the divine nature, not sinless judgeship on earth (1:4).
Priests in Jerusalem
Believers share in the divine nature, not an earthly priesthood in Jerusalem (1:4).
In 2 Peter chapter 1, believers have escaped what?
Believers “have escaped the corruption in the world caused by evil desires” (1:4).
2 Peter 1:4
The waters of the Red Sea at the exodus
Israel crossed the sea “on dry ground” at the exodus (Exodus 14:22); Peter speaks of escaping the world’s corruption.
The long Babylonian exile of their fathers
The exile to Babylon (2 Kings 25:11) is not in view; believers escaped corruption caused by evil desires (1:4).
The corruption in the world caused by evil desires
The heavy taxes imposed by Roman rulers
Jesus said, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s” (Matthew 22:21); Peter speaks of escaping moral corruption, not taxes.
The great famine that struck all Judea
Agabus foretold “a great famine” (Acts 11:28), and relief went to Judea (Acts 11:29); Peter speaks of escaping corruption.
In the spiritual growth list of 2 Peter 1, what are believers told to add to their faith first?
“Make every effort to add to your faith virtue” (1:5).
2 Peter 1:5
Hope
Hope is not in Peter’s list; faith, hope, and love appear together in 1 Corinthians 13:13.
Virtue
Patience
Patience is part of the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22); Peter adds virtue first.
Joy
Joy is in the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22), not in Peter’s chain.
Zeal
Zeal is not in Peter’s list; the first addition to faith is virtue (1:5).
In 2 Peter chapter 1, what should be added to virtue?
“And to virtue, knowledge” (1:5).
2 Peter 1:5
Love
Love comes last, added to brotherly kindness (1:7).
Peace
Peace is not in Peter’s list; it is part of the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22).
Knowledge
Humility
Humility is not in this list; virtue is followed by knowledge (1:5).
Boldness
Boldness is not in Peter’s list; virtue is followed by knowledge (1:5).
In Peter’s sequence of godly qualities in 2 Peter 1, what comes after knowledge?
“And to knowledge, self-control” (1:6).
2 Peter 1:6
Self-control
Brotherly kindness
Brotherly kindness comes later, added to godliness (1:7).
Hope
Hope is not in Peter’s chain; Paul says perseverance produces “character; and character, hope” (Romans 5:4).
Wisdom
Wisdom is not in the list; knowledge is followed by self-control (1:6).
Meekness
Meekness is not in Peter’s list; after knowledge comes self-control (1:6).
In 2 Peter 1, what quality follows perseverance?
“And to perseverance, godliness” (1:6).
2 Peter 1:6
Love
Love closes the list, added to brotherly kindness (1:7).
Godliness
Joy
Joy is part of the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22), not Peter’s chain.
Courage
Courage is not in the list; perseverance is followed by godliness (1:6).
Hospitality
Hospitality is not in Peter’s list; perseverance is followed by godliness (1:6).
In Peter’s virtue list in chapter 1, what is added to godliness?
“And to godliness, brotherly kindness” (1:7).
2 Peter 1:7
Wisdom
Wisdom is not in Peter’s list; godliness is followed by brotherly kindness (1:7).
Gentleness
Gentleness is in the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:23), not Peter’s chain.
Brotherly kindness
Prophecy
Peter speaks of prophecy at the chapter’s end (1:19–21), but it is not in the list of qualities.
Faithfulness
Faithfulness is in the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22); Peter adds brotherly kindness to godliness.
In the final step of the virtue chain in 2 Peter 1, what is added to brotherly kindness?
“And to brotherly kindness, love” (1:7), the final step in Peter’s chain.
2 Peter 1:7
Courage
Courage is not in the list; love is added to brotherly kindness (1:7).
Obedience
Obedience is not one of the eight qualities; love completes the list (1:7).
Hope
Hope is not in Peter’s chain; love completes it (1:7).
Love
Discernment
Discernment is not in the list; brotherly kindness is followed by love (1:7).
According to 2 Peter 1:8, if these qualities are yours and continue to grow, what will they keep you from being?
These qualities “will keep you from being ineffective and unproductive in your knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1:8).
2 Peter 1:8
Afflicted and poor in your daily walk among the nations of the world
Poverty and affliction are not mentioned in 1:8; growing in these qualities keeps knowledge of Christ from being unproductive.
Ineffective and unproductive in your knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ
Criticized and slandered by the false teachers who secretly creep in
Peter warns of “false teachers among you” in 2 Peter 2:1, but 1:8 is about being productive in knowing Christ.
Troubled and shaken by every storm that rises on the Sea of Galilee
Jesus calmed the winds and the sea (Matthew 8:26); Peter’s concern in 1:8 is being effective and productive.
Unknown and unnoticed among the churches of our Lord Jesus Christ
Recognition among churches is not Peter’s concern; he warns against being ineffective and unproductive (1:8).
In 2 Peter chapter 1, how does Peter describe the person who lacks these qualities?
Whoever lacks these traits “is nearsighted to the point of blindness” (1:9).
2 Peter 1:9
Deaf and mute
Jesus made “the deaf hear and the mute speak” (Mark 7:37); Peter describes spiritual nearsightedness.
Nearsighted and blind
Hard-hearted and stubborn
Hebrews warns, “do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:8); Peter calls the one lacking these traits nearsighted.
Weak and trembling
Weakness and trembling are not Peter’s terms; he says “nearsighted to the point of blindness” (1:9).
Double-minded and unstable
James calls the doubter “a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways” (James 1:8), not Peter here.
According to 2 Peter 1:9, what has the spiritually blind person forgotten?
He has forgotten “that he has been cleansed from his past sins” (1:9).
2 Peter 1:9
The covenant the LORD made at Mount Sinai
The LORD met Moses on Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:20), but Peter says the blind person forgot his cleansing from sin.
That he has been cleansed from his past sins
The crossing of the Jordan under Joshua
Israel crossed the Jordan on dry ground (Joshua 3:17); 1:9 speaks of forgetting cleansing from past sins.
The words spoken by the prophet Isaiah
Isaiah is not named in 2 Peter 1; what is forgotten is cleansing from past sins (1:9).
The fall of the walls of Jericho in Canaan
Jericho’s wall collapsed at Israel’s shout (Joshua 6:20); Peter speaks of forgetting one’s cleansing.
In 2 Peter chapter 1, what does Peter urge the brothers to make sure?
“Brothers, strive to make your calling and election sure” (1:10).
2 Peter 1:10
Their ancestry and tribe
Paul once listed his descent “of the tribe of Benjamin” (Philippians 3:5), but Peter urges a sure calling and election.
Their wisdom and speech
Wisdom and speech are not mentioned; Peter urges them to confirm their calling and election (1:10).
Their calling and election
Their place in Jerusalem
Jerusalem is not mentioned in 2 Peter 1; the goal is a sure calling and election (1:10).
Their daily offerings
Priests offered the same sacrifices “Day after day” (Hebrews 10:11); Peter urges a sure calling and election.
In the exhortation of 2 Peter 1:10, what will happen if believers practice these things?
“For if you practice these things you will never stumble” (1:10).
2 Peter 1:10
They will never suffer
Peter does not promise freedom from suffering; he promises “you will never stumble” (1:10).
They will never stumble
They will never be opposed
Opposition is not ruled out; the promise is “you will never stumble” (1:10).
They will never die
Peter himself expects to die soon (1:14); the promise is that they will never stumble.
They will never need correction
Peter keeps reminding them (1:12), so correction is not ruled out; the promise is not stumbling.
In 2 Peter 1:11, what kind of welcome does Peter say faithful believers will receive?
Believers “will receive a lavish reception into the eternal kingdom” (1:11).
2 Peter 1:11
A fearful reception
The tone is not fearful; Peter promises “a lavish reception” (1:11).
A secret reception
Nothing secret is mentioned; the reception into the eternal kingdom is lavish (1:11).
A lavish reception
A delayed reception
Peter mentions no delay; the welcome is lavish (1:11).
A doubtful reception
The welcome is not in doubt; Peter says “you will receive a lavish reception” (1:11).
In 2 Peter 1:11, into what kingdom does Peter say believers will receive a lavish reception?
The reception is “into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (1:11).
2 Peter 1:11
The kingdom of David in Jerusalem
God promised David, “your throne will be established forever” (2 Samuel 7:16), but Peter speaks of Christ’s eternal kingdom.
The eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ
The kingdom of heaven on earth immediately
Peter does not say the kingdom comes on earth immediately; he calls it “the eternal kingdom” (1:11).
The house of Levi
The house of Levi was Israel’s priestly tribe; Peter speaks of Christ’s eternal kingdom (1:11).
The throne of Caesar
Caesar’s throne is not mentioned; the kingdom is Christ’s eternal kingdom (1:11).
In the reminder section of 2 Peter chapter 1, what does Peter say he will always do?
“Therefore I will always remind you of these things” (1:12).
2 Peter 1:12
Send another apostle
Peter does not mention sending another apostle; he will remind them himself (1:12).
Remind them of these things
Appoint deacons in every city
The apostles had seven men chosen to serve in Jerusalem (Acts 6:3), but Peter promises to remind his readers.
Collect an offering
Paul organized “the collection for the saints” (1 Corinthians 16:1); Peter promises reminders.
Visit them each year
Peter expects to die soon (1:14), so he promises lasting reminders, not yearly visits.
According to 2 Peter 1:12, in what are Peter’s readers already established?
Peter’s readers “know them and are established in the truth you now have” (1:12).
2 Peter 1:12
The truth they now have
The Levitical priesthood
Hebrews contrasts the Levitical priesthood with Christ (Hebrews 7:11); Peter says they are established in the truth.
The traditions of the elders
“The tradition of the elders” was held by the Pharisees (Mark 7:3), not commended by Peter.
The wisdom of Egypt
Moses “was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians” (Acts 7:22); Peter’s readers are established in the truth.
The customs of Rome
Roman customs are not mentioned; the readers are established in the truth (1:12).
In 2 Peter chapter 1, what expression does Peter use for his present bodily life?
Peter speaks of refreshing their memory “as long as I live in the tent of my body” (1:13).
2 Peter 1:13
The house of clay
Eliphaz speaks of “those who dwell in houses of clay” (Job 4:19); Peter uses the image of a tent.
The veil of flesh
Hebrews speaks of “the curtain of His body” (Hebrews 10:20), but Peter calls his own body a tent.
The tent of my body
The prison of earth
Prison of earth is not Peter’s phrase; he says “the tent of my body” (1:13).
The garment of sorrow
Garment of sorrow is not Peter’s phrase; he calls his body a tent (1:13).
In 2 Peter 1:14, what does Peter say will soon happen to this “tent”?
“I know that this tent will soon be laid aside” (1:14), meaning Peter’s coming death.
2 Peter 1:14
It will be transformed before kings
Peter does not speak of transformation before kings; his tent “will soon be laid aside” (1:14).
It will soon be laid aside
It will be hidden in the wilderness
Peter does not speak of hiding; his body will soon be laid aside in death (1:14).
It will be rebuilt in glory
Paul speaks of “a building from God” replacing the earthly tent (2 Corinthians 5:1), but Peter says his tent will be laid aside.
It will be taken to heaven alive
Elijah “went up into heaven in a whirlwind” (2 Kings 2:11); Peter expects to die.
According to 2 Peter 1:14, who had made clear to Peter that the tent of his body would soon be laid aside?
Peter says it was “as our Lord Jesus Christ has made clear to me” (1:14); Jesus foretold Peter’s death in John 21:18–19.
2 Peter 1:14
Elijah
Elijah is not mentioned; Jesus made Peter’s death clear to him (1:14).
An angel
An angel freed Peter from prison (Acts 12:7), but it was Jesus who revealed his coming death.
Our Lord Jesus Christ
John Mark
John Mark is not mentioned in 2 Peter; Peter credits “our Lord Jesus Christ” (1:14).
The high priest
The high priest is not mentioned; Peter credits “our Lord Jesus Christ” (1:14).
In 2 Peter 1:15, after Peter’s departure, what did he want his readers to be able to do at all times?
“After my departure, you will be able to recall these things at all times” (1:15).
2 Peter 1:15
Sing psalms in Hebrew
Peter does not mention singing; he wants them to recall these things (1:15).
Recall these things
Rebuild his house
No house is mentioned; Peter wants lasting remembrance of his teaching (1:15).
Find his writings in Rome
Rome is not named in 2 Peter; Peter wants his readers to recall these things (1:15).
Identify every false prophet by name
Peter warns of false prophets and teachers in 2 Peter 2:1, but in 1:15 he wants them to recall his teaching.
In defending his message in 2 Peter chapter 1, what does Peter say the apostles did not follow?
“We did not follow cleverly devised fables” (1:16).
2 Peter 1:16
Roman myths
Paul warns against “irreverent, silly myths” (1 Timothy 4:7); Peter’s phrase is “cleverly devised fables.”
Cleverly devised fables
Temple rituals
Temple rituals are not mentioned; Peter denies following cleverly devised fables (1:16).
Visions of sleep
Peter does not mention visions in sleep; he says the apostles were eyewitnesses (1:16).
Ancestral legends only
Paul warns against “Jewish myths” (Titus 1:14); Peter denies following cleverly devised fables.
In 2 Peter 1:16, what had Peter and the others made known to believers?
“We made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1:16).
2 Peter 1:16
The location of the lost tribes
The lost tribes are not mentioned; the apostles proclaimed Christ’s power and coming (1:16).
The power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ
The date of the final judgment
Jesus said, “No one knows about that day or hour” (Mark 13:32); Peter proclaimed His power and coming, not a date.
The order of angels
The order of angels is not mentioned; Peter proclaimed Christ’s power and coming (1:16).
The secrets of the temple veil
The temple veil was torn at Jesus’ death (Matthew 27:51); Peter speaks of Christ’s power and coming.
Instead of following myths, what does Peter say he and the others were in relation to Jesus in 2 Peter 1?
“But we were eyewitnesses of His majesty” (1:16).
2 Peter 1:16
Interpreters of dreams
Joseph interpreted dreams in Egypt (Genesis 40:8); Peter claims to be an eyewitness.
Eyewitnesses of His majesty
Guardians of the ark
The priests carried the ark of the covenant (Joshua 3:17); Peter calls himself an eyewitness of Christ’s majesty.
Disciples of John the Baptist
Andrew heard John the Baptist’s testimony before following Jesus (John 1:40), but Peter calls the apostles eyewitnesses of Christ’s majesty.
Scribes of the law
Scribes of the law are not mentioned; Peter says “we were eyewitnesses of His majesty” (1:16).
In Peter’s account of Jesus on the mountain in 2 Peter 1, from whom did Jesus receive honor and glory?
“He received honor and glory from God the Father” (1:17).
2 Peter 1:17
The crowds of Galilee
Crowds in Galilee followed Jesus, but on the mountain the honor came from God the Father (1:17).
Moses and Elijah
Moses and Elijah appeared at the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:3), but honor and glory came from the Father.
God the Father
The cherubim
Cherubim are not mentioned; the Father gave Jesus honor and glory (1:17).
The Roman governor
No Roman governor is present; the honor came from God the Father (1:17).
In 2 Peter 1:17, from what source did the voice come to Jesus?
“The voice came to Him from the Majestic Glory” (1:17).
2 Peter 1:17
The temple sanctuary
The temple sanctuary is not mentioned; the voice came from the Majestic Glory (1:17).
The burning bush
God called to Moses “from within the bush” (Exodus 3:4), a different event.
The Majestic Glory
The Jordan River
At Jesus’ baptism in the Jordan “a voice from heaven” spoke (Matthew 3:17); Peter recalls the mountain and the Majestic Glory.
The cloud over the tabernacle only
The cloud covered the tabernacle in Exodus 40:34; Matthew mentions “a bright cloud” at the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:5), but Peter says “the Majestic Glory.”
In 2 Peter chapter 1, what words did the heavenly voice speak about Jesus?
The voice said, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (1:17).
2 Peter 1:17
“This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”
“Listen to Him, for He will reveal all mysteries”
“Listen to Him!” follows these words in Matthew 17:5, but Peter does not quote it, and “reveal all mysteries” is in neither.
“Behold the Lamb of God”
John the Baptist said, “Look, the Lamb of God” (John 1:29), not the voice on the mountain.
“You are My servant Israel”
“You are My Servant, Israel” is spoken in Isaiah 49:3, not at the Transfiguration.
“Rise, take up your cross”
Jesus said one must “take up his cross and follow Me” (Matthew 16:24); it is not what the voice said.
According to Peter’s eyewitness testimony in 2 Peter 1, from where did he and the others hear the voice declaring Jesus to be the beloved Son?
“We ourselves heard this voice from heaven” (1:18).
2 Peter 1:18
From the sea
The voice did not come from the sea; Peter says it came “from heaven” (1:18).
From heaven
From the crowd
A crowd once thought a voice from heaven was thunder (John 12:29), but here Peter says the voice came from heaven.
From the temple
The temple is not mentioned; the voice came from heaven (1:18).
From a cave
Elijah heard the LORD while in a cave (1 Kings 19:9); Peter heard this voice from heaven.
In 2 Peter 1:18, where were Peter and the others when they heard the heavenly voice?
“We were with Him on the holy mountain” (1:18).
2 Peter 1:18
In the upper room
The disciples gathered in the upper room after the ascension (Acts 1:13); Peter speaks of the holy mountain.
At Bethany
Lazarus lived in Bethany (John 11:1), but this voice was heard on the holy mountain.
With Him on the holy mountain
In Nazareth
Nazareth was where Jesus was brought up (Luke 4:16); Peter places this event on the holy mountain.
In the wilderness beyond the Jordan
Jesus stayed across the Jordan where John had baptized (John 10:40); the voice was heard on the mountain.
In 2 Peter 1:19, after recalling the mountain event, what does Peter say believers also have?
“We also have the word of the prophets as confirmed beyond doubt” (1:19).
2 Peter 1:19
The lost books of the ancient prophets of Israel
Peter speaks of the prophetic word they already have, not of lost books (1:19).
The word of the prophets as confirmed beyond doubt
The power to work signs and wonders among them
“The apostles performed many wonders and signs” (Acts 2:43), but 1:19 points to the confirmed prophetic word.
The priesthood of Aaron restored in Jerusalem
Hebrews contrasts Christ with “the order of Aaron” (Hebrews 7:11); Peter speaks of the word of the prophets.
The voice from Sinai spoken to them once again
The LORD descended on Sinai (Exodus 19:20); Peter says believers have the prophetic word confirmed beyond doubt.
In 2 Peter chapter 1, Peter says believers do well to pay attention to the prophetic word as to what?
Pay attention to it “as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (1:19).
2 Peter 1:19
A trumpet in battle
Trumpets sounded at Jericho (Joshua 6:20); Peter compares prophecy to a lamp.
A lamp shining in a dark place
Rain on dry ground
Rain on dry ground is not Peter’s image; he speaks of a lamp in a dark place (1:19).
A crown on a king
A crown on a king is not mentioned; prophecy is like a lamp shining in darkness (1:19).
A star over Bethlehem
The star went ahead of the Magi to the Child (Matthew 2:9); Peter speaks of a lamp, and then of the morning star rising in hearts.
In Peter’s imagery in 2 Peter 1:19, what is to rise in believers’ hearts?
“Until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (1:19).
2 Peter 1:19
The sun of noon
Malachi speaks of “the sun of righteousness” rising (Malachi 4:2); Peter speaks of the morning star.
The river of life
“A river of the water of life” appears in Revelation 22:1; Peter speaks of the morning star.
The morning star
The branch of David
Jeremiah foretold “a righteous Branch” for David (Jeremiah 23:5); Peter speaks of the morning star.
The eastern wind
The LORD drove back the sea “with a strong east wind” (Exodus 14:21); Peter speaks of the morning star rising in hearts.
In the closing teaching of 2 Peter chapter 1, what must believers understand about prophecy of Scripture?
“Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture comes from one’s own interpretation” (1:20).
2 Peter 1:20
Every prophecy comes from the private dreams of the prophets
Prophets “spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (1:21), not from private dreams.
No prophecy of Scripture comes from one’s own interpretation
Prophecy of Scripture belongs only to kings and their courts
Peter applies prophecy to all his readers, who “will do well to pay attention to it” (1:19).
Prophecy of Scripture has no value at all for the present age
Believers “will do well to pay attention to it” as a lamp in darkness (1:19), so it has present value.
Prophecy of Scripture must be kept hidden from the church
Peter urges readers to heed prophecy (1:19), not to hide it from the church.
According to 2 Peter 1:21, prophecy was never brought about through what?
“No such prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man” (1:21); “human initiative” restates this.
2 Peter 1:21
Human initiative
Angelic rebellion
Jude speaks of angels who “abandoned their proper dwelling” (Jude 1:6), but 2 Peter 1:21 does not mention angels.
Temple music
Temple music is not mentioned; prophecy did not come “by the will of man” (1:21).
Royal sponsorship
Royal sponsorship is not mentioned; prophecy came from God through the Holy Spirit (1:21).
Public debate
Public debate is not mentioned; prophets “spoke from God” (1:21).
In the final verse of 2 Peter 1, how did men speak from God?
“Men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (1:21).
2 Peter 1:21
As they mastered rhetoric
Skill in rhetoric is not the source; men spoke from God as the Spirit carried them (1:21).
As they were carried along by the Holy Spirit
As they copied sacred archives
Copying archives is not mentioned; prophecy did not come “by the will of man” (1:21).
As they followed signs in the heavens
Signs in the heavens are not mentioned; they were “carried along by the Holy Spirit” (1:21).
As they passed family traditions down
Family tradition is not the source; Peter says prophecy came from God through the Spirit (1:21).
In the promise section of 2 Peter 1, which pair of words describes what God has given?
God has given “His precious and magnificent promises” (1:4).
2 Peter 1:4
Ancient and hidden
Ancient and hidden are not Peter’s words; he calls the promises “precious and magnificent” (1:4).
Holy and fearful
Holy and fearful are not the adjectives in 1:4; the promises are precious and magnificent.
Precious and magnificent
Stern and unbreakable
Stern and unbreakable do not appear; the promises are precious and magnificent (1:4).
Mysterious and secret
Mysterious and secret are not Peter’s words; the promises are precious and magnificent (1:4).
In 2 Peter chapter 1, what does Peter identify as the cause of the world’s corruption?
The world’s corruption is “caused by evil desires” (1:4).
2 Peter 1:4
False teaching alone
Peter warns of false teachers in 2 Peter 2:1, but in 1:4 corruption is caused by evil desires.
Evil desires
Foreign conquest
Foreign conquest is not mentioned; corruption comes from evil desires (1:4).
Lack of wisdom
Lack of wisdom is not the cause named; it is evil desires (1:4).
Neglect of ritual
Neglect of ritual is not mentioned; Peter says the corruption is “caused by evil desires” (1:4).
In the verse about growing virtues in 2 Peter 1, which two negative results are specifically avoided?
These qualities “will keep you from being ineffective and unproductive” (1:8).
2 Peter 1:8
Sorrow and fear
Sorrow and fear are not the pair in 1:8; Peter says ineffective and unproductive.
Weakness and sickness
Weakness and sickness are not mentioned; the pair is ineffective and unproductive (1:8).
Ineffective and unproductive
Exile and famine
Exile and famine are not mentioned; growth keeps knowledge from being ineffective and unproductive (1:8).
Shame and reproach
Shame and reproach are not the pair; Peter names ineffective and unproductive (1:8).
In the very first verse of 2 Peter chapter 1, which full title does Peter use for Jesus Christ?
Peter speaks of “the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ” (1:1).
2 Peter 1:1
The Son of Man and Judge of Israel
“Son of Man” is Jesus’ usual title for Himself in the Gospels, but Peter’s opening says “our God and Savior.”
Our God and Savior Jesus Christ
The Holy One and True Witness
Revelation 3:7 calls Him “the One who is holy and true,” not 2 Peter 1:1.
The Alpha and the Omega only
“I am the Alpha and the Omega” is spoken in Revelation 22:13.
The King of kings from Zion
“KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS” is written on His robe in Revelation 19:16.
When Peter says in 2 Peter 1 that he wants believers to remember his teaching after his “departure,” what is he referring to?
Peter means his death: “this tent will soon be laid aside” (1:14), and he wants them to remember “after my departure” (1:15).
His move from Jerusalem to Antioch
Paul opposed Peter “When Cephas came to Antioch” (Galatians 2:11), but here “departure” means Peter’s death (1:14–15).
His release from prison
An angel released Peter from prison (Acts 12:7), but 1:14–15 speaks of laying aside his bodily tent.
His death, the laying aside of his bodily tent
His separation from the other apostles
Peter is not speaking of leaving the other apostles; his departure is laying aside his tent (1:14–15).
