A natural birthright is not mentioned; the danger is falling from secure standing.
Instead of falling, believers are commanded to grow in what?
Peter commands, “grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (3:18).
2 Peter 3:18
Miracles and signs
Miracles and signs are not the growth Peter commands; he says grace and knowledge.
Grace and knowledge
Rank and influence
Rank and influence are not what Peter wants; he says to grow in grace and knowledge.
Fasting and silence
Fasting and silence are not mentioned; Peter says grace and knowledge.
Silver and gold
Silver and gold are not what Peter commands believers to grow in; he says grace and knowledge.
In 2 Peter 3:18, whose grace and knowledge are believers to grow in?
Peter says to “grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (3:18).
2 Peter 3:18
Moses the servant of God
Moses is not the one in whose grace and knowledge believers grow; Peter names Jesus Christ.
Abraham our father
Abraham is not named in this chapter; Peter names Jesus Christ.
Elijah the prophet
Elijah is not named in this chapter; Peter names Jesus Christ.
Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ
The holy apostles collectively
The apostles are mentioned in 3:2, but the growth Peter commands is in the grace and knowledge of Jesus Christ.
To whom does Peter ascribe glory both now and to the day of eternity?
Peter ends, “To Him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen” (3:18), after naming “our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.”
2 Peter 3:18
God the Father only without naming the Son
Peter’s doxology follows his mention of Jesus Christ, not a statement about God the Father alone.
The church
The church is not the object of the doxology; the glory goes to Jesus Christ.
Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ
Peter and Paul together
Peter and Paul are not given glory; it is given to the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
The heavenly angels
Angels are not mentioned in 3:18; the glory goes to Jesus Christ.
In the opening of chapter 3, Peter says his readers should remember two sources of truth. Which pair is correct?
Peter writes of “what was foretold by the holy prophets and commanded by our Lord and Savior through your apostles” (3:2).
2 Peter 3:2
Kings and judges
Kings and judges are not named; Peter names the holy prophets and the apostles.
Dreams and omens
Dreams and omens are not mentioned; the sources are the holy prophets and your apostles.
Holy prophets and your apostles
Priests and Levites
Priests and Levites are not named in 3:2; the sources are the prophets and apostles.
Scribes and Pharisees
Scribes and Pharisees are not named; Peter names the holy prophets and your apostles.
Which question do the scoffers ask in 2 Peter 3:4 to show they doubt Christ’s return?
The scoffers ask, “Where is the promise of His coming?” (3:4).
2 Peter 3:4
Why was the temple destroyed?
Nothing in the scoffers’ words mentions the temple being destroyed.
Where is the promise of His coming?
Who will roll away the stone from the entrance of the tomb?
“Who will roll away the stone from the entrance of the tomb?” is the women’s question in Mark 16:3, not the scoffers’.
How long, O Lord?
“How long, O Lord?” is the prophet’s plea in Isaiah 6:11; it is not the scoffers’ question.
Can these bones come to life?
“Can these bones come to life?” is God’s question to Ezekiel (Ezekiel 37:3), not the scoffers’.
In Peter's argument against the scoffers, what past event proves the world has not always continued unchanged?
Peter says the world of that time “perished in the flood” (3:6), so history has not always continued unchanged.
2 Peter 3:6
The crossing of the sea during the exodus
The crossing of the sea (Exodus 14:21) was a rescue and did not perish the world; Peter cites the flood.
The collapse of Jericho’s walls before Israel
Jericho’s fall (Joshua 6:20) was a local event, not a world-ending judgment like the flood.
The flood that destroyed the ancient world
The fire from heaven on Mount Carmel
Fire fell on Carmel in 1 Kings 18:38, but Peter points to the flood that destroyed the ancient world.
The deportation of Judah to Babylon
The exile to Babylon was a judgment on Judah, not the world of that time that perished in the flood.
According to 2 Peter 3:5-7, what brought the heavens and earth into being and also reserves the present world for judgment?
Peter says “by God’s word the heavens existed” (3:5) and “by that same word, the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire” (3:7).
2 Peter 3:5-7
The covenant with Abraham
The covenant with Abraham is not mentioned in 3:5–7; Peter credits God’s word.
God's word
Angelic armies
Angelic armies are not mentioned in this passage; the cause is God’s word.
Human obedience
Human obedience is not what creates or reserves the world; Peter points to God’s word.
The stars
The stars are part of what God made (Psalm 33:6) and are not the agent; Peter credits God’s word.
In 2 Peter 3, what one perspective on time is meant to keep believers from misreading God's delay?
Peter says, “With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day” (3:8), so God’s apparent delay is not slowness.
2 Peter 3:8
Every year of delay counts as only one day to God
This distorts Peter’s comparison; he says a day is like a thousand years and a thousand years like a day.
A day with the Lord is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like a day
Time stopped passing for the world after Christ rose
Peter says nothing about time stopping after Christ rose; his point is that the Lord measures time differently.
Only the angels in heaven are allowed to know the times
Peter does not say that only the angels know the times; he explains God’s timing with the day-and-thousand-years comparison.
History repeats itself exactly in every generation of men
Peter does not say history repeats itself; the scoffers claim that things continue unchanged (3:4).
Why does Peter say the Lord has not yet brought the final day, despite His promise?
Peter says the Lord “is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance” (3:9).
2 Peter 3:9
He lacks power
Peter says the Lord is not slow in keeping His promise; the delay is not weakness.
He is waiting for a temple
A temple is not mentioned as a reason; the reason is patience wanting repentance.
He is patient, wanting repentance
He forgot the promise
Peter denies the Lord is slow (3:9); the Lord has not forgotten the promise.
He changed the covenant
Changing the covenant is not offered as the reason; Peter points to God’s patience.
Which expression does Peter use when speaking of the sudden final arrival in verse 10, rather than the expression in verse 12?
Verse 10 says “the Day of the Lord will come like a thief,” while verse 12 speaks of “the day of God.”
2 Peter 3:10
The great tribulation
The great tribulation is a phrase from other passages (Matthew 24:21) and is not used in 2 Peter 3.
The day of the Lord
The seventh trumpet
The seventh trumpet is from Revelation 11:15, not 2 Peter 3.
The year of Jubilee
The year of Jubilee is from Leviticus 25 and has no place in Peter’s description.
The kingdom of heaven
“The kingdom of heaven” is a phrase from Matthew’s Gospel, not used in 2 Peter 3.
Which expression does Peter use in the verse that tells believers to anticipate and hasten the coming final day?
Verse 12 says believers “anticipate and hasten the coming of the day of God.”
2 Peter 3:12
The day of Pentecost
Pentecost is not mentioned in this chapter; verse 12 says the day of God.
The day of the Lord
“The Day of the Lord” is the phrase in verse 10; verse 12 speaks of the day of God.
The day of God
The day of atonement
The day of atonement is from Leviticus 16, not 2 Peter 3:12.
The Lord's Passover
The Lord’s Passover is from Exodus 12 and Leviticus 23, and is not used in 2 Peter 3:12.
In the chapter where Peter describes cosmic fire, what practical question does he ask his readers?
Peter asks, “Since everything will be destroyed in this way, what kind of people ought you to be?” (3:11).
2 Peter 3:11
Who will rebuild the city?
Rebuilding the city is not Peter’s question; he asks what kind of people believers ought to be.
What kind of people ought you to be?
How can these things be?
This echoes Nicodemus’s question (“How can this be?” John 3:9), not Peter’s here.
Who is greatest in the kingdom?
“Who is greatest in the kingdom?” is the disciples’ question in the Gospels, not Peter’s in this chapter.
Where shall we buy bread?
Buying bread is not mentioned in 2 Peter 3; Peter asks about the character of believers.
According to Peter, what sort of conduct fits people who know the present world will be destroyed?
Peter says, “You ought to conduct yourselves in holiness and godliness” (3:11).
2 Peter 3:11
Holiness and godliness
Military strength and wisdom
Military strength and wisdom are not the conduct Peter commands; he says holiness and godliness.
Public display and wealth
Public display and wealth are not what Peter commands; he says holiness and godliness.
Ritual sacrifice and pilgrimage
Ritual sacrifice and pilgrimage are not what Peter commands here; he says holiness and godliness.
Silence and isolation only
Peter does not call for isolation; he calls for holiness and godliness.
What future home does Peter set before believers, in contrast to the present heavens and earth reserved for fire?
Peter says, “we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth” (3:13), in contrast with the present heavens and earth reserved for fire (3:7).
2 Peter 3:13
The land of Canaan
Canaan is not the future home Peter describes; he looks for a new heaven and new earth.
A rebuilt Babylon
Babylon is not rebuilt in this passage; believers look forward to a new heaven and a new earth.
A new heaven and a new earth
The wilderness of Sinai
Sinai’s wilderness is not Peter’s hope; he looks forward to a new heaven and new earth.
The upper room in Jerusalem
The upper room in Jerusalem is not mentioned; Peter’s hope is a new heaven and earth.
While anticipating God's promised future, what threefold condition should believers seek to be found in before Him?
Peter says, “make every effort to be found at peace—spotless and blameless in His sight” (3:14).
2 Peter 3:14
Wealthy, honored, and strong
Wealth, honor, and strength are not Peter’s aims; he says at peace, spotless, and blameless.
At peace, spotless, and blameless
Fasting, silent, and hidden
Fasting, silence, and hiding are not what Peter lists; he says at peace, spotless, and blameless.
Zealous, loud, and feared
Zeal, loudness, and being feared are not what Peter lists; he names at peace, spotless, and blameless.
Learned, famous, and bold
Learning, fame, and boldness are not on Peter’s list; he names at peace, spotless, and blameless.
In the part of 2 Peter 3 that mentions Paul, how should Christians interpret the Lord's patience?
Peter says, “Consider also that our Lord’s patience brings salvation” (3:15).
2 Peter 3:15
As lost opportunity
Peter does not see lost opportunity but salvation in the Lord’s patience.
As salvation
As indecision
Indecision is not how Peter describes the Lord’s patience; he says it brings salvation.
As wrath only
Wrath is not the emphasis; Peter says the Lord’s patience brings salvation.
As secrecy
Secrecy is not mentioned; Peter says the Lord’s patience brings salvation.
Peter says Paul wrote to these believers with wisdom that came from whom?
Peter says Paul wrote “with the wisdom God gave him” (3:15).
2 Peter 3:15
Gamaliel
Gamaliel was Paul’s teacher according to Acts 22:3, but Peter says Paul’s wisdom came from God.
Caesar
Caesar is not mentioned in this chapter; the wisdom came from God.
God
Peter
Peter does not claim to be Paul’s source; he says God gave Paul the wisdom.
James
James is not mentioned; Peter says the wisdom was God’s gift to Paul.
In 2 Peter 3, what does Peter imply about Paul's letters by saying they are distorted as they do the rest of the Scriptures?
Peter says the ignorant and unstable distort Paul’s letters “as they do the rest of the Scriptures” (3:16), placing Paul’s letters with Scripture.
2 Peter 3:16
They are merely private opinions
Peter treats Paul’s letters as Scripture, not as mere private opinion.
They are less important than the Law
Peter does not rank Paul’s letters below the Law; he places them with the rest of the Scriptures.
They belong with Scripture
They should be ignored
Ignoring Paul’s letters is not Peter’s advice; he honors them as wise and Scripture-like.
They were written in another language only
Language is not mentioned; Peter compares Paul’s letters to the rest of the Scriptures.
What two traits describe the people who twist difficult biblical writings in this chapter?
Peter says the distorters are “ignorant and unstable people” (3:16).
2 Peter 3:16
Clever and educated
Peter does not describe the distorters as clever and educated; he calls them ignorant.
Ignorant and unstable
Poor and oppressed
Poverty and oppression are not mentioned; he says ignorant and unstable.
Young and impulsive
Youth and impulsiveness are not named; he says ignorant and unstable.
Old and cautious
Age and caution are not named; he says ignorant and unstable.
Peter's warning at the end of the chapter links two dangers together. What are they?
Peter warns, “be on your guard so that you will not be carried away by the error of the lawless and fall from your secure standing” (3:17).
2 Peter 3:17
Being carried away by the error of the lawless and falling from secure standing
Losing property and family because of persecution by unbelievers
Persecution and loss are not the dangers Peter names; he warns of lawless error and falling from secure standing.
Missing the Passover and the Sabbath through carelessness in worship
Carelessness in worship is not mentioned; the dangers are lawless error and falling from secure standing.
Angering Rome and the synagogue by speaking too boldly in public
Speaking too boldly is not mentioned; Peter warns of lawless error and falling from secure standing.
Suffering sickness and famine as God’s judgment on the land
Sickness and famine as judgment are not mentioned; the dangers are lawless error and falling from secure standing.
What positive command immediately follows Peter's warning not to fall from secure standing?
Right after the warning, Peter says, “But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (3:18).
Rebuild the old paths and return to the ways of the fathers
Returning to the ways of the fathers is not Peter’s command; he says to grow in grace and knowledge.
Grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ
Separate from all Gentiles and keep the traditions of the elders
Separating from Gentiles and keeping the elders’ traditions is not in this chapter; Peter says to grow in grace and knowledge.
Await the return of Elijah before the Lord appears again
Awaiting Elijah is not mentioned in 2 Peter 3 (compare Malachi 4:5); Peter’s command is to grow in grace and knowledge.
Return to Jerusalem and wait together for the coming of the Lord
Returning to Jerusalem to wait is not mentioned; Peter says to grow in the grace and knowledge of Christ.
Looking across Peter's whole argument in chapter 3, which summary best matches his teaching?

Peter says the heavens existed by God’s word (3:5), the old world perished in the flood (3:6), the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire (3:7), and believers look for a new heaven and a new earth and are to grow in Christ (3:13, 18).
2 Peter 3:5-18
Everything has continued unchanged since creation, so believers may relax, ignore warnings of judgment, and pay no attention to holy living
This is the scoffers’ view (3:4), which Peter rejects with the flood and the coming fire; he urges holy living (3:11).
God's word created the world, judged the ancient world by flood, reserves the present heavens and earth for fire, and calls believers to holy hope in Christ
The temple in Jerusalem will protect the world from final judgment, so believers should put their hope in its sacrifices and priests
Peter never mentions the temple preventing judgment; he says the Day of the Lord will come like a thief (3:10).
Only Paul’s letters matter for the last days, because Peter’s own teaching and the rest of the Scriptures are hard to understand
Peter does not say only Paul’s letters matter; he also points to the prophets, the apostles, and the rest of the Scriptures (3:2, 16).
Scoffers are correct that the promise of His coming has failed, so believers should stop looking forward to a new heaven and earth
Peter says the scoffers are wrong; the Lord is not slow but patient (3:9), and believers look forward to a new heaven and earth (3:13).
62: In the opening of 1 John chapter 1, what does the writer say was from the beginning and was heard, seen, and touched?
1:1 calls what was from the beginning, heard, seen, gazed upon and touched “the Word of life.”
1 John 1:1
The bread of life
“I am the bread of life” is Jesus’ own claim in John 6:35, not the title used in 1 John 1:1.
The Word of life
The true vine
Jesus calls Himself “the true vine” in John 15:1; 1 John 1:1 speaks of the Word of life.
The book of life
The Book of Life is the register of names in Philippians 4:3 and Revelation 20:12, not the One the apostles saw and touched.
The living water
Living water is what Jesus offered the Samaritan woman in John 4:10; John’s letter opens with the Word of life.
According to 1 John 1:1, what did the witnesses do with their hands concerning the One they proclaim?
1:1 says the witnesses “gazed upon and touched with our own hands” the Word of life, stressing real, physical contact.
1 John 1:1
Lifted Him up
Being lifted up is Jesus’ picture of His crucifixion in John 3:14; 1 John 1:1 speaks of touching with hands.
Anointed Him
Mary anointed Jesus’ feet with nard in John 12:3; 1 John 1:1 mentions hands only for touching.
Touched Him
Clothed Him
Soldiers dressed Him in a purple robe to mock Him (Mark 15:17), which 1 John does not mention.
Buried Him
His body was wrapped in linen for burial in John 19:40; 1 John 1:1 speaks of touching the living Word.
In the first chapter of 1 John, what two things does the writer say he proclaims to readers?
1:3 says, “We proclaim to you what we have seen and heard,” grounding the message in eyewitness testimony.
1 John 1:3
What was seen and heard
What was dreamed and imagined
Dreams are never mentioned; the writer insists on what was heard, seen and touched, not imagined (1:1).
What was hidden and sealed
Far from hidden, the life “was revealed to us” and is openly proclaimed (1:2).
What was written and forgotten
Nothing is forgotten; the writer writes “so that our joy may be complete” (1:4).
What was promised and delayed
Nothing is delayed: the eternal life has already been revealed and proclaimed (1:2).
According to 1 John 1, why does the writer proclaim what he has seen and heard?
1:3 says the writer proclaims what he saw and heard “so that you also may have fellowship with us.”
1 John 1:3
So readers may become rulers
Ruling is not mentioned; the purpose is fellowship with the apostles and with the Father and the Son (1:3).
So readers may have fellowship with them
So readers may rebuild the temple
The temple is never mentioned in 1 John 1; the stated aim is shared fellowship (1:3).
So readers may speak mysteries
Uttering mysteries is Paul’s description of speaking in tongues (1 Corinthians 14:2); John’s aim is fellowship.
So readers may escape all trials
John promises no escape from trials here; he speaks of fellowship and cleansing from all sin (1:3, 1:7).
In 1 John 1:3, with whom does the writer say this fellowship truly is?
1:3 says, “this fellowship of ours is with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ.”
1 John 1:3
Abraham and Moses, the servant of God
Abraham and Moses do not appear in 1 John 1; the fellowship is “with the Father and with His Son” (1:3).
The Father and His Son Jesus Christ
The prophets and the kings of Israel
Prophets and kings are not named in 1 John 1; the fellowship is with the Father and His Son, Jesus Christ (1:3).
The twelve tribes of Israel and Judah
Israel’s tribes are never mentioned in this chapter; the fellowship is with God the Father and Jesus Christ (1:3).
The angels and the archangel Michael
The archangel Michael appears in Jude 1:9, not in 1 John, where fellowship is with the Father and the Son (1:3).
In 1 John chapter 1, why are “these things” written?
1:4 says, “We write these things so that our joy may be complete.”
1 John 1:4
So prophecy may be hidden
Nothing is hidden; the chapter is about proclaiming the life that was revealed (1:2–3).
So our joy may be complete
So judgment may begin
Judgment is not the purpose given; the writing aims at complete joy (1:4).
So the law may return
The law is not mentioned in 1 John 1; the stated purpose is that our joy may be complete (1:4).
So fasting may increase
Fasting is not mentioned; the writer’s purpose is that “our joy may be complete” (1:4).
What message does the writer say he heard and now announces in 1 John 1:5?
1:5 gives the message: “God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all.”
1 John 1:5
God is spirit
“God is Spirit” is Jesus’ teaching to the Samaritan woman in John 4:24, not the message of 1 John 1:5.
God is love
“God is love” comes later in this same letter (1 John 4:8), not in 1:5.
God is light
God is fire
Hebrews 12:29 says “our God is a consuming fire”; 1 John 1:5 says God is light.
God is peace
Paul speaks of “the God of peace” (Romans 15:33), but 1 John 1:5 says God is light.
According to 1 John 1:6, if someone says he has fellowship with God but walks in darkness, what does he do?
1:6 says that if we claim fellowship with Him yet walk in the darkness, “we lie and do not practice the truth.”
1 John 1:6
He stumbles briefly
John does not soften it to a brief stumble; claiming fellowship while walking in darkness is a lie (1:6).
He lies
He becomes blameless
Far from blameless, such a person lies and does not practice the truth (1:6).
He gains wisdom
Walking in darkness brings no wisdom here; the verse calls the claim a lie (1:6).
He enters rest
Entering God’s rest is a theme of Hebrews 4:3; 1 John 1:6 says such a person lies.
In 1 John 1:7, if believers walk in the light as God is in the light, what do they have with one another?
1:7 says, “if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another.”
1 John 1:7
Dominion
Dominion is not mentioned in 1 John 1; walking in the light brings fellowship with one another (1:7).
Fellowship
Secrecy
Secrecy belongs to darkness; walking in the light brings open fellowship with one another (1:7).
Fear
Fear is not the result named; walking in the light brings fellowship (1:7).
Strife
Strife is the opposite of what 1:7 promises, which is fellowship with one another.
According to 1 John 1, the blood mentioned there cleanses from how much sin?
1:7 says “the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin.”
1 John 1:7
Only hidden sin
The cleansing is not limited to hidden sin; it is “from all sin” (1:7).
Only deliberate sin
No limit to deliberate sin is given; the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin (1:7).
Only past sin
The verse sets no time limit; 1:7 says the blood “cleanses us from all sin.”
All sin
Half of sin
Cleansing is never partial; 1:7 says all sin, and 1:9 adds “all unrighteousness.”
In 1 John 1:8, what happens if a person says, “We have no sin”?
1:8 says, “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
1 John 1:8
He glorifies God
Denying sin does not glorify God; 1:10 says denying we have sinned makes Him out to be a liar.
He deceives himself
He becomes perfect
Claiming to have no sin does not make anyone perfect; it is self-deception (1:8).
He gains peace
Peace with God comes through confession and forgiveness (1:9), not through denying sin.
He fulfills the law
The law is not mentioned in 1 John 1; claiming to have no sin is self-deception (1:8).
Still in 1 John 1:8, what is not in a person who claims to have no sin?
1:8 ends, “and the truth is not in us.”
1 John 1:8
The law
The law is not mentioned; 1:8 says the truth is not in such a person.
The Spirit
The Spirit is not mentioned in 1 John 1; 1:8 says the truth is not in us.
The truth
The temple
The temple does not appear in 1 John; the thing missing in 1:8 is the truth.
The promise
The promise is not mentioned; the truth is not in us (1:8), and His word is not in us (1:10).
In 1 John 1:9, if believers confess their sins, what two qualities of God are named?
1:9 says, “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins.”
1 John 1:9
Holy and mighty
Holy and mighty are not the words of 1:9; God is called faithful and just.
Faithful and just
Gentle and lowly
Jesus calls Himself “gentle and humble in heart” in Matthew 11:29; 1 John 1:9 says faithful and just.
Jealous and strong
God calls Himself “a jealous God” in the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:5); 1 John 1:9 says faithful and just.
Patient and silent
Patience is not named here, and God is not silent: He is faithful and just to forgive (1:9).
According to 1 John 1:9, if sins are confessed, what does God do?
1:9 says He is faithful and just “to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
1 John 1:9
He delays judgment only
God does not merely delay judgment; He forgives and cleanses (1:9).
He forgives our sins
He forgets His covenant
God does not forget His covenant; 1:9 calls Him faithful.
He removes our names
No names are removed; Christ even promises never to blot out the overcomer’s name from the Book of Life (Revelation 3:5).
He sends a warning first
No warning is mentioned; confession is met directly with forgiveness and cleansing (1:9).
According to the last verse of 1 John chapter 1, what do we make God if we say, “We have not sinned”?
1:10 says, “If we say we have not sinned, we make Him out to be a liar, and His word is not in us.”
1 John 1:10
A witness
God is not made a witness here; denying our sin makes Him out to be a liar (1:10).
A servant
Nothing casts God as a servant; 1:10 says denial makes Him out to be a liar.
A liar
A stranger
Stranger is not the word; 1:10 says we make Him out to be a liar.
A judge only
God is not cast as judge in 1:10; denying that we have sinned makes Him out to be a liar.
In 1 John 1:2, the writer proclaims “the eternal life.” With whom was this eternal life before it was revealed?
1:2 proclaims “the eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed to us.”
1 John 1:2
With Abraham
Abraham is not mentioned in 1 John 1; the eternal life was with the Father (1:2).
With Israel
Israel is not named; the life was with the Father before it was revealed (1:2).
With the prophets
The prophets are not mentioned; 1:2 says the eternal life was with the Father.
With the Father
With the churches
The churches received the proclamation; the life itself was with the Father (1:2).
In the opening testimony of 1 John 1:1, which set of human senses is specifically mentioned?
1:1 speaks of what “we have heard,” what “we have seen with our own eyes,” and what was “touched with our own hands”: hearing, sight and touch.
1 John 1:1
Taste, smell, and hearing
Taste and smell are not mentioned; 1:1 names hearing alongside sight and touch.
Hearing, sight, and touch
Smell, sight, and balance
Smell and balance are not mentioned; 1:1 adds hearing and touch to sight.
Hearing, smell, and taste
Smell and taste are not mentioned; 1:1 names hearing, sight and touch.
Sight and taste only
Taste is not mentioned, and sight is not alone: hearing and touch are named too (1:1).
In the opening verses of 1 John, what does the writer say had been revealed, seen, testified to, and proclaimed?
1:2 says, “this is the life that was revealed; we have seen it and testified to it, and we proclaim to you the eternal life.”
1 John 1:2
The Ark of the Covenant
The ark of the covenant was built at God’s command in Exodus 25:10; 1 John 1:2 speaks of the eternal life.
The eternal life
The earthly kingdom
No earthly kingdom is proclaimed; Jesus said, “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36).
The temple veil
The temple veil was torn at Jesus’ death (Matthew 27:51); 1 John 1:2 speaks of the revealed eternal life.
The river of Eden
The river flowing out of Eden is in Genesis 2:10; 1 John 1:2 proclaims the eternal life.
Which sequence best matches 1 John 1:3?
1:3 says, “We proclaim to you what we have seen and heard, so that you also may have fellowship with us.”
1 John 1:3
We dreamed and wrote so that you may fear with us
There is no dreaming or fear; John proclaims what he saw and heard so readers may share fellowship (1:3).
We saw and heard, we proclaim to you, so that you may have fellowship with us
We fasted and prayed, so that you may rule with us
Fasting, prayer and ruling are not mentioned; 1:3 moves from seeing and hearing to fellowship.
We hid the mystery, so that you may seek with us
Nothing is hidden; the life “was revealed to us” and is proclaimed (1:2).
We suffered in silence, so that you may pity us
No silent suffering is described; the apostles openly proclaim so readers may share fellowship (1:3).
In 1 John 1:4, whose joy does the writer say may be complete?
1:4 says, “We write these things so that our joy may be complete.”
1 John 1:4

A vow of silence
Silence is not mentioned; 1:4 says grace became a license for immorality.
In Jude’s description of the intruders, whom did they deny?
1:4 says, “they deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.”
Jude 1:4
Abraham and Moses
Moses appears only in Michael’s dispute over his body (1:9); the intruders deny Jesus Christ (1:4).
The prophets and apostles
Jude tells readers to remember the apostles’ words (1:17), but the one denied is Christ (1:4).
Our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ
The temple and the priesthood
The temple and priesthood are not mentioned in Jude; they deny our only Master and Lord (1:4).
The angels of heaven
Angels appear in 1:6 and 1:9, but those denied are “our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ” (1:4).
In Jude’s reminder from Israel’s history, from what land had Jesus delivered His people?
1:5 says, “after Jesus had delivered His people out of the land of Egypt, He destroyed those who did not believe.”
Jude 1:5
Babylon
Babylon was the land of the later exile, not the deliverance Jude recalls (1:5).
Assyria
Assyria is not mentioned in Jude; the deliverance was out of Egypt (1:5).
Egypt
Canaan
Canaan was the land Israel was brought into, not out of; Jude says Egypt (1:5).
Philistia
Philistia is not mentioned; Jude recalls the exodus from Egypt (1:5).
In Jude’s example about angels, what did those angels fail to do?
1:6 speaks of “the angels who did not stay within their own domain but abandoned their proper dwelling.”
Jude 1:6
Sing before the throne
Seraphim call out praise in Isaiah 6:3; Jude says these angels did not stay within their own domain.
Stay within their own domain
Guard Eden
Cherubim guarded the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24); Jude’s angels abandoned their proper dwelling.
Deliver messages to prophets
Angels are “ministering spirits” (Hebrews 1:14), but Jude’s fault is leaving their own domain (1:6).
Protect Jerusalem
Protecting Jerusalem is not mentioned; their fault was abandoning their proper dwelling (1:6).
In Jude’s warning, what happened to the angels who abandoned their proper dwelling?
1:6 says, “these He has kept in eternal chains under darkness, bound for judgment on that great day.”
Jude 1:6
They were immediately restored to their places in heaven
They were not restored; He has kept them in eternal chains under darkness for judgment (1:6).
They were sent out to preach to the nations of the earth
Preaching to nations is not their lot; they are bound for judgment on that great day (1:6).
They were kept in eternal chains under darkness for judgment
They became rulers over the kingdoms of this present world
They rule nothing; they are kept in chains, and 2 Peter 2:4 likewise speaks of “chains of darkness.”
They were cast into the depths of the sea until the end of days
The sea is not their prison in Jude; they are kept in eternal chains under darkness (1:6).
In Jude’s comparison from the Old Testament, which cities are named as examples because they indulged in sexual immorality and pursued strange flesh?
1:7 names “Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities around them, who indulged in sexual immorality and pursued strange flesh.”
Jude 1:7
Jericho and Ai
Jericho and Ai fell to Joshua (Joshua 6:20, 8:28); they are not Jude’s example of immorality.
Nineveh and Tyre
Nineveh repented at Jonah’s preaching (Jonah 3:5), and Tyre’s doom is in Ezekiel 26:3; Jude names Sodom and Gomorrah.
Sodom and Gomorrah
Bethlehem and Hebron
Bethlehem and Hebron are not judged in Jude; 1:7 names Sodom and Gomorrah.
Shiloh and Bethel
Shiloh and Bethel are not in Jude; the LORD rained sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24).
According to Jude, what do the false teachers do “in the same way” as those judged before them?
1:8 says, “these dreamers defile their bodies, reject authority, and slander glorious beings.”
Jude 1:8
They offer lawful sacrifices at the altar and keep the appointed feasts
Sacrifices are not mentioned; 1:8 says they defile their bodies, reject authority and slander glorious beings.
They defile their bodies, reject authority, and slander glorious beings
They rebuild ruined cities and restore the ancient walls of Jerusalem
Rebuilding is not mentioned in Jude; the dreamers defile, reject authority and slander (1:8).
They honor their parents and teachers and submit to every authority
Far from submitting, 1:8 says they reject authority.
They pray day and night in the temple and fast for the sake of others
Anna worshiped night and day in the temple, fasting and praying (Luke 2:37); Jude’s dreamers defile and slander.
In Jude’s example involving the archangel Michael, over whose body was there a dispute with the devil?
1:9 says Michael “disputed with the devil over the body of Moses.”
Jude 1:9
Aaron
Aaron died on top of Mount Hor (Numbers 20:28); Jude’s dispute concerns the body of Moses.
Elijah
Elijah was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11); Jude names Moses.
Moses
Samuel
Samuel is not mentioned in Jude; the dispute was over the body of Moses (1:9).
David
David is not mentioned in Jude; Michael disputed over the body of Moses (1:9).
In Jude’s account of Michael disputing with the devil, what did Michael say?
1:9 says Michael “did not presume to bring a slanderous charge against him, but said, ‘The Lord rebuke you!’”
Jude 1:9
“Depart from me, Satan”
Jesus told Satan, “Away from Me, Satan!” (Matthew 4:10); Michael left the rebuke to the Lord.
“The Lord rebuke you!”
“It is written”
Jesus answered the tempter with “It is written” (Matthew 4:4); Michael said, “The Lord rebuke you!”
“Peace, be still”
Jesus rebuked the wind and the sea (Mark 4:39); Michael would not bring a charge himself but said, “The Lord rebuke you!”
“Woe to you”
Jesus repeatedly says “Woe to you” to the Pharisees (Matthew 23:13); in Jude, “Woe to them!” is Jude’s own cry (1:11).
In Jude’s contrast between Michael and the false teachers, what do these men slander?
1:10 says, “These men, however, slander what they do not understand.”
Jude 1:10
What they do not understand
The law they carefully studied
They have not studied carefully; they slander what they do not understand (1:10).
The poor and needy
The poor are not mentioned; they slander what they do not understand (1:10).
The kings of Israel only
Israel’s kings are not mentioned in Jude; 1:10 says they slander what they do not understand.
The city gates of Jerusalem
City gates are not mentioned; they slander what they do not understand (1:10).
In Jude’s vivid description, to what are the false teachers compared because they are destroyed by instinct?
1:10 says, “like irrational animals, they will be destroyed by the things they do instinctively.”
Jude 1:10
Strong lions
Lions are not mentioned in Jude; 1:10 compares them to irrational animals.
Wise serpents
Jesus told His disciples to be “shrewd as snakes” (Matthew 10:16); Jude compares these men to irrational animals.
Irrational animals
Swift eagles
Those who wait on the LORD “mount up with wings like eagles” (Isaiah 40:31); Jude says irrational animals.
Gentle doves
Jesus told His disciples to be “innocent as doves” (Matthew 10:16); Jude says irrational animals.
In Jude’s cry of “Woe to them!”, whose path had these corrupt people traveled?
1:11 says, “Woe to them! They have traveled the path of Cain.”
Jude 1:11
Abel
Abel was the brother Cain killed (Genesis 4:8); Jude warns of the path of Cain.
Cain
Joseph
Joseph is not mentioned in Jude; the first example of 1:11 is Cain.
Joshua
Joshua is not mentioned in Jude; 1:11 names the path of Cain.
Daniel
Daniel is not mentioned in Jude; the path they traveled is Cain’s (1:11).
In Jude’s third Old Testament example of rebellion, whose rebellion had they perished in?
1:11 ends, “they have perished in Korah’s rebellion,” after Cain and Balaam.
Jude 1:11
Absalom’s
Absalom rebelled against David (2 Samuel 15:10), but Jude names Korah, whom the earth swallowed (Numbers 16:32).
Saul’s
Saul’s disobedience cost him the kingdom, but Jude’s third example is Korah’s rebellion (1:11).
Korah’s
Achan’s
Achan’s sin was taking devoted things (Joshua 7:1); Jude’s third example is Korah.
Jehu’s
Jehu’s revolt struck down Joram (2 Kings 9:24); Jude names Korah’s rebellion.
In Jude’s warning about church fellowship meals, what does he call these dangerous people at the believers’ love feasts?
1:12 says, “These men are hidden reefs in your love feasts.”
Jude 1:12
Lamps on a stand
A lamp is set on a stand in Jesus’ teaching (Matthew 5:15); Jude calls these men hidden reefs.
Hidden reefs
Broken cisterns
Broken cisterns are Jeremiah’s picture of forsaking God (Jeremiah 2:13), not Jude’s.
Whitewashed walls
Paul called the high priest a “whitewashed wall” (Acts 23:3); Jude says hidden reefs.
Cedars of Lebanon
A cedar in Lebanon pictures the righteous flourishing (Psalm 92:12); Jude says hidden reefs.
In Jude’s picture of selfish leaders, whom were these men shepherding?
1:12 says, “shamelessly feasting with you but shepherding only themselves.”
Jude 1:12
The widows and orphans
Widows and orphans are not mentioned in Jude; these men shepherd only themselves (1:12).
The flock of God
Elders are told to “Be shepherds of God’s flock” (1 Peter 5:2), but these men shepherd only themselves.
Only themselves
The priests in the temple
The priests are not mentioned in Jude; 1:12 says they shepherd only themselves.
The children of Israel
Israel is not their flock; Jude says they shepherd only themselves (1:12).
In Jude’s chain of metaphors, what are the false teachers compared to because they promise much but provide nothing?
1:12 says, “They are clouds without water, carried along by the wind,” promising rain but giving none.
Jude 1:12
Trees planted by streams of water, yielding fruit
The tree “planted by streams of water” is the righteous man of Psalm 1:3; Jude calls these men “fruitless trees in autumn” (1:12).
Clouds without water, carried along by the wind
Rivers of living water flowing from within them
Streams of living water flow from believers in John 7:38; Jude calls these men clouds without water.
A city on a hill that cannot be hidden from view
“A city on a hill cannot be hidden” describes disciples in Matthew 5:14, not Jude’s false teachers.
A sealed fountain in a garden that is locked up
“A fountain sealed” is the bride in Song of Solomon 4:12; Jude says clouds without water (1:12).
In Jude’s sea imagery, what are the false teachers like?
1:13 says, “They are wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shame.”
Jude 1:13
Still waters that bring rest and peace to the weary
Quiet waters picture the Lord’s care in Psalm 23:2; Jude says “wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shame.”
Wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shame
Ships guided safely through the storm into harbor
No ships appear in Jude; the false teachers are restless wild waves of the sea (1:13).
Fishermen casting their nets and gathering a catch
James and John were fishermen mending nets (Matthew 4:21); Jude’s image is waves foaming up shame.
Springs of water breaking out in the dry desert
Springs in the desert picture blessing; Jude’s sea image is wild waves foaming up their own shame (1:13).
In Jude’s celestial metaphor, what is reserved forever for these “wandering stars”?
1:13 calls them “wandering stars, for whom blackest darkness has been reserved forever.”
Jude 1:13
A crown of life
The crown of life is promised to the faithful in Revelation 2:10; blackest darkness awaits these men.
A place at the altar
No altar is mentioned; blackest darkness is reserved for them (1:13).
Blackest darkness
A river of fire
The lake of fire appears in Revelation 20:10; Jude says blackest darkness is reserved for them (1:13).
A field of rest
No rest awaits them; blackest darkness has been reserved forever (1:13).
In Jude’s quotation of ancient prophecy, who is identified as “the seventh from Adam”?
1:14 says, “Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied about them.”
Jude 1:14
Noah
Noah was Lamech’s son (Genesis 5:29), the tenth generation from Adam, not the seventh.
Enoch
Methuselah
Methuselah was Enoch’s son (Genesis 5:21), the eighth from Adam.
Seth
Seth was Adam’s son (Genesis 5:3), the second in the line from Adam.
Lamech
Lamech was Methuselah’s son (Genesis 5:25), the ninth from Adam.
According to Jude’s quotation of Enoch, with whom is the Lord coming?
1:14 quotes Enoch: “Behold, the Lord is coming with myriads of His holy ones.”
Jude 1:14
Twelve tribes of Israel
The twelve tribes will be judged from twelve thrones (Matthew 19:28); Enoch speaks of myriads of holy ones.
Chariots of fire only
A chariot of fire took Elijah up (2 Kings 2:11); Jude quotes the Lord coming with myriads of holy ones.
Myriads of His holy ones
The elders of Jerusalem
Jerusalem’s elders are not mentioned; the Lord comes with myriads of His holy ones (1:14).
The beasts of the field
Beasts of the field are not mentioned; the Lord comes with myriads of His holy ones (1:14).
In Jude’s citation of Enoch, what is one stated purpose of the Lord’s coming?
1:14–15 say the Lord is coming “to execute judgment on everyone, and to convict all the ungodly.”
Jude 1:15
To establish an earthly monarchy in Samaria
No earthly monarchy is mentioned; the Lord comes to execute judgment on everyone (1:15).
To execute judgment on everyone
To rebuild the temple stones
The temple is not mentioned in Jude; the purpose is to execute judgment (1:15).
To divide the promised land again
Dividing the land is Joshua’s work, not the purpose of the Lord’s coming in 1:15.
To appoint new judges in Israel
Appointing judges is not mentioned; the Lord Himself comes to execute judgment (1:15).
In Jude’s moral description of the false teachers, what are they called regarding their attitude?
1:16 says, “These men are discontented grumblers, following after their own lusts.”
Jude 1:16
Cheerful servants
They are not cheerful servants but discontented grumblers (1:16).
Discontented grumblers
Faithful stewards
Faithful stewards are the opposite; Jude calls them discontented grumblers (1:16).
Humble worshipers
Their mouths “spew arrogance” (1:16), so they are anything but humble.
Patient laborers
Patience is not their mark; Jude calls them discontented grumblers (1:16).
According to Jude, what do these grumblers follow?
1:16 says they are grumblers, “following after their own lusts.”
Jude 1:16
The counsel of the prophets
They do not follow the prophets; they follow their own lusts (1:16).
Their own lusts
The songs of David
David’s songs are not mentioned in Jude; they follow their own lusts (1:16).
The commands of angels
Angels’ commands are not mentioned; they follow their own lusts (1:16).
The wisdom of Solomon
Solomon is not mentioned in Jude; they follow their own lusts (1:16).
In Jude’s description of their speech, why do these people flatter others?
1:16 says, “they flatter others for their own advantage.”
Jude 1:16
To bring peace in the church
Their flattery does not seek peace; Jude says they cause divisions (1:19).
To win souls for heaven
Winning souls is not their motive; they flatter for their own advantage (1:16).
For their own advantage
To honor older saints
Honoring older saints is not the motive; they flatter for their own advantage (1:16).
To imitate the apostles
They do not imitate the apostles, whose words warned about them (1:17–18).
In Jude’s appeal to believers, whose earlier words are they told to remember?
1:17 says, “remember what was foretold by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ.”
Jude 1:17
The kings of Judah who ruled in Jerusalem
Judah’s kings are not cited; Jude says to remember what the apostles foretold (1:17).
The apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ
The sons of Korah who sang in the temple
The sons of Korah are not cited in Jude; the readers are to remember the apostles (1:17).
The scribes and wise men of Babylon
Babylon is not mentioned in Jude; the readers are to remember the apostles’ words (1:17).
The elders of Israel gathered at Sinai
Israel’s elders at Sinai are not mentioned; Jude recalls the apostles’ warning about scoffers (1:17–18).
In Jude’s diagnosis of divisive people, what are they said to be lacking?
1:19 says, “These are the ones who cause divisions, who are worldly and devoid of the Spirit.”
Jude 1:19
Bread from heaven
Bread from heaven was the manna (Exodus 16:4); Jude says they are devoid of the Spirit.
Priestly garments
Priestly garments are not mentioned in Jude; they lack the Spirit (1:19).
The Spirit
Knowledge of Hebrew
Language is not the issue; they are worldly and devoid of the Spirit (1:19).
Circumcision
Circumcision is not mentioned in Jude; they are devoid of the Spirit (1:19).
In the practical instructions near the end of Jude, on what are believers to build themselves up?
1:20 says, “by building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit.”
Jude 1:20
Roman citizenship
Roman citizenship is not mentioned in Jude; believers build themselves up in their most holy faith (1:20).
Their most holy faith
The traditions of the elders
“The tradition of the elders” is the Pharisees’ concern in Matthew 15:2; Jude says your most holy faith.
Military strength
Military strength is not mentioned; believers build up in their most holy faith (1:20).
Temple rituals
Temple rituals are not mentioned in Jude; the foundation is their most holy faith (1:20).
In Jude’s commands to believers, where are they to keep themselves?
1:21 says, “keep yourselves in the love of God.”
Jude 1:21
In the courts of the temple
The temple courts are not mentioned in Jude; they are to keep themselves in the love of God (1:21).
In the love of God
In the wilderness
The wilderness is not the place; Jude says keep yourselves in the love of God (1:21).
In the upper room
The upper room is where the apostles stayed (Acts 1:13); Jude says keep yourselves in the love of God.
In the city of David
The city of David is not mentioned; believers keep themselves in the love of God (1:21).
In Jude’s closing exhortation, what are believers waiting for from the Lord Jesus Christ?
1:21 says, “as you await the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ to bring you eternal life.”
Jude 1:21
A new law carved in stone
The law was carved on stone tablets (Exodus 31:18); Jude’s readers await Christ’s mercy (1:21).
His mercy to bring eternal life
A sign in the stars
No sign in the stars is mentioned; they await the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ (1:21).
Earthly wealth and honor
Earthly wealth is not their hope; they await mercy that brings eternal life (1:21).
Freedom from Rome
Rome is not mentioned in Jude; believers await Christ’s mercy to bring eternal life (1:21).
In Jude’s instructions for dealing with struggling people, how should believers treat those who doubt?
1:22 says, “And indeed, have mercy on those who doubt.”
Jude 1:22
Exclude them immediately
Jude does not say to exclude doubters; he says to have mercy on them (1:22).
Debate them publicly
Public debate is not the instruction; 1:22 says have mercy on those who doubt.
Have mercy on them
Appoint them as teachers
Doubters are not made teachers; they are to be shown mercy (1:22).
Ignore them completely
Ignoring them is the opposite of 1:22, which says have mercy on those who doubt.
According to Jude’s rescue imagery, how are some people to be saved?
1:23 says, “save others by snatching them from the fire.”
Jude 1:23
By snatching them from the fire
By crowning them with oil
No anointing is mentioned in Jude; some are saved by being snatched from the fire (1:23).
By sending them to Egypt
Egypt appears only as the land of the exodus (1:5); 1:23 speaks of snatching people from the fire.
By placing them under a Nazirite vow
The Nazirite vow is described in Numbers 6:2; Jude speaks of snatching people from the fire.
By washing their feet at the gate
Jesus washed His disciples’ feet (John 13:5); Jude speaks of snatching others from the fire.
In Jude’s counsel about helping others, how is mercy to be shown to some people?
1:23 says, “to still others show mercy tempered with fear.”
Jude 1:23
With laughter
Laughter is not mentioned; mercy is to be tempered with fear (1:23).
Tempered with fear
Without prayer
Jude never says to show mercy without prayer; he tells believers to pray in the Holy Spirit (1:20).
Through public reward
Public reward is not mentioned; mercy is to be tempered with fear (1:23).
With loud music
Music is not mentioned in Jude; mercy is to be tempered with fear (1:23).
In Jude’s warning about moral contamination, what are believers to hate?
1:23 says believers are to show mercy, “hating even the clothing stained by the flesh.”
Jude 1:23
The city gates stained with blood
City gates are not mentioned; Jude speaks of clothing stained by the flesh (1:23).
Even the clothing stained by the flesh
Every marketplace in Jerusalem
Marketplaces are not mentioned in Jude; the warning is about clothing stained by the flesh (1:23).
The sandals of tax collectors
Tax collectors’ sandals are not mentioned; Jude says clothing stained by the flesh (1:23).
The garments of priests
Priests’ garments are not mentioned; the clothing hated is that stained by the flesh (1:23).
In the doxology at the end of Jude, what is God able to do for believers?
1:24 says, “Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling.”
Jude 1:24
Make them kings in Babylon
Babylon is not mentioned in Jude; God is able to keep believers from stumbling (1:24).
Keep them from stumbling
Build them an earthly palace
No palace is promised; God is able to keep them from stumbling (1:24).
Hide them in a desert cave
No desert cave is mentioned; He presents them in His glorious presence (1:24).
Turn stones into bread
Turning stones into bread was the tempter’s challenge to Jesus (Matthew 4:3), not Jude’s praise.
In Jude’s final praise, how will God present believers?
1:24 says He is able “to present you unblemished in His glorious presence, with great joy.”
Jude 1:24
Unblemished in His glorious presence, with great joy
Clothed in sackcloth before angels
Sackcloth signals mourning, as at Nineveh (Jonah 3:5); Jude speaks of great joy (1:24).
Seated on twelve thrones
Twelve thrones are promised to the Twelve in Matthew 19:28; Jude speaks of being presented unblemished.
Hidden from all nations
Believers are not hidden; they are presented in His glorious presence (1:24).
Burdened with many sacrifices
Sacrifices are not mentioned; believers are presented unblemished, with great joy (1:24).
In Jude’s description of rebellious “dreamers,” which trio of actions is correct?
1:8 says, “these dreamers defile their bodies, reject authority, and slander glorious beings.”
Jude 1:8
They fast often, pray loudly, and seek visions
Fasting and loud prayer are not their marks; 1:8 says they defile their bodies, reject authority and slander.
They defile their bodies, reject authority, and slander glorious beings
They rebuild altars, reject idols, and cleanse the camp
Rebuilding altars and cleansing the camp are not in Jude; the dreamers defile, reject authority and slander (1:8).
They preach repentance, heal the sick, and cast out demons
Preaching, healing and driving out demons were the Twelve’s mission (Matthew 10:7–8), the opposite of these dreamers.
They guard the law, honor kings, and serve the poor
These men reject authority (1:8) rather than honoring kings or serving the poor.
In Jude’s three Old Testament examples of corrupt behavior, which sequence is correct?
1:11 says, “They have traveled the path of Cain; they have rushed for profit into the error of Balaam; they have perished in Korah’s rebellion.”
Jude 1:11
The patience of Job, the wisdom of Solomon, and the faith of Abraham
Job, Solomon and Abraham are positive examples elsewhere; Jude’s three warnings are Cain, Balaam and Korah (1:11).
The path of Cain, the error of Balaam, and the rebellion of Korah
The courage of Gideon, the song of Deborah, and the prayer of Hannah
Gideon, Deborah and Hannah are not in Jude; 1:11 names Cain, Balaam and Korah.
The reign of David, the temple of Solomon, and the exile of Judah
David’s reign, Solomon’s temple and Judah’s exile are not in 1:11, which names Cain, Balaam and Korah.
The plagues of Egypt, the fall of Jericho, and the rebuilding of Zion
The plagues, Jericho and Zion are not Jude’s examples; 1:11 names Cain, Balaam and Korah.
In Jude’s closing exhortation to believers, which sequence matches his instructions?
1:20–21 say, “building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God as you await the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ.”
Build yourselves up in your most holy faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, and await the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ for eternal life
Offer sacrifices on the altar, sound the rams’ horns, fast for forty days, and march around the city until its walls collapse
Marching around a city recalls Jericho (Joshua 6:20); Jude 1:20–21 calls for faith, prayer in the Spirit and keeping in God’s love.
Appoint elders in every town, collect offerings for the saints, anoint new kings, and send out spies into the land
Jude gives no church-order duties here; 1:20–21 is about faith, prayer in the Holy Spirit, God’s love and awaiting Christ’s mercy.
Speak to the crowds in parables, heal all the sick, feed the multitudes, and calm the wind and the sea
Calming the sea and feeding crowds are Jesus’ own works (Mark 4:39, 6:41), not Jude’s instructions to believers.
Leave Jerusalem behind, cross the Jordan River, conquer the land of Canaan, and divide it among the tribes
Crossing the Jordan and dividing Canaan belong to Joshua’s day; Jude’s closing instructions are spiritual (1:20–21).
66: In the opening of Revelation 1, whose revelation is introduced?
The book’s first words are “This is the revelation of Jesus Christ” (1:1).
Revelation 1:1
The revelation of Moses
Moses received the Law at Sinai; Revelation opens as the revelation of Jesus Christ, not of Moses.
The revelation of John
John is the servant who receives and records it (1:1–2); the revelation itself is called “the revelation of Jesus Christ.”
The revelation of Jesus Christ
The revelation of Elijah
Elijah is not mentioned in Revelation 1; the book is introduced as the revelation of Jesus Christ.
The revelation of the seven churches
The seven churches are the recipients of the book (1:4, 11), not the ones whose revelation it is.
In Revelation 1:1, who gave this revelation to Jesus Christ?
Revelation 1:1 calls it “the revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave Him to show His servants.”
Revelation 1:1
God
An angel
The angel is the messenger who made it known to John (1:1); God is the one who gave it to Jesus Christ.
John
John receives the revelation and testifies to it (1:1–2); he did not give it to Jesus.
The elders
The twenty-four elders first appear around the throne in Revelation 4:4; they play no part in 1:1.
The seven spirits
The seven spirits are named in the greeting of 1:4 as a source of grace and peace, not as the giver of the revelation.
According to Revelation chapter 1, to whom was the revelation meant to be shown?
God gave the revelation “to show His servants what must soon come to pass” (1:1).
Revelation 1:1
The nations
The nations appear later in Revelation (e.g. 7:9), but 1:1 says the revelation was for “His servants.”
The kings of the earth
Jesus is called “the ruler of the kings of the earth” in 1:5, but the revelation was given to show His servants.
The prophets only
1:1 speaks of “His servants” in general, and 1:3 blesses everyone who reads and hears it, not prophets only.
His servants
The priests in Jerusalem
No Jerusalem priests are in view; the revelation is for His servants and is sent to seven churches in Asia (1:4).
In the first verse of Revelation, how was the message made known to John?
1:1 says “He made it known by sending His angel to His servant John.”
Revelation 1:1
By a dream in Jerusalem
John was on the island of Patmos (1:9), not in Jerusalem, and the message came through an angel, not a dream.
By sending His angel
By a cloud over Sinai
A cloud covered Mount Sinai when the Law was given (Exodus 19:16); Revelation came by sending His angel to John.
By a letter from Paul
Paul wrote letters to churches, but Revelation came to John through an angel God sent (1:1).
By the seven churches
The seven churches receive John’s scroll (1:11); they did not bring the message to him.
In the opening verse of Revelation 1, who is called “His servant”?
The opening verse says He sent His angel “to His servant John” (1:1).
Revelation 1:1
Peter
Peter is not named in Revelation 1; the servant named in 1:1 is John.
James
James calls himself “a servant of God” in James 1:1, but Revelation 1:1 names John.
Daniel
Daniel received visions in Babylon (Daniel 10:5–12), but the servant named in Revelation 1:1 is John.
Paul
Paul is not mentioned in Revelation; the servant in 1:1 is John.
John
In Revelation 1:2, what did John testify to?
John “testifies to everything he saw” (1:2).
Revelation 1:2
Everything he saw
Only the messages to the churches
The messages to the churches come in Revelation 2–3; 1:2 says he testifies to everything he saw.
The law of Moses
Revelation 1:2 speaks of “the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ,” not the law of Moses.
His journeys in Asia
John writes to churches in Asia (1:4) but says nothing of his journeys; he testifies to what he saw.
The fall of Jerusalem
Revelation 1 says nothing about Jerusalem’s fall; John testifies to everything he saw in the vision.
In the blessing at the start of Revelation, who is called blessed?
1:3 says “Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy.”
Revelation 1:3
The one who fasts and prays over the words of this prophecy
Fasting is never mentioned in Revelation 1; the blessing is on the one who reads the prophecy aloud.
The one who travels to Patmos to see where the vision came
Patmos is where John himself was (1:9); no blessing is promised for traveling there.
The one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy
The one who seals up the words of this prophecy until the end
Revelation 22:10 says “Do not seal up the words of prophecy in this book”; the reader, not someone who hides it, is blessed.
The one who builds a golden lampstand for each of the churches
The golden lampstands stand for the churches (1:20); no one is blessed for building one.
Besides the reader, who else is blessed in Revelation 1:3?
1:3 also blesses “those who hear and obey what is written in it.”
Revelation 1:3
Those who conquer Rome
Rome is never named in Revelation 1; the blessing is on those who hear and obey the prophecy.
Those who preach in Jerusalem
Preaching in Jerusalem is not in view; the blessing is for those who hear and obey what is written.
Those who memorize the law
The law is not mentioned in 1:3; the blessing is on those who hear and obey this prophecy.
Those who see angels
John is the one who sees the vision; the blessing in 1:3 is on those who hear and obey it.
Those who hear and obey what is written
In Revelation 1:3, why are the readers and hearers urged to take the prophecy seriously?
1:3 ends the blessing with the reason: “because the time is near.”
Revelation 1:3
Because the temple is rebuilt
Revelation 1 says nothing about a rebuilt temple; the reason given is “the time is near.”
Because the time is near
Because the harvest is plentiful
Jesus said “The harvest is plentiful” in Matthew 9:37; Revelation 1:3 gives “the time is near.”
Because winter is coming
No season is mentioned in 1:3; the urgency comes from “the time is near.”
Because John is old
John’s age is never mentioned; 1:3 says the time is near.
In the greeting of Revelation 1, to whom does John write?
John writes “To the seven churches in the province of Asia” (1:4).
Revelation 1:4
The twelve tribes scattered throughout Judea
James addressed “the twelve tribes of the Dispersion” (James 1:1); John writes to seven churches in Asia.
The churches in the province of Galatia
Paul wrote “To the churches of Galatia” (Galatians 1:2); John writes to the seven churches in Asia.
The believers living in the city of Rome
Paul’s letter to Rome was addressed “To all in Rome” (Romans 1:7); John’s greeting is to churches in Asia.
The seven churches in the province of Asia
The priests serving in the temple of Jerusalem
John is not writing to temple priests; his greeting is to the seven churches in the province of Asia (1:4).
In Revelation 1:4, grace and peace come first from whom?
The greeting begins “from Him who is and was and is to come” (1:4).
Revelation 1:4
Him who is and was and is to come
Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
The patriarchs are not mentioned in the greeting; grace and peace come first from Him who is and was and is to come.
The four living creatures
The four living creatures appear around the throne in Revelation 4:6, not in the greeting of 1:4.
Michael the archangel
Michael fights the dragon in Revelation 12:7; he is not named in Revelation 1.
The apostles
The apostles are not named as a source; grace and peace come from God, the seven spirits, and Jesus Christ (1:4–5).
Which title for Jesus appears in Revelation 1:5?
1:5 calls Jesus “the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth.”
Revelation 1:5
The Good Shepherd
Jesus calls Himself “the good shepherd” in John 10:11, not in Revelation 1:5.
The faithful witness
The Prince of Peace
“Prince of Peace” is one of the names given in Isaiah 9:6.
The Son of David
Matthew 1:1 calls Jesus “the son of David”; Revelation 1:5 calls Him the faithful witness.
The Man of Sorrows
Isaiah 53:3 describes the Servant as “a man of sorrows”; that phrase is not in Revelation 1.
According to Revelation 1:5, Jesus is also called what in relation to resurrection?
Revelation 1:5 calls Jesus “the firstborn from the dead,” pointing to His resurrection.
Revelation 1:5
The root of Jesse
“The Root of Jesse” comes from Isaiah 11:10; Revelation 5:5 calls Jesus “the Root of David.”
The Lion of Judah
Jesus is called “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” in Revelation 5:5, not in 1:5.
The carpenter’s son
People in Nazareth asked, “Isn’t this the carpenter’s son?” (Matthew 13:55), which has nothing to do with resurrection.
The morning sacrifice
“The morning sacrifice” is not a title of Jesus here; 1:5 calls Him the firstborn from the dead.
The firstborn from the dead
In Revelation 1:5, what title shows Jesus’ authority over earthly rulers?
1:5 calls Jesus “the ruler of the kings of the earth.”
Revelation 1:5
King over the great city of Babylon
Babylon is the great city judged later in Revelation (18:2); Jesus is not called its king.
Judge over all the tribes of Israel
Judges such as Deborah led Israel (Judges 4:4); Revelation 1:5 calls Jesus ruler of the kings of the earth.
Shepherd of the flocks of Galilee
Jesus ministered in Galilee, but no title about shepherding Galilee’s flocks appears in Revelation 1; 1:5 calls Him ruler of the kings of the earth.
Ruler of the kings of the earth
High Priest of the house of Levi
The priests came from Levi, but Jesus was from Judah (Revelation 5:5); 1:5 calls Him ruler of the kings of the earth.
In the doxology of Revelation 1, how does Jesus deal with our sins?
The doxology is “To Him who loves us and has released us from our sins by His blood” (1:5).
Revelation 1:5
He ignores them
Revelation 1:5 says Jesus released us from our sins by His blood; He did not ignore them.
He released us from our sins by His blood
He hides them in the sea
Micah 7:19 says “You will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea”; Revelation 1:5 speaks of His blood.
He transfers them to angels
Nothing in Scripture speaks of sins being transferred to angels; 1:5 says He released us by His blood.
He delays judgment for a season
Revelation 1:5 speaks of a finished release from sins by His blood, not a delay of judgment.
According to Revelation 1:6, what has Jesus made His people to be?
1:6 says He “has made us to be a kingdom, priests to His God and Father.”
Revelation 1:6
A kingdom, priests to His God and Father
Judges over the angels of the heavens
Paul wrote “we will judge angels” (1 Corinthians 6:3); Revelation 1:6 says He made us a kingdom and priests.
Builders of a new temple for His Father
No new temple is built by believers in Revelation 1; 1:6 says they are a kingdom, priests to His God and Father.
Scribes of the covenant, writing His law
Revelation 1:6 says nothing of scribes; believers are made a kingdom and priests.
Guardians of the ark of His covenant
The ark appears in God’s temple in heaven (Revelation 11:19), but 1:6 makes believers a kingdom and priests.
In Revelation 1:7, how is the coming of Christ described?
1:7 begins, “Behold, He is coming with the clouds.”
Revelation 1:7
With chariots of fire
A chariot of fire took Elijah up to heaven (2 Kings 2:11); Revelation 1:7 has Christ coming with the clouds.
On a white horse
Christ rides a white horse in Revelation 19:11, but 1:7 says He is coming with the clouds.
Through the eastern gate
The glory of the LORD entered the temple through the east gate in Ezekiel 43:4; that is not Revelation 1:7.
In secret at midnight
Revelation 1:7 says every eye will see Him; His coming is not secret.
With the clouds
According to Revelation 1:7, who will see Him?
1:7 says “every eye will see Him.”
Revelation 1:7
Only the seven churches
The seven churches receive the book (1:11), but 1:7 says every eye will see Him.
Only the righteous
1:7 says every eye will see Him, even those who pierced Him, not only the righteous.
Every eye
Only the angels
Angels are not mentioned in 1:7; every eye will see Him.
Only the tribes of Israel
1:7 says “all the tribes of the earth will mourn,” and every eye will see Him.
In Revelation 1:7, which specific group is singled out as seeing Christ at His coming?
1:7 says every eye will see Him, “even those who pierced Him.”
Revelation 1:7
Those who crossed the Red Sea
Israel crossed the Red Sea under Moses (Exodus 14:21); they are not mentioned in Revelation 1:7.
Those who rebuilt the wall
The wall of Jerusalem was rebuilt under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 6:15); that group is not in Revelation 1:7.
Those who fled to Egypt
Joseph took the Child and His mother to Egypt (Matthew 2:14); that is not mentioned in Revelation 1:7.
Those who pierced Him
Those who carried the ark
Priests carried the ark of the covenant (Joshua 3:6); Revelation 1:7 singles out those who pierced Him.
What worldwide reaction is described in Revelation 1:7 when Christ comes?
1:7 says “all the tribes of the earth will mourn because of Him.”
Revelation 1:7
The seas clap their hands
Psalm 98:8 says “Let the rivers clap their hands”; Revelation 1:7 speaks of the tribes mourning.
All the tribes of the earth will mourn
The mountains melt away
Psalm 97:5 says “The mountains melt like wax at the presence of the LORD”; that is not Revelation 1:7.
The nations sing for joy
Revelation 1:7 speaks of mourning, not singing; the tribes of the earth will mourn because of Him.
The stars fall immediately
The stars fall to the earth at the sixth seal (Revelation 6:13), not in 1:7.
In Revelation 1:8, what does the Lord God call Himself?
In 1:8 the Lord God says, “I am the Alpha and the Omega.”
Revelation 1:8
The Alpha and the Omega
The branch and the root
Jesus is called “the Root and the Offspring of David” (Revelation 22:16) and the Branch (Jeremiah 23:5), but not in 1:8.
The cloud and the fire
God led Israel by a pillar of cloud and of fire (Exodus 13:21); 1:8 says “I am the Alpha and the Omega.”
The stone and the altar
Revelation 1:8 does not mention a stone or an altar; God calls Himself the Alpha and the Omega.
The seed and the scepter
Revelation 1:8 does not use “seed” or “scepter”; the title is the Alpha and the Omega.
Who speaks the words, “I am the Alpha and the Omega,” in Revelation 1:8?
1:8 says it is spoken by “the Lord God, who is and was and is to come—the Almighty.”
Revelation 1:8
John
John is the one who records the words; 1:8 says the speaker is the Lord God.
An angel
An angel made the revelation known to John (1:1), but the Alpha and Omega words come from the Lord God.
One of the elders
An elder speaks to John in Revelation 5:5, but the speaker of 1:8 is the Lord God.
The seven spirits
The seven spirits are before His throne (1:4); they do not speak in 1:8.
The Lord God
Which title ends the declaration in Revelation 1:8?
1:8 ends, “who is and was and is to come—the Almighty.”
Revelation 1:8
The Holy One
Peter called Jesus “the Holy and Righteous One” (Acts 3:14); 1:8 ends with “the Almighty.”
The Ancient of Days
“The Ancient of Days” comes from Daniel 7:9, whose description of white hair like wool echoes 1:14.
The Almighty
The Bright Morning Star
Jesus calls Himself “the bright Morning Star” at the end of the book (Revelation 22:16), not in 1:8.
The Prince of Life
Peter called Jesus “the Author of life” (Acts 3:15); 1:8 ends with “the Almighty.”
In Revelation 1:9, where was John when he received the vision?
John says he “was on the island of Patmos” (1:9).
Revelation 1:9
Mount Zion
The Lamb stands on Mount Zion in Revelation 14:1, but John was on Patmos when he received the vision.
Ephesus
Ephesus is the first of the seven churches John wrote to (1:11), not where he was.
Caesarea
Caesarea is not mentioned in Revelation; John was on the island of Patmos (1:9).
The island of Patmos
Bethlehem
Bethlehem was the town of Jesus’ birth; John was on the island of Patmos (1:9).
According to John’s own statement in Revelation 1:9, why was he on Patmos?
John says he was on Patmos “because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus” (1:9).
Revelation 1:9
To visit the seven churches across the sea in Asia
John writes to the seven churches from Patmos (1:11); he was not there on his way to visit them.
Because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus
To escape a storm that drove his ship off its course
No storm is mentioned; John says he was there because of the word of God and his testimony about Jesus.
To study the writings of the prophets in quiet retreat
Revelation 1:9 says nothing of studying; he was there because of the word of God and his testimony.
To build a house of prayer for the believers on the island
John mentions no building; he was on Patmos because of the word of God and his testimony about Jesus.
In Revelation 1:9, how does John describe himself in relation to his readers?
John calls himself “your brother and partner in the tribulation and kingdom and perseverance” (1:9).
Revelation 1:9
Their bishop and judge
Elders are told to be shepherds of the church (Acts 20:28), but John calls himself their brother and partner.
Their prophet and king
John claims no royal title; in 1:9 he is simply their brother and partner.
Their father in the faith
John claims no fatherly role over the churches; in 1:9 he calls himself their brother and partner.
Their teacher and apostle
Jesus said “you are all brothers” (Matthew 23:8); John, too, presents himself as a brother and partner, not a teacher.
Their brother and partner
Which three shared experiences “in Jesus” does John mention in Revelation 1:9?
John shares “the tribulation and kingdom and perseverance that are in Jesus” (1:9).
Revelation 1:9
Tribulation, kingdom, and perseverance
Wisdom, wealth, and power
The Lamb is worthy to receive power and riches and wisdom (Revelation 5:12), but 1:9 names tribulation, kingdom, and perseverance.
Faith, hope, and love
“Faith, hope, and love” is Paul’s triad in 1 Corinthians 13:13.
Law, sacrifice, and covenant
Law, sacrifice, and covenant are not in 1:9; John shares tribulation, kingdom, and perseverance.
Victory, song, and harvest
Revelation 1:9 names tribulation, kingdom, and perseverance, not victory, song, and harvest.
On what day was John “in the Spirit” in Revelation 1:10?
John writes, “On the Lord’s day I was in the Spirit” (1:10).
Revelation 1:10
The Day of Atonement
The Day of Atonement fell on the tenth day of the seventh month (Leviticus 16:29); John names the Lord’s day.
The Sabbath
The Sabbath is the seventh day (Exodus 20:8); John says he was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day.
The Lord’s day
Passover
Passover began on the fourteenth day of the first month (Leviticus 23:5); John names the Lord’s day.
Pentecost
The Spirit came on the day of Pentecost in Acts 2:1; John was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day.
In Revelation 1:10, what did John hear behind him?
John “heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet” (1:10).
Revelation 1:10
A whisper like a breeze
Elijah heard “a still, small voice” (1 Kings 19:12); John heard a loud voice like a trumpet.
A choir like thunder
John heard a single loud voice, not a choir; it was like a trumpet (1:10).
A flute like a shepherd’s pipe
No flute is mentioned; the voice was like a trumpet (1:10).
A loud voice like a trumpet
A song from the temple
The voice came from behind John on Patmos and was like a trumpet, not a temple song (1:10).
What command was John given in Revelation 1:11?
The voice said, “Write on a scroll what you see and send it to the seven churches” (1:11).
Revelation 1:11
Build an altar on the island and wait there for the Lord
John was told to write, not to build an altar; he was to send what he saw to the seven churches.
Write on a scroll what you see and send it to the seven churches
Count the stars in heaven and record their number
The only stars in Revelation 1 are the seven in Christ’s right hand (1:16); John was told to write and send.
Seal up the vision and keep it secret for many years
Daniel was told to “seal the book until the time of the end” (Daniel 12:4); John was told not to seal it (Revelation 22:10).
Return at once to Jerusalem and tell the apostles
John was sent to write to churches in Asia, not to return to Jerusalem (1:11).

When John turned in Revelation 1:12, what did he see?
“And having turned, I saw seven golden lampstands” (1:12).
Revelation 1:12
A sea of glass
The sea of glass is before God’s throne in Revelation 4:6, not in John’s first vision.
Four living creatures
The four living creatures surround the throne in Revelation 4:6, later in the book.
Seven golden lampstands
A white horse
A white horse appears with the first seal (Revelation 6:2); in 1:12 John saw seven golden lampstands.
Twelve thrones
The twenty-four thrones are seen in Revelation 4:4; in 1:12 John saw lampstands.
In Revelation 1:13, who was among the lampstands?
“Among the lampstands was One like the Son of Man” (1:13).
Revelation 1:13
Moses with tablets
Moses carried the two tablets down Sinai (Exodus 32:15); he does not appear in Revelation 1.
Elijah in a mantle
Elijah’s cloak fell to Elisha (2 Kings 2:13); the figure in 1:13 is One like the Son of Man.
An archangel with a scroll
An angel with a little scroll appears in Revelation 10:1–10; among the lampstands was One like the Son of Man.
One like the Son of Man
A priest with incense
An angel with a golden censer offers incense in Revelation 8:3; that is not the figure of 1:13.
How is the figure among the lampstands clothed in Revelation 1:13?
He was “dressed in a long robe, with a golden sash around His chest” (1:13).
Revelation 1:13
Linen ephod and turban
An ephod and turban belong to Aaron’s priestly garments (Exodus 28:4); 1:13 describes a long robe and golden sash.
A long robe with a golden sash around His chest
Scarlet robe with a crown of thorns
The soldiers put a scarlet robe and a crown of thorns on Jesus at His trial (Matthew 27:28–29).
White tunic with sandals
Revelation 1:13 mentions a long robe and a golden sash, not a white tunic or sandals.
Sackcloth and ashes
The two witnesses are clothed in sackcloth (Revelation 11:3); the figure in 1:13 wears a long robe.
In Revelation 1:14, what is described as white like wool, as white as snow?
“The hair of His head was white like wool, as white as snow” (1:14).
Revelation 1:14
The hair of His head
The lampstands
The lampstands are golden (1:12), not white like wool.
The scroll
John is told to write on a scroll (1:11); the scroll is not described as white.
The clouds
Christ comes “with the clouds” (1:7), but the white-as-snow image is for His hair.
John’s garment
John says nothing about his own clothing; the white hair belongs to the One like the Son of Man.
In John’s vision in Revelation 1, what were like a blazing fire?
“His eyes were like a blazing fire” (1:14).
Revelation 1:14
His hands
His right hand holds the seven stars (1:16); His hands are not compared to fire.
His sandals
No sandals are mentioned; His feet were like polished bronze (1:15).
His robe

The stars
The seven stars are in His right hand and stand for the angels of the churches (1:20).
His eyes

Revelation 1:15
His crown
